Serious Sam 2 is a fun game that offers more ridiculous combat, but drifts a little too far from the Serious Model to be called “Great”. After the success of the original Croteam had a higher budget to put towards Serious Sam 2; sadly, Serious Sam 2 takes a path similar to the Martix 2 where an increased budget leads to a worse product. The game albeit fun has some additions which take away from the hilarity and well-crafted elements that made the series great.
Serious Sam finally meets the Sirians, the race that in the future Mental destroyed before his attack on humanity. The Sirians noticed Sam’s serious combat skills from the First and Second encounter so they portal him to their ship. It is there that they tell him of his prophecy, to defeat Mental and free the universe.  To do this Sam must venture to five planets and acquire the five pieces of the medallion. Only then will he be able to weaken mental and eliminate him once and for all. His quest will take him to five planets  in order to retrieve the pieces of the medallion from four tribes: the Simbas, Zixies, Chi Che, and Elvians. It is up to Sam to either save each of these groups from Mentals oppression and retrieve their medallion pieces.
Serious Sam 2 is divided into seven planets: M’digbo, Magnor, ChiFang, Kleer, Ellenier, Kronor, and Serius. The campaign consists of a whopping forty-two levels (including boss fight levels). Unlike the First and Second Encounter some of the levels are not nearly as long or engrossing.
Similar to the previous titles of Serious series the difficulty curve is well managed, where you can make it ridiculously hard or meticulously difficult. Serious Sam 2 introduces new weapons, and battle concepts. You can now get 200 health/armor by picking up any health packs (unlike the original where you could only go over 100 if you found special health/armor packs). By allowing you to get 200 health/armor Serious Sam 2 really builds upon the originals gameplay by giving you more control in how you will fight, but this is short lived as the weapon choices and ammo limitations dampen the combat. You will rarely find ammo throughout the campaign, and when you do you will burn through it without being able to find more. I found myself using the Auto Shotgun and Double Shotgun almost the entire campaign as I never had enough ammo for the other weapons.
Upon venturing to new planets you lose all your items, meaning you have to start collecting weapons all over again. This would be fine, but I noticed in M’digbo I only acquired nine of the fourteen weapons. Every time you start a new level you revert back to 100 health and lose your armor. This means if you performed well on the previous level all is in vain because you losing all your work anyway. You also have lives in this game, so you may think you are reloading a past save but actually its putting you back at a checkpoint with one less life.
Serious Sam is an epic first person shooter series that pushes the limit and then takes it further. The action is amazing, the bosses are intense, and the enemies are plentiful. You won’t be solving any puzzles in this one, but instead you will be gunning down the masses. There are five planets; each planet has its own unique design and unit models. The campaign offers loads of different elements that make you want to push on, making each level more epic than the last. If you want a realistic game this is not for you, but if you don’t mind going crazy having a good time Serious Sam 2 is the game for you. I would get this with the Serious complete back (only if you can grab it on sale). Honestly if you just want to try out a new game $9.99 is a little high for this game.
Pros:
+Interesting new enemies, some which play off the originals and some that are completely unique.
+Introduction of vehicles (makes some of the levels a little more serious).
+Secrets are more amusing
+Six separate planets to visit all with their quirks.
+Enemies have themes to match their locations.
+Levels offer much more variation in play-style and ambience.
+More bosses which require various tactics to defeat.
+Fun, explosive, and fast paced gameplay that keeps you wanting more.
+Netrisca can talk (you still have to read some things, but she will just tell you major clues).
+Ability to have multiple profiles, so if you are sharing a computer you can easily switch between other individuals campaigns.
+Blasting thousands of enemies to bits as you run around like a true action hero.
+Lots of nostalgia!!!!
Cons:
-Poor cinematic quality (it’s as if the cinematics are actually lower quality than the gameplay).
-Introduction of allies (you never needed them before – why now?)
-You lose your weapons upon starting up at a new planet (although this occurs also between campaign transitions in TSE the campaign for Serious Sam 2 connects each planet into a single campaign).
-You have lives (you never had lives before this)
-You always start each level with 100 health (regardless of whether you had more or less at the end).
-Some of the levels have bugs, which force you to restart the level.
-You lose Serious Bombs between levels.
-There is not one point in the campaign where you have every single weapon at one time. (Except for on the final level)
-Levels are nowhere near as large as TFE or TSE.
-Awful dialogue (attempts to be funny, but falls short atleast for me)
-Too childish (the game has cartoonish unit models that take away from the Serious in Serious Sam)

A challenging and rewarding twin stick shooter that's a blast to play coop.  The unlockable android characters are well done, and I feel like the level design and bosses push you towards utilizing different androids.  There are a lot of really enjoyable levels with a nice amount of variance and some callbacks to Bomberman stages.  Sometimes the huge numbers of swarming enemies are a bit much, and the hot floor level is a bit ridiculous, but those are minor gripes in a very enjoyable shooter.
Some of the voice acting is a little bland, but with the energetic techno and sounds of your weapons cover them up well.  When your battery runs out and you have to restart the level, do yourself a favor and listen to the song they play.  It's got to be the longest "you died" song in any video game, but it's darkly amusing and always gives me a chuckle.
One of the reasons I bought this is because it's on Linux.  Thanks devs for porting it over, the game is a good fit for SteamOS.  I had trouble getting my Steam controller to work like an actual controller instead of a mouse and keyboard, but I also have been experiencing some other annoying controller issues after an OS update so YMMV.  XB360 controllers worked great.
After beating the game make sure to use those credits you earned to unlock stuff in the store.  There's also a final android unlocked for your second playthrough along with a boss mode.  The android character playstyle design is very well done, with a fun mix of different styles and some imaginative weapons.  It would be nice if there was a little bit more info on what their abilities do, as some are not obvious from the select screen.  A power and range meter would be cool too.
Even so, this game is a lot of fun.  It was about a 6-7 hour experience for me which feels just about right for the $15 price tag.  The boss battles are old school pattern memorization affairs, that feel a little unfair until you learn the fight and then breeze right through it.  A little tip, switching your weapon gives a half-second of invulnerability for dodging some of those bullet-hell style barrages.
The level designs, android playstyle designs, and overall polish of this game make it for a great time with a buddy or three.  The game scales with the number of players, and you can even unlock a buddy AI if you're a solo player wanting to see the screen filled with death bots.  If you're even a little interested, buy this game and phone a friend.

The art style  is very typical of a dungeon rpg you have the vines hanging from the walls and the cobblestone bricks but for a dungeon it can look very pretty the monsters especially have been made very well with their stationary movements and attacks.
One of the only issues I had with this game was that some of the puzzles I just didnt understand or they just werent obvious so I had to check some youtube videos but that could just be down to my own incompetence.
I rate it a 8/10

Initially I voted Not Recommended for this game. Now that I've played Legend of Grimrock through, I decided to change my vote to Recommended with some qualification. There is a great deal to love about LoG. I only wish the developers had reconsidered a couple of design decisions.
Understand that LoG is a dungeon-crawler not truly an RPG. There is no role-playing and very little story. The only RPG elements are that you can generate your own party and determine your characters stats as they level. You interact with no other characters and converse with no one, not even your own party members. Where LoG succeeds is in its retro style and feel, but with contemporary high-quality graphics. Additionally, LoG has plenty of difficult battles, many fun and intriguing puzzles, and considerable switch-hunting (be warned). LoG is not a turn-based game as you might expect for an RPG; it's real-time. Depending on your expectations and playing style, this feature can be annoying or thrilling, because monsters can attack you unexpectedly as you view your map, manage your inventory, or even as you level up. I loved this aspect of the game.
Be aware, though, that if you have only average manual dexterity, the game can at times become very frustrating as you load, reload, ad nauseum, trying to "solve" running/timing puzzles that occur in the game. A couple of these puzzles can be bypassed, but then you will miss some of the game's most coveted items. A few are required to progress, however, and these can be game-stoppers. Worse, the movement system is not really geared to running/timing puzzles because you move one square at a time, and it's quite easy to overrun your mark--yet these puzzles require precise timing without any room for error. I found it irksome that I could understand a puzzle, but couldn't "solve" it because my fingers weren't fast enough. This dimension of the game made little sense to me; after all, the game purports to be a dungeon CRAWLER, and this genre traditionally relies on wit, thought, and tactics, not rapid finger movements like a platform game. I finally was able to deal with the two worst of these puzzles. For one of them, I found an AutoHotKey script that with minor adjustments did the work for me; for the second, inspired by the script just mentioned, I developed my own AutoHotKey script. That was more challenging and satisfying than endlessly retrying a puzzle my fingers just wouldn't do.
In another odd design choice, the developers required some commonplace items to solve a puzzle essential to progress in the game, but then didn't include the items on that level. These were the kind of items players might have easily ditched as useless levels earlier. Being compelled to trudge back several levels to search for discarded items is not fun. Fortunately, you can use the LoG console to generate the items if you don't want to bother backtracking levels.
Still, once you get beyond these issues, Legend of Grimrock is an enthralling game. If you're new to dungeon crawlers, don't expect something with the strong character interaction, huge world, and depth of story of, say, Dragon Age. That's not what Legend of Grimrock is about. But if the idea appeals to you of a dungeon-crawler/puzzler with heaps of combat, secrets, and wicked traps, go for it. You'll love Legend of Grimrock.

I'm a pretty big "Choice Of Games" booster. I've played most of them, including the Hosted Games. They're fun to play around with and some have pretty good writing. However, most of them don't live up to the concept of being a choose-your-own-adventure. Instead, they are more like customizable linear narratives. There are things that are always going to happen, you can't avoid them, all you're changing is your reaction or the broad methods you use to complete the scenarios.
Choice of Robots is easily the best CoG release. That core that exists in all CoG works is present in Robots. There are plot points you always hit, but they are more like the screws to the narrative, not the meat of it. Your choices mean a lot in Robots. The story and specifics change based on your choices. YOU, the PC, feel like much more of a character than in other CoG stuff. You feel more drawn in. The customization, the impact of choices, gives the game an insane amount replayability. Where other CoG games have you skimming through the text on replays to find the one paragraph that has changed since the last time, with this one the changes are in your face. You will experience radically different stories each time.
Secondary characters are always pretty weak in CoG games. They're not spectacular here, but they are better than usual. The romantic interests in CoG works are quite often non-characters. They tend to be little more than some text in your stat window. Here they have a little more character, picking one person over another will lead to minor events playing out differently. It's a good step that is small, but noticeable.
There's one problem with Choice of Robots (unless you consider the game being text only a problem and if that's the case you don't need to read this review to know if the game is for you) and that the lack of a save of any kind. This is standard for CoG and in the past it hasn't been too much of a problem. Here, I find it bothersome. Possibly, because in Choice of Robots it feels more like a "Game Over" than a "The End."  If the possibility of death was more prominent in the game, if it made things more tense, if it were anything more than just a narrative possibility it would be much less annoying. If you're OCD, you have to go back and try to recreate your game exactly to get back to that point.
If you're a fan of reading, a fan of CYOAs, if your favorite part of RPGs is dialogue trees, then Choice of Robots is the perfect game for you.

This game, in my opinion, doesn't compare to what I feel is a far superior version, Farming Simulator 15.  I have over 350 hours on Farming Simulator 15, and I gave this one a try since waiting for its release.
The graphics, despite what the marketing videos show, are a step down.  It looks like the devs went from pen and ink '15 version to a crayon overlay in '17.  It is so difficult to line up the cultivator or sower because it is nearly impossible to identify where you have already worked your field.  The edges of the tractors and the surrounding terrain are just not crisp and really not pleasing to look at as compared to Farming Simulator 15.
It does appear that the devs added in a lot more options for missions (which are not available in multiplayer), and you have to travel to each field to view the mission instead of a bulletin board.  There are also more locations to sell goods and new crops to choose from.  There are also trains, which only appear to travel in circles (and can really put a wallop on any tractors you accidentally left on the tracks).  There are new sound effects of crackling gravel as you drive over dirt roads, which are authentic enough to bring back memories of rural life.
Despite these very small improvements, this game just doesn't seem like the depicted improvement upon an already fantastic Farming Simulator 15.  This is the only game I have ever requested a refund on, and it hurts to say so as I was really looking forward to everything this game appeared to be.  It is simply not enjoyable, and I can't see spending more than 10 hours trudging through an inferior version of this series.

I've been looking forward to this one based on the fact that I love this genre (top down arena shooters) more than just about any other game. I'm prrreeeettty decent at them just by virtue of having played almost all of them that I've ever come across because I'm a moron, which also gives me a little bit of authority to make judgment calls on the genre. It's a hit and miss style of game for most people and I've slogged my way through some super ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones but I can say with all honesty that this one lives up to its reputation as one of the best.
It's kind of off putting at first because of how cutesy everything is, but the cutesy takes a back seat pretty quickly and then it's just balls to the wall enemies and explosions and death. The arenas change as you progress through the level and there are mandatory pickups that drop after certain waves of enemies to keep you constantly moving and ensure there's never really a lull to the action.
In addition, there are several characters to play as, each with different weapon/superweapons, and a different combat feel for each. On top of that, there are a number of pickups that you can grab, each of which is supremely helpful and add a level of tactics to the game because you can wait for the pickup type to cycle through (a la Raiden, if that means anything to you) in order to maximize your damage or control the crowd.
I got it in a bundle, but I'd honestly recommend it to just about anyone who is into the genre for sure, and anyone who thrives on almost completely mindless action as well

A SUPER HYPER ENHANCED CHAMPIONSHIP EDITION ALPHA DIAMOND DX PLUS ALPHA FES HD-PREMIUM ENHANCED GAME OF THE YEAR COLLECTOR'S EDITION REVIEW
Just kidding. Well, sort of...
The mastermind behind this project is none other than Zeboyd games. If you don't know who they are, head on over to
and check them out. Don't worry if you get distracted by their overwhelming awesomeness, I'll wait here...
Cthulhu, a cosmic entity from the Lovecraftian universe, aptly named the Cthulhu Mythos awakens from a deep slumber only to be immediately confronted by a wizard that seals his powers. As told by the narrator at the start of the story, the only way this peculiar (and reluctant) anti-hero can reclaim his power is by becoming a "true" hero.
In a proper satirical format that will quickly become prevalent throughout the story, Cthulhu wastes no time in breaking the fourth wall to engage the narrator. This may not be in good taste for everyone but I found it particularly amusing and was hooked right away. A decisive victory for the Great Old One degrades into a parody of the popular cult classics and a grand 16-bit journey ensues. Right from the beginning, Cthulhu is assaulted by a motley crew of... interesting companions from a blue-haired damsel in distress who becomes obsessed with and deemed a "groupie" by the lord of insanity after saving her, to a sentient sword known only as Sharpe, the master swordsword.
The modernized old-school graphics are as delightful as the quirky personalities given to each of the characters as the colors strike the perfect balance between vibrancy and gothic horror derived from this comical tribute's namesake. To think, the developers went as far as to add so many distinct and eye-catching layers to their map design was immensely impressive. Cthulhu Saves the World is a prime example of why I love retro styled RPG's - J and otherwise - with their charming, creative pixelated designs. The sprite work for the laundry list of enemies and NPC's alike is also worth mentioning because if that is something you look for in a game and admire the attention to detail that pixel art requires then you certainly won't be disappointed.
So, you installed the game and started a new file but before you know it, you've reached the end. Depending on your play style, you may burn through the whole thing in the advertised 6-10 hours; I on the other hand, stretched it out to about four times that, sitting at a final tally of about 24 hours, enjoying every minute of it.
Hold on a second because if just like the Great Cthulhu you hunger for more don't worry, the gameplay itself is expansive and flawless offering several different modes to explore and master making it incredibly versatile and providing loads of replayability. So go ahead, play to your heart's content because the character interaction and the hilarious dialogue are endlessly entertaining.
The faster pace and the enemy encounter limit (controlled manually through the "Fight" option in the menu) are a wonderfully dynamic solution to the traditional 'grind' that some might find irritating and time-consuming. Let's face it, the constant interruptions when all you want to do is get from point A to point B can frustrate the hell out of the best of us, we've all been there. This feature in my personal opinion is one that I think is woefully underutilized by many developers out there because just adding this one simple feature and handing the player that choice gives them a much-appreciated sense of control over their own experience.
A simplistic menu system is always a welcome sight which Cthulhu Saves the World graciously provides because a clunky, needlessly complicated GUI can easily turn an otherwise perfect game into an absolute nightmare. Seamless and responsive the menu amounts to exactly what it needs to be handing the spotlight over to other areas of the game that would benefit the player, like the branching level-up system that gives you a choice between a set of predefined parameters. When I saw this, I couldn't help thinking about those old branching adventure stores that use to be popular in the 70's and 80's.
It's hard to imagine that such a great game could be paired with an equally epic soundtrack but you'd better believe it is because the OST is OVER 9000! Gordon McNeil's brainchild will make your ears bleed and undoubtedly drive you so blissfully insane listening to it that Cthulhu himself couldn't do a better job. Just to prove how awesome they are Zeboyd is giving it away completely Free on their site, so what are you waiting for? Get over there!
Not only does he teach us all that everyone has the ability to turn over a new leaf but Cthulhu proves that even though one is deprived of their devastating, insanity-driven cosmic power, it is still possible to dish out a proper beating and make some new friends in the process.

I want to reccommend this game, as I've liked most Eugen titles over the years and I've also been wanting some kind of sequel to R.U.S.E. for quite some time now. I've played Steel Div since day 2 of the pre-order beta until a week after release.
Per se Steel Division isn't too shabby, but I would neither buy nor play this game over Wargame: Red Dragon.
Here's why:
1) AA: AA is borderline useless in Steel Division: you need to spam it up the wazoo to get some sort of effectivness, especially against bombers. It is only useful when combined with a fighter.
2) Arty: Arty was annoying in Wargame, but bareable, as decent players would recognize that to kill units, you actually need stuff on the frontline. In Steel Div, he who spams the most arty first wins, as it stuns and obliterates infantry, it stuns light vehicles, it even stuns ADVANCED MEDIUM TANKS such as the Panther in about 3-6 rounds. It's just broken.
3) Tanks: In Wargame, there were healthpoints. So even if your tank didn't manage to hit jacksh!t, it could still take a few rounds and you could retreat it / smoke it off. In Steel Div, you can have the ♥♥♥♥♥iest tank on the planet. This tank will have 2% chance to hit and 2% chance to penetrate a Tiger. That's 0,004% chance to kill a Tiger. And yet, this Tiger CAN actually die and it actually did for me once. in the same fashion, all German tanks have tons of veterancy, so they hit every round, so it's not unusual that 1 single German tank will kill off 2 or more high-end allied TDs.
4) Plane balance: The best, and pretty much only bet Allies have to counter German late-game armour is AT planes. Except, you need AT LEAST 4 to kill ONE Panther. (I've played Axis/Allies roughly 60/40, but I just find this so bullsh!t).
The immersion is great, infantry balance is ok, but the abovementioned features make this game not playworthy if you can play Wargame instead, which is graphically better, just as immersive, better balanced, and overall requires more skill, as it is not 100% rng-dependant.

This is how a dungeon crawler is done. It's really old school with lots of modern elements.
So, what's the story? Well, there sort of isn't a story, ok, yes, there is, but it's not so essential to the main plot. The plot is that three people accused of crimes are thrown into a dunegon and must escape. So they must survive while there are monsters everywhere, disgusting food, a strange dream that happens sometimes when you rest, creepy sounds and amazing atmosphere. The graphics add so much to the atmosphere too because they look very amazing and somehow this game runs very well on my terrible PC. I wish more games did that.
There are 3 main parts to this game and I will review each aspect one by one:
Combat
Puzzle Solving
Exploration
Combat-The combat in this game is an old school style one, you're party is in 4 people all linked together and you walk on square tiles. You have to gather up weapons from monsters, hidden rooms and exploring the place as so. The magic combat system and the magic system in general is you have to combine a certain combination of runes. You can find these combinations on scrolls which you find and by leveling up the certain types of skills in the game. Speaking of the skills, the skills are pretty much subclasses in classes. The 3 classes in this game are fighter, rouge and mage. (There's a fourth one too but you will have to discover that for yourself) Each class has different abilities, attributes, purposes, uses, etc. There's also traits you can have on each character. There's lots to choose from and some races have their own trait. The 4 races are Human, Minotaur, Lizardman and Insectoid. Each are good for their own class, like how the Lizardman makes a good rogue and how the minotaur makes a good fighter.
Puzzle solving-The puzzles in this game are diffucult. I had a LONG time trying to solve them. But after solving all of them, it was all worth it since it was fun and rewarding.
Exploration-Without exploration, I don't think this game would've been so great. There are TONS of secrets everywhere. Some are easy to find, some take forever to find. For all those loot lovers out there, you will love this game because of all the loot and what it takes to get it. To go into a little more depth of exploration is the moving system, to turn you can't just turn all the way around, to do that, you would have to turn sideways and look sideways again since you look always in a 90 degree angle.
To conclude, I would love to say Legend of Grimrock is a great modern day game and I would recommend it to anyone.

I'm passionate about (some of my friends would say obsessed with) robots and I like CYOAs (Choose Your Own Adventure). This made Choice of Robots a must-buy for me and so far I'm not disappointed. Definately recommended for people who like robots or soft sci-fi and who are interested in CYOA games.
For the computer I actually prefer my CYOAs in the form of interactive fiction/text adventures (like Zork, Spider and Web, or Suspended which also prominently features robots). That way the choices can become sort of puzzles and the player can have more freedom over what to do and if it's done well can lead to awesome "wow the devs thought of everything!" moments. I think Choice of Robots would also have benefitted by that form and the freedom that comes with it, especially together with its neat stat system for your robots.
The freedom of choice in the game is still reasonably good. You usually get about 3 or 4 options to choose from and most of the time they are very different from each other and every option changes the course of the game quite a bit, giving a lot of replayability.
However some big events will always or at least almost always happen at a certain point in the story as far as I can tell so far. They usually play out in a different way, depending on your choices, though.
What hurts the replayability a bit is the saving system: When you close the game while in the middle of the story, you continue at the point you had reached once you start the game again but there's no option to manually save a game state or undo a choice. Arguably this makes your choices more "meaningful". But sometimes it would be nice to be able to go back and see what happens if I had done X instead of Y in an otherwise unchanged path without going through all the same choices that came before again.
It would also help with a few choices that are worded a little too vague but the majority is worded in a way that makes it more or less obvious what your character is going to do, so that point is not a big deal.
The story and the writing itself are nice and I enjoyed all of my playthroughs so far. You start by building your robot after your own specifications, continue to develop it depending on your choices and possibly even change the course of the whole world.
You can be a misunderstood genius living in your mother's basement, CEO of a multi-million dollar robot company, try to take over the world as a mustache-twirling mad scientist, or even transcend humanity towards a life as machine.
Personally, I would have liked inclusion of at least some more common robot tropes, like assigning basic laws (Asimov's, others or none) to the robots or being able to pursue creating pure AIs but you can't have everything.
There were only a couple things I didn't like but they are little details and come down to personal preferences.
One is the mention of actual brand names for some things (like alienware or Dr Dre's headphones). I get that they probably help to characterize some of the characters but I feel like that's a missed opportunity to use the scifi genre to full effect by inventing new original devices and imagine how today's technology could develop.
Granted, the game takes place in the not-so-distant future of 2019 but there are also already sentient robots and flying cars.
Another thing: in several spots (most prominently character descriptions) the game appears to have been written with "political correctness" always in mind. I don't want to discuss PC in general at this place but I think that it doesn't work well as a literary device in a piece of fiction and grinding down the edges, so to speak, hurts the storytelling. Again this is a matter of preferences, just know what you're getting into if you're absolutely allergic against those kinds of things.
In the same vein some political aspects of the story seem a bit loaded (especially when the military, the US, or money is involved). The game is never preachy about any of this, it just seems a bit ham-fisted in some parts.
Anyway the game is not a political or economical simulator but an interactive story about robots and it does that point well, so that are only minor points. If nothing of this bothers you, Choice of Robots is a great COYA game.

Well, that went by fast.
Assault Android Cactus is, as you might already gather, a twin-stick arcade-styled shooter. Move with left stick, aim with right stick, shoot with right trigger, switch to secondary weapon with left trigger, and your secondary weapon has cooldown. There are eight androids to play all with rather different sets of weapons, four to start, another four to unlock. You fight pretty generic robots, then there are bosses.
It's not complicated, but it's very well done. Since it's not a space shooter (well, it's in space, but aboard a space-ship, and- you get the idea) it uses space well, often shifting the battle and offering new impediments, like pits or walls or hazards. (You can't fall.) It's often shifting what robots you're facing or how the battlefields work - it goes to some lengths to change the environment around you, even if it's mostly pretty standard industrial interiors and exteriors. Still, levels never feel truly the same. Some are wide-open, some are confident, some have gimmick traps- I felt like at no point was it retreading itself. Which it better not, at its basic length of a few hours to beat the main campaign. It has leaderboards survival, and optional cheats and modes to encourage you to try and play to perfection.
There are some small disappointments. The leaderboards aren't divided by character, since some androids are more suited to some levels in others, and knowing you were the best with an oddball android with a spinning sawblade or a drill attack would be good to know. Though the walking speed is generally fast enough, at times I felt that it was just a hair too slow to readily escape attack patterns I hadn't already anticipated. And some of the bosses can be overly harsh compared to the rest of the game - one in particular hits with a swarm of robots that in one attack pattern I still have no idea how certain androids are supposed to deal with it without losing a life.
Assault Android Cactus mostly just an example of how to take a classic game style and just polish it until it feels great. There's something intangible here, but circling around robots, hosing them down, singling out stronger robots to engage with missles or cannonballs, it all feels very satisfying. The characters are very basic but appealing. The story is... generic but at least not intrusive in its genericness. The continue mechanic is clever in how it subtly allows score attackers to give up at a point of failure but allow everybody else to truck on to victory without feeling like they actually failed. Ultimately, if you're in the market for a twin-stick shooter with a fun charm to it, this'll do you. It's probably the best I've played since Waves, and that's solid praise as far as I'm concerned.

This game, in my opinion, doesn't compare to what I feel is a far superior version, Farming Simulator 15.  I have over 350 hours on Farming Simulator 15, and I gave this one a try since waiting for its release.
The graphics, despite what the marketing videos show, are a step down.  It looks like the devs went from pen and ink '15 version to a crayon overlay in '17.  It is so difficult to line up the cultivator or sower because it is nearly impossible to identify where you have already worked your field.  The edges of the tractors and the surrounding terrain are just not crisp and really not pleasing to look at as compared to Farming Simulator 15.
It does appear that the devs added in a lot more options for missions (which are not available in multiplayer), and you have to travel to each field to view the mission instead of a bulletin board.  There are also more locations to sell goods and new crops to choose from.  There are also trains, which only appear to travel in circles (and can really put a wallop on any tractors you accidentally left on the tracks).  There are new sound effects of crackling gravel as you drive over dirt roads, which are authentic enough to bring back memories of rural life.
Despite these very small improvements, this game just doesn't seem like the depicted improvement upon an already fantastic Farming Simulator 15.  This is the only game I have ever requested a refund on, and it hurts to say so as I was really looking forward to everything this game appeared to be.  It is simply not enjoyable, and I can't see spending more than 10 hours trudging through an inferior version of this series.

I am well aware of Tim Schafer's Molyneux-esque decline from a position of respected industry veteran to corporate slime-ball.  I am also well aware of Spacebase DF-9's troubled development and reputation as the quintessential example of a consumer-unfriendly kickstarter failure.
So why did I pick up this game?  It was dirt cheap on sale and, in theory, it contains many elements of a game that I should enjoy.  Base construction, resource and personnel management, quirky characters to enlist or engage- all wrapped up in a sci-fi setting.  I was expecting that it would be an incomplete experience good for a couple of hours of play with no worthwhile end-game.
"Incomplete" doesn't even begin to describe this disaster of a game.  The UI is unintuitive.  The AI is incompetent.  The QA is nonexistent.  Each of these elements adds a layer of frustration to the experience that, had I known existed, I would not have bothered to play even if you payed me the price of the game to do so.  Every element is broken on some level.  Had the developers an ounce of integrity, they could have easily invested the time (for which they had been paid in advance) to bring it to a servicable level, but this is nothing more than an embarrassment for which they should be ashamed.
Do not buy this game.  Do not buy games from this developer... unless it's Psychonauts.  Buy that instead.

In one sentence: very funny with reasonable albeit unspectacular gameplay, but definitely worth it for such a low price.
As might be clear from the premise, this is not a game which takes itself seriously at all - and that is really its strongest point. The game is consistently silly in everthing from the dialogue to the enemy descriptions, and most of the jokes hit the target. Both the art style and the gameplay are very reminiscent of the old style of RPGs (think Dragon Quest, or the first few Final Fantasy games) of which the game is an affectionate parody. This does of course mean that the game does contain some of the flaws of these games - for example that combat can become rather repetitive - although it takes some steps to partially mitigate this, for instance making battles in each area optional after a certain number have been completed.
If I hade to rate the aspects of this game:
Gameplay - 7/10
Story - 7.5/10
Humour - 8.5/10
Value for money - 15/10
Madness - Cthulhu Fhtagn/10
If you like retro style RPGs, lovecraft, and having a sense of humour, this game is - insanely - good for its price.

I've been burned many times in the past by Early Access. This is the last time. Victory, in its current state, is nothing short of an underwhelming experience that left me wanting what was promised from the current release.
- Car editing is, to be honest, boring. While the livery editor is decent (if not a little fiddly), the amount of selectable blocks is low and there's no visual customisation outside of that. Customisation of the car's stats is easy but you have to pay a virtual currency to make any changes - eliminating any aspect of trial-and-error.
- Online racing is just awful. With six players maximum on the track and a lobby system that is a completely confusing mess, actually getting into a game is hard enough. Getting into a competitive one with players you can actually *race* against players instead of lapping or being lapped is even harder due to big imbalances.
- While the game isn't free to play, you can tell that it used to be at one point. You can use your gears to purchase boosts to your cars for single races (which is hugely unfair) and doing anything related to new cars costs some. For a game that advertises the freedom you get in modifying cars, you sure are locked out of doing many free things. Even modifying stats costs gears - it just goes too far.
This game has potential, but it's hugely untapped potential, and while the driving model is pretty cool and the upcoming track editor seems promising, in its current state I am not impressed.

Really had high hopes for this game. I'm an avid fan of the Wargame series and RUSE so when news broke of an WWII RTS game that combined the best of the two games I was absolutely hyped. However, this game fell short.
The game had very good ideas in the way of the Battle Phases and deck systems. The Phases created a gameplay flow that was both manageable and realistic, mimicing reinforcements and progressing resources. Decks were used in the same way as Wargame, enabling a player to tool his arsenal to his own playstyle and different scenarios. Used in conjugation, it makes a player feel comfortable with his options. I also really loved the Front Line feature, not only did it look cool but provided a different way to control the map than just rush focal points.
However, most of the other aspects of the game are unfilling, ranging from the slightly bothersome to gear-grinding awful. I'm a strategy game fan so graphics really aren't too high on my list for a game, but I can't stand the aesthics of Steel Division. The explosions are either nonexistant or completely buffoonish. I know Eugen can make better graphics, RUSE was beautiful! Again, graphics really aren't a deal breaker with me but the level to which graphics were disregarded is very unusual. It's only made worse with bad sound design, especially American and British voice acting which appartently only consists of badly cut movie references.
Gameplay is wonky with the weird LOS and combat system. Yeah, I get it. Hedgerows and towns make up 90% of Normandy. But that doesn't mean you have to create every single map exactly the same. Wargame and COH have varied maps with interesting features, but with Steel Division I have trouble telling the difference between any of the maps. Suppression was radically altered from Wargame, and all you need is your infantry to take a few shots from far away and suddenly they're out of the fight. Combat lends itself towards spamming with units that just soak up hits and refuse to die. No matter how many times you hit a unit, as long as it can retreat into cover and cower for two minutes it'll be back up to kill your units in the open like nothing happened because HP doesn't exist.
I can't go for more than 15 minutes in game without thinking, "I would be having a lot more fun if I were playing Wargame." Bottom line, if you want a great RTS experience that Steel Division was going for, just go buy Wargame. That's one of the true pinnacle of RTS games. Want a good WWII RTS? Can't go wrong with COH or Men of War. But, unless they radically overhaul this game with an update or a modder makes this game reach it's true potential, I can't recommend it with a $40 price tag. I really wanted to like this game. but I can't. To think I preordered it too.

I truly do not wish to spoil the story for anyone, mostly because the fun of this game is in going through it, making one set of decision and then looking back and saying "oh but I wonder what would happen if I had..." then going back and seeing what would have happened. Do not go in expecting "Robot Tycoon" or a Visual Novel. This is neither of those. It is a choose your own adventure novel from the 90s, rebuilt with 21st century technology. Choice of Games have made the genre better, more addicting, more entertaining, and easier to recommend. Buy it now. And if you will excuse me, I have an evil robot army to create.

Take Dragon Age Inquisition, boil off any sort of combat or action until there's just dialogue and romance and set it in some Terminator fan-fiction and you have yourself Choice of Robots. Be prepared to answer questions as simple as what material do I make my robot out of to "whats more important? My robot or my family?" to "Should I invade alaska?" culminating into some serious existentialist stuff.
You can play this game again and again and you get this butterfly effect of how things turn out. It's beautiful to behold.
If that isn't enough, at one point you can drink scotch and listen to "The Magnetic Fields - It's Only Time" which if you're anything like me means this is a mandatory purchase.

A great roguelite / platformer that involves lots of action and eccentric style.
Adventuring Gentleman is a steampunk roguelite platformer. You start your game as a gentleman in a club room: there are multiple other chaps sitting there and telling you the news (aka quests). As soon as you pick your quest: you are taken on adventure, where you need to clean 5, 10, or 15 rooms and defeat a boss. After clearing each room from enemies, you can choose a bonus which improves your weapon or your character. It can be double-jump, flight, double shot, explosive shot, etc. If you kill the boss at the end of the quest – the pool of random bonuses is increased. This improves your chances to beat the next bosses: after all, the unlocked bonuses are more powerful.
•	The enemy killing process is fun: jumping on platforms, charging your gun and killing weird enemies turns out to be awesome
•	Skill-based, challenging and adapting gameplay: most enemies are not easy to beat. You’ll have to dodge projectiles masterfully in order not to get damage. The bonus choice matters, it will affect your play style, so you can influence how each quest walkthrough plays out.
•	Amazing style and enemy variety: the game author has a great imagination and enemies won’t leave you bored: fly with a musket, robot-waiter carrying the bombs, giant mushrooms, tin soldier that uses a ballerina as a gun and much more.
•	Great Victorian-inspired atmospheric music and sounds.
•	Steampunk Style: the steampunk is pretty much underrepresented in games, so kudos to game author for making a good one.
•	Some enemy attack preparation animations are not long enough or not noticeable enough. This usually is not a problem, but this will bring you a few frustrating moments
•	When you unlock the flight bonus and pick it: controls get clunky, to the point of damaging the gameplay experience and not feeling like a drawback
•	The game is mostly about the core gameplay (not much plot): if you enjoy the run-jump-gun mechanics – the game is for you, as this turns out much cooler than it sounds like. If you’re into the games for stories – this one probably ain’t for you.
•	The style is a double-edged sword: it is well done, but you’ll either love or hate it, no middle ground
I’m really happy that I’ve discovered Adventuring Gentleman: the art and music make a great atmosphere in favor of Victorian setting. The gameplay might seem simple, but it’s easy to learn and hard to master. The good game design is also there: the player is given a real choice how to build his character, allowing to strategize between shooting and making important choices that affect the play style. Despite the flaws with some enemy animations, I loved Adventuring Gentleman and highly recommend it.

Assault Android Cactus is a top down twin stick shooter.
+ Very addicting
+ Smooth gameplay without FPS limits
+ Challenging
+ Pleasant music
+ Interesting different character personalities and gameplay styles
+ Attention to detail (e.g., each character has a different speech on each boss, dedicated music to the game over, lots of extras)
+ Replayable
+ Good voice actors
- Characters could have been better designed, i.e., they're good but I think the artist can do even better perhaps in the next game
- Sometimes it is hard to distinguish bullets, mines, lasers and such
In this game you control an android that must destroy every robot on each level. It is a top down shooter that can be controlled with either mouse and keyboard or with the analog sticks of the controller.
The only way for you to lose in this game is if your battery runs out. If your health goes to zero you just have to get up by taping your fire button. Batteries are used with time even if you don't shoot. To restore your energy you must get new batteries, which are dropped by one particular robot in each wave. So time is the most important factor in this game.
There are many characters in this game and each character has different weapons. All characters carry two weapons. The primary weapon does not have any limitations, you can fire non stop until the level ends. The secondary weapon is usually more powerful but requires some time until you can fire again. Each character has it's own advantages and disadvantages. You can choose whatever character you want in each level at any given time and in some cases a character is better than another in a particular level. All characters also have very distinct personalities, making the game more interesting.
Sometimes power-ups are dropped. There are three kinds of power-ups: tiny robots, pretty wings and blue circles. Tiny robots gives you more fire power, pretty wings makes you faster and blue circles stop every robot in screen for a limited amount of time. The power-up item changes to another power-up every few seconds. The order is always the same. If you get the same item twice, the time is extended.
There are also bosses in each section. The bosses are easy to understand but hard to defeat. As usual the bosses work with patterns. A small but welcome detail is that each boss has a different speech for each character you choose and in this way you can figure out the story of the characters.
The game does not have any FPS limitations and works very well in my 144hz monitor. Altough the models and textures aren't very detailed the game looks very good and there is a lot of variation in each level. The music never gets in your way and in fact it is pleasant to hear. The voice actors are very good and give character to each android.
Overall I enjoyed this game a lot but I have two minor issues, mostly personal opinion. The character design seems to be an attempt at chibby style 3D models but look more like bobble head action figures. The models look okay but Î think they could be better. In fact my favorite is Starsh because she's the one that looks less of a bobble head. That and the extras that she's easy to control and the funniest one. The other is that it is very hard to notice some things because the coloring is not distinguishable enough. These kinds of games usually have very bright bullets so that the player can notice them. While the bullets are bright in this game they're still easy to miss in my opinion.
After you beat the game you have some options. Option one is to beat each level in campaign with score S+. To do it you need to kill every robot in a single link and at a reasonable short amount of time. For bosses you just need to kill the boss fast enough. Another option is to beat the boss rush more, where you defeat all bosses in a row. The infinity mode is simillar but before beating the bosses you need to kill all robots that show up. Finally you can try to beat the score of other online players.
I recommend this game for anyone who wants a challenging and fun top down shooter.

This is really an amazing game. The character design is cute, and they have voice overs and dialogue lines to match. The controls are quite smooth in terms of moving your android around the map and aiming to shoot. If you have a Steam controller, I highly suggest downloading my custom control template where the trackpads do all the work as your thumbs simply hover over them, no button presses required! Well maybe except for self revival and weapon switching, but still a lot f stress of them gaming muscles.
It may get hectic from time to time with tons of enemies crowding the screen and a bunch of projectiles coming your way, but it's a blast trying to navigate the well constructed levels while also learning enemy properties all on the fly. This game forces you to pay attention to everything on screen, especially your battery. If it runs out, it's gameover. You can keep on "dying," and you can revive yourself, but the level isn't over until your battery fully runs out, so keep on an eye on that and how much you shoot. Aimless shooting will cost you your battery, so be careful and be present. If you blink, you die! If you think about anything else, you die! So pay attention.
I highly recommend this game at either full price or a significant discount. You can't go wrong with it if you want to practice making your brain really really focus on some serious hand eye coordination. I wish I'd known about this game when it came out, because it really has what I would have wanted from a modern first-person dungeon crawler. But, I wouldn't recommend it right away to everyone, even if they were looking for this kind of game. Wizardry, Eye of the Beholder, Might and Magic, Dungeon Master and many other games belong to the same genre, but they're not the same and you may not like all of them. Same with Legend of Grimrock.
Legend of Grimrock has quite simple game mechanics, and they are really easy to understand, but they have been used amazingly well to make an awful lot of challenging yet mostly fair puzzles (not all of them because it seems some people have been having problems with the timed ones, personally I haven't) and secrets to find. As you progress, the difficulty gets gradually higher. And if you really like puzzles, you can try the optional ones for rewards, which are usually harder.
The combat/skill system is a bit simple too, and most of the time it doesn't require much thinking but skills with the (clumsy) controls. You'll be either dancing with the enemy or hiding behind a wall, waiting for your cooldowns, or maybe for the enemy to get closer. But it's not always like that. There are only 3 classes, each one with their own skills that you can increase by spending points after leveling up. These skills have passive effects. Did your warrior just learn a skill to perform a special attack with swords? Well, it's up to him to use it. You just give the order to attack. But there are a lot of skills to choose from, and anyway, this makes the game easier to play (let's not forget it's a tile-based game with real time combat and pausing it is not an option). And you can choose what spell to cast with your mage (depending on what kind of mage you have), but don't expect an awful lot of spells. You'll be casting 2 spells all the time, but damn they're fun to use, mages add a lot of dynamic and variety to combat.
If there's something that this game lacks, where trying to "keep it simple" was usually (though relatively) a good idea, it's variety in its levels. Pretty much every level looks the same. Same textures, same objects, same monsters, repeating over and over.
If you are considering buying this game, expect:
Do not expect:

High quality writing and an abundance of choices that influence how the story plays out. Even choices that don't seem to be all that important can alter the outcome quite a bit.
You should bring the patience to read large amounts of text - obviously - but it's well worth it. The writing is really good and offers not only a nice technical perspective on AI and robotics but also some philosophical insights about life and humanity.

Everyone who is interested in AI and robotics and is not afraid of reading should buy this. Everyone else should at least take a look at the demo before simply skipping this game altogether.

Choice of Robots is the, as of now, latest installment of the series of text adventures called Choice of Games, complete with the series' usual tropes and occasionally annoyances. If you're familiar with these games or enjoy text adventures in general, then it's simple: pick this one up, it's the best installment yet. If you're not however, it's as good a starting point as any, especially when there's a free demo that adequately presents what the game entails.
Robots is about crafting, growing and teaching your own personal robot, and for someone familiar with the Choice of Games series, that's all you really need to know. Besides the wildly varied tone and settings, the majority of these games function nearly identically.  For those who are new, it's a text adventure, and what that boils down to is simply: You read a whole lot and make choices. There's no graphic, no music and no action (besides the ones being described with words). And if that puts you off, that's fair, still, the demo's free if you want to confirm your position.
As with most other games of the series, the choices you make influence your stats and how the story progress and, again, as with the other installments, the game encourages at least a certain degree of specializations. What is new, however, is that the protagonist have only one stat to keep track of, humanity, which tracks how kind, humane, social and emotional your decisions are. Your robot, on the other hand, has four stats: Autonomy, Military, Empathy and Grace, and the decisions you make throughout the game influence what kind of robot you will have, and, in turn, how you will influence the world. Would you end up with a mindless militaristic machine at your whim, a self-conscious and independent robotic sentient being or a curious, constantly learning robot with near (or perhaps completely) human emotions? Chances are, though, you're going to end up with a combination of all the things in between.
While, like the other Choice of Games, Robots do strongly encourage specialization in at least one or two stats, the games do not seem to punish you as harshly for deviation from your initial plans. The other Choice of Games' strategic elements usually boil down to specializing in a number of areas and then make only decisions that test your strong points and avoid your weaknesses. Robots is similar, except you have more leeway and, in fact, planning becoming a lot more difficult as decisions often have unforeseen consequences. For example, there's a point in the game where you are able to make a decision on what kind of information you want your robot to extract on the internet, and allowing it to pick up whatever it wants result in it learning things like "Big Brother is watching" and "the US is the bad guy", resulting in a substantial raise in intelligence (Autonomy) and a distrust of authority (Military). There's also a point in the game where your robot is interviewed, and if your Autonomy is high enough, the review will claim your robot is smarter than humans, giving it a boost in confidence (Autonomy) while making it more arrogant (decrease in Empathy). While the unpredictability of the gameplay structure here may hamper cold strategic decision making, it also makes the story more spontaneous and exciting, as your choices can have truly unforeseeable consequences later in the game, making the narrative incredibly dynamic. That said, depending on what you choose to focus on, the game can also end up rather difficult, requiring multiple restarts, which is even more frustrating considering the fact that the game has no manual save whatsoever, forcing a restart every time you want to change something. I believe this is to make you committed to your choices and make each playthrough special and dynamic, but I still feel that the game would benefit more from having a save system of some description, especially when you've already completed the game and don't feel like skimming through most of the story to change one decision. Robots, in particular, seems to offer more consequences and variations to your decisions than any other game in the series I've experienced (skim through the achievement list if you want to know how much you could achieve, and know that I only got 10 in one playthrough, and I thought I did pretty well). That said, personally, I don't plan on replaying the game anytime soon. This is in no way a fault of the game, but rather a strength, as I feel so attached to my first playthrough that any second attempt would feel as if I've cheated that unique experience.
But gameplay aside, this is still a text adventure, and as a game that's going to make you spend the majority of your time reading, it lives and dies on the writing. Robots, like most of its predecessor, does not disappoint in this regard. There's moment of humor, melancholy, romance (with the usual inclusiveness of the series) and, perhaps most of all, introspection. The parental relationship between you and your robot becomes clear very early on, and the game handles it extremely well. Your robot grows, imitates and reacts to your actions as you would expect, with great curiosity and bewilderment. As I watch it develops, I feel proud when it understands or questions, scared when it picks up undesirable tendencies, happy when it expresses indignant at cruelty and warm when it seems more human than any living character by the end, while still having more to learn and expressing fear of the inevitable as a child would. At least that's how it was for my Sapling (that's how I named mine, and Sapling was a she and refers to me by my real name rather than titles because that's the level of customization you have), your robot could go in so many unforeseen direction it's difficult to "plan" its development, and considering the theme, I think that's the point. The human characters, while getting less attention, are well-written and varied enough in their own right, but some, even if you choose to begin a relationship with them, will feel somewhat detached from the main storyline until the latter chapters. The game, despite its initial lightheartedness and humor, asks difficult question, present morally ambiguous choices and depicts interesting, introspective themes. The final two or three chapters are the most powerful part in the game for me because it shows the growth of your robot and how you've molded the world, for better or worse, as well as calling your ideals into question. I can only speak for myself, but my ending reflected my choices appropriately, filling me with wonder, doubt, melancholy and hope. While the game has its stronger points and weaker, more filler-y portions, the finale was undoubtedly my favorite experience of any Choice of Game story.
If you enjoy the Choice of Games text adventures, then I'll just repeat myself: Buy the damn game, it's, at least in my opinion, the best in the series yet. If you have no interest in the structure and ideas behind text adventures, then I suppose there isn't much here to convince you otherwise besides good writing. If you're new and willing to try out one of these games though, I can't think of a better place to start. Choice of Robots is inspiring, funny, well-written and introspective, and for a game about robots, it has more philosophies and humanity behind it than most games out there combined.
p.s. If you have played and enjoyed this one, do go check out the other text adventures by Choice of Games. Only a few of them are on Steam at the moment but there are quite a lot of these games on the Choice of Games website, and they all have free demos (if they aren't already free). I always thought these games don't get enough credit and exposure so please support them if you like what they're doing.

What a fantastic piece of futurist literature! I played the more peaceful route but was exposed directly and indirectly to the repercussions of my actions and that of others outside of my control. I was enlightened to the social, political, and economics prospective atmospheres of the future, with a large focus on the effects of introducing artificial intelligence (or lack thereof).  The relationships I developed felt more "real" than most other C.Y.O.A. games (the exception being the Heroes Rise Trilogy) and I genuinely felt bad when I pushed friends away for the sake of the growing demand for my robotic knowledge.  My ending felt a tad rushed but it may have been due to my overall decisions having little differentiation from my initial stance on robotics.  All in all, the author knows his subject very well and it shows in his writing (largely with robotic ethics and boundaries).  If you are trying to sate an urge to experience an Asimov tale, craving a 2001: A Space Odyssey journey, and/or wanting to discover what the future may hold for robotics from a modernized perspective, this game is for you. Grab it now!

The only complaint I would complain about is the random encounters and the mazed like levels which kind of made me want to stop playing the game

Story is mostly just background to set up the scene (though there are some developments near the end), visuals and sound are good enough. You can use either controller or mouse and keyboard for single player/local co-op.
You choose from selection of characters (four initially, one more for each boss you clear to a total of nine), each with their own primary and secondary fire. Secondary fire is usually more powerful but has a cooldown period in between uses. Different characters do better in different situations.
Powerups are dropped after defeating some enemies. They include temporary firepower boost, enemy freeze, and movement speed and I believe they cycle if you don't pick it up right away.
Battery is just a timer on how long you have to complete the level. Your battery always drains but as you kill enemies they sometimes drop battery powerups that refill the battery a bit.
There are five zones and six bosses. The regular stages were pretty standard and forgettable but I enjoyed the boss fights. The later bosses are sometimes like a bullet hell lite because they sometimes spray the traditional screen-filling bullet patterns but it's very managable compared to other bullet hells.
It was nice for me because when you get hit enough times and die you can continue (losing score and battery life) so I didn't really get stuck on a level. The way you lose is if you don't defeat enough enemies in time or let a battery powerup despawn (usually because you waste time while respawning) and run out of battery.
Worth a try if you like the idea of bullet hells/shoot em' ups but aren't at the skill level/don't have the patience to do hardcore ones.

Great game.  It is an old school dungeon crawler with modern graphics.  The puzzles can be genuinely puzzling.  Enemies range from laughable to seriously annoying and the final boss makes you work for it.  However, the greatest enemy lies in your inventory.  The game limits inventory space by weight including equipped items.  The characters must eat, though, and food has weight.  Having lots of food benefits you greatly since you can feed your party whenever they get too hungry.  It also hinders you because high weight decreases movement, and halts it if the limit is exceeded, and it occupies space which could be occupied by something else. Anyone like myself who grew up playing any of the Forgotten Realms dungeon-crawlers, or for that matter ANY of the grid-based first-person dungeon-crawlers will feel right at home.
The only thing I feel that I can say against the game, is even on a normal difficulty, it does ask a lot of the player, which at the same time I believe is a fantastic and refreshing thing(more games of similar ilk should bring back such involvement). For those who are more accustomed to RPGs that tend to hold your hand every so-often, Legend of Grimrock throws you in pants or not, and expects you to sort stuff out on the scraps it tosses you of weapons, food, clues, and chance. An adventure I'm hotly anticipating the finish of, and will likely be pouncing right on Legend of Grimrock 2 once I'm done.

Legend of Grimrock is a dungeon crawling game with puzzles. For start, let me say I usually don't like puzzle games.
In LoG, you get to create your party (nice races, classes, names, you know it) which you are leveling up throughout the game. It's fun, especially the difference between classes (Mage is the most powerful but useless without mana and can get killed quickly while Rogue is also weak but comes with interesting tricks) and positions. Yes, you heard right, positions. You'll figure that out. The casting system is also nice, although hard to remember sometimes (take that as a challenge!).
The puzzles themselves are nice and easy, but getting harder while you're progressing. I never really found a puzzle I couldn't solve, except one, but as I found out that was because I missed a hint somewhere earlier in the game. The dungeons are nicely designed and so are the traps and monsters - who are really original and (unfortunately for me, got stuck and the end of the game, gotta try a new party I guess) deadly.
The game, while being oldschool, has a modern execution so it plays rather smoothly and the graphics are nice. Furthermore, it comes with easy to learn editor!

This is my first text adventure and I don't know if this is the correct genre but it's surely not a graphic novel. But I know that I instantly fell in love with it and that I played for almost 7 hours straight.
Basically, if you are open for things like this and like thought experiments about creating robots or daydream about or whatever ... I can recommend it. The writing itself is really good. Yeah, I don't want to spoil anything about the story, you should just experience it for yourself.
I found it quite mindblowing, actually. It combines the best attributes of both video games and books. You have all the possibilities books offer, such as unmatched story telling and ways to express emotions and to imagine worlds, plus the ability to make choices from video games. This makes the whole experience so special and awesome, because it gets personal, it becomes your story and every single decision actually matters (and there are many)!
If you ever were annoyed with the shallow meaningless choices most AAA games have offered until this day, well, then, go for it - you won't be disappointed.
Yes it has no graphics and yes you definitely need to be quite imaginative to get yourself into such games - or experiences - but it's worth it. In the end, I'm just really grateful Steam opened up a niche market for these kind of games. Praise the Gaben. =)

It's difficult to attach yourself to an experience like this. Most I imagine would rather pick the most cathartic route and run with it. but even as your decisions veer up and down the scale, The story always retains its organic cohesion and compelling storyline. While one or two characters can be a tad two dimensional, every decision you make affects the story in wildly branching ways. for something this simple, little more than a flash text algorithm, I was left on the brink of tears in my first playthrough,  Not only do your decisions resonate, but they provide a good series of compelling arguments about the nature of artificial intelligence. This isn't a game. Nor is it a novel. It's a narrative experience that evolves beyond its initial "choose-your-own-adventrure" If you have any interest in sci fi, but worry that the lack of graphics might turn you off, I still recommend you give it a try. you might find it more engaging than you expect.

This game is, quite literally, interactive fiction - and very good fiction at that. Gameplay elements are minimal: You're given a choice, possibly your robots' stats changes depending on your choice, then the story continues. The focus is clearly on the (very good!) writing.  But, and this important, your choices actually matter. And that's not a buzzword for once. It's not Mass Effect-style "choose the colour of the light beams in the ending" sense, I mean that choices matter in that you get completely different stories depending on your choices. A run takes about 30 minutes, depending on how quick a reader you are, but there are so many different branches (both minor and major) that you can easily sink hours just into exploring.

The game play is seriously old-school nostalgic in the BEST way. None of the old artificial hurdles are there, so I can start and stop at any time and still feel the defeat of loss without having to start an entire area over.

1) Hired workers do their jobs better but you still need to tend to them.  If fields are too close together they will often jump from one field to the next when you don't want them too.  They still get stuck periodically but overall do a better job of getting around obstacles.
2) Being able to pick up items makes forestry possible now.  I tried forestry in FS15 and lost my mind with frusration.  With the new equipment and ability to grab items it's much better now
3) User interface is much better now and lots more information in the game
4) Much more depth to farm animals now and they can keep you very busy and be pretty profitable.
5) More advance options for tending fields that can make things more realistic/challenging.  For example, three stage fertilization, periodic plowing requirements
6) The converyors are great if not a bit frustrating from time to time.  You can put them pretty much anywhere and since you can tip anywhere it's easy to come up with creative solutions for moving crops around.  I primarily use them for Silage at the Biogas plants and they are amazing for that.
7) Built in mod management is just fantasic.
Gripes:
1) Silage on the Goldcrest valley map can be frustrating because the silos have glitches in them that create holes in the silage.  This will cause you to get stuck sometimes.  Also the silage doesn't always uncover and either requires you to hit it just right with a conveyor or hit it with a scoop.  Silage will also get stuck in the walls sometimes and either require you to edit the files or use a mod to fix it.  These are issues that could be fixed with a patch though.
2) As great as the mod management is, I'd prefer it if when you need a mod when trying to connect to a server it would let you automatically download them in the game versus taking you out of the game to a webpage
3) Would like to have hotkeys to quickly access certain parts of the information menus.  For example, no hotkey now to quickly pull up the finances screen.
4) There is no default way to store beets, potatoes or woodchips as there was in FS15.  You can either dump them somewhere with a tipper or store them in a railroad drop off but none of these options will display your total owned amount in your summary screen depsite there being a quantity of 0 displayed.
5) Would like to see more information for all owned crops that are stored in the silo AND trainyards as well as being able to designate a building that will count quantities of crops
Other obeservations:
We run our own private server and initially I was annoyed because running a server requires the purchase of an additional license while almost every other game I've ran a server for includes a dedicated server app at no additional cost.  The other downside of this is that you cannot run a dedicated server from a copy of the game purchased from Steam, it has to be a key that's redeemed directly through Giants (i.e. purchased from Amazon, Humble, etc).  Despite these issues, the FS17 server is hands down the best game server that I've ever managed.  It's all managed via a web interface and the server has lower requirements.  In addition, it's easy to make changes, add mods and so much more.  The server also allows you to upload/download any save games, has an iPhone/Android app to monitor the server and so many other nice features that it's easily worth the purchase of an additional license for all of the work and refinement that has been done.
So to conclude, this game has really peaked my interest in simulation games and has quickly become one of my favorite titles in my library.

I didnt expect much when I picked this game up at a really cheap price. From what I saw in screenshots and videos, the presentation didnt appeal to me at all, the story seemed really uninteresting, and the aestethic of it all simply didnt mesh well with me. All of those things remain true even after I have beaten the game.
However, that in no way should be an excuse to miss out on this, because what I didnt expect to find here was a videogame.
And when I say videogame, I mean it in the rawest and most primitive sense possible that the term implies.
This is the kind of game that leaves your hands sweating and your eyes glued to the screen in the hopes that you dont miss a single moment of action.
Assault Android Cactus is a twin stick shooter, where the goal is to kill every enemy in each stage of the game. Thats it. Thats all you do here, the "story" it presents is just an excuse to give some sort of context for the player to get back into the action, and besides shooting enemies, there really isnt much else for you to do here.
And thats why this game is so great. It has no pretenses about what it is, and it uses its genre to full effect to give you one of the best arcade experiences in the last few years.
Every stage is a frenetic chase to the end goal, with the screen filling with impossible levels of enemies and bullets while you do your best to avoid it all and stay alive for as long as you can, and every arena introduces a unique layout to shake things up, from floors disappearing when you step on them, to laser beams moving across the screen at certain intervals and making you run for cover just in time.
The game also introduces a brilliant game mechanic where your character has a battery that depletes as time goes by and that can only be charged back by killing a certain number of enemies. This means you can never play it safe and stick to a corner waiting for enemies to come at you, as you will have to chase them at numerous times during the game just to get that recharge before you run out and fail the stage. This is what makes the game unique among other similar titles, as it provides alot of entertaining stressful moments where you are running against time as you throw yourself at every enemy just to get a goddamn recharge.
The game has a huge list of characters to pick from, each with their own unique weapons and skills, so the game never gets stale, and gives ample room for experimentation and player preference.
It also comes with bosses, and they all significantly ramp the difficulty up with creative attack patterns and alternate forms, the Final Boss being one of the highlights of the game.
Soundtrack is amazing and perfect for this game, with one of the best Game Over tracks  I have heard in a long time, that alone is worth losing a stage on purpose.
So yeah, if you truly like engaging videogames  that actually demand the player's effort and attention, then please give this a chance, it truly deserves more love than it gets right now.
And who knows, you might actually like the characters and story more than I do
