If you like Robotron 2084 or Smash TV and love shooting at TONS of enemies, then this is another great game in the same vein! Assault Android Cactus is a twin-stick shooter in which you are the title character Cactus (or one of her 8 Android companions, when you unlock them all) attempting to stop the Section Lords on an impossibly large spaceship from planning to destroy the universe or something.
The plot is not that important, but it does have some funny dialogue and cute characters, so that's a plus. Graphically, the game is actually pretty impressive, and it can get quite hectic with the multi-colored enemies and different types of projectiles all on screen at once. Just as well, the game supports up to 4 player Local Co-Op, which is an absolute blast to play with anybody who will join you on this bullet fiesta. (Sadly no onlie multiplayer, but I understand why the devs couldn't implement it).
The gameplay is the star of the show, here, and it MORE than fulfills the desire of anyone who enjoys these types of games. Not only is there a wide variety of distinct characters to play with,  each with primary and secondary weapons, but there's so much replayability for score chasers with the rating system. Not many games have convinced me to play for so long just to make my score a *little* bit better, but with the addictive gameplay and skill-based rating system, this game inspired me.
There's plenty of replyability with the EX modes you can unlock for the campagin, finishing each stages with every character, AND Daily Challenges and a Boss Rush mode. This is a game that is ABSOLUTELY worth the price point with all the polish and content on display here.
I'll give it a 10/10. Assault Android Cactus is a perfect example of a modern entry in the twin-stick shooter genre done right. It's difficult, but it'll hook ya for sure.

Assault Android Cactus is a fantastic twin-stick area shooter.
With its innovative battery system that replaces the usual life count system, it allows for an easier access to beginner of the genre. Meanwhile, the scoring system and the leaderboards will offer worthy goals to pursue for both veterans (getting S+ ranks on all levels) and experts (getting on top of the leaderboards) of twin-stick shooters.
Moreover, the many levels of the campaign offer varied challenge that keeps each level unique and fresh. Moving platforms, night sections and environmental hazards are only some of the problems you will have to face.
Finally, the large cast of characters, each with their own weapon and special weapon, enriches the game further. First, because the small storyline and funny dialogs of each character makes the game charming, and give it some soul. Second, because it allows you to switch your playstyle depending on your preference, your skill level, or your scoring objective, making the game more enjoyable and more replayable.
Frankly, there is nothing bad I can say about Assault Android Cactus, it's a great game, that manages to strike the balance correctly between accessibility and challenge, and is fun and rewarding to play.

My interest in games was deeply inspired in my child hood years, and unlike the modern demographic of gamers it was not stemmed from Super Mario or Zelda like most kids born in the 80's. I feel at the heart of the puzzles, it is paying tribute to puzzle quests like Myst and Riven. I respect that in an indie game. As much as I love Call of Duty, it doesn't always take a multi-million dollar game studio to produce an instant cult classic. Bethesda and Activision may have helped empty my bank account on holiday sales events, but there is a real spark to Legend of Grimrock, and it has lit my fire for dungeon crawlers again.

The game is PACKED with secrets, secrets, secrets and you are constantly keeping an eye on your food meter since resting while starving does you no good. The game is well-balanced but does NOT hold your hand-- this is not for your little sister to play, even on normal difficulty.
Walking on a grid system took some getting used to, but the game is well-paced enough that by the time it hits its stride you're a master at it.
The game is going to give your the best experience during the FIRST playthrough only, though. As it is a puzzle game at heart-- the puzzles don't change. Going back through a second or third time would only be for the over-achievers that want to find all the secrets, hidden items, skulls (yes skulls), treasures and so on. I got 22/40 achievements just playing it through the first time. I only had to look up the solution to two puzzles in the entire 20hrs of gameplay, and felt halway clever the rest of the time. The game does a good job of coyly telling you what to look for, then letting you walk RIGHT past it soon after and NOT getting that cool sword that's hidden in the walls.
Be patient, Be smart, Be methodical. Grimrock IS out to get you. Food is scarce and some enemies are a bit overpowered--- again, tough but fair. You'll have a blast wandering down its tunnels. I wholly recommend it.

Transistor is a beautiful, atmospheric, and touching game. The combat system was something brand-new to me, and it felt like a breath of fresh air. The characters and their interactions are sparse but always impactful, and the story is minimalist in how it is conveyed to you, but has depth if you take the time to seek it out in the world. While not quite as obscure (or as convoluted) as Dark Souls, Transistor has a similar feel in that it forces you to spend time with the world in order to fully grasp the finer points of the story. That said, I was not intensely lore-hunting and still was able to appreciate some of these details with just a passing interest in seeking out the deeper story.
While I loved this game, I found it difficult to play for more than thirty minutes at a time. As much as I enjoyed the combat system, it felt mentally draining sometimes from how on-your-toes you have to be throughout every fight—and fights are frequent.
Strongly recommended, and I also fully recommend getting the soundtrack as well.

This game, oh good golly gee gosh this game, has successfuly sucked my free time dry.
Factorio is one of those games you go into with knowing absolutely nothing, being the complete country bumpkin, and at the end of most likely several hundred hours later, you find yourself casually discussing rocket science with your friends for quite a few hours.
The game itself doesn't have (but will have) a campaign of sorts, the only thing it offers, well...only thing...,  is a somewhat fast tutorial and then the sandbox mode, where it dumps you into a world, alone or with friends, points in a random direction and yells at you "HEY, GO NUTS!".
The point of the game is simple, start with sticks and stones and work your way up all the way into launching rockets into space and become the ultimate god of destruction for the wildlife and atmosphere of the world you are in. It's understandable if you feel intimated by seeing this game for the first time, but don't worry, through it's science and research system, Factorio does fantastic job of layering the depth and complexity in a way that is immersive and easy to understand (except combinators, god knows I still have no idea how to use those bloody things).
Before too long you will find out that despite not knowing anything, you went from moving coal into a furnace by hand, to having a fully automated factory producing uranium enriched nuclear bombs (yes that is a thing). The satisfaction factor in this game comes purely from your skill at management and it can be shocking how many things you can always do, there is always something to do, something to optimize, something to increase, something to tinker with, which is impressive when the game only has 5 basic resources that you will work with and make everything out of.
And all of this is just in the vanilla package, if you somehow find yourself not entertained with all that, you can always dip your toes into the mod scene which will get you covered. Want more powerful tiers of literally everything, we got it, want more powerful enemies to defend against, got that too. Want an entirely separate tech tree and dozen new ores and new mechanics, yep got that one too.
If all this doesn't make it obvious that this game is definitely worth 20 bucks, then let me rephrase it for you --> If you enjoy management and building games. GO GET THIS GAME IT'S AWESOME, YOU WILL LOVE IT!

Originally a mod for Unreal Tournament, Alien Swarm has since blossomed into a full-fledged, standalone product offered freely from Valve. In this unoriginal tale of malicious extraterrestrial life, you and three friends explore the ruins of several space stations, tasked with ending this foreign threat.
Your mission will take you through seven well designed locations while putting you face to face with various enemy types. It's an fun, strategic, and fast-paced adventure that just isn't offered in many games elsewhere.
Players get to choose from a variety of classes, be it a technician, medic, or soldier. Each class is vital to the team's composition, placing a heavy emphasis on teamwork. A huge selection of weapons furthers the diversity of gameplay.
For the more dedicated audience, there are plenty of achievements to obtain, ranging from speed runs to overcoming insane odds. If you look forward to these elements, you'll definitely find replay value in Alien Swarm.
Grade: B+

I bought this edition of the game as I actually felt bed for having paid sub-$10 for the original.
This game is a hidden gem. It looks very much like a GTA-clone on the surface, but there's enough that's different here that it doesn't feel like a complete rip off (ie. the Driver series).
The non-American locale is a nice change of pace. It has a melee/counter system similar to the Assassin's Creed/Batman series. A vehicle ram mechanic, jumping between cars (ie. shorter range Just Cause jump) and some character customization (clothing).
The only weak point I can see of that game is that some of the cutscene animations haven't aged well and the random NPC's you meet feel "wooden". However, the story, environment and music (ie. custom music similar to the earlier 3D GTA games) pull it out of the muck.
If you enjoy the single player of the GTA series, buy this on sale and you won't be disappointed.

I am an avid fan of racing games and racing in general. I own all the race sim games you could dream of and I go out to see as many races as I possibly can. As you can expect, I'm  not much of an arcade racing game fan, the look feel and mechanics don't appeal to me at all. Untill I played this game.
Starting up this game, you immediately notice the abandoned F2P mechanics still left in the game, you buy parts and upgrades with an ingame currency and you're able to buy boosts to your earned currency, or "gears", as well. surprisingly enough this is actually fun, it almost feels like you're a fledgling racing car driver, trying to get his team off the ground with a limited budget.
The racing itself is surprisingly good, the cars feel heavy yet powerful, the tracks are interesting to say the least and the car designs are one of the craziest yet most satisfying I've seen in any game. You can customise your own "Formula One" car from any era which leads to absolutely ridiculously satisfying designs.
The game itself looks rather bland, the cars and menus look ok at best, but the tracks, while enjoyable, look plain bad. I do realise that this is a early access game, and I sincerely hope that they adress this.
All in all this game is an unexpected diamond in the rough. I'd urge the casual racing fan and even the hardcore fans to give this a try as the customisation alone is something barely any other AAA developer has ever attempted. I consider this a well made game that mixes the wackiness of Trackmania with the accessibility and controls of Racedriver: Grid.

Assault Android Cactus is a very enjoyable twin-stick shooter with some fun mechanics. The story is pretty simple: a gigantic space cargo ship has been seized by a super AI gone rogue. A special space police force known as 'Assault Androids' send in their cop 'Cactus' who happend to be nearby to stop the AI from keeping the ship hostage. Unfortunately the ship is divided in large different area's who are all controlled by other robotic section lords who also have gone rogue. You're going to have to fight your way through the different levels to get to the core of the ship and put an end to the mutiny!
There is a large selection of characters to play with that you gradually unlock. The difference in gameplay per android is quite considerable. You don't need to worry about ammo for special attacks, instead there is a cooldown for special moves.
An interesting mechanic is your battery. This game doesn't work with continues but once the battery depletes, it's game over. Enemies will drop batteries throughout the fight and you'll have to collect them to keep going. If you get hit multiple times, you go down and you'll have to tap yourself back to life, at the cost of battery power. No matter how many times you get knocked down, as long if you have battery power you are good to go.
There is a fun combo system that revolves around chaining enemy kills. Once you killed an enemy, a counter shows up with a timer in the shape of a circle around it. You need to kill another enemy within the time limit to keep the chain going. You get a ranking based on your combo chain. Breaking the chain will end up in not managing to get the highest ranking for the level.
Other than batteries enemies will drop power-ups that give you temporarily boosts, such as extra speed, firepower assistence or freezing enemies in their tracks. They can help you a lot if you're in a pinch.
If you're a fan of twin-stick shooters this is a very, very enjoyable purchase. It feels refreshing to play and is also fun in couch co-op.

A few years ago, when I had no gaming PC, I played this on the DS, Wii, and eventually on the Xbox 360. I've enjoyed them because of the unique features that they made for each platform, and I thought they would offer the best experience when they ported it to the PC if you have a good gaming setup. Well, they weren't wrong about that.
After playing it at my friend's house, I never expected it to have a lot of bugs, glitches, and crash issues.
I gave the game another shot when I saw it on sale, knowing I might experience the same thing. Thankfully, it's more playable than the last time I remembered it...of course with the help of a few tweaks.
So far, here are my impressions after fiddling with the it:
- Xbox 360 controller option works like a charm.
- Keyboard and Mouse controls are a bit clunky, but not that bad at all if bound properly.
- You can only adjust the video resolution. Textures and other details of the game are still fixed.
- Visuals are good despite of its aging engine (played this on my HDTV).
- Loading screens on the options..everywhere.
- Camera controls are bad, but bearable.
- Force gripping/throwing enemies can be very entertaining.
- Boba Fett has a certain bug that makes him invulnerable unless you send him flying with force lightning.
- Seeing Ben Kenobi soaring and sliding across the screen after doing force combos is hilarious.
- Wampas are fragile creatures.
- Still full of bugs and glitches. Sometimes cool, most of the time funny.
- Applying the 60fps fix gave me a better experience while learning the lulz of the Force.
- I was able to fix my in-game crash issues by turning the cloth physics on and disabling the high details. Additional shadow and texture details were sacrificed in exchange of stability.
Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is an old game, and had quite a number of issues on the PC version. But as for me, it's not that bad if you apply the fixes and needed adjustments. It's still a great game and I've personally enjoyed every moment I had with it.
Verdict (tl;dr)
If you already have Star Wars: The Force Unleashed (including the DLC's) on your PS3 or Xbox 360, feel free to skip this one. As for the fans who bought this game just like me, or who wish to get it while it's on sale, be sure to check the steam community forums. There you will find some guides and links for the fixes you'll need, including the missing sounds and the 60fps unlock.
And if you're playing The Force Unleashed for the first time, you won't be disappointed. It has a well-polished storyline that any Star Wars fan would appreciate. Character customization is also a huge addition in this game. And last but not the least, the mix of lightsaber hack n' slash with the Force is fun as hell.

It's kind of a mixed bag. It is indeed fun to kill a stormtrooper with another stormtrooper and then electrocute the survivors after throwing a few off a cliff with your mind. That is awesome. Still, there are a number of issues with the gameplay I must address.
For one, it's locked at 30 fps, which is very jarring. No matter what I tried, it refused to rise above 30. There may be a 3rd party fix, but I haven't found one yet.
In addition to this, there are not many options to choose from in the graphics section. Heavy aliasing and what-not. Yeah, I know, it's a game from 7 years ago. Still, it is very clearly a badly ported console title.
Another issue is the combat. While I enjoy it for the most part, pretty much all of the enemies can stun-lock you or ragdoll you in a number of ways, leading to very frustrating moments in which you simply cannot fight back against your foes. There were several moments on Felucia, for example, where I felt that all I could do was sit back and watch as Starkiller was stunlocked for several seconds by two blue guys wielding melee weapons. Kinda takes the fun out of being an all-powerful badass sith.
And then there's the boss fights. Quick-time event after quick-time event, AOE attacks that ragdoll you and are difficult to dodge, on and on.
In short-hand, it's worth the price I got it for on sale, about $6. I would not, however, buy it at full price.
tldr:
Wait for a sale or it's not worth it.

For those downvoting the review please keep in mind that I am reviewing the Early Access Game and as such and will update my review based on the current state of the game.
Feb 19th 2014: The game is brilliant! A couple of issues such as VERY LOW fps on races, where time trials are a blistering 60+ fps, and some black flags on corners being cut on very tight lines, but I understand early access. I got quite a few hours in yesterday with nothing game breaking happening. Such a great combination of simulation and arcade with such a community driven competitive component. This brings me back to the fun times I had with Hot Pursuit 2 2002.
With the developers actively engaging the community and updates coming in fast I am very excited to see where this game goes.
Feb 17th 2014: Game won't start for me. Stays on the splash screen with only an exit button. I'm all about supporting Early Access games but only if they actually provide, access.
Day 3 with no reply on this issue. I'm beginning to think a refund may be in order.
Awesome multiplayer racing game. Driving feels just great. I don't even like Formula 1, but I love this game.

I'm going to go ahead and say this from the start, if the thumbs up didn't indicate it already. I highly recommend this game. Granted only for certain people, I understand not everyone likes racing games, especially ones that have some simulation aspects to it. This is more of a simcade, and as people have said about this before, it's easy to get into, hard to master.
I do call it how I see it though, even though one of the devs asked for me to review, I have no issue with that, and no, I'm not getting any kind of reward for it nor do I care for one, I just want to see the game succeed and get more players. Starting on developers, they are awesome. I had one personally work with me to troubleshoot an issue I had with the game crashing, and come up with a fix for it, and provided me with a modified .dll file to get the game working until the patch was released the next morning. (this was LATE at night, almost morning when it happened)
The game doesn't have many issues for me, but whatever issues it does have are being worked on by the devs atm. They listen to feedback and issues that the community encounters. Like the FPS problems some people are having. I was talking to a dev last night and they have acknowledged the issue and are working to fix it. In that process though they broke cockpit view online, once they quickly found out about that from players, they fixed it the same day. This is what more games need, devs that listen and actually work to change/fix things. I can forgive games that are broken if the devs ACTUALLY TRY. (I'm not saying this game is broken by the way, it is far from it) If you can't at least respect a developer for that, I've got nothing for you.
The community of this game, so far, is all friendly. This can of course change, as people are people and the more people that play, the higher chance for bad people to show up, that's just life, don't fault a game for that. There's a MMO like chat ingame, you have a public chat for anyone to talk in, a race chat for a race you're in, and a friends list separate from Steam and a racers tab to show EVERYONE online. You can check out their rank, nationality, and private chat from there. Quite simple and functional.
The driving mechanics ingame are quite nice in my opinion. It's definitely not a sim like Assetto Corsa, but it's not super arcadey like Need for Speed games. There's a good balance of fun and realism, combined with the options of automatic gear changing, semi auto, and manual, and various assists you can enable and disable on the fly. The cars all feel nice to drive too, they have good weight to them, you can feel the cars grip (or lack thereof), the cars respond to different surfaces, and changing car setup makes thing vary quite a bit. Running the default setup will work fine but you certainly get an advantage if you take the time to set up your car properly for a certain track, be it the under/oversteer of the car, the suspension stiffness to help cornering, the downforce levels, front/rear brake bias, and even gear ratios, and it does it in a fairly simplified but useful way. Their are descriptions for the settings on the side to help explain, and instead of some settings like camber levels and toe, and ARB settings and spoiler and wing angles, it's simple clicks left and right toward a different setting. I'm a huge fan of racing games in general, arcadey and sim. My main issue with sims is a lot are just plain better when using a racing wheel, which makes me happy to say this works EXTREMELY well with a gamepad. This itself makes it more accessible, which isn't always a bad thing.
The amount of content ingame is something I can't comment on too well right now, as I haven't played for that long. The game is only about 500mb though, so keep that in mind. There's a decent amount of tracks from what I've seen, and they're all fun, for me at least. There are preset cars ingame to buy, quite a few for each career and team, and some on the market (using ingame money).
But then we get to the car creator. You can choose between the 3 car types, and the different performance groups, then mix and match between different front, middle, and rear pieces of the car, and then change the paint and decals, and choose between a lot of different cosmetics like exhausts, brakes, rims, mudguards, steering wheels, etc. And depending on the car chosen, you get a different amount of PI to spend on your car. These are basically skill points in an MMO, you put points into things like braking, power, grip, etc. And in the same area you can select different engines and tires that will also change the PI settings of your car a bit. This adds a lot of personalization to the game and makes everyones car feel different. So in that aspect, there's a lot of content, and I'm sure there's more to be added.
A thing I forgot to put in somewhere about the car types: They're all F1 cars. There are the older ones running V6's if I remember, the Classics. Then you have the Legendary cars, I think these are using V8's ingame, I forget. They are based off more modern looking F1 cars though. Then you have the Formula class, these are using V12's ingame, and are the most modern looking cars.
When it comes to graphics, not too much to say. They aren't bad, certainly not the worst. If you really judge a game based on that, well, I don't know what to tell you. The gameplay is very good, the graphics work well and don't detract from the game. Fairly straightforward here. The only thing negative I have to say about that is with the graphics quality, there shouldn't be performance issues, but there are. BUT, like I said earlier, the developers are working on this right now. Like literally now.
Regarding peoples butthurtness towards "in app purchases". Yes, there are some. You can pay real money to get ingame money from what I understand. But it's optional. There's literally nothing you can get from that, that you can't get ingame by just playing normally, and it DOES NOT make up for lack of skill.
Any of these things are subject to change, as this game is still in Early Access and is being worked on still. This was put up on 2-14-2014. If anything changes that makes any of my points irrelevant or outdated, I'll try to remember and edit this.
I'll say again, I highly recommend this game for just about every kind of racing fan, and definitely for people that like F1 cars.
It's quite accessible too, so not being the best isn't a reason to pass this by.

A few things so far about Victory: The Age of Racing:
(This is not an actual review)
- The game menu looks quite satisfying and is clearly arranged.
- This game is definitely pay to win. Proof? The developers are presenting the "build your own car" thing as one of the main features. At the beginning you have already one car of each class so you can start right of racing. so far so good. to build your own car, you need at last (probably with extra parts and stuff a few 100 more) 5200 Gears Credits (the only ingame currency). If you win one of these early multiplayer races (don't know if its getting noticeably more when you progress) you get ~100 GC. So, to build your own the cheapest car of any class, without spending real money, wou have to win like 50 races. Races i've driven were appr. 4 - 6 minutes. In comparison: You can buy one of these predefined cars for the half of the price, which might be even a bit faster. So i think that the real money thing ones again ruins a game by slowing it down horribly, which equals pay to win to me.
- Gameplay is (after years of developement of this former-free-to-play game) like Mario Kart without Toads and bananas, but more buggy and erratic. But still quite fun to drive, a bit like trackmania. In conclusion this game is very arcadish, while it is published to have "realistic car physics".
One of the game developers once said in an interview with insidesimracing on Youtube (2012), that at the beginning, when they startet the title as free-to-play, they thought about not making one of these ptw games. Now the game is still in developement, is ptp and even ptw, too. I kind of regret buying it.
At the moment i have, to be honest, no MASSIVE complaint about the game how it is. It's okay, not more or less. But if you make the "mistake" to judge this game by what it pretends to be, it's absolutely not enough and seems like a bit of a hoax.
At the end i have to put a careful "YET", as the developers have time to and possibilities to fix these points, hopefully.

Very funny, very charming, very cool little RPG.  It doesn't take a lot to beat it, but it has some really nice elements to it, like being able to "pick a fight" in an area rather than just looking around for monsters, and there being a battle counter that, after being exausted, stops random encounters.
Also has Cthulhu, so that's a big plus.

Fun, inexpensive RPG. Despite its parodical nature, battles are super fast and combat is intuitive, especially for a turn based RPG. Enemies get 10% stronger with each turn, meaning you have to actually use each of your turns wisely to finish battles quickly. A lot of the fat from other RPGs has been trimmed here, and the game will only take a couple hours to beat, but it's not expensive and it never gets dull. Also the soundtrack is pretty solid.
Far as weak points go, most of the dungeons are kind of forgettable, the game is linear and the art is just okay (though I do love the Cthulhu wielding a sword sprite). Humor can be obvious and hit-or-miss but it has its charm and good moments.
Definitely worth the price of admission, especially during a sale.

Got it on sale for only 2,84€ and it was definitely worth it.
- The music is 100% fitting. If you like listening to it you'll enjoy what they created, if you're the kind of player who wants to blend it out and focus on the game it won't be noticeable.
- The art style is exactly what you see in the preview. You get what they present at any given time so you can check that out beforehand. Personally I found it to be stunning, simple and even found myself not playing for a few minutes from time to time just to appreciate the scene.
- The voiceover is top. Absolutely what you would want from a game like that. Could create a feeling of immersion even if the graphic style was nothing but stick figures. 10/10!
Now to the most important part: Gameplay
You control the flow. Want to take a break? Hit your spacebar and do something else. Or plan your move. Or watch the scene and appreciate the style. Love it.
Combinations of skills allow for individualized approaches to winning battles and since skills are being forcefully removed whenever you die you will learn new combos by default without having the flow of your game being interrupted or being forced to read manuals and similar.
I do have to admit that it is a bit limited and if you want to describe the game as basic as possible it's "run to x, arena gets created, fight enemies, continue to y, repeat", but it wouldn't be fair to reduce the game that harshly.
At worst you get a few hours of fun, at best you keep playing it multiple times and come back to it a few months later. It's one of the titles that can sit in your library and won't get dusty bcause you keep coming back to it every once in a while.
Since it's on sale right now I can safely recommend it for almost everyone, even if you aren't into the genre usually.
2,84€ is way too cheap for a game like this. It's almost a must-buy if you wanna kill time.
You will not be disappointed for a price like that.
As for full price: You would have to judge yourself. I wouldn't have done it, but right now it's definitely way cheaper than it should be and totally worth picking it up.

Grab a controller and get ready to have a blast.
Assault Android Cactus is a twin-stick arena shooter with local co-op.  You select a character from among a group of cute and spirited girls, and use her unique attack and special ability to kick some alien robot butt.
Once you start playing this game, it's impossible to put it down until you've cleared it.  It's a polished, arcade-style experience that feels scientifically engineered to be fun and addicting.
Even if you are not a fan of bullet-hell games, this game is not quite that.  It's more about maintaining your combo and reading the battlefield than frantic, mindless dodging.

I only have a handful of hours in this game, but if you're a fan of top-down twin-stick shooters or shmups, this is definitely worth your time. The single-player campaign's level design is such that the learning curve is gradual and the S+ goals are achievable. Every new mechanic introduced gets utilized as you discover them, which makes the later levels difficult but understandably so, given the skills you've picked up along the way.
The fact that RNG is not a factor also makes this a worthwhile addition to your library. Everything that happens, every enemy that spawns (excepting the Daily and Infiinity Drive modes) is because of your play style, not some random twiddling of bits inside your computer.
The soundtrack is almost reason enough to pick this up. Award-winning composer Jeff Van Dyck has put together a score and soundtrack that suits and enhances the frenetic play style. His sounds are the only positive in a failed run.
If you don't love this game, I'm confident you haven't played enough.

Assault Android Cactus is awesome. It's... just awesome.
The graphics are awesome. Although the super deformed look of the protagonists is a tiiny bit cringey, the animations and the personality of every character more than makes up for it. The levels are colorful and everything's perfectly identifiable despite the intense chaos that usually clutters the screen. GUI is clear and immediate, and there's a lot of detail put into the game's appearance. Shield emitters will change colors depending on your current level, shell casings will spray everywhere, lighting effects look great, and it keeps a mostly solid 60 FPS throughout.
The sound is AWESOME. The OST is catchy and upbeat, with a lot of really kickass tunes. Voice acting is cool and the sound cues are always present and identifiable. Honestly one of the best sound designs I've heard in a while.
The gameplay is awesome. The controls are a *tad* awkward since the right stick is a bit overly sensitive and being used to TBoI having to constantly aim in 360º takes a bit to get used to, but it is otherwise very fluid and fun. There is no death (you only get knocked out) and the core of the gameplay consists in killing enough enemies to spawn a battery in order to keep the timer up -a battery takes 60 secs to deplete-, resulting in a very fast paced kill-a-thon. There's a lot of enemies that can knock you out in one hit but also power-ups that help in staying mobile or killing the enemies faster. All enemies are easily identifiable and all have cues for their attacks. It feels awesome zipping around the battlefield taking out high priority targets while lasers fly everywhere.
The characters are awesome. Although they have just a couple of lines they have distinct personalities and a very different feel to them. The weapons are sort of expected but very varied and sometimes rather original, especially on the unlockable androids. Each one will have different lines on the bosses, helping replayability, and all are viable to get e throughout the game, although some will work better than the others. Overall though, they're really franchise worthy, they're that good.
The bosses are... well, on the one hand they are pretty awesome because they are bullet hell stages that feel super satisfying when you get to beat them, but on the other they can become really annoying and frustrating if you're not carrying a character that works well against them.
The play value is awesome. Every stage is pretty easy to beat, but there are ranks to them where you'll compete against your Steam friends and put on a global leaderboard as well. There's also Daily Drives and the Infinity Drive mode, which takes place on an ever shifting arena. It's really impressive to see it change shape and completely alter its mechanics Layer after Layer. You really won't get tired of it any time soon, and for the price it's going, it's a real value. There's 5 levels per stage plus one boss, and 5 stages total. After beating the game you get Boss Rush, *and* there's several unlockables that you can buy with credits which add filters, change the camera POV, give you super alternate weapons, and so on.
Assault Android Cactus checks all the boxes for a *great* game. Memorable characters, unlockables that keep you going, amazing soundtrack, great graphics, easy to get in and hard to master and polished-to-a-shine gameplay really makes it a title worth playing. The bosses can be a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥, and you'll always end up wishing for a whole campaign more, but that's the problem with good games, they eventually have to finish. For a 3 people team, this is an outstanding achievement, and truly a twinstick fan's wet dream. 9.5/10.

I am not usually one to hate on things, but this game is just bad, very bad...and here's why:
Let's start with the list of "would be pros" (things that could be good about the game if the execution wasn't so terrible):
- Fun combat system. Great, so many combos to use...if it wasn't for the fact that you will never use most of them. Especially the longer, most powerful combos are useless - weak enemies will be dead long before you finish them and strong ones will interrupt them 99% of the time. Also most of the stronger ones have superior power on melee range, so you'll just end up pouring electricity into them from safe distance until it stops being funny.
- Oh, wanted to list something more, but just realized that 'tis a part of the cmbat system as well. There is not really anything else in this game than combat anyway. So, okay - using the things lying around to fight. Sounds fun, right? Just tearing a block of metal from the wall with the Force and smashing it into your enemies. The hell it does! But it takes so long you cannot use it. First you have to target the object (more on targeting later, that's the stuff of nightmares). Use the pull ability on it, the slooooowly float it around, direct it on the enemies and release...there you go! Oh, damn, why am I lying on the floor with half HP gone? Something must have gone wrong in the process. The thing is you cannot move while doing this so you'll probably get hit by a missile or five before you get to the carnage part. Did I mention getting knocked off your feet interrupts the pull? So this one's a no go.
That's it, my list of "what could have been pros if better executed" is officially over. Now for the cons:

- Characters. They have no character whatsoever. And their behavior makes absolutely no sense. No thinking being would act like that.

- Story. There is a story? Must have missed it. Kill this, kill that, kill something more. Oh, the Dark Lord betrayed us? Let's kill him as well.
- Enemies. They are plain stupid and predictable. If you don't try to use any of the longer combos or never stop to chuck some debris around, you will pretty much never get hit with anything that hurts. Which basically limits all the abilities and combos to using 3-4 things (out of dozens) over and over again.
- Boss fights. The camera turns into a 1990 abomination during those.
And the winner of our "worst thing about The Force Unleashed" contest is (without any competition to speak of) the targetting system. You have no crosshair, no cursor or anything to pick a target. You just look in the general direction and hope the game picks the one you want. Normally it's pretty much a 50/50 thing, so it is still playable. But during the boss fights, with the atrocious camera, targeting becomes nothing short of abysmal. Most of the fight you spend running in circles around your enemy in a hopeless strive to target him/her. Mostly you hit things just by accident - when you aren't even trying to. Blocking their abilities is even worse, because you often have only around half a second to target them. I consider myself a patient person - I don't have a problem with repeating something I did wrong many times over until I get it right. Well, I'm also very stubborn, so I will keep trying even if it meant dying for the whole day. But this...this almost made me quit the game a couple times. Not because of the dying, but because I knew I didn't do anything wrong, just the mechanics are atrocious. Now that I've finished it I wish I rather quit. Not worth the time even if it was free.

Star Wars - The Force Unleashed: PLayed through from 4/29/2015 - 5/3/2015
Star Wars - The Force Unleashed is a capable hack and slash romp through the Star Wars Universe. The story is told picking up from the end of Episode III and fills in some of the abyssmal gap between the prequel trilogy and the original trilogy.
Some fair plot twists and some darn good storytelling make this a game worth playing for any Star Wars fan. There are several familiar character cameos and some nice subtle tie in's from both trilogies. All of the characters are very well voice acted and the story elements provided me with the majority of the incentive to get through the title.
Light Saber combat is fluid and fun against most of the weaker to medium foes. However, the larger enemies and boss encounters end up being an excersize in discovery and repetition. That is, you find the bosses weakness and continually exploit it until victory is achieved. I found myself spamming force lighting for most of the game to this effect.
The control scheme did not translate well to the mouse and keyboard. I would recommend a gamepad for this title. Either a 360 or PD3 controller should do the trick. Force Grip and throw seemed to be fairly useless for the most part as my inteded throw destination was often overwritten by a completely random direction. Similarly, in the boss fights the camera postioning becomes fixed and I often found myself tossing lightning around the arena rather than at my enemy.
Some simple custimization options let the player make small changes in the protagonists appearance which is a nice touch.
In the end I would give Star Wars - The Force Unleashed a 6/10 for a casual non-star wars fan for the poor combat dynamics in the boss fights. I would award it with an 8/10 for a Star Wars Fan for a spectacular universe expanding story and tie in with some serviceable lightsaber combat.

Okay my play time has been very limited and I intend to put more effort into playing this game, but heres the thing, if the game is broken it is broken no matter what amount of hours I play.
You are probably wondering what I mean by broken? Let me list it off for you:
1/. Tanks are destroyed in seconds by AT, they are completely useless against an enemy who has well placed AT and one mistake can completely wipe out a group of tanks in a very short space of time.
2/. The artillery pieces actually walk to the enemy if they are out of ammunition, so not only do you have to watch them closely they can walk off into the distance if you right click an enemy when out of ammo (WTF?).
3/. Ammunition isn't an obvious enough of a feature to be watched closely, it's also completely useless for some units such as tanks who won't last long at all on the battlefield, and units literally have no warning signs on the UI to say they are out of ammo and will just walk to the enemy.
4/. Suppression is just too OP for such a macro kind of game, I get that units should have diminishing returns but complete blackout? Come on this isn't CoH where it takes two seconds to get from one side of the map to the other but this is just too micro for such a macro game.
5/. The mechanics of the game aren't intuitive enough, the mouse has a cover colour system in it, but everything else is just confusing as buggery, I get that pressing certain buttons gives info but this is just completely confusing when tanks can be taken out in one hit from appearing behind a tree line for 2 seconds.
6/. Infantry are either OP or completely useless, make up your mind, and don't make it so that a flame thrower can wipe out an infantry squad in one shot, again that's way too micro oreintated for this type of game, if an enemy can just sneak up and wipe an entire squad in the space of 10 seconds then you have no time to even think before they are gone.
The problem with this game is it's trying to be too many things, and the pacing is completely broken, it'll take ages for your units to move but they can be wiped out in two seconds, the game's balancing is more orientated towards finding your enemies opposite which is just completely insane in a macro game.
For me the main thing this game needs is information being fed back to the player, someone's out of ammo? then flash it up and start pinging the player that the unit is out of ammo. Make the map more intuitive, maybe have a separate layer for vision maps etc.
Too few options for the player and too many niche gimicky features.

Steel Division looks like just a reskin of the Wargame titles at first glance, but it is definitely it's own game. If you've ever played Flames of War, this feels a lot like that if it were adapted into a video game. There's a nice variety of play-style between Axis/Allies and within those the different divisions - e.g. an Airborne division plays very differently from anything else. This will be a point of departure for Wargame veterans though, as within the division itself there's not many options. So whereas in Wargame you would select the DDR and then use unit composition to build 3-4 different flavors of a DDR army - in Steel Division you pick, say, 101st Airborne and you only have one or two ways to play them. I personally don't feel like this limits choices for tactical options, it just changes at which point in the composition process that you make those decisions.
The game looks as good as previous titles and makes for some great screenshots. Unfortunately you spend a lot of time zoomed out so if you really want to soak in the destruction you'll have to watch a replay. There are a few sloppy jobs in the modelling department, specifically with infantry uniforms. As of writing this hasn't been fixed but that will hopefully change in the future. UI is functional, more so than a lot of WW2 wargames. Sound isn't really exciting but different weapon systems are usually easily to identify by their sound so it at least serves it's purpose.
Where this game excels is in it's feedback to the user. A good strategy game needs to let a player experiment, and punish/reward that experimentation in ways that teach lessons to the player. Previous wargame titles were very good at this and Steel Division is no exception. What seems a daunting game at first is actually very good at teaching you what you did wrong - especially if you take the time to watch your replays, most notable the replays of matches where you lose. Don't let your impression of the learning curve scare you off, SD44 teaches you it's mechanics effectively.
The real disappointment with SD is the campaign. It's there, and it's not terrible but it feels very formulaic and by-the-numbers. MOWAS2 was guilty of this as well. Good campaigns use the advantage of scripted encounters to create interesting challenges and scenarios. My favorite examples are the missions where you attempt to hold Hill 112 in the original of Company of Heroes. There's nothing like that here which is a shame because Eugen's previous titles have shown us that they can produce a really good campaign. It's even more important in SD44 because the niche status means the multiplayer community will never rival a game like CoH2. They could've given it so much more longevity if the single-player had more depth. There's some discussion about more SP content coming out later as DLC but that seems unlikely at this point.
If you like WW2 strategy games, SD44 is worth checking out. I can't really recommend this to anyone who isn't in it for the historical time period though as you can get a better experience playing the campaign of an older Eugen title. Keep an eye out for post-release content.

Introduction:
Its the weekend before May the 4th which means its Star Wars weekend, and I’ll be looking at some of the Star Wars games over the next few days. The first being Star Wars: The Force Unleashed, it’s a hack and slash/platform style game that follows the story of Galen Marek. The story is based between the two trilogy and fills in some of the gaps in the story.
Story:
Galen Marek our protagonist is take by Vader as a child to become his secret apprentice, we meet him in the final stages of his training. The events that follow will change not only Galen’s twisted view of the world but also the course of galactic history. At least if Disney had left it as cannon, but never the less its a well written story and was written to be cannon at the time. So this means it ties in well and doesn’t try to change anything we know.
Gameplay:
The gameplay isn’t anything you haven’t seen before, its not going to blow you away. But it plays well enough and gives you an amazing feeling of power, Galen isn’t some bog standard Sith. He’s a Sith power house! he doesn’t open doors, he blows them to pieces with the force and that’s the same for all his powers. So no, nothing new and quiet repetitive but its amazingly fun too. Legend of Grimrock game review pending… (maybe forever…)  Okay, a quickie…  The game is freaking awesome!  Great old school RPG gameplay, party of 4, awesome graphics, lighting and sound, etc, etc…  Buy it!!!  Also know that Legend of Grimrock 2 is also out and you may want to get that.  I have a Mac running OS X 10.6.8.  See bottom for my full specs.
The Legend of Grimrock (LoG) "Level Editor" alone is worth the price of the game!  I seriously may never play another game accept for my own LoG adventures!  I am so addicted to this editor and pretty good at it too if I might say!
Seriously, I cannot break away from the level editor long enough to write a review about the game which is also really awesome!  Ideas just keep popping into my head for my adventure.  The editor is the easiest, most powerful game editor I have ever used.  An 8 y/o could make full blown D&D style adventures!  It's that easy.
I never once needed a manual except when scripting a couple of things.  There is good support on their website for that.  There are scripting abilities using the included Lua scripting language, but know that you "do not" need to use scripts at all to create full blown adventures with stories included, if you want to write them on walls! :-)
I used Lua to write messages on screen, instead of walls.  Say, sometimes you want to set the mood with some text as you enter a room…  You can easily place an invisible switch on the floor and link it to some scripted text.  I only needed scripting so my text would show up on the HUD.  If you want text on walls, it is much easier!  You basically set a text box on a wall and type what you want it to say.  It shows up on the wall as a golden unfamiliar text.  Kind of like the old "Lord British's Ultima textstyle".  Then you click on it to read it.
You can easily insert short or long text onto walls to create a story if you want, or to leave cryptic messages for puzzles you can create.  I believe anything that is done in the game, can be done with this editor.  If you like to build maps and levels with a D&D type theme, do not hesitate to get this game.
You'll be so proud of yourself and your creations.  You will play and tweak "your" own adventures for hours!  There are so many cool things you can do and setup!  You really are creating your own adventures and feel very good about them!  It's an incredible feeling of great accomplishment!!!  I never really scripted before this game…  You are limited to flat level designs, but can link levels together with stairs, pits and teleports.
I could go into greater detail, but just know, the level editor is awesome and will burn up your spare time fast!  You set the lighting by adding torches and/or more modern lights.  You can create some super creepy settings and add different monsters or monster spawn points to them!
If you want to just build a simple arena with endless spawning monsters that you control by the flip of a switch, you can do that too!  You can add different items to each monster so they drop different items, weapons and armor!  You have a lot of control and options and it is so simple to use!  Then, you can play them in the full game and even share them online in the Steam Workshop!  How freaking cool is that!!!  I will eventually be posting mine to try, and it is really good if I might say so myself! :-)

Assault Android Cactus caught me off guard. It was a game I bought from Humble Bundle, and I only now got around to it.
It's actually a extremely solid game of it's kind. A rather "safe" twin stick Bullet Hell.
What I mean is, unlike any other like this that I know of, taking hits won't end in immediate gameover. Instead, your true life bar drains over time, and when you take enough hits in a row in a short time, you'll topple over and shut down. You'll have to smash the fire buttons to revitalize your systems and get back to the fray. A battery in the top-middle of the screen will drain constantly, without pause. You'll have to be killing enemies by the packs constantly to spawn powerups, and the battery which is VITAL to your progress and survival.
The levels are all unique in every way. While 25 levels may seem like a lazy number, it's far from that. They truely affect the gameplay and force you to fight smarter, rather than harder. Do not expect easy victories. For those addicted, there's even Daily Drives and Infinite Drive. Daily Drives are daily levels, as expected on the tin. Infinite Drive goes on forever, until you can no longer support your android.
The characters you get to play as all cater to different styles, which is a fantastic plus. From snipers to shotguns, railguns and magma launchers, this is perfect for anyone. In fact...
One of the best things about the game is that it's 100% multiplayer friendly, allowing you to have up to four players in the mayhem. Sadly, there's no online co-op, which would've been a nice addition.
One of the things that I was surprised about is the story. This game didn't even need a story, and I assumed it didn't have one to begin with. I was wrong, and pleasantly wrong. It's not a big story, and I like the implementation. Bossfights give you good insight into the story of the characters, and there's even bios you can look into if you really want more.
The bosses are quite worthy of their position, ready to absolutely destroy players. They all have several phases and are a lot of fun to fight.
Just don't expect the game to be easy. The music is mostly techno, and is alright in my opinion.
While I struggle to reccomend this at a full purchase, anything 10$ and below, you will get your money's worth!

Facts: I'm a game moderator (voluntary user); I can be biased, but I know this game really well; also, remember that this is Early Access, so still a beta phase.
Talking about the game: first of all, despite the tags, this is NOT a simulator; it's more like an arcade racing game with realistic features (don't expect to drift on every corner or have random racing lines); still, the model is really satisfying: the racing experience and setup know-how is rewarded, while beginners won't have many problems driving their first cars. With the inclusions of new events, career mode and other stuff there's plenty to do, and car customization is one of the best ever seen in a racing game, both on visual stuff like paint and development. Good races are real fun, and the tracks are inspired and good to drive in. The devs also are very active, and try to fix bugs in a quickly way (also are active in the forums, which is nice).
Bad things: excluding random bugs (which I'm not experiencing at the moment, save for some really minor stuff) the worst part is the performance of the game in this phase. We know that graphic optimization and new shaders are coming very soon, but at the moment on many computers a race with full roster will make the fps drop. There's also the minor issue of a little population, but hopefully this will change in the next weeks (it's still early - early access), and the races and events still flow very nicely, so it's not really a problem.
What will come next: full Steam integration, procedural race tracks, track editor and Steam Workshop support. Probably some of the best features to have in a game like this.

A very soothing crafting game about making a factory as efficient as possible. It is a survival game, but I think it's best when you actually turn the enemies' aggression off, because the real meat of the game is laying out this huge sprawling factory that stretches for miles and miles. It's a sandbox game but it does have a soft ending--however, you can just keep growing that factory infinately.
What makes this stand out from other crafting survival games, is that instead of your tools simply leveling up over time, your crafting abilities evolve. You start out with a pickaxe, but you will stop using it and learn to make mining iron and other metals automated. You start by building things by hand, and then slowly the building is replaced by assembling machines to do it for you. Then, you face the issue of making assembling machines feed into eachother in a grand factory system that has to be rebuilt constantly to make room for new tech.  Each level of tech feels satisfying, but also brings in a new set of challenges that have to be solved like a puzzle.
The game has a big online community sharing ideas of how they solve their own factories, and the devs are adding new systems into the game all the time which you can opt into if you get bored of playing the vanilla version. I highly recommend. It's just a great way to relax.
One thing to keep in mind is that it assumes you know a lot going in on how to play the game. I'd recommend watching a gameplay video first, since the tutorials they have in game are fine, but are mostly about hotkeys and not so much about strategies. There's a loooot of details in this game that can go right over your head--lots of numbers and math, so seeing someone else actually play the game will make it quite easy to navigate once you go to play it yourself. But, it's quite overwhelming if you just jump into it with no context.

Take the already amazing elements that made Bastion such a joy to play being its visually impressive presentation, soundtrack and narration and add those into a new setting, a new twist and a new way of play and you've got Supergiant Games' second big hit that's just as, if not even more, impressive than their first game; Transistor.
Taking place in the sci-fi setting of Cloudbank city wherein the environment can be reprogrammed or transformed based on the popular votes of its citizens, you take control of Red; the popular singer of Cloudbank whose foiled assassination attempt has her and the powerful weapon Transistor uncover the mystery and conspiracy behind the city and the assailants attacking it.
This time around, Transistor's gameplay while retaining minor similarities to Bastion's, is a lot more fluid and mechanically complex. With the ability to pause time within the battlefield in order to plan out your moves and attacks before executing them in one burst or simply duking it out in real time; players are given many options in addition to the already abundant skills and upgrades to play the game in such variety that multiple playthroughs and experimentation is encouraged.
Transistor is Supergiant Games' second shining achievement and is the sort of game that should not be missed. Definitely highly recommended.

Steel Division isn't a horrible game, but it's just Wargame with a WW2 paintjob and some more questionable design decisions.
The artillery spam from the Wargame series is turned up to 11, exacerbated by the fact that all units are slower and easier to stun. Any infantry assault can be stopped by a pair of mortars. Any successful infantry assault can be completely wiped out by an off-map strike, of which there is no warning apart from a bunch of massive explosions. It's like a Delete button, it doesn't even require line of sight!
Airspam used to be pretty bad in W:ALB, and Steel Division is its spiritual successor. In their infinite wisdom Eugen, knowing full well the overpowered state of airstrikes, decided to nerf anti-aircraft guns to the point of uselessness. Planes appear over the battlefield in an instant, when the players have been begging for some sort of delay since at least two Wargames ago. Any assault is met immediately by a mass of bombers, which are well nigh unkillable in early phases unless you also have fighters. Tactical depth? ♥♥♥♥ no. The guns are supposed to make the planes panic and turn away, but only one gun is really capable of this early on - the 88. Others die in a shower of fire and shrapnel.
The balance is atrocious, which is on par for Eugen. I'm not complaining about that. The final verdict, however, is that Eugen can go and shove it where the sun doesn't shine. Fair warning to those who still buy it - the game has next to no playerbase two months post-release.

There's something appealing to me about old-school dungeon crawlers and Legend of Grimrock is no exception.
Creating your party = win
Exploring dungeons = win
Gaining experience/levels = win
Finding treasure = win
Spooky factor = win
Not too difficult puzzles = win
Smooth and Steady gradation of difficulty = win
What separates this first person dungeon crawler is the whiff of dry humor and psychedelics (your party will eat their share of mushrooms to stay alive). And the reason I say that is because of how smooth the gradation of difficulty/monsters/puzzles goes as your progress.
One thing I find difficult however, is spellcasting in combat. It can be challenging to manage 4 characters in real time combat much less managing the spells of the caster. You actually have to click on a recipe or sequence of 3 symbols to cast spell. A party of spellcasters? Unthinkable. Out of the question. Impossible.
And here's my solution: HOTKEYS! Why cant we use hot keys to program our top 3-5 used spells?
Backpack/Weight management can also be difficult. I took one minotar in my party and his worth in packmule and tank roles was quickly surpassed by my human fighter of average abilities save for SKILLED Feat +5 skill points. She actually has almost as many hit points as my minotar, easts less food, has higher armor rating, higher weapon rating, much more reliable.
All in all 4/5 looking forward to the Legend of Grimrock 2 after I beat this one.

This game is just a ton of fun to play!The 9 different androids all play pretty differently and make it a blast to replay levels and try out different strategies. Plus they're all really cute and full of personality! The level design is great and is constantly changing things up or throwing new surprises at you. All of them are different and have really cool visual theming too, since each one is a different section of the ship the game takes place on, like hydroponics or freight zones. The music is some awesome EDM and it really gets you pumped to blow up robots, and keeps you going when you lose and retry.
I also really like the battery mechanic, where your battery constantly drains and you have to kill enemies to get more recharges before it drains down and you die. It fits so well into the core loop of shooting and dodging enemies and their bullets, and succeeds in making a bullet hell type of game that is really freindly while still giving a great level of challenge. It also makes the action, which is already fast-paced and relentless as hell, even more tense when you're on the verge of running out and are fighting extra hard to find that one enemy holding the recharge.
Also the boss battles are great and it has a whole bunch of neat extra modes and mutators. And local co-op multiplayer!! My girlfriend and I played through a bunch together and its a really fun way to play since you share a battery meter and have to watch out for each other.
Overall this game is a ton of fun and extremely worth the money. It is a phenomenally smooth and exciting fast action game and bursting with heart and personality. Go play it!!!

I recently replayed this game without the crutch of having multiple people to play with me, and boy has this game not aged well at all. There are many points within this game where the levels feel so bland and uninspiring despite the cartoon-y apperance, and most of the levels are so cramped that it makes the previous installments feel ashamed. Speaking of bland, the enemies themselves, despite there being many of them, are just reskins of reskins, with one different stat tweek to make it look like a different enemy.
This probably wouldn't be such a big deal if they didn't stay on screen for as long as they did. The weapons in this game feel, sound, and just generally weak as hell. The shotguns make me feel like I am shooting bean bags at people, the Uzis sound like aged airsoft guns, and the rocket launcher would have more impact if it was shooting party poppers than its excuse for 'rockets'. Thanks to this, and the games constant decision to take away your ammunition, can make the game hard as balls to points where you just want to give up.
I could go on, but I think I made my point clear without touching the 'story', the horrendous hand holding, and the numerous bugs. Don't buy this game. Don't play it if you've got it from a Bundle either. Buy and play ANY of the other games, and you'll enjoy yourself so much more.

Taking place in the sci-fi setting of Cloudbank city wherein the environment can be reprogrammed or transformed based on the popular votes of its citizens, you take control of Red; the popular singer of Cloudbank whose foiled assassination attempt has her and the powerful weapon Transistor uncover the mystery and conspiracy behind the city and the assailants attacking it.
This time around, Transistor's gameplay while retaining minor similarities to Bastion's, is a lot more fluid and mechanically complex. With the ability to pause time within the battlefield in order to plan out your moves and attacks before executing them in one burst or simply duking it out in real time; players are given many options in addition to the already abundant skills and upgrades to play the game in such variety that multiple playthroughs and experimentation is encouraged.
Transistor is Supergiant Games' second shining achievement and is the sort of game that should not be missed. Definitely highly recommended.

I wanted to like this one. Really, I did. I'm all about old school RPGs, it comes with the Jim Sterling seal of approval, and I enjoy games that let me throw my own content in a bit, like with the portriats...
That said, I couldn't do it.
The combat is tiresome, tedious, and unrewarding. The interface is clunky and amatuerish. The bestiary is lifeless, the puzzels are unfulfilling, and worst of all, there's no dialog for all intents and purposes. This is as souless of a dungeon crawler as I've ever seen, devoid of wit, story, motivation, and wholly undeserving of the level of hype it's gotten.
I can put up with it's old timey grid gimmick - maybe even enjoy the novelty some. But that's all that it brings to the table, and it isn't anywhere near enough. The interface needs a complete overhaul, the combat needs a lot of work, and for the love of Skyrim put some plot and dialog in! A straight up dungeon crawl can work, but you really need to frame it better - give me more of a world, give me context and a story. Give me details and motivation and reward me with more than a set of stairs and a big spoonful of the exact same thing I just did.
I gave it a chance, and it isn't for me.

TLDR – Third person hack & slash similar to the Jedi Knight series, but you don’t get any guns, and it’s more fast paced. The game takes about 10 hours to beat the first time through and doesn’t have that much replay value.  6/10
Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a console port that doesn’t seem to have been optimized for the PC (25 GB download!).  The controls are clunky (in some areas dangerously so) and the game’s menu screens don’t use the mouse. You navigate them with keyboard only, which is a clear sign of an incomplete console port.  Oddly enough, just navigation between different options in the main menu often has its own “loading” screens.
The game’s story takes place between Star Wars Episodes 3 & 4, so it all happens a few years before the original Star Wars movie events take place. Darth Vader finds and trains a young apprentice, who he wants to eventually overthrow the Emperor with. Vader’s convoluted plan involves having his apprentice (named Starkiller) go around causing trouble and raising an army to fight Emperor Palpatine. It doesn’t make much sense to me if I’m being honest. Anyways, the moral is don’t trust the bad guys, they’re always stabbing each other in the back.
You play the Sith assassin Starkiller in the third person perspective, similar to the Jedi Academy and Darksiders games, with your lightsaber being your melee attack, and the force as your ranged weapon. Lightsaber swings are very quick this time around unlike Jedi Academy, and your force powers are more limited, but they flow better in combat. All your force powers are offensive, so you don’t really have “buff” skills to power yourself up prior to fights (except the lightning shield which only lasts a few seconds anyway). Your most used attacks will be combinations of lightsaber swings and force push / force lightning.
One of the noteworthy gameplay elements is the partially destructible environment in many areas. There is a lot of loose debris (or chunks that you rip off the walls) that you can use to throw at your enemies. Every time you kill an enemy you regen some of your life back, while your force power regenerates on its own (pretty fast too, so you can keep blasting). Along with the fact that you don’t use guns, this means that the only collectibles in the game are “force holocrons,” which can give you experience or lightsaber parts for customization. Each time you level up you get points to upgrade a few of your character’s skills or stats. Some holocrons give these skill points directly, while others give random bonuses. Holocrons are often hidden in out of the way areas or behind destructible walls, so throw force power around bountifully and be rewarded.
Pros:
+Expanded story for Star Wars fans, including the birth of the Rebel Alliance and an alternate timeline (DLC included in the Ultimate Sith Edition) where Starkiller gets all up in Luke Skywalker’s business.
+Starkiller is extremely powerful, probably a lot stronger than any of the Jedi you have played in other Star Wars games. It’s good to be bad, and I’m considering changing my legal name to Starkiller.
Cons:
-The controls are often frustratingly clunky, especially when it comes to locking onto enemies for ranged force attacks. There’s also a section involving a star destroyer that might make you want to pull your hair out. It’s not that it’s a difficult section, it’s just hard to know if you’re doing it right your first playthrough, and it just drags on and on.
-The game really is poorly designed for PC, the large download (compared to the sequel, which is like ¼ the size) and the odd menu format really stick out. Also, it might be a bug but I think you need an internet connection to launch the game. I lost my connection for about 15 minutes and found that I couldn’t load my saved game.
-The boss fights can be frustrating because there really isn’t a tutorial on dueling and it feels like I’m missing something important (especially related to blocking).
All in all, the game has significant problems but is worth playing through at least once for the story. Especially if you got this in the Humble Bundle and want to play part 2. I don’t think I’ll be playing through it a second time for a long while though. It just doesn’t bring too much to the hack slash genre.

Summary: A decent military sim ruined by glaring problems.
Score: 5.5/10
By now you already know what the game is all about, so I'll cut to the chase and tell you what I don't like about it.
First and foremost, Steel Division requires a LOT of micro-management for an RTS game of this scale.  You have to watch your units like a hawk to keep them from committing a suicidally stupid maneuver any time they're anywhere near the enemy.  If a unit strays just a few pixels too far, it's out of cover and therefore probably dead.  You might save up your pennies to buy the tank you need to turn the tide of the battle and laboriously send it to the front -- and then when it finally gets there it immediately gets killed as it blunders into the crosshairs of an AT gun that YOU knew was there, but didn't order the tank to avoid because you were too busy micromanaging the path of another unit on the other side of the map at the time.  Sure, you can mitigate this by turning down the game's speed -- but who wants to play a whole battle on super slo-mo?
Steel Division also lacks an autosave or checkpoint feature, so unless you have the discipline to save frequently, you can lose a LOT of progress if it crashes.  That wouldn't be an issue in most games, but Steel Division seems unusually unstable.  After having it crash near the end of 3 out of the 5 campaign scenarios I played, resulting in the loss of hours of gameplay, I decided that enough was enough.
And that wasn't just bad luck.  Take a look at the changelog for the recent "Duelists" update: there's a whole laundry list of fixed bugs containing the words "crash" or "freeze" in their description, and lots of other folks have complained about bugs or crashes in their reviews.  IMO the code quality of this game was highly suspect at the time of its release.
Steel Division also features the worst voice acting I've heard in ages.  The actors frequently mispronounce common military terms, which depending on your mood can be either cringeworthy or hilarious -- but either way it's poor craftsmanship.  It's a testament to the developer's commitment to quality (or lack thereof) that they didn't bother to correct something so obvious and simple to fix.
If you can look past all of that, Steel Division is a decent military simulation.  The basic game engine models the capabilities of tanks and artillery and so forth fairly well at this scale.  But for me the game's overall quality is just too low for me to want to spend any more time on it.

I play at least one match every night, even if it's just against the AI. That's how much I like this game. Sure, there's room for improvement - the graphics aren't great, sometimes your units don't act in an intuitive way, and the set up for multiplayer/skirmish (both sides rushing towards each other at the beginning) doesn't feel particularly realistic, but it's still about as perfect an WWII RTS as you are likely to find. The phase mechanic is great. It creates a real ebb and flow to each match. While some divisions share units, the different way in points are divided between phases, and the subtle differences between the cards and equipment they have, makes each one feel unique. £35 might seem a bit steep for skirmish and multiplayer but it's been worth every penny. I can imagine dipping and in and out of this for years.

Much like their previous game Bastion, Transistor also has a beautiful done art style set in a city that is experiencing a ''apocalypse'' rather than Bastion's post-apocalyptic one. The soundtrack is great or even better in this one. And like bastion it encourages second playthroughs and has a in-game organic(IMO) difficulty setting.
However when it comes to gameplay it is quite different than Bastion's direct action style. You can act in real-time: move, attack with abilities and such BUT the game is designed around the a turn-based style.
When activated the game is paused and you are allowed to plan several moves that once un-paused are done in a very quick succession that leaves the enemy no time to act. The amount of moves is determined on several factors like ability cost which can be modified via upgrades.
And that brings me to the second major difference between it and Bastion. You have no basic non-ability attack. Aside from just moving everything else is done via 1 of 4 selected abilities. These are chosen from 16 different ''functions''.
But the real kicker comes now. Each ''function'' has 3 modes: Active ability ( say shooting a energy bolt at a enemy ), upgrade ( can modify another active ability by increasing it range ) or passive ( can reduce cost of other abilities in planning mode ).
So really when it comes to experimenting with abilities and different tactics you can't go wrong with this game. Sure there will be some strategies that are clearly superior to others since dealing with enemies quickly and staying alive are pretty much the only goals you have but having the large range of choices is a huge plus IMO.
Edit: Forgot the cons.
There's really only 2 points that go against the game IMO:
1. The story while interesting and well enough done is a bit too vague. While I did have a general idea of what happened by the end it still felt a bit too open-ended with several questions left unanswered. Bastion's by contrast while leaving open a possible sequel managed to answer pretty much everything I wanted to know about it.
2. Length. Although it doesn't feel too short and knowing it's still a indie studio behind the game does feel like a slitghly longer playthrough fleshing out the world or adding some other characters to the main story would have benefited it greatly.
As it stands a determined player can finish their 1st playthrough in the same day of purchasing it.

If the only thing you want to know is whether this game is worth your money then yes,it definitely is.
Transistor is a game which you have to discover for yourself,thus I suggest avoiding any sort of reviews,videos,trailers etc that will ruin the experience even the slightest for you(that is not the case with this one,so keep on reading you lazy).
First of all I should say that transistor is a minimalistic game, rich in narrative and emotion.The feeling that you get while traversing this beautiful world set in a colourful though grim future won't be experienced in many other games.The artstyle is to put is simply,amazing,but the area where Transistor truly "shines" is its music.Transistor happens to have the best soundtrack I have ever heard both in movies and videogames.The open areas of the game host an abundant array of ambient music,while major encounters introduce you to new majestic music that may accompany you for the rest of your life.
As I said previously,Transistor is a minimalistic game,that also happens to be the case with its characters.However,there is plenty of background story to be told,that will tie up any loose ends there are and that will help you adore the characters even further(as if you won't cry enough).Plotwise,it has some very interesting elements,but I would really like it if it had expanded on its core story a little bit.
The gameplay on the other hand is pretty much a rather complete experience,consisting of some pretty interesting mechanics,though failing to captivate you till the very end.I suspect that the main reason for this is the lack of abilities,which are very unique on their own and feature a remarkable multi-use gimmick,though unfortunately there are some that are substantially better than others.Generally,I guess you could say that this is the only thing that needs improvement,but in the end combat is not all it is about.
If you want a game that will hit you right in the feels,through a journey of love,fear and uncertainty,then you simply can't miss this one.
If you want to experience a game that will banish you in a futuristic land of epic,enchanted with melodic modern electric rock music,then you simply can't miss this one.
If you just want to play a masterpiece,well you surely can't miss this one.
