King of Fighters 13 is a great game with mostly positives but a few almost devastating negatives.
The game is really hard to get into, but really fun once you get decent at it. Combos lack a buffering system, so you must time them all right. Heck, some combos require 1-2 frame accuracy, but aren't necessary to do well. To combo normals, you have to input your attack right in the freeze frames(hitlag, not hitstun) which take sometime to master. But once you do, you can really enjoy the game for what it is.
The gameplay itself is fun. There are plenty of unique characters with their own playstyles, however the roster is primarily dominanted by shotos (aka Ryu like characters). If you are sick of these types of characters, there aren't alot of characters for you. There are also minor balance issues, as characters like Kim feel significantly stronger(as in have more options in any scenerio) than a character like Elizabeth.
Combos are also handled well for the most part. Stray hits deal a good amount of damage making combos not necessary to not get a time over and also landing any hit makes you feel satisfied. The combo structure is flawed when HD cancels are considered though. When you fill up 2 gauges of "Drive Meter", you can go into a powered up state that allows you to infinitely cancel special moves into each other until the duration ends... leading to very long and boring combos. These long combos only tend to happen once a round due to how useful drive is in matches, but they are very annoying when they do occur.
Neutral game is also not that exciting or intense. It feels like Street Fighter 2 but with short hops, rolls, and some air special moves. There aren't any install supers, interesting environment affecting attacks, or anything that forces you to change your approach asides maybe some land mines. This can leave the neutral game feeling pretty mediocure when comparing it to a mvc game or Guilty Gear, but I can see that the simple neutral could appeal to some people.
Lastly, the casual content is not that good. This isn't any Neither Realm game and it shows. All you have is custom colors, Arcade, and Story mode for casual players(ignoring the obvious stuff like gallery,replays ,or online mode).
Custom colors is REALLY good as you get to unlock colors over time and you can save up to 6 colors. All characters have more than 6 colors to change on them and some can go up to the 20s, so you'll always have lots of creativity when it comes to alternate colors.
Arcade Mode does nothing special. Fight a bunch of fights then fight 2 overpowered guys. If you do it well you fight then unlock guys. That is it. No character endings, no unique thing that can make Arcade feel unique, nothing that makes the experience stand out. Well... that isn't entirely true... There are little missions you can complete mid-fights to get more meter in the battle and character dialog... which is actually well done. However, it still feels a little underwhelming.
Story Mode is just a better Arcade Mode. It's arcade mode with a dynamic pathway to choose from with multiple endings, cutscenes in between fights, and nice character dialog(which is also in Arcade mode but the whole team talks at once instead of one guy talks to another, making dialog a lot better). It's pretty good but good luck finding all the endings without an online guide. It is no "play this team and get this team". It's more "play this team at this time, then win or lose then choose that branch" type of thing.
I'd give this game a 9/10. Almost perfect. Definitely highly recommend this title. It may not be as fun at first because of the lacking single player and unaccessible controls, but damn it's really fun when you "git gud".

Spacebase DF9 is a space management simulator where a small pod of astronauts set out to create a new space colony. You have to manage oxygen, food, jobs and the happiness of your intergalactic residents. As you progress, you will need to continue expanding to make space for new residents. The game had the potential to become an enjoyable simulator, but fell short in so many ways.
PROS:
The graphics are decent.
The sound is fitting for the game.
Most of the astronauts are not human, they are alien, making for more interesting looking characters.
CONS:
The game is very repetitive. After only an hour of gameplay, all the messages are the same, all your residents are saying the same things, everyone behaves the same etc. The game is severely lacking in variety.
The A.I. is brutally stupid. Your colony can die because your mechanic is to depressed to fix the oxygen generators, killing everyone.
There is quite a limited amount of things to build. Once you build each type of room, all you can do is keep making the same things as more astronauts arrive. No matter what, the gameplay is boring after the first hour or so.
There is a lot of waiting, even when you speed things up.
When you encounter problems, there is a fixed solution to deal with them. It gets even more boring and repetitive when you are forced to do the same steps continuously as the game progresses.
It all comes down to is repetitiveness and a loss of interest. The game could be so much better if there were more scenarios and problems and multiple unique strategies to use. Unfortunately, this game is not worth the price when there are so many better alternatives available.

An expensive (if interesting) experiment with a mostly nonexistant difficulty curve.
The ideas SDN presents are interesting, paricularly the suppression/routing system (even if it feels somewhat temprimental: Weapons like the IG18 field gun (available from the start) pins entire infantry squads and light vehicles instantly and can halt entire advances while strafing runs from planes don't even slow them down), and the front lines system (the game determines in a somewhat unforgiving manor who controls certain areas of the map and awards points based on that).
However, it presents every idea it has at once, even if you've played Wargame before this you will need to spend a long time learning what every "Division" (Another concept new to this game, partly different to wargames "decks") does and how to use it in the seperate phases (New concept) in order to effectively pin enemies (New concept, sort of) move the battle lines (New concept) and win the game (Old concept).
Additionally, the active playerbase is small, meaning that if you do eventaully figure out how to play properly you will find youself waiting long times to play matches against people that have either never played before or have been playing since release.
So if you've willing to re-learn large portions of your RTSing knowladge and don't find the "WW2 stratagy game" concept saturated then this will interest you, but you really do have to be willing to learn what every division does, how to control battle lines effectively and how to work with the pinning system.
I'm not knocking the people that enjoy this - If you do, that's great, and I can see why you might, but despite an interest in the second world war and a general enjoyment of most of Eugen's games, I simply lost interest in this title because there were far too many experimental concepts that probably could have made an interesting game on their own. The end result is complicated, expensive and lacks the inter-faction depth that Wargame had that made it enjoyable to play.
Call me old fashioned, but honestly I'd prefer a "Wargame: Normandy" rather than the £35 maelstrom of experimental ideas that is Steel Division: Normandy 44.

If you read my tiny review of Breath of Death VII, not much has changed in Zeboyd's sophomore offering Cthulu Saves the World. In fact, the systems in play are identical to what we saw in BoDVII, save for a few minor tweaks.
What really changes this time around is the characters and the plot. The cast of Cthulu Saves the World is much more entertaining and the plot more interesting, than the sort of meandering nothingness we saw in Breath of Death. Cthulu is your typical "Oh no, but I'm actually evil" comedic anti-hero out to restore himself to his maximum evil potential after having his powers stripped away from him by a mysterious figure. In order to destroy the world, he's going to have to save it.

This game is... surprisingly very good. It's a steal at such a low price!
I didn't expect much from what seemed like a budgetware rpg title, no matter how infamous the titular name was. But believe it or not, there's some real meat and potatoes to this rpg. Essentially, Cthulu is trying to be a hero to undo a spell cast upon him. Due to the curse's weakening effect that is preventing him from destroying the world, he must redeem himself as a hero to get the chance to be his old self again. He soon meets up with other allies, such as a groupie of all things concerning the ocean, a talking sword, and so on.
The story is surprisingly funny and well written. There's not an over extending amount of dialogue, but enough to get the point across and there's some very amusing chatter by Cthulu (who plays a pompous windbag of an elder god if there ever was one) interacting with his party. The towns are all named after Lovecraft locations and there's numerous references throughout the game that will appeal to fans of his work.
Combat is decently tough. Each round, the enemy does more and more damage, while you can build combos and similarly thrash them. Either way, you must win fights quickly. Cthulu and his party recover after battles quickly, but they can't take a lot of punishment during. Fortunately, you have a fairly wide array of chosen abilities, including the ability to make your enemy insane, so he fights poorly against you. I enjoyed the strategy needed to win some random encounters, although you can certainly just blow through some of them. It can get grindy at times, but it won't be the sort of thing that requires you to spend hours simply leveling up.
There's higher priced RPGs out there on Steam that might look fancier and come from bigger names, but they've got nothing on Cthulu!

Hello this review is more focused on a Wargame to Steel Division Perspective, such as whats new, whats changed etc.
Disclaimer: Whilst Steel Division is a good game in many respects such as its dogfighting being incredibly exhilirating there are many gripes I have with the game. You may enjoy it, I wish i enjoyed it more.
Steel Division: Normandy 44 is as you guessed set in WW2. Its setting is pretty much as you guessed, the advent of Dday, or aka Operation: Overlord the invasion of Occupied France. For the most part this game is very well executed with detailed graphics, detailed models of units, wide selection of units, tactical depth and air superiority dynamics. But there are things that..bug me.
First of all the sound and music. They are outirght mediocre. Artillery has little to no "impact" that you would expect from shells, and none of that terrifying "train flying overhead" feel to the shells traversing the map. Gun sounds arent punchy zoomed in or out, and the overall saturation of sound is either too little or too much. the Music as well is not at all themed correctly. it feels far too modern for its setting and perhaps should of opted for a more Medal of Honor style of soundtrack (perhaps without the budget). I Muted the music and fortunately modded the sounds to accomodate for both discrepancies.
Now to gameplay. Things have changed considerably. With the addition of a "Hunt" mode which is its way of saying "attack move" without coming off too unrealistic. And also a "Unload at position" which allows you to set a position where your troops will disembark immediately without any further orders. What they have removed is the Unit company's. Means all tanks, transports, infantry are seperate units now. which means you need to micro a LOT more.
Also it should be stated, unarmed transports dissappear straight after disembarking. Probably what I think is the worst thing to remove is the Company orders panel, where you can group sets of up to four units of the same type to link up as one big unit. Sadly, Supply units by default dont reinforce squads you will have to mod that in. However the removal of sector control and making it an attrition based line in the sand game mode has made it interesting in one way yet annoying in another. It feels linear whilst offering new challenges. It essentially allows for more of a frontline mechanic meaning players must opt in a lot more units into the fray which is good and bad.
Why is it bad? Well players dont have as much choice to what they want to do now. You can tell very easily by the type of units available and their ranges and so on. The whole game is now set on you being more aggressive. Artillery ranges are reduced very considerably. For example an Ordnance 25-Pounder realistically can reach 12km with a Supercharged HE round in real life and possibly at least 6km without supercharged. In game its max range is 2.4km. a gross underestimation of the gun. Similar stories happen with other arty pieces in game. I say this because in Wargame long range shell artillery can reach 11km to 22km with ease. Why not translate it back into WW2 arty ranges? because they want you to play hard and fight. Some jokes are ok but story is lacking and consists of going to the next town and then repeat. While on towns, NPC dialog is almost inexistant. After the first three party members everyone else joins because why not?
The combat system is atrocious: groups of ten enemies spawn and you have to spam All-damage abilities to damage all these enemies at a time. Eventually you can hit attack all the time and, most of the time, it works. And this goes on and on for almost every dungeon battle except for the final boss. Some times there is a tank enemy but that's all. It is a pity because these leaves lots of skill as useless: the game forces you to use the most powerfull skill for hitting one enemy and the most powerfull for hitting all enemies while fighting regular monsters.
Enemies will ALWAYS attack first because of their higher agility and you will end up attacking after them. Combat is so unbalanced that after every battle you get a refill of your health points! It would have been more sensible to make it work so the player did have to pay attention to his health points while on a dungeon. Instead of it, you only have to pay atention to it while on combat.
Enemy sprites are totally random: crabs, starfishes and then ¿goblins? on the beach where you begin. Suddenly it all makes sense: there are literally tons of enemies, very few of them having to do with Lovecraft. ¿Unicorns? ¿Centaurs? ¿Zombie cheerleaders? ¿DINOSAURS? They are there to add numbers, and they soon become indistinct.
Every dungeon size is massive. And dungeon layout is random: every dungeon is a labyrinth with very plain decoration, and exploring is oftenly not rewarded, so you go to a dead end and... go back. User Interface is not very practical: when a character dies, all character "windows" get red, instead of only the one who actually died. Also it gets green while on medium health. Equipment menu forces you to go again for equipping a second item.
Both endings (good and bad) are mixed into, one making no sense even if you read the developer comments. Sadly, I finished this game and I don't even have an achievement to brag about it.

Legend of Grimrock was my very first RPG of its kind: grid-based, first person oldschool-type. Challenging and relentless, Grimrock kept me on my toes specially in the later dungeons when trolls and fire elementals (I forgot their actual name) started appearing. Love this game.  Spent years, nay decades waiting for another EotB type game.  The early M&M games were good, but this totally fits.

Legend of Grimrock is a certain game of twenty years ago, dressed in modern clothes. The recipe for this turned out to be surprisingly simple - leave completely untouched form the core of the game, using new technology only where it is necessary.
Legend of Grimrock has almost no plot. Yes, somewhere in the background, we have a story of four convicts who were thrown into perdition to inhabited by monsters and traps bristling labyrinth of dungeons. Throughout accompany us also to be found in various places notes made ​​by a man named Tooruma, who wandered through the corridors and halls before us. At each level during sleep appear "visions" with a few sentences. And that's basically all the elements of the story.
Interestingly, it was one of the first elements so characteristic of the classic games of this type. At a time when the "stimulus feature films" are limited to a minimum, begins to work the imagination. With scraps of information, in an atmosphere of understatement, alone, almost automatically, we are trying to fill these gaps with our own conjectures. It builds sometimes much more evocative atmosphere than most told, "film" story.
The gameplay is based on three pillars: exploration, solving puzzles and fighting.
We move through the corridors and rooms in a classic style. Levels are divided into square segments. One press of the button allows traffic to pass a single field or a reversal in the direction of 90º.
By far the biggest asset Legend of Grimrock are puzzles. At each of the thirteen levels we will get at least a few of them. Sometimes, their accumulation can be intimidating. All puzzles rely on the use of several of the same components. We have a mandatory collapse, levers, plates react to the pressure, the buttons in the walls, or portals. An absolute masterpiece of ingenuity is their use.
Although there are not too many types of enemies, they are diverse and properly assigned, so only at the end of the game started to be missing "something new". I like the fact that most of them require the use of appropriate tactics. Additionally, this old-fashioned and a bit clunky combat system perfectly conceals imperfections SI, which knows only two tactics: to follow and the encirclement. Moreover, developers have used these qualities even several times in riddles.
I must commend graphic design, but here also I have a few objections. It's basically the only "modern" element of Legend of Grimrock but it is used quite well. Textures, dynamic lighting, models of opponents and their animations look great.
Legend of Grimrock is a damn successful - I would say that close to perfection - back to the already-forgotten genre. Thought even the most hardcore enthusiasts oldschool and implemented the option to disable the automatic drawing of the map. For players remember the "good old days" and exchanging hand-trended on a piece of checkered maps, is a wonderful gift.

Ok,so as a veeeeery long KoF fan (been playing since the days of old at the local taco stores,to laundromats, to arcades,etc.) I can safely say that this game it's at best better than KoF XII, but unfortunately it does show some shortcomings
PROS:
-Nice graphics (a jump from sprites to almost handdrawn characters seem very nice)
-Inclussion of DLC characters such as Mr.Karate, N.E.S.T.S Kyo and Classic Iori
-Great compatibility with many machines (trust me, you can play this game on a potato without a hitch)
-Single Player Storyline mode
CONS:
-Veeery steep learning curve with this one, and it's a King of Fighters game
-Lackluster at best character selection
-Poor online netcoding (despite the game telling you that both players have a good connection, the lag during gameplay may tell you otherwise)
-Expect to get bodied if you don't train or play regularly
-Do not and I repeat DO NOT play this game with a keyboard or a controller, this game series as a whole were born to be played with Joystick, should  you use a controller, expect to get frustrated by playing as a jumping bean, and don't get me started with playing on a keyboard
Conclussion:
Competitively I can recommend this game, mainly on the basis of the game mechanics, which,despite being a little bit overcomplicated, it's still very satisfying to execute great combos. However, keep in mind that this game is a relatively old game, if you want to play this casually online, either expect long wait times, or players far away from you with high ping. Though to be fair, if you want to play for the story mode, do it. I mean, it's not the best presentation of it (most done through text boxes kind of like BlazBlue) but still a very great storyline nonetheless if you are into King of Fighters story (which, if you haven't checked it out, it's pretty epic and easy to follow). At this point in time, I can recommend it for now, but only to fans of the series, new players? You can still get this one, but I'd rather go for King of Fighters XIV

I'm not a huge fan of the yes/no system. Can this game be fun? Yes. Will it be frustrating? YES. Would you be missing out if you never played it? Probably not.
There's something enjoyable about this game and getting to use force powers in an excessive way. I enjoyed it on my Wii and I'm enjoying it now.
However, this game is not a very well made game. Level design is not good, enemies are either too easy or stunlock you until you die, checkpoints are not close enough together and you will ALWAYS be fighting the camera. I probably wouldn't play this without a USB gamepad. The controls are not tight at all and it's hard to get your character to do what you want him to do. You will fall off of edges a lot because the platforming is terrible. There are QTEs at the end of boss fights.
Personally, this game feels like it has a spectacle-fighter sort of vibe. Except, it lacks almost everything that makes a spectacle fighter good. If done correctly, this game could have been amazing.
The graphics are pretty good (aside from the cutscenes). But honestly, nothing dates this game more than its terrible control and camera issues.
Overall, I think the game is fun, despite its shortcomings. I would probably only get this game at a heavily discounted price though. This is a bargin-bin game (which is where I bought my Wii version). It is good fun for that kind of game. But I find myself setting the game down at least once every 30 minutes because of how frustrating it can be. Unlike something like Dark Souls, this game controls so sloppily that you do not blame yourself, you blame this poorly made game.

The side missions did nothing for the story and were just a couple bonus fights that took very little time to complete with the exception of the temple mission which as i mentioned there was a more extensive version included in the regular force unleashed i bought years prior to playing the sith edition. lost hilt customization entirely but there is crystal customization. Boss fights were done pretty well,though sadly lost a few in this version for the main story. This did however feature several various types of storm troopers i did not see in the regular. The game is adequate at best in my opinion and for every gain with this i feel there the loss of something as well.

Roller Coaster Tycoon: Deluxe is an isometric tycoon game where you manage your own them park. Not just one, but each of the game's 70+ scenario is a different park. The scenarios get broken into four different categories: original, loopy landscapes, corkscrew follies, real life parks and extra parks. There is no fast forward button, so you're stuck going at the same pace. A game year would be an hour of real life time and several scenarios go between 3 - 4 hours. Each scenario has success conditions like have X amount of people in your park by year 3 with a rating of over 600. Others are more complex like double the park value without taking out a loan. Then after the time expires, you can keep playing if you'd like. There is around 210+ hours of game in these scenarios.
As the manager of the theme park, you can plop down rides. From there, you can paint them, change their music and entrances. Even change different options on each one like how many times does a Ferris wheel go around? You'll build walkways to get to places and lanes to get to ride entrances. Without lanes no one will stand in line. The longer the lanes, the longer people need to wait in line. You can even raise and lower terrain, add water all at a price.
The joy here is designing your own tracks. Roller coasters, go carts, flumes, slides and every other type of track. The game comes with premade tracks, but you can design your own as you go. Couture them to your land, have them dive into tunnels, over walkways. Heck design them to launch the trains off the track to kill people. This is your game, you do what you want. Just don't expect anyone to ever ride a crashed roller coaster again. You can even take away bridges to drown your patrons.
Building the tracks is fun, there are a lot of roller coasters to chose from. Standing steel, sitting steel, inverted steel, wooden, twisting steel, diving coasters that can drop at 90 degree angles, hanging steel and far too many others to list. Different rides have different needs. Some need to be a smoother ride with less sharp turns. Others like the wild mouse roller coaster need sharp turns everywhere. The only down side is you make it as you go. There is no way to construct your perfect coaster, then add it into the game like you can with Roller Coaster Tycoon 2. You can still save any track design to your premade tracks to use at a different time.
Each ride has stats broken into three categories, excitement, intensity and nausea. Every patron has their own stats. If they're looking for something calm, intense or exciting. If your ride is 18 loops back to back with an excitement stat of 23, but an intensity level of 23, don't expect many riders. If rides are too gentle, like kid slides and bumper cars, you'll hear about it. You need to pace things, blend gentle rides next to thrill rides. The more nauseating the ride, the more people will throw up unless you have enough benches outside the ride exit for them to sit down on.
If someone throws up, you'll need to hire handymen to clean it up. They'll also water gardens, mow grass, empty trash cans and so on. You can even set the land they cover. When your rides break down, you will need mechanics not just to fix them, but inspect them. This ensures rides run with less down time and no one randomly dies due to brakes cutting out and one trains smashes into another. There are security guards for when patrons get too angry. Costumed characters can get hired to keep people happy while they're waiting in line.
Decorations also boost patron enjoyment. Plant flowers near walkways, statues near lines, plants and trees next to rides. Its all up to you. Decorations next to a ride will slightly increase its excitement value. For the most part, designing a ride track under, over and next to either itself or a different ride will boost its excitement level. With enough effort, you can make a merry go round into an exciting ride, but its easier to make anything else in the park exciting.
There is a thought view of everyone in the park, so you can determine what the people want. Are they hungry? Thirsty? Sick? Do they need to 'go?' Well then build food stalls, drink stalls, benches and bathrooms. There are a lot of different stalls and you can set the price on everything in the park including setting all your drink stalls to charge the same price. Not just that, but there are plenty of merchandise stalls full of things for your patrons to buy when they're happy enough.
So how do you get different stalls, rides, coasters and decorations? You devote X amount of dollars each month to ride development. Minimum, medium, maximum or no funding at all. This will be how quickly you'll unlock something for the park you're managing. There are even check boxes for what you want to research. Gentle rides, thrill rides, roller coasters, shops & stalls, scenery and ride improvements. Ride improvements are simple things like putting a wooden roller coaster train backward.
The game is very flexible when it comes to finances. Each scenario will usually start you off with a hefty bank loan that has minimal interest. You can get a bank loan up to a certain amount, depending on the scenario. Having money always lets you keep playing and growing. If you outgrow your park, then just buy land tile by tile. Its a little tedious, but whatever. Sometimes you need to buy rights to have your coasters go over roads, because you can't buy the land itself. While you can charge money for each ride, you can also make them all free with a park entry fee. Some scenarios force you to do certain things financially. The restrictions, coupled with the different parks make it interesting. Instead of just having the perfect park over and over again.
On top of that, there is promotion for your park. Pay X amount for park or ride marketing for X number of weeks. Free ride vouchers, free food, half price entry for the park and so on. Its all to draw people in when you need it. Without patrons you can't make money, but all you really need are fresh rides. Old rides start breaking down more often. People visit them less in favor of newer rides. No one wants to spend $4 to ride your 3 year old roller coaster and so on.
The patrons themselves seem pretty dumb. They'll walk in circles, so I've found straight lines are the best way to get them around the park. In one of the expansions of the deluxe version, there is a no entrance sign that you can post. People can't enter, but they can come out. Its helpful, especially for scenarios that start you in a park that has dozens of paths. Patrons get lost and start destroying things.
I've owned Roller Coaster Tycoon for 15+ years. Its one of the first PC games that I bought with my own money after playing the 3 scenario demo. Not just that, but then I proceeded to buy all the expansion packs. I've completed the game on 5 different computers. I am big into management and tycoon games and I think this is one of the best if not the best.
Even though a lot of people enjoy Roller Coaster Tycoon 2 more for its much larger parks, I still like the original better. I still feel its the best management game, but I can understand that the game can play itself at some point. You can walk away for two hours and come back with the scenario completed. Unless of course a roller coaster explodes or something. Its a relaxing low stress game, even if you're put in charge of a place that people could die... and you can kill them.

Factorio works like this,
You start the game, nothing but the basic mining machine and tech to work with. You start harvesting with your machine and begin building a base, research your first tech upgrade and begin to build a bigger base.
Its about 5 hours in you realize you've been building all wrong and have to start again.
Once you start again, you plan your base better and things begin to run smooth. From here you automate using research technology and grow your base more..
Your third play through, you think you mastered the layouts, how to build proper automation lines, your oil fields look like something from an oil enthusiasts dream. You've built yourself a tank and hunt down aliens for more research packs. But you run into another problem.. your base? It wasn't big enough. Your automation? Not nearly vast enough. Your Mining and Oil Empire? Sorry, ruin.
You're 15 hours in, its time to start one last time.
Your fourth playthrough, you have more mines then the world combined. Your power generation could reliably run the West Coast forever without interruption. You're trains run smoother then the Japanese trains could dream. The chinese envy your assembly lines. Screaming  "YOU WANNA LIVE FOREVER" as you drive your tank over those damn bugs. There is nothing that can stop your rocket lauch now.
And there isn't, once the you've grown your base and are defended the only thing to do is wait.
and wait some more.
While I really like this game, and I came in thinking it wasn't going to be this addicting. But it is, it really is. You always see things and ways you could have built your base. You tear down and rebuild so many times, and if you like base building and effiency in design then you are going to love this.
I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys playing Civilization or Simcity, but because you have time on your hands and arn't looking for immediate results. Probably best played while also doing something else, maybe watching some TV, or playing with a pet?
Also, some good things to note.
1) Iron is key, you are going to need lots. And when you think you have enough, more.
2) Do not neglect your power generation when expanding your base. Its easy to forget.
3) Red / Green wires are very difficult(I found), but if you were a red wire wizard in Minecraft you should do fine.
4) Aliens are punks. You're going to need bullets.. lots and LOTS of bullets. Even when you go attacking, bring LOTS.
5) It takes a while to get it working, but logistics and constructions robots can be a huge asset.
I aimed for a large base, central to all the resources I need and then transport belted them to my main base. Trains are a great way to move large cargo quickly. Build some walls, get yourself turrets either fed by belt, or logistics robots and secure your base. Past that build some pretty assebly lines and get cracking!

In this game you apply very basic principles to build very complex structures. You will have to use problem solving skills and logic to build an automated factory that you will be improving as you learn more and more about the game. If you like other management games like for example Cities: Skylines then you will definitely fall in love with this game. There are a lot of mods that enhance the possibilities of the game even further.
Although Factorio still carries the Early-Access tag the game very polished already and is totally worth your money even if the developers would quit their jobs tomorrow. They do release patches on a weekly basis, sometimes even biweekly and make improvements to the games aesthetics and gameplay while taking the feedback of the playerbase into consideration. The community is very friendly and active with a recommendable subreddit for those who wish to learn from the experience of others. Just trying and working things out for yourself is also fun on it's own. There is no need to watch or read excessive tutorials to finish the game because even a non-efficient factory will eventually get you into the end game.
Talking about end game I have to talk about a negative point (for some!) aswell. The game doesn't have a solid victory state as of now. Technically starting a rocket is the main goal but that can be achieved without really dipping into the complexity that you can get from the games mechanics. If you have no problem with sandbox gameplay and can motivate yourself to try and make your factory better and better then you won't have any problem with it at all.
Factorio is also fantastic as a multiplayer game and I would definitely recommend playing it with a few friends. Don't be turned off if you don't have anyone to play with though as the game is very fun in singleplayer too.

With 53.2 hours under my belt, I have enough hours in the field to give a review which reflects this game's quality.
As a huge fan of the Close Combat series, I was greatly anticipating the release of this game back in May. I was not to be disappointed. The game is outstanding. I am a great advocate for historical realsim in RTS's and Steel Division's reliance on actual aerial photography to depict it's wide range of maps is a great relief.
The AI is almost too difficult at times but no one plays an RTS hoping for an easy time right? I wooped with joy the first time I beat the AI on hard difficulty (yes, there is a very hard setting too). You really have to earn your stars in this game.
The 18 divisions based off iconic divisions of the Normandy campaign are beautifully modelled and are well balanced, A player can have at their disposal air, land and sea (in the form of offshore artillery) at their disposal. The battles are hugely entertaining given their large scope and watching your units battle highly intelligent AI is a joy to watch and command!
Mod support will ensure this game has a long life. The audio mods are particulary impressive and really enhance the atmosphere on top of what is already a very good audio system.
Of course, you can also do battle in multiplayer with as many as 10vs10 battling it out very large maps (map size depends on how many players are involved).
There is a Campaign (12 missions divided between Germany, Britian and America) which is beautifully done with a great emphasis on voice acting and stock footage cut scenes to give the game a historic edge. Skirmish mode is also highly entertaining and where I have so far practised alone to compete with those in multiplayer,

If you enjoyed the Wargame series that Eugen Systems has developed, a fan of WWII history (especially Operation Overlord) or a fan of real-time tactics games, you owe it to yourself to try out this game.
Pros:
Excellently modelled units and divisions: the game is not merely focused on Americans, British, and Germans, but also incorporates Canadians, Polish, and French divisions - as well as the colonial / allied units that appeared for both axis and allies (i.e. Spanish "Nueve" serving in French 2nd Armored or Italian "volunteer" units serving with  716 Eichenlaub)
3 phases of battle means that games don't just necessarily devolve into tank spam fests
Morale system means you don't necessarily need to kill units to be able to weaken offensive pushes; artillery is more useful
Focus on "front warfare" means no more cheesy "Command unit sniping"
Air combat is not as lethal as Wargame series, and there is an increased importance of combined arms with AA units
Infantry become very useful on offense as well as defense thanks to new LOS mechanics
Cons:
Single player campaign is merely a string of missions (yes, unit preservation is still important, but it's nowhere nearly as good as Airland Battle's campaign)
Bit of a learning curve, especially for new players trying to understand the scouting and line of sight mechanics

I am I HUGE fan of dungeon crawler games one of my favourites being Wizards and Warriors on the old Windows 98 PC and I’ve had no luck finding anything as good not till I started playing Legend of Grimrock.
I first saw this game when I was browsing a friend’s steam account and decided to give it a go and was super impressed by it.
Let’s get right into the review though now shall we, I’m going to brake this up into three parts: A brief description of the game, it pros and it cons and then a final verdict.
Description:
Legend of Grimrock is a grid based, first person role playing, dungeon crawler (try saying that ten times fast) that has you taking the role of four prisoners who are thrown into a mountain in order to earn their pardons for their crime.
Pros:
* This is an easy game to pick up and play using only a few sets of keys to move your characters, open maps and inventories and so on.
* Creating your characters is easy as well. Choosing from one of three classes and four races the game even lets you add in your own custom character portraits and gives It a lot more depth also making it feel a little like a Dungeons and Dragons game.

* Maps are well spread out with all types of hidden goodies and short cuts for you to find and if you finish the main game and have this on steam you can download more story modes and maps to explore on and even import characters from other games to use on your team.
* Combat is rather easy to get the hang of and the multiple skills your characters can learn do make it much easier. For example if you have no throwing weapons for your rogue and don’t want to switch position of your characters during combat you can make him learn a skill that lets him attack from the back row.
Cons:
* My only really nit-pick I have on the games combat is the magic system making you memorise runes and picking the right ones in order to cast spells. All though there are some easy to remember spells, its having to click on each rune in order to cast it that can be a real battle killer and sometimes braking the flow of game play.
Verdict:
Other than my one complaint with the game it’s still one of the best dungeon crawlers to date and is worth picking up for both beginners and hard-core fans of this type of game, throw in the fact that you can download more maps from the steam workshop, gives this game loads of replay value. I give this game 9.5 out of 10.

There was really no correlation between base level and defense systems and the difficulty of any enemies. Seriously, you know no effort has been put into balance when you have 2 entirely unrelated raider boarding parties entering your base when you're barely 10 minutes into the game.

In conclusion, I think this game is a bit of a lost cause. It had potential, but it was thwarted by bugs, balance, and lazy devs. It's a shame, really. I recommend taking a look at Prison Architect if you still want a game similar to this, but far more in depth and absolutely worth the price.

The good is all there: great audio and visuals, pleasant to look at and getting one pumped, the fantastic feeling of most weapons and satisfaction brought by the mayhem. Creative and dynamic levels that are stimulating by asking the player to adjust on the fly, similarly creative bosses that switch things around quite fast. So, how can I not recommend this game?
Because it is plagued with the most atrocious design flaws it possibly could've been, that is why. If you want a tl;dr, I will say this: easily the most frustrating game I played in a long time, seemingly dedicated to obsessive masochistic OCD perfectionists. Deeper explanation below.
The battery/revive system is interesting, but my god why did the idea of weapon dropping to null power whenever you die make it to the campaign is beyond me. In all the score-focused modes, yes, keep that in. But the campaign is the whole different story, there are many bottleneck places in the levels where if you die (and they are hard moments) you are ♥♥♥♥ed. Because now you need to somehow clean up this hard part with severely diminished firepower, which leads to more deaths. On top of the fact that lowered firepower makes it quite hard to catch up with killing, which is needed to refill the damned battery. This becomes even most absurd in the boss fights which are, for the most part, quite tight timing-wise, on top of being extremely stingy with orbs that you can actually pick up. And no picking up == no weapon powering up.
An additional problem with the bosses is that the battery refills usually spawn right at the point where they stood when the phase of the fight ended, so usually right behind the boss. Retrieving these is often paramount to suicide, and since batteries disappear in time... yeah, enjoy.
The health bar could almost not be there, really. The game has an unhealthy obsession with one-hit deaths (and we already established how much going down hurts) and will throw them at the player all the time. This is coupled very annoyingly with how ridiculous the terrain can get; while enemies generally provide visual feedback to when they will strike, the terrain can be very subtle with when it wants to kill you, leading to many frustrating deaths. Also, bonus points here for the terrain spewing enemies out with no warning right onto your face. Especially when some of them blow up. Instant death if you didn't restart the map X times to finally understand what and when happens.
But there is one thing that adds an insult to the injury and it is the nonexistent post-hit invincibility. Doesn't matter that your character has several hit points, if there is a cluster of bullets coming at you, failing to dodge it will just outright kill you. A favourite thing on the bosses, they weave real rich patterns of bullets, one wrong step and you are dead. The second boss is the most sadistic here, requiring strong weaponry to deal with an absurd amount of adds that she summons while being deviously adept at killing the player right when her third phase triggers. The swarm of little flies will just ram into you and drain your health in a second or two.
All of the stuff presented above wouldn't be as fun as it is without yet another thing that just makes me shake my head in disbelief. And it is a catastrophic lack of visual clarity. The game is flashy and visually noisy like a glittery Twilight vampire, and it can lead to easy demise. When I said the health bar could almost not be there, I neglected to mention some humanitarian enemies that actually shoot stray bullets. Which, for reasons unknown to me, are smaller than every other bullet, including yours. It is possible to get randomly hit with something just because amidst all of these explosions and spray of your own weapon, something will hit you. And pray it is not a rocket. You see, some enemies shoot a rocket into the sky, and it will fall down on a designated location. And instakill you. Would be fair, it is delayed, there is a targeting reticle indicating where that will happen. So why for the love of god it is the least flashy, most dimmed and blurred thing in the entire game? On some arenas, it is more subtle than the actual environmental lighting. Just astounding, really.
As an added complaint, the devs didn't bother to design stages in a way that makes sure each of them is reasonably doable with each and every of the long list of characters offered to the players. Sure, if you grind for long enough, you will become the god of Cactus and master every character in every stage, but this is exactly the overarching problem with this game.
It is not considerate of anybody but mad perfectionists who will time the sparse invincibility frames down to a millisecond, and learn how to get through each level without dying once. People who won't be deterred by hundreds of re-tries of boss fights. In a great many cases, the game demands such an obnoxious level of perfection just to get through the damned stage without cursing all of the creation while hammering the revive button (absolutely pointless that you need to do that, btw, and just fuels the anger) that it is simply not worth the nerves. I am going to beat this, as of writing this review I am nearly done, but I won't lie: enjoyment was rare, frustration and annoyance ruled.

The life system works off of small shield and disabling your character if you take too much damage. You're really battling the clock because your android runs out of life the longer you are playing each level. Take too long between battery recharge pickups and it's game over. It's good to see the options for unlockables WITHIN THE GAME and not as DLC, which gives this arcade-y title an old school feel.
Now, the final boss. Waaaaaay too hard. The second phase removes battery pick-ups and it's INCREDIBLY challenging to deal enough damage to survive without your battery running out. My go-to for bosses was often Coral because of high shotgun damage. Even with her, I was one second or less away from dying when I beat the last boss/phase. This is not counting the dozen or so times I came within 3-4 blocks of winning and ran out of battery due to the way the final boss phase is designed. Introducing a fractional recharge from enemies would have been useful (aka, as long as you are fighting and not disabled, you will be able to survive to the end. Hey, Hey you... Yes you, the person who's about to thumbs down my review. Did you notice that I actually LIKE the game? Just because I didn't recommend the game didn't mean I didn't enjoy it.
This game fell right between the lines of "recommend" and "not recommend" and that's a sign to me that most people probably would rather play something else. You're welcome to disagree with me, but at least comment to tell me why.

Ever want to blast people with "UNLIMITED POWER"? Like the idea of picking up stormtroopers and throwing them into the abyss? Have you ever wanted to try mixing lightsaber moves with various force techniques?
...Then this... ....
... ...be the game for you?


you play as Starkiller, Darth Vaders Secret apprentice. Star killers been put into a twisting story of nearly constant betrayal, being a spy and agent for Lord Vader tends to have that effect on you.
Starkiller's soul purpose is to hunt down the enemies of the empire and bring them to justice, Starkiller learns various force and lightsaber techniques to assist him in his hunt. The story takes place after the clone wars, but before the first Death Star is fully constructed.
You can play through the story in maybe 6-12 hours, depending on how much extra collecting you do and difficulty you play on. The game also does the cheap fork-story-ending, so you need to go back and make your choice over again, if you want to see both endings.

This is where the game hurts... sometimes literally.
this game was designed to be played with a controller, but even with a controller the game is a mess, the camera is tricky, targeting is terrible, you need to spend a majority of the first few levels learning simply how to pick up the correct object (since it's linked to which way Starkiller is facing, INSTEAD OF MY CAMERA. Sheesh)
To be quite blunt and fair, the controls of this game are a very good reason for people to steer clear and spend their money on a game they might actually enjoy playing. However this game did have great potential, and brought a lot of great concepts, but it definitely needed more work before it was released.
To talk really briefly about the various attacks, you have force lightning, force push, lightsaber attack, and block. There are various combinations of these four to make up your combat type in the game. The game seems to prefer you supplement your lightsaber strikes with force moves, instead of going full blown Master Yoda mode.
There is one final thing to say about the Game Play... Screw Quick Time events. They don't NEED to be bad, but they are in this game. You'll also have them memorized; it gets repetitious fast.

There were achievements on the Xbox version, there might be achievements some time but as of now there are none (03/19/15). We should probably count ourselves lucky. However, the accomplishments, unlockables and extra's are still in the game so you still can obtain them, if you so desire.

I purchased The Force Unleashed: Ultimate Sith Edition from a humble bundle, so naturally I suggest waiting for sales before purchasing. The standard price for The Force Unleashed on steam is $19.99. Not a fair price, in my opinion. I will be squeezing out more hours of the game doing the extra content.

I don't know that I can really recommend this game for anyone who ISN'T already a star wars fan, if you knew nothing of the franchise, or just simply didn't care one way or another, this game is a skip for you.
If you happen to consider yourself the avid Star Wars nerd/fan you'll probably be able to overlook the games follies and enjoy watching/playing/listening to the story of Starkiller.

I don't often write reviews, but out of all the games in my library this one has kept me entertained the longest so I will write a review for it.
As a foreword I would like to praise the development team for this game. They very thoroughly playtest and bugfix before releasing their updates. This may be the most stable game I've ever played. Even an update's beta branch before it is officially released has fewer bugs in it than many 1.0 releases.
That said this game really deserves all the positive reviews it gets. Although there is combat in it, this game isn't very action-y. If you are an action gamer and tend to only enjoy fast-paced games, then this may not be the game for you. Factorio is very self paced. There are aliens to fight, but they expand fairly slowly and won't be much of an issue if you move slowly yourself. However, if you build up your factory very quickly the aliens will become aggressive because pollution will start to build up and the aliens, like hippies, hate pollution.
So what's the point of the game?
Well, there are really 2 main goals and many small ones. The game is centered around the mass production of various objects. Each time you automate production of a given item it is a milestone that gets you closer to your first major goal of launching a rocket, which takes many different raw materials being processed into intermediate items before finally being combined into rocket parts which are used to build the rocket. The first time you manage to launch a rocket it is a graduation of sorts. You are no longer a newbie and you move onto the next main goal, optimization.
Launching a rocket would more-or-less be the end of the game except that you can ALWAYS build bigger, faster, more efficient factories. There are a handful of "research" items you can sink all of your extra resources into. Some of them grant bonuses to mining raw materials or damage bonuses for your weapons and these go on forever, but become more expensive after each one is researched. This encourages you to build larger and more efficient factories to supply ever increasing quantities of items. Therein lies the beauty of Factorio's late game. If you played and enjoyed the game up until launching the rocket, you'll probably have a few ideas on how you could have done better and after implementing them, you'll take a step back and just take in everything that you've built. I recently had over 15,000 circuits being produced every minute and just watching all the moving parts that going into doing something like that is amazing, but know that it was YOU who built it is immensely gratifying.
If you enjoy games where you build things you should give this game a try. Especially if you want a building game that challenges you.

----Update----
Whilst I do still enjoy the game, I have found a growing disatisfaction with some elements of the "Mega Brutal" difficulty level(I've completed much of the game at this setting beating down on a pathogen or senerio until biohazards are maxed). Whilst various combinations can be found which offer a high chance of success, the almost "blind luck" of infection to a handful of nortorious nations does offer little in terms of skill. The "luck" element of fan favourites, such as New Zealand, Madagascar and Greenland, for example, seems to have the same intrinsic failure of 4x games (where the AI doesn't actually get smarter but rather gets to push resource boundries--volume over substance or in this context luck over skill).
There should be a random element to this game--any infection stream would be in the real world. However, the degree of such seems skewed at the higher difficulty levels, so much so, that the tactics used are far less important than the "blind luck" of a "red" boat or a plane.
The game is still enjoyable and I still recommend it. However, the "luck factor" is over emphasised on higher difficulty levels and seems to be quite unrealistic.
Suggestions to afford greater realisation in terms of infection routes to nations:
Birds fly. Many birds fly very long distances. Many of the island nations are well within the flight range of various species of birds. Why then, using Madagascar as an example, do birds not traverse the waterway to the island? Why, in terms of the various animal and water transmission streams is there no infection route for say "sea life". I would expect that Greenland would be far more readily infectable if there was an animal transmission via sea life/seafood (a significant staple of many arctic nations). etc etc.

Absolutely gorgeous. All the art is done is stunning detail in the futuristic sci-fi city of Cloud Bank. As for the enemies easily identifiable but with enough color variation to make sure you can react appropriately to them in a combat situation.

Quite simple at first but turns into an absolutely complex blast that let’s the players imagine exactly how they want to play the game. As an explanation, you’ll have one weapon ,the Transistor, but many different abilities to play around with starting with something as simple as slamming your Transistor into an enemy and then eventually making your Transistor a black hole generator that can obliterate a dozen enemies at a time. The game also takes these abilities and gives the player full control of customizing in the form of passive abilities for your primary skills that you use in combat ,say turning a death beam into a splitting death beam that goes in 3 directions and can bounce off enemies. As well as passive abilities for just the character such as being able to pull objects from farther away and having more health. Overall, this gives the player tons of freedom in combat playstyle.

Again, simple at first with running around in a locked arena, dodging your enemies, and using your abilities but quite early on the game introduces the unique mechanic of “turns”, which is basically pausing the game and deciding precisely which moves and abilities you want to use and then executing it in a speedy fashion allowing the player to do some absolutely ridiculous damage combos. However, the drawback of using a turn is that you can’t use any abilities (without special enhancements) until your turn has fully recharged so it’s important that you leave enough space between you and the enemies to make sure you don’t lose a ton of health when your turn is up. A simple but super fun mechanic that makes you feel like a god when you dodge a ton of projectiles then proceed to turn around and annihilate everyone.

Possibly Transistor’s strongest selling point this soundtrack is so simple and mesmerizing but also fits the mood of the game perfectly for when you’re taking in more information on the lore of the world or for when you’re fighting and take a “turn” and you hear the soothing voice of Red as you plan your next action.

Serious Sam 2 feels like a console game from the late 90s. Complete with all the absurd amounts of color and giant blocky polygons. This is not worth the playthrough.

In about half the levels, beheaded kamikaze are replaced with fat, giggling clowns on unicycles holding exploding cakes. That about tells you all you need to know.
Serious Sam wasn't ever serious, but this one is absolutely stuffed to the gills with zany. There's a lot of awkward, miss-the-mark humour in it. The old bestiary have been remade as silly cartoons, although bizzarely some of the new additions are unimaginative humanoids, and some of them commit the sin of having hitscan weapons, making them priority targets despite being lowly minions.
You still mow things down with a minigun, then do it some more, then finally maybe it'll let your index finger uncurl for some dancing-with-kleer and a double shotgun. Except both at the same time. While popping off some rockets at a giant spider in the distance, and sniping a helicopter sweeping across the fray. The offhand grenades are an excellent addition for adding a little extra firepower and rewarding you for herding enemies into clumps.
You still can't rocket-jump without taking your legs off below the knee, but you can still run at 30MPH on your last hitpoint, desperately dancing and weaving through laser blasts toward a health pickup. Cover is something you blow up to deny it to the enemy. It's still Serious Sam, and it's not got the vast expanses of the first, but it's still big. And twice as long as you might think at first. A lot of stuff happens, and it's not lacking in variety of scenery and experience. Even the turret and vehicle sections are welcome shake-ups to what otherwise might be twenty hours of the minigun spinning.
And it's nice to have Sam moving *towards* MENTAL for once, not sideways, or backwards into prequels. For all its screwed-up tone, and some lousy and unfun early-level design (what were they THINKING with the single shotgun?), by the finale it's one adrenaline build-up after another.

Apart from that it's more or less the same as the first games, but it isn't in HD. If you liked the colour and silliness in the first games, you'll like this. If you're looking for a more serious game, try Sam 3 BFE instead. Chronologically Sam2 is the latest in the series, so you won't spoil anything by jumping straight to 3. You've heard of a "book you can't put down"?  Well this is a game you can't put down.  It's resource and assembly line management with a little train sim tossed in for added joy.  The controls are fantastic and really remove the barrier so many builder games have that restricts your creativity with a clunky UI.  Everything I wished I could do in Minecraft (build epic automated rail system and have things construct themselves) you can do here.  Oh, and copy and paste via "blue prints".  That concept alone makes it worth my money, then having builder bots launch off your customizable modular armor and go place all the pieces for you is icing on the cake.
The game is just fantastically balanced with a good evolution of tech that always gives you something to aim for, and something new to learn how to use.  You start off digging coal and stone by hand to build a furnace so it can further refine ore for you, and by the end I have networks of solar powered electric miners in half a dozen outposts loading ore onto trains via conveyer belts and bringing them back to my refinery base to get processed in bulk... all while managing power production and consumption so your laser turrets don't power down while being attacked by creatures aggravated by the pollution you are creating.
I haven't loved a game this much in a long time.  Go check out the demo to scratch the surface, but I got a good 70 hours of gameplay in the paid game  out of my first freeplay base alone.

Legend Of Grimrock is one of my favorite games released over the last couple of years, and hands-down the best from an indie developer. People call it "the game that revived the dungeon-crawling genre", and this couldn't be more accurate in my case.
I grew up playing Lands Of Lore: The Throne Of Chaos. A similar, two dimensional, tile-sliding real time fantasy rpg. Nothing could top it, and Grimrock brought me something I had always hoped for: a modern re-imagining of this style of game.
Having played through the regular game twice, and trying out a number of the great user-created content packs, this game has almost everything I'd want. A great variety of gameplay challenges and obstacles, gorgeous graphics, captivating atmosphere and story, tons of danger. Plenty of challenge is present, as well as an easy means of scaling difficulty to one's personal preference. Additionally, the custom dungeon workshop has provided an easy way for creative fans to build using the game's engine very easily and intuitively. There are some mods that even top the core game itself!
While I recognize that Grimrock's appeal is somewhat niche, those who aren't addicted to first-person games, have patience for difficult combat, and enjoy the challenge of a dungeon delve with many survival elements like light sources, food management, and mapping your environment will undoubtedly find this interesting, if not fantastic. The only criticism I can think of is wishing for character voicing and enlarging the world/taking the game outside of a subterranean environment at least some of the time.
Thankfully, Grimrock 2 is being released in...ten minutes as of writing this, and promises to do the latter.
This game is a modern classic and will always be on the tip of my tongue. It's a thrilling and refreshing experience in the world of modern gaming. I challenge you to take your first step...

This is one of the worst console ports I've ever played.
First of all, let's talk about the controls - they're terrible.  I'm sure that on an xbox or playstation controller, this game plays well.  But when you take the layout of a console controller and try to match it on a keyboard, the end result is sloppy, clunky, and poorly-designed.  Even when I remapped much of the interface, the controls still didn't feel intuitive and some of the combos in the game simply cannot be performed given the keyboard layout.  This was subject to much frustration during my playthrough.
Now let's talk about the sound.  The score itself is fantastic and there's no complaints there.  However, this is only valid WHEN the sound chooses to work.  For the first half of the game, everything appeared to go well.  But for the later half, there'd be levels where the music wouldn't be playing, or the sound effects wouldn't play, or nothing at all would play (except the sound of my character running).  Maybe this is to signify that my character has gone deaf, because the world could be blowing up around me, but I won't hear a bit of it.  Likewise, the sound itself doesn't seem "rich" at all.  It almost sounds like the game was optimized to play through a single channel, versus surround sound (think mono vs. stereo).  Even playing with headphones, the sound appeared bland and non-immersive.  And good luck trying to fix that given the audio controls in the game....they don't work.
And finally, let's talk about the game itself.  I know that on the console versions, you have the ability to lock onto an opponent.  The same can be done in the PC version, but due to poorly-mapped controls (see above) trying to fight a boss who's calling in multiple minions at once becomes a complete and absolute mess if you're trying to target a single character.  But that's nothing compared to the single most inexcusable moment of the game (SPOILERS BELOW)
Near the end of the game, you're tasked with pulling a star destroyer out of the sky.  That alone, should be the single-coolest moment of the game.  What you get instead is a broken, frustrating, and utterly terrible experience.  You are tasked with manipulating the star destroyer's angle using the keyboard and mouse while you pull it in.  As you do so though, you have to fight waves of TIE fighters.  Destroy the TIEs quickly, then pull the star destroyer.  Unfortunately, the mouse movements are so slow that you barely move the star destroyer at all before another wave of TIEs roar in.  It gets to a point where you can no longer move the star destroyer at all!  You just keep fighting wave after wave of TIEs!  On the console, where the controls are more fluid, this problem is avoided.  But on the PC, you are left to suffer.  The only way to even get past this point is to move the mouse VERY slowly in the direction necessary.  Do so, and that should be sufficient to finally get the star destroyer down.  However, this is a problem that never should have existed in the first place.
In summation, save your money, don't get the PC version of this game, and get it on either xbox or playstation.  The game itself is fun (when it works) and I'm sure it's a blast on the consoles.  But on the PC, it's a load of garbage.  And if you have no other option and are forced to endure this game on the PC, save yourself some hassle and at least get a USB xbox controller to use.  It'll make your life a little easier.

As someone who has played all the Wargame games, this game was not entirely what I expected. However, this is not necessarily a bad thing.
The Good
-Great UI.
-Very good WWII feel to it, includes many historic tanks and such.
-The maps are very good, with many strategical points to hold, the gameplay is always exciting.
-The cover system is much better than the previous games, allowing tactics to play much more of a role than simply overpowering your enemy.
-The frontline system is really clever and allows you to estimate where you are losing the battle and quickly reinforce.
-The battles feel very tense and managing to get your infantry to overrun the enemy is a very rewarding feeling. Also the surrendering while units are pinned down is a really cool feature requiring all new tactics not seen in the previous games.
-The difference in strengths and weaknesses of divisions truly plays to their roles. Some divisions are great early game and have a ton of light tanks and such to overpower your opponent early on. Some are more balanced, while others are focused on late game and relying on help in the beginning. This diversity really makes the fights feel different every time.
The Meh
-Not entirely sure how I feel about the stage system. I cant tell if I like it or not but it is definitely something that changes the dynamics of battles.
-The unit orders are not all there from previous Wargame games, but I cant expect all of those in a different game. However the auto cover command is very useful for not having to worry about that every time you move a unit.
The Bad
-WHY DO TROOP TRANSPORTS DESPAWN AFTER DROPPING TROOPS OFF, I WANT TO USE THEM AGAIN!!!
-While I get the pen chance is realistic, I find it rediculous that a wolverine with 16 AP can pen my King Tiger from 1.2km from the front. RNG is not kind to me.
-Multiplayer or the lack thereof. The servers are almost always empty and when you do manage to find a match half the people just quit. There needs to be some sort of penalty for quitting mid match. Servers rubber band unless you have really good connection. Definitely felt that the previous Wargame Games had much better matchmaking.
-Controlling and managing a larger group of units, god forbid from different directions
, is impossible unless you use the time slowdown feature. This does make it much easier but lowers the realism factor for me.
Conclusion
I really like the game and despite some minor bad points, will remain on my PC for a while. It has a similar, but not the same feel as the other Wargame games and will likely be welcome to you if you have played them.

I recommend this game, but only if it's the type of game that you'd enjoy. It's about putting details under scrutiny and detecting discrepancies, which are often well hidden and satisfying to catch (especially when nobody has tried the same trick yet). It's also about testing your morals, and being willing to interrupt your reputation as the greatest bureaucratic inspection machine to let or not let people into the country based on other factors. Many people may live and die because of your actions, including your own relatives and people that you let into the country. Can you afford to keep them alive?
Throughout the experience, you gain more familiarity with your job as a border inspector. Complex patterns of inspection arise in the player's nature as the game gets tougher, and more types of documents are thrown at you. Organizing your desk becomes one of the games challenges, too. It can be tedious, but it's varied and satisfied enough that it can be played with the intention of having a lot of fun.
There are elements of the game that show how well planned the game is. Patterns of more people coming from specifc countries on certain days can be detected. The game will intentionally train you with a "random" person that you must deny. Dull colors, faces that blend in with one another, repetitive intro music, the sound of cars moving by the checkpoint, and gunshots without any music playing compliment the themes.
From playing the game almost blindly, I'm pretty sure that this game takes place in a communistic country in Europe during the year 1982 an alternate history where the Soviets were more successful. Too much of the game's plot is easy to spoil, and talking about anything in the game after the first two in-game days could be considered a spoiler.
Final verdict:
Try Papers, Please if it looks interesting to you. Don't try it if it doesn't.

For those of us not quite old enough to have enjoyed the Cold War, Papers Please gives us the chance to make the tough choices available to a border employee.  Do you follow all the rules of glorious Arstotzka or do you accept bribes to prevent your family from starving?

Warmly recommanded! A casual yet fun subpar open-world RPG. Especially good if you do not have tens of hours to spent diving into the land of Tamriel.
Pros:
+ You can fly on a giant eagle given to you by a waterfall!
+ You can also ride pterosaurs. I mean, do you have to read more?
+ You fight giant carnosauts with a crossbow and a sword. Still not convinced?
+ Fireball spell is actually a firethrower
+ Runs on low-config old machines
+ No game-breaking bugs
+ All the boring parts of an open-world RPG have been ripped off the game
+ Skill progression is rather entertaining
+ Nice landscapes
+ Beautiful music
+ Ennemies attacks are nicely animated (especially the Raptors)
+ Easy grinding
+ Most voices are convincing
+ You can be everything at once (mage, warrior, thief)
Cons:
- No depth in universe and in story
- Very limited loot
- Maps are empty
- No proper dungeons
- Lack of challenge
- Ennemies are all of equal strength more or less
- It is NOT Oblivion or Divinity II or Two Worlds or Risen or Gothic. Nothing of that kind here.
Verdict: A casual, low ambition game, yet seriously fun. Short and fast-paced. And dinosaurs! And flight!
Long version: This game is hard to judge. In every aspect, it tries to remind to you of Oblivion, especially in the first city, where the music is almost the same. And yet it is highly delusional. This game is a CASUAL open-world RPG. Seems paradoxical? Sure it is! A few examples: All merchants buy everything you have to sell at the same price. Lack of immersion, for sure, but it's fast and efficient. Houses are closed if there is no quest inside. People have no name if they do not have something to sell or some quest to give. Maps are quite simplistic, with no caves, no dungeons, only a few wandering ennemies that you can kill at will. They happen to respawn near instantly, but as they are very passive, it is only a massive grindfest.
So, this game is subpar in every aspects. Everything is simplistic; but everything works as it supposed to do. Some landscapes are really nice and charming (the Terraces, for instance), music is nice and epic, fighting system is good, skills are a constant fun to improve, etc. If you can explore the different regions in any order, the game is quite linear in the sense that you have nothing to do in the so-called regions except a meagre handful of straightforward quests.
This game provides a chep yet solid fun, which will content every one who like to hunt Raptors in the swamps with a magical sword and the sound of drums humming in the air.

I want to first point out that this could be a good game but their are problems, many problems.
Firstly - I have never played any of the Wargames but was a massive fan of R.U.S.E which initially made me attracted to this game as some of the developers worked on R.U.S.E.
The game has three small campaigns which can be somewhat challenging and a basic tutorial with missions. The game is quite easy to learn and from my Wargame friends they have also said its easier to learn then that. The main focus of this game is planning your battle-group, you can choose between allies or Axis with different divisions to choose from. Their are phases between A - B - C and you have a limited amount of slots per each category i.e Infantry - Support ect.
Depending on skirmish with the A.I or VS with real players, a typical game puts you in a historical focused map that is based off real photographs from WW2 with either an all out annihilation mode or a map focused border control, the more territory you have your troops in / remove the enemies the more you win territory and this can shift - Your allies will be on one side, the enemies on the other and the battle begins in phase A. Any units you had selected from the battle-group from phase "A" will be available, after time then it will be phase "B" and then later "C". Depending on what you selected from the Battle-Groups - units will have a cost and you will initially start with resources to use throughout the game and this will accumulate every min or so with more points to purchase new units.
The problem I have with this game is the balance and the servers. Support units are very OP and can annihilate entire regiments of infantry within seconds. Planes are almost immune to everything inc. AA and their just seems to be an inbalance with the AXIS being much more superior then the allies. Games can be as large as 10v10 and within the beta the servers were fine and ran smooth however after release its completely buggy and feels as if its on an entire different server, a recent patch has included dedicated servers however I have not tested it as of yet.
Lastly is the player count - unlike Wargame or R.U.S.E for that matter it doesn't seem like this game sold very well, as an Aussie during my time the player count hardly hovers over 400 people and if I do get a match its usually with someone from Russia. The patches honestly seem to be released way too late and feels like it isn't getting the support that it clearly needs.
In my honest opinion under its layer of issues it is a great game - but its just not worth its asking price, even if its less then usual games.

As an ardent Lovecraft and RPG fan, I whole-heartedly recommend this game.
If you're familiar with Breath of Death VII, then you already know what this game is like. If you're not, read on...
CSTW is a light-hearted homage to both the classic JRPG's of yesteryear as well as H.P. Lovecrafts work. In this game, you play as Cthulu, cosmic horror supreme, who undergoes a bit of a dilemma: rather than destroying the world, Cthulu is tasked with saving it (hence the name.) Along the way, Cthulu encounters many different characters and locales, many of which are pulled straight from Lovecraft's stories. Some help and join you, while most just want to fight.
As for the core gameplay, it's traditional turn-based RPG fare. You choose your options, watch everything unfold, and go for it again. There are plenty of characters to mix and match for your active party, all of which obtain their own unique skills and abilites. The level-up system from BoDVII is back, giving players a choice in how they want to build their characters upon gaining a level. Simple, but it adds a nice sense of strategy. The good ol' "stand next to a save point and grind out all of the battles in an area until they're gone" strategy is still the best way to break the game, so that's nice.
Overall, the game is fun and quirky. It's not very deep, and especially with the Diablo III's and Skyrim's and WoW's out today, CSTW might seem a little too simple. But RPG's started somewhere and this game does a fine job at looking back lovingly.
If you're a fan of either classic RPG's or Lovecraft, this is a solid buy.
