A greatly simplified action 'RPG'. You level up, increase stat points, not really any special skills. If you don't need shiny graphics, this game delivers some interesting and diversely themed locations to fight various monsters in: jungle with dinosaurs, snowy mountains with trolls, forest with goblins, deer & boars, plains with bears, caves with elves, tropical area with crabs and flying (i guess dinosaurs?). Combat is simple, you can block and attack with melee, or shoot with a bow. You can also equip a rune to 'shoot' elemental damage. There are both first and third person views available.
I really enjoyed this game for it's simplicity. Nothing new I had to learn, no lore I had to cram my head full of in order to understand what was going on. No complex combat systems or complex item/equipment stat balances that required hours of deliberation to max my stats. (Each unique area: this gear sucks, this gear also sucks, this gear is good, this gear is the best) It was just an adventure with real time combat. Yes the graphics are very sub-par but I didn't need that, it was still fun to explorer all the unique environments. I played this almost exclusively for nearly a week until I beat it. (about 10hrs to finish) It was just so easy & simple to get into after work when I didn't have hours to invest in a deep, involved, time consuming RPG. Totally worth it on sale at 80% or 90% off.

This game has a wonderful atmosphere and a very unique take on turn-based combat. It's very difficult to describe, because I've played anything quite like it.
The mood of the game reminds me a bit of Gun Grave, and the premise is similar. You're in this cyberpunk environment, heavy on the noir vibe the genere sometimes has. You're out to get revenge on the people who ruined your life. You travel through the world, slowly learning about it as you meet and take out those who conspired against you.
The main character is mute, so the majority of the dialogue comes from the consciousness within your sword. The voice gives you comfort and counsel. Through this method of storytelling, you get a great feel for what the person trapped in the sword meant to the main character. The person in the sword also names all the enemies as they show up, giving them names like "Jerk" and "Creep." It gives the game a unique personality.
The gameplay is also unique, so much so that I find it much harder to explain than the story and atmosphere. As said earlier, it's turn-based...sort of. Once your energy is charged up, you can pause the game and plan out your moves. Your character will then perform those moves, and you will then have to dodge attacks until your energy recharges. It's a little bit like the VATS system in Fallout, in that regard, but that comparison doesn't quite do it justice.
If you don't mind the kind of story where you slowly learn the details, piece by piece, you'll probably love this story. I certainly did.

Certainly, the present indie games are founding the new genres for the future gaming reality.
Transistor is going to be one of them. It focuses heavily on art style and combat design, utilizes as much resoureces as they can to output the maximized artistic style of a game. Artifying a game.
We always know that game is a combination of art and entertainment, such a game heaviliy focusing on art makes it stand out among all other indie games. Even today, we hardly find this kind of refreshing game based off the limited resources they have had.
The combat system is well-crafted to be diversified and fun, you can combine multiple perks into one action, and that one attack action would provoke the perks' effects out. Different perks different combinations, it's very cool to see it. And the system uses a real time engage clock, which is a pause in combat that allows you to draw out a tactic route to attack enemies. Something like the tactical view of Dragon Age, but rather the real time engage clock makes it kind of turn based.
With this, we also have a niche story, even the story is kind of cliche but I really appreciate the voice acting of the characters in this game. The man in the sword's voice is just too good to be true. Story itself is interesting not yet engaging enough. But for the love of the arts in this game, you might as well appreciate that rather than the plot.
Overall, 7/10.

Spacebase DF-9 is a survival game in the wide-reaching void of, you guessed it, space. Your mission is work with a trio of astronauts and build the most sophisticated, comprehensive and long-lasting space station anyone has ever seen. That sounds amazing on paper, and being developed from the veterans over at Double Fine Productions, you’d almost be assured a great game. However, the product falls short and development has long since died for this title, leaving an ugly mess in its wake. In space, nobody can hear you complain.
The game opens up with an interesting concept at first – a map laid out with all the locations in the galaxy, letting you pick where you want to start and factoring in variables like meteor showers, derelict ships, traffic for earning more crew members [good and bad] and resources. Once your base is selected, you’re launched into space with three crew members, a space pod for power and oddly, no spaceship; the game starts you out in the dead of space with limited oxygen, limited supplies and a very short time span before your whole crew perishes from asphyxiation. From a logical standpoint, the start of the game makes absolutely no sense and it only gets worse from there.
You must quickly build a functioning center with enough life support for your crew. You’ll gather material from nearby asteroids that oddly resemble play-doh, which you will ingeniously craft into oxygen recyclers and stations for power with nothing but a blowtorch and your wits. As the base grows, you’re able to expand, making different rooms that can be retrofitted into housing, laboratories, pubs, infirmaries and more.
I like the aspect of building a base to my own liking, but Double Fine really chokes the life out of personalizing it as you see fit: limited items to use, each room can only use furniture from one list of items [I.E. only residential furniture in a residence] which forces you to build a lot of unnecessary rooms for no reason at all. However, my biggest complaint is being in space and not being able to build along the Z axis; you can only build outward, not vertically, which seems like a huge oversight since you’re not hindered by the laws of gravity.
As you continue playing, you’ll encounter hazards that you must overcome, such as illness, resource management [marginally], machine repairs, raiders [space pirates] and meteor showers. Most obstacles aren’t all that exciting: meteor showers are not impressive and barely noticeable if the game didn’t tell you it was happening, space pirates have terrible AI capabilities and can easily be killed with a few well-placed defense turrets and most ailments can be cured by simply sending them to the doctor, curing them nearly instantly. Oddly, some of the ailments have auto-cures, such as when I was afflicted with “Space Blindness”, which I was promptly told there was already a cure so I didn’t have to do anything.
The real gem to this travesty is the writing, or the lack of a proper writer. Here’s an example of the type of “communications” you’ll received while in space:
I felt secondhand embarrassment just reading it. The writing is dreadful, out of place and just downright terrible. Couple that with other gems like my dead astronaut having a “kinda happy” job satisfaction while simultaneously being dead, but the real winner is that her location is “space”:
Yes, everything in this game has "space" attached to it. Your location, beds are called "space beds" and even rugs are called "space rugs" because your typical Ikea rug is not suitable for the vacuum of space apparently.
I could go on and on with all the issues with this game, but in the end it has been abandoned completely by Double Fine and is left at the hands of 3rd party modders if they feel like investing their time in such a project. Much like my crew member Nashira Corrino, this game is dead, asphyxiated by its own mediocrity.


Overall, Spacebase DF-9 is an absolute mess with broken AI, poor graphics, terrible UI and even worse sound effects. There is literally no reason for you to play this unless you’re punishing yourself and even less reason to buy it unless you’re sending it to someone in hopes of terminating a friendship.

Legend of Grimrock employs a great deal of forward thinking to what seems to be a long-forgotten genre of RPGs.  The first-person tile-based dungeon crawl has recently been dominated by Japanese developers, mostly ATLUS, and while great games in their own right, they lack the feeling that the early Wizardy and Might & Magic games had.  Every single bit of Grimrock feels deliberate; crisp visuals give way to crisp sound, providing a surprising depth of ambiance and atmosphere.  Indeed, each room and item has a purpose for it's placement, adding to the immersion.
Grimrock's combat moves to a beat - each monster moves at a certain pace, and moving with it is the key to surviving.  The brings a certain amount of tension to each fight, and moving around the environment has its own unique challenges.  Twitchy fingers are practically a requirement on Hard but this is common in dungeon crawls, and after a small amount of time movements between attacks become second-nature.  Magic in Grimrock is fairly straightforward - a board of 9 runes comprise each spell in the game, and combinations are explained in scrolls found throughout the dungeon.  This is probably the biggest misstep Grimrock makes.  It's very easy to progress down a skilltree in a specific element of magic, only to find one or two scrolls relating to the element.  It's a frustrating feeling, and makes the player feel like knowledge of the exact location of each spell is required.
As good as the combat is, the heart of Grimrock is exploration and puzzle solving, something that is (thankfully) executed flawlessly.  Constant observation of your environment is a must especially in the later levels where it's required for progression.  It's tough to explain the puzzle system without giving too much away - but each level of the prison brings new challenges and secrets.
Legend of Grimrock is the breath of life into a genre nowadays only found on handhelds, and aside from a few hiccups,  presents a polished experience that indie RPGs should aspire.

A fun open-world combining the gameplay of GTA, the combo-based fist fights of Mortal Kombat (with a dash of Arkham City), and classic cover-based shooting

8/10. Open world sandbox rather similar to other open world sandboxes but set in Hong Kong with a surprisingly gripping story and a hand to hand combat ‘Arkham’ system where you can’t just hammer the counter button.
Sleeping Dogs. Not quite as popular as Saints Row or Grand Theft Auto, but what can you expect when you steal basically all of your gameplay from them, and your CQC combat from Arkham like every OTHER game? What do you bring Sleeping Dogs?
“The ability to doorslam someone’s head in, throw someone onto a swordfish to impale them, and drop an engine block on them.”
♥♥♥♥ING SOLD!
Like other sandboxes you can drive or walk around the map. Driving is smooth with some nice handbrake drift possibilities. Running around introduces a light parkour mechanic where you push a button to vault smoothly over objects, or smash into them and climb over afterwards with a hint of shame.
No flying is present in Sleeping Dogs, but there sure are a metric ton of boats. Unlike other sandboxes though, you don’t really have guns at your disposal. This isn’t America, this is Hong Kong, which means less gun crime. Which means the main style of combat is hand to hand ‘Arkham’ based combat. Light attacks, heavy attacks, grapple, and counters, along with some melee weapon attacks. What’s more interesting is the obvious real life martial arts connection, making combos seem like something out of a Bruce Lee/Jackie Chan film (which the game does heavily parody in one set piece). It’s very fluid and fun to bash someone’s head in with a lovely 5 hit heavy combo.
Also, the spam counter mechanic is gone. If you mash the counter button when no one is attacking, Wei Shen will just look around like a lost puppy before some goon charges up a heavy attack and bashes your skull in, so props for making us have to press a button with timing now.
The main draw of Sleeping Dogs is in the environmental grapples. You can slam your opponents against walls, smash their heads on tables, you name it. There are also special grapples where an object is highlighted red. Drag someone into these and you can do a powerful and stylish one hit move which usually involves mortally wounding the other fighter in some horrible way. These balance out by only being a one time use per fight, so you can’t just environmental grapple your way to victory.
There are also different enemy types. There’s the usual guys, then the guys who block all normal attacks, then the guys who can’t be grappled, some guys who carry weapons, and some guys who counter. A lovely little bit of variety to keep you on your toes.
When you aren’t fighting hand to hand, you sometimes get a gun. Gun combat is weird with a controller, but it has an auto lock on which helps, but you’ll still miss half your shots. You can also do slow motion bullet time moments by aiming while vaulting over cover for example. This is extremely fun to do and will be the main way of killing everyone in a room.
There are also 3 types of experience points. Triad (basically being a stylish killer), Cop (driving safe and avoiding innocent casualties), and Face (your overall rep). Each of these unlocks a respective upgrade in that skill tree. For example, upgrading your Cop experience will make you be able to find guns in cop cars or steal cars without setting off an alarm. Annoyingly though, Triad experience for some reason is so hard to get near the end game that you might have to replay a few missions to get full Triad exp. There’s also other side stuff, like small cop jobs, karaoke, street races, fight clubs, and more.
You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop who infiltrates the Hong Kong triads. Hilariously, the police force send you in almost right after their other undercover cop was found out, tortured for sport, and buried alive. A brilliant way to set-up what will happen to you if you get found out.
The story isn’t what I expected. It’s surprisingly gripping; emotional and full of little side bits that flesh out the world and I invite you to actually read the reports you receive. I also like how the game really actually cares about building a realistic world. For example, people speak both English and Cantonese which are the most popular languages in Hong Kong. Also, everytime you pass someone trying to sell you something, they yell out to you to attract your attention. It’s quite believable in a night market setting, where some guy trying to see you a pork bun judges your masculinity on sight to entice you.
You do certain actions (like how many thugs you can punch to death, or how much money can I get at once from the parking meters) and a little box pops up and shows you how good you are versus your other friends who have also done the same task. Interesting, but pointless. I would very much like to drive around Hong Kong with a friend. Looking at you, Sleeping Dogs 2.
The game is rather pretty and depicts Hong Kong nicely. Even on Low and Medium, the game still looks nice. I wish the blood was a little more visceral. When I curb stomp some guy’s head, I expect a puddle of blood on the footpath, not a tiny spray like a bleeding nose.
I beat the game twice, once a year ago where I barely paid attention, and once this week where I completed the whole game 100% including all the side mission stuff. It’s addicting really when you’re collecting stuff and filling out a checklist. But once everything’s done, there’s not much else unless you want to screw about in the sandbox, but without multiplayer, it kind of falls flat.
Going through and finishing each individual collectable line will reward you with extra vehicles, extra powers, more health, etc with the final reward being a small box that rewards the 100% achievement. Kind of an anti-climax, but it’s more about the journey.
It took me 35 hours to beat the story the first time through, doing a little bit of the side stuff. It took me 52 hours to, from the start of the game again, completely 100% the game including achievements and all the DLC side story stuff.
All in all, that 87 hours I sunk into this game in case you couldn’t read my hours played nimwit.
I’d wait for the eventual sale.
Just like any sandbox open world game, the cracks in the design do start to show, but usually in a humorous way. Once I saw a man who was stuck in a couch in a karaoke bar. I sung him a few songs then left and came back, only to see him out of the couch and looking at me with a perplexed expression. Only one crash and that was when I set off several car explosions at once, so the game is stable.
All original DLC’s are already added. These include extra missions, costumes, vehicles and side stories. The side story DLC’s (Nightmare at North Point and Year of the Snake) are both short end-game fun that will take about 2 hours each to complete 100%.
Quick pros
+ Fun open world game which takes the best bits from others that preceded it
+ Hand to hand combat is nice and fluid
+ World is immersive and story is engaging
Quick cons
- Weird voice acting at times
- Repetitive mission structure
- Getting stuck outside in the water without a boat is a painful experience
Sleeping Dogs isn’t exactly a clone but it’s not exactly original. However, it still provides a fun sandbox experience for any who decide to pick it up.

This is a difficult game to recommend for everyone, but it certainly has its audience, so let me start by saying:
Ravensword: Shadowlands is a game for you if you:
On the other hand, if you are purist of the genre or have very high expectations, I would not recommend this game to you. You'll only get frustrated, or bored. And life is too short to be either.
Ravensword: Shadowlands is a simple game, with simple aspirations. The world is built with thick, not too careful brush strokes, and the story follows the same pattern. Still, it works, and that's as much as you can ask of it. The gameplay is kind of barebones for an RPG, with a small skill tree where most branches aren't really needed. Also, you'll find places where difficulty spikes are big, seemingly to encourage longer playtimes.
However, there are interesting ideas in the package. And the game is pretty optimized for a casual audience. The quests aren't overly long and can be easily followed, inventory management is reduced to a minimal expression (only weight can give you some problems from time to time) and the world is attractive enough to keep you engaged for the relatively modest amount of hours you need to dedicate to the game.
I am recommending the game based on the premise at the beginning, and also because, for me, it filled a very simple place in my library: a simple distraction from more complicated games. Sometimes, that's exactly what's needed.

This game is a lot of fun for somebody who is focused, strategic, and patient. It also helps to be a little bit of a completionist.
Plague Inc: Evolved is the PC version of the popular app game Plague Inc. The game was sponsored by the movie "Dawn of the Planet of the Apes" when it came out, as shown by the number of references and achievements related to the movie. The goal of Plague Inc: Evolved is to infect and then kill the entire world with your disease as fast as possible before the humans develop a cure. Sounds easy, right? Unfortunately, it gets to be much more complicated than you may think.
There are many different forms of disease that you can choose from. I will give a brief explanation of each.
Bacteria: Incredibly easy to use once you know how to play the game. On your first try on Normal setting, it may seem difficult to use since you don't know what you're doing. But trust me, it's really easy and kills people really fast. There's even an achievement for winning with the Bacteria in under 365 days. If you don't know, that is a REALLY SHORT time in this game.
Virus: Somewhat difficult. It's special ability is that it mutates symptoms ALL THE TIME. This may sound good. Free symptoms? Awesome! Not really, though. The more symptoms your disease has, the higher its severity is, which means humanity will notice it faster, which means they'll make a cure faster, which means you'll lose faster. Using the Virus is all about controlling when symptoms should evolve.
Fungus: Hard to use because it doesn't move very far. This is the essential principle in Plague Inc: Evolved. Your disease has to infect everyone before humanity can shut down the borders. There's a reason Greenland and Madagascar are so hated by the community: they have the polar extremes of weather and they each have only one port for the Fungus to access. Using the Fungus is all about staying hidden and having high Infectivity levels.
Parasite: Tough to stay hidden. The parasite starts with a high Severity level, meaning humanity will notice it incredibly fast. You also don't gain nearly as many DNA points (used to evolve your disease) from infecting people as you would with any other disease type. Its Special Abilities reduce its severity levels, so save up your DNA points from transmission and the abilities.
Prion: Not incredibly difficult, but not incredibly fun either. It's hard to cure in the first place, and then its special abilities make it even harder to cure, but it takes a longer time to react to any new evolutions. Again, not incredibly fun because every aspect of the disease is slow.
Nano-Virus: Considered by most to be one of the top 3 most difficult to use plagues. The Nano-Virus's story is that it is a microscopic robot that was accidentally released from a laboratory. The humans are now trying to shut it down with a kill code. What this translates to in the game is that the cure starts the second you pick a starting country. Stressful, right? Well, to compensate for this, the Nano-Virus has a higher starting Infectivity level, all of its special abilities go towards slowing down the "kill code", and all symptom costs are relatively cheap. Still very difficult to win with, though.
Bio-Weapon: For me, this is the second-most-difficult plague type (this is also a popular opinion). The Bio-Weapon starts out already lethal. As soon as it has infected 200 people, five will already be dead. And its Lethality level will continue to increase throughout the game until all hosts are dead. This is bad because you usually end up killing about 50% of the world, but the other half hasn't been infected because all the infected are dead. The Bio-Weapon's abilities reduce its lethality, it has a somewhat higher Infectivity level, and it functions better in rich countries than other plague types. Still incredibly hard to use.
Neurax Worm: Considered by almost everybody to be the most fun plague type because of it's interesting symptoms and abilities as well as the fact that it is relatively easy to master. The Neurax Worm is a worm that attaches to the brain and takes control of the host. Its ability is the Trojan Plane, which is a plane bubble that pops up for the player. The player pops the bubble and then chooses where the plane will go to infect. The Trojan Planes ignore all closed airports, making infecting countries like Greenland and Madagascar very easy. DNA points accumulate very fast with this plague type. The Neurax Worm has multiple different special forms of transmission, such as Eggs, as well as two different ways to win. The first is to go the normal route and kill everybody, but the second way involves evolving the left side of the symptom tree. This will give symptoms where the infected worship the Neurax Worm as a god. You can now win by enslaving humanity. The only downsides for the Neurax Worm are that increasing Infectivity also increases Severity and that the symptoms are more expensive than usual.
Necroa Virus: Zombies, to put it simply. Infect a bunch of people, turn them into zombies, make the zombies kill the healthy people before the zombies die. Not simple at all, but not hard enough to be one of the top 3. The Necroa Virus has lots of new transmission abilities, such as Blood and Saliva. It also gains a zombie symptom tree once the Cytopathic Reanimation symptom is evolved as well as zombie abilities on the Abilities page. There are a couple of positives about this plague type. The first is that once zombies are created, DNA points come really fast. The second is that the cure will not affect your zombies, only healthy people infected with the virus (if that makes sense XD). The third is that some abilities make infecting new countries much easier. The fourth is that it has lots of Steam achievements, making it fun to use for any completionist. The downsides are very high, though. Increasing transmission increases the chance of the virus mutating, meaning it may get noticed earlier. It's hard to win without creating zombies (Normal), as that's where most of the infection and death comes from. The cure will develop INCREDIBLY FAST! Finally, once zombies are created, humanity will create ZCom. This is a zombie-elimination task force that will set up base in healthy countries. They will rapidly kill any zombies if their fortress is not destroyed quickly.
Simian Flu: Inspired by and sponsored by the Dawn of the Planet of the Apes movie. Infect people, infect apes, make apes intelligent, kill the humans and make the apes rulers of the world. The hardest plague type to win with. Humans are testing a cure for Alzheimer's on apes, but secretly it's infecting the humans as well. The Simian Flu is very similar in format to the Necroa Virus. Once the Simian Flu becomes severe or lethal, the cure will immediately start and be developed very fast. Lots of new transmissions, ape abilities and ape symptoms, new human symptoms. You have to evolve a symptom which makes apes get the flu and become intelligent, causing them to break out of labs and spread the flu to other apes. There are not many positives to this disease. Ape abilities make them stronger and increase their combat skills. However, cure research is very fast, it does not infect very fast, drone strikes will attack ape colonies, there are only 600-something thousand apes to infect, et cetera. Make sure you've beat every other plague on normal before you try this one. Also, almost all of the Simian Flu achievements are at the very bottom of the global achievement stats on the store page. Only one achievement has been received by more than 20% of people.
Wow, this is a long review. Finally what's good about this game:
-Lots of achievements
-Lots of ways to infect/kill/evolve
-Necroa Virus
-Neurax Worm
-Multiplayer is pretty fun and pretty intense
-Gives a fairly realistic simulation of what would actually happen
Con:
Not really worth $15.

Despite the fact that I am a Cthulhu Mythos fanatic and a great enthusiast of the RPG genre (including cRPG) I have found this game bringing moderate fun only.
The story is tries to be witty and humorous but achieves this goal only a few times during the game. The jokes are usually poor, the whole concept of character knowing he is a part of game/movie/novel/etc. has been used for too many times already. Jokes in the names or descriptions of monster remind me of high school times - in this case it's not a 'pro' feature.
The characters are plain and one dimensional.
The world of the game is absurd, not necessarily in a good way. It's a mix of Cthulhu Mythos and fantasy worlds (with goblins etc.), there is a concept of insanity, but other than that the mechanics of the fight and magic is D&D-like - nothing really specific for the CoC.
The gameplay is very simple - you walk, find loot, fight in all too many random encounters (which are tiring, not bringing any fun). The dungeons are boring and involve lots of walking (probably so that there is enough time to fill the game with random encounters), There are some puzzles, but the main puzzle is to find yourself around in these mazes (thank devs for the 'run; mode).
Battles with bosses require some thinking and are interesting.
Music is decent, but too repetitive.
So why the 'thumb up'? As I've said earlier, I'm a fanatic, so if they made a Tic-tac-toe and named it 'Cthulhu Riddle' I'd probably recommend it.
Also keep in mind that this game comes in a package with 'Breath of Death VII'. From what I have senn both games are very very similar, so there is really no need to choose the lesser evil.

Bad Company 2 was mostly praise worthy due to it's timing.
The singleplayer campaign, while decent, is more-or-less forgettable aside from the fact that its seemingly self-aware characters liked to poke fun at the modern shooter genre and specifically Battlefield's nemesis Call of Duty.
What really made this title what it was was the multiplayer. Coming out the spring after Modern Warfare 2, BC2 provided a nice change of pace for those of us who were getting burnt out on Activision's latest affair. Unlockables and a levelling system provided familiar ground for the CoD fans while drivable vehicles, huge maps, and a larger emphasis on "realism" offered up new challenges and endless fun.
Revitalizing the Battlefield name in the realm of online multiplayer, there's no doubt in my mind that BC2 went on to convince EA to reboot the Medal of Honor franchise and finally release a contemporary installment in the main Battlefield series.

Do you love video games? If you don't have this game, you sure don't.
Assault Android Cactus is one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time. A phenomenal love letter to arcade shooters that's bursting with unique qualities. It's easy to pick up and play, but hard to master. This is the quality of great games. I've absolutely fallen in love with it and became addicted.
It's hard to imagine that a small handful of people have created such a beautiful, charming, polished, engaging, and just plain joyful product. If there's one game you absolutely need in your library, it's this one. Forget the AAA walking simulators, and treat yourself right. It's a steal at full price.
AAC is a twin stick shooter where you play as androids. There's a lot of characters to choose from and each one has unique weapons and shooting patterns. You'll want to play them all since they're not just for looks, but actually play completely differently. There's a play style for just about anyone, and plenty of options for breaking out of your comfort zone.
The goal is to survive to the end of each level and fight the bosses of each world. Go to town dodging enemy attacks, power up your weapon, finding batteries to keep you going, collect temporary power-ups, and shooting everything in your path. There's dozens of enemies, every level has a unique concept, and each boss has several phases and unique attacks.
All these small things will overwhelm and keep you on your toes at all times. You will die, and it will be fun. You'll actually have to gain some skill, learn some things, and improve to beat the levels.
The real challenge is getting S+ on every single level though. To do that, you must keep the chain meter going and defeat every enemy without it breaking. Incredibly challenging and you'll keep coming back again and again to try it. The game even features an option to reset the level automatically when the chain breaks.
The game is challenging, but the average player can beat it with persistence. S+ ranks will involve quite a bit of optional skill.
The game has a lot of unlockable bonuses and extras ranging from vanity to cheat like options. You'll have to play a lot to unlock them all. If you play normally and are really into the game, you won't have to grind for them. This leads to a well balanced stream of enticement while playing the game.
The game could run on a toaster, and it supports unlocked framerate, making it not only play better, but a great showcase for a high refresh rate monitor, as any decent hardware can max out its potential.
It supports local cooperative play with up to 4 players simultaneously and scales the difficulty depending how many users play.
It isn't perfect, but nothing is. There's some minor quibbles that will lead to some unfortunate or frustrating deaths. The camera can be wonky with how it frames the action, and it can be difficult to tell where missiles will land when the screen is loaded with enemies, but you'll have so much fun, that even after you die, you'll say one more time. The short and easy to easy to digest levels make it easy to keep coming back.
The game hasn't sold well, so this is definitely a game that needs more support. You can easily put in 50 hours into the game, and there's a ton of quality content in it. Grab it right now.

What a great, charming game!
Even if you aren't a fan of bullet hell games, the game still allows you to get through without too many problems.  However for the more hardcore, there is a good challenge in trying to S+ rank every level.  I haven't even had chance to play the infinite/daily game modes yet as I've been having so much fun trying to perfect the campaign!
The controls are tight, which is really needed in a twin-stick shooter.  There is an interesting dodge mechanic in that switching between your character's primary and secondary weapons renders you temporarilty invulnerable.  This works really well and encourages you to use both of your characters' weapons to the full.
The characters are varied and interesting.  There will be a lot of replayability in terms of learning the best strategies for each android, and seeing which suits you best.
The game is slightly lacking in the visual department in places, however the fast action usually distracts you from some of the shortcomings.  The stages chopping and changing around you is a really nice touch however, and keeps the arena shooting style without being bland.
I took a bit of a punt picking up AAC, but I'm glad I did!
If you enjoy twin-stick shooters, you owe it to yourself to play this game. Very solid in every aspect.

Lets start off with the basics, This is a very good game.
The idea is that you are a general of an army division. You have to select what troops to take into combat, how to deploy them and how best to use them. The resources you have are limited and the idea of a Zerg Rush simply isn't a possibility. each unit is mostly historically accurate and is organised into a realistic sized squad. As such, you need to actually think and develop strategy, not just counter-deploy weapons as in other RTS. This is the thinking mans game!
This game does a number of things very well. One mechanic I like very much is the deployment time idea. In other RTS games, when you deploy a unit it either spawns at a base and slogs to where it’s needed or just “magically” appears at your desired location- not here. Each unit comes with a transport, more often than not a truck. You have to allow time and a safe passage for that transport to get to where it is actually needed and allow your troops to get out of said truck.  This means you need to think about the front line, the reserve line, supply lines, being flanked and how you deploy your units where you think is best. It makes the game more in depth and forces you to consider may aspects when deploying troops.
Another excellent mechanic is the phase system. The battle is divided into 3 phases, separated by a timer. Phase A is typically light vehicles deployment, recon and basic infantry. Phase B often sees artillery included as well as tank destroyers and phase C is the heaviest stuff your army has. This system, whilst berated by some who don’t appreciate thoughtful games, simply stops players from just spamming panzers and romping all over the map- It stops the “whoever has the most armour wins” exploit that is so common in other games.  After all, a phase C heavy tank can be knocked out by a phase A 6lb  anti-tank gun. It also means that players must use all of their units in a successful way.
Officers play a good role here too. Instead of being some macho, uber elite bullet sponge of a unit, they are actually just as standard in fighting as your most basic infantry. What they do well however is to buff all nearby stats for resilience and accuracy for your other units. This means that units led by officers are much hardier and can hit harder than others. The officer group also tends to carry anti-tank missiles for short range, meaning that infantry are a serious threat to tanks that get close.
This game is also very mod friendly- meaning that you can adapt it as you like and the community has already created hundreds of mods to allow this game to expand.
The last word of praise for this game would be the length of battles. In some games such as DOW etc, games can last for as little as 5 minutes (usually as the space marines just roll over you or the elder spam you with banshees). Here games last upwards of an hour and the tide can often be turned by small actions that you thought were insignificant. Leaving units on the front line too long depletes their supplies of ammunition, making them less effective over time. To replenish the ammo, you need supply runners such as ammo trucks- again this harks back to the supply lines that you should have kept open if you were thinking about what you were doing.
However, this game does have some serious flaws. To me they are nothing game breaking  but they are niggles and problems non the less.
The first major flaw is that the AXIS seem to have far superior units. In all games I have played, they have been more accurate, faster moving, more resilient and generally “better” at everything. An American anti tank gun identifies a target at extreme range and takes 4 shells to knock the tank out- the Germans can one shot it.  A British rifles group is suppressed by an MG after 6 seconds, German troops can weather the storm for 20. Canadian storm troopers outnumber and attack a German house resulting in close combat- the Germans win. For some reason, the axis seem to be rather OP at time of writing and this tends to hamper online games.
Line of sight doesn’t match up. There have been instances where unit A has opened fire on unit B, but unit B won’t fire back because they have no line of sight. Last I checked, light and bullets travel in straight lines and as such, if they can see you, you can see them. I’m not sure why this happens, but it happens more often than I am comfortable with.
My final problem that I would like to see addressed is that of the AI. Put frankly, it cheats. Enemy artillery knows exactly where your artillery is parked and fires on them- even when there is no possible way that they can be seen. Your hidden troops are targeted by artillery “blind firing” or “area bombarding” with pin- point accuracy. Out of the 500m long forest, it just happens to shell the 20m that my troops are occupying. Hand that… The enemy bombers will target your officers on the way to the front, despite the fact that they are about 4km from the front line and there is no way that they could have been seen by the enemy.
In conclusion, solid game. Well polished, excellent to play. Some faults, but nothing hugely major, no matter how infuriating. I would recommend this game at full price as frankly if you’re an RTS fan, you’ll like its complexity and depth.
If you’re more of an action player, this game may still be for you, but wait until it goes on sale.

If you enjoyed Wargame, and find WW2 interesting, you will likely find this game great. If you're new or bad at RTS games, I'd take a pass. Like the Wargame series and other Paradox games, the game has a steep learning curve and many complex mechanics. It helps a lot to have a prior knowledge of equipment, but most people do not have that. As a Wargame VETERAN (1k hours), I picked up most new mechanics within about 25 minutes. I have no idea how long it would take for someone who's never played Wargame to get comfortable with this.
Pros:
Better visuals than Wargame.
Better unit pathing/movement than Wargame (you can tell units where to go in the deployment phase)
Dramatically better AI than Wargame (It actually seems to use more passive tactics and calculated pushes instead of sending 500 low tier tanks at you 2 minutes into the game)
Towed guns
Mortar Infantry
Less emphasis on air combat (Wargame had an airspam problem that was realistic but annoying)
LOS tool
Tanks are more useful for supporting infantry
Singular machine guns are actually a threat
No ATGM
No heli-spam
Murica
Interesting phase system
Reasonably balanced decks (No, I don't think the Germans have a dramatic advantage. Allies and Axis are different playstyles, just like RedVBlue in WG.)
Mod support on launch
Slower pace than Wargame
Phase system is cool
Cons:
Sometimes units are still idiots like in Wargame (moving out into the open, for example)
Infantry divisions are sometimes terrible on open maps with no towns/minimal forests
DD Shermans look stupid (Wouldn't they take off the swimming gear when they got on the beach?)
Steep learning curve
Nazis
No Hans Landa ace unit
Vehicles are sometimes too slow off-road (Open fields should allow for near-road speed, at least for tanks)
Vehicles (especially tanks) cannot move through minimal forests, creating complex fatal funnels. (You should be able to burn or blow your way through 25 feet of forest)
No Jagdtiger
In fact, not really any experimental units (Wargame had tons)
Only has the Western front (currently)
Because of the last con, there is (currently) no glorious Mosin Nagant in the game
Paradox (which means lots of micros in the future :)
No Naval (It would fit A LOT better in this than it did in Red Dragon)
Infantry feels too limited at times (You used to be able to get 5-10X more in Wargame under certain circumstances)
Tl;Dr
If you liked Wargame, buy it.
If you're new or bad, take a pass and get a more basic RTS.
It's a fantastic game otherwise

Pro's:

Con's:

Cthulhu. Saves. The World.
What's not to like?

In the same vein as brother-in-arms Breath Of Death 7, CstW lampoons old 16-bit RPG tropes in a story that has you playing the bad guy. Cthulhu awakens to bring chaos and insanity but immediately has his powers removed by some goody-two-shoes jerk. So begins a quest to regain his powers and bring ruin to those who would oppose him.
In terms of BoD7, CstW is everything that was but made bigger and better. The sensible additions BoD introduced such as limited encounters are still here, but the whole thing feels like a more complete package overall with sidequests and party construction.
The humour remains consistently funny throughout and the joke never seems to wear thin, with enemy descriptions being a highlight of awful puns and one-liners that will make you smile and groan in equal measure.
After Breath of Death VII, we go from 8-bit to 16-bit Rpg. It's twice as good and (almost) twice as long than BoD VII. At that price and with BoD VII, I don't know why you haven't bought it already !

I don't often write reviews, but out of all the games in my library this one has kept me entertained the longest so I will write a review for it.
As a foreword I would like to praise the development team for this game. They very thoroughly playtest and bugfix before releasing their updates. This may be the most stable game I've ever played. Even an update's beta branch before it is officially released has fewer bugs in it than many 1.0 releases.
That said this game really deserves all the positive reviews it gets. Although there is combat in it, this game isn't very action-y. If you are an action gamer and tend to only enjoy fast-paced games, then this may not be the game for you. Factorio is very self paced. There are aliens to fight, but they expand fairly slowly and won't be much of an issue if you move slowly yourself. However, if you build up your factory very quickly the aliens will become aggressive because pollution will start to build up and the aliens, like hippies, hate pollution.
So what's the point of the game?
Well, there are really 2 main goals and many small ones. The game is centered around the mass production of various objects. Each time you automate production of a given item it is a milestone that gets you closer to your first major goal of launching a rocket, which takes many different raw materials being processed into intermediate items before finally being combined into rocket parts which are used to build the rocket. The first time you manage to launch a rocket it is a graduation of sorts. You are no longer a newbie and you move onto the next main goal, optimization.
Launching a rocket would more-or-less be the end of the game except that you can ALWAYS build bigger, faster, more efficient factories. There are a handful of "research" items you can sink all of your extra resources into. Some of them grant bonuses to mining raw materials or damage bonuses for your weapons and these go on forever, but become more expensive after each one is researched. This encourages you to build larger and more efficient factories to supply ever increasing quantities of items. Therein lies the beauty of Factorio's late game. If you played and enjoyed the game up until launching the rocket, you'll probably have a few ideas on how you could have done better and after implementing them, you'll take a step back and just take in everything that you've built. I recently had over 15,000 circuits being produced every minute and just watching all the moving parts that going into doing something like that is amazing, but know that it was YOU who built it is immensely gratifying.
If you enjoy games where you build things you should give this game a try. Especially if you want a building game that challenges you.

Legend of Grimrock is an old-school dungeon crawling game which is inspired by games like Dungeon Master oder Eye of the Beholder.
The game tells a story of four criminals whose crimes are forgotten by getting tossed into the maw of mount Grimrock. A massive mountain which holds a huge dungeon of untold horrors. No one has ever managed to escape this atrocity. No one but, well you might guessed it, you !
You are in control of the four criminals. You can either chose a preset of four ready-to-go characters or create your own party. Once you are in the Dungeon your job is to find a way out. You can move your party from tile to tile and can only perform 90° turns to the left or right. This sounds quite simple and to many quite boring, but Legend of Grimrock does a fantastic job of keeping things fresh and interesting.
As you progress through the dungeon you have to solve puzzles which become increasingly harder and sometimes force you to think in unconventional ways. But they are never unfair and can be solved with a decent amount of thinking and experimenting. The puzzles are the highlights of the game which are quite rewarding in most cases and keep you motivated as you progress deeper into the dungeon.
The combat system is rather simple but still challenging. As already mentioned you control four characters which are always standing on the same tile. On the bottom right of the screen you got the avatars of you characters which are also used to control you characters. If you left-click on a equipped melee weapon you will perform an attack with this weapon. The twist about this system is that the upper row of your characters represent the front row on the tile you are standing. Characters in the back row cant hit targets with melee weapons / attacks (with a few exceptions). So you are forced to build a solid mix of beefy warriors / melee characters that stand in front and weaker but also very useful range characters that stand in the back and cast spells or use throwing weapons or other types of ranged attacks.
If you have a mage in your party things really become interesting. The spell-system requires you to combine several runes in order to sucessfully cast a spell. And you have to do this during the fight in real time. So things can get a bit stressful if you fight off several enemies because you still want to use your other characters. There are no shortcuts you could use. You have to memorize the runes and the combinations to put your mage to use. To some of you this might sound disappealing but if you get the hang of it, it feels really great.
Technically the developers have done a great job. Some light effects in Legend of Grimrock are really great to look at, the textures are very sharp, the animations of enemies are great and fluid.
One of the downsides of this game is that it may lack a bit of variation. There are only 3 different looks in the dungeon. Some of you might think that this it no problem because a dungeon is a dungeon but even in that particular scenario you could do more than three different types of wall textures.
All in All Legend of Grimrock is a great expierence if you like solving challenging but rewarding puzzles and if you love exploration because you get to explore a lot. There are a lot of secrets to uncover in this vast dungeon.

For a port of a mobile game it isn't all that bad. It obviously does not offer the experience you might expect from a full fledged game but it nonetheless offers an enjoyable, though short RPG adventure.
The game does surprisingly well in many departments. Each environment (though the graphics still suffer from their (former) mobile limitations) are pretty and unique. The soundtrack is surprisingly high quality and pleasant to listen to. Combat is simple but satisfying, and the game offers a generous amount of quests to complete.
There are still some aspects in which it falls flat, however. The developers attempted to add a variety of playstyles, the only practical of which seems to be melee (there are stealth and ranged options. No magic). Stealth just seems useless and your character moves painfully slow whilst sneaking. Bows do what you'd expect, though they won't give you much of an edge as your enemy soon closes in to kill you. The game is also extremely punishing in difficulty unless you manage to get very good gear early on. There are horse mounts in the game, which are not all that useful since they are quite slow and can rarely be used in most areas. Finally, there are quest markers, but they don't always point to the right location. Sometimes it will tell you to go through a door, then tell you to go back through that same door again. This makes finding the quest locations very difficult, and the quest descriptions are often too vague to be of any help. The game has it's fair share of bugs, but only one of which I experienced was game breaking (I just loaded a save from a minute ago and fixed it though).
It's a decent sized RPG game which, for a few dollars less, might be worth a buy.

Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is basically a remastered version of the original released in 2012. You play as Wei Shen, and undercover cop working for both the HKPD and for a triad to defeat them from within. You climb up the ladders as you gain XP for both cop and gang related missions. Along with this you also gain face XP which gives you a better reputation with vendors and civilians. Being and open world, there are a ton of missions other than the main story that can be completed, meaning this game has plenty of content.
The game does a good job making you feel like you're actually in Hong Kong, with busting streets, markets and sidewalks filled with vendors and citizens. You can actually interact with most of them, buying food, getting massages or doing favours. The graphics are actually not half bad, which adds to this.
You can except good martial arts related combat from this game. You can achieve several unique combos as you beat down your enemies, unlocking cooler and better moves as you become stronger.
Not only does this game deliver in the unarmed department, but also the armed. The style of shooting is hiding behind cover and popping out to go guns-blazing. You can also aim while vaulting, you will be put into slow motion allowing you to clear rooms with one vault, which is pretty badass.
As you progress in the game, you start to meet very interesting and unique characters, both friend and foe. The voice acting, character models, tone, speech, everything suits each character well and adds to the immersive factor of this game.
Although it's quite simple with just a few tricks like vaulting, jumping up to high places and stuff like that, I must admit it is still quite fun to do.

Whether you're sprinting, driving, reversing or fighting near a wall, the camera angle seems to mess up and either clip through walls, not allow you to turn around and look behind you or just snap into a random direction. It happens quite often, but it's nothing major.
Majority of the missions are quite fun, but there are a handful that are basically the same thing repeated over and over again, only difference being the person giving the mission and a slightly different location.

Assault Android Cactus is a great game! It's got a lot of style and clearly had a lot of love put into its development. The game has a large focus on the wide cast of characters, and there's a strong emphasis on the high score chase. If you're on the fence, there is a demo, give it a shot!
Very fluent gameplay, cool style, i like it!

Take note, indie developers. Hell, even some AAA developers. This is how you polish a game!
You can clearly tell that the developers of Assault Android Cactus loved what they were creating, they shared a creative passion and wanted to bring it to life, to share it with the gaming community. And did they ever! Every single part of this game was polished until chrome, from the characters (each character has a different animation for being selected, cancelling character selection, entering a level, and completing a level, along with different primary and secondary weapons, some of which use completely different mechanics than any other character) to the boss battles (each boss is completely different, with pre-fight dialogue that's different for every character, and after defeating them you unlock new characters) to the arcade style interfaces, complete with credits and drop-ins.
Probably should mention the gameplay, because it's nothing like anything I've ever played. A top-down bullet-hell style game where getting hit doesn't matter, because what's really important is your battery. Taking damage simply stuns you, but when you're on limited battery, you really have to make sure you make every second count. I'm pretty sure that's the game's exact motto. When a battery drops, you (and your friends if you're playing coop) make a beeline for it, because that's your health. You miss a battery, you're as good as dead.
There's even special game modifiers you can buy with your credits, such as AI teammates, or even a fully fledged FIRST PERSON MODE. The developers of this game put effort into something that was completely optional, something I didn't even notice until I already beat the game. That's awesome. That should be the industry standard, like it used to be, where games boasted dozens of cheat codes that let you play it any way you wanted, because they wanted you to ENJOY WHAT THEY CREATED, not so you could line their pockets with cash.
My complaints? The game's pretty short, as the strong point of the game is definitely the boss fights.
I wish I had friends to play it with.

This game gets an 8/10 from me. It's a really relaxing game when taken for what it is. I am reviewing it as version 1.06 Mac OSX no mods installed. I had a free version for months before finding it on steam for 99¢ and just had to buy it to encourage the developers just a little bit with my tiny contribution. I would easily pay $5 bucks for it.
You're basically thrown into space, given 3 guys and very little resources to start building your space base. In the beginning you need to start as small as possible, building just the bare necessities. Once you have a small (3x3) airlock room, another room just large enough to hold 3 oxygen recyclers, and a room just large enough for a matter refinery, the rest is a piece of cake.
The game is 90% relaxing, mining and building, welcoming new (weird & silly) inhabitants, and pretty much trying to keep everyone fed, breathing, and happy - or as happy as one can be in a fragile domicile in space. You need to begin early considering how to protect your base from bad guys that pop in periodically, and asteroid impact damages.
Aside from the few (easy) dangers, it's just a relaxing sandbox style building game where you can be creative in making a space base to be proud of. The interface is pretty much well organized, which is an aspect that many games like this get wrong. I enjoy the weird types of characters/aliens and their thoughts and interactions.
Many people complain about the AI being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but you have to pay attention to what each character is good or bad at and by what degree they would suck at a job. You have to assign them to duties they are good at and actually enjoy doing. Some are good at a job, but hate doing it, so yeah, they'll stand around playing games on their pads instead of doing any work, unless you assign them to a duty they enjoy. I find this aspect completely adorable, as it really adds to the immersion and how you feel or care for each individual. I also love the names - imagining how an alien would pronounce his name written as "Uneekly (nicely)" - that sorta thing.
It's currently (for the past several months) been my favorite game for when I just want to relax and make a creative little space base. The few, easy dangers add just enough of that random aspect to keep you on your toes and influence the shape and direction your base takes. Have lots of good tech guys and your base will run smoothly - put lotsa gun turrets all around the outside walls and you'll be safe enough to survive a large attack that eventually happens. And just have fun building and watching how your inhabitants get along.
My only complaint is - once you get a VERY LARGE base, things go bad fast. Machines start failing, catching on fire, destroying themselves everywhere, no matter how many techs you have to fix them. But I guess this is just a sign that I've gone way too far with this base and should just start a new one, haha.
Lotsa people be hatin' on it, but it's been one of my favorite, relaxing games that I keep going back to.

Make no mistake: there will be times when you hate this game. And it will hate you right back, relishing in your every misstep and failure.
That said, this is also a beautiful, smooth-running, addictive twin-stick shooter made for the hardcore arcade enthusiast. For some, it will be enough to work through the campaign for a few white knuckled hours and call it good. For others, the allure of beating your old scores and slowly creeping up the leaderboards could provide dozens of hours of replay value.
The premise is simple: pick a character with a unique attack style, and then jump in to a small arena and destroy swarms upon swarms of robots, keeping an eye out for battery powerups. You can die and resurrect an infinite number of times, but once the battery is depleted, you die for real.
The makers of this game get a standing ovation for providing a free demo to try, something that is criminally rare these days. While the demo - which features a few levels from the first zone - is deceptively easy compared to the full game, it allows you to get a good feel of the game mechanics. By all means, check it out.
At the time I'm writing this, I've only put 2.6 hours on the game. I usually play 30 minute sessions, and most of them so far have ended abruptly with me spewing hateful words at my monitor and slamming my controller down. But I always seem to come back.
(Edit: I should add that progressing through the campaign itself isn't particularly difficult; getting high grades on the individual levels is where the real difficulty is to be found.)

To begin, I want to note that it's never tiring looking at the visuals in this. It's probably my favorite aspect of this game. They're very dreamy and striking, and never lack lore to add to the game. This brings me to my second favorite aspect of this game: the story. The story is obviously not relatable, yet the narrative does well in expressing itself with raw emotions (which in this game is generally fear, love, and awe), and those are translated mostly through the characters, which allows the player to feel the charaters on an adequate level. The last aspect I wanted to note was the soundtrack. The soundtrack, like the previous two aspects, brings life to the game. Every song fits the atmosphere and is the right tempo for each situation. It makes the game feel like  a complex piece of clockwork, where every gear has been oiled for a smooth experience.
Of course, no game has no flaws, yet there is but one flaw that I'd say is noticeable for everyone. The one thing I'd note about this game as a flaw is the action. At first, the concept of slowing down time and planning your moves to prove yourself a worthy foe to your enemies is attractive, but you quickly lose enthusiam over it as you get used to it in just the first fight. Afterwards, the action teeters on a sharp, thin blade, where on one side, the action is frustrating, and on the other side, too easy. The game manages to balance on this blade, and only ever sways to one side or the other, but, of course, staying too long on this sharp blade instead of falling will just result in a "cut". This is noticeable during the end of the game, where the boss fight is ultimately dissappointing, because the action was always the same, just like in the previous fights, and where previously these fights succeeded in being generally enjoyable for balancing every factor that a good fight requires, this balance is against the ending experience's favor.
Overall, this is generally just a great game that I think everyone can enjoy. It probably won't become a favorite of yours, but a memorable experience nonetheless.

The Bad: Medicore, frequently repetitive gameplay with often unresponsive controls and a very cool Force throwing system with utterly impenetrable aiming mechanics (At best, you can move the object/individual you're trying to throw vaguely in the direction you intend it to go in, and hope that it lands somewhere in the vicinity. More often than not it just drops straight down, or goes flying in a completely different direction...I'm still not sure why.)
Occasionally hairpullingly frustrating when there are massed ranged troops, some of whom have weapons that can stun you or knock you back, leading to instances where you get chain stunned and take an enormous amount of damage with little to nothing you can do about it. I'm assuming that in these instances you're supposed to use your incredible Force powers to hurl some of the random debris that sits around every environment in the game into the groups of your enemies but the aformentioned uncontrollable aiming system makes trying to hit anything that you're not locked onto an exercise in futility, so the debris mostly gets in the way (you can also Force-grab enemies, but in some areas the debris is so thick that half the time Starkiller ended up grabbing random detritus and violently throwing it out of the way of his foes like some sort of telekinetic custodian clearing away trash in mortal fear of a personal injury lawsuit) so you're reduced to wading into the thick of your foes as best you can, Force-dashing along the way to avoid the stream of rockets, electric rounds, etc. that are being shot at you, and then flailing about with your lightsaber.
There are a number of simple combos that you can use in combat, but after about halfway through the game most of the enemies have shields that block your Force powers until you do enough damage to them, at which point they're almost dead anyway, so in practice you wind up spamming attack a lot.
Now and again you'll come across a larger enemy (Rancor, AT-ST, etc.) and that'll be cool the first few times, but after the third or fourth you'll realize that you can kill it by popping out of cover, zapping it with a full bar of Force Lightning, then popping back into cover and waiting for your mana to regenerate (which it does almost instantly) until its health is in the red and you can run up to it and kill it with a quicktime event. The combination of this, the aformentioned stunlock issue, and the Force-blocking shields mean that a squad of Stormtroopers in 'Force Unleashed' is generally much more dangerous to you than a pair of Rancors.
Possibly the crowning achievement of the game's bad design occurs near the end of the game, where an event that should've been an incredible, 'holy crap' experience is instead reduced by an actively deceptive onscreen prompt and poor controls into an exercise in absolute, controller-throwing frustration.
The Good: Absolutely spot-on voice acting (Vader sounds like Vader, Palpatine sounds like Palpatine, all of the new characters are on point as well), a very strong story, and gameplay that is often fun despite itself. It has its (many, many) flaws, but the core mechanic of Force manipulation is enough to sustain the game. Almost every level has some sort of awful. hilarious thing you can do to your foes, from dropping an Ugnaught into an active carbonite bath, to slowly pressing a Jawa against a laser fence, to throwing a Stormtrooper through a window and into a stream of flaming railgun exhaust (or into the vast void of space, or into a Sarlacc's mouth, or...) to just plain hurling them against the wall until they stop moving. The Force Push also figures into this, and the first time the stars align and you chain it into a combo that targets a cluster of unshielded troops, hurling them screaming off of a platform, it will be absolute magic.
If you're a Star Wars fan (and honestly, who isn't?) I'd grab it, but I can't recommend it to someone who isn't attached to the mythos and is just looking for a good game to play.

War Operations is the sort of piddling junk you'd expect to see on an app store, for free, laden with about five dozen ads featuring games that are more often than not exact duplicates of it. But nope, it's on Steam thanks to the late Steam Greenlight, which despite allowing games like this on the storefront was still better than Steam Direct. At this rate you'd expect Valve to cut out even more middlemen and sign sponsorship deals with competitive eaters, given the way they're dedicated to removing crap from their service.
Anyway, this game sucks. Of course, you knew that already. I don't even know if it reaches some new depth of suckitude previously unknown to humankind, given the kind of stuff that usually came through Greenlight - and now Steam Direct, like a leaky oil pipeline being replaced with a bigger, leakier one - but it does definitely suck the big one. This masterpiece offers menus that make most other freeware games produced in developing countries look like fine art, a quit function that just spits out an error message, a store description that straight up lies to you, and we haven't even gotten to the gameplay yet.
Well, technically the store blurb isn't all lies. It is most definitely not an FPS, but it is, I suppose, a game which requires all of your skill and wit to complete. Partly because it could very well win a Guinness Gamer's Edition world record for 'worst controls in a top-down game' if they gave out awards for sucking. The AI isn't all that intelligent, since all they do is patrol predetermined routes, but they do "react to even the smallest sound" by almost instantly killing you the moment you fire a gun or enter their line of sight. They don't react so harshly to silenced weaponry, which only one of the two soldiers under your control has, making one of them effectively useless apart from the mythical bomb-planting ability I have yet to witness because War Operations gives I Wanna Be The Guy a run for its money.
I mean, there are multiple levels in this game kind of like if some weirdo janitor decided to stack six urinal cakes on top of each other (and they're about as necessary as a sextuple-decker urinal cake), but I'll be damned if I'll see any of them, let alone figure out how to win the first level. Enemy reaction times are so fast, and their weapons outrange yours by so much, I think actually finishing this game would make a good record. Forget Dark Souls, forget Ghosts 'n Goblins,
is the real test of a real gamer.
This game isn't even so bad it's good, so I'm not really sure why I bought it in the first place. I had more fun writing this review than playing it, if you can say I even played it. All I know is that this is just one piece of flotsam in the great garbage patch that is Steam's average output, and a relatively inoffensive one at that compared to the asset flips and cynical clownboats infesting the platform now, because Valve has lost the ability to think about thinking about quality control except when scumbag developers are doing things like trying to sue their own customers for accurately pointing out that they're scumbags. Lord.

Fantastic RTS with great competitive play. Best played as 2v2 though 1v1 scene is more active. Large number of quality-of-life improvements over previous wargame entries, including planning phase orders, line-of-sight at cursor and unload-at-position.
All the divisions feel unique and play out differently. Divisions are put together pre-game through a deck-building mechanic in which the set of units available are unique to the division. The more veteran divisions are generally stronger, even if the number of units they can field is strictly lower. The number of units you can take [activation] is limited in a total number and also in terms of number of a single type of unit. The types of unit are: ‘Scout’, ‘Infantry’, ‘Tank’, ‘Support’, ‘Anti-Tank’, ‘Anti-Air’, ‘Artillery’ and ‘Air’. For example, a division might limit you to 40 activation but only let you place a maximum of 4 into your ‘Air’ tab. A single activation in your ‘Air’ tab might get you two Spitfire fighters, or one Typhoon with AT Rockets.
In a match, requisition is gained each minute. The amount is based on how far into the match you are and which division you’re playing. Requisition is spent to deploy units from your deck, allowing you to be flexible but limited with your responses. Identifying targets and shoring up weaknesses in your line is key.
There is a phase system, which limits units to become available for deployment based on how far into the game you are. Phase A lasts for the first 10minutes, B for the second 10minutes, and C for the remainder. In addition to gaining access to more units for deployment, your requisition income also increases. Generally the strength and expense of units goes up as the game goes on.
The game requires attention to lines-of-sight and unit positioning. It favours skilled use of combined arms, which necessitates a mix of infantry and armour based on both your and your opponent’s capabilities. Encounters are generally won through surprise, key units deployed at key locations being leveraged to suppress enemy’s strengths and exploit their weaknesses.  Infantry gives you presence to your frontline, but can struggle to kill units. Towed guns are cheaper than self-propelled and can move through forested areas – which can be useful to take units by surprise at short range. But they are slow and weak to fire support like artillery, machine-guns and bombers. Tanks and self-propelled guns are almost the exact opposite. They’re speedier, and resilient against most attacks, but are weak to being flanked and surprised by anti-tank weaponry – towed AT guns and Bazookas, and struggle to move directly to where their fire is needed. Finding the balance is the path to success.
In conquest, the most popular game mode, the game is won and lost based on the amount of territory each side has claim to. More territory, more victory points are gained per second, though you have to approach 60% of the map taken to gain a +2points tick-rate. The game is played to 40minutes or until 2500 points have been gained by one side. Most units exert influence, with infantry being the cheapest and most numerous.
In conclusion, this game is fantastic and if you have an interest in RTS, I highly recommend this game. It is a fresh take on what has been a stale genre for the past few years.

I really like Steel Division, however there are a few things you should think about prior to purchasing.  Before I get into any reservations that one may have, lets start with the good:
GOOD:
+ Actually the EXCELLENT... the moving front line is by far the most INOVATIVE additon to an RTS in a very very long time!  It works very well in the fact that it forces people to move foward and not just camp at a SECTOR as in all Eugene's prior Wargames.  Not only does it make one move forward, it provides them with the opportunity to choose where!!!  Now that's novel!
+  Graphics are great... the Landscape (actually designed from air reconnonace of WW2) not only provides great eye appeal, the asymetry makes for more immersion.
+  BattleGroups is much better than WG.  The choices are less miniscue;  In WG there were sooooo many choices that it seemed that if you picked between a M1, M1A1, M1A2 you may be at a disadvantage... and don't even get me started with all the choices of units and carriers!!!  I sometimes spent more time in Making my army in WarGame than actually using it!  The system in SD44 is clean, easy... allows for choice, but doesn't overwhelm someone with such small varations.
+  Gameplay is Fun!!!  For some it may be too slow... and for others too fast.  I like the options to adjust the time scale, however I never use it becuase it seems good to me... not a click fest, but fast enough to feel that when you need your units to move to an area they get there at a reasonable time!
BAD:
- The worst part, and I am bias, is multiplayer!!!  I love SD44's Multiplayer... however, being part of the VIP Beta for all WarGames... even back to RUSE... I stressed the Importance of a MATCHMAKER SYSTEM.  Many others who were part of pretesting did so for previous Eugene Games and for once Eugene said, during the ViP Beta Forums that they would consider it... eveyone jumped in and they officially said they would implement it!!!  Awesome.... but not, in conjunction to creating something they called 'Quick Play', they also resubmitted 'Ranked'  a week prior to the Open Beta which used the exact same system to pair players (side note - none were avalible for the testers and were grayed out, but many people noticed this and voiced their concern).  In addition, they still kept the Custom Game Lobbies that eveyone hated!!!  This divided the choice to 3... what we wanted was a Quick and Fair way to get a game in SD44... they tried, but implemented too much and it failed.
Right now the Population is slowly shrinking... but hopefully with the summer sale it will pick up again.
Final Thoughts:
I really like SD44... and all I do is play MP now; typically Ranked.  I only wish they implemented the MP system better so people didn't get lost in the Custom Battles or were too scared to play Ranked.  The only problem is that if I get on and the population is low... I will probably not get a game in Ranked and will have to search Custom games with is a pain in the butt!

I've had these games since FS13 so you could say I'm a seasoned vet. FS17 is a welcome improvement over 15, but its definitely and evolution rather than a revolution. Sure there are some additions, but it's nothing ground breaking.
- There is now an in-game reason to plow, as long as you enable the option to require occasional re-plowing
- There are now 3 (maximum) stages of fertilizaion, which you can set between 1-3 in the settings requiring you to fertilize your field more than once for optimal yield
- pigs -- similar to cows but can't be milked
- trains -- slightly gimmicky, no real reason to use them aside from selling harvest in locations that only accept a train car and not a normal wagon tipper. But cool nevertheless. Physics aren't realistic, but they are authentic in that it takes a while for the train to get up to speed and requires you to brake far in advance of your stopping point.
- vehicle customization -- you can now get different sized tires (which are even better if you have the crop destruction mod enabled which requires you to use Narrow Tires to be able to drive through your crop without destroying it), different engine sizes, different colors, and getting a frontloader attachment. Not all options are available on all tractors, but most can be customized in some kind of way. This is a VERY welcome addition.
Unfortunately some stuff has been taken out as well.
- No more mowing/pallet driving side missions, which have been replaced by doing field-work chores for other fake farmers -- the more you do the better price you get when you buy the field from them.
- They also removed some starting equipment, which is a real shame since they added more reason to plow and fertilize. Guess which equipment they removed? (the fertilizer and plower in case I need to spell it out)
Overall, if you've played Farming Sim before you know what you're getting into. Might want to wait til its on sale tho, I got it for $30 since I couldn't wait any longer but ideally I'd want to get it for around $20. If you haven't played FS17 before, this is the perfect place to start. The graphics, physics, and sound have all been improved over the last versions and it has tweaks here and there that just make it a more immersive experience than before. It's not a groundbreaking game but it works exactly as advertised. Sure it'd be nice to see some more changes especially since they have 2 years to work on the sequel, but the game is fun as-is. If you're into this genre of games, I'd recommend.
