I don't know why so many people say this is a bad game. Sure, I'd be disappointed if I had paid $15 for the game, but it only costs $7 now, and I got it on sale at Humble Bundle for $0.99 back in May, so I think I got a great deal on it.
There's plenty wrong with the game, but nothing that really kills the enjoyability of it. No, it's not Skyrim. It's a mobile game that has been ported. From what I can tell, there isn't even any major expansion in this port, except for one additional step in the main quest and actually having to aim in a bow competition, which is fine at the current price. If I'm wrong about this, someone please let me know since I've never played the mobile version. Most of the problems can be traced back to Unity. Some of the glitches can hinder gameplay, like getting stuck in the environment, which only happened to me once, so it's important to save on a regular basis, especially before and after doing something dangerous or challenging.
The basic gameplay was enjoyable for me, and I liked the straight forward quests. I would like to see more quests added to expand on the game. I really liked that the best gear is found, and not bought, although, you may need to buy some gear so you can survive to get the better equipment later in the game. On a first play-through, I kind of like a little bit of grinding, whether it's for experience or for gold, but in a shorter game like this, it would kill replay value.
Basically, don't expect this to be Skyrim because it's not. Personally, I would hate to try playing this on my phone, so I'm glad I got it on PC. If you can't accept that it's a port of a mobile game, of course you will think it's lousy.
I give it about 7.5/10

Calling this a budget Skyrim is an understatement. That said, the game isn't without merit. The best thing I can say for it is that the game doesn't wear out its welcome. Where it becomes an absolute chore for me to finish sprawling RPGs like an Elder Scrolls game, the main quest with some extras in Ravensword: Shadowlands took me about six hours. The combat mechanic is simple, but that's no different than most ARPGs. The screenshots posted are representative of the in game graphics, which look two console generations old at this point, but definitely not an eyesore. My biggest complaint is the plot. It is not at all compelling and the dialogue is painful. The main reason I finished this game was to take it off the pile. If your PC hardware is very oudated and you are unable to run Morrowind or Oblivion, or you are just looking for a short ARPG fix, you will probably get you $7 worth out of it, but you can definitely find a better game if you are willing to wait for a sale.

I feel like this game was built around a great idea. The Transistor. This weapon gets functions from the people it embodies. These functions can be mixed and matched to use in battle as active, secondary, or passive skills. There are a total of 16 different functions to unlock through your first playthrough, although if you decide to "recurse" (subsequent playthroughs) you unlock duplicates, bringing them up to 32.
Playing around with these different possible combinations is where the magic happens, and the game is aware of this. For instance, when leveling up you choose one skill in a small selection, so the order you unlock them is slightly random.
(not all since some are story related)
Another example is dying. When your health bar is depleted in battle you will be punished by losing your most valued function in return for a full health bar. This function will remain locked for a few fights forcing you to try new combinations. This can hinder you or open your eyes to devastating new tactics. It is only after losing all active functions that you die.
Limited ressources and knowledge can make the beginning of the game more difficult than intended. But once you find those game breaking combos no amount of limiters will hold you back. Limiters offer you a chance to increase the challenge in exchange for bonus xp. They also unlock as you level.
I like how the functions and limiters have little profile cards for the characters and the process (enemies) respectively. It gives depth to the transistor.
The story on the other hand is relatively short and intentionally cryptic. As I mentioned you have the possibility to recurse. Depending on how complete you want your experience to be, it might be necessary. There is an area in the game called the Backdoor containing different types of challenges. These tests are unlocked through your player level and after a single run some will remain locked. I would say it takes between 2 and 3 playthroughs to get max level (30) depending on the number of limiters you use.
Under the cloud of mystery and the sci-fi allure of the narrative is hidden a pretty simple story. It didn't bother me much but I would understand if some of you find it underwhelming.
The turn base and strategy side of this game is not as prevelant as I thought and aiming in real time can feel clumsy.
The last thing I want to mention is the level design. In spite of the stunning graphics the levels were lacking. It's mainly walking in hallways between combat. In battle is where you want to be, so these lackluster levels don't really affect the fun of the game. Paradoxically a second playthrough doesn't feel all that repetitive because it is just a continuation of the battle/walk/battle formula the game already had going.
Sometimes in battle, a "cell" can become hidden by terrain which can unnecessarily lengthen a fight.
In conclusion, this game is guided by a single well developed fun idea leaving the rest feel like an afterthought, disappointing but not enough to drag this down.

Overall, not a bad game. It has a few problems, but it's still a solid game.
Good
-----------
-An actual need for fairly realistic tactics. You can't expect to win a battle with only one type of units. Tanks, Infantry, and IFVs actually need to be co-ordinated to sucessfully fight.
-A decent level of realism among the units. The infantry have proper weapons, the tanks are correct with their weapons, and the planes carry the correct ordanance.
-Proper maps. You're actually fighting over real locations. Omaha Beach is laid out just like Omaha beach was on D-Day. An ambitious move, but it really helps with the level of realism.
Bad
----------
-Small Campaign. Each section of the campaign only has 4 missions. Personally, I would have wanted more missions, but the ones that are available are very good.
-Limited choices among units. I understand the reasons for this, but in some cases, it's a bit silly. An example is the Me-109s the Germans get to use. They all have gunpods mounted, but many pilots didn't like using the pods unless they had to go against heavier targets like bombers. It'd be nice to be able to pick the loadouts and have a list of proper options. So, those 109s would have options for nothing, gunpods, rockets, or bombs of various sizes depending on the version of 109.
-Difficulty of cover and how vision works. These systems are far better than some other games, but they still have issues. For example, why are forests not counted as a form of cover? If the tree is large enough, you could gain an amount of protection from it, at least against small arms fire. Also, why is there not a "fortification" option? It'd be great to be able to order units to dig in and make foxholes or a small trench that they then use as cover. Plus, vehicles don't go through forests. Most tanks just pushed trees aside, and smaller vehicles can just manuver around the trees.
-Balance between certain units. This is very true among the tanks. A Sherman Jumbo really shouldn't be as survivable as a King Tiger. It's a more survivable tank than a normal Sherman, but it's still classified as a "Medium tank". Plus, when one unit has the ability to start murdering entire sets of units with no support, it needs some fixing. (And yes, I've done that with King Tigers, so I know they need some tweaks also)
Ugly
----------
-The AI. The AI is not "Intelligent". It cheats. If you spawn a unit and tell it to move somewhere, the AI instantly knows what you did and counters it. This just kills the enjoyment and the possibilities of using proper tactics. Perfect example is the campaign. In a certain German mission, you need to assault an Allied position. Unfortunately, the AI knows exactly where you're moving your units and just throws its units at you. You can not (as far as every try I've made) get past them, because they keep throwing their units at you. Realistically this is just not a proper strategy for the Allies (unless your Russia~). Custom Soundtrack

The Force Unleashed is a unique Star Wars game that combines very fast lightsaber swordplay and devastating Force powers combat system as well as some pretty cool envoronmental physics puzzles and interaction. Its core gameplay is simple, you need to get to a certain point in a level while trying to stay alive and defeat enemies along the way, but how you choose to do it is whats fun. You can beat them up with many different lightsaber combos, fry them with lightning power or infuse your lightsaber with the power of lightning and do both at the same time, push them away or throw them in any desired direction with little effort like a rag doll! Or maybe you prefer to throw explosives or drop heavy objects on them? Whatever you option for, you can do it, and you can do it as much as you like and at any time and you can even get creative while doing it. There is also a character progression system that keeps the gameplay fresh so you will constantly be unlocking new combos and force powers to play with as well as a few minor lightsaber modifications that you can choose from. Regarding gameplays bad aspects, i can only think of a cheap boss battles(possible minor spoilers  regarding gameplay mechanic ahead) that are not rly battles in my opinion and i say this because the way it works, its impossible to actually fight with a boss since they always win, by easily interrupting your combo no matter what you do and how you approach it and deal some heavy damage to you in just 1 hit most of the time. Bosses are defeated by finding a specific move that will incapacitate them in some way, being that a lightning strike stun or a knockdown of sorts and then dealing as much damage as u can before they get up and once they do, you have to do the same thing over and over again until its HP bar is depleted because, doing anything else will result in your character being wrecked 90% of the time. Thats pretty much everything regarding the gameplay for the Star Wars: The Force Unleashed.
As for the visuals, the game looks fantastic and the overuse of physics really contributes to the feeling of the Force power since the world around you will react to its impact and objects will often bend or break as you unleash it on your enemies, tho, as i said, its really demanding and you can expect some FPS drops here and there, but, unchecking the "High Details" box in the launcher seems to improve performance quite a lot and doesnt really take away anything from the visuals so...
So, another faulty port that is still super fun and enjoyable despite all of its technical flaws simply because of its amazingly enjoyable gameplay. 9/10, awesome game, would play again

If you are a fan of Star Wars, you should definitely play this game.
If you are a fan of action games, this is also a game for you.
The Force Unleashed is an excellent action game with a pretty good story.  You play as Starkiller, Darth Vader's apprentice, and at the beginning of the game are tasked with killing the last remaining Jedi. The rest of the story is a bit predictable, but the excellent cutscenes, backed up by great writing and voice acting, make it very enjoyable. There are a couple of insanely cool moments you will remember for a while, such as
. Backed up by great art and music, you can easily feel what the characters feel and get emotionally involved in the story. In my opinion, Starkiller is especialy well developed and is very easy to relate to.
The gameplay is excellent most of the time. It is a standard action hack 'n' slash game. Levels consist of platforming sequences and sections where you fight a lot of enemies. Fighting is excellent, and makes you feel like a real Jedi because you can freely throw everything and everyone around as you wish. It is even more fun because of the ragdoll physics and it can be really fun seeing your enemies tumble around in air as you throw them.
The game does have a few setbacks. The camera can go crazy. Boss fights, despite usually ending in great executions which are simple and short QTEs, can vary in quality. Some are too easy and can be easily button-mashed, and others require you to follow just one pattern over and over again slowly. Another issue is a lack of replayability, since you only have one ls/ds choice and it is at the end of the game, so you can just reload and see it. There are challenges and collectables you can pursue, but they don't really offer much, and the story can be finished in some 5-6 hours, maybe even less.
This is still an excellent game, and it is a shame LucasArts/Disney decided to ignore the extended universe since this was a great addition to it. Definitely recommend it to all, both for it's action and for the story.

Giving a simple thumbs-up or thumbs-down to Legend of Grimrock seems to me to miss the point of the game; it was consciously designed for a very specific audience, and your enjoyment will depend upon your belonging to said audience.
I'd describe Grimrock as a puzzle game with an RPG overlay. You're dumped on top of a mountain and have to fight and puzzle your way through a series of dungeon levels in order to get to the exit at the bottom. There's an opening graphic about being condemned to the maze and offered a slim chance at survival as punishment for unspecified crimes, like eating puppies or promoting Justin Bieber's music or somesuch. Unimportant; it's a reason for your four-person party to wind up stuck in a dungeon. Players of the Recent Might and Magic X: Legacy will find it has less involved, less tactically sophisticated combat but much tougher puzzles (it pains me to admit that I got stumped fairly early on); you look for a hidden switch that opens a door somewhere on the other end of the level that leads to a dead end with another switch disguised as a torch sconce that when pulled opens the gate you saw three turns back which leads to a scrap of paper with a password on it for that magical barrier you couldn't get past before...
I've given Legend of Grimrock a thumbs-up because it seems to do what it set out to do: it provides a series of tougher and tougher dungeon puzzles for the player to obsess over, with some simple combat to leaven it. The game's a bit like extra-dark chocolate in that respect: people who already find it to their taste will love it, while people who don't will find it has a bitter, gritty flavour that sort of reminds them of something they like.
There's an optional rhythm game-esque puzzle. 10/10

Battlefield: Bad Company 2 brings back the fun of the Battlefield series in a very thrilling way. While many online fans are saying death to Modern Warfare 2, I’m not going to make those comparisons. Modern Warfare 2 is a different style of game and cannot be compared apples to apples. Battlefield is a vehicular combat shooter with huge, open maps, which goes without saying since you wouldn’t want to roll around in a tank on a 4×4 map.
If you were a fan of the original Bad Company, by story alone, you will not be completely disappointed. The story has a lot of funny moments to it, some that will have you laughing out loud, while still maintaining a seriousness about it. The original felt more like a comedy-action, but they’ve managed to switch the roles this time around with an action game with comical moments. Some of that comical relief comes from taking cheap-shots at Modern Warfare 2. If you’re a fan of Modern Warfare or not, the snowmobile shot is very well placed and funny. Especially coming from Haggard, the games stereotypical right-wing Texan.
Bad Company is no longer on the quest for gold bars but instead, is still just looking to complete that last mission to get out of the war. It starts out back in World War II, where a group of soldiers are escorting a Japanese scientist to go back to the States. Without spoiling anything, the game shifts back to the current day, you are Preston Marlowe and joined with the same B-company crew as the original. B-company is after an WMD that is of some unique significance. The game pits you against Russians, of whom are also after the same WMD you’re after.
The game is fairly easy when playing on hard. Part of the reason is that you’re not constantly dodging grenades, the enemies are not always auto targeting you when you stick your head out, and there’s no respawning of enemies when you’re trying to advance. You clear an area, and move on. They also took auto the healing tool, so no longer are you going to need to heal yourself. They went to the standard of today’s shooters: regeneration. The AI is a decent, but don’t expect them to outsmart you in combat. They’ll duck and cover, but mostly you’re going to enjoy a nice game of target practice.
If you were looking for a single player experience and have no ambitions of playing online, you might want to wait for the bargain bin. The single player experience is over in 6-8 hours and there’s not too many reasons to go back. Even the collectables are easy to get, as I found all of them (guns and satellite points) in one sitting.
This game was truly built for a better online experience. If you were a fan of the PC version of Battlefield 2, there’s no reason to really read about the multiplayer; you should know what to expect. This game brings back a lot of what Battlefield 2 brought to the PC world when it first came out. Open worlds, lots of objectives (and explosions), and intense squad battles. You’re set up with different kits, from sniper gear to medic gear, and it’s really just up to you how you want to play. However, picking a class is more than just picking a gun. You need to take the role of that class. It’s ridiculous to see a medic going solo to assault the other team.
If you’re not familiar how Battlefield works, it’s squad based and not meant to be a deathmatch game. Trying to solo everything is not going to work and will result in a less than satisfying experience. For instance, having a sniper and a medic together is one of the more deadlier forces to reckon with compared to a great assault soldier who is doing it solo. Dying is a learning experience as well. Instead of just hammering the same area over and over, you’ll need to switch your kits to find out which is going to be most effective.
The ranking system is back with all the digital glory and stat-keeping. One of the fun features that was probably ignored (but brought back to life) is knifing. Being able to see the gamer tags of friends or foes that took a knife to the face is beyond fun. It’s like collecting Pokemon, except I really do want to collect them all! In all seriousness, stats are well fun and don’t feel as time consuming as some games put out there. Is the multiplayer time consuming? Yes, and I like it that way.
Currently, though, there are some server issues. Ironically, the server issues are being worked on as we speak and should be good to go in a few days.
As far as technical aspects go, there’s a lot to brag about and hardly anything to complain about. There’s a new sound option called “War Theater”, which seems to put out a bit more battle sounds in the background. Graphically, it’s superior to the original in almost every way. I never saw frame drops. I haven’t ran into lock-ups. I’ve only ran into walls, only to blow them out of the way. The destruction in this game is a bit better than the original (being able to crumble a building with enemies is just too much fun), however, it’s about on-par with the original beyond that. Which isn’t bad. There’s not too many shooter outs there that let me reshape the terrain and buildings around me.
If you’re looking for something more than shooting infantry in a shooter, give Bad Company 2 a try. It’s a load of fun, and a great game to master. If anything, it brings back some of the golden days of shooting from the king of the shooters: the PC.

Serious Sam 2 is a game with a proper budget and is worse for it. This might sound a little strange but part of the charm of the original Encounters were their simplicity. They were the most first person shooter you had ever seen in a first person shooter. Their success has now lead Croteam to develop Serious Sam 2 with some loftier goals in mind and unfortunately this only makes the game worse for wear.
The first new introduction you'll get is to the storyline which now takes a front seat in the game together with cut-scenes. Both are unfortunately very poorly made and do nothing to pull you further into the game. On the contrary the constant breaks in the action where you have to sit around and watch Sam try to be funny ruins the pace of the game and makes the dreaded boredom begin to set in.
Sam was always a funny character in the originals. In the same way that Duke was fun back in Duke 3D. The cute little adolescent one liners made you giggle a little in between stomping out alien scum. In Serious Sam 2 however these one liners have been ramped up and pushed into the cut scenes and the increased intensity of the, coupled with the fact that you are no longer playing the game when they happen, you are sitting around waiting for the cut scene to end, means that you will begin to get sick of them very quickly.
Serious Sam 2 does maintain some the good qualities too and make a few cool additions of it's own. The weapons are still fun and varied, sound great and feel great. The levels are still massive with hordes of enemies and an absolutely absurd amount of color thrown in there to offset the modern shooter's often too heavily reliance on brown and grey.
The enemies look great and are every bit as varied and insane as in the original, everything from headless bombers to giant American footballers and psycho clowns on unicycles.
All in all Serious Sam 2 isn't a bad game. Underneath it all it still got everything that made the First and Second Encounters so enjoyable. It's just picked up some bad habits which hurt the overall feel of the game.

Finally finished this little gem of a game which I put off playing for sooooo long.
First of It has some issues, but nothing really game breaking (for me anyway). I loaded this up set it to full hd 1080p graphics are all set to the max, xbox 360 controller supported sat back and played away like a good little Jedi. The game ran perfectly with no major issues at all nothing game breaking, maybe a few random bad bits of level design but nothing that can't be avoided in the first place. The combat was good, a little stiff and sometimes sluggish especially when standing back up after being knocked down and then getting knocked down straight away and to have that repeat 3 or 4 times is very annoying, but not game breaking.
I had an issue on the last level of the game where my sound was missing i could hear slight lightsabre effects but everything else was missing, but this was cured when i downloaded the fixed files from the forum and took seconds to do and was easy to do.
The game itself is alright nothing spectacular it reminded me of Devil May Cry meets Star Wars, its a lot of hack and slash but with force powers and cool lightsabres. You dont use any pistols or ranged weapons other than force powers and throwing of the lightsabre, so dont expect to use rifles etc because you cant. There is a basic but effective leveling up system for your character and the force powers, you can also collect crystals for your sabre to change colour and to add perks to your weapon. These can be found through the levels and by completing various challenged throughout the game.
The game can be frustrating and sometimes lacks proper intruction but nothing major i found and completed all objectives/side missions and enjoyed doing so. One thing I would recommend is that you take breaks when playing this game i spanned it over 3 nights playing for a couple of hours at a time. I did that because its repetetive the same enemies over and over some with added powers/abilities and the odd mini boss before the inevitable end level boss.
That brings me onto the next point i had, Bosses, they didnt seem very tough at all, in fact i found the mini-boss battles with the AT-ST and others that wont be mentioned were a lot tougher at points during the game. The bosses seemed to be over in a few minutes and a lot of them were defeated the exact same way as the previous one but because they were so short i wasnt too fussed.
Now the music, the music. What can i say we all know what the Soundtrack to anything Star Wars is gonna sound like and this game does not fail in providing us with the well known star wars classics. They really do make the game feel more epic than it actually is, i was enjoying my lightsabre massacre with the epic star was soundtrack playing in tempo to the slaying of many, many clone troopers. I would say the soundtrack alone made me enjoy this game more than i should of.

With an extremely hard learning curve this game is for diehards.
There is no inutive way to understand what units are a rock, which are paper and which are scissors.
This despite the game very much playing this way. In example - AA unit does not actually shoot down planes.
This means you are often as a new player, finding yourself losing engagements without knowing why.
A fractured playerbase split between "custom games" and "quickmatch/ranked" further does the game a disservice.
There is no way to veto maps, which in turn means that games are often decided before place any units based on your division choice.
The internal balance between playable divisions, especially in 1v1, is attrocious.
The game revolves around airpower, assault infantry armed with flamethrowers or grenades.
Medium tanks are never worth their points as the game mechanics doesnt make them usefull against infantry.
Further, the stress impact induced by non-AT weaponry on AFV's means that tanks often find themselves missing or being forced retreated by mortars and other support weaponry.
Allied light tanks are outclassed by 20mm cannon Armoured cars, which means in many matches an allied player will find half his starting force destroyed by 4x armored cars.
Although patches have been introduced to reduce the extremeties of certain support weapons, the core gameplay mechaincs remian uninteresting due to extremely lackluster balancing between divisions.
This game should never be bought with competetive play in mind.
It is reasonably enjoyable to play the game with friends as the balance becomes much better. The game units are greatly modelled and the scenery looks great, with the maps paying amazing attention to detail.
The game has all the components to be a great, however extremely poor user interface design and game mechanic design betrays it dramatically.
I would recommend Company of Heroes 2 for anyone looking for a better, more competetive strategy game in the same historical setting.

Transistor is a game that presents a unique mixture of turn based and real time gameplay, using RPG progressioin elements to strengthen your character as you play the game. As you progress, you unlock more options for how to build your hero and approach fights. Initially, the leveling system seems solid, as does the opportunity to approach battles in a manner that suits your play style. When fighting, you can access up to nearly a dozen abilities by the end of your first playthrough, which, being roughly 5-6 hours, is a heck of a lot of progression in such a short time. Each of the powers interacts with another in a specific way, meaning there are literally endless possibilities for how you can approach fights. If you have played Magicka, in which you can create spells from basic magick essences, then you should have a good grasp of how many combinations you can potentially make.
My first hour or so playing this game was very positive. I love the Narrator design mechanic, something that was carried over from Bastion, which this game mimics in a lot of ways, though also differs in a few crucial areas. The game can be paused to issue commands in a sequence (similar to Mass Effect, etc.) in order to take on multiple enemies at once. The world is easily interacted with, and the many side interactions you have initially flesh out the world, adding a level of mystery to what you are doing. I finished the first third of the game wondering many things: what events led up to this? Who exactly am I? How is all this possible? True intrigue drove me into the middle of the game.
Unfortunatley, this is where many of the game's issues began to crop up. While the turn-based action is complex and deep, it often winds up being very frustrating to carry out. After each turn, there is a cooldown period for your ability to pause and issue commands. Normally this wouldn't be a problem; however, in Transistor, the ability to aim in real time is radically difficult and unreliable. Since you will routinely find yourself in small spaces fighting multiple mobile enemies, targeting, or the lack thereof, can become quite frustrating. The alternative to poor real time mechanics is to simply run around like a dog with its tail between its legs until your turn comes off cooldown (unless your powers are set up in a very specific way, which means your options become severly limited). Not very heroine-esque.
Some of the combat mechanics feel very cheap; your character is relatively slow, especially compared with some of the enemies. It can be very easy to get cornered with no real way out as you get bombarded to death. The narrator, while sporting an excellent voice, becomes repetetive and useless rather quickly, which leads me to mentioning the story that really falls flat. While the beginning of the game builds and makes you question what is going on (in a good way), the end of the game fizzles and falters into something largely uninteresting. I finished the game with very little caring for what was going on. Its difficult to put into words just how unimpressed I was with how the game finished.
Part of the reason these issues became so noticeable is because the game is too short. While some games are perfect if they last 6 hours, the length of Transistor made it feel rushed, empty, and lacking in good story-telling content. It felt, at the same time, stretched out as long as it could be and finished too quickly. I wanted a chance to really use my powers once I had attained them all, putting my learned combat skills to practice. While this happens briefly, it is far too short of a window to be satisfying.
Overall, despite having an excellent and uniuqe fighting system with interesting and seemingly endless possibilities, along with a cool narrator and an initially interesting and mysterious world, Transistor quickly becomes a frustrating, repetetive, and disappointing experience. It seems to have a hard time deciding what kind of a game it wants to be. For a better story, better gameplay and a better narrator, I would recommend Bastion, which is also made by this developer.

The O.S.T has some memorable tracks and the visuals are great. There are also daily challenges, infinite run mode, and a boss rush like most arcade like games. The battery system is intersting and keeps you at your toes. Also, the bullet hell in the boss fights are fun and a blast. If you like Pac-Man and Nuclear Throne, this game is for you. Also, all the enemies are varried and the level design is different each time so your never bored. One gripe I have with the game is that the battery has this magentic attraction to you when you go near it to get it. Yet if you move to fast, it will never reach you and result in a lot of stupid game overs. Overall, its a great game that I'm glad I was able to find and play. Thank you so much Witch Beam for this game and I'm excited for your next! I give it an 8/10.

Great game. Similar to Wargame (great in itself) series, but
- Better UI and controls
- Better AI
- Better campaign
- Less units, easier to learn. Without really losing anything essential
- WW2 theme makes the gameplay slower paced, in a good way
I was first put off by the "Frontline" mechanic, but it's actually really good.

Some units (Recon, paratroopers) don't affect it, so even when you seemingly control an area, it doesn't necessarily mean it's cleared.
In most videos the Frontline is visually intrusive, which I heavily disliked. But you can turn it from Options menu so, that only a thin line is shown, no colored terrain. Looks way better, without losing any info.
There is also some other "gamey" mechanics, compared to Wargame. For example, unarmed transports disappear, after passengers are unmounted. But it is actually better for the gameplay, once you get used to the idea.
Recommended for RTS and strategy fans. This is not about actions-per-minute fast clicking or micromanagement, but about actual strategy, even when it's real-time.
Eugen did balance updates for Wargame for years, so they always keep polishing the game. Seems they intend to do the same with Steel Division, which no doubt has some minor balancing issues. To be expected with hundreds of units. Oh, and it has in-built Steam Workshop mod support, including mods by the Eugen devs.
Also, if this game sparked your interest, check out also Wargame: Red Dragon. It's slightly more hardcore, more units (way more, 1400+) to learn. Dumber, more spammy AI, although Steel Division AI is exceptionally good. But Red Dragon still has an active multiplayer scene.

If you're looking for an rpg in the tradition of modern titles such as The Elder Scrolls: III-V, be prepared to learn how the movement controls work, as they are vastly different. Not in a bad way though. While this does make the game more difficult, I found the game to be enjoyable and rewarding once I got the hang of the movement.
If you lack patience, then this title may not be for you, but for those who are willing to take the time, it will be a worthwhile experience of discovery and adventure.

This game takes me back to my childhood in the '80's over at my friends house with graph paper and our two characters (my elf and his minotaur) trying to figure out which way to go to make it through the dungeon.
Also a nice throwback to the early Might and Magic on the NES but this is so much better.
So, time for the review:
The best part of the game is they tell you only how to move and interact with things.  The rest of the game you have to figure out on your own! It makes it fun and interesting and very much like we were really just dropped into a maze-like jail/dungeon (which is the storyline of the game).
It's amazing how they managed to really capture the atmosphere.  I continuously asked myself, "what's going on?" or "wait, why is it suddenly shaking and rumbling really loudly" (the volume actually rose during an earthquake, not all the volume...just the quake.  Nice touch!), or "have I come this way before?"
The combat is satisfying and actually a very nice pace for a first person grid dungeon crawler. Each character/class has their own abilities.  They stay in a square formation, 2 in front 2 in the rear, but you can switch at any time, including in battle which is nice when your minotaur can hit ANYTHING but can get hit by a giant snail...
My only real beef so far with the game is the puzzles (so far) have been pretty standard fare.  I had a little difficulty with one but figured it out (hint: watch the shadows).  I am sure they will get harder as I get further down into the dungeon.

Anyways, amazing game.
10/10 for nostalgia
9/10 for the graphics (yes, I like the fact they went old school and used the same brick layouts)
10/10 for sound (the sound travels through walls, around corners.  As long as you have stereo or surround sound and not mono you will know where to look for sound triggers (like baddies))
9/10 for music (this would be 10/10 if there was more than one composition; however, that composition is excellent)
10/10 for gameplay (ohmigosh! addictive and way too fun.  This game does NOT disappoint.  It delivers everything I wanted in an old school grid style dungeon game).
9.6/10 overall!

This addition to Battlefield franchise had a slow start but once it gained momentum it become a really great experience.
It still delivers the classic battlefield experience one would expect. Being a part of a well coordinated squad is worth in gold for it's enjoyment. What this game does well is expand the gameplay from the standard imbalanced run and gun most modern military shooters face today. It creates a focus on the battlefield itself with vehicles, positioning, awareness and knowledge of the game itself as more important factors than one camping behind a fridge and no scoping anyone passing by. As far as a tactical team game, this game most certainly delivers.
This is not without problems, latency and hit registration issues can hamper the experience, but are not too common to make it unplayable. With good internet and using close servers one can minimize the problems to next to nothing. There is also lack of good voice communication system. While not necessary, due to programs like vent/mumble/ts etc, it would have been nice to have.
Overall this is a very enjoyable tactical military shooter, that despite of small bumps along the way it delivers a really fun experience.

I got this game because I was a big fan on Bastion.  Much like that game, this has a great art style, interesting gameplay mechanics, and is overall a very polished game. I like how strategic you need to be, and how you aren't a whole lot stronger than the enemies you're facing. I have a few gripes though:
1. The game is very un-intuitive. It never explains what most of the terminology means and tutorials are lacking. After a couple hours, I found myself needing to start the game from the beginning because of learning things too late.
2. It is also un-intuitive because it punishes you for not doing well. Due to how linear the game is, this only makes the game harder. To continue my first complaint, the game also doesn't tell you that you can restart battles - something you should definitely do if you find yourself losing or else you're going to get frustrated about how hard the game gets.
3. Though there is a lot of detail in the plot, the story is a bit hard to follow and not very captivating.
4. Some doorways bring you to another "local" spot, while others permanently bring you somewhere else without warning. As someone who likes to explore, this gets irritating.
5. Some enemies have nearly unavoidable attacks. Normally this wouldn't matter since you can pause time in this game, but there's a good chance you aren't going to kill one of these enemies in a single turn without putting yourself at even more risk by ignoring everything else.
I'm not sure if I'd say I *recommend* this game, but I don't regret getting it.  The game is fun once you play it long enough.

I have had this for a very long time, yet had never installed and tried it.  It came with one of the many Humble Bundles I purchased.  When I saw that there was no controller support, I immediately dismissed it (I play with my laptop hooked up to my TV, so it is much more convienant for me to use a gamepad).  It also looked to me like a bad Elder Scrolls, Gothic, the Witcher, or Two Worlds ripoff.  Today I decided to go ahead and give it a shot, and I am actually glad that I did.  The art style is a little bit different than Oblivion or Skyrim, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing.  It grew on me rather quickly.  Again, having next to no great expectations (and that COULD be why things turned out as they did), I was actually impressed with things from the start.  The combat is just a notch above hack and slash, but with a bit of (somewhat picky) Elder Scrolls thrown in.  It can seem sluggesh, but once you get the hang of it then it is pretty satisfying.  I have only begun, so I cannot judge the story or dialogue so harshly yet, but it isn't terrible so far.  The more I play it, the more I see things that I like about it.
Considering I had no intention of buying this might factor into my impressions (again, I have not played for very long at all--I did see enough to know that I want to see more that it has to offer, and that is actually saying something compaired to most things I have played lately.  My review may change as I progress, but as for now, I recommend this game.  There is something about it, despite how I know it looks, that is compelling.  Even though I was irritated by not being able to use my xbox controller, once I got over it, the controls really weren't all that bad.  I had to switch "use" with "jump" but hey, at least it let me do that.  :D  Surprisingly, a lot of the games I have been playing recently don't give you the option to, but that might be because I have been playing a lot of Early Access games.
To conclude, give this game some thought and research before you immediately dismiss it.  I'm not sure offhand what the price of it is, but I don't recall it being  all that high.
[edit: At the time of writing this, it is $6.99, and that isn't on sale or anything.  I haven't a clue as to the length of the game, but even if it ends up being rather short, that seems like a generously low price.]

Emily is Away is one of those games I couldn't forget... Emily is away offers something different from most "visual novels".
Emily is Away takes place years before Skype and Facebook, the years when AIM was king. You create a screenname and profile pic and begin talking with your friend Emily. As years you and Emily talk through IM, sharing personal stories, you learn more about the choices you make throughout.
The gameplay is straight-forward, you log on, you're given 3 things to choose from to say to Emily. Each choice you make can change the story. The game does a really good job at making players feel as if they're in the 90s-early 2000s, sounds in the background such as your keyboard as you type along with computer helps the game feel much more "atmosphereic"
Emily is Away is a really good game despite its length and simplicity, the game gives off a really good vibe and a story that can really touch your emotions.
Overall: 8/10

What a strange game this is. Detailed historical units and maps, but gameplay that is basically the same as any other RTS and voiceovers made by people who don't know how to pronounce 'kraut' or 'cavalry'. *cringe* Machine guns that can fire in 360 degrees of direction, despite them being listed as two man teams, allowing them to completely annihilate any opposing force. Flanking? Impossible, the enemy has already set up positions everywhere. Suppressive fire? Only if you use artillery. Trying to get your units to follow routes that are unobserved by the enemy is like herding cats. Reinforcements come in exact units, even for airborne units that in real life got dropped in the wrong spot and had to spend a lot of time to gather themselves together and make it to their objectives. An AI enemy that just keeps spawning new units at certain spawn points and sending them towards the enemy by the shortest possible route, only getting out of their transport vehicles once fired upon, even if the enemy positions are already well-known. And if you're not properly dug in, meaning, if you have your troops not set up in an unassailable bunker, I mean, some random house or farm, tough luck, because th AI enemy will just overrun your positions with a never ending stream of reinforcements. Missions that can only be done one way, as that is the way they were conceived. Skirmish battles taking place on 'Omaha' Beach result in the Allies holding one part of the beach and the Germans holding another, instead of the Allies getting the beach and the Germans positions inland. I could go on. I won't say this game isn't fun, although your mileage may vary, but historical? Nah.
TLDR: if you're looking for a game that is faithful to the history of WW2, which does justice to strategy and tactics of that era, look further. The units will be recognizable, but that is about it. Too bad. With a little more work, this game could have been exceptional, now it is mediocre at best. Let's hope the Steam Workshop comes to the rescue again, to turn this game into something that is actually worthwhile if you know anything about the history of WW2 and Normandy in particular.

Over the years the Call of Duty series has set the bar for immersive, action-packed, cinematic FPS gaming, and no matter what camp you're from there's no denying the franchise's influence on the industry. When Infinity Ward moved from the classic World War II setting and blazed new ground with Modern Warfare we saw the first obvious split within the world of Call of Duty. The series dropped its historic focus, created a new cast of characters, and began treading on new ground by taking the first-person shooter genre to new locales, and pushing the boundaries of what military games are willing to show. With Modern Warfare 2, the sheer amount of hype has been practically inescapable, with preorders alone setting it up as one of the biggest selling games of all time, the addition of even more multiplayer modes and features, and the game's new Special Operations mode has set Infinity Ward's lastest up as the game to beat this year.
The real question: has it been worth the wait, and can Modern Warfare 2 live up to the precedent set by over half a decade of Call of Duty tradition?
Modern Warfare 2 is by far the least traditional of the series, with the core package broken up into three main pillars of gameplay. Single-player fans have their main campaign, if you're down for more co-op gameplay either locally or via online connection you've got the new Spec Ops mode, and Modern Warfare's groundbreaking multiplayer is back, and truly better than ever. There's an overwhelming amount of content to experience, but with each mode being 100% standalone in nature, you're getting three completely different experiences all in one. That, however, also plays a huge factor into how your final opinion of Modern Warfare 2 as a whole turns out.
First and foremost is the single-player experience. As the anchor of the Call of Duty world, campaign mode is back, and it's intense. You'll instantly get a sense of just how far the improved engine has come when you're thrown into the bustling streets of Rio de Janeiro's favela, the ice-capped mountains of Kazakhstan, the dusty roads of Afghanistan, and other unexpected locales. On the visual side of things, Modern Warfare 2 is an obvious step up over Call of Duty 4 and World at War, with a stronger emphasis on complex terrain in the environments, weather effects, destructible objects, and the overall sense of action and chaos that comes with so many visual improvements. This is only complemented further by the increased attention to sound design, with the effects of many returning weapons being re-recorded,even more in-level chatter amongst your allies, and a truly captivating score by Hans Zimmer which builds based on specific in-game moments. Modern Warfare 2 feels like an action movie through and through, with the production values alone dating Infinity Ward's last game, Call of Duty 4, quite a bit.
At the same time, the single-player campaign has its issues. For starters, it's short. I've been playing Call of Duty 4 steadily since its release, and my first completion of the Modern Warfare 2 campaign came in at just under five hours on regular difficulty. Playing through on hardened will add another hour and a half onto that. Modern Warfare 2 is definitely more chaotic this time around – partially due to the new visual effects and upped production values – and with the improved enemy AI and tough scenario design you'll be fighting for every checkpoint. One of the larger visual changes to the game's heads-up display this time around is the blood splatter system. In previous Call of Duty offerings you'd get damaged, the screen would start to shade red, and you'd be required to seek cover before your vision returned to normal. Modern Warfare 2 employs a new system, actually having a thicker blood layer added to up the realism. There's been some discussion on whether the splatter is too distracting, and in my experience with the game it's far from an issue. You'll be able to take more hits on easier difficulty settings, so while a few well-placed shots will drop players on hardened or veteran modes the added splatter is an acceptable trade-off for more overall health.
Thankfully many of the glaring issues from last time around have been fixed. You won't find unlimited enemy spawns in areas, there's always a waypoint icon on-screen showing you where to go or who to follow, and the amount of in-game chatter from your team is simply astounding. It isn't often in games that you'll hear your squad call out specific areas on the map and have it mean anything. When your friend shouts, "Two tangos behind the yellow station wagon!" you'll actually see two enemies behind a yellow station wagon. It's a pretty engaging experience. You'll still have random issues with friendly AI, specifically with blocking your movement or deciding to walk in front of you mid-firefight, but for the most part it's a better experience than the first Modern Warfare.
Where Modern Warfare 2's campaign drops the ball, however, is in its actual storytelling. With no historic anchor it's up to the Infinity Ward to not only put players in the moment, but also build and develop the world around those moments. That's one area where Modern Warfare 2 could have used more polish time or specific direction to get right. Events fly by, story is told only through load screens or in-game via NPC chatter (usually amidst firefights, where reading text isn't exactly priority one) and the story is so gigantically over-the-top that you'll often find yourself catching your breath after a mission, feeling like you had fun, and then trying to figure out what you just did in the context of the story. Though this may prove an issue for some, I was able to catch the plot, enjoy the characters, follow the twists, and truly care about the story. But then again, I've also been dedicated to nothing but Modern Warfare 2 for the last six months. The game often expects you to already know the characters, extrapolate on one line of dialogue or a quick cut-scene, and then figure out the story from there. In the end though, there's no real weight to anything you're doing. Outside of playing a couple missions as a soldier taking orders from the top you never get a true feel for scale, or any actual emotional attachment to the events. Something as simple as a newscast reel, or moment of downtime while on the field would have gone a long way. The end result is a game that has the feel of an '80s action movie with huge plot holes covered by plenty of epic moments, but never a believable, cohesive set of events.
There are definitely still great moments to be had in single player though. There's a laundry list of awesome gameplay concepts and new tech at your disposal. It just doesn't stack up against some of the previous Call of Duty story modes, where single player was the obvious focus throughout the entire package.
For the vast majority of the experience, Modern Warfare 2 is best enjoyed with friends either locally or via online. The core campaign may have taken a bit of a hit, but in its place is an incredibly well done debut mode called Spec Ops. For those that don't know, Special Operations mode is an arcade-inspired challenge mode that can be played single player for the most part (minus a few co-op specific challenges), but is obviously designed around two-person team play. The mode is broken up into five tiers, each with missions that have a possible three stars to gain based on difficulty level in each of the 23 missions. You'll see a lot of repeating areas, some pulled directly from the single-player campaign, but the actual objectives (and most of the time, the exact layout of the level) is all new. You won't find leaderboards for this mode, unfortunately.

Note: I'm not a professional in any way, I'm just a guy who likes writing reviews. I try to remain unbiased, but take note that this is a positive review; I like this game, so don't expect me to be thinking too clearly. :P I'm not being payed or trying to persuade you to buy the game, I'm just relating my experience.
TL;DR
Android Assault Cactus turns this type of game in its head with backwards and chaotic gameplay. While its story and graphics may not be spectacular, it makes up for it with unique and intense gameplay.
You know those guys who charge around without strategy constantly firing at everything and repeatedly getting themselves killed? You know how everyone hates them for being a stupid liability? Have you ever stopped to consider how they feel or WHY exactly they have no strategy? The reason is revealed in this game; cry no more, that guy! The game pushes you to use this chaotic strategy, whether you like it or not. Guerrilla tactics, sniping, and farming have no effect as the only way to stay alive is to kill everyone as fast as possible. People who play this game will quickly learn that most power ups are worth more than your life and recklessly charge into a hoard of enemies, firing constantly. Trust me, this doesn't subtract from the strategy. To understand it better, look up gameplay. All of this makes up for how very generic the game looks at first.


You thought that was all? The game gets twice as crazy when you try to get a good score. This game is no longer casual when trying to get an S+! Suddenly, local multiplayer becomes an added difficulty and life is precious. Strategy and planning are essential and must be carried out to the millisecond in order to work. Nothing less than a perfect marriage of brilliance and skill will work. (So I'm obviously at a loss. :P)
(Only because it's not completely original.)
Although the game is notably long, it still has a fair amount of replayability. In fact, some can argue it has too much. With two different multiple different game modes that both focus highly on score, you could literally play this game for months without being satisfied with your completion... The definition of hell for some. However, to a less hardcore gamer, it'll still be fun for a while. After you tire of the many central elements, there's the EX options to change up the game. Among the more notable ones are FPS mode, AI partners, super weapons, duplicate characters, and [ALT CAMERA WHT DOWS IT DO]. Though for some... The immensely fun gameplay, character variety, and local multiplayer could be enough In itself. Perhaps the only problem with playing it over and over is the lack of randomness. I think the only thing that's random is the things dropped by enemies... But you could still argue that it has a great amount of replayability.
Anyone with FPS mode can say that the graphics are unnecessarily good. It has a sufficient amount of settings to suit your computer and playstyle... I'm unconcerned with graphics unless you can't see crap or if they lag my admittedly bad computer. This game does neither, so I see no problem with it. For someone who likes playing with graphics, there are plenty of options for that... Which brings me to customization. As mentioned above, you can change the graphics. Other necessary options at included, but they have extras that go above and beyond. I mentioned a few of the EX options earlier, but there are many more. Some make the game more challenging, others make it easier. Some relate to graphics and music, and others fundamentally change the game. Most are serious, some are silly. While the game isn't spectacular in either of these aspects, everyone can agree that it does well.
I would not buy the game for the story alone. Not that it's terrible; I've seen much worse. The problem is that it's not the BEST. The integration of story with graphics and gameplay is poor... Death robots pop up out of nowhere and brainlessly attack you, and three untrained androids manage to grab extremely powerful weapons and use them for a presumably long time with SIXTY-SECOND BATTERIES by ripping out and draining the batteries or enemies... Just ignore that. Dialogue is infrequent, but characters still have a shocking amount of personality from voice lines in and out of battle. This raises new questions about how they got to be like that, but I'll count it as a plus since personality counts for story in my book. I could go on, but I don't like saying bad things about this game. Let's just say that there are good and bad things that mostly balance each other out.

Kung Fu films have their classics. “The 36th Chamber of Shaolin”, “Last Hurrah for Chivalry” and “Heroes of the East” are a few movies that spring to mind. For Kung Fu video games I’d pick “Double Dragon II”, “River City Ransom” and “Sleeping Dogs”.
The Definitive Edition has all the DLC from the original title. Including the two stand alone story missions. The graphics and PC performance has also been improved.
The problem with games like Grand Theft Auto is that the playable characters are all career criminals. With no chance of redemption. I cannot even hope to empathize with the likes of “crazy” Trevor or “corrupted family guy” Michael from GTA5. Sleeping Dogs is different. You play as undercover cop Wei Shen. He's a good guy caught up in a bad situation. I can understand his struggle and appreciate his point of view.
I love Skyrim. I’ve poured over 100 hours into the game on my PS3 (don’t laugh). But still the melee combat leaves a lot to be desired. It can be a little clunky at the best of times. In comparison the combat in Sleeping Dogs is near flawless. Wei can track his targets and counter attack with ease. Even when you’re fighting ten guys in the pouring rain the combat remains fluid and fun. Using a gamepad to play is strongly recommended if you want to have the best experience.
The City of Hong Kong is a vibrant place with it’s neon lights, market stalls and Karaoke bars (Wei’s actually a pretty good singer!). Performance wise the Definitive Edition runs at a rock solid 60fps at 1080p. (Visit my Steam profile for PC specs) There are also some excellent FAQ's in the Steam community if you get stuck on something.
Criminally overshadowed by the GTA series. Sleeping Dogs is better in every Wei.

Will Transistor be any good, will this live up to the older brother Bastion? These were the questions I asked when I booted up Transistor for the first time. So let me let you on the little secret of what exactly is Transistor.
There is no dancing around the bushes the game radiates Bastion for better or for worse so most of the time I will be comparing the two.
Let's start with the good things. The combat, which was absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥in Bastion, is greatly improved this time around. You now get the option to combine various skills and abilities into combinations that change the battle dynamics completely. There are a metric tone of combinations to try out (ofc some are better than others). So that means no more tedious battles where you sigh once you see an enemy looming in the distance just after finishing another battle that felt just the same as 10 before, right? Sadly it falls into the same pit again, but more on that later.
As was with Bastion, the game looks bio-tea-full. And I mean Gorgeous, with saturated contrasting colors, fluid animations, and interesting color effects.
Music is again of outstanding quality, and you get a dedicated button to play with the music withing the game. That's a bold art-house pretentious decision, but in the end I would say Transistor runs with it.
Again, as with Bastion (sigh) you get Supergiant Games' way of telling the story as you go about your game related business. For me this way of storytelling is too much distracting (and you sorta can miss out on details if you activate certain things too early), but I do appreciate it.
Now the bad things.
Transistor has the most abyssmal UI I had encountered in a very long time or maybe even

Throughout history people have asked, “What does it mean to be a man?”
Does it mean having a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥- and at least one ball - attached to one’s body? Does it mean turning women into cats, domestic and feral? Does it mean punching other men, and then crushing their families with a bus?
“What does it mean to be a man?” – the question seems immortal; and to it there have been many answers (a few examples: the Odyssey by Homer, Lord Jim by Joseph Conrad, Godzilla by Japan). And here we have Supergiant Games’ answer. Released in 2014, it is brilliant, flawed, and even a little brave.
Specifically, I’m speaking of the Presentation of their answer, which isn’t so much with words but mainly illustrations: the characters, the backgrounds, the action. THAT: is brilliant yet flawed.
As for the answer itself – That to be a man means to have a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and/or at least one ball, or to have HAD a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or to have HAD at least one ball, loss of either due to injury, plus male human DNA at some point – as much as I don’t care for this answer Supergiant states through Transistor’s visuals, I applaud them for their artistry in showing their truth.
To comprehend their message, take one group of their illustrations: the enemies. The first thing you’ll notice upon seeing them is that none show you one or more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nor one or more balls, nor evidence of castration, nor any test results showing human, male DNA. Not once. And thus the player can't help but conclude that the enemies in the game aren’t men, but something altogether different, like Carthaginians.
Or take our protagonist, Red. She’s a singer. Yet at no point (in the game) does she whip out her♥♥♥♥♥♥and/or a ball, nor does she provide DNA test results. In fact, the game never mentions her ever having had a DNA test...
Given the pattern set by the rest of the game, Red evidently is not a man.
And what of her talking sword? The Transistor has a low voice, a trait not uncommon in men. Yet, never does it show us its♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and never does it show us its ball(s); and never does it show us its DNA results; nor does it show evidence of crotch-based injury. Therefore, by Supergiant’s logic, we have no reasons to consider the Transistor a man.
And all this is brave on Supergiant’s part.
In 2014 they published their answer for judging if one’s a man. And it is still available, though propounding any answer to the question is bound to lose customers. I myself, for the record, don’t agree with their answer and, again, couldn’t care less, and am only judging their Presentation, which is brilliant yet flawed, flawed especially when my XBOX 360 controller suddenly couldn't do attack moves. That, by the way, forced me to use my mouse and keyboard for the rest of the game, which will affect the review score!
Having said that, I do want to say that Supergiant’s answer to the immortal question can’t be right. I mean just think of it. There are a lot of male human-seeming characters in the game, none of which show us male human genitals, nor human male DNA. Soooo none of these characters are men? Really Supergiant?

Plus, isn’t it kinda absurd that one HAS to have a DNA test to prove one is a man? Or to maintain evidence that show that one violently lost one’s male human genitals? Not that I’m against Art featuring no men; I myself am an open-minded man, with a male, human♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and balls and DNA.

Madness and Glory to the great Cthulhu! Cthulhu Saves The World is an excellent, quiet well designed game that is a definite throwback to 'old-school' RPGs while being quite accessible to new players. I certainly enjoyed it, and if you can get in the double pack alongside Breath of Death VII it's a steal. Only problem I found was that the dungeons were far too long and confusing, and you might be put off in trying to complete some of them. Still, the particular mechanic of having a limited amount of mandatory dungeon battles is practically a(n old)godsend as it allows gamers of different types to approach dungeons how they wish, to a certain extent. If you can take your time with the game, it will reward you. The director's commentary is always a nice treat as well.
Pros: Solid Humor, references to RPGs and Lovecraft aplenty, large world to explore, good variety of foes
Cons: Long, somewhat steep difficulty, dungeon design confusingly, MADDENINGLY tedious.
Overall: 4/5

This was a really well made game that took less than a half hour to finish the first time through. The story is heartbreaking. I used to use MSN back in the early 2000's instead of AIM, but Emily reminded me a lot of the days when I still used an IM and of various people that I had talked to and befriended when I was still a teenager. The music and culture references are on point, and in a lot of ways made me feel like I was back in middle school again. The feeling of nostalgia and the relatability of both the main character and the titular Emily and their relationship is something I found very impressive.
That said, I found Emily to be an extremely annoying, unlikable and bland character... Which is something I see a lot of people critiscizing the game for, but the thing is that her portrayal was great because it's something that I have seen so many times in other people that are real. Just because a virtual character would really suck as a person doesn't mean that the character was poorly constructed.

For being 6 years old, the graphics aren't that bad. It runs perfectly and hasn't crashed once. The force powers are relatively equal in strength so there is a reason to use different force abilities based on the situation. All things considered, this is a pretty fun game...until you reach the bosses.
The bosses are a long sequence of frustration that brings you on the edge of breaking. While constantly blocking, you rarely get to hit them with your lightsaber. They are also immune to force much of the time. The only strategy to beat them is to just use different force abilities until you happen to hit him when he is not immune for a bit. One of the things that makes enrages me the worst is when they can use Force Push. They will use it, throwing you to the ground, and by the time you get back to your feet, they launched another one, throwing you back again. I literally had this happen five times in a row before I was finally able to move out of the way. These fights are long, frustrating, and just plain boring. I enjoy playing this game, but I dread boss fights just because they were so poorly made without the gamer's interest in mind.
Throughout, there are a few long and boring parts (such as the sequence where you pull a Star Destroyer out of the sky), where I just thought that they should have made it shorter. I would much rather sacrifice a few minutes of the game's length then have to repeat this long and tedious process multiple times.
Conclusion: 6/10

If the fact that 97.4% (639/656) of all the reviews for this game are positive isn't enough to convince you to buy it, please read my story:
TL;DR: Download the demo. If the first 5 levels don't get you excited enough to buy the game at a totally reasonable price of $15, then I'm worried you are the kind of person who doesn't smile or know what immeasurable bliss and joy feels like.
The True Story
April 5
1:30 AM: "Assault Android Cactus.....that is probably the weirdest name for a game I've ever heard....Oh, it's like 1941, but with androids instead of WWII airplanes. Okay, I'll get the demo and check it out. I like these kinds of games."
2:00 AM, upon finishing the demo: "Oh my gosh, that was so fun. I want to play it all again with a different character. Holly looks cool."
2:30 AM, after finishing another play through of the demo: "This game is amazing. I'm buying this." So I bought the game + DLC because the soundtrack is amazing.
10:30 PM: I start playing from the beginning again with one of my good friends in my house. He loves it.
11:30 PM: Another friend hops in as he gets home, and I can't tell if he's tired or just mildly interested, but he wasn't exactly rushing to the computer.
11:40 PM; The second friend is totally in the zone, and a third friend we invite says "Okay, but I only have time for one round." Yeah, right. Sure. Okay. Go for it.
11:55 PM: The third friend decides to help us with the boss fight, and as he plays as Cactus, he goes right up to the boss and is using the flamethrower relentlessly. I say, "Dude! You're so hardcore! You're right up in there!" He laughs and says, "Yeah man! I'm gonna get this guy!" I am reminded of when he said he'd only do "one level." Yeah, right. Uh-huh. Sure. That's like saying "Okay, but I'll just have one Pringle." Never happens.
April 6
12:00 AM: We beat the second boss three or four levels later and the third friend is like "Dude. This game is so sick." Sadly, he did finally drop out after going through the last half of the second section to go to bed.
12:30 AM: Me and the other two friends finish the third section of the game and finally decide that this is the best time to call it quits since we all have class or work in the morning.
It's charming. I don't give that kind of description to many games nowadays. It is charming and reminds me of the innocent fun we all used to have in the 90's before everything turned into a dark, harsh, nickle-and-dime, profanity-laced online mulitplayer FPS universe. It reminds of a time when games were games and it was just good fun. The characters are witty, there are lots of little things that make the game fun (like the characters being disappointed when you change your mind on who to select), and even an entire section that gives you the backstory on each character, NPC, and enemy. It even gives you info on stuff you won't encounter that is only mentioned in dialogue. It's like you get all the fun preface stuff from your old video game manuals built into the game! Surely any 90's gamer will remember such game manuals.
At this point you're still here because you're looking for an excuse not to buy it, but deep down you know you want it. Buy it. It's fun, and that's all it is. Just cut loose, don't be stingy or nitpicky, and have fun. There's a reason this game has a 97% approval rating. Play it and go back to a day when games were simple, silly, and charming.

Does it mean having a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥- and at least one ball - attached to one’s body? Does it mean turning women into cats, domestic and feral? Does it mean punching other men, and then crushing their families with a bus?
“What does it mean to be a man?” – the question seems immortal; and to it there have been many answers (a few examples: the Odyssey by Homer, Lord Jim by Joseph Conrad, Godzilla by Japan). And here we have Supergiant Games’ answer. Released in 2014, it is brilliant, flawed, and even a little brave.
Specifically, I’m speaking of the Presentation of their answer, which isn’t so much with words but mainly illustrations: the characters, the backgrounds, the action. THAT: is brilliant yet flawed.
As for the answer itself – That to be a man means to have a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and/or at least one ball, or to have HAD a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or to have HAD at least one ball, loss of either due to injury, plus male human DNA at some point – as much as I don’t care for this answer Supergiant states through Transistor’s visuals, I applaud them for their artistry in showing their truth.
To comprehend their message, take one group of their illustrations: the enemies. The first thing you’ll notice upon seeing them is that none show you one or more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nor one or more balls, nor evidence of castration, nor any test results showing human, male DNA. Not once. And thus the player can't help but conclude that the enemies in the game aren’t men, but something altogether different, like Carthaginians.
Or take our protagonist, Red. She’s a singer. Yet at no point (in the game) does she whip out her♥♥♥♥♥♥and/or a ball, nor does she provide DNA test results. In fact, the game never mentions her ever having had a DNA test...
Given the pattern set by the rest of the game, Red evidently is not a man.
And what of her talking sword? The Transistor has a low voice, a trait not uncommon in men. Yet, never does it show us its♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and never does it show us its ball(s); and never does it show us its DNA results; nor does it show evidence of crotch-based injury. Therefore, by Supergiant’s logic, we have no reasons to consider the Transistor a man.
And all this is brave on Supergiant’s part.
In 2014 they published their answer for judging if one’s a man. And it is still available, though propounding any answer to the question is bound to lose customers. That, by the way, forced me to use my mouse and keyboard for the rest of the game, which will affect the review score!
Having said that, I do want to say that Supergiant’s answer to the immortal question can’t be right. I mean just think of it. Transistor is a game that's as much a game as it is a beautiful, moving piece of art. From the gorgeous visual style, the stellar music, an emotional and layered story and impeccable voice acting, not to mention the deep and mutating gameplay, it has near about everything that I crave from a videogame.
The narrative is essentially about the relationship between a woman without a voice and man without a body. You are in a cyberpunk city called Cloudbank and something bad has just happened to you (the woman), causing you to lose your ability to speak and the man getting killed and his consciousness getting trapped inside the Transistor, the swordlike thing the woman carries. His voice constantly speaks to you, describes the happenings of the city and guides you. From here on out, Red - your character, must figure out who were behind this attack and make them pay. Before long you sense something is wrong with the city as well and it's changing too. Red and the Transistor's journey through this decaying city in persuit of vengeance is what makes up the story of this game. It's a very layered story with lots of subliminal themes, and it's told expertly and movingly, but none of these details are handed to you. You have to work for it and they are unlocked as you use different abilities in the game; while some people might find that off-putting, as far as I'm concerned that's a good gameplay design as it incentivizes experimentation and discovery of the numerous skill combinations you can put in place.
The gameplay consists of turns where you pause the action and plan your steps and then unpause to watch the action roll out. You can also play it as a standard third-person game in real time but in more complex encounters this is neither feasible nor nearly as much fun as watching a perfectly planned attack execute. In the game you discover different 'functions', which are souls(?) of dead people you come across The interesting thing is that while most other RPGs have designated active and passive abilities, all the abilities in this game, these functions, can be used as active, secondary or passive abilities without restriction. So while for example Spark() lets loose a flurry of explosive shells when used as a primary function, it imbues a splitting and subdividing character to other function when combined with them as a secondary, and as a passive ability it spawns a copy of Red when under attack that'll divert enemy attention for a short time. Each function has different primary, secondary and passive characteristics like this and you're constantly judging whether a function will be more useful as a primary or perhaps augmenting another one. It is this gameplay element which immediately sets it apart from other RPGs, and leads to a potentially infinite loadouts as you can mix and match these functions to find completely different ways of dealing with enemies.
A great game overall. Supergiant Games has quickly become one of my favourite developers and with the kind of work they did on Bastion and now Transistor, I'd be looking forward to their next game with baited breath. And yes, just like Bastion you'll cry at the end of this game as well. I know I did.

As a game from my childhood, I may or may not hold some bias in favor of this game.
However, this will not be evident in my review. Let's answer some questions.
"What is this game?"
Rollercoaster Tycoon is a franchise where the player becomes an amusement park owner with the power to create tracks, customize everything from the terrain and decor to the ride names and colors, and even charging people to use the BATHROOM. Great idea. Think the sims, but without families and more workers and rides.
"Any ACTUAL skills I can get from this game?"
Yes. Balancing out a budget is seen by the money amount you are given in loans. These allow you to buy rides, stands, construct in general, advertise, et cetera. These loans CAN be paid off so you can run the park and not have your money taken away every month for loans. Also, there is keeping things cleaned/organized. The park gets awards based on how you run it, ranging from "Safest Park in The Country" to "Worst Looking Park". In order to keep good PR, you want to hire some handymen who sweep up all the vomit and trash people leave lying around.
"Anything popular come out of this game?"
I WANT TO GET OFF MR.BONES' WILD RIDE
I WANT TO GET OFF MR.BONES' WILD RIDE
I WANT TO GET OFF MR.BONES' WILD RIDE
I WANT TO GET OFF MR.BONES' WILD RIDE
"Why not just RCT3?"
RCT3 is just, eh. It's hard to explain. RCT3 is not a bad game at all, trust me, I own that one as well and its fantastic. But, it will never have the same bouncy feel the early ones do. RCT3 is more calming and orderly. RCT 1 and 2 are bouncy, chaotic, and generally more enjoyable. In the earlier games, you get more of a RCT feel and less of a Sims. The gui in RCT3 even looks like the Sims. Still tho, try both and see which is your cup of tea.
"DLC?"
"Any bugs?"
The game is being updated constantly due to being on steam, mainly in language support from what I've seen, but that doesn't mean its lost some if its old bugs. Sometimes, mechanics pay no attention to rides and they just get fixed on their own by some means. Guests still just wander off park when you delete the path they're on instead of finding another path. RCT was made in 1999, so its not really a suprise when these things happen. You just have to push them in the right direction and it's all figured out (by that I mean pick them up and throw them at the ride's enterance until they get it RIGHT).
"Is the music good?"
You can set music differently for each ride, so if you don't appreciate one song, just pick another!
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Basically, get this game. You will not regret it.
