Where to start? This game is not just entertaining, it is most certainly also a piece of art. The music, atmosphere and dialogue all fit in together perfectly and complement each other. The game is relatively short (~6 hours) but can be replayed and is still entertaining a second time around.
Story-wise, the game is also very good. It took me a while to realise how the story is told, but you are given atricles which explain the stories behind influential people, most of whom you never actually meet in-game, but who you are presumed to know. There is a lot of guesswork involved in figuring out the full story, although certain elements are presented directly through cutscenes.
Graphics are one of the strongest points for this game. All levels are meticulously drawn in fantastic detail, and the game runs like a charm too. In all my playtime so far, I haven't experienced any glitches or bugs and the game has always run as intended, something I cant say about a lot of games nowadays.
Gameplay is original, with classic RPG elements set in a futuristic setting, with your weapon acting as a USB stick of death which can have different functions installed on it. Simultaneousl, the game allows you to plan your actions in advance, adding an element of strategy to it too. The cooldown bar prevents you from over-using this option. As you progress, the enemies are upgraded and become tougher to fight. More points can be gained by installing limiters, which make your life harder but allow for you to level-up faster. Levelling-up gives access to more limiters, functions and as a result, more information on the events unfolding in-game.
The music, which is certainly a strong point of the game, accompanies the gameplay perfectly and is part of the entire experience. As such, the soundtrack should  not be listened to before finishing the game, as it can contain spoilers about events in-game.
Personally, this has had to be my best buy ever, I got it on sale for 4 bucks. If you are planning on playing the game multiple times, I would say even paying the full price for the game is worth it, although for the price you get relatively little play time.
TL;DR
Pros:
-Graphics
-Music
-Story (and ending)
-Setting
-Gameplay
-Good replay value
Cons:
-Relatively short (~6 hours)
-Regular price is a bit high
I havent even scratched the surface of how much i love this game, but I'll stop here and let you decide whether your wallet can warrant this purchase. Trust me, If you enjoy RPG's, you'll love this.

The skill system is just really amazing. Every skill can be used in three ways: As an active skill, as an addition to another active skill altering its effect, or as a passive. Transistor's an odd one. Odd, but definitely pretty. I was expecting Bastion 2, and I KINDA, SORTA-ish got it, but ultimately Transistor is a whole different beast altogether with great ideas of its own, even if the combat isn't as fast as its predecessor.
The biggest difference between this and Bastion is the "Turn()" system, which freezes time and give you the opportunity to queue up a list of actions, not unlike VATS from Fallout. Like VATS, you'll have to wait to use it again, but unlike VATS, movement can be queued as well, which makes it useful to get out of a hairy situation, at the expense of the cooldown, which prevents you from attacking or using Turn() again until it is available again.
Turn() and the subsequent cooldown from using it will be something not everyone's going to like, but it can be largely ignored in favor of the real-time combat (if you're gud), which is comparable to Bastion before it. My favorite aspect of the combat, however, are the Functions(), which you can think of as modular, customizable attacks. You can combine attack properties to create more powerful Functions() at the expense of combat options, or sometimes even movement options.
Whole load of stuff to talk about there, but at this point you'd learn more about it when you play. My eyes liked it, my ears liked it, and I am compelled to dive right back in for New Game +.

This is definetely the promised land after a long time of thirsty waiting for new land in the rts genre! Despite everything that you can say about the game, if you already played everything, if "you had it all but you wanted more", you will just LOVE this game!
If you understand the game, you will never have problems with the issues that some of the reviewers have. (And you will never want to drop the game anymore).
The Problem is to come to that point. Just like Wargame Red Dragon or Act of Aggression, you need to give the game a chance, it is a bit rough and also difficult to win at the beginning, but if you survive the first 30 hours learning the way this game works, the push backs that new players suffer, be it in the multiplayer, in the campaign or with things that seem boring in the first minute, become MOST excitning once you made your lesson with that.
You are not powerless. What you get stomped with at start, is what you can also give out at the game! And that makes a heck lot of fun! You feel so powerful and destroying things feels SO GOOD!
If you learned your own bandit's tools, the units you loose do not hurt you anymore, but you just give back what you receive, you dont need to take the punch and allow it to rest on you, but revenge yourself!
Somebody is spamming you with Rocket artillery? Revenge yourself!
Somebody is crushing you relentlessly? Revenge yourself!
The campaign gives you the loss 2 minutes before you win or the AI is laughing down on you, is relentlessly after you? (It really does!) - Revenge yourself!
And as you do, the game becomes great!
If you have a bit trouble with the seemingly high difficulty? 1. The difficulty vanishes, it doesn't stay (for longer, in some ten's of hours you solved the problem).
2. The boot camp gives you a soft way to learn. Much better than any Wargame or Act of Aggression.
3. If you think that the Boot camp is not enough for you, aim for the Deluxe edition, because the Tactical guide and the Battle log give you a helpful strategical discussion about ALL the maps and more important ALL the divisions, to help you further getting into multiplayer. Discovering all 18 Division can take some time. You can do it alone, and its fun, but if you want quickly into multiplayer, speed things up, TAKE the additional help to get a solid foot.
So as you understand the game, your concerns with it will proof more and more wrong, and you get rewarded with a finally fresh game after 10-15 years of not so much innovation, besides the old generals, company of heroes, and tiles that are good, but played until the end of the world, you are SO happy to finally get water again after a LONG waiting time, especially with the missing C&C games from earlier and other either missing or too narrowly considered sequels of BIG hopes of the genre.
"you had it all but you wanted more"
If you dont get enough content with this game, which is actually very solid, but you wished for so much more of that, (Campaign is a good start - but - you think that its still far from enough!) - then listen to this song ...
... because the song describes the situation. :-) It really hits for me! - So when you are lacking content, then its more probable that you get it with taking the start than taking it not, because the developers do rather listen to what the people want than they do not, with the power that they have.
The game may have some childhood illnesses (heck no!) - but if you think so, then its much less than anything else in the genre.
The multiplayer topic that people are concerned about is one that was already SOLVED in the beta! (you can play small games, but large games get disconnects... this will surely be fixed in few weeks).
If you ask me, you definetely get the promised land that you were looking for. There are just some last preparations to be made for full enjoyment.
LOOK into the music I mentioned above. It REALLY feels like the situation if you played RTS for 20 years like me and it took SO long for another island to take.
Taking the island earlier will heal more than taking it later.
I did really get some deficides the months before the game, that no other title could give me.
So, if "you have it all, but you wanted more", then this is the approach to improve the situation, if you dont take the approach, it will rather become worse.
So, go beyond the horizon and enjoy the next generation of rts, because you will miss it!

Where to begin? RollerCoaster Tycoon is arguably the best tycoon game of all time. The game's development was mostly credited to only one man (Chris Sawyer), and was released in 1999. There were four games that defined my childhood. The Sims, Age of Empires II, Dungeon Keeper 2, and this.
RollerCoaster Tycoon truly gives you the power to make exactly the kind of amusement park you want to build. Even in the scenarios, it largely feels like a free building game; the game does not ask you to do anything you don't want to do. For example, instead of asking you to build a park based on nothing but rollercoasters like some games might have implemented, Rollercoaster Tycoon simply plops you down on a plot of land and basically says, "Get this many guests and have a good park rating in three years. Have fun and buh-bye!" This game should be truly applauded for being a tycoon game that is not only great fun, but never turns into a chore by forcing you into situations where you feel you're only doing something to beat a level. It gives you an end goal, and it's up to you, the player, to decide exactly how you'll get there.
The game allows you to build your own rollercoaster, water slide, log flume, monorail, railroad (and many more) designs from scratch, which gives you endless possibilities in each level (and you will be playing levels over and over again simply for the fun of doing them multiple ways). You can build these rides around one another, underground, over water...there are few limitations. You can also decide what color themes each ride has (or not), even down to making each car in a rollercoaster train a different color. Also, put shops and food stalls around your park and decide how much to charge. You can even charge for guests to use the bathroom, bringing out the greedy capitalist in each of us (I usually make a profit over running costs with my bathrooms, charging just $0.10 per visit).
You can even name guests and track them, which brings another level of fun to an already ridiculously great game. Read a guest's thoughts, pick him up and drop him in front of a ride you think he'll like, see what things he's bought from your park that are in his inventory. Hey, you can even drop him in a lake if he's so angry he's potentially messing with your park rating and drown him. It's up to you!
RollerCoaster Tycoon is also, in my opinion, better than its sequels. Other than some rides not being available in some levels, it will never revoke your abilities. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, there were levels where you had to meet a scenario goal without charging any entry fee for your park, for example, which only ended up taking freedom from the player's hands while pushing itself into the "chore tycoon" category. RollerCoaster Tycoon never crosses that line.
In summary, RollerCoaster Tycoon is a fantastic classic game that is perfect as it is. While the graphics may be simplistic by today's standards, it would be simply ignorant to pass up the game because of it. This game is fun, relaxing, rewarding, timeless, and close to flawless. If you don't yet own this game, pick it up. Otherwise, the only one who is missing out is you. ;)

I can understand every bad ending for this game, but I would like everyone to consider that this game is a bit more than just getting rejected over and over. It's a bit of a life lesson game.
Go into this game thinking of the girl who got away. The girl who was the "one-time" memory girl. In a way, this game is theraputic. We all have an "Emily" in our lives. Go into this game thinking of that girl and you'll understand. I highly recommend that you keep trying to get with Emily. Whatever conclusions you come to about the game are you own.
Spoilers here, so if you want to stop reading go ahead but let me continue on.
...
...
...
So as every other reviewer says, "Thanks for letting me get friendzoned." "Friendzone simulator" this game is a bit more of, "Look, the winning move with that girl who got away, your "Emily" is to let it go. Let it end. You'll probably play this game once. You'll get a bad ending, you'll say, "Okay, let me try again." You'll try again and once again, no emily. You can keep trying and it'll never happen. You decide to be a total jerk. Emily decides to not talk to you. By the end of it, you'll realize that really the only winning movie is to get to the last chapter, let Emily be done with you and you need to be done with Emily. Let me repeat that.
You need to be done with Emily. That's it. There's no changing it, everything goes the same way kind of like with that one girl who did friendzone you. The point of the game is to get over it and live your life. You can make all the choices you want but it'll always end the same way. You had your moment with her, let it go. Either you kissed in high school or you had sex in college, it's always the same and she's always going to feel bad about it because each time was never a romantic thing.
Let's get real, you were always just instant messaging her, was it really going to end up anywhere on that? Consider the other situations, all in all, things will never change because of all the circumstances in place. Emily is who she is. Your differeing educations are what they are. Your both living different lives and somehow feel like you can bring it together and make it work, but can it really?
I highly recommend looking into yourself as you play this game and realize that there are things we can change and things we can't change. We can hope to have do-overs all the time and that won't happen. This game is the closest you can get but the results are always the same. Here are the winnning moves, or thoughts...
Let what happens happen. Your choices are your own. Even though they're controlled by an incredibly limited game, they are still your own choices.
Remember that you did it though, you still got with her. You may not have her as a romantic partner, but Emily did happen. Even if it was only for one moment, even if it didn't go anywhere. You still did it.
Realize that being the nice guy and being the bad guy both typically end up the same way and don't matter at all in the scope of this game. In a way, you take away that nothing matters in the scope of this game.
Lastly, I think you can actually learn something from Emily. Emily HAD a crush on you, there's no changing that. You two have been friends for a while, but that's just it, friends. She tells you she'd rather not dwell on the past, so listen to that. Don't dwell on the past.
Again, could it have really worked with the two of you going to different schools? You're trying to keep a flame alive while both standing a considerable amount of distance away from it.
In the end, I think this game is more therapy than it is a game. So go into it, with that in mind. Go into it with your "Emily" in mind and leave the game feeling like a better person.

I quite loved the potential for this game, but in practise it is horribly disapponting!
My first playthrough went fine, pretty basic management fare but then a raider showed up and I discovered that the 'security' crew assignments I'd made meant people couldn't last two seconds against the lone raider..
Alright then, it was the first go and in tutorial so I can accept an hours play lost and decided to start a new game.
First realisation, there was no "this will erase your data" or "do you want to save" warning. Surprising and not great, but as said, I hadn't planned to anyway so I went ahead with a new real start.

My plan... reassign every crewmen to security and overwhelm in numbers! XD
Not great I know.. but it worked, though highly tiresome to have to remember and reassign everyone back to their old jobs as you can't assign saved positions to default back to.
Then of course, things went bad again...
I find a derelict ship, so badly laid out it could've been a rushed post-battle vessel from Galaxy Truckers.
So of course, I decide to tear everything out as salvage materials.
Unknown to me, one crew decided to remove the ships oxegen generator and then the door of another room from the inside.. leaving him stuck and likely gormless, as there was no notification of him being stuck.
I'll admit a possibly mistake on my part: Not painstakingly watching and assigning each item removed one at a time, but when I tried that previously the crew had a habit of just heading off to bed or returning to my base for a minute to build some shelves I'd requested another builder to build, before coming back.. which is why this time I just left them to it.
Anyway, I found Mr.Gormless and got him to let himself out of the room but before he got any further the oxegen in the ship got too low and it turns out people panic when they realise the oxegen is low (fair enough I'm sure).
Unfortunately, this panic was apparently too much to allow the builder to obey my orders to rebuild an oxegen generator.
Close to frustration I see my second builder heading over in a space suit to save the day..
Unfortunately, Gormlessness is clearly contagious as our superhero stepped out of the airlock, went into a panic himself, rushed back into the airlock and flushed himself into space...
So yea, there you have it. My adventures in Spacebase DF-9. I advise you against having any of your own.

I'm sure everyone knows this, but I must include it on my review. This game has been abandoned by the developers.
The developers are also expecting modders to finish the game for them...but didn't make a workshop compatability...*facepalm*. Seriously devs? so at the moment, there are very few mods out there and they are scattered all over the internet, and google search is no help.
However, there is a new mod called "unoffical patch" to fix some bugs and add some features. I recommend you download that mod or be greeted with bugs apocalypse.
Now lets talk gameplay.
I don't know what they normally call them, settlers? austronaut? pawn? I'll just name it "people".
Unfortunately, you can't move your people, which can be very annoying when raiders are on sight.
You can assign them up to 9 jobs, some people are more skilled on certain job and also enjoy/hate certain job.
The jobs are;
Builder: self explanatory
Technician: maintain and fixes objects
Miner: self explanatory
Security: shoot hostile enemy, and follow security beacon that you can set.
Bartender: Tends the bar which increase happiness.
Botanist: tends the garden.
Scientist: Make researches to unlock things.
Doctor: Heal and cure diseases/illness
Janitor: Clean corpses
Unassigned: default
People have needs, and they can go up and down shown on a graph. I don't know what most of these does to the person.
Duty, Social, Morale, Stuff, Energy, Hunger, Fun. Those are the 7 needs of a person.
People also have "thoughts" that you can read. Some of them are about friends and enemy they made, an object they built, or even a certain doom they are about to encounter. Thoughts really define them and I enjoy pausing the game and reading them.
They also have a nice hand drawn avatar so you know what they look like and perks, if they have low self esteem or they are anxious, etc.
Each person really is different from the rest and it's amazing how much detail they have. It's ashamed this game is abandoned.
Now let's talk about building.
There are 13 rooms you can build, and they are;
Airlock: In and out of the space station
Life Support: For placing Oxygen machine
Reactor: for powering the entire space station
Refinery: smelting rocks into matter (money)
Residence: Build beds to increase population limit
Pub: increase happiness
Garden: Grow food
Fitness: gym
Research: build research table for scientist
Infirmary: Hospital
Brig: prison
Command: Threat monitoring
Unzoned: plain old room
Each of these rooms have certain objects that can only be placed on that room. All objects (and wall/floor) cost matter to build.
Matter can be obtained by mining rocks and smelting it on a refinery machine.
To build a room, you need to inclosed it with walls and floors. If a wall or a floor is destroyed, and a person is in that room, they will be sucked into the vacume of space and die.
Walls/floors and objects can be destroyed from astroids and raiders.
There are random encounter in the game.
There are people that you can communicate with that randomly pops up (when they are near you).
If you respond to their message, then you can either gain a person or be targeted by raiders.
This is the risk you need to think about before accepting their calls.
There are also an actual spaceship that shows in your game. You can either send your security (via security beacon) or leave it alone until it leaves the game.
Spacebase DF9 had potentials, but its been abandon before it can even fly. I really wish someone would make a similar game. SOMEONE PLEASE!
That being said, would I recommend this game? Not on full price. Buy this game when it's 90% on sale.

First up, I will say that I have personally enjoyed playing it overall, despite the many gripes I have. However, the sheer quantity of gripes means I simply cannot in good conscience recommend the game to others.
To put it simply, the game is really, really hard, because the AI is awful and the game hardly gives you a chance to recover from one raider attack to the next. I literally end up with 10s of bodies littered around the inside and outside of the space-station because the medical staff (who are supposed to clean these bodies up) do so at a slower rate than new bodies are generated. Your station crew love attacking eachother due to unhappiness, with no obvious way of resolving their unhappiness. Your non-security personnel love to run directly into the line of fire of the raider boarding party, whilst your actual security personnel will slowly amble over from the other end of the base, even though you put down a beacon more than 30 seconds ago.
However, the fact the game is hard due to the rubbish AI is, I think, what makes me enjoy it. I can build a successful space-station despite the crew being my worst enemy.
The game also, in general, feels unfinished - which is probably not surprising because, despite what Double Fine Productions may tell you, it simply isn't. They basically cancelled the game and released a Version "1.0" which did tidy up some loose ends but by no means all of them, nor did it add any sorely-needed late-game content.

One word: Powerful. This game takes something seemingly boring, checking papers at an immigration post, and creates a compelling narrative. Not only does the game make you think about your mistakes, but about your choices as well. Do I let this woman get reunited with her husband, when she has a missing ID card? Do I report this man for human trafficking? It’s all up to you and your morality.
Your choices have real consequences. Your actions matter. The deeper you get into the game, the more you learn about the world the game sets you in. You learn about each country, their government, small and large details. You feel as if you are in a real world, and each person is real. There are
different endings, which are all based on your choices.
The real nail-biting part of this game is in each inspection. As you play, more and more rules are added. Maybe now, tickets are invalid, and you need an entry permit to enter the country, or maybe forged documents now appear. After each check, there’s always that dreaded feeling of being notified that you inspected incorrectly, and must face charges. You are always on your toes, because, with your limited money, and your need to support your family, each mistake could mean life or death. The compelling gameplay fits well with what the game presents to you.
If any of this sounds remotely interesting to you, I recommend you give this game a try. It’s a puzzle-ish game, with a unique concept never done before. If you are into investigation games, mystery games, or puzzle games, this is one worth trying out.

The game features three single-player campaigns of four missions each; the conflicts are large in scale, but they are presented in a linear order with no grand strategy on a large map of the region as in the later Wargame titles. Skirmish games against the AI and online contests are also available. There is a good number of detailed maps that scale according to the number of players. Before each match, you must design your battlegroup, choosing units (recon, infantry, tank, anti-tank, air, anti-air, artillery, and support) based on the division you are commanding. The two new innovations of Steel Division are compelling: three phase gameplay and the frontline. Each match is divided into three phases (A, B, and C) that determine which units in your battlegroup can be called into action (typically, more numerous and more powerful units can be brought in later). This adds another layer of strategy to battlegroup deck building. The frontline is displayed on the map (and used to determine victory points), giving a rough indication of where enemy units are. This is a much more effective mechanic for determining map control than placing a command unit in an arbitrary zone. Steel Division retains much of the game mechanics of Wargame (suppression, line of sight, supply, ballistics, units automatically attacking and finding cover), but operates at a slower overall pace and is thus more accessible. The AI is a quite capable opponent and will provide a good challenge offline. Through its approachable gameplay and various innovations, and despite a lackluster campaign mode, Steel Division: Normandy 44 improves upon the formula established by the Wargame series and is a must-play World War II real-time strategy game.

Steel Division is an awesome experience where you can follow one pilots journey or an entire companies war. The scale is unprecedented especially in 10v10 matches. The campaign is short, but creates interesting scenarios that make you think differently about how you play. It runs well, the gameplay is tight, multiplayer is extremely fun and the attention to historical detail is excellent.

INTRO
Silent Service is a nautical simulator set in the World War II where you have to shoot your way on different convoy and patrol missions on the Pacific Ocean, destroying all kinds of ships, cargo, destructors, tanks and others.
IN-GAME
You can first select the practice option where you have 3 still ships ready to be destroyed. I advise to read the manual and learn the basics and terminologies before going into the convoy missions option so you don't get frustrated the first time you launch it.
CONTROLS
The manual doesn't come with the keyboard controls for this version, IBM version is kinda like this one. I managed to find them pressing all the keys. That's why I'm saving you time and writing them here, because nobody did. When you launch practice or the convoy missions, you'll start on the conning tower menu, where you can choose between the various battle stations.
BATTLE STATIONS KEYS: "F1": Map ("Z" Map zoom+ ,"X": Map zoom-), "F2": Bridge (Check visibility), "F3": Periscope, "F4": Instruments and gauges, "F5": Damage status, "F6": Ships sunk info, "F8": End the mission.
CONNING TOWER SCREEN MENU: "SPACE": Brings you back to the Conning tower screen menu.
Then, you can move your submarine with these ones:

Dissapointing....  Back when the game was in early development I fell victim to its "appeal".  I saw a game with potential and I was all and all hopeful.  In those ealier days the game was riddled with bugs and glitches, and when I found out they were dropping the game and rushing development, I was hopeful they would eliminate those bugs and glitches in the game.  So as a review of the official release of version 1.06 here is the breakdown.  I'll have a simple review and more in depth... or in this game... anger driven review...
----- Simple ----
The game is crap... It had so much potential but since it got the axe and a speedy release... it has so many issues.  I honestly tried to play the game again... but yet I wasn't able to play longer than 10 minues.  I would not recommend this game to anybody unless it's less than a dollar or given to you free.  It's buggy... rough to control, and just honestly crap.
----- Angered Version -----
Graphics:
As this is not a "Highly graphical" game I wouls say they are acceptable.  The sprites perform actions that is befiting, and nothing to standoutish.  However in aspect of gameplay the "isometric" angle makes the game difficult to know exactly what is going on.  In the typical fashion the walls disappear in a way to allow you to see in the rooms, however being able to roatate the camera would be nice.
Gameplay:
This is where the game loses me.  Although the controls aren't "hard" they are difficult in there own way.  I've played many builder games, and most games play similarily with minor adjustments to the controls.  In more recent terms since the era of shooter games almost every game depends upon the W-A-S-D model.  This game doesn't stray too far fram that idea and it feels comfortable... at least until you start building.  At that point the game takes a turn for the worst.  Edge scrolling doesn't feel like it's in existence, so your dependant upon the WASD model, but once you open the construction menu, foul language fills the mouth as when you click with your mouse to select the item and press "D" to move your contruction item changes.  As soon as that construction menu comes up the game shifts from a comfortable WASD model to a point and click model.  This wouldn't be a problem if they didn't establish you could use the WASD in the first place....   So that is annoying.  Then it gets worse.  As you play you decide to speed up the game, and most games using some button near the WASD (tab, 123, something) changes the game speed, but in comes the mouse model, and you have to click the speed options.  Now I wouldn't have an issue with this, if it wasn't for the fact that when any ship arrived or any notification appears the game switches back to speed 1.... and DOES NOT RETURN.....I find it quite annoying because I'll be in the middle of waiting for my characters to build a room... then all the sudden a message... then the question, "Why are my guys moving so slow"... then oh gotta click that speed... then the game goes NOPE... and another message.  It just continually pesteres you until you get so angry that you give up.
AI:
I don't normally judge AI as it's always an issue with all games.  It is always about finding that right balance between what the computer needs to process and what the character prioritizes.... unfortunately it appears that this game said, "F*$k it... have the guys do whatever."  And like loyal programs they do whatever.  You have absolutely no control over the individual character, so when your trying to finish that bed... your have to wait until the game decides... "know what I think I should build that bed."  But at that point your characters are now falling over because they are so tired... that they have no energy... then get depressed and not want to work... so now that bed will never get done.... it annoying the bleeping crap out of me as I was just trying to enjoy the game.
Glitches and Bugs:
Yes I'm bringing it up... as a "fully" released game you would expect most of the bugs and glitches to be taken care of... in fact thats what most of the follow up forums established... but know what.... turns out that your characters get stuck (dumb AI) and because you can't do that they sufficate.... yeah... so just started finished the basic build... airlock... air... and such... but oh no... two of my guys just sat there... doing... NOTHING... could it be AI? probably... but to me that's a bug.   But it's not the worst oh no... in my honest to goodness no opinion try I got "invaded" another ship attached itself to me, and I was assulted.  After killing the AI I noticed, Hey there is a gun outside...  Then I slowly watched one of my security guards go out to take care of it.... two shots later dead.... ok..... so what does the AI do?  "Well he's dead... probably should take care of that... but naa...."  Guess where my miners had to go to get resources?  Right in the line of fire.... so there goes two of my miners...  Well maybe I can control a security... oh wait can't control the guys so whoops... maybe set a security point for them.... nope... dead... dead and dead.....  I'm happy they incorperated the guns for defences... but when a gun is established as enemy and even if you took over everything it appears that that guns still acts hostile....  My frustrations knows no bounds.
Overall the game is fine.... just fine.... not great... not good... just fine.... if you want something new to distract you for 10 minutes... here is the perfect game for you... but don't buy unless it's on uber sale.... and by uber sale like... I dunno $0.99 per copy... or heck maybe if the company pays you to play... becuase honestly this game isn't worth anything more.

Ok, I've not put many hours into this game, but I think I can already describe it to you.

***Minor Spoiler ahead***
You are Starkiller. Darth Vader has adopted you after killing your father, because the Force is strong in you. He has trained you for Jedi-killing, until one day the Emperor discover your existence and cast away.
So you will be a dark jedi for the first part of the game (in which at the moment of the review I actually am), but I sense, as the story progresses, that you will find the light...

The urge for writing this review came for the really bad things you will find.
First of all I think that every bug I encountered depends on a disappointing PC port.
-The game is buggy as hell. I think no game other than Alpha Protocol in my library have forced me to restart the pc more than this one.
You will find yourself frustated a lot during the course of the game because every now and then it crashes without a motive.
-In some cases you will fall between the layers of the level. In that case you are forced to restart the mission (if you don't have a previous save).
-The boss battle are terrible. It's the first time in a game that I actually hate to be in a boss fight. The force system depends on you facing the item/character you want to use your powers on. I often couldn't face quickly the boss, and this is a game in which speed is essential.
-The sound is perfect but something has gone wrong, because I can not hear the voice of the actors during the cutscenes (which are crucial to the understanding of the story and actually well-done). So I have to play with my headphones and this actually solved the problem.(???)

In 2007, it was revealed the winner of that years world cricket tournement would be presented with a diamond studded cricket ball with gold trim estimated to be worth $68500. If you've haven't seen pictures of it then go take a look because it is really quite a stunning peice of craftsmanship and artistic design - it is also completely useless and could never be used to play cricket with. Transistor is that cricketball in every way.
Visually Transistor is visually stunning. Gorgeous to look at with a distinctive art-style that clearly had a ton of work put into it. The audio design is pleasing with some great voice acting that puts a wierd spin on the 1920s era with some Tron-esque elements. Unfortunately, the same effort didn't go into the game itself as it is clunky, tedious, short and not at all engaging. How anyone could consider this a good game boggles my mind because I heard of this game from a number of sources as being a great indie title but clearly these people were either bamboozled by the visuals or they have limited experience with this type of game.
In terms of how it works, its a strange mix of real-time and turn-based combat. You can pause the game to chain up lightning fast attacks and movement but when you have used your allocated chunk of time you have to wait for your turn-bar to recharge. During this time you have to run around avoiding attacks or use your abilities that quite often root you to the spot so its better to avoid attacking during this time. As such, it would be a mistake to call this an action-rpg at all. The trouble is that causes combat to move in fits and starts and the limited size of the areas you are contained in during these battles means that tactics really are shallow at best. The ability to mix functions (the games method creating attacks and abilities) is initially interesting but since it doesn't have a distinct offense/defense/support design you are left with all attacks - either ranged, melee or summons. As you can imagine, this means the appeal of this system quickly wears off as you realize your choices only impact the distance at which you need to engage threats.
Speaking of the 'threats'. The game has no memorable encounters. Enemies lack personality and are very limited in variety. There are some 'bosses' but these are just damage sponges rather than being difficult to defeat due to clever design. As I said, all the effort went into the look of the game and the game itself was left as an afterthought causing it to become a tedious and boring mess partly due to how plain the combat is and also due to how it is so linear as you progress from area to area with the game leading you by the nose. So it even lacks any meaningful replay value.
All in all, I could never recommend this game even on sale. It is a diamond ball of eye-candy without substance to its gameplay or the storyline.

I had played this game for a bit in the past, less then a few minutes because I could never figure out how combat worked and would always get killed off from the snail. Then the other night I started it up again and tried playing once more not expecting to get far or play to long. However I found myself playing for over an hour and was able to figure out what I couldn't before, so here is my review on a very awesome game.
The Legend of Grimrock, a game I bought on Steam a couple years ago during the 2012 summer sale event made by
.
The game is an old school RPG that is not turn based but live action. In other words you are able to move, cast spells, select items from your inventory and rest without waiting for creatures to take their turn. As your trying to get your spell cast or looking for a throwing item in your inventory the creature will be attacking you and won't sit there and wait till your done.
I really found this game to have that pen and paper D&D feel to it and I like the idea of selecting the option to not have the game do the mapping as I explore and then I can map it out with graph paper and a pencil (I didn't do this of course).
The character creation screen is very simple with 4 races and 3 classes to choose from.  The inventory and character screen isn't complex or confusing but very intuitive and easy to figure out and understand.
The spell's though are based on symbols and you have to select the right symbols or combination of to cast the spell. I found that you couldn't get the spell unless you found the scroll for the right spell but this could have been because I wasn't selecting the right symbol until I found the scroll.
When venturing through the dungeon your characters will get hungry and there will be a symbol of food in there avatar picture indicating they need to eat. When you kill of creatures they will sometimes leave a meat chunk behind and you will want to get these to eat along with any food things you find along the way.
During combat along the way some of your party member may die, take heart because they are not gone for good. You will be able to access their inventory while dead to. There will be these big blue floating crystals that when touched will restore your party to full health and energy and raid the dead. Remember where these ones are. Once they are used you will have to wait for a bit till it can be clicked on again.
Now as for combat, where I originally had most of my troubles. To attack all you need simply do is right click on your hand under your avatar (wither their is a weapon in it or not). If your a spell caster you will want to keep at least one hand empty for right clicking to bring up the symbol window for spell casting.
When you left click on a throwing weapon it will be attached to your mouse cursor and if you click with it again with your mouse pointer above the midline of the screen (the top half of the window) then it will be thrown. If you click below the midline (bottom half of the screen) then it get dropped on the floor.
This is a keyboard and mouse type game and no controller support.
Now that I have been able to find out something about the game and how combat works, along with the abilities to make your own dungeon's and storyline and the Steam Workshop to try some community based dungeons, The Legend of Grimrock is one game to have in your collection.

As of late we've seen more and more smartphone games get ported over to PC, with mixed results. This is because they're usually saturated in heavy microtransactions, which are very common on the smartphone marketplace. Rarely do we see a port and not see microtransactions, Ravensword: Shadowlands is one of these examples.
The PC Port itself is a mixed bag; it improves its graphical fidelity with improved textures and post effects, re-bindable keys and an improved control scheme which is vastly superior to its smartphone counterpart. That’s where things end; the UI cannot be customised and is very clunky as it's made to be used with limited screen space. Everything in the menus can only be done through mouse clicks, leading to frustrations after continued use.
Animations are clunky, actions feel unresponsive, combat and movement inputs override each other causing unrealistic actions, such as performing an attack followed up by a roll which shows a standing attack animation but you move as if you’re rolling. The RPG elements are very basic, all the talents, stats and gear are simple increase X or Y with no real flare to them, there are no tough options and it’s hard to see your character truly progress.

Legend of Grimrock is one of a very small litter of games that attempts to create a classic dungeon crawler similar to those of the old days such as Dungeon Master and succeeds in not only emulating that style, but updating it enough to make it a refreshing experience for modern gamers, as well as a familiar one.
A feature I found to be charming (as well as terrifying) was the option to play the game on a Classic difficulty that forces you to draw your own maps out on grid paper, much like old pen-and-paper tabletop games. I myself haven't been brave enough to give this playthrough a try yet, but I still find it to be a wonderful option for true gluttons of punishment.
As deeply rewarding as it is challenging, with lots of replay value, and great Steam Workshop options to keep the game new for even the most frequent players, LoG is a for sure winner. I'll be eagerly awaiting the release of the second game, ready to brave the dangers between the dungeon walls once more.

Papers, Please is a very unique indie game made by one talented man named Lucas Pope. It's a great game that will make you happy, sad, and make you feel heartless and dreadful. It's a bit addicting, and a must-own for anyone looking for a challanging game. It is worth your money, and I recommend everyone to play this game!
The game revolves around you. You were selected from the October labor lottery to become the border patrol officer at the Grestin Border Checkpoint at Arstotzka. Everyone that arrives at your counter must present all documentation, and it is your job to validate it. You must check everything, including obvious things like matching pictures, names,  and ID numbers, to very precise things like their height and weight. There's many reasons to deny people, ranging from expired and missing documents, to new rules in your rulebook. You can also arrest and detain people for things such as forged documents, attempting to smuggle contraband or weapons into Arstotzka, or their face being on the most wanted criminals list. Your job is very important, and you must take it very seriously to keep Arstotzka safe.
One thing that I find amazing is the different ways you can play this game. Will you play the strict officer that abides by the book to keep his job intact and will deny anyone that doesn't follow procedures, which include denying people desperately running for their lives? Will you play the heartful officer that will let these people in to save their lives, and help everyone that requests legal help, despite going against protocal? Will you play the corrupt officer that assists criminal organizations and breaks promises you made to put more money in your pocket? There's likely more ways to play Papers Please, but these are the ones I came up with. I played my first playthrough as a mix between the strict officer and the heartful officer, abiding by the book strictly but giving exceptions to a few people that I showed compassion to, and I plan to play the corrupt officer in my next playthrough.
Papers, Please is a fantastic indie game that must be played by everyone that wants a challange. It's a joy to play, and is one of the most unique and interesting games I have ever played.

Papers, Please. Probably (I use this word a lot), the second best indie game I've ever played (The Binding of Isaac is the best). A game that is simple but so addictive that you won't notice the hours flying. This game is a good run if you're stressed playing Counter Strike, Dota or other big game. It's, in some way, fun, easy but you need to think, like, a lot, before you actually give the green stamp, and of course, the storyline is nice, a little short but with more than 5 different endings, so every major point of the story has its other side.
The game is cheap, so it should fit in everybody budget, and it is worth every penny, as it'll take more than 24 hours of game to complete it to its fullest. If you like indie games and games to cool your head after a stressing run, then this is a must play.

Papers Please is a stark look into the brutal nature of an uncaring bureaucracy, and offers a glimpse as to how such systems persist. When you start Papers Please the rules are simple, 'only let in Arstotzkans'. It's an easy rule to follow so you are able to process many people, and keep you family fed. But soon more rules are implemented, it takes longer to process people and you start to make mistakes. You receive citations (too many and you're fired), your pay drops because you cant keep up, and your family suffers. All the while peoples lives are in your hands.  They are fleeing civil war, trying to reunite with long lost family, desperate for work, and you decide their future in 30 seconds because 'five more processed and I can afford medicine for my son'.
You are faced with impossible choices. Do I help these strangers, or throw them under the bus to save my family? Do I try to help end this brutal regime and risk death, or keep my head down to survive another day? And never once does the game tell you if what you are doing is right or wrong, it only shows you the consequences. The terrible, brutal, consequences.
If you ever need an example of games as art, here it is.

Assault Android Cactus is what you get when you cross Touhou and Smash TV... More or less at any rate. It's a twin stick shooter set in the future starring a bunch of androids trapped on a ship filled with homicidal robots. The titular Cactus is an Assault Android sent to investigate why the ship, the Genki Star, shut down contact with its other vessels, and is the type who prefers to let her trigger finger do the talking.
As a result, mayhem, explosions, and heavy weapons fire ensues. With a bunch of other surviving androids along for the ride (more unlocked as you progress through the campaign), there is a lot of action to be had, and a lot of beautiful bullet patterns to be avoided/destroy yourself on whilst you (possibly fail to) eliminate your enemies.
Adding to the challenge of dodging and weaving around gorgeous blooming bullet flowers and huge beam lasers and kamikaze mines and rockets and such, you have to not get too close to enemies which usually have some kind of devastating melee attack which they will attempt to hit you with, keep your battery topped up with battery pickups, and evade/make use of the levels' various hazards and traps...
All of this to a fantastic soundtrack ,and with plenty of EX Options to unlock, which will up the difficulty further if you so wish. Can you S+ rank every level by making sure you never drop your combo and never get knocked down? Can you beat every boss flawlessly before your battery runs out? Can you discover why the robots on board have turned against the humans?
Whilst primarily a single player experience, local co-op exists of up to four players and is purportedly lots of fun (as well it should be). There's also lots of fun things to unlock and even a first person perspective mode if you really want to ramp up the difficulty. Also at only £10.99 it's a real steal!
Get it now, join the fun, blow up robots.

What might seem like a shameless and unoriginal GTA clone on the surface is shown to be unique, fun, and more charismatic with its amazing characters, fun mechanics, and beautiful open world.

Sleeping Dogs reminds me of True Crime: Streets of LA in a few ways and that's a good thing. Instead of taking the GTA approach this open world game focuses more on melee combat and that's where it shines. Fighting mechanics are similar to Mad Max (which I'm told is similar to the Arkham series). There is gunplay and it works well but there isn't as much variety as there is in the melee combat. The driving and racing is very similar to a GTA game but it'll take a little while to get used to Hong Kong traffic.
I never played the original edition on PC but I will say that the Definitive Edition runs smoothly and I rarely had any problems out of it during long play sessions. For achievement hunting this game has a lot to offer. None of the achievements are particularly rage inducing but there is plenty to keep you busy so make sure you're willing to devote the time to this game. Overall, if you're looking for an open world game that's not GTA or Saints Row I would recommend this game. Factorio is an early-access survival crafting game. Those words might frighten the majority of people, and make them think that this is just 'another one of those games', but that's far from the truth.
The goal of Factorio isn't to mine resources just to make tools to mine more resources. While it is true that you need to do mining and crafting, you don't need to do those things yourself. Instead of making pickaxes and mining everything yourself, you can create machines to do the work for you. The machines start off pretty weak (mining drills and furnaces that require fuel to operate), but the game starts to get more and more interesting as you get further in the game. You can get machines that can automatically craft items for you (or your factory) pretty early in the game. In the late game, you can even get robots to automatically build large segments of your factory.
This all sounds pretty boring 'Am I just making the game play itself?', but it's far from boring. The challenge in this game comes from 2 sides. The first side is the enemies that attack your base. Unlike most games, these enemies don't attack you for no reason. As your factory grows, it spews out pollution, which actually attracts the enemies. The second side comes the logistical aspect of this game. Recipies later in the game can require multiple inputs, and it can be quite tricky to route items to their destination if your base is one giant mess.
I would suggest to play the demo if this game before you're going to buy the full version. If you like the demo, you will totally enjoy the full game.

LEGEND OF GRIMROCK is so perfect in its execution of old school retro hack and slash its supernatural. The balance of puzzle difficulty and battling enemies is as perfect as humanly possible. Dungeons are buetifully designed in their retro design ala DUNGEON MASTER. Lighting and shadows give an eerie haunting ambience as they flicker about walls and cast their forms on stone floors. Some times shadows are moving about violently due to some ghastly horror standing in front of a light source about to pounce on my party of four dungeon prisoners trying to survive to earn their freedom.
Monster design and animations are amazing and terrifying. Its like actually being in the world of DUNGEONS AND DRAGONS with familiar classics from the table top games gracing ones eye with their artistic beauty. Running into new enemies is a major adrenaline rush bringing back memories of playing EYE OF THE BEHOLDER etc where part of the reward of continuing was seeing the great looking monsters.
Combat is a strategic joy as giant bats lunge and fly at my party repeatedly as we try to time our acttacks for best effect and hopefully a critical or two. Animations really add to the immersion making one get lost in the excitement of the moment. Alot of times i'll find myself having to acttack from long range or retreat lest my entire party is slaughtered with no one left alive to bring them to huge blue crystals which can bring your fellow adventurers back from the dead.
Sound effects are subtle and all consuming adding to the realism of the experiance with plenty of retro inducing emotional thrills. Its nice for a change to actually hear my characters give a blood curdling scream as they die compared to other rpgs where they hardly give out a whimper. So far the only music i have heard is the intro theme which is fabulous alive with old school adventure as if from a 1980s Conan movie or b-movie. While traveling in dungeons of Grimrock my ears are sweetly embraced by spooky ambient sound effects.
Character creation and developement is handled very well with a comfortable amount of detail to make each adventurer in ones party feel unique. You can add points to strength, dexterity etc and also put points into certain character based skills only available to certain types of characters. So certain skills will only be available to a particular class such as a rogue and others to a mage etc.
If you loved old school hardcore rpgs back in the day such as Dungeon Master and Black Crypt you owe it to your happiness to get LEGEND OF GRIMROCK. There really isnt any excuse. Just pick up a STEAM card at your local game shop such as GAMESTOP or BEST BUY add some money and go buy the game online without worrying about the hassle of credit cards etc.
LEGEND OF GRIMROCK. Truly it is legend.

TL; DR: It's a free game, just try it.  You don't need reviews to help you avoid losing money on this one :)
Each match you make in this match-3 summons adorable troops to fight their way through enemies who are also adorable, and who bleed a lot.  Even the skeletons.  The bigger the match, the more units are called.  A level is finished when your troops have destroyed all four gates in their path.  Each level may work in one of two ways: either you're allowed to make a certain number of matches at whatever pace you like, or you need to make as many as you can within a time limit.  These are the two play modes mentioned in a few other reviews, but note that the mode is chosen by the level rather than by the player.  At the end of each level, whether you win or not, you receive coins that can be used to upgrade your units to make them even better at causing their adorable enemies to bleed and die :D
After you run out of moves or time, your units continue to fight until the gate is destroyed (at which point, unless it was the final gate, you receive more moves/time).  This transitional period is no longer tedious thanks to the addition of a fast-forward button; and if that ~3 seconds is still too long for you to wait, it seems to now be possible to remove focus from the app window without having the game pause (i.e. the battle continues even if you click away to another window).
Is there a lot of grinding in this game? You betcha.  It it excessive? Perhaps.  I found it to be a bit too much, and i actually like grinding.  I think that this game may be better suited to its mobile origins, since time spent waiting for a bus or an appointment or whatever is less goal-focused in the player brain.  If you're not into PC grinding, but enjoy making cute little cartoon characters slaughter each other, why not try the mobile version? I'm guessing that's also free, but i'm too lazy to look into it to be able to tell you for sure.
As for the microtransactions, i found the ones in this game to be quite inoffensive.  Cash is NOT required to progress or win, and the player is NOT asked for the truly "micro" microtransactions you see in some games where they ask for $0.99 to continue playing a single level.  You are offered the
of paying -- as of this writing -- between 1 and 30 USD for gold coins (which are gray, for some reason) that can be used to upgrade your units.  You don't wanna pay? It's cool, you can earn silver-colored gold by grinding.  $30 may be a bit ambitious of them to expect, but i found the $8 option agreeable enough that i went for it, simply because i felt i'd gotten $8 worth of enjoyment out of the game.  TBH, if i'd paid the money just to get the coins, i might have been a wee bit disappointed by the mileage i got out of them.  But i was viewing it as a Voluntary Entertainment Tax, so it all worked out.
It is true that the difficulty takes a sharp, steep incline somewhere in the teen levels.  That's the bad news.  But you can turn this into good news if you consider the fact that when you fail a level more than twice in a row, you get double the coins; connect this with the need for grinding, and the clever player may see in this an opportunity to cut his or her grinding time in half...
The two bugs i did experience (using a Mac, if that matters) did not interfere with gameplay in any serious way -- in fact, one actually helped me, and the other might not have even been a bug.  The one closest to being "bad" was that in levels above 50, destroying the 2nd gate doesn't give you more moves/time; this did not prevent me from getting 3 stars on any of them, but it did make it a bit more challenging, so this may have been by design for all i know.
One of the nice things about this game is how well the two modes (move-limited vs.  time-limited) are handled.  In move-limited mode, there's a slight delay after you make a match before you can make another one, which is probably as it should be.  This delay is just long enough for the pieces on the board to settle, which really just has the effect of only allowing you to make one move at a time.  In time-limited mode, this delay is
present; you can make your second move while the board is still settling from your first one.  Not only does this speed things up, it allows you to make what i'll call "mid-air matches," since i don't know if there's actually a word for this thing i'm about to describe.  Of course you know that when you make a match, the matched pieces disappear, and the pieces above the gap fall down to fill it in.  In Battle for Blood, you have a split second before this fall happens to grab one of those pieces which is about to fall and use it for another match.  This allows you to effectively move pieces small distances across the board to make bigger, fancier matches than you might otherwise be able to make.  Also faster.
The game ends a little abruptly at level 60, and i say "abruptly" not because the game seems too short, but because there's no fanfare or congratulations or cute little animations or anything.  You finish level 60 just like every other level, and then you know the game's over only because there aren't any more levels after that.  It appears the developer had originally planned for more, but it also appears that this plan may have been ditched.  It's a shame, because i would love to have more.  If i hadn't already paid my Voluntary Entertainment Tax, i would even say i'd
for more levels as DLC -- IF they were to toss me some kind of meaningless kudos for completing the first 60 levels.  I'm not made of stone here.
Seems to me that the addition of an endless mode would be the simplest way to make this game a little more PC-friendly while simultaneously mitigating the problem of excessive grinding.  If each gate in this mode were to give a progressively larger coin reward, players would be able to amuse themselves by trying get as far as possible, and when they were done, they'd have a little chunk of change they could use to get further next time.

This game is a match the tiles kind of game, similar to Candy Crush, Chuzzle, Bejewelled etc. However, there's one thing that's different - when you match a minimum of three tiles you summon a unit, the icons on the tile represent a type of unit, you can summon two units by matching 4 tiles, 3 by matching 5 and it's possible to summon more if you're lucky.
There are 60 different levels and 12 units, the difficulty increases quite soon after you reach the double digit levels, fortunately, there's an upgrade system you can utilize to improve unit stats, the effectiveness of items as well as the health of your 'base'(a wagon) and the amount of coins you receive when matching coin tiles. Upgrades do cost quite a bit, you can either buy more coins with real life money or slowly grind for upgrades(despite the grinding being rather slow, each 'match' can take seconds to minutes) and yes you can replay completed levels.
Quite a fun matching game but you have to be quick as there are time/match limits that vary with different levels.

Assault Android Cactus is a twin stick shooter that sees you progress through an overtaken space ship destroying hordes of enemies and bullet hell style bosses.
There is a selection of robots to choose between each with a very different set of available weapons ranging from the fairly standard gun of Cactus to the more bizarre bladed helicopter of Aubergine. Each character also has a more powerful weapon that can be used to destroy large enemies more quickly but this weapon can only be used on a rechargeable basis.
Each level is completed while constantly trying to look to recharge your battery which constantly depletes. This means that each level is essentially completed against the clock and death acts as a time delay rather than an all-out game ender. I love this mechanic and think it is the best idea to happen to the shooter or bullet hell genre in recent memory and I hope more developers take this idea on board as it makes death… something that happens frequently… into a managed penalty rather than the end criteria.
The game is extremely accessible to casual players and can be blown through in a couple of hours but achieving high scores can easily become an obsession as you look for the best strategies and best androids to complete each stage.
The level design is superb with platforms, conveyor belts and rearranging floors making the games level unique and engaging in what could otherwise be a repetitive game. The enemy design is equally as interesting with particular stand out types being the dog type androids who ground you in place and the swarms of insect androids that appear from the destroyed android hives.
The endgame in AAC sees you push for increasingly higher and high scores to gain better rankings. Gaining an S rank in a level, involves completing it without a single knock-down. S+ involves no knock-downs but also killing every enemy in the level in one long successful chain. This is equivalent to getting perfect in a guitar hero game or never missing a beat.
Overall the game is a joy to play and definitely one of my favourite twin stick shooters of all time. An extremely varied roster and wonderful charming presentation makes this a must buy for fans of the genre.

I've never played a twin stick shooter before. The closest thing I've played are Touhou games, and I was never that good at them (I think I've only ever beaten a couple in Easy mode). So, as a casual noob to this genre, I have to say Assault Android Cactus was loads of fun, providing challenging but fun gameplay that was smooth as silk and high on adrenaline. The action never stops, thanks to a forgiving health mechanic where you can take a few number of hits before you die, and if your health is low, all you have to do is not get hit for a few (felt like five?) seconds and your heath regens to full. Also, when you switch weapons you get a few frames of invulnerability. This allows you to dive for those power ups and, more importantly, batteries.
The battery mechanic encourages aggressive gameplay, since your power constantly drains and the only way to get more power is by killing enemies for battery drops. If your power drains to zero, it's game over. This gives you the perfect excuse to go ham on those mobs. Besides batteries, there are three types of power ups that drop. If left on the ground, the power ups change between each of the three types. So if you want a specific power up that isn't currently on the ground, you can run around killing mobs until the power up changes to what you want (it feels like five seconds or so between each change). This becomes an interesting tactic as you balance killing high priority mobs with power up timings, taking into account how many seconds it takes to run to that mob, kill it, and run back in time so the power up has changed to the one you want.
There are nine playable androids (four to start, the others unlocked as you go), each with their own unique primary and secondary weapons. All of them are a joy to play, though I found myself gravitating towards three or so favorites. The story is light and fun spirited. It's easy to get behind the androids even with the dearth of character development, simply due to how cute and enthusiastic they are. The campaign took me about 5 to 6 hours to complete, including all the fails and retries for some of the harder levels (the final boss was the hardest, taking me about 15 attempts to beat). But, as I said earlier, I'm a complete noob to this genre, so it will probably take you less time. I personally found the difficulty level to be that sweet spot of challenging but still enjoyable. Some of the bosses have bullet patterns that resemble Touhou games, but with maybe half the bullet density.
There is a decent amount of replayability to be found in the Infinity Drive game mode, as well as trying to beat your high score on the campaign levels. The gameplay is slick, the soundtrack is amazing, and the level design is beautiful-- all this, along with the ability to choose between nine different androids, makes replaying levels a blast. That feeling when you S+ a level is quite satisfying as well.
As someone who is not really into these types of games, I really enjoyed AAC. The gameplay is smooth and addicting, the sound and level design are top notch, the characters are lovable, and the difficulty level is just perfect in my experience. Highly recommended.

An interesting variation on the match 3 genre, Battle for Blood doesn't simply have you matching pieces on a board in order to get points; but rather, it has you building an army with the matches you make. Before each level, you get to choose which "troops" to take with you (each with their own abilities, and specific odds of showing up in the board); once you start playing, you get a Bejeweled-like board with a small combat area on top. Each time you make a match, you'll summon troops to fight the enemy on said combat area; like any match-3 games, higher matches give you better bonuses (in this case, more units per match). You can also get coins during each match to upgrade your units, and there's also special abilities you can use to help them with the fight.
I must say, I was kind of impressed with this game. While I'll admit this one is very simple (and really feels like a mobile port, all the way to the game window being similar to a phone screen in terms of width/height ratio), the concept really interested me, and I could see a more "complex" game built around it. I should also say that this game is very good to pass the time, as it's not really hard, it offers some casual fun.
Well, in my opinion, this game is recommendable for some light, casual fun, when you just want to relax a bit. There are better games in the match-3 genre, of course, but this one's free, so that's a plus.

Battle for Blood - Epic battles within 30 seconds! is a game developed by YFC games. The game is a mobile port, the mobile game have been released 3 months before the pc version. The game is a gem matching game,match3 if you want to call it that, with a twist. With each match you summon troops or get coins, more complex matches getting more troops or coins, with which you must defeat the enemy troops and destroy their base to clear the level. The game have 60 levels, each level having few "zones"( they are something like enemy camps, and at the end of the level a fortress ), two levels modes: limited number of moves or time limit, getting aditional moves/time after each "zone" is finished.
The game have 12 kind of troops, from which you start with 3(I could say 4 as the first troop unlocks after you finish the first level) and unlock the others along your gameplay. There are also 5 items, you get 5 of each when you unlock it, if you use them all you can purchase others with coins. There is also an upgrade system with which you can upgrade your troops, items, your camp life and the ammount of coins received when you make a coins match.
The game have microtransactions which only give the option to buy coins. The game can be completed without them.
The sounds are fitting, although they use some from their previous game, they added more for this one.
The game doesn't have a story, you just pass through levels.
The bad side of the game is that around level 15 the difficulty sky-rockets and you end up grinding some time. After you get your troops level to mid-max range you will progress easier to the end of the game. At least for me, finished the game on my third time, the first two times abandoning it because the huge difficulty raise mentioned earlier and the loss of the save files, which are stored in registry, from OS replacement.
If you interested in this aspect, the game features both trading cards and achievement, but where the game is free to play for card drops you need to invest 9$ or you can just use the booster crafting implemented by steam some time ago.
Altought the third time I kinda enjoyed the game, I will have to give this game a negative review because of the huge difficulty increase that I mentioned earlier and the lack of resolution change.

This game's combat system just got better and better, it's a shame the game wasn't bigger.
The game gives you an interesting way to control your progression that is not just another point allocation system.  The game also provides a cool way for you to control the difficulty.
One thing I was worried about going in was that the game was going to be a push-over, and maybe it could be, but the game gives you something called "limiters".  Limiters are basically power-ups that you are giving the the enemies and/or handicaps that you are giving yourself in a fight that can cause a variety of effects ranging from faster respawns to double damage to reduced memory for your abilities.  The benifit to stacking them is that each Limiter then gives a bonus percentage of experience at the end of the fight.  They are integral to doing well in the game and can really make the game hard as rocks if you want that exp.
It's well known that the soundtrack is stellar, even worth picking up seperately if it falls into what you might normally listen to.
The game could do a better job explaining itself, some of its concepts (such as limiters) are just not really explained and need to be googled.

Assault Android Cactus is an arcade style twin stick shooter set in a vivid sci-fi universe.
I recommend playing it solo for hunting those highscores, but full 4 player couch-coop is lots of fun too!
- Dozens of awesome Bossfights (with bullet-hell attack patterns)
- 25 levels with a few cutscenes
- Survival Mode
- Daily Drive (a randomized daily level with changing enemies and bosses)
- 3 color-coded powerups that you don't want to miss!
- 9 different playable androids, each with their own unique primary and secondary attacks
- Cute but solid visuals that fit the genre really well
- 4 player local co-op
- Expressive Soundtrack
Its current post-release state is fantastic and I couldn’t find any bugs.
For those not looking for repeat plays to compete for score, the price might be a too high.
That said I still feel it’s absolutely worth the money and I’d recommend it to anyone who has any interest in twin stick shooters or bullet hell games.

Nostalgic convenience.  Certainly brings back a lot of the fun of 16-bit RPGs, but includes a lot of nice additions that many of those older games did not such as being able to save anywhere at any time, conveniently placed restore points (especially before boss battles), ability to "one-up" if you die and want to try a battle again, free inns, able to warp to any town at pretty much anytime (even from dungeons), limited number of random encounters, and a run button.  I wish all those older games had these features as it pobably would have saved my parents from yelling at me to hurry up as I'm trying to fight my way back to an inn just to save my progress.
CSTW is really geared towards the fun aspect of these older RPGs.  Combat is overall simplistic and I found myself settling in on the same attacks over and over.  This may turn off some players but I didn't mind it too much.  There are some attacks and "team-up" attacks that I did not use at all or maybe once.
Some parts of the game aren't explained very well such as the "insanity" mode that some attacks will cause.  When I used it, the monsters caused more damage, but also took more damage from player attacks.  Apparently this mode can also unlock special attacks from certain monsters.  The monster's picture will also change slightly to show that it is "insane".
There were a couple of nit-picky items that did not affect gameplay a whole lot but I thought were a little annoying.  First of all, the animations during the battles was very minimal.  The monsters did not move and only flashed when hit.  You can see your character's attacks in the form of a swipe or some kind of spell effect, but that was about it.  Also, some indicators on character status during fights would have been nice to show if they were poisoned, stunned, etc.  The game will tell you in the text box if a character's status is impacted, but its so easy to just click past these messages from habit that its easy to miss.
Overall this is a good game that took up about 20 hours of my time.  There were still some optional dungeons to complete and I may still do those.  If you like old-school RPGs or want to take a break with something more casual, then I would recommend this game to scratch that itch.  Plus you can get it on sale for less coin than what you probably have clinking around in your car's cup-holder.

Battle for Blood came to my attention when I was fixing up a computer for a friend and I was setting it up to have something that their grand-kid could play as opposed to playing flash games and downloading viruses from various websites. Thus Steam was downloaded and some FTP games were installed.
I’m a fairly decent fan of Match-3 games in as much as they are more blatantly time-wasters more so than your usual games are. A lot of games will try to give you a deep story where in Match-3 games, the stories are pretty bland and used more as filler between and explaining why the levels exist in the order they do. Battle for Blood is basically the same thing with a mild twist.
With so many Match-3’s out there, if you are to make a new one and want it to compete, you’ll have to do something different. What Battle for Blood does is reward you in real-time with units for the fight you are currently engaging in above the Match-3 board. The bigger the match, the larger the number of units are brought into the field. You’ll probably encounter some super BS baddies, but give it time and you’ll end up with some of your own. The flip-side of the coin is that there are “penalties” to using said powerful units… well for you. The computer just does whatever it wants.
As you progress you gain access to more powerful units, however there is one more thing you need to pay attention to. Each unit has a cost (which also corresponds to the rate at which their pieces will appear on the board). More powerful units cost a lot less, but you’ll still have to send a level specific amount of units onto the field. Weaker units will fill this need quicker since they have a higher cost. The more powerful units won’t fill this bar much at all. That means to get up to the level specific amount of units, you’ll have to bring more troops. That also means there are more tiles on the board and it will be harder to create large matches or matches at all really. You’ll have to decide if the cost is worth the benefit, and sometimes it is. I didn’t like taking more than 4-5 units in if I didn’t have to.
With each round won or lost, you’ll gain money. You’ll be using this to upgrade many aspects of each troop individually.  This is where the grind can come in. Some levels will be designed as difficulty barriers. You’ll probably have to try some of these levels a few times. Some have complained about the grinding in this game, however they have obviously never played a game with real grinding ala Monster Hunter. That said, sometimes upgrading your troops doesn’t guarantee victory. I’ve simply played a level a time or three and suddenly the RNG was with me and I straight wrecked the level that previously trounced me. Whatever works I guess, right?
Score Gewd./Tasty!
While Battle for Blood does slap you with RNG, it at least isn’t taking math lessons from X-Com. There is some grinding to be found, but it’s really nothing to be worried about since the core concept of the game is rather fun. If you’re having a rough go about the game, mix up your picks. I tended to stick with the low-cost units, healer and one big DPS/tank. Remember that a smaller, but stronger army is better. The only other thing that can get frustrating is earning three starts because it tends to rely on the amount of things you kill. If you don’t get three stars, stay until you do. It’ll be harder if you have to come back with stronger units. If you do well, you can probably destroy all the content in about ten hours. That’s more than some time I’ve spent in games that cost me money.  If you enjoy Match-3 games, you have no real excuse for not playing Battle for Blood. I am waiting for the additional content that Battle for Blood says is coming.
