Factorio is an early-access survival crafting game. Those words might frighten the majority of people, and make them think that this is just 'another one of those games', but that's far from the truth.
The goal of Factorio isn't to mine resources just to make tools to mine more resources. While it is true that you need to do mining and crafting, you don't need to do those things yourself. Instead of making pickaxes and mining everything yourself, you can create machines to do the work for you. The machines start off pretty weak (mining drills and furnaces that require fuel to operate), but the game starts to get more and more interesting as you get further in the game. You can get machines that can automatically craft items for you (or your factory) pretty early in the game. In the late game, you can even get robots to automatically build large segments of your factory.
This all sounds pretty boring 'Am I just making the game play itself?', but it's far from boring. The challenge in this game comes from 2 sides. The first side is the enemies that attack your base. Unlike most games, these enemies don't attack you for no reason. As your factory grows, it spews out pollution, which actually attracts the enemies. The second side comes the logistical aspect of this game. Recipies later in the game can require multiple inputs, and it can be quite tricky to route items to their destination if your base is one giant mess.
I would suggest to play the demo if this game before you're going to buy the full version. If you like the demo, you will totally enjoy the full game.

Summary: Potentially a fun experience, if a few aspects don't bother you.
Unfortunately, Steam reviews are limited to yes/no recommendation, as I'd recommend this game... under certain circumstances. If you like high difficulty and an occasionally uncooperative camera, BUY IT. If not, probably best to avoid.
Assault Android Cactus is a very fast paced, intense game. It has great humor and a varied cast of characters, each of which have their own strengths, weaknesses and charm.
The gameplay is unforgiving, but also very satisfying when you achieve victory. If you love games that stack the deck against you and force you to fight for every inch of progress, you can skip the rest of the review, as this game is for you.
As for why I don't give the game a shining recommendation? A few flaws (some a little more subjective than others, I'll admit) hold it back:
* The camera. It's set up to keep your character centered on the screen or, if in a group (I tested it with AI teammates) to keep all players on the screen. This means that the edges of the arena are sometimes hidden. This is especially prevalent in co-op, where I often found myself attacked by enemies I could not see.
* The battery. This one may be a strength, depending on how difficult you want the experience. In addition to having to master a character's play style and learn boss patterns to beat the game, you're also on a very tight timer in the way of your battery. Killing enough enemies or clearing a phase of a boss fight drops a powerup to refill the battery somewhat, but it's still a very tight time limit. If you miss a single powerup (which is plausible, considering how fragile the characters can be), you will lose, guaranteed.
* Lack of difficulty options. As I hope I've made clear, this game is hard. Very hard. I will admit that I'm not all that good at action games, so I prefer playing on a lower difficulty so I can enjoy the game without putting too much strain on my heart. AAC has a campaign mode, an Infinite mode (apparently a survival mode, judging by the description) and a 'daily' mode that I also didn't look into. The point is, the campaign mode has a single difficulty. Personally, I'd have rather it had a standard easy/normal/hard set, with easy being detrimental (or disabling) your score.
* The Ex Options. This isn't a flaw, just a related observation to the last point. You earn credits by playing the game that can be used to unlock options. These include adjusting the characters to human proportions, unlocking AI teammates or two options I'd like to mention in detail:
First, the ability to play a co-op game solo, meaning more enemies with more health. Effectively a hard mode, I suppose, which may appear to conflict with my previous statement about difficulties. The idea of unlocking a harder challenge sound like a good inclusion to me, since it means a player unlocking the option is confident in their ability. It seems more emotionally rewarding, at least to me. But it adds context to my next point:
Second, the ability to toggle on stronger weapons. This sounds a bit like an easy mode (and in fact, a friend suggested it to me specifically when I mentioned being stuck), except the option costs 5000 credits, versus the 1000 most other options (including AI co-op) cost. It also disables your score. To me, that feels like paying twice. First I have to grind for credits (since I'm only getting double digit rewards from each stage) just to afford it, and then I'm barred from the leader board. The AI co-op option also locks you out of scoring, but only costs 1000 credits.
Though considering I care very little about high scores, personally, this doesn't bother me. I'm just a little confused about why it's implemented that way.
So to sum up my thoughts: I love the game. Genuinely adore it. But I'm a filthy casual and would love it more if it had an easy mode.
On a side note, I had difficulty playing with a controller due to it being very hard to aim with the right stick. A slight movement would have my character firing in a completely different direction. So I swapped to keyboard + mouse controls and found it much easier, so my thanks to Witch Beam for including keyboard controls.
I also apologize for the length of the review. There are a lot of points I felt needed to be mentioned, and I wish I could select "Yes, but..." as a review option instead of just yes or no.

I've never written a review for a game on Steam before, but AAC was for me personally such a surprisingly enjoyable experience, that I simply couldn't resist writing a few lines about how great this game is.
AAC provides you with a multitude of different characters, each with their own unique weapon layouts, that you can use to either blast your way through the game‘s story mode, or through various other modes like a high score attack or boss rush mode. While some of these characters are available from the very start of the game, others must be unlocked by playing through the game's story mode, and each of them brings its own unique playstyle to the table.
While the story mode can be completed within a few hours, the real allure of the game lies in its high score system. I can't remember the last time a game has successfully motivated me to try scoring for an S+ rank on every single stage, but AAC is so masterfully designed, that I didn't mind playing a stage over and over again until I had achieved a perfect score. No matter how often I had to restart a stage, the gameplay just always felt great and when I had finally managed to reach an S+ ranking, the sense of satisfaction was simply overwhelming. And even after reaching a perfect score on a stage, I would just replay it again later with a different character, to see whether I could reach another S+ with a completely different weapon layout. (A quick note for all Gurren Lagann fans: One of the characters even carries a giant drill into battle that you can use to pierce your enemies as well as the heavens ;))
I could probably go on and on about how much I love this game, but I'm afraid eventually you readers would lose all interest in my ramblings, so tl;dr:
Great game, best twin stick shooter I've played in years, I want more of it.

And unlike other games, choices here make a direct difference :P Either way I have found myself really quite enjoying this game and have done really well on some daily challenges and some levels. There is some character inbalance, for example Startch is mindlessly easy to play and is very easy to rack up insane scores on while, Aubergine takes a great deal of focus to do half as good as swigning your second stick around randomly with Starch. The level designs are interesting if simplistic. There is one near the end of the game where the floor is constantly being made and unmade under your feet; this is an amazing level. The boss fights are a lot of fun, I found some of them frustrating, until I simply gave up and owned them with Startch. There is a silly story line that is kind of irrelevant in the enjoyment of this game.
Overall the game looks good and plays nicely. I reccoemnd it to anyone looking for a solid dual-stick arcade game.
One minor complain: I cannot get the game to register any input after the menu screens on my Linux Box (Debian Jesse 8). Not a big deal just =\

No words could describe this game's beauty.

Transistor is probably best described as a "tactical hack & slash." That odd combo of descriptors speaks to a set of game mechanics that is unique and, at times, complex. The "trials" they present you are especially challenging puzzles, as are boss fights. The game offers a wide array of stylistic capabilities, as well as "limiters" - options which you can turn on to enhance the difficulty (and your reward).
The story is really nothing to speak of - the flimsiest outline of a plot, loosely carried along by vague, non-specific lines of dialogue uttered by cardboard characters with cool portraits but little personality. Don't get this expecting to find an engaging narrative - the gameplay is the real strength here.
I paid this game the ultimate compliment and actually beat it. The game is satisfying, albeit frustrating at times - the "challenge puzzles" usually have a trick to figure out. Until you do it can feel like you're beating your head against a brick wall - sometimes unsure whether it's your tactics or your ability to execute that's at fault. That being said, the game is well worth it, especially if you enjoyed Bastion - and, frankly, I would recommend Bastion to anyone who's never played a SuperGiant game before I'd send them to Transistor.

While I do give Battle for Blood a thumbs up, I don't necessarily absolutely recommend this game.
The match 3 mechanic is an old, rather solid one, and combined with the upgrading system of the different units throughout the game, it is rather easy to get the hang of it. What is not so nice is the fact that it is nigh impossible to earn a lot of coins by repeating stages. Even more so, it will become incredibly difficult to make the necessary coins to affors the pricier upgrades. Hence, we are back at what we loathe - micro-transactions, to get the best out of the units, and even if you only want to do a couple of them.
And it isn't a particularly long game either. Battle for Blood only took me approximately 3.5 hours to really complete with one straight playthrough (aided by a micro-transaction, though it rather felt like a macro-transaction). As said, it is easy to play, but the coin-earning is a pain. And even with my love for grinding, I have to say: what you get from the already completed levels is far too little to really warrant leniency there.

The question you need to answer before you sit down to play Cthulhu Saves The World is: what are your tastes in humor? Do you like stories that poke fun at the trappings and cliches of their genre while reverently following those cliches, for good or ill? Did you think Shrek was a fun ride but could have name-checked 1930s horror literature more often?
If so, Cthulhu Saves the World has plenty to offer. Otherwise, you probably don't have to keep reading, since the game lives and dies on its gags.
If you're looking for more cerebral references to Lovecraft's work, you won't find much to work with here: the inspiration is pretty surface-level, beginning with town names and ending with boss battles with (twee parodies of) shoggoths. It all adds up, essentially, to one long schtick contrasting the Final Fantasy atmosphere and plot with the Lovecraftian setting elements, seasoned with JRPG lampshading.
While the jokes are shallow and unambitious, there certainly are a lot of them -- this is a game where every bookshelf has an amusing book to examine and every NPC has a snippet or two of tone-appropriate dialogue.
The actual gameplay is standard turn-based material, with the extra wrinkles of an "insanity" status effect that invites good or ill depending on who it affects and a gimmicky but engaging combo mechanic, which, combined, provide a little thought to the usual "buff-debuff-sword-fireball" litany and carries you from one comedic scene to another.
If you've read this far, you can probably already tell that Cthulhu Saves The World has something to offer, and at this price point, that means I can recommend giving it a shot.

I have never played a game like this before and as my very first try at a first person dungeon crawler, I have to say this was a great experience. Yes, I know, it's a whiny statement, but let me kind of explain why I feel this way and perhaps it'll make more sense.
I get the dungeon crawl concept. I've played them before, and roguelikes. Against all expectations, I beat the hardest of hardcore modes on Dungeons of Dredmor, I went through a couple playthroughs of Dark Souls, all that stuff. When I lose in those games, I feel it's because I did something to mess up, missed a move or made a wrong decision.
With this game, there is no wrong decision to make, because no matter what you decide, you get thrown up against a difficulty spike that you can't possibly be ready for until you die at least once to it. If it isn't the obtuse puzzles that only make sense about half the time, it's the enemies that pop out of nowhere, can take forty times as many hits as any of your characters, and deal out damage that can kill you in seconds in a straight fight.
I know a lot of people may disagree with this, and they certainly have a right to. But to me, this game isn't a challenge, or a dungeon crawl. It's just mashing my face against random walls in the hopes of finding a hidden switch, and getting killed a dozen times by the same overpowered monster group until I find the hidden cheese tactic that somehow lets me go down another floor.

Transistor is probably best described as a "tactical hack & slash." That odd combo of descriptors speaks to a set of game mechanics that is unique and, at times, complex. The "trials" they present you are especially challenging puzzles, as are boss fights. The game offers a wide array of stylistic capabilities, as well as "limiters" - options which you can turn on to enhance the difficulty (and your reward).
The story is really nothing to speak of - the flimsiest outline of a plot, loosely carried along by vague, non-specific lines of dialogue uttered by cardboard characters with cool portraits but little personality. Don't get this expecting to find an engaging narrative - the gameplay is the real strength here.
I paid this game the ultimate compliment and actually beat it. The game is satisfying, albeit frustrating at times - the "challenge puzzles" usually have a trick to figure out. Until you do it can feel like you're beating your head against a brick wall - sometimes unsure whether it's your tactics or your ability to execute that's at fault. That being said, the game is well worth it, especially if you enjoyed Bastion - and, frankly, I would recommend Bastion to anyone who's never played a SuperGiant game before I'd send them to Transistor.

This game is unique.
The art, music, story and voice acting are all fantastic, and a lot of people talk about it a lot, so I'm going to go straight to the gameplay, because to me, that's what really makes this game stand out.
The gameplay in transistor is an interesting and deep blend of strategy, tactics, and action RPG. It looks like an action RPG - one character, running around the game world in real time, trying to pull off attack combos. And you can play it like that, if you get good at the controls. But you can also stop time and program perfectly timed combos to occur.
That alone sets this game apart. The balance between those two completely different mechanics - using your moves in real time, and planning out moves in a safe, stopped, environment - straddles two completely different genres, and thus two completely different play styles. Besides the real time action RPG style of gameplay, you can more or less impose a turn based style of game play - the mechanic for stopping time is even called /turn. On your /turn, you try to deal as much damage as possible to your opponents by planning out the right moves in the right order so that they don't get blocked or cancelled. Then, you can just run around the board, dodging attacks until the meter reloads and you can take your /turn again.
Obviously, most of the time, you find yourself doing a bit of both. You figure out good move combinations to use in /turn, and then while turn is loading, you try to use those same combos in real time to deal more damage. Sometimes, you find yourself using Turn primarily to dodge or reposition yourself, and doing all your real damage in real time. You find the middle ground that best suits you.
But the real complexity and beauty comes in the wealth of moves available. You end up learning a bunch of different moves, and the moves can be adapted to three forms - they can be moves, they can modify other moves, or they can modify your player character. You like explosions, but the explosion move is too slow for your playstyle? Slap it onto one of your faster attacks to give it an extra punch. Or, slap your fastest attack on it, to remove its drawbacks. The combinations and complexity available is staggering, and it makes the game more personal and more fun. When you discover a great synnergy between two moves, that was your discovery, and you can feel proud of it.
All of this makes the death mechanic in the game hit even harder. You have a health bar in this game, but when it gets to zero, you lose one of your moves - usually the one that's been most modified, so probably your best move. If you built your playstyle around one synnergy, you effectively have one life. If you have a lot of moves, you live longer, but each hit still really hurts, as it takes away one of your tools, and probably one you designed a little yourself and are proud of. This makes the 'death' of your moves matter to you, and makes the tension of the game more real.
Since you can only reinstall moves at a save point, and your ''dead' moves will be unavailable for the next new save point you find, this also changes how you use your save points. In an insane reversal of usual game logic, you might choose not to use the save point that's right in front of a hard battle or a boss, so that you can go to it after the battle, restock, and get back your main moves more quickly.
All of this is to say, there isn't another game fully like Transistor. It has elements from several different genres, and playstyles or strategies that you have from those other games might apply to it. But as a whole, this game is a unique experience, and one that is unque all the way down its considerable depths.
It's also a very fun, immersive, and beautiful experience, and it can be extremely challenging if that's what you want, but also extremely casual if that's not.
It is free and worth every single penny. :) <3

Transistor is an isometric hack and slash RPG from the creators of Bastion. You play as a famous singer who lost her voice, and it's all the Process' fault.
Transistor is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played to date. Everything in the game feels so... alive... Everything is hand painted and looks spectacular, you can really feel the artist's motivation and power. The cutscenes are amazingly well done and really helps you connect with Red, the main character. Everything from the enemies, levels, and even ambient background objects are incredibly detailed. Kudos to the artist(s) for the job well done.
One of the featured tags on Transistor's store page is Great Soundtrack, and, well, it does indeed have a great soundtrack. Actually, scratch that. It has an incredible soundtrack unmatched by other indie titles. You are Red, a famous singer that actually sings in the soundtrack. The soundtrack is mesmerizing, and the singer for Red did a fabulous job. Sometimes you just have to take a moment and listen to the breathtaking tracks. The voice acting for the Transistor is marvelous as well. You can really hear the passion in the voice of a sentient sword. My favourite line spoken by the Transistor is "Don't let me go". The voice actor has a lot of meaning and soft power behind his lines.
My only problem with the soundtrack is they didn't use the amazing vocals of Red enough, which makes sense if you tie it in with the story.
Favourite Track:
Transistor is very story rich and deep. You play as Red, a once famous singer with a vengeance against those who stripped her of her beautiful singing voice, and, as I mentioned previously, one that you can actually hear in the soundtrack. You are accompanied by Transistor, a sword that embodies you with the power of a thousand suns as you rain hellfire upon those who wronged you. The cutscenes and news stories supply the perfect amount of exposition for you to understand just what is going on, what happened to Red, and why you have to take your sweet, sweet revenge.
I love the combat in Transistor. You can choose between turn based combat and real time hack and slash. You can carefully plan out your moves in the turn based combat system but you can also fully enjoy your power in the hack and slash mode. You can change out each ability and you can also modify them. There are endless possibilities you can use to exact your revenge. There is a lot of strategy that goes into Transistor. The turn based combat system has a cooldown that leaves you vulnerable to enemies. You have to plan out what abilities and modifiers you use to exploit your enemies weaknesses. Everything, including the realtime hack and slash, has to be planned out in a way that keeps you entertained.

Steel Division: Normandy 44 is a Tactical Real-Time Strategy (RTS) game, developed by Eugen Systems, the creators of titles like Wargame and R.U.S.E. This new game puts players in command of detailed, historically accurate tanks, troops, and vehicles at the height of World War II. Players can measure their tactical skills against several opponents in big multiplayer battles or against enemies in a challenging single-player campaign. Steel Division: Normandy 44 allows players to take control over legendary military divisions from six different countries, such as the American 101st Airborne, the German armored 21st Panzer or the 3rd Canadian Division, during the invasion of Normandy in 1944.
Main Features:
Command Over 400 Historically Accurate Units:
Whether fighting for control in intense multiplayer battles with up to 10-vs-10 players going head-to-head, playing alone or working with friends in ranked matches, players will need to coordinate their selection of historically accurate infantry, tanks, aircraft, and support vehicles to counter enemy units in this Tactical RTS game.
Real-world Tactics:
Battles rage over three distinct phases, where different units unlock over time, mimicking the movements of real-world armies and adding variety to the ever-changing theatre of war. A dynamic front line illustrates the ebb and flow of the conflict. Pin down your opponent's infantry to gain the advantage and force a retreat, or push through with a perfectly executed plan.
Real-world Setting:
Using the latest version of Eugen’s IRISZOOM engine, players can smoothly zoom from a tactical aerial view all the way down to a single unit, and see 400 different real-world vehicles and units designed with careful historical detail and accuracy. Maps are designed based on actual aerial reconnaissance photos of Normandy in 1944, requiring real-world tactics and strategies to cover and control.
Outplan, Outsmart, Outgun:
From battlegroup customization to troop positioning and maneuvering, winning battles requires cunning and strategy, not just raw firepower. Each unit lost presents a growing tactical disadvantage, and players will need to fight to gain -- and keep -- the upper hand.
From commanding historically accurate infantry, tanks, and vehicles, to troop positioning and real-time engagement with the enemy, players will need to be clever and resourceful in order to win. Every unit counts as the battle presses on, and raw firepower alone will not be enough to claim victory. Whether viewing the entire battle from an aerial perspective, or following a single tank into a firefight, players will need to cleverly manage the dynamic front line in order to execute ambushes and advances.

Cthulhu Saves the World is a game about Cthulhu,
, a being so terrible that just being around him makes everyone go insane. So, how does one stop such unstoppable madness? Have a stranger zap his power away. Then make him become a true hero and his powers will return to him. Yeah, the plot is rather...unexplained. But that’s not important because we have madder things to deal with! Like groupies, heroes, undead monsters and Cthulhu saving the world. It’s a pretty fun and funny time, with plenty of references to go around. This is a 2D jRPG with a minimal upgrade system for armor, weapons and skills.
Cthulhu builds upon the combat system designed in Breath of Death VII. Refining the lightning-quick turn-based combat to a new level. Now, there’s a new system called Insanity. When enemies become insane via certain abilities you can use, they take and give out double the normal damage. It’s a tricky trade-off to make sure you don’t accidentally power up an enemy before you can strike a killing blow. There’s also retries to start a battle over if you messed up too badly and some tweaks to status effects to make them more useful.
There’s also a fairly basic upgrade system. Everytime you level up, you get a choice of abilities to select and hopefully improve your combat performance. (Though I get the feeling that the wrong choices could really hurt you without you knowing it). Weapons and armor can also be upgraded from the shop and loot found in the world. There’s usually only a couple of choices per weapon and armor “level” so it comes down to what stat you prefer the most.
I found that after 10 hours, the combat system was becoming too dull to work through. Half the battles were a cakewalk and the other half the difficulty would seem to suddenly spike and I would die repeatedly. It didn’t help that there was a constant rinse-and-repeat of entering battle, select the same combo of attacks and win/lose. Which has made me realize that perhaps jRPGs as a genre aren’t for me anymore. I used to enjoy them a lot when I was younger. Now? I find the repetition tedious. It’s a case where minimal visuals may have worked against the game, because there’s no interesting eye candy to watch. It’s a trade-off.
Cthulhu is very well optimized and won’t strain your system at all. Crashing and bugs should be rare as well. The devs clearly knew how to make a polished jRPG. That being said, the game only supports 1280x720 and 640x360 in addition to fullscreen mode. Frame rate is also capped at 60FPS. There aren’t any other visual settings to be found here. There’s also no mouse support but that’s largely unimportant. Remapping of keys is here as well as support for controllers. Separate volume controls exist as well. Largely bare-boned and mostly I just miss resolution options. Outside of that, it’s just fine.
I want to like Cthulhu Saves the World. I really do. But I think CSTW has indicated that the jRPG genre might not be for me anymore. The premise of Cthulhu stripped of his powers until he becomes a great hero is very amusing. But the game’s dry combat system is simply too boring for me to enjoy it. Especially when I take the experience grind into account. That all said, if jRPGs are your kind of genre, Cthulhu Saves the World is well worth checking out. Especially since it’s a combo pack with the other well done jRPG, Breath of Death VII: The Beginning.

Cthulhu is very well optimized and won’t strain your system at all. Crashing and bugs should be rare as well. The devs clearly knew how to make a polished jRPG. That being said, the game only supports 1280x720 and 640x360 in addition to fullscreen mode. Frame rate is also capped at 60FPS. There aren’t any other visual settings to be found here. There’s also no mouse support but that’s largely unimportant. Remapping of keys is here as well as support for controllers. Separate volume controls exist as well. Largely bare-boned and mostly I just miss resolution options. Outside of that, it’s just fine.
I want to like Cthulhu Saves the World. I really do. But I think CSTW has indicated that the jRPG genre might not be for me anymore. The premise of Cthulhu stripped of his powers until he becomes a great hero is very amusing. But the game’s dry combat system is simply too boring for me to enjoy it. Especially when I take the experience grind into account. That all said, if jRPGs are your kind of genre, Cthulhu Saves the World is well worth checking out. Especially since it’s a combo pack with the other well done jRPG, Breath of Death VII: The Beginning.

The first sign that Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a mediocre port comes as soon as you boot up the game: you can’t navigate the menus with a mouse. On its own, this isn't an awful fact, but it's an omen of bad things to come. Aside from resolution and brightness options, there are no visual options to tweak. There is no antialiasing and no way to enable it. And frame rate troubles will haunt your every saber swing. It's too bad that so little respect was shown for the platform--and to those that will spend money on this product--because the underlying game is rather good. As Darth Vader's secret apprentice, you slice through grunting Rodians with your glowing lightsaber, go head-to-head with slobbering rancors, and punt jawas into the distance as if they were pigskins. You might be lucky enough to avoid this troubled port's technical flaws and experience the full pleasures of The Force Unleashed, but be warned: Picking up a copy of this physics-heavy action game is one gamble that may not pay off.

Even the cheap tactic of force grip and throwing someone to damage/kill them is still not very functional due to the HORRIBLE targetting mechanics. You will end up not being able to grab anyone because you never get to target your enemy even when they're literally 4 feet from you. NOTHING about the gameplay is fluid. Skill is absolutely not a factor.
Do you want to be a Jedi or Sith? Unfortunately you have only a one time choice and it's at the end of the game. It's not even obvious that there is a choice. Look it up and you'll see what I mean, no spoilers here.
Want to force throw 3 large items at once? You got it!.. Want to hit the only enemy around with 3 said objects? NOPE! Aiming things you throw is almost random and unfortunately you have to do it to pick down the bosses so you can actually have a lightsaber fight when they're at about 5% health.
The checkpoint system is terrible, the UI is bad, the menu/options screen is the worst I've ever seen.
Want to skip a cutscene? Sure! Press all buttons.. nothing. Press enter though and you'll just open the menu to save your game!.. Handy feature that is.. Saving mid cutscene.
I could go on for hours.. I hate this game, I play it for the story because I like Star Wars... Going in I wanted to be a Jedi, now I'm definitely turned to the dark side.
Oh, yeah.. and the game is capped at 30 fps and 5.1 sound so enjoy the choppy gameplay and very poor audio unless you have a 5.1 speaker setup in your house.

What can I say that hasn't been already said? Nothing really, just that Papers, Please didn't resonate with me like it did with other people.  Did I have fun plaything Papers, Please? Yes, yes I did. Are there worse games I could of played? Yes, yes there are, Do I think Papers, Please is a good game? Yes, yes I do, which leaves me in the weird spot recommending the game even though I wasn't as blown away by it as other people.
For those of you who have been living under a rock, and don't know what Papers, Please is I will tell you. Papers, Please is a job simulator, but instead of driving a tractor or tractor trailer you are a border guard. You guard the border of a fictitious landlocked Cold War Era Eastern European/Former Soviet Republic. Think one of the countries ending in -stan you have a good idea how everything looks and feels. Everyday before you go to work you read the newspaper. The newspaper lets you know world events going on, and what your previous actions affected. During your shift you admit immigrants into the country depending on their credentials. The more people you admit the more money you get, but admit to many people with the wrong credentials and you will be fined by the Ministry of Admission (M.O.A). At the end the of the day you use the money to feed your family, keep them healthy, and keep the heat on. This is the first big tension of the game trying to work fast enough to keep yourself and family a float without making to many mistakes that the M.O.A starts sending you literal pink slips and fines. To complicate matters worse as the days go on more and you will have to check more and more paperwork of the immigrants coming across the border. The second major tension coming from the immigrants themselves. Everyone has a story and it's your job to figure if you believe them or not. Personally I had no problem denying people with sob stories if they didn't have the correct paperwork and just doing my job. Though I can see if you weren't so cold hearted as me. How this could be a major headache and make the game much more than a job simulator. With all that being said I would say give the game a shot. It's fairly cheap and usually on a Steam sale, so even if you don't end up being blown away by it. It won't cost you a pretty penny.

I used to have a board game called Hero Quest when I was a kid.  I loved it!  It was a gateway game to harder dru...erm, games like D&D, Vampire, and other table top games and eventually back to board games (I'm a proud board game geek).  Coincidentally, I also began to take a second look at dungeon crawlers.  Before this time, my largest exposure to first person RPGs of the like was Bard's Tale and I hated that game.  I bought "Eye of the Beholder" and "Shining in the Darkness" back then.  I dabbled with them, but quickly moved onto other RPGs.
Fast forward twelve years later and I picked up and finally beat Shining, giving it more respect and reigniting an appreciation for that style of RPG.  Two years after Shining, I beat Phantasy Star.  Two years after Phantasy Star, I beat Shadowgate and now Legend of Grimrock.
I love top ten lists, cause I'm a sucker for order. Given the four dungeon crawls I beat, Grimrock would rank second after Shining.  The game is great, but I'm not sure it was enough to pull me back for more.  I enjoyed the opening music and the sound effects were atmospheric.  Graphics are decent and are done well for being programmed in Lua, but the effects do make certain reflective surfaces appear artificially shiny.  Gameplay is pretty straightforward.  Find better gear and attack bad guys.  The battle system is very simplistic as it really just comes down to right clicking.  The joy in combat actually comes from side stepping and dodging enemies to smack them.  It really is pleasing to be able to pull this off flawlessly after some practice. If done correctly, you can go floors before even getting hit.
I played on Hard and Old School mode and it hurt me emotionally. I ended up getting lost several times, despite best efforts at maps and some enemies made me swear bad things against their offspring.
The story is nearly nonexistent, but tidbits of flavor in the form of Toorum's notes and the ever detached presence pushing you forward is enough as the story takes back seat to the puzzles on each floor.  "You're dumped into a dungeon, find your way out," is what is it comes down to.  The final boss was unexpected until you got down to the 12th floor and the battle wasn't overly difficult, but was a tad too long as I would dish out a few hits, drop down to the lower floor, heal, save, repeat.   The artwork for the ending is well done and I was surprised that a game this well made was done by four people.  It's worth a play if you're into this type of thing.

Now this is an old-school game. A geniune dungeon-crawler, but with shiny modern graphics. The floors are all really well laid out, the difficulty progression is not too bad, and the puzzles are tough but manageable. The inventory is a bit stiff and the controls for casting spells are a bit frustrating in the heat of the moment. Still, the game has great customization and an awesome level editor. I am also pretty sure the sequel is addressing all the complaints. Give it a try, but watch out for spiders!

Legend of Grimrock is a wonderful Dungeon Master love-in and a fantastic technical achievement from a team of just four people.

Seriously, Legend of Grimrock is one of the best games you could ever purchase.

Overall, this is a very good game with several great aspects but the few negatives keep it from being top tier.
The story and pacing are well done and left me wanting more, the music is just about perfect (even the songs with lyrics which I usually find annoying in games), and visually it is distinct and sharp looking.
On the negative side, it is very short (about 5 hours for a playthrough) so the story that is set up ultimately disappoints because it wraps up too quickly. Additionally, the game is quite easy though there is a built-in mechanism to make it more difficult if you like. The combat, while fun for the most part, is a fairly standard ability/cooldown system and doesn't do anything new or exciting.
Overall it's definitely worth your time and your money, though you should not expect a deep RPG experience from it. 8/10

When Battlefield Bad Company 2 (BFBC2) first launched in 2010, it made headlines for having one of the most realistic graphic and physics engines. Frostbite (engine) was groundbreaking, way ahead of Call of Duty, even to this day. Now with other Battlefield games using newer generation Frostbite engines, this game can still stand the test of time. The real population exists on the PC version, with dedicated servers, and better performance and even better quality.
Today in 2015, the singleplayer is nastalgic, the multiplayer is still as addictive as ever, and the dedicated community that still populates it's servers are nothing short of hardcore BFBC2 pros. The attention to detail during development of this game is readily apparent. My personal favorite, the realistic sounds of death echoing throughout the map when people die is something I'll always remember when I think of BFBC2. An insignificant detail to some, but unlike Call of Duty, or any other game for that matter, the voice acting of a character dying has been perfected in this engine. It cannot be explained in words, it is the most realistic death sound I've ever encountered in a video game.
But the real gem within this game is the "Vietnam" DLC. Battlefield 3, 4, and Hardline, just can't compare to the addictive nature of such an amazing yet simple DLC. Only consisting of 5 maps and a handful of guns. The Vietnam era voice acting, music, maps, models, guns, tracers, animations, textures, vehicles, atmosphere, and guerilla tactics make this game my all time favorite FPS. No game has ever hyped me up as BFBC2 Vietnam.
The North Vietnamese Army (NVA) voice acting is unforgettable. It's a mixture of humor and intensity. Fighting as a GI and trying to retake a NVA stronghold on Conquest, you find yourself being overun by Guerilla's screaming "You Kill my friend!", "For my Brother!", and "Go Home GI!" with realistic tracers flying by your head, as well as the sounds of everything blowing up around you, you become immersed in a world long forgotten by the main stream.
I will continue to play this game until the day I die. And we've been hoping for Bad Company 3 for too long now. If you havn't tried this game it's still a must have. You will not regret it.

Factorio is an early-access survival crafting game. Those words might frighten the majority of people, and make them think that this is just 'another one of those games', but that's far from the truth.
The goal of Factorio isn't to mine resources just to make tools to mine more resources. While it is true that you need to do mining and crafting, you don't need to do those things yourself. Instead of making pickaxes and mining everything yourself, you can create machines to do the work for you. The machines start off pretty weak (mining drills and furnaces that require fuel to operate), but the game starts to get more and more interesting as you get further in the game. You can get machines that can automatically craft items for you (or your factory) pretty early in the game. In the late game, you can even get robots to automatically build large segments of your factory.
This all sounds pretty boring 'Am I just making the game play itself?', but it's far from boring. The challenge in this game comes from 2 sides. The first side is the enemies that attack your base. Unlike most games, these enemies don't attack you for no reason. As your factory grows, it spews out pollution, which actually attracts the enemies. The second side comes the logistical aspect of this game. Recipies later in the game can require multiple inputs, and it can be quite tricky to route items to their destination if your base is one giant mess.
I would suggest to play the demo if this game before you're going to buy the full version. If you like the demo, you will totally enjoy the full game.

I checked the earlier reviews, and the pathing and terrain issues have been talked about quite a bit. The way you can walk into some walls, walk out of bounds in many areas, that weird one-way bridge. Not to mention there are a number of rooms(usually off to the side) that you might miss altogether if you're not paying careful attention, and the occasional doorway that throws up a message(in Portuguese? Spanish?) when you try to enter it. It's just weird and makes everything feel incomplete, like whoever made this was in a big hurry.
So I'll add something new that I didn't see mentioned yet -- the broken "sick girl" quest. Pretty early in the game(maybe 2 to 4 hours in, depending on how fast you play), there's a side quest that's triggered by talking to a man who appears after you investigate a "rat infestation" in the sewers that ends up revealing a poisoning attempt. You'll see him on your way to the palace to talk to the Queen. He directs you to a house in the same district as the sewer entrance, and you'll find a bed-ridden girl with a doctor and another person(her mother?). They say it's terminal, and send you to get the priest to give her last rites. If you haven't talked to the Queen, you can't enter that area of town yet. So you talk to the Queen. Now you can enter the area, but . . . the priest isn't in the church! So you continue with the next story quest, come back, and go back to the church.
The priest is now there! As are a couple of his assistants. None of them do anything when you talk to them. No mention of the dying little girl. Nothing.
The man who started this entire quest is still giving his spiel about how he hopes the little girl will make it.
If you visit her house, the little girl is walking around just fine! She's talking about how she feels kinda sick, but she's not bedridden or anything.
The doctor is back at his place a couple houses east of your character's house.
. . . congratulations, because you talked to an NPC when he appeared instead of psychically knowing that you should wait(I assume) until after certain other events, the quest is broken!
I also have another complaint. Compared to the pathing/terrain issues and at least 1 broken quest early on, it might seem minor, but . . . the game is slow! Walking is slow, with no dash feature available. You can't disable battle animations, and they are really slow too. Screen transitions are annoyingly slow(and annoyingly common), which there's no excuse for in a game that's just a step or 2 above SNES quality in terms of graphics and sound. I've played a number of RPGMaker games, so I know that RPGMaker has tools to deal with most(if not all) of these. It's just so weird that whoever made this wouldn't make use of them.

This is another game from Warfare published by Aldorlea that (like Midnight's Blessing) takes a bit of time to get into. And, like MB, the payoff for patience is very rewarding. The game is deep in character development and story.
You begin the game seeing a young girl (Kismet) being shipped off by her family to work as a maid for a well to do man in another town, then the tale picks up 6 years later. At that time, Kismet is ready for a bit more in her life in her new town, and, after several "prologue" chores and adventures meets new party members, fights some minor battles (for leveling up and acquiring supplies), and discovers the complexities of just what is going on in her world.
It is then that she is made a guardian of the realm, and is sent back to her hometown to investigate some disappearances that the real action begins. Because the narrative is laid out very carefully, it takes a little time, but the effort is worth it ---- so you can settle in for quite a long game.
The story itself is very well told, and done so with a good amount of humor considering the gravity of the situation the party faces. (evil enemies, a monster-turning illness, etc). You can easily find yourself getting involved with these characters, and that always adds to the overall game experience, or fun factor.
And there is plenty of exploration ---- you have to look everywhere and talk to everyone to discover all the secrets and aspects of the game. And, there are choices to make as to which quests to undertake that seem to affect the course of the game which adds to the replay value ---- or you can just use the multiple save slots and follow the different directions the game offers simultaneously.
The battle scenes are very nicely done, there is a world map to help you along, the music is very nice, and the artwork is good.
So, lots of things to do, interesting choices to make, a good length, nice characterizations and flawless gameplay add up to a winning adventure that grows on you more and more the longer you play. Nicely done, and recommended.

I've been waiting for years for a game like this. Let's start with the fact that I'm a fan of "Eye of the Beholder"-like games. You know... these first person RPGs with the primitive movement (one button click, one square-step) where you never see the sun and you're wandering in underground mazes full of puzzles dealing with buttons,plates, teleporters and the like.
The game has pretty good visuals, certainly good enough for this kind of game. But the thing it excels at is the puzzles. The creators have achieved just the perfect level of difficulty. Plenty of puzzles that are not easy enough (plague of modern games) but not too tough on the other hand to make you quit the game. You get the satisfaction of solving a puzzle without hitting your head on the wall (except for maybe a couple of cases :)), one of the cornerstones of great gameplay.
Overall the game is great and cannot recommend it enough!  Just hope there were more games like this one

I remember playing the original "Where in the World is carmen Sandiego?" detective game for hours on end at a friends house when I was 6 or 7 years old.  The game was painfully slow paced, repetitive, had terrible music, and borderline unfinishable.  The only reward for playing was a gradually increasing rank that became increasingly difficult to improve.  No changes to gameplay, no higher stakes.  Just one long boring slog through the same bifurcated screen, tracking an uncatchable thief and her band of cronies across indiscernible international locales.
I am forced to recall this as the style of "Paers, Please" is so clearly remiscient of those early games. But instead of attempting to confuse you into thinking the game is making a jet-setter out of you, "Papers, Please" does everything in it's power to instill in you the existential dread of being a cog in a communist machine, trapped from one day to the next ina cramped cubicle, constantly racing against the clock, stranded, morally speaking, between a rock and a firing squad.  What enjoyment can be taken from the game is visceral; not accomplishment, but survival. Endurance and speed are developed not to raise ones arms, but to lower ones head, walk home silently and without attracting any attention from your superiors.
Not a game for everyone, but I loved it.

I like the old GTAs. 3, Vice City and San Andreas where great. With GTA4 the GTA series started to become stagnant. In GTA4 they left out
that made San Andreas so good. I didn't play GTA5, but at that point i was already so bored of GTA, which is always the same.
Guy in a USA City Roams around.
I have to say, i did enjoy the silent protagonist in GTA3 most; the ever increasing foul language and super Stereotype of "bad guys" that appears in each new game was just not interesting enough.
Now to Sleeping Dogs. I played the original version back on my PS3. The things that make it stand out from GTA and all those other GTA-like games is allot.
First you are in Hong Kong, which is a total different enviroment then any USA City. Something total fresh ... and you have to rdrive on the left side of the road. I can't count, how often this threw me off when i started to play it ;p.
The game mainly revolves around Kung Fu, especially those Police movies with Chackie Chan and other Hong Kong movie Stars.
The main fighting system is all around Kung Fu. You can pull off several different Combo's seen in allot of those kind Movies, Counter like in the Batman Arkham Games ... or Shadow over Mordor or Grab people and Break Legs and Arms. Always a chuckle how the rest of the enemies react when you do that ;p.
You can also Grab people and drag them around, interact with
in the game world, which acts then as a finisher.
There is also Gunplay in it, but for some reason the Aiming is
bad with a controller. It is perfectly fine with a Mouse ... at least for me. There is a Cover system which works very well.
You can also Drive Cars, and there are certain Action moves where you can jump out of your Car onto another one ... while driving. Then you crawl to the Driver Cabin and pull him out ... very fun to watch. There are shooting Scenes while drivint, either your Character Drives ... or someone else Drives ... just sad that the most effective strategy is to shoot the Tires ... with devastating effect ;p.
Overall, i can only suggest to give Sleeping Dogs a try. The game has
variety. There are Mafia Missions, Police Missions, Racing Missions, "Face" Missions and they all are not too Repetitive.
The Story is also
good, it shows the twists and turns of the main Protagonist, who struggles being a Police Officer undercover in the Chinese Mafia ... where he is with allot people he know from his Childhood. I really like the Story of this game allot.

This game offers very little besides the wacky title.
What passes for a story is Cthulhu going around doing heroic things in his own way, which is sometimes something funny like saving innocent zombies from the thing controlling them but mostly things like returning a lost dog or healing an illness  by finding magic water.
There is very little cast development, the characters stay mostly one dimensional and while the character concepts like a talking sword or an alien cat might seem interesting at first, very little is done with them.
The music is nothing worth remembering, not even the final boss theme was that catchy.
The dungeon design is bad, the only puzzles are barriers that can be opened with a button press and a falling/rising water level. The levels are designed to make the player get lost, probably to extend the short playtime, if you want to find the right way, take the path that looks the least like it will lead to progress.
Of course, the graphics are also nothing noteworthy, they go for a "retro" pixel style, but this is just an excuse for being lazy with the graphics since they are nowhere near actually good looking detailed pixel art like:
The gameplay is one good aspect, you are often in danger of dying and all of your HP get's refreshed after each fight, even if a party member dies, thus making even a victory with only one fighter left standing worth it. The only thing to look out for between fights is the MP count, since it isn't completely replenished. This game also makes buffs and debuffs useful, even in non boss fights. You still have a lot of skills you rarely or never use though. The danger of loosing is sadly undermined by being able to save anywhere, although this might not be the case on harder difficulties.
Like any jrpg though, fighting get's tedious after some time and since there is little else worth looking at in this title, I suggest you avoid it.

A very light hearted adventue in the style of classic NES/Genisis RPGs. The system is very well done for an indie game and it's quite possable to custom your main character towards sword play or sorcery as well as a few other characters. Some (October, no techs, but a good weapon) are much more liner minded but can still become a physicaly played character. The Game has additional modes after the first play (most notable Cthulu's angels with a dirrent/alterd cast. Also has diffrent difficulties (a lot of the negative reveiws seemed to have missed this in there complaint of just clicking to compleat without tactics.). A little shy on equipment choices, but there are more then one set of weapons for a few of the characters to choose from based on users melee/skill/magic prefrence. Also some hard choices at times on lv. up between skill selection, or diffrent growth paths. The battles per area system is a very intreasting mechanic which many other games could learn from, you can barebones (expwise) rush a boss for a challenge, grind a lil as necisary to reduce frustration, or go full grind to maximise PT strength to cake walk over anything you'll encounter at the next area.
Biggest (legit) complaints I have seen is the lack of Darkness and Horror since it is a game staring Cthulu. This game is light on story but has some pretty funny moments/comments (I literally spent over an hour cheacking Zombies to see if any had alternate dialog, unfortunatly no...but gravestones are awsome). As I said light hearted.
Still for what your paying and what you get it's well worth your money, especialy if your like me and foundly remember classic rpgs of the 80's and 90's.  Now I'm going back to racking up more hours of insanity!
Ps: You can walk under bridges =D

King of Fighters XIII should be renamed to "Controller Destroyer Simulator", because god damn, a controller of 6 years in great shape became unusable within six hours of this game. Six hours later, my new one's analog stick's becoming loose.
Painfully truthful jokes aside, this is an excellent game and worth the disposible controllers. Cast is extensive and, for the most part, each unique in their own way.
Controls are incredibly smooth and responsive (I'm just too rough apparently), and its fairly easy to pick up and play (i.e: button mash) but the combat and combos are really worth learning; you'll WANT to spend hours and hours in training mode to improve your skills (I'm still trying to successfully pull off a 40 hit combo with Leona I saw in some video). Is it necessary? Probably not, but it's a lot of fun to experiment and then brag to your friend who doesn't give a rat's bum about it before he goes back to talking about catgirls or whatever; I don't bother paying attention; after that 20 hit combo, I'll fight his catgirl 1v1.
The graphics are beautiful and stylish; the character sprites are well detailed, the animation is great, special effects are flashy, and the backgrounds are pretty; some of the backgrounds have people watching you fight, and I swear they're on something because they move faster than a McLaren F1 with the rev limiter removed being driven by Michael Schumacher while hearing the Emerald Hill Zone music from Sonic 2 in the background.  It's hilarious.
I will lastly add that I speak for single-player and local-multiplayer only. I haven't the slightest clue how well online play is.
All in all, this is one of the best damn fighting games I've ever played and worth a purchase even at full price. Bring your friends, buy some spare controllers and be ready to fight; we got all night and no girlfriends.

28 hours in and still loving it (I'm only on mission three in the US solo campaign).
If you watch vids online or read through the guides, I'm sure you'll get through these missions quicker, but I chose to go it the old school way and actually play the game. It's taken me a little bit of time to learn the hot keys (line of sight, rate of fire, speed, range) are all really important and it's intuitive to learn if you play for a couple of hours.
The missions are scripted for the most part, but the AI will throw occassional curveballs. Even with the scripted missions, it still takes strategy and planning your battlegroups out in order to be successful.
I've replayed the first two missions several times (I'm on standard difficulty- honestly, I haven't bothered to change it, because it feels really balanced, challenging and satisfying when you finally beat a mission.
I've been playing strategy games for over twenty years, but am new to games from this dev. So while not completely a newb, it took a few hours to really appreciate the mechanics.
Is it worth forty bucks? For me, yes. There's several missions and additional campaigns to complete, and I haven't even messed around with skirmish or multiplayer yet. I've already logged plenty of time to feel like it was worth the price for me.
One small gripe: I wish there was some sort of carry-over of unit experience or their stats (kill counts) from mission to mission in a campaign. Kudos for tracking stats for each mission, but wish the aforementioned features were implemented. I'm sure balance was an issue with such a system, but even if they carried over kill count, it would have made me happy. Still a good game,  but hope something like this is implemented or made available via modding.

When I first played this on the 360 I really had a lot of fun. I never understood the negative reviews and arbitrary hate this game recieved. That said, the PC, specifically the STEAM version has some pretty negative points that you may overlook, but I find pretty disheartening.
First off, 2 levels lose their audio partially. All you can hear is your lightasber, powers, sometimes music and stormtrooper screams as you cut them donwn. The issue is within the files downloaded from the Steam server, as retail disc versions do not have this issue. It's been 6 years since release and no official fix has been presented. You have to replace the faulty files yourself from whichever source you can get.
Aside from that, and I'm sure other reviews cover this, there's the issue with the visuals. The extent of graphics customization is limited to resolution and a check box for high detail, that's it.
If you want to enjoy the gameplay, an Xbox 360 controller is a must-have. Mouse and keyboard is very clunky and I am not aware if there is any other third party gamepad support.
As for the core game, it is fairly entertaining and challenging at parts. It does suffer from invincibility frames, enemies pulling off attacks that you cannot block and sometimes not even evade.
All in all, it is playable and a very decent game, but the technical issues are not warranted for something you paid for.

I remember playing the original "Where in the World is carmen Sandiego?" detective game for hours on end at a friends house when I was 6 or 7 years old.  The game was painfully slow paced, repetitive, had terrible music, and borderline unfinishable.  The only reward for playing was a gradually increasing rank that became increasingly difficult to improve.  No changes to gameplay, no higher stakes.  Just one long boring slog through the same bifurcated screen, tracking an uncatchable thief and her band of cronies across indiscernible international locales.
I am forced to recall this as the style of "Paers, Please" is so clearly remiscient of those early games. But instead of attempting to confuse you into thinking the game is making a jet-setter out of you, "Papers, Please" does everything in it's power to instill in you the existential dread of being a cog in a communist machine, trapped from one day to the next ina cramped cubicle, constantly racing against the clock, stranded, morally speaking, between a rock and a firing squad.  What enjoyment can be taken from the game is visceral; not accomplishment, but survival. Endurance and speed are developed not to raise ones arms, but to lower ones head, walk home silently and without attracting any attention from your superiors.
Not a game for everyone, but I loved it.

This game is simply not for me.  Why you ask?  Because I seem to solve puzzles differently than how the game developer intended in Legend of Grimrock.  The game itself is fairly good for a dungeon crawler, with decent graphics, simple gameplay, and not too demanding hardware specifications.  The game relies on solving a series of puzzles and finding things to advance to the next level.  The game is linear, and if you don't solve the problem in the exact manner intended by the game developer, you WILL BE STUCK, like I've been.
The first time I time I played, I used a custom party of 1 fighter, 1 rogue, 2 mages, and I found the mages to be useless cheerleaders due to a lack of access to spells.  No problem.  Start a new game.  Second round of 2 fighters, 1 rogue, 1 mage seemed to be a better fit for the challenges awaiting me on level one.  However, there was a portion of the dungeon with 1 pit and 2 pressure plates, with snails waiting behind the gate.  I got past the pit with no trouble, and the gate lifted.  However, during the encounter I moved off the plate, and the gate slammed shut, with no way to lift.  From my previous playthrough with my abandoned party, I knew that this area was important in order to advance to the next stage.  With no way to lift the gate, I was stuck.  Thus, I needed to restart the level.
Moving on to level 2, I almost cleared out the entire dungeon, if I could only find the two keys for the keyholes to the left and right out of gate, with a portal beckoning me to enter.  Unfortunately, I got stuck again.  Why? Because at the portion of the dungeon with two hidden rooms, I did not realize there was a second hidden room, with a key located there. I found 1 key in the room past the teleport trap, and used it.  When I retraced my step, I couldn't get the door to the second hidden room to open no matter how many times I pressed the hidden switch.  It appears that by using the key, I broke the script.  So now I've put five hours into the game, and I'm looking at the prospect of a third restart of the game.  Not worth it. :(

A parody of Lovecraft's masterpieces. It tries to be fun, tries too hard sometimes.
If you can bear with the spoiler amount in the title itself, I can summarize the topic as an evil thing loses its powers and tries to regain them by trying to be a nice guy once in a while. A santa with alzheimer, A mermaid with legs, A kitty who is actually an alien, and a hovering sword comes to his help. I did not finish the game yet, I am about to, but I dont think the other characters will be exceptions in terms of weirdness of the cast. Not really well thought or something, and mostly just interesting for the sake of being interesting. The story revolves around our hero, there are some 4th wall breaking moments etc. But actually let alone a few interesting lines in the graveyard, writing gets dull too easily.
Do we need such a title? Parody is basically a thing which is pointed towards too overrated things. At least that is what I am used to. Lovecraft is one of the milestones for western horror genre, if not one of the founding fathers. Nobody reads him too much, nobody mentions him too much, and in gaming, in movies, in books etc, actually if there is a thing, it is underrepresentation. So what is the point of taking a demigod from his book, and ridiculing him? I am not sure.
I am playing this with developer commentary. He seems like a fun guy. I enjoyed my time with him. And I actually think that this notes could be included in Narrator versus Cthulhu dialogue lines. A missed opportunity.
Music is mediocre. Good for a while, gets repetitive too fast. Does not get annoying. Nothing to shame upon, nothing to praise.
Okay, so what about gameplay. I am not that familiar with this kind of RPG titles, so my comments would be coming from a rookie in this genre. But I seriously dont think that having an algorithm as simple as the following for winning is a good sign:
-Press enter repetitively until all of your enemies die or one of your guys get about to die.
-Heal, if there are more than half remaining, nuke two or three times.
-Repeat.
RPG side is  a bit lacking. With each level, you choose an ability out of two for each character. The maximum level is 30. So There are 2^30 "setups" for each character. This is not as good as it sounds, since most of the upgrades are just basic stat upgrades. Mechanics of the game is not well explained, I still did not understand what is making them insane is doing. I dont know whether water attacks work more against fire-like enemies. I am not sure what each Stat is doing, but I am only guessing. And enemy explanations are nothing more than "witty-oneliners", so there are a lot of missing things here.
Other than that, getting interrupted by random encounters is just too disorienting for my tastes. I played Pokemon before, so I know that this is WAD, but I think experiencing this to the point of forgetting where was I in levels with labirynthine designs  with no minimap, remembering it in some 10 seconds, then getting disrupted again... Till getting angry, is no good design.
There are potions. They resurrect or fully heal your party members. Especially for the Ape Princess, use of it is definitely needed. There are enough weapon finds out in the wild, so I did not spend almost any money.  Imbalance? I think so.There is a 1UP mechanics which helps u to ressurrect at the same point....But I did not use it as well. Since it basically works like an autosave feature, but a limited one, so instead of using it, I just kept saving and reloading (savescumming) almost infinitely. Since most of the fights were pressing enter repeatedly, not saving does not help the feeling of thrill, only frustration. So 1up was a mechanism which is meaningless. Before I start my review of this game, I would just like to say that I have been a fan of the RollerCoaster Tycoon series ever since I started playing it when I was five years old, and the first game will always be in my memory. Alright, lets get this review on the roll.
Ever wondered what it would be like to run your very own amusement park, to build rides at the click of a button, and such, then RollerCoaster Tycoon is definetly for you! RollerCoaster Tycoon is one of the best PC games of all time, and it deserves it's place in history as it. The story as to how RollerCoaster Tycoon began was when Scottish video game developer Chris Sawyer, who developed the legendary Transport Tycoon, was planning on making a sequel to the previously mentioned game, but when in the process of making it, Sawyer developed a keen interest in rollercoasters, and with that being done, he shifted his focus from that to making RollerCoaster Tycoon, and thus, a masterpiece was born.
The basic gameplay of RollerCoaster Tycoon is simple. You're tasked with a specific park of your choosing, and your job there is to reach the goal that is given to you at hand without completely destroying the reputation of the park itself. This can either mean to achieve a certain park rating, amount of guests, and other such tasks that can keep you busy for a while, and with that being said and done, it's time to start building!
You mainly play from a thirdperson view of the park itself, and you can build whatever you want in it, as long as you have sufficient funds. The game has a variety of different attractions to build, ranging from the gently ferris wheel, to the pulse-pounding steel roller coaster. Doing all this is very fun and addicting and can keep you occupied for a very long time. Since this is also deluxe, you'll have some extra fun with additional scenarios to play in, so you can be sure to have endless hours of gameplay. As the "Tycoon" that you are, building all these rollercoasters, rides, stalls, scenery, and paying all your staff in the park is costly, you'll need to be more careful with what you spend your money on, or else you'll need to start taking loans out, and that's never a good thing. With all being said and done, RollerCoaster Tycoon is one of the best games of this generation, and a must have for everyone of all ages.
In conclusion, RollerCoaster Tycoon is definitely a must own, and is a materpiece that could never be remade.

Geometry Wars has company.  Assault Android Cactus is quite the score based twin stick arena shooter.  The game also supports mouse and keyboard.  I've tried both controller and keyboard and each method of control is more than precise enough for this genre.
Multiple characters are available, four initially and five unlock-able, each with different load outs and each requiring their own strategy for you to perfect, and I do mean perfect.  Every little detail in Assault Android Cactus has been methodically thought out and implemented by the veteran developers and it is up to the player to not only play but observe and learn the characters and arenas in order to maximize scores.  The Austrailian developer team's lineage has roots in Midway, Electronic Arts, Sega and Professional Gaming Leagues.
The ranking system is of the D to S / S+ variety.  In AAC, to maximize scores, it is not only about dispatching enemies as quickly as possible but how you dispatch them.  Maintaining chains is paramount.  Strategy is important and seeing players with 100+ hours in the game speaks volumes of depth and replay-ability.
AAC features a battery mechanic, essentially an energy charging pickup that prevents death.  In simple terms, your battery runs out and it's the scrap heap for you.  Hits alone will not explicitly kill you but will make your demise imminent if you accrue too many.  The player character has a limited number of recharging hit points of which a count of zero will render the player incapacitated requiring resuscitation by mashing the fire button.   When rendered incapacitated you will lose some of the energy pellets you've been accumulating to power level your weapons resulting in a powered down weapon and ruining any chance for leader board supremacy.
The game spawns not only batteries but a power-up, one of three types.  Speed, companion orbs to accelerate weapon discharge and stasis.   Not all types are optimal for every situation or every character in every arena.  The three types will rotate in place until the type you desire is picked up.
AAC features a twenty five stage campaign encompassing five themed levels made of five arenas with difficulty increasing with progression.  AAC is high intensity, very challenging and will require a degree of dedication in order to maximize efficiency.  Arenas may contain environmental obstacles and will on occasion morph.   Each of the themed levels is capped with a very challenging boss battle.  Boss battles are typically multi layered and require advanced pattern recognition.  In addition to the campaign, there are additional modes such as survival, daily and local coop with up to four players.  Coop games are also recorded on the leader-boards.    Locally, game pads and mouse / keyboard combinations may be mixed on the same computer.
I mentioned Geometry Wars.   The spawns in the AAC, both battery and power-ups are designed to encourage aggressive game-play.  Having played my share of Geometry Wars, obsessively battling for score dominance with a lovely friend of mine, I'm reminded of a similar design.  Baiting the player to take risks to maximize scores but yet encourage mastery by rewarding success with ascension up the leader boards.   From experience in both games you might think that you've achieved your score goal only to stare in disbelief at the final total.  One more time .........  and so it goes.

Battle for Blood - Epic battles within 30 seconds! is a tile-matching game ported from the mobile/tablet. The game's unique feature is that for every tile matched, soldiers are deployed on to the battlefield. The symbol of the tile determines the type of soldier deployed on to the battlefield. You can also upgrade your soldiers stats from attack power, defense, HP, attack rate and critical rate using your gold earned from your battles.
The build of the game is basically pay-to-win but you can actually clear the game without spending a single penny. It just takes some strategy depending on how you upgrade your army. The pay-to-win part only speeds up your progression with cash being converted to gold but there's no need for it. I actually cleared the game 100% (well, unless there are new updates) for about 15 hours.
It's a decent mini-game and yeah, there's no need to rant about this game since it's actually free. In my opinion, there's nothing bad about having mobile/tablet games being ported to PC and being sold on Steam. There are games out there that are only available to mobiles/tablets. The PC community is lucky to have such games but if you hate them so much then just don't buy them or play them. Simple as that.
Anyways, I recommend this game to those who are looking for mini-games that can burn off some of your free time.

This game has a great idea with a fantastic story, but the gameplay itself is executed terribly. The controls feel awkward, the force powers aren't as fluid as they could be. Enemies can hit you while you're on the ground which can be very frustrating as health does not automatically regenerate. The worst part of the gameplay is the terribly done boss fights. Each one gives you a terrible camera view and lightsaber fights are not nearly as cool as they could have been. If you even try to swing your lightsaber at the boss, they just defelect it with the same annoying animation every single time. Most of the more difficult enemies just require you to spam force push/lighting with follow up short lightsaber attacks and they're just not fun at all. The worst part of the game was probably in the last few levels where you're tasked with destroying a ship using force push powers and the objects never travel in the direction your aiming, making it very difficult to take out enemy TIE fighters. Another pretty stupid part of the game was one of the levels bosses. The developers thought it would be cool for you to fight Darth Maul, so they had your comic relief robot hologram character randomly fight you in the middle of the mission. It just came off as lazy and frustrating.
The graphics are expected for a game from 2009. Unfortunetly, the game is a pretty obvious console port, with a painful 30fps lock that keeps the game from running as fluid as it could. The lighting and textures are average but what really stands out is the fantastic physics engine. While the controls are terrible making it difficult to do, it is still awesome to be able to pull objects off the walls and throw them at your enemies just like you would see in the movies.
The story is this games only saving grace. It takes place between the original trilogy and the newer prequel series with Darth Vader hunting down the last remanents of the Jedis in the galaxy. You play the roll of a new apprentice "Starkiller" who is tasked with going to planets (all of which are locations Star Wars fans will recognize) to kill a bunch of locals and hunt down the jedi hiding there. The cutscenes are done very well with great voice acting and new original characters that fit perfetly into the Star Wars universe. The scenes even have that cheap looking transitional fade that the original movies had which really shows the attention to detail in making what appears to be a real Star Wars movie. The ending does feature two endings depending on what you do, but I won't spoil why/how.
Unfortunetly, this is a video game, and the story alone is not enough to be able to fairly recommend this game. If you love star wars, you can probably make it through the terrible gameplay just to see the cool cutscenes and story, but if not, avoid this game.

Just like real life! ENJOY!

I've been a Wargame series fanatic ever since the release of European Escalation.
If that describes you, then you need to buy Steel Division:  Normandy 44.  It's that simple.
Eugen has teamed with Paradox to bring back almost everything you loved about Wargame, except this time set in a WW2 timeframe.
There's enough "newness" to this game to give even a veteran Wargamer a learning curve...I probably spent the first 30 hours or so re-learning the particular dynamics of this new game.  The three-phase battle sequence is the biggest and most interesting, IMHO.  The damage model has been revamped - no longer can you pull units back for repair and resupply...once your unit is damaged, that's it.  Anti-tank warfare is another big change...you'll need to scout lines of sight, shepherd your guns, and guard strategic crossroads.  Which reminds me - roads are key.  Travel across open land in this new iteration is painstakingly slow, making crossroad control vital.
AI is improved as well - especially when it comes to probing and exploiting weak points in your line.  I would skirmish the Red Dragon AI on "Very Hard" and win consistently with a variety of decks and approaches.  I struggled to get past "Medium" AI for quite some time in this game.
All in all, a must-have for fans of the Wargame series.  Money well spent.
