Prepare to die, again and again. 'Legend of Grimrock' is a hardcore RPG even in normal difficulty. Either I made all the wrong choices either your party is always at a (more than slight) disadvantage as you get to higher levels. I've been poisoned and eaten alive by spiders, incinerated by those flying armored mages, and even chewed up by frosty lizards. The devs really want you to suffer in this dungeon that often seems like a dead end as it's almost impossible to fight and defeat more than one enemy at the time. All the fighting is done real time but there are no shortcuts or hotkeys, therefore the computer will always be quicker then you as you will struggle to command the attack with your mouse - especially with the spells that need several inputs : choosing the wand, choosing 1-4 runes, and then pressing on the attack button AGAIN! But most of all the puzzles will drive you crazy: 'The Maze of Madness' will drive you as mad as hell until you can't take it anymore (or find the improbable solution with no hints whatsoever) and the mostly random logic will leave your characters and yourself starving while you bang your head against the wall.
The minimalistic nature of the game is classy, but the lack of real meaning to many of the puzzles is frustrating; some are genuinely good and easy to understand thanks to a scroll (the shadow maze for instance), but now I'm currently stuck in an endless hall in level 9. There's probably a hint I'm missing somewhere in the slaughterfest but maybe I'll die before I find it. I might never see the light of day, after all I've been there for over 24h already...Grimrock don't roll, it's a total headbanger!
PS: I eventually found the scroll and got to the game's over-the-top goofy conclusion; you have to see it to believe it! Also the level editor is great and relatively easy to use and some of the mods are actuallly way more enjoyable than the original, there's this awesome Mine of Malan Vael and The Tower of Bones that could both easily be official DLCs while we are all waiting for the sequel.

Combine that to an attack system triggered by a right mouse click on 4 squares at the bottom right of your screen, with recharge times for every attack and movement along a grid and you'll understand what the issue is: more than fighting enemies you're fighting the interface. Steel Division is a fantastic game with a complex  real time tactical gameplay environment. I was a VIP beta and Beta tester and frequently mentor new players. These comments reflect my experience with the game.
Pros :
* for the first time in Eugen's development history, a robust and full featured tutorial that explains most elements of tactical combat
* complex air combat simulation, complete with RTS friendly boom and zoom implementation for the lovingly detailed P51D Mustang and P47 Thunderbolt. Careful micro, good use of AA and veteran planes can allow a skilled player to win 2v1 or even 3v1 fighter duels.
* good balance since the latest patches which fixed notorious bugbears like AA interaction, veterancy, excessive Jagdpanther availability and numerous other issues
* faithful modeling of armored warfare, complete with ammo, a reasonable armor/armor penetration system and some basic simulation of systems failure. Sherman vs King Tiger is a tough fight that can only be won through careful tactical decision making and good use of combined arms warfare. The simulation takes into account things like turret rotation, the vertical gyrostabilizer of the Sherman, optics and numerous other components, but manages to boil it all down into a set of easily understood stats on the unit card.
* infantry combat that is a good compromise between the large scale of the combat environment and the reality of infantry combat in Normandy during WW2. This includes grenades, smoke grenades, modeling of individual infantry weapons systems, flamethrowers, HMG teams, infantry mortars, towed weapons and the ability to enter and exit individual buildings as opposed to the blocks in previous titles. Fans of CoH2 and WW2 sims will find the lack of window modeling a little jarring and the omnidirectional cover less involved than the careful manipuplation of cover in those games, but will appreciate the huge leap in scale and realism
* probably the widest number of vehicles and weapon systems ever represented in a WW2 game set in Normandy. This includes early war favorites like the Pz1, Pz2, B2 and R35, as well as less common infantry weapon systems like the MG15. Eugen cares a great deal about historical authenticity and it shows. Forces not usually portrayed in WW2 games such as 1 Pancera (Poles), 3ID Canadian, 15ID Scots, 2e DB (French) and even Italian and Russian troops fighting on behalf of the Germans (sometimes of their own free will, sometimes not).
* Eugen's deck system continues to be a fun way to individualize combat formations and ensure that no two battles even against the same division will ever be the same. All divisions come with a detailed biography of the division and the individual leading it. Divisions are represented as they were during the actual campaign, and players build battle groups from them which contain a subset of units available to the division. Players receive division specific income during the three game phases which allow them to bring in a subset of units in their battlegroup.
* 2v2 through 4v4 games are an incredible experience. Divisions can compensate for one another's strengths and weaknesses and can engage in truly impressive team play reminiscent of the World in Conflict experience. This is best experienced with a friend, but there are a large number of games in this size and it is generally very easy to just drop in and play and have a good time.
* Campaigns are short, but the missions are well designed and no longer simply skirmishes with a frame story as in previous Eugen games. Campaigns marked hard are indeed very hard and should only be attempted after you are experienced with the game. Missions have multiple sub objectives and are generally both complex and possible to complete with multiple strategies. Campaigns for the 101st Airborne, 21st Panzer Division and 15th Scots are currently in the game, with Eugen promising a co-op mission content drop in the near future. IMO the only thing the single player content is missing is a scoring system.
* UI is massively improved from other titles. There is a line of sight tool accessible through the C key that allows you to see the line of site and distances at any point on the map where you put your cursor. This is especially helpful for new players and looks gorgeous.
* The graphics and unit models are phenomenal.
Cons
* The 1v1 experience isn't particularly interesting in my experience. Divisions are clearly designed around teamplay and it shows, with only a small number of divisions viable in 1v1 without excellent play, understanding of game mechanics and high APM. It can still be fun, but this is not my preferred way to play. During beta and the early period of post release the balance was poor, but things have improved and it is now more enjoyable so I'm giving it a second chance.
* The 10v10 experience is fantastic on the 10v10 map where maneuver and good micro/map awareness can allow a single player to have an outsize influence, but the community largely prefers 10v10 games on 4v4 maps. This results in horrible balance and a massive bias toward heavily armored late game German decks and artillery spam. Avoid the 4v4 map variant, but if you see a 10v10 map variant filling up get in there quick!
* The learning curve can be a bit rough. An experienced player can shred a new player with incredible ease because of the complexity of the mechanics. Deck design is tough and involves game knowledge that new players lack. The best way to learn the game is to play through the tutorial, then the campaigns in order of difficulty, then a few skirmishes against the AI. If you are new and friend me, I will be happy to give jump into a comp stomp with you and explain game mechanics.
* The community does not make use of the matchmaker and this results in lobby sitting simulator at off peak hours. After being spoiled by the COH2/DOW2 matchmakers, it is tough returning to this style of multiplayer.
I recommend it for fans of Eugen's other games, for fans of Relic RTS games like DoW2 and CoH2, fans of the Men of War series, and fans of sims like the Graviteam Tactics and Close Combat series.  It is easily my favorite game of the year and looks set to remain that way unless HOI4 gets some insane patches. If you have any questions about the game please feel free to hit me up with a friend request and a PM.

This really is a superb game with tight mechanics, fair difficulty that doesn't ruin the game, and a crap ton of gameplay variety due to all the characters. Bullet patterns feel fantastic to move around and really give you and empowering feeling when you make it through a wave of them without getting touched. Getting strategies down to complete stages or beat bosses just feel so good and really gets you pumped up to tackle on the next obstacle. I had to pull myself away from the games after wanting to push forward to complete more areas.
The biggest part about this game that makes it so amazing for me are the stages and how they are laid out and even dynamically change during gameplay. It stage transformations happen so smoothly and look so beautifully that sometimes you loose yourself to it and forget that you have bullets flying in all directions. Who ever the stage designers were for this game deserve some sort of award. They are that amazing to watch.
One thing that I found to be relieving is how fast the load times are for restarting stages when you know you are trying to make it through without getting hit or getting knocked out. It's so quick. Even boss fights with dialogue at the beginning are skipped when restarting the boss fight. I just wish more games like this would implement this system. It really helps with getting practice in certain areas without wasting time.

I would welcome it for other modes in the game where a extra set hands would definitely help. But personally, I feel like play the campaign of the game with 2 people would really take away from the feeling you would by taking each stage on yourself.
All in all this is one game that should be in every STG and Twin Stick Shooter fan's library of games. It is, in my opinion, THE best twin stick shooter on STEAM right now. Don't hesitate.

A really good remaster. While there was originally confusion as to what improvements were made, the list is actually quite large, and the more you play it the more you realize a lot of different aspects of the game were changed. Anything from draw distance to certain graphical effects to neon signs having animation to pollution haze and fog to sounds, physics, and controls have been improved here.
On the surface when you watched one of the poorly done comparison videos, it seems like they just upped the gamma and added in some fog. That isn't nearly the case. You can change the brightness in-game, or you can redo the gamma on your TV. Problem solved. For whatever reason they did make it too bright on default here. Honestly, I just put the in-game brightness slider down a bit, and I am happy with the night time looking pretty good. Graphical effects improvements range from various lighting issues, to animation, to reflections and beyond. When you really compare the past version and then this one like for like you understand that a decent amount of work went into this game.
The DLC has been totally integrated as well, which is very nice. It's simply better to have a the full game here with no BS. The game also runs very well on my rig with top settings and supersampling. I found the tone of the original to be too static. Despite lowering the neon bloom of the original--I have no idea why PC players are in love with overbloomed signs--to look more realistic, the signs are actually animated. While not close to as animated as the real Hong Kong, the city always looked dead as hell without any fog or pollution haze. I'm sorry but those things are two HUGE characteristics of the city at hand. Not having them kind of makes your city look unpolished.
I have seen the numerous complaints when this game first released. It was not offered for free, and the changes were just kind of being seen from a hivemind based on one or two videos that did not accurately sum up the new game. Even Digital Foundry's article, done when they were just getting started on comparisons, was a bit poorly made with only the first couple of areas in the game being shown.
Once you start driving and exploring the city it becomes apparent that at least the DE brings the game up to modern standards a bit. It's not a gigantic change that you will spot anywhere, but it's all the little things. Like taking down the obnoxious ads attached to skyscrapers that made the skyline awful. Like actual physics on breakable objects during fights. Like ANIMATED signs in the city or eyes on characters not looking like zombies. Like particles floating around a really polluted and busy city giving it a hazy look and vendors actually being detailed while selling proper merchandise. Like having actual controller support! The city is populated and busier than it ever was, and I get the feelling I am actually in a city with this version.
I could go on and on. Rest assured that on PC this is the definitive version of the game. I have them both, and I would never go back to the old one. The game still remains an excellent rendition of the genre, and there is nothing else like it out there.

This game is a masterpiece. There are a lot of games out there with cops, thugs, racing, car chase, shooting and all things good and bad. So what makes this game different?
1. Environment: It's so refreshing to get out of the States. Every current world story is made with a base in the States. Hong Kong feels a welcome breath of fresh air with it's vibrant colors, streets, people, language, food, buildings, cars, bikes and clothing. It's really great to be somewhere other than the States in a game.
2. The main story: The main story is amazing. Sure it's about an undercover cop who is trying to take down the triad that is eating away at his city, at the same time getting emotionally attached with the triad, at the same time trying to fight demons, old and new, at the same time having no clarity of thought regarding who he actually is cheering for. It's a gritty, marvellously written piece of narrative that'll make sure you stick to your screen until you're through.
3. The graphics: Yeah yeah. I know. With all the new games I'm still going on about the graphics. Drive on the roads of Hong Kong when it's raining and look at the road. You'll know what I'm talking about.
4. Fighting mechanics - Hand to hand: THIS is the bomb! Flawless hand to hand martial arts like in no other game before. And it's look and feels amazing. Every fight is new. Every confrontation is a challenge of it's own. There are combos that only doesn't look crazy but actually are. Best hand to hand combat ever. And that's counting Arkham series.
5. Shooting mechanics - All kinds of guns: Shooting mechanics are pretty much normal with Max Payne inspired slow motion cams included. You can use all kind of guns. But the best parts are shooting in a car chase. When I first saw at how shooting at the tires made the car fly, I just shed a tear,
6. Open world events: Sometimes repetative. But overall enjoyable.
7. DLC 1 - Nightmare in North Point: A step away from the serious cop saga and more into the domain of Saints Row stuff. You got demons to fight off, zombies and undead to deal with (Yes. Those two are different things.) Not great stuff, but for a short DLC, it's pretty sweet.
8. DLC 2 - Year of the Snake: Get back again into the cop saga but this time, no undercover stuff. You're a cop now. With all the duties and obligations of one. And it's new year and a cult threatens to blow half of Hong Kong away. It's a neat, race against time thing to stop that from happening. And the way this DLC is made, you actually feel the rush.
That's it. If you haven't bought this game and looking for something that'll engage you but not make you impatient and irritated with it's 200+ hours of gameplay which is repitative as hell, go for this.
Oh and definitely try out the Karaoke.

When your looking for a game thats got a more relatable character than anything GTA can throw at you (Yes Trevor, we're looking at you) and is still as gritty (so basically no Saint's Row) get this. Most of my playtime on this game is through the stand alone client, so hours shown here are not accurate.
PROS:
- If you're playing with friends , it definitely makes the experience more enjoyable, though you'll be playing together mostly during dungeons / instances.
- Great graphics.
- Interesting job/class system which allows you to play any profession/class with a single created character.
- Boss fights are fun, and can get a bit challenging at times.
- Entertaining story when at times, though I did find myself skipping through a lot of it, and mostly watching only the scenes with voice in them.
CONS:
- If you're not a tank or a healer, expect LONG queue times. I've sat in the queue for over an over at times unable to get into a dungeon/raid/boss fight.
- If you're playing alone, it may be hard to get motivated at times to keep doing the same cycle of things (leveling up in Palace of the Dead, or running fates, etc). The story does do pretty well at covering most of the leveling, though.
- Grinding side jobs (cooking, alchemy, etc) is more of a chore and hardly ever fun.
- After the initial learning curve (learning your best spell rotations, etc) , combat gets a bit boring and annoying at times when you're trying to keep in rotation, but having to avoid hits makes it so you have to start the rotation over again.
If you're playing with friends, I'd give this game 8/10, without, probably a 7/10 or less. I do recommend playing it if it's your first time, as it does provide plenty of enjoyment for the new player.

Before each battle, you have an opportunity to customise your Battlegroup, first picking a division to draw units from and then adding them to your Battlegroup with a card-based system. Each of the three countries you can play as have a number of different divisions, each with their own unique personalities and backgrounds that Eugen have researched and recreated. One German division is made up of the low morale conscripts from the Eastern Front, Polish troops fill the ranks of the Allies’ Black Division, there’s infantry divisions, paratrooper, and armoured divisions, just as you’d expect to see in Normandy 1944.
Patience and attention to detail are basic requirements, as is not just knowing but caring what makes one of six different tanks or recon units different from the others. The pace is weird, sometimes slow then suddenly too fast to cope with. I don’t like to say it, but Steel Division can be hard work.
But with the patience and the will to learn, Steel Division can also be exciting and absorbing. By the time the campaign had me holding off German divisions in a central village while exploring for anti-tank guns behind enemy lines, I was having a good time. Massive-scale battles with multiple tank groups rolling around the countryside, machine-gunners and bazookas garrisoned in the towns, aircraft looping and duelling overhead, makes all that strategy seem pretty cinematic. It is, as I said, a wargame, but not as dry as the usual efforts.
First of all, each Steel Division battle goes through three different phases, the phases determining which units you can deploy. Your requisition point tally keeps climbing, minute by minute, but some of the most expensive and powerful units can only be brought into action in the first or second phases, and there’s always a question over whether it’s wiser to splash out on the big guns or reinforce with weaker but cheaper units.
Picking your units also forces you to think about the long game and the length of battle. You’re given more resources to spend every minute, which you can pool up and spend together or dole out a little bit at a time, but the rate of resources changes through the three stages of a battle – A, B and C. Some divisions have more resources early on, others have more later on, and unit cards unlock during different phases as well, sometimes letting you redeem them multiple times. Do you want to have one tank early on, or the ability to call in two or three tanks later? Are mortars enough in the late game, or will the long range of howitzers help turn the battle? It’s a clever system that doesn’t devolve into the cheapness of card systems in some other games.
Secondly, Steel Division has an active frontline; an instant, constantly shifting visualisation on the battlefield that shows exactly who’s dominating and where. In Skirmish, you get victory points for the percentage of the map you control, so the frontline isn’t just informative, but a very big deal.
PROS
+Impressive historical detail
+Authentic maps and units
+Deep and engaging strategy
+Extensive Battlegroup system
CONS
-Hard to get into
-Heavy on the micro-management
Neutral:
=Imbalances with certain unit types and between divisions
=Voice overs simply put through audio bank playback
=Audio sometimes not matching gunfire
Conclusion
While there’s a distinct appeal to Steel Division: Normandy 44, this is a game that caters to a particular niche audience of hardcore strategy fans. Its depiction of the Second World War focuses on realism, with a reliance on ambushes and weight of fire in infantry combat and a surprising fragility to the tanks, but this difficult to master game won’t be for everyone.
Verdict:4/5 Considernig that this is by the same people who made RUSE and the Wargame series: Very much yes.

Fun throwback to ye olden days RPG, or JRPG if you prefer. The game is in the style of the old Final Fantasy games which for me does have some nostalgia value since I remember playing FF 4 or 5 on my old Gameboy Color.
But the game itself is pretty entertaining. The story is amusing, I've had a few good laughs throughout my playthrough so far. The aesthetic is fairly good if you like the 16 bit style. I've had a couple problems with the UI but nothing major after I got used to it, my biggest complaint is that the game doesn't seem to want to let you Alt-tab out of it.
One thing you DO NEED TO KNOW is that if you lose a fight and don't want to spend a 1-up to try again, hitting backspace to quit will force you to reload your last save file. So save frequently and if you're thinking about quiting out of a fight consider how long it's been since your last save. :P
The dungeons are maybe a bit too large and somes feel convoluted, I definitely got lost a time or two. And due to the nature of exploring through being constantly attacked with random encounters this can mean the game can drag on a little. Personally I've enjoyed the game enough this has not bothered me, but if you're expecting this to be a quick little experience you may find otherwise. So far I've played probably around 8 or 10 hours on Hard difficulty and I still haven't reached the ending.
Speaking of difficulty, I found the game a bit too easy on Normal so I had to stick it out through Hard even though at the start MP management is a pain (mana points). Now that's almost disappeared as a concern since all my characters have over 100 MP and some even over 300 and the spell costs didn't really grow in proportion, but I consider that a good thing. Some dungeons are still long enough that I'm starting to run out of MP near the end, for a couple I've even had to go back to town and come back to refill on MP. It can be a bit tedious but Normal difficulty just felt too easy. Though if you just want to blitz through the game just for the story, then going on Normal or Easy is probably the way to do so.
The character development in terms of combat is interesting because it genuinely does feel like it's possible to have your characters fill the role you wish them to, at least to a certain point. For example your first party member Umi at first seems like a great mage but I think she's actually a better fighter/support and should focus on Str which will really come into form when you pick up Thor's Call somewhere above lvl 20. As she levels you can try to push her down the mage tree but I honestly don't think she'll ever be as good as October. Similarly it's possible to try to make Cthulhu a mage, but I don't think he'd do all that well either, and for both characters I feel this is mostly due to a lack of spells. October gets the access to the full wizard toolkit, while Umi and Cthulhu can only really pick up the occasional spell. And unfortunately it seems once you make a level up choice there is no way to alter your choices, so later on you may regret spending points in one direction or another.
Generally most characters feel useful in some capacity or another, except for maybe Paws. He has extremely high Agility, can toggle the enemy group's insanity on or off, and that's about it? He just seems to be lacking any combat skills to make him effective and even when he gets a couple they don't really do enough damage. The insanity bit is interesting but I don't see a reason to bring him along when Dacre can support much better, both Umi and October are better Mages, and Umi, October, and Sharpe all do way more damage. He's a sort of Jack off All Trades, Master of None in that he can do a bit of just about everything, but all of it is kinda weak. I think he'd have been better if he had been more focused on something.
Overall I would say the combat is competent, which is fine since I think humor is meant to also be a large part of the attraction and in my opinion it works. And I do like the fact you can skip through all the combat text if you so desire, so combat only takes as long as you want it to. Though some of the harder fights did require me to pay attention.
The Insanity mechanic is pretty interesting in that you can get buffs from enemies being insane and it looks funny/cool, and I know the devs intended for it to be a double edged sword, but I tend to find the edge that cuts back at me is a bit too sharp. It's fun seeing October cast Void on an insane group and do 1400 dmg in aoe to a massive crowd, or seeing Cthulhu Dark Strike an insane enemy for like 3k dmg, but it's not so much fun when the enemies start throwing their insanity buffed nukes at you and party members start dropping like flies. All in all I've found it better to avoid turning most enemies insane and just mess around with it from time to time rather than trying to rely on it.
Steam says I have played 12 hours but it's really more like 8-10, but I still haven't finished the game or tried the extra game modes so I hope to be entertained even more by the mighty Cthulhu as he strives to be a true hero.
tl;dr version: A funny, quirky game in the style of oldschool RPGs like the early Final Fantasy titles. Not perfect but it's fun enough to kill a good few hours and has a generous amount of content at a generous price, so imo well worth effort.

My Detailed opinion:
Even with this new games already outstanding update in graphics and realism, they still managed to add in more detailed gameplay than in previous titles. Whether it's the better feel of a true campaign with the addition of helping other farmers, or the ability to make minor adjustments to personalize your farm with buildings and placeable objects. The devs have really done good on their part by polishing a previously great game series by bringing in better graphics and a more well rounded game with a lot more to keep you occupied instead of walking away from your computer until your next harvest is available. The ability to continue to play while other parts of the game, like waiting for your crops to grow, can do so much to improve the amount of enjoyment people get.
Sort-of-cons: Slow going on the early gameplay
During my initial playthrough, for those that have already played other farming sims, I did eventually come to a point where I would have liked to buy bigger and better stuff to expand my farm. Which in all honesty is the point of it all, but I felt myself coming to a split in my decision on how to do it, eventually I decided it would be easier to sell everything and farm up about 100 beehouses to have a large free income while I spent my real world time eating, watching videos, or doing other useless things around my house. On the other hand I could have just went to other local farms and worked their fields while I waited for my own to be harvestable, but I quickly realised that while I was speeding up game time while I was waiting, the mission system puts everything back at normal speed. Which to be fair is how it should be, seeing as the game uses the time clock to monitor how fast you work the fields. This made me feel like I was lacking in getting my fields closer to being ready, so I opted to go the AFK free money route until I could have free income to progress the game a little faster.

Most of the feud with this game is that it's a free to play that is apparently "Pay to Win". Many free games are pay2win; however, that doesn't really matter as much as this game is not multiplayer in any way, so you will not be outmatched if you play freely. Paying will definitely make the game much quicker than it should, but you do not need to pay to make progress in the game and it really does not have a grind element. If you fail a level too many times, it begins giving you consolidation coins which equals the amount you earned through the failure.

So much fun. I don't know if a twin-stick shooter could get any better than this, or if anything this entertaining. The game escalate towards insanity, but it's all put together so well that as things get crazier on screen, the experience only gets better.
It can sound pretty simple when you describe it: you choose one of nine playable androids (five of them need to be unlocked), each android has a unique primary attack and special, and you shoot the baddies. You have a battery meter that will slowly decrease, but can be recharged with battery drops from the said baddies. This isn't anything to worry about unless you're taking a lot of hits - this is a bullet hell game at its core - when you take too many hits you can become stunned, and this is when the battery meter can become an issue. It's all about time management, and getting stunned saps at it. But even after bouts of badluck and poor play, things have rarely felt completely hopeless. Come backs feel like a real thing if you up your game. There are also powerups that drop and you primary weapon progressively gets more powerful until being reset when knocked down.
That's all pretty straight forward. Things get interesting because of the levels you're fighting in. To call them dynamic might be a bit of an understatement. From circular rooms with spinning wheels to square grids that reconstitute at will, things wont get boring anytime soon.
The boss fights are a blast. Each android feels unique. And I could play so many of these levels again and again. There are even a couple added modes I've yet to dive into, and I haven't even finished the core campaign. So much fun.

Here's what you need to know.
The basic robot-shooting gameplay is practically flawless.  The controls are sharp, with both gamepad and mouse / keyboard working just fine (although I personally find using a gamepad much more fun).  There's no ammo or need to reload, meaning you can put out a never-ending barrage of firepower against the constant stream of enemies.  Visual design is superb, with all the robots having distinct looks, making it easy to remember and react to their attack patterns in the middle of the chaos.  Despite the ridiculous number of exploding robots on screen, I never find it overwhelming - everything reads well and the times when you die to something you didn't have a clear warning about are very rare.  The battery system (which is effectively a timer + checkpoint system, with a bit of a twist) keeps the pace up and forces you to be aggressive.
Sound design is great too.  Audio cues are easy to pick up on (such as the "woop woop" when you reach low health, or the little "tink" when your secondary weapon recharges), even while having your face melted off by the soundtrack.
All the little details feel right - the speed at which the power ups cycle, the range at which you can collect the weapon orb things, the time it takes for the secondary weapons to reacharge - and it all comes together to make a game that is just plain fun.
On top of all that, the difficulty curve is handled well.  There's a smooth progression from playing just to clear levels, onto playing for S+ ranks (along with a robot voice saying "S plus!" that makes you feel special inside), onto playing for pure score on the leaderboards.  There are no real difficulty spikes - by the time you've cleared most of the levels, getting the top rank on the first stage is easy, and from there you can just keep going.
Having said that, I do have a couple if issues with the game, the only one worth mentioning here is that I don't think it works very well in co-op mode if you have a bit of a skill mismatch.  Due to the battery mechanic, every member of the team needs to contribute to killing robots as fast as possible in order to reach the next battery drop.  If you have a less experienced player who falls behind, it's not like you can wait for them to catch up - the other players need to immediately pick up the slack by killing robots even faster.  While this is possible, it's no fun for the player at the bottom, as they will be constantly dying, having their weapon level lowered, being unable to keep up with the damage, and then dying again.
In single-player, however, this is a game that I can recommend unequivocally if you have any interest in fast arcade games.

A really good remaster. While there was originally confusion as to what improvements were made, the list is actually quite large, and the more you play it the more you realize a lot of different aspects of the game were changed. Anything from draw distance to certain graphical effects to neon signs having animation to pollution haze and fog to sounds, physics, and controls have been improved here.
On the surface when you watched one of the poorly done comparison videos, it seems like they just upped the gamma and added in some fog. That isn't nearly the case. You can change the brightness in-game, or you can redo the gamma on your TV. Problem solved. For whatever reason they did make it too bright on default here. Honestly, I just put the in-game brightness slider down a bit, and I am happy with the night time looking pretty good. Graphical effects improvements range from various lighting issues, to animation, to reflections and beyond. When you really compare the past version and then this one like for like you understand that a decent amount of work went into this game.
The DLC has been totally integrated as well, which is very nice. It's simply better to have a the full game here with no BS. The game also runs very well on my rig with top settings and supersampling. I found the tone of the original to be too static. Despite lowering the neon bloom of the original--I have no idea why PC players are in love with overbloomed signs--to look more realistic, the signs are actually animated. While not close to as animated as the real Hong Kong, the city always looked dead as hell without any fog or pollution haze. I'm sorry but those things are two HUGE characteristics of the city at hand. Not having them kind of makes your city look unpolished.
I have seen the numerous complaints when this game first released. It was not offered for free, and the changes were just kind of being seen from a hivemind based on one or two videos that did not accurately sum up the new game. Even Digital Foundry's article, done when they were just getting started on comparisons, was a bit poorly made with only the first couple of areas in the game being shown.
Once you start driving and exploring the city it becomes apparent that at least the DE brings the game up to modern standards a bit. It's not a gigantic change that you will spot anywhere, but it's all the little things. Like taking down the obnoxious ads attached to skyscrapers that made the skyline awful. Like actual physics on breakable objects during fights. Like ANIMATED signs in the city or eyes on characters not looking like zombies. Like particles floating around a really polluted and busy city giving it a hazy look and vendors actually being detailed while selling proper merchandise. Like having actual controller support! The city is populated and busier than it ever was, and I get the feelling I am actually in a city with this version.
I could go on and on. Rest assured that on PC this is the definitive version of the game. I have them both, and I would never go back to the old one. The game still remains an excellent rendition of the genre, and there is nothing else like it out there.

This game is a masterpiece. There are a lot of games out there with cops, thugs, racing, car chase, shooting and all things good and bad. So what makes this game different?
1. Environment: It's so refreshing to get out of the States. Every current world story is made with a base in the States. Hong Kong feels a welcome breath of fresh air with it's vibrant colors, streets, people, language, food, buildings, cars, bikes and clothing. It's really great to be somewhere other than the States in a game.
2. The main story: The main story is amazing. Sure it's about an undercover cop who is trying to take down the triad that is eating away at his city, at the same time getting emotionally attached with the triad, at the same time trying to fight demons, old and new, at the same time having no clarity of thought regarding who he actually is cheering for. It's a gritty, marvellously written piece of narrative that'll make sure you stick to your screen until you're through.
3. The graphics: Yeah yeah. I know. With all the new games I'm still going on about the graphics. Drive on the roads of Hong Kong when it's raining and look at the road. You'll know what I'm talking about.
4. Fighting mechanics - Hand to hand: THIS is the bomb! Flawless hand to hand martial arts like in no other game before. And it's look and feels amazing. Every fight is new. Every confrontation is a challenge of it's own. There are combos that only doesn't look crazy but actually are. Best hand to hand combat ever. And that's counting Arkham series.
5. Shooting mechanics - All kinds of guns: Shooting mechanics are pretty much normal with Max Payne inspired slow motion cams included. You can use all kind of guns. But the best parts are shooting in a car chase. When I first saw at how shooting at the tires made the car fly, I just shed a tear,
6. Open world events: Sometimes repetative. But overall enjoyable.
7. DLC 1 - Nightmare in North Point: A step away from the serious cop saga and more into the domain of Saints Row stuff. You got demons to fight off, zombies and undead to deal with (Yes. Those two are different things.) Not great stuff, but for a short DLC, it's pretty sweet.
8. DLC 2 - Year of the Snake: Get back again into the cop saga but this time, no undercover stuff. You're a cop now. With all the duties and obligations of one. And it's new year and a cult threatens to blow half of Hong Kong away. It's a neat, race against time thing to stop that from happening. And the way this DLC is made, you actually feel the rush.
That's it. If you haven't bought this game and looking for something that'll engage you but not make you impatient and irritated with it's 200+ hours of gameplay which is repitative as hell, go for this.
Oh and definitely try out the Karaoke.

...Okay, time for an actual review.  I impulse bought this game while it was on sale for about 4 bucks, thinking that I'd play through it once and then be done with it.  Boy, was I wrong.  I love this game, and part of me feels bad for only paying four dollars for this masterpiece.  The rest of me is a cheap little lump of crap though, so there was no way I would have paid full price for it.  I would now, though.  Now, time for some details.
Gameplay:
I would describe the gameplay as 'Moba-esque'.  Top down perspective, and you use skills, or as they are called in the game, 'functions' to attack.  There is a diverse set of functions which is made far more diverse by the upgrade system.  You can take any function and equip it in an active slot, and then depending on what you've unlocked, one function is called 'spark ()' where you launched out a small projectile that spawns several more which explode nearby, and there is another function called 'purge ()' which fires out a single projectile that slows and deals damage over time to a target.  Placing purge () into the upgrade slot adds the slow and damage effects to spark (), increasing the overall damage.  Depending on your progress, you can place up to two functions in upgrade slots for a single function.
Of course, that's just how you prepare for combat.  It's simple, but also has plenty of depth.  Actual combat is interesting on its own.  There are two strategies, one can move around and attack your enemies in real time, utilizing all of your abilities, or you can utilize 'turn (),' which allows you to pause time and plan out a series of attacks.  Personally, I prefer a merging of these two, fighting against the relatively weak enemies in real time, and utilizing turn () in order to stack huge amounts of damage against the tougher ones.
I like the way that you are just dropped into the game and given only a minimal tutorial that tells you the very basics of how to play, making you have to figure out how to play on your own.  Some people may not like that, but I personally do.
I also like the way that experimentation in what functions you use is encouraged.  There are three possible ways to use a function, as an active function, as an upgrade for another function, or as a passive to give you a buff.  Using a function in any of these ways will unlock some background information.  It isn't critical to the plot to know this information, but it's a nice addition so that you can get more of a feel for what's going on.  You also end up using every function in every slot, so you can get a definite feel for what funcions you like in what slots.  In trying to unlock all of the information, you just may end up finding that you like a function that you never would have tried otherwise.
Soundtrack:
A lot of games have good soundtracks, but not many have
ones.  Music from a good soundtrack can fit in very well with what's happening in the game, or it can stand on its own seperate from the game well.  It doesn't do both.  In the vast majority of games I play, it's one or the other.  Only truly great soundtracks blend seamlessly in with the gameplay and yet also stand solidly on their own when listened to outside of the game, and the soundtrack of Transistor does both of these.  Look up and listen to a song from the soundtrack, even if you haven't played the game, you won't be dissapointed.  I'd reccomend listening to one of my favorites, 'The Spine,' but then don't listen to any more until after you've played through the game.  It's better that way.
Story:
The story isn't exactly obvious.  As I've said before, you're just sort of thrown into the game and have to figure out which way's up, both in terms of gameplay and narrative.  Of course, enough of the story will be explained just through playing the game, but you unlock and read all of the additional information, it really helps complete the story and flesh out the world more.  Overall, the story is great.  I can't really go into more detail without spoiling it, so I won't.
Overall rating:
Talking Sword Boyfriend/10
(Not as ridiculous as it sounds.)

I picked up this little game because it happened to be on sale, and it has been my obsession for the past couple of days.  Everything about this game is gorgeous: the combat system, the art design, the storyline, the voice-over work, and the soundtrack... especially the soundtrack!
What to expect: Well, it's a top-down action game with some light RPG elements set in a futuristic world that is quite different than the usual fare.  Combat seems straight-forward at the beginning, but as you begin to pick up more abilities, and learn how to combine them in new and differant ways, it has surprising depth and leaves a lot of room to develop your own unique style.
The game does very little hand-holding as far as the background story goes, only dropping little hints as to what is really going on, and leaving you to pick up the plot in pieces as you go all the way to the end.  Some may not enjoy the confusion that style of storytelling can cause, but I feel it was a great choice on the part of the writers.  The characters' journey as they make their way through the story together is very compelling at an emotional level - at least it was for me - and this in due in large part to the excellent voice-over work of your ever-present and yet unnamed compaion.
Is Transistor worth getting?  It took me 18 hours to complete two runthroughs and get 100% of the acheivements.  For some, that might not be enough gameplay to justify the purchase, but for me, it absolutley was.  Even if I had paid full price, I still would feel that I got my money's worth on this one.

The scale of the maps feel right - and you get a lovely sense of the range of higher caliber weaponry. I like that tank warfare is about penetration/non-penetration and critical hits and suppression rather than an incremental health bar (as per other games) this means positioning, combined arms and flanking is very important.
The game handles multiplayer fights well, even 2-1 or mismatched sides due to the reinforcement value being balanced across the side - there's plenty of variety in the national divisions and some truly huge 10v10 maps across entire miles wide sections of the battlefield.
If you care more about the single player campaign or skirmish and are worried about it being too twitchy don't be concerned you can freely dial the speed down to "bullet time" or pause and give orders and then speed it up again. This allows you to properly micro-manage everything against the computer if you like - though obviously playing against other people is a more strenous and demanding proposition. It is however (like wargame) a game about scouting and setting up ambushes and clearing opposition with combined arms rather than simply building 20 tanks and rushing in blindly.
All in all its an excellent development on the already quality wargame franchise and if you are remotely interested in the genre and setting (rts and ww2) you should consider giving Eugen Systems your money to encourage them to keep on innovating in this genre of games - they are currently a very interesting studio and deserve the support.

You are appalled by superheroism like in Company of, well Heroes?
You don't want to build factories to produce tanks and breed soldiers directly on the battlefield?
Visible hitpoints on tanks and magical healing of infantry seems weird?
You do like medium paced multiplayer games that prefer tactics and knowledge above klicks per minute and perfect microing?
You do like to build decks? Each one based on historically pretty accurately modelled Divisions? Both for Allies and Axis?
This game might be for you. I certainly do like it.
So, what's the deal?
Steel Division is mostly built around a system of hard-counters to certain threats. The game relies heavily on the concepts of combined arms, recon (recon and even more recon) and supressive fire. Yes, there IS a supression bar. Units can get panicked and will surrender if their situation is hopeless.
Steel Division features a tactical KI that will prioritize targets and send infantrymen and towed equipment like AT guns or flak into the next cover (can be switched off.). Wayfinding still need serious improvement though. It's sometimes embarrasing to see sibling units starting just behind each other take two vastly different paths to the target. Yeah. Kind of a mixed bag here.
So, this game is surely NOT a simulation. Although you might encounter a lot of compromises between "realism" and "game balance/fun" it's a good and very engaging mixture that never looses to impress with details and historical plausibility.
It's built on the experiences of the three Wargame titles previoulsy made by Eugen. It's obvious tha many lessons have been learnt. Core concepts got improved, new features have been added.
You might call it Wargame IV. But in fact it transcends the Wargame series by adding three phases to each battle in which you might field a certain set of specific units from your decks.
There is also dynamic front-line that can be used as a visual indicator of your progress in conquest. Or as a tool to isolate enemy units and to create pockets.
At first, deck building seems pretty limited compared to, say: Wargame:Air Land Battle or Red Dragon.
But by introducing the different phases in which you can only field certain units (no Tigers in phase A, mate) flavourful units like the Char 1 bis, Somua, Pz III, StuG III etc. become meaningful and important assets that would have otherwise not have had any use on the battlefield.
Wargame had so many redundant units. Steel division has not. You got to choose, choices will be hard. Over strenghening one phase in your deck to field more "super-units" in a later phase will lead to failure. It's...different. You'll have to adapt to this challenge.
So, if you're ready to by-pass all 10 versus 10 (clown games. No balance here. It's meant to be broken forever) and 1v1 games (much better balanced than 10vs10. You might enjoy it if you like to be spanked) and ignore destruction mode while not expecting to have a perfectly dramatized singleplayer experience you will get a very engaging tactical RTS.

It should be known that I played this game vigorously on Xbox 360, so in terms of storyline, cannon, and other non-machine related topics, I have at least 300 hours of experience in this title.
Star Wars The Force Unleashed, is possibly one of the most entertaining Star Wars games I've ever had the pleasure of playing! It is not a game fitting for the avid lightsaber fight loving Jedi/Sith personality, as this game's name; 'the force unleashed', is quite literal. You get 'way' more options in this game in terms of using the force, than you do with lightsaber combat...Frankly, lightsaber combat in this game is more of a 'last resort' deal, or if the enemies are so weak/few that it honestly would take longer to beat them with the force.
In terms of gameplay, however, the game is extremely entertaining, and thanks to the game's commendable difficulty curve, from Apprentice to Sith Master(last one has to be unlocked), the game sports an absolute TON of replayability, from alternative endings, to new lightsaber colors, to new unlockable costumes and entirely new characters, the game is one of those gems which has you coming back for more!
In terms of lore, the Force Unleashed opens a new, previously unexplained gap between two movies, I believe its number II and III(not the newer videos). It tells the story of a rogue Sith apprentice to Darth Vader, codenamed simply as Starkiller, who works under the strict and vicicous tutelage of the Dark Lord himself, effectively hunting down exiled Jedi. However, as the story presses on, the young Sith apprentice begins, for varying reasons, to feel less secure in his apprenticeship to Lord Vader, and his life takes a complete U-turn when he meets his new ship pilot, Juno.
The story is believable, as it fills in a lore gap to explain what happened in the space between movie II and III.
Graphics wise, this game is on par with modern video games, and takes quite a bit of effort on your GPUs part to keep up the Framerate counter, however, it can easily be resolved by lowering the resolution, and unchecking the High detail box prior to starting the game, which pretty much eliminates framerate lag(Unless your computer is a potato with copper wires in it)
Do I think this game, and its sequel, are worth adding to your Star Wars game collection? Without a doubt. This game's shere popularity, and Lore accuracy, makes it a 'must play' in order to get insight into a truly intense and entertaining part of the untold-in-the-movies story!

I often think about what games can do that other forms of art can't. Is there actually any added value in interaction? After playing Papers, Please, the answer is a million times yes. This is a game where you're tasked with running a border checkpoint. You check passports, verify personal information, and follow a routine set of rules to make sure a person's paperwork is in order. That might sound boring, but it's incredibly challenging as more and more rules are passed down to you along the way.
But what's so great here is how this tackles a real world issue. This is a game about immigration, which aims to make the player understand the complexity of the situation. Every day, you're tasked with emotionally intense situations. In my first hour or so with the game, I found myself continually staring at the screen upset and dumbfounded as to how I was supposed to handle certain things. Was I going to have to break up a family? How could I admit a known sex offender, but turn away so many others? It's heavy, but I think that's where its strength reveals itself. We can read about immigration all day and debate about it like we're experts. But very few of us will actually ever be in a situation where we have to deal with the gravity of it. Papers, Please gives players a chance to go into the role and see how it feels to bear those responsibilities. Is this a perfect substitute for actually working in immigration? Obviously not. But that level of interaction makes it more effective than a movie in many regards.
But it's not simply good for the statement it makes. The core mechanic at play here is brilliant, turning paperwork into a difficult puzzle game. And while this could have been a quick 3 hour, 1-play game, it's packed with a surprising amount of replayability. Within an hour, I actually restarted the game entirely because I wasn't satisfied with my decisions. And even when I finished the game, I still felt like I could have done better. The game features 20 endings, and getting the best ones require a lot of skill and a sharp memory.
I can't recommend this highly enough. This is, without a doubt, one of the best games I have ever played. It's bold, intelligent, emotionally engaging, and fun (when it's not completely crushing your soul). This is how gameplay can enrich our lives, rather than just serve as a fun distraction from them.
(Note: I received this as a gift from a friend, though I would have bought this myself in a heartbeat.)

A modern take on the old-school tile-based dungeon crawler, was something of a surprise hit. Blending a close to perfect mix of horror, suspense, mystery, puzzles, and combat, Legend of Grimrock enticed my inner adventurer. The game itself is quite enjoyable, the grim-dark atmosphere lends itself perfectly to the setting, and the tile-based movement adds an interesting mechanic to it all. The is a game where you will make mistakes, there’s no avoiding that, you will fumble and fall and lose party members and grumble as you backtrack to a crystal. You’ll jump and curse when spiders sneak up on you, groan and rage as traps trigger and surround you with enemies, and kick yourself for not saving more often. You’ll experiment in the skill tree and find out that you’ve invested in something useless, or that you’ve given points wrong, or expended one-use items on the wrong character. Sometimes you’ll wish you’d taken the other loot, or wondered what was in the other locked room, so you’ll reload and find out, then compare before reloading again and deciding. You’ll rage as monsters surround you, you’ll rage as you find a character suddenly out of ammo, mana, poisoned, or just plain dead. You’ll rage as you run from Ogres, you’ll rage as Fire Elementals hit your back-row characters, you’ll rage as you’re confronted with new horrors the dungeon has to offer. But most of all, you will rage at the puzzles.
The game does not hold your hand, which is both beautiful and mildly infuriating at times. There’s a lot of trial an error when it comes to solving puzzles, and you will die a lot trying. But that’s what this game is, a lot of trial and error. It can be harsh, but it’s never unfair, so long as you use your brain and save every 5 minutes. The only genuine complaint I have with the game is the inventory/loot system; space was simple to manage so long as you saved your sacks and boxes, but the weight mechanic was a little challenging at times, when I discover that the Kayran Nipple I just looted and put in a character’s inventory has weighed them down and has made the party slow as hell. What really got me was that there was no loot selling or anything like that, things just became obsolete and you had no reason to keep them, other than maybe convenient replacements for rocks.
All in all I love this game to death, and had that rare compulsion to play it every second I had free time, though the game is best enjoyed, in my opinion, in longer sessions. That way you remember all the little details you were going over and you don’t miss out on something. That being said, I went over the entire dungeon with a fine-toothed come and still managed to miss some secrets, as the statistics will tell you. Half-way through my first playthrough I realized my lizardman rogue was relatively useless when I could have just gone double fighter mage combo, since I had teched him into ranged and throwing. And that was a mistake. You MUST specialize your character if you want to survive, if you choose to go down swords, you stick with swords, if you want axes, don’t switch out for maces because you found one and it was better, and try to keep to one or two disciplines of magic.
For anyone who likes grim-dark fantasy, dungeon crawling, RPG’s, mystery, puzzles, and/or tile-based combat, Legend of Grimrock is definitely a must. Your inner loot-♥♥♥♥♥ will be pleased, your inner puzzler will be perplexed, and your inner adventurer will be grinning all the while. Enter Mount Grimrock, and make your way to the horrors within, best of luck.

Don't have much to say about FS17, other than the modding community for the previous games has been such an excitement and I can't wait to see what comes next.
My Detailed opinion:
Even with this new games already outstanding update in graphics and realism, they still managed to add in more detailed gameplay than in previous titles. Whether it's the better feel of a true campaign with the addition of helping other farmers, or the ability to make minor adjustments to personalize your farm with buildings and placeable objects. The devs have really done good on their part by polishing a previously great game series by bringing in better graphics and a more well rounded game with a lot more to keep you occupied instead of walking away from your computer until your next harvest is available. The ability to continue to play while other parts of the game, like waiting for your crops to grow, can do so much to improve the amount of enjoyment people get.
Sort-of-cons: Slow going on the early gameplay
During my initial playthrough, for those that have already played other farming sims, I did eventually come to a point where I would have liked to buy bigger and better stuff to expand my farm. Which in all honesty is the point of it all, but I felt myself coming to a split in my decision on how to do it, eventually I decided it would be easier to sell everything and farm up about 100 beehouses to have a large free income while I spent my real world time eating, watching videos, or doing other useless things around my house. On the other hand I could have just went to other local farms and worked their fields while I waited for my own to be harvestable, but I quickly realised that while I was speeding up game time while I was waiting, the mission system puts everything back at normal speed. Which to be fair is how it should be, seeing as the game uses the time clock to monitor how fast you work the fields. This made me feel like I was lacking in getting my fields closer to being ready, so I opted to go the AFK free money route until I could have free income to progress the game a little faster.

TL;DR version: It’s good. It’s fun. Buy it.
Although I only have a few hours into this game, I've been playing the Farming Simulator series since the first one was released. Even though this version is new, it is leaps and bounds above even the most recent Farm Sim 15. There is a greater diversity in crops and animals in this version than previous as well as things which can be done with harvested crops.
I grew up on a farm when I was younger. While this game, in no way, gives you the feel of driving an actual tractor, some of the aspects are better in this version i.e. continually having to buy seed or fertilizer to replenish what you’ve used, a requirement to till the soil after a period of time in order to produce greater yield, and continue fertilization of crops throughout its lifespan to produce highest potential of yield. If you’re a fan of the previous versions and don’t think you would like these settings, no worries…you can toggle them on/off.
One thing which would make the game a better simulator of real farming would be random breakdowns of equipment which require you to either fix the equipment in the field, or tow it back to the main house/garage to work on it there. Been there, done that…
And, yes…there are still plenty of mods out there. Giant is even releasing more this time around.
Overall, I’m enjoying this new version. If you’re a fan of the series, you won’t be disappointed. If you’re a first time player, spend a little less and get an older version of the game to be sure this is something you would like to get into. If you find that it’s for you and you might want to explore this version, remember this: there are trains in this version, and you can also strap down your loads that you’re delivering.

I want to start off by saying that never before this game have I played any sort of top-down game, let alone a top-down (old-school) RPG like this one, so I hold no nostalgia factor for games like this one. This is from the perspective of a man who has been PC gaming since 2002 (was 10 y/o) and is just introduced to this type of RPGs.
It's very difficult to give a good game a downvote, but even if everything else is done great, if your main mechanic (the combat) is done poorly, then the game loses all it's value and becomes bad and frustrating.
Let's begin with the praises first:
As I mentioned, most aspects of the game are done great, we will start off with the:
The art for the characters is great, when you see emotion, the picture changes according to the mood of the character. There is lots of variety between most of the monsters and you don't feel like fighting a different version of the same creature over and over again, even through some are just re-skinned and re-colored.
Great ! Music is awesome and the sound effects while fighting vary from each-other.
Again, great ! I love how you are a hero, but also not. You want to be evil, but you have to do good things in order to be able to do bad things. I know, right ? Mind=blown. The ending is very disappointing though, I really hoped that the opposite of what happened to happen.
Oh thank you, thank you, thank you for adding a sprint button, also thank you for making the "attack" command to be the default one. That helps with spamming ENTER in order to get out of the garbage fighting system as fast as possible.
...and now the bad...
I wish it wasn't this long honestly. Every dungeon frustrated me and I blitzed though it as fast as possible. I am so glad I chose the easy difficulty, otherwise I had to spend a lot more time planning my moves and forget where I was going by the time the fight is over.
Whenever you are in a dungeon (or outside one, doesn't matter) you will constantly get interrupted by random encounters. For some it's possible to spam the ENTER key in order to pass them fastly, but for the later ones that option goes down the drain.
Picture this: I am happily strolling down a dungeon, thinking of how to reach the end, I see the layout and think of the best path to take.... and all of a sudden.... BAM! A RANDOM ENCOUNTER. These things can take 5+ minutes. You have to concentrate, think of your best powers to use, look at your MP, HP and stats, look at the monsters' stats and so on. You get so involved it the fight that when you finish, you completely forgot where the hell you were going and forgot your plan completely.
So you set off again, walk a bit, find the way and BAM! AGAIN A RANDOM ENCOUNTER. This repeats 30 times, making you walk the same path 30 times, seeing the same thing over and over and over(x27) again. This is not fun, it completely ruined the game for me. Exploration is out of the question in this game. I cannot enjoy the look of the dungeon even, if the gameplay constantly gets interrupted by random encounters.
That is why I don't recommend the game and I am sorry I bought it (only for 31 cents, but even free I wouldn't have played it if I knew how bad it was). It's a shame really because the game does everything else fine.

...Okay, time for an actual review.  I impulse bought this game while it was on sale for about 4 bucks, thinking that I'd play through it once and then be done with it.  Boy, was I wrong.  I love this game, and part of me feels bad for only paying four dollars for this masterpiece.  The rest of me is a cheap little lump of crap though, so there was no way I would have paid full price for it.  I would now, though.  Now, time for some details.
Gameplay:
I would describe the gameplay as 'Moba-esque'.  Top down perspective, and you use skills, or as they are called in the game, 'functions' to attack.  There is a diverse set of functions which is made far more diverse by the upgrade system.  You can take any function and equip it in an active slot, and then depending on what you've unlocked, one function is called 'spark ()' where you launched out a small projectile that spawns several more which explode nearby, and there is another function called 'purge ()' which fires out a single projectile that slows and deals damage over time to a target.  Placing purge () into the upgrade slot adds the slow and damage effects to spark (), increasing the overall damage.  Depending on your progress, you can place up to two functions in upgrade slots for a single function.
Of course, that's just how you prepare for combat.  It's simple, but also has plenty of depth.  Actual combat is interesting on its own.  There are two strategies, one can move around and attack your enemies in real time, utilizing all of your abilities, or you can utilize 'turn (),' which allows you to pause time and plan out a series of attacks.  Personally, I prefer a merging of these two, fighting against the relatively weak enemies in real time, and utilizing turn () in order to stack huge amounts of damage against the tougher ones.
I like the way that you are just dropped into the game and given only a minimal tutorial that tells you the very basics of how to play, making you have to figure out how to play on your own.  Some people may not like that, but I personally do.
I also like the way that experimentation in what functions you use is encouraged.  There are three possible ways to use a function, as an active function, as an upgrade for another function, or as a passive to give you a buff.  Using a function in any of these ways will unlock some background information.  It isn't critical to the plot to know this information, but it's a nice addition so that you can get more of a feel for what's going on.  You also end up using every function in every slot, so you can get a definite feel for what funcions you like in what slots.  In trying to unlock all of the information, you just may end up finding that you like a function that you never would have tried otherwise.
Soundtrack:
A lot of games have good soundtracks, but not many have
ones.  Music from a good soundtrack can fit in very well with what's happening in the game, or it can stand on its own seperate from the game well.  It doesn't do both.  In the vast majority of games I play, it's one or the other.  Only truly great soundtracks blend seamlessly in with the gameplay and yet also stand solidly on their own when listened to outside of the game, and the soundtrack of Transistor does both of these.  Look up and listen to a song from the soundtrack, even if you haven't played the game, you won't be dissapointed.  I'd reccomend listening to one of my favorites, 'The Spine,' but then don't listen to any more until after you've played through the game.  It's better that way.
Story:
The story isn't exactly obvious.  As I've said before, you're just sort of thrown into the game and have to figure out which way's up, both in terms of gameplay and narrative.  Of course, enough of the story will be explained just through playing the game, but you unlock and read all of the additional information, it really helps complete the story and flesh out the world more.  Overall, the story is great.  I can't really go into more detail without spoiling it, so I won't.
Overall rating:
Talking Sword Boyfriend/10

I can't recommend Transistor enough. I bought it myself on sale for four dollars and after playing a few minutes bought it for some of my friends too. It's fantastic and, I feel, completely worth full price at $20.
This game has an interesting playstyle though it doesn't go too deep into explaining it to you. It's top-down with a number of "functions" that act like spells. You can use these to destroy enemies with combat being sectioned off almost into different rooms or areas in the game, each separate from the next. Combat can be difficult at times but I actually went through the game without dying. Some functions are better than others in combat and you'll figure out which these are yourself. If you lose all of your life, you'll lose access to a function rather than dying which makes remaining combat in the area harder but your function will return eventually. I actually do like this mechanic because it forces you to switch up your function use.
The story to this game rolls out slowly and thoughtfully. It takes its time to show you what it has to offer so you have to be patient and think more closesly. Some have issues with the direction of the story but I quite enjoyed it - I would rather not say more about it. In short, you're a singer named "Red" and you've fallen into possession of - something - and you're out to find out what happened to you and right the wrongs done. The city itself has quite a bit of character too though as you'll find out. The atmosphere in this game is phenominal and in my opinion the best part of the whole thing. The soundtrack only helps set the scene of a city on the rise, but a bit wistful with hints of sadness and longing.
The game isn't especially long but well worth it for the price.
I can do nothing but recommend this game highly to anyone who would listen. I don't normally write reviews but I felt that this one is well deserving of it.

I picked up this little game because it happened to be on sale, and it has been my obsession for the past couple of days.  Everything about this game is gorgeous: the combat system, the art design, the storyline, the voice-over work, and the soundtrack... especially the soundtrack!
What to expect: Well, it's a top-down action game with some light RPG elements set in a futuristic world that is quite different than the usual fare.  Combat seems straight-forward at the beginning, but as you begin to pick up more abilities, and learn how to combine them in new and differant ways, it has surprising depth and leaves a lot of room to develop your own unique style.
The game does very little hand-holding as far as the background story goes, only dropping little hints as to what is really going on, and leaving you to pick up the plot in pieces as you go all the way to the end.  Some may not enjoy the confusion that style of storytelling can cause, but I feel it was a great choice on the part of the writers.  The characters' journey as they make their way through the story together is very compelling at an emotional level - at least it was for me - and this in due in large part to the excellent voice-over work of your ever-present and yet unnamed compaion.
Is Transistor worth getting?  It took me 18 hours to complete two runthroughs and get 100% of the acheivements.  For some, that might not be enough gameplay to justify the purchase, but for me, it absolutley was.  Even if I had paid full price, I still would feel that I got my money's worth on this one.

The story is the main draw of this game for many people in my opinion. It's scope and depth is well beyond most normal MMO fare and will take you from humble adventurer beginnings to seeing you to becoming
and beyond across the base game and at current count two expansions. So it's quite easy to say that there is a lot of story available to sink your teeth into. In fact it took me about 200 hours to get through the base game's story and 100 hours for each additional expansion. YMMV as I like to take my time and do every quest and side quest available. The expansions in particular are quite good. Do yourself a favor and don't be in a rush to end game(or worse spoil it by purchasing a skip potion from the Mog Station) or you will miss out on a huge part of the game.
FFXIV is almost exactly like a standard MMO when it comes to most gameplay mechanics. However, it takes those mechanics and excels at it better than every other MMO currently on the market and adds extra stuff besides. The amount of content in this game is staggering. There is so much to do in this game you will get lost and it may end up seeming overwhelming at first. I've sunk over 1,300 hours in this game(on PC, I also played on Playstation previously before switching to PC) and I've still not done everything the game has to offer. End game you can do anything from Raid to your hearts content, delving into dungeons, participating in PvP matches, Crafting or Gathering, participate in hunts against high level and difficult world boss type monsters, playing pretend Sims and decorate your house or do some gardening in one of the wards of player housing available, creating glamours for your character, playing music if you're a Bard, collecting minions, playing mini-games, participating in seasonal events, ect the list can go on. Suffice it to say you will never lack something to do. The best part is content is reguarly added as well every 1.5 to 3 month intervals. The next patch 4.2 should be coming sometime in Jan 2018 and will have a ton of new content and dungeons to play.
Now to the downsides. The biggest would probably be the Mog Station is very controversial in the game. It is essentially a cash shop in a subscription based game that sells mostly cosmetic gear and mounts for sometimes very steep prices. However, it also started selling "Jump Potions" that will instantly level a character to level 60 in one of the combat classes. This is NOT the max level currently as that is 70 so they will still need to do some work to catch up.
