Disclaimer: I love wargame but...
First off, this is quite similar as Wargame, but not really. It's MUCH easier to get into as you don't have to research for a long time what everything means on a units statcard and what the speciality is for every faction.
It's also much slower and better structured than wargame because it introduces phases. Games are divided into 3 Phases A / B / C  whereas in A you can field only relatively basic units and in C the heavy stuff hopefully is rolling out to victory, so contrary to Wargame you can't field your best unit right away, you have to hold your ground before you can bring that shiny king tiger to the field, and that can be quite a challenge in itself as heavy armor divisions for instance tend to be weak in early phases - because every division has a fixed but diffrerent income each phase. This gives those famous units much more weight and meaning than just the culmination of their stats.
For instance the French sport much more income than the allied tank division in Phase A making them superb to take ALOT of ground early but they struggle holding their ground against the heavy tank divisions in later stages. This leads to interesting choices especially in multiplayer as the balance of power constantly shifts and you have to adapt. You can't just take all heavy armor divisions and hope to hold your ground against strong infantrydivisions as it could mean you're not even going to see the Phase where you're strong at.
These are interesting design choices coupled with a streamlined system of damage: your tanks are either alive or dead, no partial damage. Your Panther can absolutely die to a silly sherman round but it's just not very likely. I was skeptical of this first but it leads to epic moments, taking down that King Tiger that proofed to be invincible for so long is a feeling to be remembered - you still get rewarded for working these probabilities but it never feels unfair. On top of that system you have the supression mechanic which works on vehicles as well, a tank crew is not getting phased by a few MG42 bullets but it definitely starts to question their choices of profession once the 10th shell of AT guns bounced off their chassis rendering them useless and retreating.
Another point that not alot of people note is the speed of the game, it's rather slow (but not relaxing, dont be fooled). You're constantly busy moving the slugish frontline to get more area under your control while the enemy does the same but you have time to do your decisions, noone will outdo you because they click faster. It makes sense to learn some useful hotkeys but essentially it's your fault if you lose a tank because you just moved it into reach of that pesky AT gun the enemey silently moved up. The lack of air deployable troops and that you can't just walk past an enemies front without them noticing focuses the game brilliantly on the frontline and nowhere else. (You still have a ton of options to use artillery, planes, tanks, infantry, mech troops in any way you like, but an army is no covert ops operation)
You almost never get frustrated with the controls, it's all about what and how you do it. There's very few games that do this well and Steel Division is one of them (and probably one of the best) because it's far less crowded than Wargame, individual units actually mean something here, by the time you see 4 Tanks pushing on a frontline with infantry it's probably already over.
It's also notable that the airgame in this seems to work much better than in wargame, planes fill a vital role and str hard to take down but you dont need to apply nifty tricks like in wargame to make them work. Their (slower) speed also seems to fit their realworld counterparts, they do exactly what they are supposed to but dont win wars alone.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game in it's current state, it is a fantastic RTS and lives right now in my Top 3 of RTS easily, it's THAT good for either newcomers and veterans alike.

I bought this game at the start of the early access beta, and at the time of writing have 78 hours in game (1 day after full release). As a bit of background I am a veteran of all three of Eugen's (the developer) previous Wargame titles, and am a regular player of a number of Paradox (the publisher) titles.
Overall, I am very happy with the game. The single player campaigns are reminiscent of Wargame: European Escalation, which had, in my mind, the best campaigns of all the Wargame series. Multiplayer is stable and fun, although please make sure you have a good internet connection and decent hardware! In contrast to some of the negative reviews, I have found the majority of the player base to be pretty good natured and friendly, both in game and in the forums, and there is more teamwork going on in Steel Division than there ever was in Wargame.
An important thing to note is that if you are expecting perfect competitive balance between all of the divisions in the game then you will be disappointed. Eugen have taken a historical approach to the game (although there are a few gameplay allowances) so some divisions are better at certain things than others. However, I have found that EVERY division is capable of winning a game, if handled correctly.
On a final note, if you are one of those casual historians who believes that German tanks were the best tanks of WW2 and could never be killed, you need to revise that belief BEFORE playing the game, otherwise you'll be very sad when your Tiger is sideshotted by a veteran M10 Tank Destroyer on its first shot!
The game is fun, looks nice, rewards teamwork and good tactical play, and I would highly recommend it.

I am going to qualify this review by indicating that I'm not a big fan of fighting games. Especially ones that are very technical. So, if you are a fan of fighting games requiring a high degree of technical proficiency, you can probably skip my review.
I gave this game a fair play through. I obtained this with a bunch of other games via a Humble Bundle purchase. It wasn't part of the reason I bought the bundle, but I figured I'd at least give every game a fair shot. This game provides 7 Steam Cards for playing it as well, which is nice.
However, grinding out those 7 cards was exceptionally painful. I only become "passably familiar" with a single character over my entire time playing this game. When I say that, I mean it's difficult even to get past the first few stages in Training!
Now, it is true that this game when I first acquired it wouldn't recognize my controller at all. So, maybe it was insanely difficult to enter combinations due to it not properly supporting it or something along those lines. I can only comment on my experience.
As for the game itself, I quickly grew bored with the poorly-translated dialog which plays at the beginning of almost every fight. There was almost as much button mashing just to skip dialog as there is when playing the game! And despite the fact that they obviously made an effort to translate the game's text, there is absolutely no audio translation... which makes it very difficult to find any appeal for the characters unless you happen to speak the language. I'm assuming it is Japaneese, but that's only because I believe Japan is the largest game producer in Asia, so take that with a grain of salt.
After my compaints in the translation department, you also have the art style. It's obviously an anime-style fighting game. It's even complete with the horribly sexist character models you would come to expect. I remember one of the female characters they clearly put a lot of time into making sure her breasts "jiggled" as much as possible. Maybe it was done mockingly or something, but all "personality" of the character comes through in audio... which I couldn't understand!
Honestly, I do feel that there's quite a set of people who might enjoy this game, but it definitely wasn't for me. If there was a "meh" option, I would choose that instead of "not recommended," but I don't have that option.

the most important part to enjoying this game is the spectacle. there are scores of games that do this better. don’t expect dynasty warriors or even the god of war it rips off. it’s painfully paint-by-numbers with an ignorant combat system that discourages melee and has no difference in combo versatility other than length. what creates the spectacle is, after all, the ranged combat. starkiller dumps lightning from his fingers and has better hadokens than any street fighter. all you gotta do is blast the rag dolls away with your midichlorian powers. if being a magical laser deathmachine isn’t on your list of ‘entertaining spectacles’ then you’re going to take issue with this game. that’s not to say there are no redeeming qualities - there absolutely are - but its success hinges so much on enjoying being a destructive brutish jedi.
you have a four string combo and that’s pretty much it. it can be delayed to get more hits in but since enemies have armor values it ends up doing less damage, which is a pretty amazing oversight. at any point of your combo you can opt for a finisher, either lightning style or spirit gun. lightning knocks bads down and blasts knock them away. finishing the tail end of your combo with force will instead knock an enemy up, symmetry be damned, leading into a second air combo. if you were to play to efficiently, you'd do this to every enemy, and end with a throw. it does overwhelmly more damage than any other string, though playing like that would become mind-numbing. I ended up using different finishers arbitrarily, pretending like the invincibility frames from grabbing were needed, the aoe of the lightning swipe was tactical, and that blasting the enemies away secured my safety. the depth could be there, but it’s rendered brainless by design flaws.
I’m torn over which is the worst offender, so I’ll relate linearly. force unleashed’s cardinal sin is having a level up system. whatever depth we can allow the game doesn’t matter; it’s locked out to you. it’s not even as if there’s a gradual curve compensating for your progression like a rpg, enemies from the second mission forward get no bulkier, which isn’t something I wanted mind you. it does take considerably less points to acquire every combo, though maybe it was simple luck that allowed me to have them all before the end, because of another beautiful offender: level ups are also tied to hidden collectibles. if you’re a sleuth hound (or play with a guide) you’ll have a nonsensical advantage over the player whose focus is on combating the level. I’m not against progression in a beat ‘em up, but if the progression overrides basic skill and locks out mechanics that should be in the game to begin with then it’s served no purpose.
its next big ticket in wasted design is very poor enemy philosophy. arrangement of enemies is not all important in a beat ‘em up. some games do this very well, others do not realize there is a purpose to it. both approaches honestly serve just as well and the force unleashed is not without finesse. sometimes it crafts thoughtful encounters. now I’m not so concerned about its technical design, because its ruined from the gate. difficulty is supplanted by giving enemies specific immunities to your jedi magic. the force powers are the most fun part of the game, so this is lamentable, but respectable considering their overpowered nature. however, they couple such immunities with enemies that are immune to knockdowns and hitstun. it’s absolutely stupid for a beat ‘em up to have enemies with constant super armor, because it downplays what should be the focus of the game, its close combat action. on top of diluting its focus, it shuts down a half of your ranged attacked, hampered further by the fact that you might have spent all of your levels on your favorite force powers. you have to grind out high hp enemies using attacks that you don’t favor. there are all kinds of solutions, like putting a window of vulnerability after the enemies attack string, or a successful finisher staggering the enemy. on that note, mechanical enemies weak to electric always stagger to sith attacks and are immune to force. which means the best way to dispatch is repeating the same three hit electric combo. absolutely monotonous.
note that despite these flaws, unleashed is still satisfying to play visually, and is not broken, just a far cry of being sophisticated. starkiller moves quick and is carefully animated. hit detection feels great, favoring you instead of enemies, though sometimes the priority seems wrong. the ragdoll physics are absurd but I wouldn’t want it any other way. my spirit palm should send every idiot flying. rooms are continually different, I was more than surprised, and enjoyed the level design more than anything else in the game. if two missions (that’s like a fourth of the game) didn’t take place on the exact same planets as the first two missions, and if the final level didn’t feel so rushed, I would be singing fat praises. as it stands, though, two levels are remixed environments. they’re still a lot different from the source they reuse, but without the different enemy models and textures the game had been throwing at you up to this point it loses a ton of its momentum. at least starkiller’s fashion always changes between levels, something I still can’t get over.
graphically the game is great, high-budget values everywhere. I’m probably ignorant of games from 2008 but damn it looks good. nice and shiny with an art direction that’s definitely star wars. I don’t remember if it’s the first or second time you go to raxus prime, that’s the stupid game’s fault, but there’s a part where you’re in a huge mushroom-thing with interconnected bridges sprawling upward. it’s like something pulled out of nintendo’s playbook. there’s a lot of detail on the planets and in the space ships. this stems from a desire of having all kinds of things to throw at badguys, even when it stops being useful, the clutter is less than clutter and is real organic. this degree of detail that will probably go unnoticed, simply because the gameplay is no where near as detailed. even better than the graphics is the game’s music. it’s probably star wars standard to have rearranged star wars tunes for their games, but holy crap is this some top shelf classical. makes all kinds of modern games sound like a joke.
now the story is nothing more than a saturday morning cartoon. it doesn’t feel stupid or contrived, but it seems more motivated to get starkiller to fight certain things than to orchestrate his apprenticeship. I found the voice acting awesome and able to carry the whole game and darth vader to be absolutely convincing, sealing the simplistic premise to something I could wholly enjoy. the only thing that would make darth vader cooler is if he was an exiled prince of zeon. it’s not incredibly in-depth, but you know, neither is the phantom menace. it has some hard hitting moments and the writing is pretty serviceable. frankly it’s not the best or the worst, so take it as is and have a ball. the dlc levels are slipshod compared to the main game, I’m not going to grace them with my words, but I’d like to shout out the hoth campaign where starkiller gets luke to turn to the dark side and make luke his apprentice. that’s freakin cool.
so yeah, this is just a spectacle brawler. it has great levels and great theming, but doesn’t quite sink in the gameplay. it isn’t mangacore either, so its missing its targert market, heh. if you’re down to shoot thunder and lighting, to bend spines with your fingers, to cut puppety flesh like cheese with a glowstick, and fly around inside a neutered space opera, then the force unleashed is a successful game. those are all things I wanted to do, I just didn’t know I wanted to do them

TL;DR version: It’s good. It’s fun. Buy it.
Although I only have a few hours into this game, I've been playing the Farming Simulator series since the first one was released. Even though this version is new, it is leaps and bounds above even the most recent Farm Sim 15. There is a greater diversity in crops and animals in this version than previous as well as things which can be done with harvested crops.
I grew up on a farm when I was younger. While this game, in no way, gives you the feel of driving an actual tractor, some of the aspects are better in this version i.e. continually having to buy seed or fertilizer to replenish what you’ve used, a requirement to till the soil after a period of time in order to produce greater yield, and continue fertilization of crops throughout its lifespan to produce highest potential of yield. If you’re a fan of the previous versions and don’t think you would like these settings, no worries…you can toggle them on/off.
One thing which would make the game a better simulator of real farming would be random breakdowns of equipment which require you to either fix the equipment in the field, or tow it back to the main house/garage to work on it there. Been there, done that…
And, yes…there are still plenty of mods out there. Giant is even releasing more this time around.
Overall, I’m enjoying this new version. If you’re a fan of the series, you won’t be disappointed. If you’re a first time player, spend a little less and get an older version of the game to be sure this is something you would like to get into. If you find that it’s for you and you might want to explore this version, remember this: there are trains in this version, and you can also strap down your loads that you’re delivering.

In my opinion, Sleeping Dogs is like a greatly refined version of True Crime: Streets of LA. It is also relatively similar to GTA, Saints Row, and even Crackdown in the sense of the open world freedom with the addition of also being a cop/agent.
One of my favorite things about this game is how short the missions are. That sounds weird at first but honestly there are so many missions and side missions, all of which feel rewarding to complete, so I'm glad they're short so you can easily beat a few in a decent amount of time. Plus you can save at anytime (but you will always load at your nearest safe house).
The driving is one thing that I've seen a few people complain about but personally I love it. It's not nearly as easy as GTA, but like anything, if you just take it a bit slow at first, you can easily get used to it.
Overall: The story is awesome and exciting, the setting in Hong Kong is beautifully made, and the gameplay is very fun and addictive

Legitimately one of the best MMO's out there, if not the best.
An actual interesting and deep story in an MMO? Get outta town. But seriously, the story may not click even for the first few dozen hours or so of playtime, but once it does, (particularly in heavensward) you're gonna understand. Cutscenes and voice acting doesn't occur all the time, but you get it enough that it's an awesome reward for making it through an arc. And there are MANY arcs. The story is big enough that once it starts to reflect on events 50+ hours back in your playthrough, it feels like a genuine history you've been a part of. It's an experience unlike any other
In the meantime, you have tons of things to do. Dungeons, raids, world events, actual enjoyable side missions, even way into late game and so much more. As well as a crafting system that's more complex and rewarding than any other MMO ever, and only gets deeper in late game. And the ability to switch to any class you like on the fly, great for joining your friends while they level.
Cannot reccomend this enough, and now that you can play for free up to level 35, with NO TIME RESTRICTION there's no excuse not to give it a try. Make sure to join a guild early, and partake in one of the most helpful and friendly game communities out there.

My quick thoughts thus far, after just a couple skirmishes:
#1 - The balance still needs work. Right now, the most problematic balance issue is the recon and sight range of non-recon units. Armored units right now feel extraordinarily vulnerable, and the reason is the ridiculously poor sight-range they have. I totally understand if my armor doesn't see enemy units that are stationary in a forest nearby and take a close-range AT weapon hit and go up in flames. What is harder to understand is when an enemy infantry unit is moving in open ground right a little ways away, yet manages to still take the tank out because they weren't seen until the tank was on top of them *in an open field, while the enemy was moving*.
#2 - Anti-air vs Anti-tank efficiency is insane. AT weapons can frequently 1 or 2 shot a tank... anti-air seemed to never make a single kill against air units (though they do have some power against infantry and ground targets). It seems wildly inconsistent that anti-tank units do pretty well, while my only prayer of actually destroying enemy aircraft is with my own. I mean, come on: I have 88-mm AA guns spread around the area I know the enemy aircraft will enter, and they enter only to be nothing more than scared off. I get that my own aircraft should be better at destroying enemy air-power, but if I have multiple AA guns firing on a target, I should have more than a 5% chance to shoot it down.
#3 - I'm not sure I'm a fan of the phase system. It's pretty arbitrary, even in terms of game mechanics and balance... previous games Eugen made basically used the income economics to regulate when you got a chance to get out particular units, which was more flexible and allowed players to rush out an expensive unit quite early at the risk of not having the support units to back it up. This time around, the phase system arbitrarily keeps units out of the game until X amount of time passes.
#4 - I like the dynamic battlelines element. It means that map control can be approached very fluidly and flexibly. Rather than have some static point to capture, the entire map itself is worth something, netting extra income to players that find ways to break the enemy line and squeeze a few units through.
#5 - CPU play is solid, and probably a step up from the already decent play of the Wargame series' CPU. The only thing I've seen thus far that is problematic is that the CPU sure likes to bunch up its units, allowing human players to really get a lot out of their artillery and bombers.
Overall, it's fun. A bit more micro-intensive than Total War games, a little harder to know what is and isn't in cover compared to CoH2, but a lot more action-packed than the typical Paradox games (I love EU-IV and Stellaris, but exercises in intense planning and weighing of risk/reward sometimes needs to give way to a couple hours of actually controlling the combat and watching stuff blow up).

If you played
then you should know what you're in for and, as such, can expect the same experience and be happy that you'll get an arguably better one from Transistor. If you haven't played Bastion, then continue reading.
Transistor is right up there with Bastion in "best games I've ever played" for many of the same reasons as well; I'll start by discussing the gameplay itself. I played through the game using an Xbox360 Afterglow controller, and the controls are very intuitive and remappable in the options menu. Of course, the game can be played without a controller. In terms of difficulty, it's that comfortable difficulty that isn't easy but isn't frustratingly impossible; it's sometimes challenging, but it's nothing an average player shouldn't be able to handle. There are unlockable and completely optional "limiters" that make the game harder and give greater rewards from battle as a result. As you progress through the game, you'll unlock several different abilities that can be equipped in various ways, allowing you to find out for yourself which abilities and combat styles you personally prefer; there's no punishment for not using a certain ability, and (outside of the challenge rooms) you have complete freedom as to how you wish to tackle the many battles in the game.
If I were to attempt to describe the combat mechanics, it'd be a turn-based real-time hybrid; you can attack in real-time (which is rather difficult, as most attacks have short start-up and ending cooldown animations), or you could take advantage of the Turn() function, which is the game's core combat mechanic. By activating Turn(), you essentially freeze time and are able to move and perform actions; when time is frozen, you don't actually
the actions until time is unfrozen, in which you then proceed to wreak havoc on the enemies. However, after you use this, there's a set cooldown period where you cannot use
actions except for running around and evading enemy attacks until you can use Turn() again. It takes a little bit of getting used to and the game provides helpful tips at the top of the screen, as well as the first battle.
As for the non-gameplay aspects, the pacing of the story in tandem with the narrative serves to keep the game entertaining and flowing smoothly. The plot develops the more you play, and you can unlock more information about character backstories by using different abilities in combat. The soundtrack is dynamic as it changes depending on the stage of battle. The entire game can be played in one long sitting (4~6 hours), but it auto-saves at each in-game terminal or whenever you enter a new area, so it's fine to play in short intervals if you don't have the time.
For the record, I shouldn't even be able to run this game, as I don't meet the minimum requirements; however, turning down the resolution and a few other settings, I was able to play the game with an acceptable framerate with little to no issues. Of course, doing such things isn't good for my processor (pun intended).
Excellent artwork, superb soundtrack, and a touching story. A must have.

TL;DR: This game is good, and I recommend it.
I'll mention up front that I bought it on sale for $4, so my review may be a little skewed due to that fact. Alright, jumpin' right in:
Graphics
The graphics are pretty good. The 2D art (backgrounds and cutscenes) is good, and has a fun style to it. Sometimes the 3D boundary collision doesn't quite match up with the background, which produces a weird effect sometimes. The 3D art (characters and enemies) is also good. The only issue there is that changing direction based on input is pretty abrupt. Suddenly the main character is facing a different way.
Sound/Music
The sound and music are both very good. The music sounds very professional, although it's not particularly memorable. Sound effects pop up exactly where you'd expect them to.
Gameplay
The main "gimmick" of this game is that you can pause time and plan and queue up moves. This is a lot of fun, because it adds some fun tactis to an otherwise real-time game. As you progress through the game and level up, you'll gain access to new abilities that can be used in one of three ways: as an active ability, as an upgrade for another active ability, or as a passive ability. EVERY ability obtained can be used in each of these three ways, though not all at once. Choosing your loadout at the various save points is important, though some loadouts are obviously better than others. Sometimes things don't quite work as expected, though, for reasons that don't really make sense. This was frustrating when I was shown specifically by the planning GUI that a monster would die, and I ended up doing only half of the predicted damage for no discernable reason. Also note that the game is quite short; after 9 hours of playing I completed the story. I definitely didn't do everything. There are many challenges that I didn't do, and there's a "Recursion Mode" available after completing the game once, analagous to "New Game+".
Story
The story is... interesting. It's partly an intriguing personal story about two lovers separated but... not. It's also party a story about a dystopian-style city with an interesting twist. Both of the stories are tied together in interesting ways. Unfortunately, it's rather vague. I kept expecting a "big reveal" that never really came. Does it take place inside a computer? Is it the real world? Are the people real, or not? None of these questions are definitively answered. It's definitely food for thought, but it's like a tough, overdone steak: lots of chewing for something that's not entirely worth the work.
All in all, despite a vague story, it was enough to keep me going through the game, and it was supported by great (but not perfect) gameplay. I recommend this game!

Spacebase DF-9 lets you create your own space station, managing crew and resources all while staving off pirates and taking hails. It sounds like a lot of fun for anyone that was into Star Trek or even games like Dungeon Keeper 2, but it turns into all of the management and none of the fun. The big issues that I have with the game is that its tough to survive the first few moments of a normal game and beyond that, its just a dull game that forces you to assimilate all metal to keep growing your station to accommodate more crew.
Your objective is to keep your crew alive against first asphyxiation and later raiders. Even when your crew dies and the game tells you start a new game, it still continues. It is a game over without being concrete or giving you a final score before you have to start a new game.
To start with, there's an optional easy how to play tutorial level that will guide you through the basics without feeling forced upon you. The tutorial makes it easy to get up and running. Assign crew to the roster of jobs. Builders build when you construct rooms or objects. Miners will mine ore to be refined to get more matter to construct with. Technicians fix things and that's about as far as the tutorial gets.
You'll need a few things to get a space base operational. The first is power that comes in the form of reactors or a seed to start with. The second is the base itself which can be a giant room. You'll need an oxygen recycler since you are in space after all. After your space base has O2, an enclosed room and power, there's another matter and that's getting in. To do this you need to setup an air lock with two airlock doors one to the interior and the other to the exterior. This room also needs to have a locker for space suits.
Outside of the tutorial the giant problem that I have with the game is the level of difficulty when you're even getting started. The tutorial is nice and setup and it does let you continue on playing which is perhaps the best method. Consider that easy mode. You get to select your location and the game tells you how rich in ore and the frequency of attacks. Its a nice choice of difficulty without being a blunt difficulty slider.
In normal play, the game starts you with a seed for power and three crew in space suits with limited oxygen. There is so much that can go wrong. Running out of matter before your crew is in oxygen will doom you. So you need to budget building a small room to house the seed, a recycler, food dispenser, and a second for the air lock. Then you need to wait for the station to fill with oxygen and even for the air lock to cycle air in and out. Your spacemen can die in their suits when waiting for an air lock to pressurize. Oh but there is another nail to get caught on and that's the fact ore needs to be converted into matter, so it requires a matter refinery. This getting started kicks off the game and it will scare people away.
On paper, interesting things do happen. Derelict space stations will come into your area for you to explore and spaceships will dock with you. From there you have a choice, send your security over to investigate them or ignore them. The spaceships become part of your base where then you need to claim each room, which can be tedious and cumbersome since many small rooms are just tough to click on.
People can come aboard infected with a disease and then your science station will be put to work finding the cure. To do so, click whatever science room you've setup and select whatever they should research. There are a number of diseases to cure and upgrades to unlock. Upgrades include things like body armor and heavier doors.
You will get attacked from time to time. Raiders will float out in space and either try to shoot your miners as they pass by or they will board your station. Other times vessels will dock with your station and you'll be invaded. The catch is, unless you're watching a mining operation, its easy to spot and prepare for. You can have your security waiting for them, unless they're busy putting out a fire. It seems like more of an annoyance than a fun or cool challenge. You can also purchase wall mounted defense turrets.
Normal crew will still engage the enemy if they're in the same room, but to send crew in to fight hostiles, you'll need to assign crew to the security. From there you can make a security beacon that draws them to the area. It feels like an extra step and even marking the point and calling off security seems like it could be streamlined. A lot of the game needs to be streamlined.
Once attackers are incapacitated you can act to cuff, uncuff or execute them. In fact you can chose to execute or cuff any of your crew. Its just a little odd. Sometimes they will even chose to join your crew. Once resources become scarce, its just easier to execute them and dump them into the refiners to make matter.
Sometimes there is an issue where a firefight in an airlock can down the only crew inside the station. So anyone outside the station is forced to suffocate over time because the air lock refuses to open when someone is in there without a suit. It gets more hilarious because in smaller stations, crew will just stand in the air lock when its too crowded everywhere else. Spacebase DF-9 is an amazing game to watch because of its logic.
Speaking of logic, I managed to glitch the game into thinking there was no airlock. Those outside the station would die of asphyxiation and those inside the station would stay in there. Even crew joining would stay outside until they died. Destroying the airlock doors and rebuilding had no effect. Yet I could manually keep a door open so the spacemen could float into my base still in their suits. They would still suffer the same fate with no oxygen. The only way I was able to get people in and out was to build a new airlock.
In terms of crew management, when it comes to the roster everyone has an emotion to specific jobs no matter what their skill level is. You can have someone great at botany, yet hates doing it. Crew member you're the best doctor we have! Yeah but they get sad while doing it. Its a realistic and offers a level of micro management. Once you get to a point where you have crew of every class it gets easier since you no longer have people flip jobs such as having a miner one day and builder the next.
You get constant hails to answer and decide if you want them to join. It feels like a chore so I opt to avoid the calls. Sometimes the hails are to lull you into security so they can get "in your base, killing your dudes." Their transmissions all seems sketchy. There is no one that sounds like a clear cut good or bad choice. They all sound like they're trying to be funny and questionable, because that's what people like in their games, humor and charm. Well both fall flat and it feels forced.
Its also annoying having to press the faster speed setting, because the game will drop to normal speed whenever a yellow notice appears. It could be worse by being a popup box that you have to click like in so many other games. These warnings are things such as a crew member is starving or running out of oxygen. These warnings are color coated. Green means an overall hint on what's needed in your station such as more self space. Yellow and brown seem to be specific crew have achieved something or need something. Major warnings like crew being attacked or raiders about to board are in yellow so they blend in. A lot of times I realize we've been attacked after I see the number of crew go down. Raiders look similar to your own crew.
Spacebase DF-9 is just a tough game to love when it feels like a tough start followed by dull and uninspired management. It does feel like a fleshed out game with a lot of annoyances. I think scenarios would help extend my interest, but within a few hours I feel like I've seen everything there is to see. With all of that said, it is still worth the one dollar I paid for it.

is an action style game where you collect various resources to repair and upgrade your ship which crashed on an unknown planet.  Day and night cycles pass as you gather various types of resource to take back and deposit in your ship's bank.  Dying will cause any collected resources to be destroyed, and you are teleported back to your ship.  The ship itself has a health meter, and during night phases, you get teleported back to your ship to defend it from invaders on the far side of the battle area.
There are currently three types of weapons, or tools you are equipped with.  Certain combinations of resources can be used to add extra upgrades or effects to your tools.  There's a regular sword-style weapon, a mining hammer to search the ground, and a thrown weapon that acts sort of like a boomerang, but the angle will change when it hits something.  Return damage is much higher if you line yourself up so it hits targets.  You have a suit that can be upgraded as well with the resources, and you can create other used items, to recharge your health or energy for example.
The gameplay has you on a specific map where you can go down some various paths, and there are a few enemies that remain consistent in some areas, while most change up.  Resources also seem to change up, and some are fairly hard to acquire so far in my experience.  There are a lot of different behavior types and tendencies with enemies.  I really have enjoyed the variations so far in different types of enemies attacks or ways to best kill them.  Many have different ways of weakening or destroying them.  Successfully beating them can drop red tokens, while dodging many attacks in a row, or blocking their courses of action can yield blue respect tokens, and eventually cause them to flee and drop some resources and many times an item for you as well.
Most of the unlocks need the blue or red tokens along with resources.  The ship takes in solar energy, so you can only exchange during the day and some of the night phase.  There is a counter at the bottom left when the ship will have no more energy to deposit what you have collected.  The ship unlocks can be pretty nice.  There is also a portal that will take you to a random place in exchange for a few resources, and it takes you somewhere random.  Collecting everything there can give you a bonus at the end, but you cannot leave until you find the exit or get killed.  They can have harder to find resources at times, so the resources required tradeoff always pays off there.  Not a hard to acquire resource that is needed to open portals.
Movement is click area and Mr. Donovan goes that direction.  There's an easy mouse button dodge, and I have found the controls very smooth and solid response-wise.  There is one area you can get to that requires multiple teleport/dodges in a row that I don't quite understand how to do.  Also once one gains that ability to teleport through certain smaller areas, it's not easy to find where those spots are.  Indicators would be nice, I think.  It's still kind of early on to really say how this will progress, but your crash zone is not too big, and it feels a bit grindy right now for me, since I see stuff over and over again while trying to acquire one thing in particular to upgrade and get closer to end progression with the crashed ship.
Anyway, I'll mention a few pros and cons so far, since I've been just mainly explaining some of the general gameplay and using a lot of text to do so:
Movement is really responsive.  Doesn't feel at all clunky to me once I got used to it.
Many enemy variations depending on the type.  Some are upgraded versions that seem a bit harder to deal with, or have added mechanics.
Pretty nice learning curve.  Not too difficult to understand for the most part.  Starts to get easier, but there are some difficult enemies from time to time.  Can be a little too easy sometimes, but I prefer that to frustratingly difficult games.
Varied environments when you travel through the portals.  The crash zone varies too in certain ways, and changes each time you play, as far as what you encounter, resources you collect,  stuff you can dig up with your hammer which includes health or energy zones on the ground.
There are pets you can attack or something...  they will give you bonus abilities if you use them, kind of like items.  I'm not sure of the exact workings of them though.  Pressing a button summons the particular pet a certain amount of time.  There are also hearts to signify something with pets, but I am also unsure how these are gotten and how that system works.
I had a bug I encountered, and it took the developer some time to respond to my issue, but when they did, a fix was incorporated in the next patch.  Good to hear things get actively worked on!
Right now, feels a little grindy.  Some resources are very scarce, while others I already have the maximum amount collected.  I would like to see slightly more balance here.
Your crash zone area is not very big, and it could use a little more area.  It would be harder to get back to your ship though, since you have to go back and forth, and you only get teleported there in nighttime attacks on your ship.  Can't deposit resources until morning.
Attacks on your ship are a bit monotonous also. They happen too often - I think every single night so far, or close to it.  Enemies are a bit of a pain to have to kill over and over in this manner.  I do not like this right now for whatever reason.  Auto weaponry or traps I could create near my ship to take these guys out would be a nice addition.
It is hard to figure out where everything is in the zones you can teleport to. I have only found every single resource one time so far. There is a particular enemy that chases you with a field that harms if you get hit by it. Once they are activated, they will chase until you leave, and there is no way to defeat them that I can tell.
Unrelated to gameplay, but it took around a week to get a response about my issue when using Steam forums to report a bug.  I am patient though, so it wasn't a really big gripe from my side of things.  Stuff happens, and I expected to get this review out over a month ago, but ran into a few hardships that slowed me down.  Hopefully what I have laid out here is fairly comprehensive, though.
There are a lot of games around $18 right now that are further along, but for an early access game, this isn't a bad purchase right now. I don't think it's for everybody, and I do wish there was a demo around for people to try first (I could not find one, but I might have missed it) since the style of game is hard to put into really good words, or stick a particular genre on it completely. This could go either way for me at the current price, depending on what happens with progression.
It definitely has a lot of good points right now. I'd be more comfortable around half the price, personally, but since it is early in development, things could really improve if care and time are taken, and it continues to go the direction it is going. I don't have a lot of complaints about the game itself.  It is a little monotonous in its current state to keep me interested for longer periods of time, but that being said, overall it's really becoming a nice game. I'd like more of a balance with resource gathering, and some extras to keep it interesting for longer grinds at a time. It's not really clear on what or where it's going either while you are running around, aside from the need to fix your ship, and gather resources to improve your ship, weapons, armor, and trade in for consumables or portal runs, so there could be more of an interaction going on instead of feeling like I am mindlessly going through each day searching for resources.
If you're on budget, and really scoping this one out, wait a bit, or grab it at a good discount!  It's definitely turning into a quality game.

Not many video games today can brag about inventing a new subgenre, but Mr. Donovan lays claim to this rare title. Debutante developer Swizzle llc coined the term “SOBO” which stands for Singleplayer Online Battle Open-world. That’s a mouthful but I have to say, with proper and constant treatment in the form of content-adding updates and performance patches, Mr. Donovan might be the start of something noteworthy.
The story is the least coherent part of the game, sadly. It’s rather thin on content: you’re an astronaut named Donovan, who's stranded on a strange planet. Almost the entire wildlife wishes to kill you, along with conveniently placed traps as if the terrain itself wishes to consume you as well. You must survive and gather up sufficient resources (summarized by power-ups of sorts) to repair your damaged space shuttle and escape this Sci-Fi hellscape. Apart from a flimsy tutorial section, no further context is being given and no valid reason for the crash landing on this nameless planet either.
You can catch some more friendly creatures and use them for defense purposes against the hostile ones, in a similar manner devised by Pokémon. Some explanation and an intro sequence, would really benefit this title a lot. A MOBA (multiplayer online battle arena) sure doesn’t require much in terms of a plotline or distinguishable characters yet Mr. Donovan seems to be proud of the fact that it’s a singleplayer experience. Well if the SP mode needs something in order to stand out, that is a proper story to captivate even players that prefer the social interaction from MP-only titles.
Another creative use of Unity Engine 5 assets which translate into lush and exotic vegetation while also rendering some spectacular combat effects for the hefty arsenal used against your many foes. I think I’ve seen so far Unity used in every gaming genre that I can think of and I'm still surprised by it’s potential and flexibility. As for the developer, I am certain that he had the best intentions in mind and the skill to back them up. The performance was as stable as it’ll ever get. I didn’t even encounter bugs, glitches or resolution issues, as some player complained in the game’s Community tab on Steam. Donovan was run at 4K@60fps without a single frame rate drop or crash to desktop, so I really can complain that I didn’t like what I was seeing. Native monitor resolution and refresh rate, despite the simplistic settings menu.
Unfortunately, the pretty graphics were’t  supplemented by equally pleasant sounds. Those were few and far in between. The soundtrack was highly repetitive and I ended up muting it and playing my own tracklist instead. Epic music to the rescue, as always. It goes without saying, that there is no voice acting either but since the story is barebones as it is, that’s only a minor sin.
Depending on how much you prefer repeating the same task under different visual conditions, you may actually enjoy playing Mr. Donovan for longer than I did. When you’re not harvesting consumables by smashing the ground with a warhammer, you can slash your alien opponents with a giant sword or blast them from a safe distance with your robotic arm. At least before you’ll be able to upgrade your space suit. I never claimed there’s no incentive to explore the maps (which also feature day/night cycle and weather effects) and kill nearly everything that moves. Remember the feelings here are mutual.
I actually doubt those “cute pets” our space survivor seems to enjoy collecting, prefer doing his bidding. The pets once deployed across the map, act like towers of sorts and may defend key areas such as the space shipwreck, which might get attacked by random waves of spawning aliens. Health regeneration is weird, to say the least. It is activated much like some power-ups and you need to enter an “effect radius” in order to receive back any hitpoints lost during combat. And fighting is pretty much the central gameplay mechanic in Mr. Donovan.
The enemy is as diversified as it is odd shaped and colored. A bestiary or trivia codex would be welcome additions. Being the only human being in such a hostile environment is pretty bad as it is, no need to force one fight afer another and not even offer information on what the flying snake or the organic turrent before it, represent. Yeah, I got bored fast enough since the AI can barely offer a challenge. Perhaps the Dark Souls series has taught me how to dodge attacks at all times and always be on the move, but I could swear more than half of those alien opponents must have been blind as bats.
It certainly doesn’t help Mr. Donovan one bit, the fact that I consider it overpriced given its repetitive nature and lack of a proper story. No amount of upgrades and collectible pets could convince me to spend any more time in-game than what I already did. The Achievements are fairly easy to obtain so at least that was a silver lining to this digital fight for survival. I’d dare call Mr. Donovan a classic case of graphics that attempt to distract attention from a deficient gameplay. It rarely succeeds, but perhaps MOBA enthusiasts might consider this title funny enough in a twisted spin-off manner. The game needs a price cut even after it leaves its Early Access stage and I sincerely hope the developer will offer more content to it soon enough. For now, purchase it during a Steam Sale or bundle if you wish to ensure future support for Donovan and his flight back home.
+ Beautiful graphics.
+ Steam Achievements
+ Plenty of terrain and enemy variety.
- Lack of a proper storyline and clearly defined objectives.
- No Steam Trading Cards.
- Repetitive sounds.
- Overpriced.

Mr. Donovan:
~~~~~~~~~~

Your mission is to find and explore distant planets; that’s what astronauts do! After successfully initiating a light jump, your spaceship re-appears right in the middle of an asteroid belt. The shield warning is pumping up every few seconds until it goes down. And then the inevitable occurs . . . an asteroid strikes your vessel causing extreme damage. Your only hope is to survive a crash landing on a totally unknown planet. Good luck, Mr. Donovan!
Mr. Donovan is an Action / Adventure game where you control an astronaut who is stranded on an unknown planet. His mission is to find resources to repair his spaceship and also to defend it from incoming waves of aliens.
But before you do so, you can take a small tutorial where you will learn the fundamentals of the game, including how to fight and how to guide your astronaut within the environment. Or you can just jump right into the game and find out by yourself while playing!
First, you’ll need to find your spaceship crash site. Look for the pentagon transport platform tiles; you will need to have the right resources to be able to use them.  Therefore, make sure to look around and collect all available resources to use the platform. Every time you use the platform, you’ll get closer to the crash site. When you find it, you can use the ship console. Here, you can upgrade and repair your spaceship, unlock and equip new abilities, purchase items or even track the pets you captured. Remember, everything costs a specific number of resources (apart from the pets).
The game play is rather fun! Your character has three different utensils within his inventory: a sword, a pickaxe and a cannon of some sort. As you explore the planet, you will come across giant flowers, robots, dragons, aliens and other fun enemies. You will also find resource points (well, that’s what I call them); use your pickaxe on them and you’ll collect several types of resources. You’ll be able to use your pickaxe on flowers as well as on blue and yellow cracks on the surface of the planet. They can reveal resources, healing and energy recharge to restore your character’s health and energy. They could also reveal traps and considerably damage your astronaut health. There are tiles with signs on them; step on them and you’ll activate fire traps, electric traps (flying balls) and more.  A very important point - make sure to download your resources onto your ship during the course of the day and not at night. In the event of death, you will lose all resources that you were carrying.
When you win a battle against an enemy, pretty much hack and slash with your melee weapons; they usually drop a blood point or a respect point which you’ll need to upgrade your weapons and suit at the ship console.
Visually, Mr. Donovan looks very good and I really like the environments on the planet. The only downside at this stage is the limitation in regards to the resolution - the highest you can go is 1920 x 1080. The soundtrack is good and rather calming, I must say. In regards to the controls, I would like to see them smoother and the cursor needs to be more obvious. A few bugs here and there as you would expect on an early access title.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Interesting enemies
-	Large number of upgrades and items to purchase
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls need to be tweaked a bit
-	Need to have a better cursor (more obvious)
-	No Trading cards
Overall, Mr. Donovan is a solid early access game and worth having a look at.
7/10

Everyone loves and fears Cthulhu, the Great Old One, He who slumbers below the waves of the sea. He will awake someday from His slumber, and He will bring ruin to the world. And now, in Cthulhu Saves The World, you can play through that great event whenever you want.
Cthulhu Saves The World, or rather Cthulhu Saves the World: Super Hyper Enhanced Championship Edition Alpha Diamond DX Plus Alpha FES HD – Premium Enhanced Game of the Year Collector’s Edition (without Avatars!) which is the official name, is a retro-style RPG available on the Xbox 360 and on Steam.
Well, it's not so much an RPG as it is an RPG parody. A spoof of the role-playing games of old, like older Dragon Warrior/Quest or Final Fantasy games.
Cthulhu Saves The World is quite possibly the stupidest game I've ever enjoyed playing.
Cthulhu has arisen to destroy the world, but has his powers sapped. And the only way to regain them is to become a true hero. And so, Cthulhu sets off on a quest to save the world in order to destroy the world.
You'll have to enlist the help of a colorful band of allies, including an alien cat and a talking sword. Cthulhu even enlists some pretty female characters, which I'm 100% sure were put there purely in hopes of someone R34-ing it.
I mean, that's what I'd do if I made a game about Cthulhu.
If the premise of the game isn't goofy enough, it's sure to drive the punchline home within the first few seconds of the game. Before you can even take control of Cthulhu, the fourth wall is pretty much obliterated. And it stays that way for the entire game. Cthulhu and pals will pick fights with the narrator, point out the glaring "RPG logic" plot holes in the story, and reference the fact that they're in a game multiple times.
Not that it's a problem by any means. It's actually the highlight of the game.
The writing and dialogue in the game is hilarious, stupid, and sometimes even witty.
Each enemy will have a short description when you get into a fight. Something like "Wizard - Fun at birthday parties" or "Ghost Knight - Totally not a palette swap". They can range from incredibly witty to stupidly nonsensical, but are entertaining nonetheless.
I found myself talking to every NPC, investigating every bookshelf and cupboard, and pretty much searching the entire game for anywhere that may contain more juicy bits of text. The writing is definitely strong, and anyone with a sense of humor and a love of retro RPG's will definitely be able to appreciate the subtle references and jokes.
Joke games can usually go either way though. If too much emphasis is on the humor to the point where the game is unpolished or unplayable, it won't get too far based on the humor alone. Laughing at a game and laughing with a game are too entirely different types of entertainment.
Lucky for Cthulhu though, we're laughing with him.
Cthulhu Saves The World has your standard retro RPG setup. Turn-based combat, dungeon-crawling, random encounters for experience and gold for leveling up and getting better equipment. All of that is there, with a few twists.
The biggest twist has to be that Cthulhu doesn't have amnesia. Or brightly colored hair. But his skin is green, though. That's close enough.
The battles seem to encourage the idea of speed. Of striking hard, and striking fast.
With tentacles.
Enemies will grow stronger each turn, meaning if you're too slow they'll eventually double or even triple in strength. Enough to kill your entire party in a few hits. You have a similar feature though. A combo meter that will build up with every hit, which will boost damage on certain combo finisher moves.
Even the items in the game are short and to the point. In fact, there's really only two. And only one of those you can freely use in battle. Unlike a standard RPG where you'd be weighed down with Phoenix Downs, status recoveries for every possible ailment, and all sorts of stuff you need to stock up on but rarely ever use.
You'll have 1-ups to revive your entire party if you fall, and Potions to fully restore an ally. That's pretty much it.
There's a number of features like this to make the experience smoother and quicker. You can save anywhere, and your party heals all HP and a bit of MP after each battle.
But most importantly, probably the best idea out of this whole game, is the random encounter limit.
Each dungeon will have a set amount of battles. Roughly 20-ish for most. But after you've defeated them all, you're done. You can casually explore as much as you like after, and nothing will pop up and attack you. The choice is still there if you'd like to fight; there's a button on the menu that will trigger battles for you if you'd still like to grind more. But at that point, you'd be pretty much as strong as you'd need to be anyway.
Like any retro RPG, it does seem to drag on at times. It can get pretty repetitive and grindy towards the end, especially after you've read every funny monster description and just mash the button to kill things. But it's definitely a solid RPG game.
For those that find it to their liking, they'll be pleased to find a number of bonus things to do after the game is over. Multiple bonus modes to play, and collectibles to unlock.
Your party members even have crude "skill trees" as they level up. And by that, I mean "You can choose to make Cthulhu a physical attacker or a magical attacker". Not anything as fancy as modern RPG's, but it gives you a bit more to play with every playthrough I guess.
It even has a pretty nice soundtrack, like any RPG should.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of an intriguing little Simulator-type game called Plague, Inc. Plague, Inc has been around on mobile devices for a while, and on Steam since February 20, 2014. It is still in Early Access, but Publisher/Developer Ndemic Creations is VERY active, having just recently added the highly anticipated Competitive Multiplayer mode.
(NOTE: This was a review from a game in my own Steam library, it was NOT provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Great game, good casual way to pass time OR you can ramp up the difficulty and give yourself fits. Highly replayable. Active Devs. Another 4/5 on an incomplete game? Yup. Worth $15 easily.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
I picked this game up a long time ago on my iPhone and loved it, so when it came to Steam I picked it up about a year ago around Xmas. I stashed it away, awaiting it's release from Early Access. Well, I couldn't wait and the newly updated Multiplayer mode gave me an excuse to review it anyways! Now, I didn't review the MP mode simply because I wanted gamers to get a feel for the actual game itself first. This game is a simulation game where you are trying to spread a disease and essentially wipe out mankind. You get points to evolve your disease in different categories (Transmission, Symptoms, Abilities) to try and help it spread and eradicate humanity. Meanwhile, the world works against you by crafting a cure, shutting down airports/harbors, etc. Pesky humans, you'll find, are quite resiliant. As you play and get better at the game you unlick different types of diseases and starting genomes for your disease. There is a lot here and this is all fun on it's own, but then you incorporate things like Steam Workshop, User Made Scenarios, Multiplayer and the like, and the replayability shoots through the roof. The best part....they aren't even done yet and are obviously very active in the games continued development. Hop on board now, this is not one to miss. 4/5 easily, even in it's incomplete state. There is MORE than enough to play here, nothing game breaking going on, they just keep adding more and more awesome stuff!! Well worth the $15!
Happy Gaming!!!

An Hour In: First Impressions
From my first impressions, Steel Division has proven to be a phenomenal game. I haven't felt the intensity of WWII in a strategy game in quite some time. Sure, Company of Heroes has been packed full of intense moments, but never in this way.
Outside of the strong tone and thematic integration, the gameplay itself is solid, but slow. This is not a game where you play a quick ten minute match, at least not from what I've seen. The multiple phases of combat which grow in scale is a solid choice, and really makes it feel like a true battle is going on; the wide roster of units is also impressive.
My two big gripes with gameplay come largely from the learning curve and micromanagement. It is NOT an easy game to pick up or master. The tutorials will give you enough to know the basics but there is a lot to the game beyond that.
As well, there is a lot of micromanagement. This isn't inherently a bad thing, but there are some things I have to manually do that seem a bit unnecessary, such as having to ALWAYS manually direct artillery fire. It would be nice to be able to put them on a return fire mode, or simply to automatically shell enemies. Mortars and artillery are extremely powerful and useful, but can be difficult to keep up with while also directing infantry, AT, and vehicles.
Steel Division's single player excels in capturing the insurmountable odds you're up against, the bravery of the average soldier, and the necessity of sound tactical choice.
By just the second mission, I was impressed. I found myself tasked with relieving and resupplying a division desparately trying to hold on to a town. I had thiryt minutes to hold that town. And by the last ten, I was struggling. Reinforcements were low, and the Germans managed to cut off my only alley into the town. I watched my numbers dwindle, dwindle, dwindle. As my forces shrunk, we were forced into the very city center, all while watching that clock tick down.
With a minute left, I thought it was game over. Yet somehow, my three units managed to hold on. They were relieved, the Germans retreated.
It's a fantastic game so far. The constant push and pull of the battlefield is captivating, and there are some really, REALLY close moments.
Complex, fun, intense. Absolutely recommend.

Assault Android Cactus was one of my early purchases since joining Steam a couple of years ago, and even in its Early Access stage, had remained one of my favorite games from my library.  Now that it's finally complete, I would love for anyone who's been on the fence to give this wonderful arcade blast-a-thon a go.
What makes AAC such a great videogame is that it is just that -- a damn videogame.  There's no need here for bloaty features like RPG elements, perks, weapon customization, or what have you.  If you just wanna turn off your brain an' go out gunz a-blazin' with unlimited ammo, this game is it, and the three-person Witch Beam crew were steadfast in delivering that experience.  With little to get in your way, AAC is perfect pick-up-and-play fun for both casual players and S+ experts.
After a short tutorial and a couple of cutscenes, the game catapults your chosen Android into a campaign filled with relentless robots ready to wreck you.  Using your unique primary and secondary weapons, as well as some helpful temporary powerups, you must destroy wave after wave of bots or duke it out with a fearsome Section Lord before proceeding to the next stage.  Five hits will knock your character down, but you can press the buttons repeatedly to get back up and continue the fight, no problem!  But don't party just yet -- Assault Android Cactus also features an interesting gimmick in the form of the Battery Meter.  Instead of relying on a limited number of Lives, the Game Over screen gleefully waits for your Android's power to completely drain during battle, so be on the lookout for occasional Battery drops from enemies to keep yourself afloat.  This feature adds to the intensity of the game, as you're encouraged to balance between being careful and getting aggressive.
If you wanna take a break from AAC's Campaign, there are indeed other modes to try out:  Boss Rush, the Daily Drive, and the endless Infinity Drive.  There are also fun unlockables ("funlockables"?), such as other playable Androids, and with enough hard-earned in-game credits, you can purchase character art and bios, story info, and the excellent EX Mode features.  The EX Modes alter the game in cool ways, such as placing the gameplay in First Person view, changing the graphics (can you handle Psychedelic?), or even allowing helpful A.I.-controlled Androids to assist you for faux co-op play.
Speaking of co-op, while up to four players can have at it, I should mention that it is local only, as Witch Beam did not have the means to work in online multiplayer.  AAC was originally to be only single-player, but they were able to change that at least.  I sincerely hope the lack of online co-op doesn't deter you from trying out this game, and that perhaps the unlockable A.I. mode will suffice.
Again, if you're looking for simply "a damn videogame", and don't mind local co-op, I highly and wholeheartedly recommend Assault Android Cactus.  A lot of love was put into this game, and it definitely shows.  Pick up an' play it!

The game's main selling point is its physics engine. It combines Havok, Euphoria (of GTA4 fame), and DMM to rather remarkable results. And for those of you who don't know, DMM is a more in depth material modelling engine. The idea being that you get objects which bend and break like their real world counterparts. Glass shatters, wood splinters, metal bends, and plants swing. And it's remarkably effective. Often it adds to the wreckless destruction your jedi powers leave in their wake, as all sorts on the sidelines gets caught in your wrath. And at other times, it's used to open doors. Two layers of steel blocking the way? Not a problem, just punch it out of the way!
However it's not an open ended game. It ultimately has you navigate a linear path, which is fine. But in order to do this, it has to put up immovable barriers to keep you there. Which rather horribly juxtaposes all that dynamic damage they have going on. In fact, in order to make sure the game's still completable, there's a lot of indestructable level geometry. The only bridge across a chasm won't break, for instance. But next to the impressive DMM magic, it feels astonishingly cheap. At times, that damage engine can just feel like a gimick you get brief glimpses of, as some areas make very sparing use of it, so the game falls back on raw gameplay for enjoyment.
Which brings me to the biggest problem I have with this game. The levels feel very drawn out and artificially lengthened, and get tedious quickly. Especially as fighting enemies isn't particularly fun. The infantry type enemies don't pose any real threat, leaving you only with the choice of which force power or lightsaber combo to kill them with, coupled with how cruel your sense of humor is. The boss fights are more interesting, with moves like blocking suddenly becoming useful, but even those drag on enormously.
On top of that, there's a few issues with the PC version. It's locked to 30fps and the lack of detail leaves a lot of the game looking rather bleak and apocalyptic in ways it's clearly not supposed to.

I'm currently a level 40 WHM.
I have played a ton of MMO's during my time as a gamer and I can say without a shadow of a doubt that this is BY FAR the worst leveling/questing system I have ever seen.
You want quest variety? Too bad. There's like 4 differen't types of quests. "Hey you go fetch me this", "Hey you go kill that", "Hey you go do this dungeon", "Hey you go deliver this". What makes this even worse is the fact that you're sent all over the world. Before you get your mount the vast majority of the time you're just constantly running from one place to the next. When you do finally get your mount you're still doing this only slightly faster. Why doesn't the game teleport you back to the quest giver after you finish a scenario? There's zero reason not to. Instead you've gotten spend more time travelling. There is also little to no humour at all to relieve the tediium.
This entire experience so far has been dry, tedious and not very fun at all. The scary part is is that according to just about every single person I have met there is a quest grind at level 50 that is so much worse. I don't even know how that is possible but it seems every single person I have talked to is in complete agreement.
EDIT: #1 Level 53 WHM
After a rather long grind I have finally finished the base game and I have moved onto Heavensward(The first expansion). While the story ending of the base expansion was excellent, the questing left much to be desired. Again there was simply no real quest variety and there was so much POINTLESS travelling again. I'm hoping this changes in Heavensward but so far after doing maybe 10~ quests it is seeming unlikely.
Another massive complaint I have is that you HAVE to do the raids to advance the main story. Despite playing a healer(A desired role with supposed quick queue timers) twice I waited over 30 minutes for a queue pop, once I waited 40 minutes. And the average seems to be 15.
The sad part is is that the dungeons (4 player parties) and raids (8 member parties) are actually excellent and while you do get to do some while leveling they're too far apart and you need to slog through monotonous quests to get to them.

Here we have a simple puzzle-quest oriented match them up with a unique concept. If you've ever played any of the Puzzle Quest series these games aren't a simply bash your face into the keyboard when it comes to matching and expect to win. There is actually strategy involved.
The "Gems" you match spawn units on your side of the field that march to the opposite side of the field in a Tug-O'-War style. That's where the strategy get's involved. From DPS archers that if enemy units get up to they get smacked, to Tanky Knights that stand in the frontline and take damage, to even Melee DPS longswordsman that need a tank in front of them or they get mowed over.
On TOP of selecting your unit roster and hoping you get the gems in the right place (Or if you're skilled enough manipulating the board to get what you want), You get to selectively upgrade your unit stats. Attack, Defense, Crit, HP, are the basic upgrades but at least with this you can fill in weakspots or boost strengths. Add in you can upgrade your "camp" and your "powerups" this game is quite refreshing IF you like the puzzle genre.

I adore this game.  Video review below with text thoughts after:
Assault Android Cactus is a game that I feel sets the bar higher for what indie studios can produce.  Not only is it mechanically sound and a blast to play, but the presentation is simply out of this world.
You take the role of Cactus (or 1 of 8 other androids) in a fast paced, arcade style, twin stick shooter environment for 1-4 players in local co-op, blasting robots and attempting to restore peace to the inhabitants of the Genki Star.  The Campaign mode in Assault Android Cactus spans across 5 areas each with a handful of levels apiece, each topped with a challenging and visually impressive boss fight.  Each stage is unique and beautifully crafted.  In fact, the only 'downside' I see in AAC is simply that I wish there were more campaign stages, purely for how well they're made.
Everything about Assault Android Cactus shines.  The graphics are charming and clearly display information in the intense environment, the soundtrack is
, the voice acting is solid, cutscenes are engaging, the controls are tight and response, everything simply flows together for a fantastic experience.
While the Campaign may only take you a few hours if you're skilled, Assault Android Cactus is all about replayability.  You're ranked on your performance and in-game leaderboards keep the competition hot.  Additionally, the game provides an unlockable 'Pro Mode' that you can setup to facilitate better rank monitoring or quick resets if you're going for that perfect run.
In addition to the Campaign leaderboards, there's also the 'Daily Drive' which is a ranked Daily Challenge for 1-4 players, with each category separated.  You only get one shot at this and everybody plays the same level.  The Daily Challenge spans 10 'layers' of a shifting arena with a variety of enemies and bosses.  Beyond that, there's also the Infinity Drive, an endless mode that works much like the Daily Challenge but can be replayed as often as you'd like, seeing how far you can get.  Also included is an unlockable Boss Rush mode if you want to practice against the bosses or simply challenge yourself to back to back boss fights.
Oh you want more unlockables?  Done.  Playing the game earns credits, much like many older games or early entries in the Uncharted series, which you can use to unlock a variety of different things.  Lore entries, artwork, or even gameplay adjustments in the form of visual changes, AI companions, or powered up weapons (the latter of which turn off leaderboards for that run of course).
Assault Android Cactus is chock full of options and replayability to a level that's typically reserved for AAA games, many of which have even been lacking in the past few years.  Highly recommended!
