I know im on the minority here, but i want to express an important point no one really likes to talk about.
At first, i play this game for years now, long before it went on Steam and have many playhours that i enjoyed.
The problem i have with this game, and that isnt visible until you invest more time playing it, is that it doesnt deliver a purpose of actually doing what you do through a lack of depth in some mechanics.
I dont mean, making sense in playing a videogame. I mean theres no real freedom and the game sadly runs in circles of pointless crafting for no "reason".
Let me explain that.
You start in automating the process of harvesting resources and producing items/goods/products. Call the endresult how you feel fit.
But the only purpose is, to be able to automate the production of sciencepacks, to then research new ways to enhance that process, only to be more effective into producing sciencepacks.
You see, this goes in circles and goes nowhere.
When you play Factorio, you are only there to do what you do, for no reason other to be more effective in this pointless process.
Yes, there is combat in Factorio. Its the weakest mechanic in the whole game and despite the focus of the game, isnt automated.
What i liked about Factorio is the idea of getting rid of handcrafting everything and automating this with using machines, robotarms and belts. And it achieved that in 3 of 4 main aspects of the game. If i was more precise i would say 2.5 of 4.
Factorio is about these aspects:
- Building and Producing
- Exploring the map for resources and enemies
- fighting enemies and defend your structures
- Research new ways of doing all of that
The Research aspect and the building/producing aspect received numerous additions in updates to be fully automated and deliver enough ways to get it working.
The exploration aspect, only consists of either moving out by yourself, with a car or by foot, or using radar scaners, which are limited in range. So that process could maybe be considered automated, but with restrictions (A scout unit could make the trick here).
What is lacking and missing, is the combat. Its weak, often plain out boring and underdeveloped (barely any updates for combat).
Not only does the tower defense aspect not really deliver, but doing attacks on alien nests yourself is tedious busywork that needs something fresh and new to be interesting.
Which gets me back to the initial point. The game has no main purpose of why im doing all of that, beside being more effective at doing really nothing.
Which led me to the question, why not "simply" make combat automated and add Combat Robotics?
Producing items in Factorio would finally serve a purpose and have an end of a chain.
Whenever i played factorio, i built an effective and well made factory producing thousands of items a minute, only to...
Yeah what exactly? These products serve no purpose. Why would i massproduce copperplates exactly? I can pump out enough science packs easily without having to massproduce anything.
All the weapons and combat related researches, are a waste and only give the player items he/she might craft ONE time, and then never again.
Why would i massproduce armor or a gun? I can only carry one, so having more than two would be pointless.
Not if i had combat robotics to have my factory autobuild droids that i can send out to fight the aliens.
It would add a complex mechanic, give this whole prodouction a second goal/approach (waging war at aliens) and basically making it one of the best RTS Games you could imagine.
And dont get me wrong, there are attempts of that. A mod introduced Combat Robotics, doing exactly what i hope they will include into the vanilla game later.
But its of lesser quality, robots arent animated and it doesnt feel as well made as if it was done by the developer.
Sadly, this game might be great in many aspects, but lacks in the most important thing i could think of, giving me freedom.
And after i played enough to experiment with factory designs, theres nothing to it you can do otherwise.
Which means, that PvP also isnt really interesting to begin with, as missing "attack" options for a player, wont get you playing PvP.
Both players building a factory, which takes hours for most people, only to place some turrets and attacking your enemy, meaning you had to go there personally to deal with his/her turrets, is boring and not really interesting.
But producing units and sending them out to fight, as in an RTS, would deliver that though.
To show off how ridiculously obvious it is, that the lacking combat and point of producing is kicking the game down, is that you really dont need to massproduce efficiently to get to the "goal".
You can build a small factory, research your stuff and get your rocket off, well done.
No need to really massproduce and expand your base by much.
You dont even have to leave your first base and still be able to hit the endgame.
If they release their game without proper combat mechanics and production chains related to that, i feel that the game lacks a real lategame alltogether.
It has an endgame but no lategame.
You can reach a goal of shooting a rocket up and "escape". It doesnt encourage playing lategame though, as keeping on producing has no other point than that (like continue war).
An example, to underline this point: I played with a friend and when we started (he was new to the game) i explained him how it works.
He then just asked "And why are we doing all of this? Why would we spent hours of work to get a good factory running?". I couldnt give him an answer, because there is none.
I thought to myself, i would have liked to tell him "to be able to produce robots of different kinds, which we then can send out to raid alien nests, because those get large in numbers and grow stronger each hour we play, turning it into a Coop Real Time Strategy Game where we build bases and train units, like in the old C&C and Dune Days when we played CompStomp Matches."
The next time i loaded the Combat Robotics Mod with him, it was a much better session.
We had much more fun producing things and trying to build new bases.
We felt great massproducing weapons, armor and ammo for "soldiers", so we could send them out to die in a big war.
Which was great.
If the developers took that mod (or a bunch, because there are really good ones), polished it and included it into the vanilla game, I would easily say that this game is finally a step up from the RTS Genre to a new era of strategy gaming, but also being a must-buy overall.
A genious game for a low price for what it delivers.
But in the state it is, lacking in such a big aspect, i can say that this is only true for those who just want to mess around with factory designs and occasional fights.
If its just experimenting with production designs while occasionally building some towers and walls to stop aliens annoying you while you do that, feel free to buy it. As you will get an awesome game.
If you however want a game where producing has a point and research not only makes you more efficient but also gives you proper stuff to use your resources for, if you want to fight aliens and spend time to create a deadly factory.
Dont buy it as that part is a shallow placeholder.
The whole main idea of the game is to automate processes so the player only has to deal with macro tasks, commanding, managing, taking care of the strategy.
But currently this only applies to the production of new resources, and nothing else.
Which is a break with the whole idea to begin with.
If they manage to find a way to tackle that issue or just include the already given idea of combat robotics that many players want, use and deemed a great idea, i will change this review to a completely positive one, as i cant think of any flaw apart of the described one.
They now need to bring combat/exploration on the same depth-level as building and researching. Otherwise half of its features stay underdeveloped.

I've played this game a lot, and I'm still drawn to it. Your time is spent designing and expanding your factory. The better the factory, the cooler stuff you have, and you progress from being extremely week at the beginning to godlike in power by the end. Then you look at your factory, think of all the ways it could be done better, see other amazing factories, and want to do it all over again.
At any given moment, you are solving puzzles of your own invention. As such, it is never too challenging or too boring. There is always something to do, either a) increasing your resource production, b) expanding your factory, or c) improving your production chain to fix bottlenecks. And if you ever need a break from that, you can go out and dish out some well-earned hostility to the murderous alien insects that surround your little bastion of engineering prowess.
I've had it about a year at this point, and the entire time there have been weekly updates from the development team, as they focus on increasing content, improving computing efficiency (which I appreciate with a laptop), and making quality of life improvements. They listen to the community and go out of their way to encourage modding, making it the easiest game to mod I've ever played.
I definitely recommend this game without reservation. If you're still unsure, try the demo.

In my world, Legend Of Grimrock would be called "The reincarnation of Eye Of The Beholder", or something of the sort, as I have really good memories of the first Eye Of The Beholder game from the early 1990s (although I never beat it), and Legend Of Grimrock looks just like it. Just recently I realized Eye Of The Beholder itself was a reincarnation (or what some people would call "a clone" or "a ripoff") of a similar game called "Dungeon Master" from the 1980s (which I've never heard of until recently), but 'nuff said about that.
Back to Legend Of Grimrock -
The game is a first person dungeon crawling Action/RPG. You play a group of 4 adventurers (aka convicted criminals, but nevermind about that :P), whose goal is to survive the dungeon by means of solving puzzles and fighting monsters while staying alive in the process.
The default party consists of two fighters (one human, one minotaur), one wizard and one rogue, set in a fixed formation of two rows - two characters in front, two more behind them. You can choose which character to place where and change it while playing, but you can't change the formation. The idea is that the two front characters use melee attacks, while the other two need to attack from long range (either magic, throwing weapons such as knives, or missile weapons such as bows).
Up until now (8-10 hours ingame), I'm really having fun. Technically, everything looks and feels good. There's nothing overwhelming about the graphics or the music, but they are definitely good enough. Come to think of it, there's hardly any music ingame, and I think it's a really good idea. The lack of music makes the game feel more realistic, and it lets you pay the worthy attention to the sound effects, which just like with Eye Of The Beholder, play an important role, as they serve as warning signs from certain enemies.  The controls are simple and intuitive (left click to move items, right click to attack when it comes to battles). Some of the puzzles are very easy, others are more difficult. I did find it necessary to look for help online in a couple of incidents so far, but I did manage to solve most of the puzzles myself (up to where I am at the moment, can't say anything about the puzzles I haven't reached yet).
All in all, this game is fun. If you like dungeon crawlers, get it. It might not be a masterpiece, but it is fun to play.

An utterly frenetic bullet-hell shooter that encourages (and sometimes even demands) that the player(s) take risks. If you're not in the absolute thick of it, blasting the circuitry out of robots at point-blank range, you're probably wasting time... And if you're wasting time, you're doing it wrong, because these badass loli-droids are on a VERY tight schedule.
Collecting batteries grants you more time, but the problem is that the game doesn't actually explain the mechanics behind battery drops very well, and this can lead to frustration for new players. However, battery drops are NOT random. They are tied to the quantity AND quality of enemies you destroy. The act of destroying a hulking enemy with a ton of hitpoints will often get you a lot closer to a fresh battery drop than destroying squads of low-end cannon-fodder. The key is learning who to attack, and when, and with what weapon.
Once you become familiar with those concepts, the game becomes ridiculously fun... Unless you're someone who REALLY likes to play it safe. In which case you'll die repeatedly as your battery runs out.

There's obviously lots of games in this general category -- company of heroes, men of war, and prior entries in the Wargame series all have a bunch of the core elements that are in SD:N. One major axis is size of the battle space. In order of small scale to large scale: CoH, MoW, SD:N, Wargame. In terms of pace, SD:N is slower and less micro-intensive than basically any other game on that list. Units don't really have special abilities tha tneed to be targetted. The only real "special" move is smoke; otherwise units make reasonable choices about what weapons to use against which targets on their own. You don't need to, like, press the "shoot bazooka" button if you want your AT-equipped infantry to shoot a tank. There's also relatively little game-y ness that plagues something like CoH. You don't build buildings that produce troops, you don't magically heal or replinish squads. You don't repair tanks on the battlefield. There are concessions for playability for sure (plane/AA interactions, limited but readable penetration models for armor, etc.) but they're not super glaring.
I find that particular mix pretty compelling. You're operating at a nice level of abstraction where combined arms really shines. You have to make meaningful choices about where to deploy different units and how they're going to work together to achive something. There's enough micro around armor to feel satisfying but not so much that if all you're doing is driving your precious tank. Definitely worth a look!

This game will really appeal to anyone who has enjoyed the Wargame series - especially if you mostly enjoyed tank charges and infantry battles but didn't enjoy the missle spam of some of the games. When I got Bastion, I thought nothing could top that experience for a top-down narrative rpg.  Then Transistor came along, wiped the table of all the things I expected.  Was it going to be a two weapon smash like Bastion?  NOPE.  The combat is more complex.
This game can be played with either slow-paced tactical precision, or as a fast paced action game.  Like planning out your mode of attack?  This game's got that.  Want to just run around and spam your skills or play a more action-y style? This game provides that.  Want to be stealthy, or be like a trickster?  This game will surprise you.
The "skill" system provided is extremely versatile, allowing players to choose their own specific skill-set, then enhance those skills by powering them with extra abilities from un-used skills.
The story, well... wow, can't even explain how beautiful it is.  The dialog and the tone.  The feelings portrayed by the art and subtle sounds.
The one thing I can surely comment on is the music.  The music just naturally gets the player to empathize with the situation.  Its not the type of music that hypes players up.  There are very few games where the music can also tell the story and set the tone properly, and this is one of those games.

I haven't finished this yet, but as I spent many hours yesterday playing it I am more than comfortable reviewing it.
Pros;
+ Soundtrack is fantastic
+ Story is good, considering it's a game poking fun at JRPGs
+ "Narrator"/character interaction plays well
+ Fantastic dialogue (I laughed really hard at many points)
+ Excellent art for the style, vibrant and varied
+ Good level design for a 2D JRPG mockery
+ Streamlined interface/mechanics (i.e. levelling up gives you a choice of two bonuses, usually a trade off between a weak group/ stronger single target spell or upping some stats in place of others)
+ Multiple character art portraits for different moods in dialogue
+ You're a cutesy 8-bit Cthulhu
+ You can search stuff like bookshelves/drawers in that typical JRPG style, often with funny results

This game is addictive like crack cocaine. It makes time fly like nothing else. If you're looking for something to relax with while you drink your coffee and have nothing better to do then this is it.
Graphically the game might not look like much but do not let that fool you. This game is the best managerial game that I have ever played. It takes a lot of thinking, planning and constructing to get something working properly. There's a constant balance between production output and consumption. Too much of one and it will create issues that more often than not creates a chain reaction that requires more fixing.
Research progress keeps things fresh by unlocking better machines, more technologies and whole new industries. You can focus on one specific part of the tech tree or you can try and juggle multiple types of industries at the same time. You can for example make robots that make more robots, create very intricate computing systems inside of your production & setup a railway with cargo trains between your different facilities.
There's a learning curve to the game and a lot of things are so advanced that you will have to watch tutorials repeatedly. Or at least that's what I've had to do. You can still get started and do quite a lot of stuff before digging into the more advanced stuff that requires tutorials. I still did not learn everything there is to this game and after more than 20 hours it still feels fun and “unexplored”.
On top of difficulties juggling the problems that occur in your industry you’ll also have to defend yourself from aliens expanding and sometimes attacking your base. The more you pollute the more frequently you will get attacked. Setup turrets, walls and equip a weapon to defend yourself.
I read another review where the author described Factorio as a game where you fix problems of your own making & I think that description fits perfectly.
Multiplayer is really fun and you can create huge factories with a group of other people. You can setup a private server for you and your friends or join a public server.
There’s mod support in both single- & multiplayer which is great.
If you like these kinds of managerial games I’d say it’s a must-buy in its current state. The developer is really active and the tag of ~20€ is underpriced in my opinion.

Well, here's my two-cents on Factorio:
Short summary:
Factorio is an amazing, challenging game. Graphics are great for such a indie title. And it's got a brilliant  (Czech I believe) development team behind it which loves the game. They update the game quite often. When playing on steam, enable beta builds, as they've just added nuclear fission technology, grand! If you've finished the game? (The game is officially on 0.14, but the beta 0.15.x version already has a ton of mods with many more being added daily)
I've played this game for about 45 hours now, and plan on playing a lot more since I've booted up a new playthrough with a more efficient factory.
Pro's:
- Healthy playerbase + modding community, boosted from their own website forums.
- Challenging concepts
- Variety in enemies, but I will get to this later
- Lots of content (without mods, and much more with them enabled)
Con:
- Though it boasts a healthy variety of enemies, they become unchallenging really quickly. Mods can solve this, but I'd like a take from the developers, see how they invision a harder, smarter enemy. (As of now, the alien enemy evolves due to the pollution your factory creates, but also evolves when you destroy their homes or kills their friends in an effort to keep them away from your factory. Due to this, it boasts more evolved aliens with more damage and a higher HP. But, one you have Mk2 Power Armor and a flame thrower, none shall pass.
I'm looking forward to more updates, to keep my autistic brain in an efficiency endorsing loop working on bigger and badder factories.

NOTE: This game is Free to Play, so you lose nothing by playing it just for 30 minutes. Do not take my review seriously as you shouldn't with anyone else's due to that fact. See for your own eyes how good the game is.
Battle for Blood is a VERY obvious Mobile game port that doesn't seem to be any different from the original game, maknig the whole existence of this game on PC very debatable.
The game is basically a match-3-style game where matches summon units to attack enemies in a way that reminds me of Starjeweled, a Starcraft 2 custom game that is equally free to play.
Only here, there are different tiles and each tile type corresponds to a unit type, only unfortunately, they unlock as you complete the levels. The game would benefit from each unit type being rebalanced to allow this as it might add some more replayability, which given the fact that facebook, Kongregate, and even Steam itself offers far suprerior match-3 games...
The game doesn't really do well.
You can upgrade units, but ofcourse it doesn't matter too much as the game somewhat depends on RNG, hence being a match-3 game.
The Lives would work only on a phone where you can be notified when you get more, so you can play more, and the skills feel a bit lacking, the first being one to kill units on the screen, which is really all I used or got.
Altogether the game's art style does remind me of Castle Crashers, so there's that, and the soundtrack is decent, but altogether, the game doesn't stand out to me in any real way.
The game's mechanics don't work on a PC format too well, and it's obviously an unaltered mobile port.
If it cost money, you could bet that the reviews would be even harsher, so due to it being Free to Play, reviews don't really mean much, mine included.
I liked it, but once I got stuck, I immediately uninstalled and lost interest. I've played too many far better Match-3s on PC for this game to be at all relevant beyond the .6 hours I played.
This game gets a 5/10 with me. Just average, despite having a neat set of mechanics that would work better if they were improved upon for the PC version.

Didn't lose a battle until level 12, then you have to grind a little. I liked it enough to go get it for my tablet, where it plays better. For a free game it's fine, but shouldn't be on pc. It's a phone game. Would NOT pay for it though.

The idea that running out of moves should penalize the player, is a horrible one and seems to only further the overall pay to play system, which leaves one wanting more to delete the game then repeat the monotony or spend actual money.
Had this been put up for $2 without the pay to play system and more emphasis on puzzles, I think it would have been ok (as a developers first game), but it's clearly a port from IOS or Android, with little thought to the standards of PC players, it seems more like it's about getting it to the masses to soak up revenue from in-app purchases.

Assault Android Cactus is an absolute joy to play. It has some mechanics that set it apart from other twin stick shooters, such as the depleting battery meter that must be kept charged at all times.
There are a slew of characters to choose out of, each one with their own unique primary and secondary weapons. I played the game mostly as an unlockable character by the name of Starch, and thoroughly enjoy lasering everything in my path. The game supports local co-op, which makes the game immediately twice as fun as it was before. I played the game from start to finish with my brother, and we had more fun playing through this game together than we have had in a long time.
That's not to say that the game is without it's flaws though. There are a few things in the game that feel a bit unbalanced or a bit unfair. Some of the weapons used by enemies will instantly deplete your health meter, and at times the screen can be so packed full of enemies that it can be easy to lose track of your character. Let alone dodge the walls of projectiles coming from all sides. That's not including all the explosions and enemies that grab you to keep you from moving. Unlimited deaths helps to ease this a bit, but it can still be frustrating to get up and immediately be knocked back down.
This game can get HARD. The last world is brutal. But we pushed through and beat it, and had fun doing so.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that is a bullet hell, or twin stick shooter fan.

Wonderful RTS with nail biting tension. No more fighting over pylons or points. Steel Division has you fight over ground which is a much interesting and accurate representation of warfare on the front line.  Have you ever wanted to call in a plane to strafe enemy soldiers, if so, this is the game for you. In response the enemy will call in a plane of their own and soon you will have a dog fight happening on your screen.  For those that have played Wargame, you will feel right at home. For those that have not here are a few things that make this one special: Soldiers'' lives matter, you have a fixed number to bring in and veteran troops are rare (not something you pay 100 gems to unlock). This game is simply outstanding.  I've already racked up about 25 hours of gameplay and it hasn't even properly released yet.
If you enjoy strategy games where everyone starts off on the same level and the outcome is solely decided by your actions on the battlefield then this is the game for you.  If you want to feel conflicted about whether you should commit your reserve troops to the front lines or try to shoot through the gap, flank the enemy, and completely change the course of the entire battle... this is the game for you.  If you want to watch your best laid plans crumble, reform, crumble again, reform, succeed, gain some ground, lose it again... you get the idea.  This is the game for you.
I've seen some comments and reviews discussing how some people don't like certain aspects of the game.  How some units are "OP" and the morale system is ridiculous because "my infantry squads shouldn't be instantly suppressed by a machine gunner".  Well, some units in real life were "OP" and the opposing forces just had to find a way around or through them.  As for getting pinned by a machine gun, you have a .50 cal round snap past your head and then tell me what you would do.  It is the management of these things, along with numerous others, that make Steel Division so great.  I'm going to be playing this one for a long time and I look forward to what the devs do with it in the future.
Tl;dr - This game is fantastic and it hasn't even released yet.

Cthulhu Saves the World is an RPG with new twists on an old formula. If you haven't already, you should look at my (or any) review on Breath of Death VII by the same developers prior to this game. Cthulhu Saves the World does a lot to expand on that. For those of you who don't want to bother looking at that first... well get ready for this review then.
Cthulhu Saves the World has all your basic RPG stuff in it, leveling up, equipment management, going from town to town, talking to people, random encounters, spells, a four person party... all that good stuff. And the story, basically, is that Cthulhu has had his powers taken from him. In order to restore them, he must become a hero. Of course, being an evil creature such he, this makes for some goofy situations and banter between characters, the narrator, and Cthulhu himself along the way. So what makes this game stand out exactly?
Well, if that premise of playing as a reluctant hero isn't enough, consider some of these things. The combat consists of a basic attack, technical attacks, and spells. Technical attacks and spells take MP. Using most moves will result in your combo going up, based on the number of hits. There are some moves that are very powerful or very useful, but may break this combo when used. There are also a few moves that are combo finishers. This means that the higher the combo, the more damage these moves will do. This is very useful to take advantage of on bosses. There's also a status effect in this game called insanity. Generally, moves that cause insanity will be quite powerful, and enemies that are insane may increase your stats a bit based on your passive skills. However, insane enemies tend to do more damage as well, so it can be a risky trade off. Another neat thing is that, upon leveling up, you can choose to select one of two available upgrades. They might be increased stats, new moves, enhanced old moves, passives, or any combination of the choices. This gives some good replayability and customization options. To really appreciate this game, you have to look at where it shines... convenience.
This game is clearly designed by people who know how annoying RPGs can be, and they have taken measures to try and lessen the natural burdens of the genre. One way is simply allowing you to move around faster at the push of a button. There's also the ability to teleport to any city you've been to at any time, which is really nice for fast travel. The fights can move along quickly, which is nice for grinding. Animations for attacks are short, enemies are still images, and the display gives you fast information. After a battle, you will have some MP restored, full HP restored, and all party memebers revived... provided that you won. This makes it very easy to keep moving forward. No need to hoard healing items, use up MP on healing outside of battles, or travel back to healing areas. But by far the best addition is how this game handles random encounters. You see, every area has its own set number of random encounters. This means you'll find battles randomly that many times in the area. Once you've fought that many battles, the number reaches zero and you will no longer encounter enemies there randomly. This allows you to focus on your exploring, which is super nice in the mazier places. However, if you wish to grind in an area even after all the random encounters are up, you can! Simply go to the menu and select the option called fight. Then you will get to find a battle immediately without walking around randomly. It's the best of both worlds and I really love this feature.
The art style is cool, basically a 16 bit type of representation, more or less. Colorful areas and monsters, plus I really like the neat attention to detail with the in-battle backgrounds that change depending on the area and terrain. A nice touch that made me get a little more into it. I can't speak for the music since I had the sound off while grinding and watching stuff... so sorry but... grinding. Some of the dialogue can be pretty funny at times. Sometimes not so much, but it depends. There's even a cool mode you can turn on to get little notes from the developer in the game about its development. It's neat! Also, I'd like to bring up that there are some fun bonus modes to try out here too. I personally really liked the Cthulhu's Angels bonus mode, which is almost a totally new campaign aside from many of the areas and enmies reused. New story and dialogue, not to mention new characters, made it well worth going through.
However, there are some bad things about the game. The extra modes are among them. The higher difficulties are just more frustrating, as is highlader mode which only lets you use one person at a time to fight. These seem more like filler modes than actually being more conent, and for a game that's designed for the ease of use, making harder modes seems a bit counterproductive. But it's for more harcore players I guess. The other issue with the game is that, while it does try to fix the natural burdens of classic RPG design, it simply treats the symptoms rather than curing the problem. Basically, while it does make those aspects more enjoyable, it still has them.
In the end, Cthulhu Saves the world is a really fun RPG for those who like simpler RPGs and want a smooth experience with a classic feel. I can only seem to find it in a package with Breath of Death VII for 3 bucks, and even for just this game, it's worth it. If you want to know more about Breath of Death VII, check out my review of that (or other people's reviews) and see for yourself. It's basically the same as this, but smaller and a little less polished. I'd say that if you get the pack, play that first to really appreciate the changes in this one. It's a pretty good deal for what you get. Cthulhu Saves the World gets an 8/10 for being a solid classically styled RPG with some great innovations to make the old formula much more enjoyable.

So as you can see from my playtime, I have played a long time. I enjoy this game immensely and is the best MMO I have played so far, well worth the sub fee.
The free updates and content are great, usually on a monthly basis, with season events and the two Expensions. unlike other games with expansions *coughDestiny2cough* this actually adds alot of content and items and skills. With level cap raises and a combat system with new resource bars and abilities, this makes each class and job actually feel somewhat different.
The story is suprisingly good considering it's an MMO. You have good characters, some you can actually get attached to, and learn more about your allies, the world, and your purpose. It's a step up from the latest titles like FF15 in terms of a story and overall plot.
I main a Black Mage, so when Red Mage was released, I was very excited. I love it, with magical combos and physical attacks it's a great change from the constant Fire Rotation of Black Mage. Paladin is different from Dark knight and Warrior and Scholar is different from White Mage and Astrolagist, so even each job with a same role have a good amoutn fo differences to them. I recommend Astrologian for Healing, Paladin for Tanking, and Red Mage for DPS.
For new players, I do recommend giving this a shot since you do get 30 days free. You also get faster exp gain until level 60 which is a huge boon. The Mentor system makes it so experienced players are around to help newbies out and the Duty Finder is also a huge help, even if the DPS queues are long.
TLDR; a fun mmo with a great story, combat system, and community. If you have a chance, try it out. You can either research each class/job and learn everything from videos, or do what I did are run in blind and learn as you go. Your play style, your choice.

So I get the purpose of the game. Look at the documents, compare to the rules you've been given and make decisions about whether or not to let folks into the country. I also get that the game is allegory and is trying to tell you a story of how horrible it is in authoritarian countries and how bad it is to be a border agent.
Here's my issue: The game does the last two things a bit too well. You know what would have made this game better? Keyboard shortcuts that you don't have to pay for! Or, maybe a bit better way to display information about what the fine folks in central HQ want you to do. Yes - I get it. That would disrupt the narrative! I guess my issue is, narrative is fine but it shouldn't get in the way of gameplay.
This is one game where I feel like the gameplay suffers horrendously because the designer is trying to drive home the message of "LIFE IS BAD IN THESE PLACES." Ok, good! You have driven home that message. I don't live in these places and will no longer be playing this game which seems to be designed to annoy me.
Last bit - There are some substories here which do make for some interesting decisions. Unfortunately I couldn't get to too many of them because the game turned me off real hard by day 9. Double the length of the day, double the money you get for letting people in, double the physical space I have to cross reference documents and I will happily sit through the gameplay to get to the narrative.
Stress me out and annoy me because of the time crunches and I'll just uninstall - because I live in a Free country and we can do that here!

I found the game to be difficult and confusing but not in a good way. Other reviews have stated that the game doesn't "hold your hand" and that is an understatement. The game tells you almost literally nothing. You get the basic control scheme and that is pretty much it.
The interface and HUD are a bit clunky. The first puzzle in the game is... well... starting the game. I clicked on "play", selected my difficulty setting which then disapears and then I sat there for 30 seconds waiting for the game to start before figuring out that I have to click "play" a 2nd time to get it to go. You are then brought to a small room in zero gravity with some of the controls listed on the wall and a whole mess of numbers in the corner of the screen. One is a clock that is ticking down to something and a few other indicators that I still don't know what they all mean. I figured out that one is a health indicator, not sure about the others. I get that the game is supposed to be hard but some things in a game should be explained, like for example, what the stuff on your HUD is for and what it means. You also start with a note that simply says "Lab 20" on it (I assume that is my objective) and perhaps one of the worst flashlights in video game history. The game is very dark and I think the flashlight makes it worse by putting a large white spot on one side of the screen while also failing to actually light anything. You also move very slowly. At first I thought it might be an FPS issue, but moving my head and other moving objects are moving fluidly with no lag soooo I think you just move slowly.
There are also these wierd physics puzzles I guess scattered around. You fly into this yellow circular structure in the wall and then you have to bounce around like a billard ball into another circle and it teleports you to another room. You have no free move controls in these puzzles you just aim at the wall and hope that you bounce off it at the right angle to land in the circle. Prepare to do many of them again and again and again and again just to get to the next room. It isn't really "hard" it is more like "frustrating".
The game has potential. The atmosphere of the game is good and the graphics are very nice for an indy title. It just needs a little bit of polish. I think a little backstory and some more indepth instructions besides "press ? for controls" and welcome to a defunct space station, now go find lab 20 - would be a big improvement. The developer seems like he is making constant improvements based on feedback and that is always a good thing.
I have a hard time recomending this game. If you do decide to play it I recomend setting aside a few hours and a pen and paper (seems to be one of those kinds of games...) to make maps and notes. I might give the game a 2nd chance later when I can do just that. If that is your cup of tea and you don't mind a bit of inappropriate furstration then give the game a try.

This game is just a failed experiment I suppose? Basic playability is barely functional.
At a base level in games, you generally want to know what you can and can't do, and a certain amount of intuitiveness is necessary in UI elements.
You cannot place objects on walls if they face ne/nw (Isometric view). You cannot rotate a camera despite the 3D models, I spent about five minutes confused thinking no surely you must be able to make it face the other way? Considering objects are NECESSARY in one room, to go into another, (Two spacesuits in a room, with an airlock, to move out) the only answer is making gigantic rooms or a ton of small rooms. The tutorial doesn't really tell you to do this, and while you can then retry, and do it "right", it sets the tone for the game. You won't be using your intellect or planning skills, you will learn that the game isn't capable of some things, and how to work around it. There is no space efficiency, which is one of the key "fun" things to do in a base building game.
Learning is of course a key part of games and design, but they should be learning mechanics not limitations.
In ten minutes I ran into several of these little "Oh. You can't do that? Or am I doing it wrong?".

Steel Division is pretty great. At its core, it is essentially Wargame EE/ALB/RD with a few additional tweaks to the formula. The minor changes however can dynamically alter the gameplay and give Steel Division are more realistic feel to the way battles unfold. Chief among these is the front line system. Now it feels like every inch of ground is important. The result is I have forces fighting for territory everywhere. At any given moment, I can have units defending zones, making counter attacks, moving forward for hard flanks everywhere on the map.
The setting change also contributes greatly to this feeling. Infantry is much more important. Armor is harder to take out because of limited AT. It makes most of the unit in the game feel crucial as an infantry squad or MG in the right place can make all the difference. Watching a german heavy tank laugh shell after shell of its hull as it slowly make its push and then having a signle squad with an anti-tank grenade save the day is a wonderful and satisfying feeling.
There are some negatives. I miss the resupply system and the unit experience system. The pinned down and surrender mechanic is a neat additon, but doesn't always work like it should in sometimes a stray shot can force a pin and any unit near by will cause that unit surrender. The result can sometimes feel wonky. It would also be nice if there were more nations involved. (I know some of them were not in Normandy)
That said, this game is the pretty awesome when looked at from the sum of its parts. If you like wargame series, Steel Division is for you.

This is a good game similar to the Wargame franchise but with notable changes. I esspecially like the conquest mode and the phase system.
The normal match takes 40+ minutes and starts with phase A which lasts ten minutes, then entering phase B lasting ten minutes too, then entering phase C.
Your strongest units are likely not available in Phase A (or B), so you use weaker ones in this Phase(s). Together with the deck building mechanic, you have to really make compromises which units and how many of them to use in your deck in Phase A,B or C.
The conquest mode got a moving front line. Which really encourages player activity in all phases. The side controlling more of the map scores points.
The maps are nice based on historical maps.
Game is slower than Wargame RD, which I like.
The major bad point for me is how leaving players in multi player are handled.
If a player leaves a specific player gets control of the leaving players units. If other players leave the same player (!!!) gets control of those players units too, overwhelming him very likely.
Eugen already promised to make a change here.
(Got about 10% crashes-disconnects too. Not an issue in other games for me.)
Edit: After release the KI takes over the control over units from leaving players. So I give this game now a full thumbs up.

This game is great, but it does have some drawbacks. Unlike most other MMORPG's this game has sort of a single-player aspect to it in regard to the main story, which they refer to as the Main Scenario Quest(MSQ). There are quite a few times that you have to complete something solo, meaning you must drop out of your group. The story itself is extremely detailed and enjoyable, as one would expect of a Final Fantasy title. I wish all of the story was voice-acted as well, but only certain cutscenes are. Another initial drawback is the combat, compared to other MMORPG's, it feels a bit sluggish, due to the 2.5 second global cooldown. Eventually you obtain skills that can be used outside of the global cooldown and then you'll have more buttons to press making combat seem more fluid. The dungeons and raids are pretty dang fun and the music score is amazing. Overall, I'd recommend this game with the caveat that you give it a fair chance.

And once you've thought that there weren't enough side scrolling 2D shooters out there, along comes Who's that Flying?! Although simple and mindless, it's actually fun. There's plenty of action going on at all times keeps it from getting stale. It offers a short cartoon campaign with a story to save different cities around the world. The goal is to keep 50 enemies from getting past you which is harder than it sounds on some of the levels. Add in a different assortment of boss battles and it's actually a real treat.
You get a special one-time powerful beam every time you kill a certain number of monsters, but the charge will deplete if an enemy gets past. It has controller support which is nice. And once you finish the campaign there are a couple dozen challenge levels and an infinite mode to keep you entertained even further.
The in-between time waiting for levels to load seemed a bit long though, but not overly excessive. Decent dollar menu game.

Story 9: Sleeping Dogs (not about sleeping puppies, sadly) puts you in the shoes of Wei Shen. A hunky♥♥♥♥♥individual who's a native of Hong Kong who returned from the U.S. He becomes a member of the Sun On Yee triads, only to be arrested shortly after and somehow becoming a part-time police officer. Now Wei has to fight to protect his freedom, his triad family, and he has to choose which side he will be on. Overall, it's a great story that actually takes itself seriously despite some flashes of goofy humor here and there.
Visuals 7.5: Sleeping Dogs isn't the most beautiful game, but it's handsome enough. On the good side, this fictional version of Hong Kong can look pretty at night with its neon signs, the animations are convincing, and it can run on a pretty wide range of hardware. On the flip side, character models look like creepy mannequins up close and the fog effect added to the Definitive Edition can vary depending on your tastes.
Audio 9: The voice acting from big name celebrities like Emma Stone and Lucy Liu are pretty good. But it's the main performances that steal the show and the mix of English and Cantonese is a very nice touch. The cultural sound effects in the menus are pretty distracting, though.
Gameplay 8.5: Combat is kind of like the Batman Arkham games except its more realistic. It's not as amazing as the aforementioned games, but the mix of light and heavy attacks feel pretty good. Plus, you can use the environment to brutally takedown your opponents. Driving through the GTA-like open world of Hong Kong is also great. The vehicles have a combination of speed and handling that feels too good and the action hijacking is satisfying. Shooting isn't as interesting, but it feels pretty good to land headshots. Getting to cover can feel pretty awkward, though. The only problem with combat and driving is the wonky camera. During combat the camera can be a problem in tight spaces. While driving, the camera always pans to the front of the vehicle while backing up which can be confusing. Also, as to be expected with games long in development, there are minor bugs. There are also things to do on the side like errands, cop jobs, races, karaoke, and dates.
DLC (Doesn't affect final score): The DLC aren't must-plays, but it's cool that they're here. Nightmare On North Point is a cheesy and fun, if repetitive, Halloween expansion (7) and Year of the Snake is a better, if dully plotted, New Years expansion (7.5).
Overall: Sleeping Dogs is a fun open world game with a well writen story, fun combat and driving, and plenty to do. While a clunky camera and some minor bugs do take away the immersion, it's fun to take a vacation to Hong Kong. Hopefully it's not as violent in real life.

Video Game Review
CIU110.1 Critical Thinking in Creative Media
Assault Android Cactus
Video Game from Witch Beam
Review by Carlos Melo
From the Brisbane-based developer team Witch Beam, Android Assault Cactus will immerse you in the role of a Police Android named Cactus, that responds to the call of a stranded space freighter “The Genki Star”. Once inside the ship, she finds out that all the robot workers have rebelled because some malfunctioning. Attempting to save the ship, Cactus fights hordes of robots and bosses that control different decks of The Genki Star, together with 7 other androids that she recruits along the way to reach the brain of the ship while trying to find out the cause of the malfunction.
This game is a Twin Stick action arena shooter with an isometric top-down view that up to 4 players can play in co-op mode. It was firstly made for PC, but it will be available for PS4, Vita and Wii U, and although the game is still in Early Access, it is extremely refined and polished, it has great 3D graphics and great performance, it runs very smoothly even when the arena is packed with enemies.
The art style reminds me of Jet Force Gemini and Megaman with influence of anime, and every android is remarkably different, not only in appearance but also in gameplay, each one of the androids has a unique primary and secondary weapon. The primary weapons go from an assault machine gun with high precision to a shotgun with more spread shooting that can help with crowds. The secondary weapons are very powerful and have short cooldowns, they help a lot when taking down the big robots, and as if it wasn't enough you can power up the primary weapon by collecting energy, and there are also 3 pickups that can assist you in your fire rate and speed.
Each level consist of two objectives, the first one is to destroy all the enemies, and the second one is to collect the batteries that the robots drop when they are destroyed, so you can keep fighting. This battery system works as a timer and in fact, the only way you can lose is by running out of battery which will shut down your android. Apart from that, getting hit a few times will eventually stunt your android, making you press the shooting button repeatedly in order to get up and keep fighting, this doesn’t count as dying but it does drain your battery.
Now, what makes ACC one of the best games of its genre that I have played is the mechanics of the game and the amazing dynamic levels, the arena changes while you are fighting, moving and rearranging itself, this can play in your favour or against you by making you take decisions really fast and being spontaneous. There are 20 levels and 5 bosses, which are very different and challenging.

I would like to say that I'm really impressed with the work these developers have made, the game is getting close to its final stage but they keep adding more awesome stuff, like the bonus features on the EX options where you spend credits for more features like more visual filters, A.I. partners and a First Person Shooter Camera MIND BLOWN!.

Don't be discouraged by the Alpha state.  This game is more polished and stable than most full releases.  It runs flawlessly on reasonable hardware. Basically:  the core of the game is complete and future updates will cosmetic updates to a few levels, minor balance changes, additional game modes, and lore/story/info bits. AAC has a few mechanics (such as the battery mechanic) which simultaneously lower the skill floor and raise the skill ceiling.  This makes the game accessible for novices but also very competitive if you like chasing high scores.  Otherwise, it has pretty much every feature you'd want in a game like this.  Level select for the levels that you've cleared.  An infinite arena mode.  A daily 10-wave mode that is different every day which adds a ton of replay-ability.  Quick access to different menus for character/level/mode select.

You can have up to 4 players and you can mix and match control schemes (you can play 3 person co-op with 2 controllers and one keyboard/mouse) but it has to be done old-school-console style.  This makes AAC a really great co-op game if you have an HTPC or living room PC.

Lucus Pope, originally a developer for Naughty Dog on the Uncharted series, left Naughty Dog after the 2nd Uncharted. He went on his own Wim and after going through international boarders seeing the border crossing security in action who was inspired to make a game, where the player is this security guard. Pope was the only one to work on this project.
This game is brought together by its sound which to cut the need of voice actors he’s used his own voice, and pixelated the sound, so everyone genuinely sounds the same. The design aspect which he has used a sort of pixelated layout. The intended effects are to give the player an experience of challenge and feeling of rushed and questions your moral.
This is a fantasy game, where the player’s role is as the Border Crossing Security. The graphics and some of the audio has a pixelated theme. This is due to the design of the creator. Having the audio and design the way it is, a lot of it is very pixelated reminding the user that this is a fantasy experience. Also there are no bright colours at all, the game is mainly made up of greys and black and the environment is simulating something similar to the cold war being over and people are starting to rebuild their lives. Even though its pixeled the game is designed to show you interesting things and sometimes overtly crazy things that you wouldn’t expect, such as you failing to scan them and the game lets you know you’ve made a mistake by making the sound of a fax machine then showing you either penalised by how much money, or by giving you a warning. then once they are through they walk over to the security fence and blow themselves up because they don’t like Arstotzka and they had explosives attached to them which you happen to miss, when doing your searches. While searching through people’s ID and document for discrepancies it can be noted that each document needs to be handled individually, you can’t just click a button and it does everything for you. You are to sort through each document otherwise you can easily fail and be penalised and possibly risk the end of the game. Which luckily saves each successful night, or new day.
Above all these things, I must say I had an interesting and sprightful experience playing this game. Although there are moments where you question your morality, when you are given an option and you choose for example, when a husband and wife come up to you, and the wife has a typo in her name, are you wanting to decline her for the glory of Arstotzka or take a penalty and let her through. Not to mention you have seconds to decide. This is not the only thing that gets you on your feet. I'm going to assume you have some knowledge about this game, regardless whether you have played it or not. So, spoilers. Deal with it.
You are Starkiller, Darth Vader's secret apprentice. But you never really feel like a Sith. Nor a Jedi. Starkiller seems a bit of a badass in-between character, with skills that hint at both.
The story feels quite engaging, if you are into Star Wars. If you are a fan, you'll gleefully smile at the references, appearances and the style of everything.
I'm not an expert, but all the locations truly feel like they are Star Wars planets. And Starkiller's outfit design that comes with every level is a notable feature too.
Gameplay wise, aside the quirks an old game is expected to have, the game runs smooth. The cutscenes have frequent syncing hiccups, but it's easy enough to find them on Youtube and watch them with Overlay.
While I really want to say the controls react perfectly, they don't...not really. There are many moments where an attack animation can't be interrupted, especially with a dash. Leaving you at the mercy of your foe (and their heavy attack)  whether you'll be punted away.
If you aren't being thrown around, though, you'll usually have proper controls.
The quality of the game is pretty nice, especially since Patch 1.2 comes with an HQ pack (comes with the installation). It's not super modern looking, but it's still pretty nice.
With the Sith edition comes many new outfits, even from characters that don't or make a single appearance. Such as Proxy, Starkiller's "assistant" and training droid, turning himself into a holographic Darth Maul to battle-train him.
Which was a tough fight, I'll have you know.
The real fan service comes in the form of extra missions.
The first one is from the old Jedi Temple, providing him with a small and personal adventure (in the shape of the Jedi Trials), showing Starkiller his "possible" future.
Which possible future you may ask? You might already know this, but the main story end leaves you with a Light or Dark Side choice. Save your friends from The Emperor, or kill Darth Vader, whom you already had beaten right before that (but who seems fine to do it all over again).
This is where things get interesting for the fans. The Light side choice (defeating Palpatine) is the canon ending. With Starkiller saving his friends, allowing them to start the Rebellion, and him dieing in what I consider a sense of sacrifice.
But the Dark Side choice is pretty badass in on itself. Not only do you replace Vader, but a little 'incident' (which I won't spoil for you) causes him to be gravely wounded as well. Resulting in him being assigned a pretty unique helmet with a breather that sounds a little bit like that of Vader. However, his design is much more designed for Acrobacy, and he also has kept his limbs, so there's that.
By the way, everything is unlocked in the extra missions, including all the lightsabre crystals, except for a few skills in the Jedi Temple one.
This is the point where the other two extra missions take place. You are now the Emporer's enforcer as Vader was. One mission takes place in Tatooine, where you hunt for two familiar sounding droids...
This has you passing by familiar characters, such as Jabba the Hut and Ben Kenobi, whom you have to kill, twice, in succession. Yeah, something about that spirit of his...
The second mission, and my personal favorite, takes place in Hoth during the famous assault on the Rebel Base. Starkiller has donned an outfit similar to that of Darth Vader, but built for acrobacy and flexibility. In my opinion, it looks ten times more badass than that of Vader. And I don't say this lightly.
But the real fan climax comes when you fight Luke for the second time. What happens there at the end gives so much fantasizing juice. Makes you feel bad that Lucas Arts didn't design a whole game around Starkiller taking the Dark Side.
The game is old, and it shows. But the story is strong and the gameplay is fun, but tough enough. It's been quite the trip, and I can't say I've really regretted it at any point.

Steel Division harnesses the unique and exceptional gameplay of the Wargame franchise while incorporating many updates and modifications that range from flat improvements (Line of sight tools, more complex infantry behavior, increased unit movement assignment options) to era specification modifications that more closely mimic the style of combat during WWII (decreased lethality of air support and decreased effectiveness of AA, restricted vehicle movement through dense forests, glancing blows and bounces from shots against armored vehicles).
Eugen does for modern warfare what Creative Assembly's Total War franchise did for historical and pre-industrial warfare. While lacking the grand campaign of the Total War franchise, SD:44 focuses its efforts on cultivating its unique gameplay into its competitive multiplayer scene. If you are a fan of multiplayer RTSs which focus heavily on gameplay and tactics rather than resource management and logistics then SD:44 will certainly be a new favorite.
If you are already a fan of Wargame then you will enjoy Steel Division. Its deck building system doesn't provide the amount of diversity (or, perhaps, the illusion of diversity) that exists in Wargame but its gameplay is tighter. If you have no experience with the Wargame series then I suggest SD:44 if you want a more limited but polished experience and I would recommend Wargame: Red Dragon if you prefer a more modern setting and don't mind getting rocked by the veteran, well-established multiplayer community.

Transistor isn't a bad game, it's just not particulary good.  The story is ho-hum and the dialogue throughout isn't interesting.  Characters aren't well fleshed out, so you'll never be drawn to or care about any of them.  The game is intentionally vague on its' mechanics which doesn't serve it well and makes the start game portion confusing.  I was 2 hours in and didn't realize you could actually die until I looked it up online.  The combat system is interesting at first but there's not much depth to it, as you'll repeat the same tactics over and over.  It also makes combat fairly simple and I didn't die a single time. You can choose to apply limiters (combat debuffs) to yourself to make the combat more difficult & gain more xp, but I didn't care enough about the game to really want to activate them.  On the positive side, you're given plenty of options on customizing combat actions, buffs for those actions, and passive abilities.  I found the inventory system to be a tad counter-intuitive.  Each function has an upgrade tab that tells you what other processes will do with it when attached as upgrades, but what you really want is actually the opposite of that.  You want to know what that function will do as an upgrade for each other function.  They should've made that the upgrade tab or included it as its own seperate tab.  It can be very time consuming looking up what a function will do as an upgrade for each other function.  The game never really drew me in & never made me want to keep playing or come back for more.  I started this back at the beginning of November and didn't bother getting around to finishing it until the end of Janurary.

Almost every single positive review will mention the art style & music as their first two positive notes.  There is usually a problem with a game when things like art style and music overshadow the plot, stories, characters, dialogue, and actual gameplay.  While I enjoy those things and they can serve to make a game better, they are usually the least important elements of a game.  Overall, it's an ok game that doesn't have much wrong with it; it just doesn't do alot of things well.  This is a game I'll never play again or remember much about.

Differences between this and the mobile version:
- Better Music
- Better Graphics
- No microtransactions (unlock everything just by playing)
- Scenario editor (you can make your own scenarios and play user made scenarios [you can wipe out humanity with fridges!])
- The freshly added Multiplayer
- The upcoming Co-op mode
Is it worth it?
- Yes!
In this game you choose between different plague types to wipe out humainty.
While certainly not easy (mostly because there's no tutorial, but since it's early access it will be added in the future) it is rewarding for a while once you know the drill (mostly because it's almost the same tactic for every plague type). There are also 3 special plagues (neurax worm, necroa virus, simian flu) that require different tactics. You'll unlock genes for every win to modify your plague. After that, you can try to beat the game on Mega Brutal.
Then you move on to scenarios. They are different from the normal game and therefore you still have to put thought in your actions. After that you basically have seen everything from singleplayer. Now you can play some custom made scenarios.
It's time for the Multiplayer! You have to either infect 100% of the world population or have the other plague getting wiped out by making humanity focus on the cure for the other plague or kill all it's hosts (passively or actively). More modes are coming.
Every game of multiplayer is different, because the enemy has different tactics (unlike in singleplayer). You'll have to adapt and use their mistakes to your advantage to win. There are special transmissions, symptoms and abilities just for multiplayer.
I can't write about the co-op mode because it's not out yet.

I would have been way more interested in the game if they hadn't made the asinine decision to have all content / levels unlocked immediately, as another reviewer noted this kills ALL sense of progress and nullified any minimal interest I had remaining in the game.

I don't mean to tarnish the game as it obviously had very few people working on it, and I'm sure they weren't "shooting for the moon" with this title by any means, but it's very indie /limited resources / effects etc and very "what you see is what you get." It would have been a kickass PC game in like 1995, and maybe it would have benefited if it leaned more into that it was depicting a bygone, retro era with limited features, but as-is it feels simplistic/limited.

Do you like twin-stick shooters?  Do you know what SHMUP is?  "Yes" to either = get this game.   AAC is pure arcade shooter fun.
Don't be discouraged by the Alpha state.  This game is more polished and stable than most full releases.  It runs flawlessly on reasonable hardware.  Control (gamepad or keyboard/mouse) is smooth and really tight which are important for games like this.    Basically:  the core of the game is complete and future updates will cosmetic updates to a few levels, minor balance changes, additional game modes, and lore/story/info bits. AAC has a few mechanics (such as the battery mechanic) which simultaneously lower the skill floor and raise the skill ceiling. This makes AAC a really great co-op game if you have an HTPC or living room PC.
Player base is small-ish but they are pretty dedicated to dominating the leaderboards so expect some stiff competition that's your thing.

Assault Android Cactus is one of those games I didn't know I wanted until I got my hands on it. The game takes the simple premise of being a bullet hell-ish arena shooter, peppers it with unique and memorable morphing levels and eight playable androids with different kinds of playstyles, strengths and weaknesses (four of which are playable from the start), and tops it with a race against time to beat the levels before your batteries run out (yes, even boss levels work like this!).
Even though levels tend to get downright overrun by enemies really often, I never felt like I lost sight of where I was (I did mix up my character on ocassion with that of other players) or that I didn't stand a chance agaisnt them, and the enemy variety is enough that you'll feel challenged by them, and will have to think fast when some particularily pesky ones decide to show up.
Unlike with regular stages, bosses are fought one-on one, with you pelting them with all you've got while struggling to get them to drop the next battery in time. Again, I feel like they are challenging and can get to overwhelm you, but still do so in a fair way (gotta learn their attack patterns!).
Even if you don't care about the score attack aspects of the game you can have plenty of fun with the crazy levels and huge number of enemies that get thrown your way. Still, the game really shines when playing local co-op, so I'd definitely recommend Assault Android Cactus to those of you who know other people you can play it with more than to people looking for a satisfying single-player experience (except for score attack enthusiasts, of course).
Having personally met the team behind it, I'd say that their concept of designing levels with easily identifiable features (ie: the popping lava level, the conveyor belt one, the one where the lights go out...) was a really good decission, making for a wide variety of fun and interesting arenas which also have the added bonus of letting different characters excel at each of them.

Short version: This game will make you want to move to Hong Kong and be either a cop or a gangster.  Play it.
This is an open world game in a flavor similar to GTA or Saint's Row.  It sticks to it's core competencies of storytelling, fighting, and driving.  The mechanics of the game are not especially remarkable: You'll spend most of your time defeating your opponents using Kung Fu.  The martial arts system isn't especially deep, but as you unlock a variety of moves over the course of the game you'll develop a reasonable amount of flexibility.  The firearms mechanics are underwhleming, but serviceable for the relatively infrequent gun battles.  The driving mechanics are solid, and include the ability to manually initiate a ram on your opponents.
You play as Wei Shen, an American cop who has gone home to Hong Kong for an undercover assignment infiltrating a Triad.  Every mission you will accrue experience as both a cop (for avoiding injuring/killing bystanders and damage to public property) and a Triad member (for Kung Fu, shooting, fast talking, and sometimes driving).  Each type of exp unlocks a series of appropriate upgrades, such as improved striking damage and damage resistance (Triad) and the ability to slimjim a parked car without setting off the alarm or retrieve rare firearms from the trunk of parked police cars (Cop).
Now, for what makes this game a must-play, especially at sale prices: the story and the voice acting are excellent throughout.  I'll avoid story spoilers, but this game has a high-enough quality story and cinematics that I'd be happy to sit and watch somebody else play through the story missions.  Also, the city of Hong Kong is a delight to explore.  While parts of the city feel relatively generic, the first chunk of the game takes place largely in a night market, and the background conversations are frequently in Cantonese.  The game has a lot of fun with it's environment, including a mission where you break into an enemy's house to mess up his feng shui and somebody who asks you to take a dive in a karaoke competition.
Bottom Line: This is a great game with a lot of character.  $20 is a little steep, but I definitely recommend picking it up next time it goes on sale.

This game is the dream child of an engineer and a programmer.  The automation is beautiful and absolutely instrumental - you quite literally can't win by crafting everything in your inventory.
Tips I've learned the hard way:
Iron is your best friend, get as much of it as possible, then double that amount.  If you have less than three chests of iron plates at any time after achieving automation, you're doing it wrong.
After you get a working knowledge of the game, once you find where you want to begin, make sure to pause the game and plan everything out via the map.  It'll take a long time, but not having to undo your stuff to expand later is brilliant.
Make a main bus.  Use long-handled inserters and fast inserters to input/output your resources to an open area for when you continue automating later.
As soon as you can, get fast conveyors and automate construction of them.
Once you get enough resources to build a steam generator, don't.  Find water near a source of coal, and make it auto-feed a line of boilers and a line of generators.
DO NOT NEGLECT TURRETS!  Early-game the biters aren't such a big deal, but after a while they start to go from cute little zerglings to ultralisks and smash through your base if you aren't prepaed.
The only real issue I've found is if you don't plan out where everything needs to go, you're screwed later on.  I'd also recommend adding a pollution cleaner-esque thing (which doesnt actually reverse or even stop the spread of pollution, it just sharply reduces it) because I'm about 4 hours into my map and I'm getting absolutely crushed by the bugs - I can't just kill them because they're big enough to crush me, and my base is decently protected but I can't leave it to settle elsewhere and my resources are nearly depleted.  Also, we need a way to "uncraft" things, so we can turn the useless burner stuff at the start back into materials instead of having them be inefficient or just sitting in a random chest.

Transistor is a pretty interesting game, though definitely confusing. You begin the game "in media res," with things falling apart and jumping into some uncertain combat with some creatures known as The Process. Your character, Red, seems to have lost her voice, which is odd, and I will get to that later as a criticism related to Supergiant Games. The only thing that speaks to you (as the character and player) for most of the game is actually your weapon, the Transistor itself.
The story is not all given to you. In fact, you must piece a lot of it together - what the world is, where the people in it are, who the people you meet along your journey are, and what you are actually doing in the first place, among many other questions. Supergiant was very lightweight on what they give you, as you only learn small pieces here and there, with a few side details as you explore and find items such as terminals, which have news posts or recorded audio.
Other story details revolve around your powers in combat. As you go along in the game, you earn new attack skills for the Transistor, and you can map out which skills you have at a time. There are 4 active skill slots you can hold at any one moment. Each skill can be upgraded with a max of 2 other skills at a single time. And further, there are 4 passive skill slots that you can hold, which will cause certain effects during combat. Each new skill will give you 3 pieces of story information revolving around a singular character. To unlock the information, you must use each skill as Active, Upgrade, and Passive. Doing so will give you new blocks of text about each character's background.
Note that there is Memory that you have in the game, and equipping each skill uses up the Memory. Its purpose is to limit the amount of active, passive, and upgrade skills you have at any time. Further, you gain experience to level up in combat, common to RPG-style games. Leveling up is how you unlock certain new skills, and also how you unlock the usage of the new slots for active/passive/upgrade.
A very heavy piece of combat, which is basically a requirement to survive the game, is something called Turn(). Essentially, it stalls combat (freezes time) and gives you a limited energy bar to plan out what you want to do. Moving around and using skills will eat up the energy, though you can undo moves and keep changing your plan until you finalize it by ending Turn(). Doing so will trigger everything you chose in faster than usual speed, with most enemies barely moving while it all happens. Turn() is a way to increase damage against enemies, escape bad areas of battle, or even just a way to look around the area to figure out what to do.
While I do think that the usage of such a system was pretty efficient, and the fact that using skills in those 3 different ways allows for good customization, I do not think that Turn() necessarily blew the game away. A big reason why it is not all that is the fact that it really must be used a ton, or else you simply die. Many enemies cannot be efficiently beaten without it. Some of them are even chasing and attacking you every single second, as if they are in their own Turn() mode the whole battle, such as these dog enemies called "Fetch." While you find certain skills to hide or run away, most battle areas end up being relatively small and having large amounts of enemies, meaning that no place is exactly a safe spot.
In fact, the later into the game I got (and during my second playthrough in "Recursion"), I ended up using the exact same set of skills and spamming Turn() in order to get through. The game had certain side battles called Tests, one of which is called Performance Tests. In them, you must fight waves of enemies with randomly generated skills, as a means to get associated with more skills than just a few you like. However, most of those were simply not possible with certain skills and required many retries to get stronger ones, showing that not every skill is enough to beat the game.
The graphics of the game are pretty good, though I found way too many areas to be extremely bright/to have high contrast to where things were blending together. I could not find a good reason for this, because my computer and the game settings were nothing abnormal. No such brightness/contrast issues exist for any other games I have played, or for any applications I have used.
As for the sound, most of the effects are nothing too special, while some of the music and voice acting were done well, with limitations. In total, you only hear about 4 characters in the entire game, with 3 of them being for very short periods of time. Supergiant Games seems to not get many people acting as characters, and in both of their popular games so far, that minimalism exists. The other game is Bastion, of course, a game which many people compare Transistor to, as Bastion came out a few years before in a similar vein. Both games have very little voice besides one main character talking as a semi-narrator, and one or two songs made for the games.
Now, as just mentioned, Supergiant has the other big hit Bastion. As has seemed to be a large topic for players of these games, many people question and answer which of the two hits are better. A majority of people I've seen so far say Bastion - and in my opinion, I would agree with them.
While Transistor is definitely strong and I still recommend playing it, I feel like Bastion has more charm and better setup than Transistor does. I enjoy the gameplay setup of Bastion more, with a hub that you return to, a map that you traverse to specific areas with vastly different styles, and a purely active combat style. I also enjoyed the story and characters of Bastion more, with you getting to learn more about them and the world.
Supergiant made Bastion with very tight-knit story and gameplay, while Transistor has more breadth. Bastion gives you almost every single background detail possible, which I would not say Transistor needs to do - but I still think that Transistor did not go as deep as it should have. A lot of the story just feels like it is randomly pieced together, while Bastion feels very connected. Further, Transistor is a rather shorter game in comparison to Bastion.
Despite the above, I think Transistor is definitely a game worth trying out, as it is a nice experience overall. However, I believe that Bastion has a higher replayability as well, and I do not see myself returning to Transistor much.

This game is a departure from the side-scrolling shooter genre, while at the same time being a good hommage to its ancestral roots.  The endless waves of identical baddies are there, flying in bizarre formations, just waiting for you to blast them out of the sky.  What's different, however, is the sense of humor the game brings, and the fact that, unlike most shooters, your "ship" (in this case, a blaster-armed, showboating Guardian of Earth) is invincible!  Getting hit by the baddies doesn't kill you; it only slows you down.  This doesn't mean there is no consequence for failure, however; If you let the little Ravager aliens escape, they will devour part of the population of Earth.  Let 50 of them pass, and it's game over. And, like I said, if you do get hit by them, they will slow you down and prevent you from shooting for a brief time. Being invincible does make the character feel much more epic and powerful, though, unlike the old-school games where you pilot a fragile spaceship.

I also liked combat system. Building up your combo points and finishing the combo can really make difference in harder boss fights.
