I really recommend both of these games if you are at least a little into old school 8 bit rpg's. If you are unsure, start Cthulhu Saves the world and see if humor catches you up. Personally I'm definitely going to play rest of the developers games through at least once.

Review from the PoV of moderate skill level [fighting games] and fairly new to the KoF universe.
+Low system requirements
+Great variety of characters and colors
+Good control
+Multi-path story mode.
-Barebones Tutorial
-Story frames do not help to identify who is talking.  You are expected to know all the names and backgrounds already.
-Limited resolution setttings
-Uneven difficulty progression.
-Could really use a key rebind for menu pageup and pagedown
The game runs very smoothly on my J-series intel [2GHz] + 820M setup.  The tutorial mode is nowhere near the skullgirls level, but the practice mode is good [easy access to command list].   The Story mode is like a choose-your-own-adventure which is fun, but for someone who is new, I struggled to put a face to the speaker, often not knowing who                                                        was talking until the frame scanned to the other side at the end of the scene.  Also my major gripe is with the difficulty spike at the end.  I can clear out story mode with ease, often using only one character per fight, yet the final boss will get perfect matches against me.  Yes, it will make his defeat more rewarding, but it cheapens the rest of the fights.  I like Street Fighters progression more, where each fight is more difficult than the last, so that I can better gauge how well I am improving with a character.
Aside form all that, the game is really fun.  The fighting is solid and the variety of approaches to the story mode give it some replay value for people like me who like to know character backgrounds.
I have not tried online multiplayer mode, and wont until I have stable internet.

you start out in the menu screen, a well animated character by the name of cactus off to the side giving a "fine" impression like this is yet simply just a small game which sucks like many others on greenlight at the time of writing this. you head to the campaign... to almost instantly notice the music, the up-beat tone giving you a feeling like your about do something a little crasy. you play the tutorial, and you use the basic WASD and mouse keys noting the over-head view like that of the familiar M,O,B,A comforting you in the fact that what is used is tried and true. then the first level begins. it isnt like the beat of before, now these enemies fall like dominoes before a playfull child, and the more enemies killed the more of these "orbs" plop about, collecting them like points you begin to feel quite a bit like a bad♥♥♥♥♥as you gun suddenly seems able to mow through them like a knife... not through butter, no no NO! more like... it's going throught them like a "whisk to water"  of course that high point was followed by an imidiate low of you getting your character knocked face first against the floor! the music almost stopping, waiting for you to get back up, then once you do the beat kicks right back to where it was at the beginning but you find it easy to get the music pumping as a smile comes right accross your face. then the level ends. and you feel a water in your mouth, almost jarring yourself as you imidiately surge yourself into the next level.
This, dear readers, is Assault android cactus. now, that was my first impressions and they were quite good and a hell of a time was had. with that lets get into the thick of it. after all this is a review not a fan-fare!
this game involves multiple characters on a journey aboard the "genki star" a 25 level ship filled to the brim with robots quite intent on trying to kick your shiny♥♥♥♥♥to the ground and hope it stays that way. i personally went through the campaign moslty with the shotgun weilding "Coral" and "Lemon" the latter of which i can describe as more like that of a the ye-old "tripple shot" buff from Bullet hells which i'm no stranger to on kongregate and a bit of the touhou series. now.. this game can be described in a nutshell as what i will call a "bullet hell hybrid" now why hybrid? that batterry beter at the top of the screen is one justification for that as you getting knocked down doesn't mean life lost. it means PRECIOUS time is lost.. i put that in caps to emphasize that quite immensely, especially with the characters I was playing as.
there is more of an emphasis on mowing down enemy after enemy, the music helps the feel of the game, the better you do the better the music that plays, period. which for me tends to put a damn good smile on my face. The mechanics are quite"snow-bally" in that if your doing good you'll soon find yourself doing better but make a mistake or five rather and you'll have lost all momentum which can quite easilly be a serious pain trying to climb back up with your batterry at around half, which i cvan note it does feel like once the batterry goes red, it drains faster which while emphasizing the need to grab the batterry and re-charge the meter that does get frustrating at times and sometimes it's much easier to simply hit escape and restart the level then to try and pull the round back into a good position.
Now lets talk about the levels themselves, each level has a set "gimmick" to it be it turning off the lights, or flinging you accross the stage and turning the camera about alah, the transit level. each of  these levels are fun, intense, and easilly quite enjoyable after the first round of it where i find myself sutdying it, and then going at it again with calculation, and a little bit of luck and reaction time. now while that's all done and good, beside in the level select there is NO correlation between one level and the next besides maybe a matching theme of colors. you seem to drop down from one level to the next but you do not really feel that you are on a ship but you are exploring a "complex" if it was in space my best guess is this being some sort of station floating through space, not really a ship and certainly more based towards looks than function. which while being the largest nit-pick i have and any other complaints i have are usually found in the midst of thought, like the time you wish something was nerfed or buffed for "insert random event here" which looking at those i find them to be not worthy of mention as you have many ways you can go aboutn a situation. which leads me to the "bullet hell" of the game. the bosses!
This bit is hard to type down simply because i wish to avoid spoiling what story this game provides, which is all found in the interaction from your character to the bosses themselves so i'll stick to the first boss "embryo" which quite obviously by his looks is a mix of eggman and the crasy weapons guy.. you know the one guy who has an absolute love for weapons explosions and anything involving trying to use them to get you. never heard of him? well... damn.. nevermind then. now as you begin he has a seperate set of dialog for each character, and quite good interactions between you and the boss for me coral straight out called embryo a punching bag, which i found hillarious at the time. now the boss plays out with as many sections as his health bar has, with a surprise nearing the end of the fight. for example embryo cowers a little bit and begins throwing absolutely EVERYTHING he has at you. i'm not joking either on that one it's like a test "lets see if you actually can deal with all of this aat once" which is quite rewarding and at the end of it leads to some damn good clutch moments with bosses, with the third boss i killed him/it/her (let you geuss or you can buy it to find that out) i found myself with 0 batterry and killing the boss right as he killed me which was definitely one of those ... uhh... what do people say? "omg yeessssss" or something along a sigh of releif comes to mind. i myself can't do them justice, all the elements of the boss are found in previous levels and each boss acts as a test before you can go to the next set of levels which isw how it should be.
personally i find this game to be stupidly good for just going nuts and having a whale of a time. if you got the spare cash, go right on and grab it. no don't go off to another game to look at. trust me with what little impressions i have with you, and grab, the, GAME! it's worth the time and i personally had and will continue to have a damn good time playing it. also if you aren't conviced... grab the god-damned demo... by god man the demo is FREE! if you need a slice of gameplay grab the damned thing!

Assault Android Cactus caught me by surprise as a very competent arena shooter that is loads of fun.
If you've ever played Smash TV from back in the day, this game will feel immediately familiar to you. After selecting your android of choice, you enter a room of varying design with hazards and mobs of robots. Each character has two weapons: a primary which can be leveled, and a powerful limited use secondary that has a cooldown period. The eight playable characters (half of which are unlocked with gameplay progression) each offer a unique play style that can be vastly different from one android to the next. For example, Shiitake uses a high damage, low rate of fire railgun that is devastating  to lines of enemies, while Lemon uses a spread gun to evenly dish out firepower in wide area.
There are lots of elements to keep the game interesting. Right off the bat, you'll notice that score is a big part of replayability. In its current form, you'll spend a good chunk of time chasing those better score rankings and leaderboard positions. When you achieve S rank and the coveted S+ rank scores, you feel like you really earned it along with a sense of pride. The level design throws specific challegnes at you (like evading a white-hot torch as it spins) while you dispatch hordes of robots that range from missile launchers to quadrapedal melee brawlers to spectral teleporters with beam weapons. As you might expect, the later levels are very difficult. The number of enemies that can effectively one-shot you grows in number. Not to worry though, as pickups like Firepower, Acclerate, and Shutdown help you keep the playing field level. On top of all those challenges, you have to keep an eye on your battery meter. Without regular recharge pickups, you will fail the level if you let it run out.
Apart from the great story mode maps is a survival mode called Infinity Drive. Here, the environment changes on the fly in a fixed-size arena as you face an endless waves of enemies.  A Boss Rush mode is also offered to let you practice against each of the game's tough bosses. Local Co-op is there, but I am really pining for some Online Co-op. Unfortunately, that's not in the cards as the dev has admitted that due to technical limitations and a small team, it won't be happening.
The controls are tight whether you go with mouse/keyboard or a gamepad and both options are comfortable to use. Your android choice may affect which control style you go with, as some characters require more precise aim than others.
In summary, for an EAG this is far from your run of the mill broken beta release. It has a lot of polish, plenty of content to enjoy, and the communication from a passionate developer shows what EA can and should be. Each update brings more fixes and even more shine and shimmer to an already glowing product. It's an easy recommendation for fans of twin-stick shooters and old arcade games. I realize I've been raving about this game the whole time, but I really can't find a lot of fault with it. Even at this stage, bugs are rare and the ones that are found (and well documented) get addressed quickly. If you've been sitting on the fence about it, I can assure you it's worth every bit of the asking price.

Note: I did not try to play the game with the keyboard.  This "review" is based on my gameplay impressions using a 360 pad.
Quick facts:
-------------
Game version at the time of this review: 10.6
My Playtime (for a single run through): about 4 hours
Bought the game because of the demo.
I was on the fence about this one for a while for whatever reason.  If you're not sure if you want to buy it, try the demo.  If you enjoy the demo, buy the game.  It's great.  Certainly worth the price, discount or not.
ACC has a very "arcade-y" style feel going on.  If AAC was actually an arcade game, I can tell that it would be rather hard on my wallet.  It's a hard game to put down.
It's super fast with tons of enemies and tons of bullets on-screen.  Seriously glorious chaotic fun.  Difficulty and chaos increase exponentially the further you get into the game.  The bosses are well designed and borrow elements of Bullet-hell type shmups.  Transforming levels and the battery mechanic do a great job of keeping you on your toes.  It's rather satisfying once you find your best character and dance your way across a level racking up that massive 200+ Hit combo and never getting downed once.  Enemy mechanics do not feel cheap.  Any time I felt frustrated, it was over my own lack of skill.
The art-style is very colorful, and looks great.  It also never gets in the way or becomes overly busy.  I do not recall every losing track of my character because of all the chaos onscreen.
I read somewhere that someone compared this game to Smash TV and they were right in making that comparison.  AAC does remind me of that game.
Game did not crash once, no frame-drops or other bugs. Cranked the settings up to max and it still runs like a dream.
Overall very impressive for an Early Access title.  Very much looking forward to more content and release day.
I wish I had someone to play coop with if for no other reason than to see how crazy it gets with more players.

Assault Android Cactus is one of my favorite games on Steam. It's over the top, it's adorable, and it knows how to keep it's audience playing. The satisfaction that comes from pulling off a satisfying rank is always well emphasized- from the music letting you know you're on a roll, to your character's voice exclaiming how unstoppable she is, to your weapon kicking into high gear and unleashing a flurry of projectiles. This is a fun game, with a charming cast of characters and enough interesting dialogue to keep you invested. The bosses are pretty OP, so if you want that S+ rank for every level, you have your work cut out for you. This is a lot of fun.

Are you tired of empty promises? Vague planes of what will be in the game and what will not? Developers who have very little communication with their community? All the stuff that happens one Early Access? Well then, take a look at Assault Android Cactus! There's a clear goal of what they want to be in the game at launch and how much is in it at the time you're buying it, right there on the store page! A lesson to the majority of developers that put their game out there on Early Access
But what about the game itself? Is it any good? The short answer is: Yes.
The long answer is the amount of time you'll find that you sink into the game. With four characters to boot and another one unlocked with every boss leaves us at 8 in total. All of them unique in their own way. They all have a primary and a secondary weapon which drastically changes the way they are played.
There's a whole heap of different enemies for you to blast to bits and rack up the points in a total of 25 planned levels! 23 of them available as of the time of writing this. And in addition to that you have Boss Rush and Infinity Drive game modes. The latter of which might need a bit of explaining, It's basically a wave survival mode.
So you're having a good time blasting enemies and all that, and then you suddenly get your first S+ rating. Meaning that you got through a level with an unbroken chain of kills. Nailing the level perfectly. And this is where your dark descent begins. This high is something you'll keep chasing, again and again on each of the levels, with your ranking going higher and higher on the global leaderboards.
The music and sound design is fantastic and fits the game like a glove. Not much more to say about that really.
So, why should you buy this game? Well, all the reasons above really. You'll be supporting a hard working team that, as a previous review stated, "short of the developers being visited by aliens and having their brains replaced with cottage cheese and pineapple chunks - this should be an easy recommendation, and a big thumbs up from me."
..At least do try the Demo. The first one is always free, remember?

The ideal quality MMO. While it's not exactly the most affordable (being not free to play), you gain a lot in quality by investing your time and money into it. Many things you'll have to pay for in other free to play games (changing appearance, for example) are done strictly using in-game currency.
Changing classes is very easy as well. You do not have to make multiple characters to experience every class - you can switch at will. Each has its own separate leveling track, ensuring you don't get to max level for all classes in the blink of an eye.
The microtransactions that are present are entirely cosmetic and optional, perhaps the sole exception being faster mounts. However, at level 20, every player gets a chocobo mount that can also serve in combat. Furthermore, you buy these items using actual money - there is no need to buy a premium currency.
The quests that are available are fairly standard - most of them being "fetch, flay, or fedex" quests. However, the "flay" quests rarely ask for more than six enemies killed, and items that do require monster-specific drops have (as far as I can tell) a 100% drop rate, ensuring players don't get hung up on farming a specific enemy waiting for that one quest-related item to drop for them. The quests are nothing groundbreaking (unlike, for example, the quests in The Secret World), but good writing and low requirements ensure they don't overstay their welcome.
This is a premium, high-quality MMO. This is the difference between a gourmet burger and a Big Mac. FF14 asks a lot, but gives a lot. While not recommended for those on a budget, if you have the coin and the time and are in the market for an MMO, here it is.

Okay! Here is an updated review after launch.
As you may have seen in my Pre-Release review...I was, UNFOND of this game to say the least.
After release, I am even moreso unfond of it.
In fact, I am willing to go out on a limb and say I absolutely hate this game. And that is REALLY saying something.
But I hate it for multiple reasons, and I do not use the word hate lightly.
First and foremost, the game let me down. From it's conception, it looked like we had finally found our successor to Close Combat. I was thrilled, I was ready!
My gaming experience started in 1997 with one of the best games I have ever owned, Close Combat, Bridge too Far. It was the first game I ever became addicted to. I saved up allowence to get a CD drive for my old computer just to play it. I installed it on every computer at every house I was sent to over the Summer.
I know there are some reviews out there, that are saying this game indeed, is the new Close Combat.
Let me say flat out, no, no it is not. It is nothing like Close Combat. The scale of the game alone makes that impossible. But looking past even that, nothing about this game is mechanically similar to Close Combat. Whereas Close Combat was and is a game of very deep strategic thought, and a slower paced, thinking man's game. This game is either a hollow shell trying to trick people into thinking it is that, or a very casual light version of that, depending on how you decide to look at it.
While Close Combat (And other games, like Combat Mission and Graviteam Tactics), have a very complex model for everything from Morale, to fire effectiveness, to armour penetration, Steel Division takes those concepts and places arbitrary numbers to them. Steel Division is a game that is trying to APPEAR deep, but is infact very shallow.
And like a misleading hotel swimming pool, if you dive in head first expecting depth, you are likely going to be in pain.
In fact, this game IS  the misleading hotel swimming pool of Strategy Games.
You know what I mean, when you go to a hotel, and you see the pool and it looks lovely, but you get into it and it's too shallow and it has this goofy chemical smell that burns your nose? And when you are done you feel like it was a waste of time to go to the pool and now you have to walk back to your room all wet and crap?
This game is that, only the goofy chemical that burns your nose is the horrible community that burns your will to live.
So let's get these thoughts in order shall we?
First lets address the "Morale" Mechanic:
The Morale Mechanic was the thing that turned me on to this game, and gave me the feeling we were looking at another Close Combat! But boy is it a mess.
All the Morale Mechanic does in this game, is make it far too easy to stop an attack. And really, it turns the game into a stalemate of people playing Rock Paper Scissors with support weapons.
Units have two stages of "Morale", Pinned and Falling back.  There is a meter at the top of each unit that fills up at various rates of speed determined by...I don't know...the Eugen Gods, and once it fills up, the unit becomes pinned and absolutely useless. The only option to fix this is to fall the unit back, and once you select this order, the pinned unit will then run like a chicken with it's head cut off, oblivious to danger, towards the enemy, away from the enemy, through open fields, through forests....Eugen seems to have confused "Fall Back" with "Rout Blindly!" OH! And my favourite part, if a unit becomes pinned down, and another unit approachs it, they will surrended.
This leads to hilarious exploits in the morale system, where you can pin down an enemy with an off map artillery strike, and then bee-line a small vehicle like a jeep, through the middle of the AOE, and capture all the squads pinned down by the artillery. I think my personal record is capturing about 4 full squads of German infantry with one M20 Command car, and this also applies to tanks...meaning, a tank that is "Falling Back", can be captured by a 2 man infantry squad.
And when I say the morale bar fills up at a rate of speed determined by the "Eugen Gods" I mean, I have no idea how they figure what effects morale at what rate. Weapons that can't damage tanks, make them lose their freaking minds, artillery hitting in the same zip code as your infantry makes them all go to ground and become useless. But at the same time, you can watch a  plane fly through flak so thick you can walk on it, drop it's bombs, and happily skip away laughing at you as it ♥♥♥♥♥ on your dreams.
Which would be okay I guess, if the game  wasn't built around offense....
The game itself revolves around a front line system that must be "Pushed" to gain points. Now add this game mode, with a morale system where it is possible to "Stun Lock" enemy units like some bad MOBA, and you have the general frustration with Steel Division.
The next problem is the Balance:
I don't even want to get too far into this one, other than to say, Eugen cannot do Balance. They have never been able to. The Balance here is no better than Wargame, in fact it might be worse.
A game based in Normandy, needs Asymetrical Balance, but Eugen cannot fathom that, due to the fact that they can't even pose off "SYMETRICAL" balance.
The developers tout "Historical Accuracy", but when you get into a battle and realize the German's are holding bombing the hell out of you from the skies over Normandy, while your P-51's flail away helplessly at the hordes of German aircraft, you will start to wonder just what version of history Eugen get's it's information from.
This comes to the third problem...the air game itself.
Now one would think that aircraft would handle something like vehicles? Right? I mean, they are planes and all, they would likely take damage, have fuel leaks, have engines blow out, have control cables snap and all? I mean, in Wagame their engines flamed out, or they lost radar, and this, that and the other, so here, they should be just as fragile right?
Wrong! Airplanes have the same mechanics as infantry squads! Because of course they do!
This means that to counter planes, you are spending most of the time trying to break their "Morale", to get them to "Fall Back" hopefully before their bombs kill you.
So lets take a look and put some numbers together. An average ground attack plane takes about 140 requisition points. The average AA Gun costs about 50 points. Now, it will likely take you 4 or 5 AA guns shooting at that plane to "Stun" it.
So already, you are needing about 200 points just to STUN the 140 point aircraft. But now lets add the need to DESTROY the plane, you will need your own 140 point fighter to do that! Because the AA Guns you purchased only damage the planes morale! So you have about 340 points invested into stopping a 140 point plane....and that's just to stop ONE! Compound this with each enemy plane, and you have the pants ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ frustration of SD.

Paradox tired of its niche status and wants to be major publisher specializing in strategies. All kind of strategies. They started with the powerful collaboration and then continue with destroying region prices on their games, like most of the big boys do. Yeah, let's make it about politics. It’s not like bullying the way through their loyal community is the new tactic for Paradox. Crazy DLC politic is the great example. But what’s more important is what let them do anything they want and it’s their card of uniqueness. You won’t find any alternatives to paradox games.  But you won’t find anything like Eugene’s  game either, that’s why SD might be so important to paradox.
Eugene delivered solid gameplay with an uncanny similarity to their Wargame Series. The main feature is the frontline which moves with the units. Neat idea on the surface turns out to be more of a gimmick. Even so, Eugene says that’s the main part of gameplay, in the end, it didn’t really change it, but make it more noob-friendly. And this is the main theme of SD. Wargame series are well known for its total unfriendliness toward new players, the game doesn’t have a proper tutorial, it got 2000+ units you better learn (how they perform and even looks).  So they decide to cut the corners. Now we got 400 units, fewer stats for each unit, "autodeckcreator", we lost few tactics; like helicopter rush (no one would miss it, but still helicopters gave more tactical choices), we cannot get around and strike opponent to the back (because frontline shows there we got units, except recon infantry). Tactical choices reduced to constant push-build defense line-push/retreat.  Maps became wider and units became sooo much slower, which is make sense but still might be frustrating. People who wished the infantry would be the kings of the Steal division (spoiler alert it doesn’t) would find themselves disappointed. Roles didn’t switch, dynamic didn’t change drastically, artillery became more powerful than ever. Even new stress system feels just like a light touch.
Paradox is… that game is still semi-realistic and really complex for the newcomers, while wargame veterans will get “less of the same”. I think I appreciate the gentle approach, no one want’s to learn everything from the scratch, but at the same time, I can’t find anything that justifies the transfer from Red Dragon to Steel Division. Surprisingly enough SD doesn’t look as good as you might expect, models look shabbier than their brothers from Wargame DLCs. But animation became smoother; infantry doesn’t slide through the hills like they used to do.  Anyway, I doubt you would notice it during the game, cause all you need to see is pictograms of your units on the whole wide map.  The best new thing is the circle which allows you see how much vision each point on the map will give to you units, that’s what Red Dragon surely missed.
Steal division doesn’t feel like a step back, more like “confident mudding-through”.

Starts off sweet but quickly becomes sour.
As far as abandon titles go, this one seems like it is close to being complete. However, two big elements are missing.
First, there is gameplay balance. The game starts off feeling like you can do anything in it, if you just put the time and effort into it. And for the first 20 or 30 minutes this feels true.  You expand your base, explore ships, and manage your people to get the most out of them.  But then the raiders, and meteor strikes happen. And this is where the missing gameplay balance is most obvious.  Negative events are important to any game, if things were always good, than there wouldn't be any challenge. But the speed, and frequency of the negative events needs to be balance out against what the play can and cannot do, so that they can overcome them, and not just suffer.  I found that during the few games that I played, that I would get close to having a decent base going, only to have ruin by constant attacks, to the point where I was losing a lot more people than I was generating. Which resulted in me having a large empty base that I had no chance of defending or using.
The second element is content. There isn't much in this game...
Overall, this is not a game that you should spend money or time in.

King of Fighters 13 was my first ever fighting game I owned in life. I have no controller/stick, just a plain old keyboard.
After 30+ hours it has been quite a trip learning myself this game from scratch using a keyboard.
Why did I stay? Because the game is awesome and here is why:
First of all, the game is stylish and colourful, the aesthetic is nice yet not over the top. The animations are fluid as you'd expect from a decent 2D fighter, and effects are beautiful.
Character design is different from the usual designs. Some sprites have their flaws (yuri's big head) (shen's long neck) but these make all characters feel unique except for Ralph and Clark who share the same legs.
Different body types, different colours and PLENTY of colours to choose from to customize your favorite characters.
The gameplay is difficult, in-depht and there is always something to learn.
Pulling off the moves, combos and all these CANCELS CAN GET SO HARD.
One neat feature of this game is the Hyperdrive, allowing you to cancel special moves into others or even bigger moves, allowing you to extend an already awesome combo. Half a bar allows for one ''Drive'' or ''Super'' cancel.
A full bar means you can go into HD mode and just unleash unlimited cancels for a short amount of time.
The game in general is fast and requires quick-thinking with plenty of room for punishments.
With all these features added the game becomes quite execuction heavy the more skilled you become.
As I said, there is always something learn. The roster is diverse with 30+ characters each with their own set of moves and possible combos. For the characters you want to master you can always sharpen your skills, making sure you don't drop the combo and just unleash hell whenever you desire.
As for my negatives:
-The netcode. It's good, but only when you find someone close-by to fight with. Getting a friend to play this with you is recommended. In random matches, try to stick to either a 3-latency or 4-latency.
- A minor complaint would be that the pixels showing themselves. Mind that this is a game that got released in 2011. You might or might not be ticked off by this.
- If you own a HDD that can hold more than 1 tb, you're going to have some technical issues if you install it on that HDD.
To avoid them, try installing the game on a cheap let's say... 256 GB drive.
Thanks for reading my review :)
It's called the KING of fighters for a reason.

Assault Android Cactus is a very simple game that demonstrates just how important good execution is in game development.
This is a twin stick shooter with multiple characters that have two weapons (one upgrade-able spammed primary, another more powerful attack on short cooldown).  The health-death mechanic is bit different because health loss costs you score/weapon level and you only really 'die' by running out of time limit.
The levels work mostly by changing the terrain on the fly rather than having you move towards something.  So instead of more traditional 'scroll left' type of map, think of an arena where walls and grounds are changing every now and then.
The enemy variations are pretty good IMO.  You got your standard slow dumb cannon fodders to bigger mooks with varying tactics (some shoots seekers at you, some ground pound for shockwave, etc.), swarmers to turrets  to verticle missile launching robot dogs, it's got healthy variety in both design and function.
So all of this probably reads rather conservative in terms of mechanics and yes, you probably have seen all of these bits and pieces before but you probably haven't seen them to this degree of polish.  Dare I say it, this game plays like indie take on twinstick shooter with the famous "Blizzard polish".  Fans of the genre would be amiss to not have this in their library, and for new comers this game is really good introduction to the genre.

This is the best engineering/resource management/factory planning game I have ever seen. Seriously.
Factorio is a super complex basebuilder that has you automating almost everything there is to do with conveyor belts, robotic arms, other machines, FLYING ROBOTS, trains, and for the really hardcore players, computers. If you like big, complicated logistics and engineering problems then this is the game for you.
Okay, so Factorio is super cool, complicated, and is worth its money. BUT it still has some problems with real-world physics and especially some parts of the newly minted nuclear dynamics. For instance:
Ore Processing
Iron and copper ore can basically be thrown on a pile of hot coals in a special building and get refined into pure, shiny, malleable plate form. Let's overlook the obvious here, that this doesn't really happen in the real world. Now, what this process is called in the real world is reduction smelting. This works for most types of ore, but isn't perfect for all of them, like aluminum which has to get electrolyzed into polycrystalline sapphire before it can be reduced. It just really irks me that you can just throw every single flippin' ore (of which there are only two) into a strategically built pile of rocks that can ignite coal spontaneously and expect to get a 100% pure, clean, and FLAT piece of corresponding metal. Maybe in the future they can add more ores and processing techniques that work for certain ones and NOT EVERYTHING. Electrical smelting does make sense though, in the lighter sense of the word in that you CAN melt ores into molten metal and get rid of the gas that's stuck in there and then you can reharden them in a cast of some sort into a more or less flat plate of semi-pure metal. However, if the ore is only made out of metals (let's say naturally occuring bronze), then this wouldn't work. You would get two types of molten metal floating on top of each other, and they would probably reharden into one bronze plate with highly variant composition throughout, with highly coppery bronze on the bottom and highly stannic (tinny) bronze on the top. Of course, the ores in Factorio are simply Copper oxides and Iron oxides. Nobody really knows or can know what exactly the Uranium ore is made of. Point is, ores are too simplistic and processing is too, even if it works really nicely and falls in line with most other types of ore processing in other games.
Uranium Processing
Unlike every other ore you need sulfuric acid pumped into your miner to mine it. That's a nice touch, and it adds a dynamic that I think would be good to add to other materials; sometimes, you can't just hit it with your bare hands and get some with a little patience. Another unique thing about Uranium ore is that you can't actually smelt it into plates, which is both really contrary to Factorio trends and also doesn't jive very well with the real world. in the real world, we take Uranium ore and refine it into Uranium hexafluoride, which is a vile, dangerous, and toxic liquid that is pretty similar to sulfuric acid as in the game. Then it gets centrifuged into 3.5-5% U-235 enriched nuclear fuel, gets cast into pretty little ceramic pellets, amd then thrown into a nuclear power plant. This process generates a lot of depleted Uranium, which goes off to make tank penetrators and other really weird niche uses. The fuel is put into the reactor, and when enough of the fuel gets turned into *not* Uranium they pull it out and centrifuge it again. This is called reprocessing. From this process we get some Plutonium, some Americium, some Neptunium, and a bunch of other cool radioactive elements like that. Plutonium primarily gets reprocessed back into nuclear fuel in what is called MOX fuel, where it can be put with depleted uranium and have a chance to 'breed' it into U-235 which can be used to generate energy in the reactor. Then, when this wears out it gets reprocessed again, and again, and again until we run out of nuclear material, which is highly unlikely. So. Where's the Plutonium? Plutonium is an essential part of the life cycle of nuclear fuel. No, really, it's not just because I want the other cool radioactive element. The other byproducts could probably just get grouped in with Plutonium, honestly. But seriously, Mixed OXide fuel is a major source of energy, and while it's kinda weird you need it if you want to make an sort of energetic return from nuclear fuel processing.
MOAR ELEMENTS & STUFF
It is really weird to play such an advanced tech game with only three (Four?) metals. Iron is a necessity. Copper makes sense. Uranium is cool. Coal is basically carbon. What the heck is stone? And then I guess steel is a nice progression from Iron (It's really WAY too expensive, since steel is basically just iron with some ash and a couple more cool elements smattered in there). But what about tin? Bronze (I know it's an alloy but it's so well known)? Silicon? Gold? Silver maybe? I mean, it's unreasonable to say that you can just walk around with three and a half tons of copper and iron and be able to make the whole first half of Factorio. And then electronic circuits... ugh. Basic ones make sense for their recipe. Don't really understand how you can make a directional circuit with some copper ribbon and slab of iron, but the recipe makes sense for some reason. Advanced circuits are a little cooler but make less sense since plastic does not conduct electricity at all and I would assume advanced circuits are using semiconductors. Processors make very little sense because of this. I mean, everything in the recipe makes sense and should be there, but it's missing (you guessed it) SILICON. Processors only actually work with semiconductors. You can't simply engrave your way out of that problem, even with sulfuric acid. However, this problem can be easily remedied by making 'stone' into 'silicate', which is the fancy scientific name for most of what you pick up on the ground. Silicates can be reduced into pure silicon, and then this silicon can be further pruified into varying degrees determined by tech level and the amount of energy you can expend to centrifuging it. Purer silicon makes better and potentially smaller semiconductors, which can go into making processors and advanced circuits. What about bronze? Bronze is honestly a bit superfluous in Factorio what with steel, but it still has a really nice color. Gold would make a cool endgame resource that you use to just embellish your base with the opulence it deserves, or, if you actually want practicality, better circuits. Other elements could definitely find a warm home in Factorio. Silver is a fantastic conductor if they ever want to add in limited transfer rates to power conduits. Tungsten is literally the toughest metal. Cesium explodes very violently and impressively with water, and would probably have the same effect on aliens. Molybdenum, manganese, zirconium, vanadium, and nickel are all used in iron alloys to make steel. Germanium is a substiute for silicon if centrifuges are too hard. The point is, there are about 88 practically usable elements on the periodic table. Not asking the Factorio devs to put praseodymium and and dysprosium in there, but just put some neat chemicals in there. Really, you guys are working your butts off for this game and we are all so thankful for it. The whole point of this review was to basically inform you about some of the stuff in the game that could be improved. Everything that wasn't mentioned is fine, I was just trying to list and talk about some of the things about Factorio that I think should be fixed, or optimized, or whatever. The factory and engineering aspect is incredible. It's perfect. It's just... 70 million copper plates and 190 million iron plates look pretty barren compared to the periodic table, and Uranium refining doesn't work quite like that. Otherwise, keep up the good work. Loving the experimental! 1 last thing. Plz chge uzd ful cel to depleted.

This game is the dream child of an engineer and a programmer.  The automation is beautiful and absolutely instrumental - you quite literally can't win by crafting everything in your inventory.
Tips I've learned the hard way:
Iron is your best friend, get as much of it as possible, then double that amount.  If you have less than three chests of iron plates at any time after achieving automation, you're doing it wrong.
After you get a working knowledge of the game, once you find where you want to begin, make sure to pause the game and plan everything out via the map.  It'll take a long time, but not having to undo your stuff to expand later is brilliant.
Make a main bus.  Use long-handled inserters and fast inserters to input/output your resources to an open area for when you continue automating later.
As soon as you can, get fast conveyors and automate construction of them.
Once you get enough resources to build a steam generator, don't.  Find water near a source of coal, and make it auto-feed a line of boilers and a line of generators.
DO NOT NEGLECT TURRETS!  Early-game the biters aren't such a big deal, but after a while they start to go from cute little zerglings to ultralisks and smash through your base if you aren't prepaed.
The only real issue I've found is if you don't plan out where everything needs to go, you're screwed later on.  I'd also recommend adding a pollution cleaner-esque thing (which doesnt actually reverse or even stop the spread of pollution, it just sharply reduces it) because I'm about 4 hours into my map and I'm getting absolutely crushed by the bugs - I can't just kill them because they're big enough to crush me, and my base is decently protected but I can't leave it to settle elsewhere and my resources are nearly depleted.  Also, we need a way to "uncraft" things, so we can turn the useless burner stuff at the start back into materials instead of having them be inefficient or just sitting in a random chest.

The fusion of WW2 with the Wargame series that I've been waiting for since RUSE.
This game is exemplary. It's not a simulator, but it does very well when it comes to getting across the feel of WW2 combat in Normandy without the painful amounts of micro that sims require.
The addtion/adjustment of several gameplay mechanics such as a LOS tool, a better morale system, and command units to name a few makes Steel Division the best game Eugen has ever made in my opinion.
The deckbuilding system has been reworked, and the addition of the phase system means that combat flows natrually through Combat Recon, Skirmish, and Battle phases. The revamped conquest mode combined with the new frontline system is exemplary.
The maps are extremely well-made and detailed (based off of reconnaisance photos taken before and during the invasion) with plentiful variations in terrain.
Haven't had access to the campaigns yet as we're still in beta. Will update when the game releases.
TL;DR: If you enjoy WW2 rts's but don't like flat out sims, this game is exemplary. It's an excellent showcase of how combined arms and maneuver warfare worked at that time in history. Additionally, the game is only $40 for the baseline edition without additional visual content.

The new mechanics, the frontline and phases all really help with gameplay and immersion.
Finally, and possibly best of all, historical accuracy is spot on. German tanks are like other tanks, their infantry is mostly conscripts, their equipment from whatever they could scrounge. If you're expecting Company of Heroes level superhuman Germans in all their Nazi-apologetic glory, you will cry and whine about this game. The Sherman is not made of paper armor and watching a 17 pounder anti-tank gun rip through a Koingstiger is probably one of the best moments possible in the game.
Definately my favorite RTS, it has set the bar for the genre.

Best RTS I have played in a while. Very in-debt. I really love the historical theme with the different divisions that play out a lot like the separate armies of Wargame Red Dragon.
There is a certain uniqueness to the different divisions, they all have their balance of strength and weaknesses and are effected greatly by the amount and type of units you can bring onto the field.
Some have strong focus on infantry while limiting your armored or air force options later on and some divisions start out with nothing but a token force to delay the enemy until your economy picks up in the later phases of battle, where you use your superior units to break trough and claim back any lost ground. Just make sure you don't lose that expensive king tiger to an inexpensive and well hidden infantry squad with a bazooka!
You are not tied to a single kind of selection, meaning that you can customize your army group to great extend, like focus on an early rush with light vehicles and tanks, or setting up a defensive line with AT, artillery and machine guns.
Other tactics include a focus on holding a strong position like a bridgehead, forest or town with infantry and ambush anything that comes close while you safe up points for a mighty air force, landing surgical strikes to disrupt and slow down the enemy's advance.
These are but a few examples and I hope it demonstrates the feel of the gameplay.
There is a great amount of focus on strategic dept and combined arms in this game.
Line of sight and spotting are fundamental and even the heaviest armor will struggle if not supported by other troops. There is an important factor of warfare featured in this game and that is suppression. Inexperienced troops will panic when under fire by aircraft or artillery and sometimes and entire advance can be halted by a single artillery barrage.The use of firepower in this game is not only meant for destroying the enemy, but more often to to disrupt their combat effectiveness and drive them back.

Line of sight and stealth are vital. Ambush and shock are an integral part, as is momentum and supplies.
You need to plan deliberately and not get tunnel visioned to succeed in this game, since holding territory is so important you can not really allow any part of the map to be unguarded. An open flank will allow your opponent to simply put a few cheap units forward and capture precious ground unopposed, giving them an easy win on the strategic level, no matter how well you are winning tactically.
There are some issues with the game too right now.
It's a steep learning curve and some players experience instability and crashes.
Matches are pretty long, often up to 40 minutes. Gameplay can grow stagnant quickly, with neither side being able to push forward.
This makes the initial phase vital and an early setback may lose you the game, with nothing you can do to break out. Often times the only thing you need to do is push up early and then just hold ground, pushing trough a defense is very hard, especially in the early phases. Team games are great but can be super frustrating when players drop out and suddenly you have to focus on controlling a lot more units and ground. When someone disconnect in multiplayer another player may suddenly get a lot more units under his command, meaning a lot of extra micro management.
Once you are on the losing end you tend to lose more and more, and in a game with long rounds of 40 minutes or more this can feel pretty boring and frustrating.
Overall I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of RTS-Games with a focus on deliberate strategy opposed to quick reflexes and spamming hotkeys. The different divisions all feel unique and well represented. The battle phases and dynamic frontline is a good addition to the game. Keep in mind that early on your performance might not be the best since it takes a bit of a learning curve and the game still has some crash related stability issues with online play which I hope will be fixed soon.

Do you like classic rpgs? If the answer is yes then you must own this game!
Coming fresh off of Zeboyd Games smash hit Breath Of Death VII, I knew I was in for a great game. What I was unprepared for was that this game was more then great, it is magnificent! This has everything Breath Of Death has and improved upon it in every way possible.
You take control of Cthulhu, mankind's worst nightmare who lost all of his powers. How can he get them back? By doing heroic deeds for mankind! With a story like this you can only expect something epic and wacky at the same time and this is just what the developer is known for. Throughout your adventure you will laugh with hilarious jokes and scenarios that will keep you entertained and wanting more.
This game is high on humor but don't let that fool you to think this is a not so serious rpg. Beyond the story the developer has taken a major overhaul to the graphics compared to it's last game Breath Of Death VII. Instead of taking a 8bit graphic style it went full force with 16 bit and looks as good as Final Fantasy 3 and Chrono Trigger on SNES. Overall the graphics are detailed and much more dynamic then the last game. The music for Cthulhu is like Breath Of Death VII having a more cd quality sound then chip tunes it worked well. In fact too well! I must express that the music in this game is completely mind blowing!
The combat is much like classic Dragon Warrior on NES with more depth and very rewarding overall. Each turn the enemies grows stronger so you must think fast. At your disposal you have your standard attacks, magic attacks and tech attacks but you also a unique attack called unite. Using unite will team up with other party members for damage or helpful status effects. Upon defeating your enemies, you get your life refilled however your magic will refill slightly depending on how fast you finish the fight. You must manage your attacks and kill monsters efficiently or you could be in big trouble in later dungeons. As you level up you have the option to choose how your characters develop so if you want a more magic focused or combat focused character is completely up to you.
Zeboyd Games know how to make classic rpgs more up to date and it shows with this game. While this game has random battles, each dungeon zone has a limit of random battles and when you break this limit, you are free to explore. If you wish to grind further you have the option to do so in your main menu. Also in this menu you can travel to past towns at anytime and also save your game.
Unlike most rpgs, this game has replay value to keep you playing again and again. You have different difficulty levels so how you want to play the game is up to you. Upon completing the game you have harder difficulty levels and even more modes of play! You even have the option to play the game with director commentary and read about the thoughts the developer had in different key parts of the game. This alone not only makes the game worth it but worth beyond the value it sells for. This game is complete perfection and I highly recommend to any classic rpg gamer.

This game is awesome. It's quick, it's fun and you're going to replay levels to try to beat your best score. It's in early access, yes, but if the final product is anything like this, it's totally worth the price. I would like to see the graphics improved slightly (there doesn't seem to be any anti aliasing) and support for more widescreen and HD resolutions (like 1366x768) but it is an awesome game.
The price is a steal and the developers are onto something here. They understand gaming doesn't always have to be serious and we are in this to have fun. This game is fun, colourful and you unlock more characters as you go along. Each character comes with a standard and alternative weapon, but they're all different, which makes for interesting combinations in multiplayer. If you're unsure, there is a demo available, though I do believe you're getting more value than what they're asking for it.
As for the technical stuff, it is a top down shooter, which supports keyboard and mouse, or a gamepad. It has local co-op too so that's a plus if you have friends over. As I mentioned before, the graphics could do with a few tweaks, but it is by no means unattractive. The gameplay is fluid and you will be moving around the arena a lot while gunning down hordes of machines. There are powerups available, which also encourage you to keep moving. The music is upbeat and adds to the fast-paced atmosphere.
I'd give it a solid 8/10, with the hope that the final product will be as fun, or even more so.

If you don't know, let me start with giving this tiny piece of information: Sleeping Dogs was actually supposed to be the third installment in the True Crime franchise, called "True Crime: Hong Kong". Although I tried so hard to love True Crime, I eventually realized that it's not my cup of tea. It was actually good for them to scrap this idea off because Sleeping Dogs feels like another game on its own, surpassing True Crime in every possible way, basically including an impressive story and diversive gameplay.
You step in the shoes of Wei Shen, an undercover HKPD detective who is tasked with infiltrating and bringing down Sun On Yee - a very powerful Triad organization reigning in Hong Kong. To admit, the story has some easily predictable twists, but the story still comes out as one of the strongest suits of this game. This cut-throat, dog-eat-dog story has a satisfying finale, but something about the ending still seems cheesy to me: SPOILER ALERT!
Although they share the same formula, describing Sleeping Dogs as a "straight GTA rip-off" is not fair at all. The atmosphere and open world created for Sleeping Dogs is astonishing and the developers at least tried to do everything they could to make sure that Sleeping Dogs is distinguishable from GTA and its clones. Let's start by hand-to-hand combat. You'll be busier with your fists than you'll be with your trigger finger because hand-to-hand combat is the main core of this game. Hand-to-hand combat already feels unique even by the beginning of the game, and you can improve the experience more by unlocking new moves (like leg breaking, arm breaking, stun moves, combo strikes) by getting Triad XP or going to the martial arts club. Gun fighting is way less emphasized compared to hand-to-hand fighting, so it's not the best selling point of this game but it is still fun though (Vault Shoot, everybody).
Speaking of Triad XP, the missions reward you with Triad and Cop XP which give you some special perks for leveling up. Both Cop and Face XP (which is efficient in a lot of ways, for instance buying new clothes and vehicles) are easy to level up but Triad XP is a little bit troubling because once you finish the main story, there's very little to do for leveling it up (there are few side quests that can boost your Triad XP, so you generally end up replaying the missions for getting the max Triad level).
The game may not be that rich in terms of side quests, but they still manage to keep you busy for a long time: Going for 100% completion takes about 48 hours, which is noticably fair. The side quests include street racing, debt collecting, stealing cars, hi-jacking security vans, doing favors (which kind of works like GTA IV's Random Encounters, but shallow in context). Praying at health shrines boosts your health bar, and opening lockboxes sometimes rewards you with unique clothes. Oh, and you can also bust drug dealers as a free-time activity which works like this: First, you clear a street corner off the thugs, then you hack the camera. After that, you use your survelliance system to identify to drug dealer and command your fellow officers to arrest him. Busting drug dealers was probably my top favourite side quest.
Definitive Edition comes with two distinctive story DLCs, namely A Nightmare in North Point and Year of the Snake - they add approximately six more hours of gameplay. To be honest, A Nightmare in North Point becomes pretty boring after the first 15-30 minutes because the game is lacking in extra content and it's just about kicking ghost and demon butts. Both DLCs do not live up to the glory of Vanilla Sleeping Dogs, but Year of the Snake is the better one. In Year of the Snake, you control Wei as a beat cop going after a crazy cult in the main campaign, and making patrol shifts as side quests. It also enables you to handcuff and tazer enemies when fighting them.
The game has some few issues regarding the grappling/interacting button like:
- The grappling button "E" doesn't work fine for me, switching it to mouse wheel did the trick though.
- For some reason, I can't interact with street vendors to buy food or clothes. Getting away from them or starting a fight can work. If not, reload the game.
- Wei sometimes refuses to get in vehicles because of the same reason. The solution is the same as above.
The real question is "Should there be a Sleeping Dogs 2?". Absolutely. Sleeping Dogs has proven to be successful, interesting and innovative enough to deserve a second game. However, I think they should give Wei Shen a break here. As much as Wei is a great protagonist, going too hard on him would be "watering him down". I know that one of the distinctive features of Sleeping Dogs is that it heavily feeds on Chinese/Far East culture, but I also see good potential otherwise. What about a game set in 70's Boston focusing on Irish Mob? Or a Donnie Brasco-esque game with Italian Mob theme? An undercover cop cracking down on French Connection maybe? I think they're good enough to put in consideration and work.

Steel Division is set as you would expect, in Normandy during 1944.  Units for the most part, represent what was deployed and in existance during that part of the war.  If you liked Wargame then you should like Steel Division as most of the mechanics came over from there.  Additionally, other things have been added for improvement, like the sight system that lets you see what your unit can see.
For those that don't know what Wargame is about, then I will explain Steel Division a bit.  There is absolutely no base building or economy to manage outside of points that you use  and accumulate to bring in more units from off of the map.  You use cover to hide and get better defending positions, scouts to see, and use a combination of units to get the job done.  Units can panic and get pinned or fall back on their own, units are generally smart enough to fire on their own if you leave them be and need to go tend to other duties on the map.
Other aspects of the game, like utilizing combined arms is extremely important.  He who spams loses.  If you try to send infantry against medium tanks without some sort of anti-armor capability you are in for a short ride.  Artillery, air force to include bombing, interceptors, anti tank strikes, scouting, and high caliber guns for soft targets are all part of the game.  Using supply trucks to keep your units supplied with ammo is critical, without them, you are essentially sending in soldiers to fist fight against guns and you know how that is going to end up.
The graphics, controls, sounds, interface, all of it is well thought out and designed.  Markers to indicate what you want to do are available, sich as attack, defend, etc.  Additionally, You choose your own units for your army.  You build a deck of cards which consists of units.  These units all have a varying set of capabilities for different situations.  They have statistics that need to be taken into account such as range, armor penetration, high explosive capability, ammo count, speed, optics, armor, the list goes on.  This is not a comapny of heroes game where you send things in and if it gets lost, then make more.  What you bring to battle is it, you call stuff in as you can and as you need to.  Unit preservation is paramount and using veteran units and command units soup up your chances of survival and winning.
The goals to win are either conquest in taking map control or destruction where you must get a certain amount of points through kills to win.  Destruction may seem tempting but offers little reward for taking territory.  It is far better to take territory and think about how to win versus unloading everything and hoping for the best.  In the future, I hope there are expansions that add to the game.  Things like an Eastern front expansion and Asian front would be a welcome enhancement.  As of now, there is enough here to satisfy a person and keep them busy for a long time.
One final note, if you are a wargame player, don't expect the level of intricacy with the units.  There is far less to take into consideration.  That isn't to say its dumbed down, but instead of having 500 different units of the same thing with slightly different stats, you now only have a handful.

Easily one of my top 10 favorite video games of all time. The story is great despite how short and compact it is (you can easily beat this game in a day).  But what really takes this game to the next level are the atmosphere and soundtrack. They are breathtaking. Get the highest quality headphones you can find, crank up the volume, and lose yourself in this creative and immersive game.

If you're familiar with their other game, Bastion, then you have a good idea of what to expect.
The game begins with the female main character, Red, pulling the sword named Transistor out of someone who has just been killed.  The rest of the game is essentially her seeking answers and battling with the fallout of that individual's death in this really unique and original world they've created.
The game is extremely polished.  Like Bastion, they pair the visuals, music, and narration perfectly.  The game is absolutely dripping with style and attention to detail.  The combat system is really solid (and pretty challenging) as well.  You have four main abilities, or functions, that can be active at one time.  Each function you gain in the game contains the essence of a fallen individual of the city, whose lore you can read about once you possess it.  Each function has a main, secondary, and passive property.  Each one also requires a certain amount of memory, so which abilities you can run at the same time will depend on how much you have invested in increasing your max memory capacity.  The combat can be performed in real time or you can execute the turn() function and plan your moves ahead like a turn based game.  It's highly customizeable, albeit a little overwhelming at first (there is no tutorial but you do run have occasional access to a practice zone throughout).  I completed the playthrough without unlocking all of the passives or secondaries.  I guess that is supposed to draw you towards playing it again.
My complaint is that the game is so compact.  It took me about 5 hours to complete.  I guess I played with minimum limiters (kind of like talents you pick to make certain aspects of the game more difficult in return for bonus xp), but if you need to have a multitude of these limiters to stretch out the experience of the game, then maybe somethings wrong.  Additionally, there are only a handful of enemy types (they get progressively more difficult as you advance in the game).  This leads to the combat getting a little repetitive in some combat filled areas.
The game is very unique and well made, and I would absolutely recommend it.  However the $20 price-tag seems to have been made with the notion that the buyer would do multiple playthroughs.  I'd pick it up on sale instead.

Okay, so I loved Bastion, but I've been bitten before, assuming another game by the same studio would be good so I had jammed this on my wishlist but never quite gotten around to getting it.
Got given it as a New Year's gift (tyty!) and started it up rather nervously...
...Immediately captivated.
It is beautiful. It's also (despite the similar viewpoint) not Bastion, and part of me really feels for them because there were always going to be comparisons drawn rather than letting the game stand entirely on its own two feet.
The combat is quite unique (at least to me) as a mix between real time action and phases where you effectively pause time and then carefully plan out your next few moves. The skills system is... hmm... it's a really nice idea. Every skill can be used as an active skill, a passive skill or a modifier for another skill and this offers myriad ways to combine them. The game then encourages you try different things as using the skills in different ways unlocks more information. Screw up and get hit too much and one of your skills will burn out and you'll probably want to try using something else while you progress enough for it to repair.
In practice though the interface was clunky, there was no way to easily save/load builds and the sheer amount of choice available was either overwhelming or (later on especially) you tended towards specific combinations and just settled into a little rut there. I think if the interface had been better there it might have encouraged more flexibility.
The story is lovely and poignant, albeit a little short. Many of the details are only available if you explore or play with your skills to unlock more information and some areas of the story are deliberately vague, but it all makes sense (whether you delve or not) by the end. I felt it worked very well.
You pause after every fight - literally everything stops and a board pops up while you gain the exp from that encounter. I found that a little jarring and immersion breaking at first but i got used to it.
The game is entirely linear (other than a small hub with the challenge maps) and although you can play a New Game+ mode it is still just a beginning to end deal, there is no real option to explore freely or amble around fighting random stuff.
The difficulty is tweakable with the use of limiters that power up the enemy or mess with you to make things harder.
The challenges are challenging and range from more puzzly/strategy oriented ones through to surviving waves of increasingly hard monsters.
Overall I would say it is worth it - the story and graphics alone sell it, however I imagine that the combat may not be to everyone's tastes, so probably worth watching a little gameplay to see if you'll like it.

Spheroid is product of a fan of the Armored Core series by FROM SOFTWARE. Spheroid is like the original Armored Core from original PlayStation in concept, but without providing any form of customization and adding in a few unique changes that make it feel more like a blend between Armored Core and Transformers BeastMachines. The music used in the preview was created in similararity to music from Armored Core Nexus. Not sure if Frame Gride or Murakumo Mech Assalt were also inspiration in the design or if I'm entirely wrng and its VirtualOn in the mix.
Why do I not recommend this? Mainly it is the lack of controller support, the fact that the menus are weird, and the game appears to do a full reset after completing a "mission".
It doesn't seem terrible, just it seems like I paid for a fairly polished preview that will hopefully fund the next (improved) version -which is what FROM SOFTWARE did every console game on PS1 into the last title for PS2. Every game was playable, but always had quirks, or had implemented entirely new concept dynamics from previous that were not fully tested and ironed out for any kind of balance, etc.
I can't say enough how its the lack of controller support that is the main reason I can not recommend this.

Worth the buy just to see how Early Access can be done right, full stop. But it helps that the game is fantastic, I guess.
Great music, graphics that look like a great PS2 game with perfect IQ, frenetic but highly fluid action that runs well even on a fairly poor PC. One of the best twin stick shooters I've played; controller recommended but mouse works fine. Note the game is pretty hard, and score MATTERS; your "life" is a battery that constantly drains (not by taking damage, by time), and you get battery pickups by scoring. You will have to be good to beat this game.
As for the Early Access, this is how it's done. From the very start it was clear what was done, what was being worked on. The place holder graphics were clearly not final but polished in their own way that it's not quite so jarring to play an unfinished level. More than enough good music to make it feel like a final release, and gameplay is extremely tight.
Overall it feels like you're playing a curated selection of a finished game rather than unfinished chunks of randomness that the creators will polish later. Everything you experience feels polished enough to let real people play, even if it's not finalized it's still playable and not too hard on the eyes, ears or fingers.

A great grand strategy game that I can't get enough of. This type of RTS (Wargame series etc.) is such a perfect fit for a World War 2 setting. You get everything you expect in a Eugen RTS. Loads of units, lots of customization, tons of finely crafted maps, and great solid multiplayer. Even solid single player, something fairly new for this series. If you've never played a Eugen RTS before, this is a great place to start. If you're a solid fan, this is an amazing follow up and a must own.
-Solo campaign. I've only played the US Allied missions so far, and they are outstanding. They are re-creations of the famous battles of WW2. Start off behind enemy lines as a paratrooper division, take out guns firing on the landing, secure towns. It's all done so well. The history buff will love this stuff.
-The new frontline mechanic is a really nice touch. Instead of capturing sectors, there is now a dynamic front line that gets moved up with your command units. It shows you exactly what is happening on parts of the map immediately. It's intuitive and works great.
-The new phase mechanics slowlys gives you more income and grants you stronger units. You're in Phase A for 10 minutes, then Phase B until 20 minutes, then Phase C for the rest of the game. This makes each game have a nice feel where the early game is scouting and securing area. Smaller scale combat. Then Phase B ups it a bit as you both build larger armies. By 20 minutes in Phase C you have giant grand armies that only keep getting larger and more advanced. It really makes you feel like a general.
-The multiplayer works great like it always has in previous games. There is a lot of fun to be had online, there is probably a little work to be done in terms of balance.
-Making a deck is almost as fun as the actual game. If you're into building the perfect deck there is so much to do. You pick a historic division (armored, airborne, mechinzed etc.) from certain nations/generals, and begin building your fully customized division. You pick from all the category of units and then give it a try. See where it's weak, change it up. It's a lot of fun and you will soon have loads of decks to pick from. You'll keep getting ideas for a new deck.
Eugen to me is a great company. They release these great real time strategy games and patch them frequently. They will be sure to add a lot of new maps and new units and divisions. They support their games. All of this, and for $40 brand new, I will forever support this company.
If you like Grand RTS, buy this game right now.

While I do understand when games have to be abandoned, with the new Early Access system, this is one many people got burned, and burned bad with. What was supposed to occur with the game, and what actually happened, were narrow. They released the game from Early Access and called that that. Did a few fast patches to shut people up about the big items and continued on their way. The dollar signs weren't big in front of Doublefine's eyes apparently, and took what they had and ran. I wish Steam would have forced their hands in this situation, but didn't, and Doublefine continues along its way like nothing happened.
I'm even more disappointed with Doublefine that they put it on sale right before they terminated development (And I can't imagine them NOT knowing they were going to can it a couple weeks before they did) and continue to sell it with no disclaimer anywhere on the Steam page that it is abandonware and no longer being worked on, AND have also put it for sale as if it's still being acknowledged.
I will not purchase another Doublefine title (or anyone who is part of their team if they move on again) in prerelease, and I am GREATLY nervous about buying a title from them ever again.

So as I read this statement "Do you recommend this game?" I wonder....do I truly?
Yes. All of my yes. This is actually my first purchase on Steam that was FULL PRICE. All of my friends that know me, know you gotta do a lot to make me pay for anything full price. What makes this game good?
First off, let's begin with gameplay. Gameplay can be described as a combination between Smash TV with the aestetics of Bomberman. Sounds weird but plays great. You have a primary and secondary weapon which you can switch between. That simple. There are multiple characters and actual unlockable ones. I'm being honest when I say that these aren't just simple re-skins. With how the engine runs, every character playstyle is drastically different. Only thing that stays the same is you have to keep moving regardless of character.
The controls are not complicated at all. R-trigger shoots. Right stick aims. Left Stick moves. I think left trigger swaps weapons. Pay attention to your cooldown time with weapons, keep moving, and priotitize. If you do this then you're golden.
Music is very catchy. It's not exactly the same as the trailer music was originally. All tracks start of mellow making you slightly bob your head which snowballs when the beat drops. I'm halfway through the game and a perfect example would be the hive. The checkpoint stage I couldnt help but shoot to the beat like I was Ulala or something. Would I download the soundtrack? You beat you sweet and/or sour bottom I would!
Now everybody wants to be a critic and say "What about the graphics?". It's not Crisis 3 nor does it need to be. It's art style compliments the gameplay. This is the first Eugen game I have played online and I am enjoying it alot.
Its slower paced than the wargame series and you can actually enjoy watching  the combat.
There are two game modes, destruction and conquest.
Conquest is probably the harder mode as it requires you to attack and hold territory. In destruction you can get away with just defending.  Both modes have their merits but destruction mode usually favour the german deck with stong phase C units while conquest favours allies due to the stronger phase A units.  If the allies do well in conquest the game can usually be won before phase C kicks in.
Apart from the two modes that play different you can have 1v1, 2v2, 3v3, 4v4 and 10v10.  Eugen have balanced this game around the 3v3 and 4v4 to encourage combining the strengths of each division to cover each divisions weakness.
In 1v1 some divisions will easily beat others, and to a lesser extent in 2v2, so I can imagine in these games players will probably pick the strongest all round decks or phase A rush decks (looking at you Fench division).
10v10 are good place to start with just to learn the mechanics, you also have less responsibility in these games.  But they play different to 3v3 and 4v4.
Playing against medium AI is also good place to learn on 1v1.
Finally get customising your decks, the default ones are very average.   Its good practise to have 3 custom decks of each division, one for 10vs10, one for 3v3 and 4v4 and another for 1v1 and 2v2.
I would recommend trying this game, there is still a week of open beta left and 10 of the divisions are playable and about 8-9 maps.

Being a fan of the Cthulhu Mythos and an avid reader of many of HP Lovecraft's works, you can imagine my surprise when I found a Cthulhu-themed game on Steam and iOS. Having wanted this for a very long time, this game is a surprisingly pleasant pi ss take on the both the Cthulhu Mythos and the RPG genre in general.
In Cthulhu Saves the World, you play as none other than the Elder God of Madness himself, Cthulhu. Having all of his powers taken away by a powerful wizard, Cthulhu sets out on a journey to become a true hero and save the land in an effort to regain his powers, so he may use them to destroy the world.
The game plays very similarly to that of Final Fantasy, Pokémon or Shin Megami Tensei, so people who are familar with those games, or turn-based RPGs in general will feel right at home playing this. With a wide variety of skills and enemies, Cthulhu Saves the World plays out like a comedy, but feels like an adventure all the same.
