If you're familiar with their other game, Bastion, then you have a good idea of what to expect.
The game begins with the female main character, Red, pulling the sword named Transistor out of someone who has just been killed.  The rest of the game is essentially her seeking answers and battling with the fallout of that individual's death in this really unique and original world they've created.
The game is extremely polished.  Like Bastion, they pair the visuals, music, and narration perfectly.  The game is absolutely dripping with style and attention to detail.  The combat system is really solid (and pretty challenging) as well.  You have four main abilities, or functions, that can be active at one time.  Each function you gain in the game contains the essence of a fallen individual of the city, whose lore you can read about once you possess it.  Each function has a main, secondary, and passive property.  Each one also requires a certain amount of memory, so which abilities you can run at the same time will depend on how much you have invested in increasing your max memory capacity.  The combat can be performed in real time or you can execute the turn() function and plan your moves ahead like a turn based game.  It's highly customizeable, albeit a little overwhelming at first (there is no tutorial but you do run have occasional access to a practice zone throughout).  I completed the playthrough without unlocking all of the passives or secondaries.  I guess that is supposed to draw you towards playing it again.
My complaint is that the game is so compact.  It took me about 5 hours to complete.  I guess I played with minimum limiters (kind of like talents you pick to make certain aspects of the game more difficult in return for bonus xp), but if you need to have a multitude of these limiters to stretch out the experience of the game, then maybe somethings wrong.  Additionally, there are only a handful of enemy types (they get progressively more difficult as you advance in the game).  This leads to the combat getting a little repetitive in some combat filled areas.
The game is very unique and well made, and I would absolutely recommend it.  However the $20 price-tag seems to have been made with the notion that the buyer would do multiple playthroughs.  I'd pick it up on sale instead.

Okay, so I loved Bastion, but I've been bitten before, assuming another game by the same studio would be good so I had jammed this on my wishlist but never quite gotten around to getting it.
Got given it as a New Year's gift (tyty!) and started it up rather nervously...
...Immediately captivated.
It is beautiful. It's also (despite the similar viewpoint) not Bastion, and part of me really feels for them because there were always going to be comparisons drawn rather than letting the game stand entirely on its own two feet.
The combat is quite unique (at least to me) as a mix between real time action and phases where you effectively pause time and then carefully plan out your next few moves. The skills system is... hmm... it's a really nice idea. Every skill can be used as an active skill, a passive skill or a modifier for another skill and this offers myriad ways to combine them. The game then encourages you try different things as using the skills in different ways unlocks more information. Screw up and get hit too much and one of your skills will burn out and you'll probably want to try using something else while you progress enough for it to repair.
In practice though the interface was clunky, there was no way to easily save/load builds and the sheer amount of choice available was either overwhelming or (later on especially) you tended towards specific combinations and just settled into a little rut there. I think if the interface had been better there it might have encouraged more flexibility.
The story is lovely and poignant, albeit a little short. Many of the details are only available if you explore or play with your skills to unlock more information and some areas of the story are deliberately vague, but it all makes sense (whether you delve or not) by the end. I felt it worked very well.
You pause after every fight - literally everything stops and a board pops up while you gain the exp from that encounter. I found that a little jarring and immersion breaking at first but i got used to it.
The game is entirely linear (other than a small hub with the challenge maps) and although you can play a New Game+ mode it is still just a beginning to end deal, there is no real option to explore freely or amble around fighting random stuff.
The difficulty is tweakable with the use of limiters that power up the enemy or mess with you to make things harder.
The challenges are challenging and range from more puzzly/strategy oriented ones through to surviving waves of increasingly hard monsters.
Overall I would say it is worth it - the story and graphics alone sell it, however I imagine that the combat may not be to everyone's tastes, so probably worth watching a little gameplay to see if you'll like it.

That said, they could have gotten a little more creative with the combat scalling or at least taken it one more step forward.
While story does not introduce many choices along the way, gameplay certainly does. Picking and matching your abilities, creating level of difficulty just for yourself, trying to figure out just how many crazy applications your tools can have. It is probably my favourite take on fully customising your character and while I believe the whole system is held back just a tiny bit by the way the game introduces new mechanics to you, overal experience was immensly enjoyable and jumping to NG+ still suprised me with yet another layer of complexity for your own choices.
Definetly check it out.

Ok, so this game.  Great concept.  Great idea, and it is done really well.  Except for one main thing.  The game constantly throws stuff at you, and sometimes there isn't actually a good answer.  Let me explain.  You are building a big section of your base.  Things are going well.  You then see a message appear on the side of the screen saying how one of your builder's space suit oxygen is running low.  Sometimes they quickly make their own way back to the airlock, stopping them from dieing.  Sometimes they just carry on working and then die.  You can try to avoid this by sending them to the infirmary (which is obviously inside) manually.  But sometimes they don't bother to listen and still die.
Another example of this game throwing rubbish into your face would be those raiders who have high tech weaponry.  It takes one of them to take out tonnes of vital parts to your station as well as many many people with inferior weaponry, and thats it.  Your space base is broken and/or on fire and half your population dead.  Yay.
The random space debris causing major fires and ruptures within your base can easily kill a room full of sleeping people, again almost half your bases population.
But the main thing that gets me is that for a game that is meant to be a mix between economy and fighting, all the fighting is unfair (see the first paragraph) and the economy lacks whats really needed.  The AI don't know when to prioritise fixing vital oxygen recyclers over fixing an unused door.  They also don't know when it is useful to take a break - many will take a break and not perform tasks during critical points in gameplay, causing negative effects (most prominently the players mood).
In conclusion this game has a lot of potential.  A lot.  But it doesn't have basic concepts like manual prioritization and decent AI.  The whole game needs a huge amount of balancing, and until this happens I recommend you simply follow this game, rather than get it.  If and when the devs make the changes necessary this game will definately worth the money.  But for now, I recommend you spend it elsewhere.
And one other thing.  I can't for the life of me find out a way of keeping the people happy.  It may just be my incompetance, or this too may need balancing...

Can't recommend this game right now due to the state it is in, this close to release.  If you didn't like Wargame Red Dragon, you will not like this.  In many ways this is worse.  Just be aware that this is not any different to any competitive RTS fromthe last 20 years.  It is a WW2 setting, it does have a Paradox label on it, but strategy and tactics are not really much use here.
The basic units can't do anything without micro-management, So if you are not clicking constantly for 40 minutes at avery high rate, you cant play this game.
The solo game has a very poor AI, that despite all the developers protestations to the contrary either cheats, or has the most amazing luck with the basic to hit and penetration mechanics.  This means that the game ends up being a pretty standard RTS with you just trying to overwhelm the AI.  Encounter 5 half-tracks at 600meters with 3 panzers and your panzers are toast.  You probably will not get a shot off.  There are AI settings but the gap between Easy and Medium is a gulf most players will not cross.
As you can't train in any useful way against the AI, Multiplayer is a bit of a challenge.  The community is toxic.  They are not forgiving and they don't like noobs.  Most of the players will wipe you off the map in 40 seconds.  The game at the moment is extremely unforgiving, and the dominant tactic is a rush with cheap over-powered units that will overwhelm anyone new from the start.
Maybe they will do a last minute turn and straighten things out, but if you are a strategic WG fan, but not a competitive RTS player, stay well away from this one.

I have played wargame games in the past and been mildly pleased with them but this game is fantastic.
So first to warn you, this is not Coh2, this is not Sudden Strike, it is much more tactical. More mass scale, but still a lot to micro. Think 5-6 panthers supported by AT guns, infantry, and anti air vehicles, also air support you control vs. 1-2 tanks and  never really worrying about air superiority.
The graphics are quite good, but to be honest you won't zoom in all the way too often, because you will be positioning your troops, calling in reinforcements, checking on your allies an what they need. To be good at this game you have to get out of the "I am in it only for me tunnel. If you set up a good defense and are not being pushed call in a few units for your ally, or provide them air cover.
The historical accuracy of the units is amazing. That being said, there is a learning curve to knowing what unit does what. Line of sight and range are key to understanding how to best use your units. Artillery is as devasting as it is in real life, so if you bunch up your units expect a kick in the teeth.
Build your own deck, try it and adjust. Do not use the standard decks. Each division (8 in the beta, many more in full game) has it's own strength and weaknesses. There are some standard things you should get like a few arty, few tanks, amo trucks etc. but you need to play around and play against opponents to see where your deck is strong and weak.
There are also phases, so phase A you can call in troops from your deck only with an A on the card. This makes you balance the game, because you might be able to call in planes in phase, A, but do you want to wait for phase B to get more planes etc. All chocie you have tomake based of experience int he field. I am sure there are guides to god decks, but I like making my own.

Even though this gem is still in Alpha, it thankfully escaped the feeling of emptiness that usually comes with that label. The gameplay is so tight and feels so good that you may just forget that it's in Alpha. This game's levels are an adrenaline rush from start to finish, a high-energy high-pressure robot laser massacre that forces the player to be aggressive instead of allowing them to hang back and snipe. The Weapon Level system, Battery system and Power-ups encourage the player to get in close, and this creates a feeling of urgency and danger that is unique among twin-stick shooters.
Every level is an ambush. Hundreds of robots will attack you in the span of a couple minutes and attempt to overwhelm you with sheer numbers. Good thing your weapons are so powerful. And this is just in singleplayer -- if you have any buddies playing with you, the robot count may rise into the thousands... Good luck!
This game is excellent for a coffee break. The rounds are typically 2-3 minutes, so you can hop in and play a quick game whenever you want. And then you'll want to play just one more level.
Did I mention the incredible production value? Assault Android Cactus's art style reminds me of Jimmy Neutron. Everything looks really cool, without eating too much of your processor. This game can run very well on even low-end computers. The exciting Drum n' Bass music, tight controls and high skill ceiling puts this game in the same tier as Super Meat Boy and the likes.
Buy it. It is ABSOLUTELY worth the $15.

Sleeping Dogs really, really wants to be a Hong Kong movie. Somewhere along the way, during its development, it met a genie that granted its wish.
Sleeping dog is an open world variation on the GTA theme taking place in Hong Kong and letting players take control of Wei Chen, an undercover cop in a mission to infiltrate and destroy the triads.
Faithful to the genre, the game will punctuate its main story with a slew of side missions and events. On-foot pursuits, races and gunfights are, of course, involved, but only serve as a seasoning for the game's main dish: its hand to hand combat.
Clearing missions for either the triads or the police will earn you experience points to build up several skill trees, mostly dedicated to bashing your opponents with a the violent kind of grace you'd expect from a HK flick.
Even if the combat system was already popularised by the Arkham series at the launch of Sleeping Dogs, fighting remains glorious and gets spiced up by the use of the environment. Tired of punching and kicking? Dunk their head in a toilet bowl. Don't like this kind of practice? A free lobotomy on a circular saw will do the trick. Not a fan? Go back to punching, kicking and countering. Still glorious.
The story itself, even if rather predictable, is well written. Without any noticeable plot holes, it gives character to its characters, and is supported by a fantastic rendition of the East Asian urban ambiance, complete with adequate radio stations and shady massage parlors (Cliché? yes. Myth? No.)
But, there has to be a but. The game far, very far from being perfect. Capitalising on the open world concept is one thing, but developers have to be smart enough so players don't feel like they are only playing a series of mini-games spread over a map. There, Sleeping Dogs fails and, beside its main story, the experience feels like content has be added for the sake of it.
It wouldn't be too bad if... if the game were polished enough that the activities offered by the side missions and events were smooth enough to justify their repetition. Unfortunately, driving everything but a motorbike feels like a chore, (also, the GPS is all over the place), gun fights lack precision, hacking, bugging, and phone tracing are tedious, and even fighting can be atrocious at times.
Yes, fighting. The one aspect in which the game really shines is marred by a lack of consistency in the time windows for counters and interrupts. As a result, some fights will make you feel than luck is a more important factor than tactics or skill. This may make you want to swallow your controller just so you can poop it later.
The game is also rather buggy and it really shouldn't be. Sleeping Dogs: Definitive edition is supposed to be an overhauled version of its older iteration, you'd think that the developers would have done something about invisible props, drunk drivers and mission breaking bugs (How are you supposed to protect your mate if he commits suicide? Tell me?). But no. Bad developers, bad!
And yet... yet...
Yet this minigame compilation on a map, this frustrating, unpolished piece is tied up so well by its story, characters and ambiance that it remains highly entertaining. Will Dog Eyes bite the dust? Will Wei get in more trouble than he already is? Can you really trust a matriarch who spends her days handling a cleaver? All these questions have to be answered between two servings of pork bun, because pork buns make a man complete.
All in all, Sleeping Dogs is an enjoyable experience that's worth Wei more (haha) than the sum of its parts. I do recommend it, especially if you're into Hong Kong movies. Wait for it to be on sales so you won't pay extra for the bugs, then go spill some street guts!

This is a first-person RPG in the style of Eye of the Beholder.  The plot is simple but appropriately so.  You are four convicts who have been exiled to Mount Grimrock.  You receive a pardon upon being exiled because nobody makes it down and out of the mountain.  Ever.  This game is an epic dungeon crawl and it knows it.  You need to find light sources or you will die.  You need to find food or you will die.  You need to manage your inventory and weight loads or, yes, you will die.  The game is pretty tough on the normal difficulty and you can ramp it up with a hard mode as well as an old-school mode where you must create your own maps out-of-game.  The itemization, art direction, and music all contribute to an ambiance that other games from top-tier studios would be wise to emulate.  It is not without its flaws.  The combat system is rather clunky and the grid-layout of the game allows many enenmies killed through mechanical exploitation.  The real difficulty is in the carefully crafted puzzles that push the limitations of the grid-based system to new levels of awesome and often require precision movement and perfect timing.  This game goes on sale often but it is worth it at full price.

Farming Simulator is the best Farming Simulator in the series today imo. The bale handling is improved over previous games, the textures are better and I like the new mission systems, which make more sense as you are doing actual farm field chores for other farmers instead of just mowing or transporting crates.

Pig farming has now been included and all animals (cows, sheep & pigs) can now breed, with you being able to haul excess animals to the sell points too.

You can now place various buildings around the map, including grain silos, hay barns etc.. and you can buy seed and fertiliser packs to transport to your farm.

I came in here to write a short comment, what resulted was anything but...
Having played and not been the greatest fan of the previous macro-strategy games (Eugen's Wargame games) as they always felt lacking, in that the diversity of available units did not equal a diversity of fielded units compared to micro-strategy games (Men of War, Company of Heroes).
That is to say: do not approach this game as you would Men of War, or Company of Heroes; both are different enough to take you off guard if you play them in the same manner, and just because you like Men of War or Company of Heroes, does not mean you'll enjoy the gameplay of this one.
However, having said that, I am happy to say that so far I have been enjoying this game quite a bit and have found the need to field all types of units available without said unit not feeling inadequate in comparison to similarly priced units (as with the Wargame series). Every unit has a niche that it resides in with little to no overlap of units that fill another role as well (but this is probably due to the game's setting of WWII, when most things had a singular purpose, a real rock-paper-scissors war).
So far I have only played cooperatively with and againt AI (I am yet to play against players, I am strongly advising my friends to purchase this game as well), both have proved to be suitable allies and opponents.
The AI are fielding the entire breadth of units available to them and using them effectively: my artillery is being counter artilleried, scouts are well placed to see things behind my front line, mortars will bombard a grouping of buildings I have occupied, fighter planes will counter my bombers and, along with their own bombers, harrass my ground units.
The battles, once they get going, are a fantastic spectacle and even enjoyable to watch on replay as a spectator.
The default game mode, Conquest Mode, is a very interesting take on the (now classic) capture sectors to gain points game mode. Now instead of capturing specific sectors to increase your points, the portion of the battlefield you control, from the rear to your front line, is your sector, and the percentage of the overall map you control determines whether or not you are receiving points and how many per tick.
The game with this game mode is amazing, it's always encouraging you to keep pushing forward, keep pushing their front line back and to only take a defensive strategy as a temporary measure. This turned what was a defensive game mode of capture the sector and hold onto it, into a fantastically offense mode. You can see the ebb and flow as the front line keeps moving across the map like a low and high tide at battle with the beach, and it will keep you on your toes the entire time.
This game is graphically well done but take this with a grain of salt as I only have a R7 360 (still waiting on Vega) playing on medium-ish (mish-mash of high, low and off) settings at about 30fps. Taking note of that I haven't had any performance problems that made the game grind to a painfull low despite the amount of action on-screen at the time.
As of this time with 7 hours played I have only had the game freeze/crash once, but the game is still in beta with a couple more weeks to go.
I've always had a problem getting into these macro-strategy game without the finer placement controls available to the micro-strategy games, I've always wanted to enjoy them, I just could not find to enthusiasm to played them regularly, but I am happy to say that this game appears to have broken that spell and is a worthwhile purchase, even as the beta state it is in.
To me Men of War and this game, (even though both occupy the WWII strategy category) are different enough for me to have the fine control of units and positioning in Men of War, and have this game sit along side an in my list of regularly played games.

Transistor is an extremely solid indie game from the makers of Bastion (if you've played that, then you'll probably enjoy this). The game takes place in the strange but beautiful city of Cloudbank. You play a singer named Red, who wields a swordlike machine called the Transisitor. You're trying to figure out where the hostile machines called the Process come from, and how to defeat them. The story overall is pretty interesting, but can be hard to follow, and you don't get a full explanation of what's happening. But that's OK, because the story isn't really meant to be the best part.
The gameplay is a combination of turn-based and real-time action, though for the most part, you'll depend on the turn-based segments (which charges up, then lets you unleash a chain of attacks without leaving enemies much chance to react). You have a set of "functions" that you unlock and equip on the Transistor, which allow you to customize how you fight. There are so many options here, so you can truly play how you want - be stealthy, deal massive damage, cripple enemies slowly, you name it.
As far as graphics and sound go, they are nearly flawless. There is so a lot of color until the end of the game, when things start getting a bit grayer (for story reasons I won't explain here). The electronic-ish soundtrack is excellent; I bought it with the game and don't regret it.
The game is somewhat short. I finished in about 7 hours, tops, and I am not much of a quick player (I took the time to explore things in the world), so it can be finished sooner. There is a sort of New Game+ mode that restarts the story with all your level-ups, and the end-game difficulty level from enemies is also retained, so it's not just a walk in the park for you. There are also challenges you can work on beating, and you can continue experimenting with your functions, so there is stuff to do. But the story is pretty linear, which probably will make a replay somewhat more dull, hearing all the plot again.

TL;DR
Story 7/10
Graphics 9/10
Sound/Music 9/10
Gameplay 9/10
Replayability 6/10
Overall score: 4/5
If this game is on sale, BUY IT immediately (and maybe get the soundtrack too). If not, weigh the price versus what I've said above. I vastly enjoyed the game and strongly recommend it.

I've never heard of the Supergiant Games studio before, nor about any of their games, so a recommendation I've heard from my friend about Transistor was completely new to me. Not knowing anything at all about the game, buying it on its next sale was a bit of a risk, but one I'm very glad I made. Admittedly, I didn't think much of this little gem at first - played it for a few hours, got bored, and left it for many months - but revisiting and completing it again recently made me love it, and compelled me to write this review.
Great things:
- Beautiful art style. Very colourful, detailed and full of light, that never gets obnoxious at any point. It creates a strangely warm, inviting atmosphere to the world despite the rather grim events going on in the story.
- One of the best soundtracks I've heard in a game, I want to find all of those songs to listen to in my own time (any help with that is appreciated).
- Lovely protagonist, despite not having a voice Red is nonetheless a fascinating, strong character that gets very well developed over the short course of the game and whom you can really grow to resonate with and root for.
- Engaging, well paced, mature storytelling, helped by your sword boyfriend's brilliant narrating skills.
- Some unique mechanics - such as the Limiters, which handicap your combat in some way for a nice amount of bonus experience, and every "Function", the in game combat skills, having all sorts of active, upgrading and passive effects, allowing for loads of customization in your fights.
- Red can hum to the melody of whatever song is currently playing, which is a very minor thing but one I found very amusing and I often idled in the game just doing that.
- Luna.
Good things:
- Combat isn't entirely groundbreaking, but it's fun, the "functions" are diverse and great to play with, and has lots of strategy element to it - utilizing the turns as much as possible to create different combos tends to get you a lot farther than just bashing the Process over the heads with one skill over and over. It mixes turn based with fast paced combat and pulls it off, what is very nice to see and work with.
- Nicely done character development of most introduced characters, including the main villains and the Camerata, despite the limited actual time dedicated to it.
- Achievements aren't hard to get, the backdoor room challenges can get pretty tough when you progress through their stages but all of them are solveable with a bit of focused thinking. It's also great that besides achievements, those challenges give you a good bit of ingame experience, which you can't increase with limiters from what I observed but is very helpful either way. I recommend doing all of them at some point in every playthrough, if not for the boons then at least just to unlock more brilliant songs to idle around with.
- Completion of the game's main story allows you to start a recursion playthrough, revisiting all of it with stronger enemies while retaining your level and all your functions, which is great.
Cons (everything has some, I guess)
- If you're interested in the deeper backstory of the game's main characters, the decryption system that unlocks bits of it is confusing and weird to get used to. You only get access to it by unlocking different combinations of functions, which takes a long time and doesn't feel worth it for ultimately just bits of reading.
- Very linear and short. You do get your time to explore Cloudbank and other bits of the world, but your sword boyfriend pushes you through a solid set path that could really do with being longer.
- Spoilerish, a more personal bit of input:
Overall, this game proves that games can be a gorgeous work of art as well as an interactive medium of fun, and I couldn't recommend it more to anyone looking to play through an adventure like no other. I will make sure to give Bastion a go one day and see if I enjoy it as much as this.

Evaluating this game is hard. I would say I do recommend it, but to avoid disappointment, the potential player needs to be aware that its level of quality is not on par with Bastion, no matter what you may hear elsewhere. It just isn't.
That said, both art and sound have the high level of quality expected that has come to be expected from Supergiant Games. I can't explain why for the sake of avoiding spoilers, but its graphical quality does drop towards the end, which I didn't like much. Gameplay is quite innovative and feels cohesive, implementing engaging turn-based with pause battles that you actually have fun with. The attempt at giving this title an organic start was slightly too disorienting, and while the world and its particularities are interesting, the lack of context for the plot is too big, crossing over from mystery to just simple confusion.
The whole experience is just quite short and rushed, and leaves you wishing there was something more to it. It's still a good game, but it's not what it could have been.

Sleeping Dogs really, really wants to be a Hong Kong movie. Somewhere along the way, during its development, it met a genie that granted its wish.
Sleeping dog is an open world variation on the GTA theme taking place in Hong Kong and letting players take control of Wei Chen, an undercover cop in a mission to infiltrate and destroy the triads.
Faithful to the genre, the game will punctuate its main story with a slew of side missions and events. On-foot pursuits, races and gunfights are, of course, involved, but only serve as a seasoning for the game's main dish: its hand to hand combat.
Clearing missions for either the triads or the police will earn you experience points to build up several skill trees, mostly dedicated to bashing your opponents with a the violent kind of grace you'd expect from a HK flick.
Even if the combat system was already popularised by the Arkham series at the launch of Sleeping Dogs, fighting remains glorious and gets spiced up by the use of the environment. Tired of punching and kicking? Dunk their head in a toilet bowl. Don't like this kind of practice? A free lobotomy on a circular saw will do the trick. Not a fan? Go back to punching, kicking and countering. Still glorious.
The story itself, even if rather predictable, is well written. Without any noticeable plot holes, it gives character to its characters, and is supported by a fantastic rendition of the East Asian urban ambiance, complete with adequate radio stations and shady massage parlors (Cliché? yes. Myth? No.)
But, there has to be a but. The game far, very far from being perfect. Capitalising on the open world concept is one thing, but developers have to be smart enough so players don't feel like they are only playing a series of mini-games spread over a map. There, Sleeping Dogs fails and, beside its main story, the experience feels like content has be added for the sake of it.
It wouldn't be too bad if... if the game were polished enough that the activities offered by the side missions and events were smooth enough to justify their repetition. Unfortunately, driving everything but a motorbike feels like a chore, (also, the GPS is all over the place), gun fights lack precision, hacking, bugging, and phone tracing are tedious, and even fighting can be atrocious at times.
Yes, fighting. The one aspect in which the game really shines is marred by a lack of consistency in the time windows for counters and interrupts. As a result, some fights will make you feel than luck is a more important factor than tactics or skill. This may make you want to swallow your controller just so you can poop it later.
The game is also rather buggy and it really shouldn't be. Sleeping Dogs: Definitive edition is supposed to be an overhauled version of its older iteration, you'd think that the developers would have done something about invisible props, drunk drivers and mission breaking bugs (How are you supposed to protect your mate if he commits suicide? Tell me?). But no. Bad developers, bad!
And yet... yet...
Yet this minigame compilation on a map, this frustrating, unpolished piece is tied up so well by its story, characters and ambiance that it remains highly entertaining. Will Dog Eyes bite the dust? Will Wei get in more trouble than he already is? Can you really trust a matriarch who spends her days handling a cleaver? All these questions have to be answered between two servings of pork bun, because pork buns make a man complete.
All in all, Sleeping Dogs is an enjoyable experience that's worth Wei more (haha) than the sum of its parts. I do recommend it, especially if you're into Hong Kong movies. Wait for it to be on sales so you won't pay extra for the bugs, then go spill some street guts!

Right. So. The title. It makes about as much sense as the game does. But hell, whatever. There's been more crazy names thrown around in the Steam universe. Let's roll with it. What are we looking at?
Assault Android Cactus, and from this point on I shall merely refer to it as Cactus, is an arena score shooter. Where you pick from a stable of androids, each with their own weapon loadouts and personalities and looks, and then select a level from an ever expanding list and have at it, dealing with wave upon wave of horribleness in the time honoured tradition of Arena Shooters everywhere. With obscene firepower.
On my rig, it runs beautifully, after the first run on a level which for some strange reason it needs a bit of time to shake out the cobwebs it will invariably run at 1920x1080 with all the shiny set to max, and with nary a judder. The movement is slick and the animation is crisp. The effects are bright and the game moves along at a rapid clip, controls are ridiculously simple, you have four keys for movement, you use your mouse to aim, one button to fire, the other to switch between primary and "power" weapons.
And that's it. Kill everything that isn't you.
Thank god, because this is all about instinct, you pretty much are on the move from start to finish, dodging bullets and badguys in a near incessant firestorm of incomming pain and rage in the form of various mechanical and I -think- biomechanical baddies, I didn't get time to admire the scenery too much. Kinda hard when everything is trying to kill you.
The graphics are excellent and the story, what there is at this point is witty and well presented, in the style of some sort of adult teen anime, there seems to have been some kind of robot mutiny, and the androids you control are tasked with restoring order. Each of the androids has a very specific personality, which shows through quite nicely in the boss fights, their expressions and their playstyles. Music and sound effects are also uniformly excellent, with each "area" having a thumping soundtrack that keeps a high tempo and keeps you pretty much immersed in what's going on.
And this is an early alpha.
This review will evolve but bluntly - short of the developers being visited by aliens and having their brains replaced with cottage cheese and pineapple chunks - this should be an easy recommendation, and a big thumbs up from me.

So as I read this statement "Do you recommend this game?" I wonder....do I truly?
Yes. All of my yes. This is actually my first purchase on Steam that was FULL PRICE. All of my friends that know me, know you gotta do alot to make me pay for anything full price. What makes this game good?
First off, let's begin with gameplay. Gameplay can be described as a combination between Smash TV with the aestetics of Bomberman. Sounds weird but plays great. You have a primary and secondary weapon which you can switch between. That simple. There are multiple characters and actual unlockable ones. I must say these are not simple re-skins. With how the engine runs, every character playstyle is drastically different. Only thing that stays the same is you have to keep moving regardless of character.
The controls are not complicated at all. R-trigger shoots. Right stick aims. Left Stick moves. I think left trigger swaps weapons. Pay attention to your cool down time with weapons, keep moving, and priotitize. If you do this then your golden.
Music is very catchy. It's not like how the trailer's music is originally. All tracks start of mellow making you slightly bob your head which snowballs when the beat drops. I'm halfway through the game and a perfect example would be the hive. The checkpoint stage I couldnt help but shoot to the beat like I was Ulala or something. Would I download the soundtrack? You beat you sweet and/or sour bottom I would!
Now everybody want's to be a critic and say "What about the graphics?". It's not Crisis 3 nor does it need to be. It's art style compliments the gameplay. Why would I want to play a top down shooter that has over the top graphics. There is too much that goes on in this game and truthfully you need the change in colors so you don't foolishly just run into the bullets because you can't tell that they're bullets. Can't say it's too colorful or too dark. It's just right.
Final notes: I can't believe this is still just an Alpha. That scares the crap out of me. I'm happy to own this game and hope you get it. The only turn off could possibly be the art style since that may not be for everyone. All in all I suggest buying it. There's not much I can peg this game for and it's challenging. Like old school challenging also while being played as a respectable shump.

The pixel horror game "Into The Gloom" drops you in a mysterious circumstance filled with questions of what is going on. Why is everyone dead around you? What caused everyone to hang themselves? Why are you here?
Using pixelated graphics can often be seen as a drawback. What can pixels do that realistic graphics can't? Into The Gloom uses them effectively, with everything being very detailed and adds more of a disturbing touch to the enemies and the hanging bodies. This also allows the horror to come from other places, such as the soundtrack, the element of mystery, and the overarching story that reveals more with each ending. Jumpscares are scarce, never overstaying their welcome, with the main enemy of their respected section causing panic. Into The Gloom does well during first playthroughs with each branching path. With each death, the player gains more information on how to survive till the end.
The puzzles are difficult, but not too difficult that the player would get frusturated as it does show progression. Each ending branches off from each other, giving something new for the progression and the different choice the player made. The game also comes with a way to unlock notes about the background of entities and people to encourage players to do and find ways to unlock them. Coupled with background music with eack new area and different sounds accompaning each enemy, Into The Gloom does not overstay its welcome.
The only problem is that it is easy to get caught on corners, and while you are being chased this can be a temperary annoyance.
Overall, Into The Gloom is an effective horror game that creeps the player with almost every element implemended. Don't let the pixelated graphics turn you away from this well crafted horror game.

THE CAMERA DOESN'T HOLD STILL
The game uses an immersive camera that never stops moving, giving one the feeling of playing a live, breathing character. Even when you are not touching anything, the screen is moving around in slight circles. There is also stride bobbing when moving the character around. These effects may not affect everyone, but it makes me feel sick when I play. As far as I can tell, there is no way to work around these gameplay effects. It makes it very unpleasant when I try to play it, so I just don't play anymore. I can't recommend a game I can't play without feeling nauseated.

Other people have said it far better than I am going to attempt to, but I simply have to add my praise to this game.
Pixelated?  Yep.  Mostly montone color scheme?  Yes.  One of the best horror games I've played in years?  Very much so.
This is not a typical pixelated walking simulator with jumpscares.  This game is a true horror game.  And every time I look through my lists for horror games yet to be played I find myself again and again wishing there were more Into the Gloom's to play.
I have been playing horror games since the days of Haunted house on the Atari 2600.  I have been reading horror stories, and watching horror movies since I was 10.  I have played Amnesia, Penumbra, Outlast, The lurking horror, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Cryostasis, Anna extended, Clock Tower, Hired Guns, Undying, Fatal Frame, and more AAA, indie horror games, and obscure horror titles almost no one has even heard of than I could ever list in one post.
This game has moments where it ranks with the best of them.
Does it have AAA production values? No. Does it have 1000+ hours of playtime? No. But what it does have, it has in spades.  It is well worth the $3.00 price and I can only hope the developer makes an Into the Gloom 2.  I would rank that on my wishlist right next to Outlast 2 and a true Amnesia sequel.

A great iteration on the Wargames franchise.

Great game whether you are a RTS fan or just have an interest in WW II. You build your deck from one of 18 divisions present at Normandy recreated using the historical TO&E. At any one time you probably control what amount to a small battalion of infantry, tanks, artillery, and even air support. Maps are great and were apparently created using aerial photos of the battlefields as they appeared in WW II. I think the game excels at capturing the spirit of the hedgerow fighting where every field and every hedgerow was turned into a small fortress. Learning to properly reconnoiter, manage line of sight, and employ combined arms is essential. You can micro as much as you want; not as much as in a squad based tactics game, but your units can survive on their own without needing to constantly babysit them. Firefights look and sound gorgeous, zoom in on a fight and turn your volume up, you won't regret it. There should be three campaigns to play offline and I think the AI is a noticeable step up from Wargame's.
Cons:
Needs further optimization could run smoother, but it is a beta and improvements are in the works.
Running the game can be a heavy load on you processor, however mine is only clocked at 2.4ghz, but I can still run the game on high settings.
Final opinion: Some of the best fun I've had in a long time and one of the best RTS I have ever played, even though it's still in beta.

Before you buy...
1.This game is not meant to be easy, there are mechanics to learn and master.
2.War is not balanced, don't expect your units to be a 1 to 1 match of the enemy units. example a Sherman is not a tiger it never will be but it can kill one if you play well.
3. this is about smart plays and well thought out plans, before battle you make a deck/division of troops, each troop has a role and they perform best in said role, a scout squad is not infantry squad so on.
4.Learn to play in different styles and be adaptable.
In all honesty this is a great game and worth the price my suggestion is that you give it a go and it is most certainly best played with a friend or even a stranger as communication is a great helper as some divisions lack certain units, Inf divisions have the minimal amount of tanks but a massive amount of artillary and infantry while a airborne or a division with historical ties to the airforce will have some amazing options in the air.
The game also implements a feature which is good and bad at the same time. Phases, battles usually begin small with the allies having a advantage in quality of troop choices but fall off as the game progresses as german divisions are able to muster a resistance with some of their best toys like kingtigers and panthers.

I highly recommend this game, its obviously not for those who expect a lot to happen in a short space of time, its very repetitive but isn't that the point? Anyway, here are the good and bad points.
GOOD:
Very high attention to detail: The models in this game are very realistic, slightly better than the previous game but still better.
Mod Manager: Although there aren't many mods available on the Mod Manager, there are still enough to make the game noticeably different. I also love how most of the mods are actually by GIANTS and are FREE which is very respectable because if it was any other developer they would have released them as paid DLC.
Radio: There are 4 radio stations, Rock, Pop, Electro and Country even though the songlist isn't that big its still a decent improvement and hopefully in the future the ability to add your own songs or a radio mod.
New Crops and Vehicles: Its awesome to see new crops in Farming Simulator it obviously adds a lot more realism and at the same time, more work to do.
New Maps: Goldcrest Valley and Soznovka. At the moment I have only played on Goldcrest which is a very well laid out map, so I assume Soznovka will be laid out very well too, I just don't like it because it looks very rustic and I prefer modern.
Vehicle modifications: This is my favourite addition by far, the ability to modify your vehicles adds a bit more flexibility to the vehicles you buy, althought not every vehicle can be modified there are still a lot that can.
BAD:
Animal Animations: They aren't really that bad, but they could be a little bit smoother. When the animals walk they sort of judder and the transition from animations are instant but either way they are still not too bad.
No Crop damage: This can be rectified by downloading a mod using the in-game mod manager, but it would be nice to see that little bit of realism added by default, it could even be toggleable.
Maps: There are only 2 maps, although they are very VERY nice maps, itt would be nice to see more maps by the masters at Giants rather than fan-made. I don't know about you, but the game feels more official when you play on a map made by the devs rather than fans.
Well, thats about it, I know I have only played 42.1 hours as of posting this review but thats still a pretty long time in my opinion considering I do play other games too. So again, I highly recommend this game, especially if you have more than one monitor, its really fun to just play this and watch Netflix on another screen, a great way to chill out :D

Playing King of Fighters 13 is more enjoyable than eating a grape-flavored popsicle on a scorching 200°F saturday afternoon.  If you think I'm joking then try it out for yourself.  Once you do, you'll quickly realize the errors of your ways, and that this is one of the best fighting games available.
Let me begin by saying that this fighter is not an easy one to learn.  For those who aren't used to playing fighting games, special move inputs can be difficult, combos can be difficult, understanding what is even happening can be difficult.  But the reward of learning this game and pulling off super saucy cream dream HD combos is vast and satisfying.  It is a feeling that is similar to what we feel when we viciously chew on a crispy strip of bacon.  I'm sure you all get what I'm saying.
The cast of characters is FANTASTIC. Most of the great KOF classics like Terry Bogard, K', Iori Yagami, and Ryo Sakazaki return, so long-time SNK fans will be pleased.  The visuals are MAGNIFICIENT.  They have chosen to stick with the 2-D sprite style which looks ultra sick nasty, and some of the special moves just look crazy godlike.  Hitting opponents with the POWAH GEYSAH gives me one of the greatest feelings that a man could pursue.  And don't even get me started on the musical greatness that KOF13 features.  The characters, visuals, and music are all top-notch godlike, of this I can assure you.
I've played a decent amount of online matches and I am happy to say that it runs great. Nice improvement over 2015. Some mods available for 2015 are now standard in 2017. The graphics are slightly better, and a nice group of new vehicles/equipment including some new types of equipment (conveyors etc). FINALLY we have more animals (pigs) instead of just sheep, cows, and chickens.
The only Cons I will give are the maps and the in-game map system. In the 2015 and earlier versions you could pull up the map, see your equipment all over the place and click on anything and be instantly taken to that piece of machinery. In 2017, you can't. The map does nothing more than SHOW you where they are. You can either drive over to them in another vehicle or tab through until you land in the machine you want. Also, the default maps kind of stink. As a US based person, I only have interest in the US themed map and it is poorly laid out. A very, very small home-base farm with little to no storage for equipment (and no place to put additional storage) and fields all over the place. The geography is a very poor representation of most US farm land. The "town" itself is nicely laid out though and very well detailed to look American.
The train system is a nice addition, but I feel it is a bit uneccessary. Also, the trains themselves are European styled so they don't fit in at all on an American map.
I will play this game much, much more when there is an add-on MOD map that I like made available. Until then, I'll just wait and see because as I said the US map is just too annoying for me to play on.

The atmosphere was perfect. The puzzles were challenging yet had a decent learning curb and the story was actually really interesting, with 5 different endings and some of those endings leaving an opening for a possible sequel.
After completing all endings, I highly recommend this game. A really good example of it's genre, the only complaint is that it leaves you wanting more, as all that it does is done well.
*
- Makes you feel like you're there, it goes from creepy to calm to soothing and back around again with great timing. This is complimented really well with the music, sound effects and visuals.
*
- Challenging yet fair (some really challenging), each different with a decent learning curb to them and some 1 or 2 that are quite sneaky.
*
- By interacting with the world and examining things, picking up letters, reaching checkpoints and getting to endings, you put the pieces of the story together and experience it as you're right there in the world itself, this is done really well.
*
- All though the game does what it does really well, and the endings are fine, it leaves you wanting more, and some proper closure, a feeling tha the story could go on.
*
- Though it does feel very open at times, you often find that "this door is locked" or "this door is jammed" comes up a lot, even though there are 5 different endings and a point in the game that you can make a major decision that effects the story, it leaves with the idea that there more possiblities that haven't been explored.

In the Steam awards 2017, I nominated FFXIV for the labor of love award for the simple reason that the director, Naoki Yoshida, loves this game, loves the community, and continues to show that love in the content he produces. Watch the noclip documentary on YouTube about the rebirth of FFXIV from the mess that another director released as v1.0 and it's clear that Yoshi-P (as the community and his co-workers call him) has put together a dream team of many of the best in Square Enix to create a wonderful fantasy world. I've clocked a thousand or so hours in the world of Final Fantasy XIV (between the Steam/non-Steam PC versions and the PS4 version, all of which on the same character/server/world) and it continues to impress and excite me with new content "patches" being released regularly. While V2.0 (the original "A Realm Reborn" storyline) did feel somewhat rushed and bloated filler fetch quests at times, FFXIV's Heavensward expansion was widely heralded as the glorious return of the Final Fantasy franchise to the world of dungeons and dragons styled high fantasy with rich new expansions to the world, moody and epic music, and moving storytelling (something especially rare in MMOs). Stormblood has similarly impressed reviewers and players alike and as long as Naoki Yoshida continues to man the helm this ship is expected to continue on its impressive course as one of the top MMOs out there.

FFXIV Online is a fantastic MMORPG and I believe that if you give it a try, you'll enjoy it as much as I do.
The Story:
Like some other MMOs, the game has a main scenario questline that you can follow. IMO it has an amazing storyline, though the first portion (lv1-lv50 ARR) of the MSQ doesn't feel as exciting until the beginning of post ARR quests and so forth. Heavensward MSQ was my personal favorite, with Stormblood as a close second. The MSQ also introduces you many gameplay mechanics that exist in the game, such as materia melding (kind of like enchanting or upgrading you gear) and etc. The primary issue for some people may lie in the fact that the MSQ is the main way for progression in the game. I do not mean in terms of leveling as there do exist alternative methods. However, the MSQ is the primary way of unlocking most of the game's content like dungeons, trials (boss fights), and raids. You also need certain MSQ quests in order to obtain a job for your class; for example, you need the MSQ quest of "Sylph Management" completed in order for you to get your job at lvl 30 for the ARR classes. If you are a new player and don't mind the quest grind and actually enjoy immersing yourself in the world, then by all means go through the MSQ. If you are the type of new player that just wants to quickly catch up with the current expansion and go through content like grinding for gear and stuff, SQEX does offer a story skip and a job boost (choosing a class and boosting to 60) for a price on the Mogstation website. Overall, the MSQ is a great experience if you enjoy a good storyline.
Combat, Classes/Job, Gear:
FFXIV has a combat system that shares similarities to other MMOs like WoW. You have a hotbar where you can bind skills to certain keys that you wish. You can tab target or, if you are strange, you can click on the target. Your character has an auto attack that often mixes in damage with your other skills. The game has three primary roles: tank, healer, DPS. Tank and healer are kind of self-explanatory. Tank has the job of making sure they have all the mobs aggro directed towards themselves. Tanks have many skills that can create more emnity (what they call aggro in this game), have skills that can reduce damage, and some ahve skills that can assist other party members. Healers have the job of healing....yeah, that's obviously expected isn't it. Some healers have skills that have other effects like regen (heal over time), shielding (preventing certain amount of damage), or providing a variety of different buffs to party members. Healers also have spells that do single target damage, damage over time, and aoe damage. DPS have the role as the party's primary source of dealing damage. There are also different types of DPS: melee dps, caster dps, and ranged physical dps. All these different types have their own playstyles and sometimes either has their own kind of gear or share it with other classes/jobs. As of the current state of the game, you no longer put attribute points into stats, rather it will do it for you and will place them in stats depending on what class/job you are leveling. Even though you have to pick a class to start off in when you first create you character (cannot select Heavensward or Stormblood jobs for starting character), at some point in the game, it will allow you to try out other classes/jobs, meaning that you could level and max out every single class/job on a single character. Gear provides defense and extra stats to your character. Gear is typically classified into 4 categories: all classes, disciple of war (tanks, melee dps, and physical ranged dps), disciple of magic( healers and casters), and the tanky gear (tanks and sometimes the lancer/dragoon). You can meld materia in order to add additiional stats, use crafting skills to make gear have highher quality, and can either dye the gear into different colors or glamour it (the ability to change the look of a piece of gear into the look of another piece of gear/article of clothing/etc).
Combat content and noncombat content:
Typically in FFXIV, outside of MSQ, there are other pieces of content that you use to grind levels and gear for your character. These include levequests (tasks), FATEs (area of event), "logs", dungeons, trials, and raids. There is also PvP content, though it isn't a popular piece of content compared to other MMOs. For dungeons and trials, you typically are grouped with other players into a party of 4 or 8, depending on which dungeon/trial, and go through the instance with those members. A typical dungeon will have your party go through the map, killing low tier mobs and/or completing specific objectives, fight a few mini bosses that have their own specific mechanics, and, when finally reaching the end, your party will battle with the final boss. After defeating the minibosses and final boss, there will be a treasure coffer with the dungeon specific drops. The mechanic for the loot will consist of the coffer giving you drops and you and your party members have to vote "Need", "Greed", or "Pass". Rolling Need or Greed will randomly generate a number between 1-100, with the highest number in the party obtaining the item. Rolling Pass will give an automatic zero and will not give you the item. Trials are boss fights, with trials usually being unlocked during the MSQ. Your battle fights a boss that has their own special mechanics. Raids consist of either 8-man or 24-man parties and are similar to dungeons, although are usually larger in scale and more difficult. Some dungeons, trials, and raids also have harder modes which you can unlock. These are usually much tougher and introduce additional mechanics. Overall the content that requires some combat are usually very fun and one way to grind for gear in the game.
The noncombat content mainly consists of two things: gatherer/crafter classes and social aspects. For gatherer/crafter classes, they are self explanatory. You play classes that have the ability to either gather certain things (like mining) or craft certain things (like cooking). These classes level similarly to the combat classes, with their own way to grind levels and gear. The social aspect consists of different things like making friends or joining a Free Company (guild) and etc.
Community:
The FFXIV community, IMO, is very friendly and often sociable. For example, let's say you are a new player and it's your first time in a dungeon. If you let your party members know, usually they'll be nice and try to guide you through the dungeon, often giving tips and advice. The community, in my view, can be categorized into 3 types, with one type having 2 subtypes. Type 1 is your casual joe. They just want to play the game and enjoy their time. They are often friendly, sociable, and sometimes act as a helpful advisor to newbies. The majority of FFXIV players, or at least the ones I interacted with, fit into this category. Type 2 is hardcore bob. These are the ones that are the hard grinder, no nonsense during my raid kind of people. This type falls into 2 subtypes: the serious and the jerk. The serious hardcore player is exactly as they sound. During a raid, you may see them often being the serious shotcaller and what not. They are not meanies per say, they just take themselves seriously. The jerk is like the serious but will often flame and be toxic, sometimes without reason. Deal with them civily and kick them if they get too bad. Type 3 is the roleplayer. These people are a rarity but are a bundle of fun. They'll usually interact with others in a way that fits with their chosen role.
If you read up to this point, then I congratulate you and thank you for taking time to read all off this. It's my first time writing a review so I may have overdone it. FFXIV is a great game and I do recommend it. The game allows for a free trial period where you can play up to lvl 35, giving you a chance to see if you like it or not. Have fun and game on!

Not many modern RPGs can boast the presentation of a genuine challenge. Legend of Grimrock does, in mother♥♥♥♥ing spades. Thrown into a dark, dank, critter and/or zombie infested dungeon (the eponymous Grimrock), your four plucky prisoners must use any means at their disposal to escape from Grimrock, or, as is often the case, keep from becoming a stain on the rough-hewn cobblestone wall, while contending with the constant threat of hunger and/or giant venomous murder spiders.
Every level was designed by hand; every trap, monster, mushroom, and weapon lovingly tucked exactly where it needed to be to make your experience as harrowingly awesome as possible. This is an old-school dungeon crawl through and through, and it'll never let you forget it. If you're, like me, too impatient and dense to check every nook and cranny for a secret cache of items, you won't see a longsword until you're 45 minutes in.
The game has got some shortfalls, however. The tile-based movement means that it's pretty easy to take advantage of the enemy AI (something the rogue's assassination ability is built to take advantage of). Trolls, which are practically LoG's mascot and therfore built up as being incredibly badass, are kind of disappointing to fight because of this, since their charge attack (which they do whenever you're at least one tile away from them) leaves them wide open for a backstab. They will, however, give you a thundering ♥♥♥♥♥-slap for your trouble if you try to dance around them as per usual. The puzzles can somethimes get a little frustrating, too, if you're used to having more than a cryptic, vague line of text to go on.
Overall, it's pretty great, and triumphing over an army of poisonous ents and badass,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off mudcrabs makes you feel awesome like few other things can.

I should have learned my lesson from Red Dragon.
As much as I have enjoyed my time with Wargame (discounting Red Dragon), and RUSE before it, I cannot support Eugen anymore.
This game has taken the worst parts from RUSE and Wargame and thrown them into one horribly put together and exceptionally imbalanced game, with questionable historical accuracy to boot. As a player that used to be heavily involved (and successful) in the competitive scene of Wargame, I had fallen out of touch with competitive gaming, and quite frankly stopped caring for it, so I approached Steel Division from a more casual perspective.
Sadly, even from a casual perspective, the game is filled with far more frustration than anything else. Phasing system is a recycled idea from RUSE that didn't work back then, and doesn't work now. Perhaps it could work if done by a company that can balance the game, but considering Wargame took 3-4 years and two games to balance, only to then be completely unbalanced by Eugen listening to the voices of many rather than the experienced few, I really don't want to be sitting around waiting for balance. As it stands, the balance is far from good, and yes it's beta, and yes there isn't all the content yet, but you don't throw in all the content and then balance it at the end. You start with a balanced foundation and then add content that doesn't throw it off balance (See every successful competitive RTS, FPS, MOBA game).
Edit:
To be fair there is some improvements that do deserve my praise, but honestly I can't believe it's taken this long for them to be added to what is essentially Wargame: 1944 (<--- a better title than what you chose btw). Edit2: I forgot it was published by Paradox, I guess Focus Home own the rights to the Wargame name.
Allowing units to be given orders in the deployment phase is amazing, and would have been nice to have in Wargame. Also the ability to see your line of site is a useful tool that was in RUSE anyway, but not Wargame.
Well I doubt my review will influence many peoples decisions, but for those of you who like the game, enjoy the flavour of the month battlegroups and units for the next 2 years until you finally concede and move onto a different game.

After a fairly rough start to its open beta, with a lack of content, poor optimization and graphical performance, I'm glad to say that the game is shaping up to look quite promising. As the beta has progressed Eugen has given us a trickle of new content in the form of new divisions, new maps and a few balance changes here and there to adress the main problems of the game.
I'm happy to see that Steel Division doesn't fully copy the Wargame series and comes up with a few new ideas of its own, that coupled with a change of setting, and to some extent scale, makes Steel Division feel like a familiar but nonetheless fresh experience.
The new frontline mechanic coupled with the hedge-filled maps make every bit of territory gain and outmaneouvering of your opponent feel much more satisfying, Command units are no longer limited to just hiding in a forest for the entirety of the game and now accompany your troops and provide them with tangible bonuses and at times invaluable support. Planes feel better to use and more effective overall as even your fighter planes can swoop down to supress enemy artillery or AT guns. The units might move a bit slower with truck and tanks struggling to conquer the rough terrain yet despite of this, every engagement and firefight seems every bit as fast and violent as those of previous games.
All of these little new ideas and changes come together to make Steel Division feel like a promising new strategy game in a genre that rarely has the courage to stray away from the tried and tested methods.
*I should also add that - at least for me - the last patches have visibly improved both performance and graphical quality, though there is still work to be done on that front.

I can't remember the last time I got so giddy over smooth game controls.
Honestly, I had very little interest in Helicopter simulators growing up. I recalled seeing Comanche on game shelves back in the day and the boxart featuring explosions and burning tree’s wooed me until I realized just how many buttons would need to be pushed just so I could take off.
And I REALLY wish I did pick it up, because this game plays like a dream!
I bought Comanche just recently alongside another helicopter sim “FairStrike”. Spoiler warning, it was♥♥♥♥♥♥ Feeling burned by one sim I felt reluctant to give this a go but after one long shift I sat down and gave it a whirl.
And one take off later, I fell in love.
Comanche is a simple game. You are a helicopter pilot who commands the mother of all attack gunships and travels the globe blowing tanks, rogue governments, terror cells and opposing helicopter pilots sky high. There is a plethora of characters who assist you in your missions, which range from search and destroy to stealth flying through canyons to avoid SAM’s and other pilots.
Graphics themselves are also very bleached and look hideous up close, but that is to be expected for such an old game set in massive levels. Speaking of which, there are 31 in all, yet they go by in the blink of an eye. I Played around 8 hours (internet’s been jumpy so not all hours were clocked) so I wouldn’t call it a long-burn of a game.
All and all, graphics aren’t exactly eye-catching and the story is shrug-worthy yet does the job in establishing who is who and what needs to be blown up. So, what made me fall in love in such a short time-span?
I’m not going to sugar coat anything, this game features perhaps some of the best helicopter controls I have ever seen. Yes, there are far more buttons and commands compared to more mainstream games yet I quickly came to memorize them without even scanning the options menu! Everything from deploying flares, calling for backup, selecting weapon-modes to camera angles and even navigating obstacles with the WSAD layout feels so precise and buttery smooth!
Hell, the only gripe I ever had with the controls was how the auto-elevation on easier settings would lock up your speed for a brief second, that’s it! I never once felt frustrated playing this, I always felt that every failure or death was at my own hands when the going got tough!
As someone who rarely plays simulators, I can’t recommend Comanche 4 enough. The game hasn’t aged well but if you are in the mood for blowing up oil fields with sharp controls that can cater to newbies and enthusiasts alike, then look no further! This game is a little on the short side, but it’s a blast!

Skip to the bottom for a summary.
Gameplay- Pretty typical JRPG as far as gameplay goes. You have your party and you explore dungeons, towns, and the overworld. As with most JRPG’s you can find a wide variety of armour and weapons, each with their own special abilities. The only feature that separates this game from any other JRPG is its combat. It is turn based, with the unique twist; after each turn the monsters slowly get more powerful. Ultimately all this normally does is forces you to use the spells that cause the most damage, and subsequently use up the most of your magic points. After the battle is over your characters will regain full health and a portion of their magic points back. This at first is pretty fun, however after a few hours you will only be playing this game for its storyline, as it is pretty repetitive. Also, each area has a predefined amount of monsters you can fight, which for me really encouraged exploration as I wouldn’t have to fight endless enemies. I would definitely recommend turning on the developer commentary as it is always optional to read, and is usually funny/insightful to read. 6.5/10
Sound- Really not much to say here, some catchy little tunes and mostly generic sounds. 5.5/10
Graphics- They are stylized to look retro and I believe it works out pretty well for the most part. The overworld and towns always look pretty good, and handcrafted. The dungeons on the other hand look all pretty similar and boring. The monster sprites however are beautiful. There are many, many monsters in this game and they all are unique and awesome! 7/10
Storyline- This is what makes this game rise above other similar games. This is an epic tale describing Cthulhu's struggle to regain his powers, and to do so he must become a hero. This is a very original idea, and was wonderfully delivered. Cthulhu is a great anti hero. All the side characters are well thought out and enjoyable. This game is funny, and is able to remain so for the entire game. This is by far the greatest aspect of the game. But I do feel as if the combat and exploration sometimes was not broken up enough by story bits. Honestly I would have preferred a shorter game that focused much more on the story than anything else. 9/10
Summary- What a wonderful little gem, and an addicting one at that. Despite the generic gameplay, the storyline rises this above most of its competition. The graphics achieve what they set out to do, as does the sound.

Legend of Grimrock is a old school dungeon crawler offering intense combat, puzzles, exploration, and most of all survival. This game actually reminds me of Shining In The Darkness. Legend of Grimrock offers some really neat features like the ability to eat so you won’t starve. This might throw more casual players off the game because you’ll be managing a entire party and you have to make sure each person/thing in your party is well fed, has plenty of health, weapons, armor, and torches before you decide to continue on your descent into this maze like prison that you’re trapped in. The character creator in this game is awesome. It’s very old school like dungeons and dragons. Basically you choose a portrait, decide on what class you want that character to be, then choose their strengths, and traits. No one character will be good at everything so be careful on what you choose. I always have two warriors, a rogue, and a mage in my party and i’m doing pretty good with them.
The way you learn magical spells is by finding them on pieces of paper scattered around the dungeon. These papers will have the correct way for you to cast the spell. You can also randomly try and cast them but when you’re in a fight you really don’t have time to experiment with your spells. As you find weapons and armor throughout the dungeon you’ll be faced with a choice. Who will you give them too? This is what I love about this game. You won’t find enough equipment for everyone and you have to decide who you want to have them. I usually get my warriors set up for battle before anyone else. I gave the bow to my assassin, staff to me mage, axe to my minotaur, and sword and shield to my human/warrior/tank. Combat in this game is also very old schools. You click on your weapon to attack the enemy in front of you and watch as your sword cuts through the enemy. It’s very basic and easy to learn but it’s up to you to strategize and use tactics when you encounter a large group of enemies.
You don’t want to get surrounded in this game and risk losing one of your party members because they will not come back. Once they die they’re gone until you can find a giant sized blue crystal to revive them and that’s not always easy. In order for you to recover some health you can either rest by pressing the R button or by using a health potion that you’ll eventually find. You can also heal with a magic spell but I wouldn’t advise that since it’s not all that useful. The best ways to heal are by resting, or using a healing potion. When you rest your characters will get hungry so you’ll have to feed them. It’s up to you to decide when to rest and if you have enough food to eat when you’re done resting. ugly

As of 2017, this is the only MMO worth paying a sub fee for, and I'd argue worth the time investment as well. There are a signifigant lack of RNG or gambling mechanics that are immensely present in the competition so this is easily the most popular MMO that subscribes the least to predatory anti-consumer tactics. At times, it feels like an antithesis to the standard formula that Activision Blizzard has set; FFXIV is a game made of genuine passion with an inspiring production story and has some great ideas that breed quality of life mechanics without sacrificing much in terms of rewarding gameplay that isn't watered down in an effort to appeal to less intuitive players. Of course, the game can be enjoyed on many levels of difficulty, but FFXIV will test your ability to juggle a sometimes overwhelming (even as of 4.0) amount of skills as well as the various hazards of combat, though operating at peak performance is never quite required in casual play. The lack of things like damage meters is hugely beneficial for the community, leaving group leaders to find more conventional methods of judging a players contribution, and thorough additions like Mentorship and the Novice Network serve to make this one of more friendly communities. Of course it is an online game so you will meet some bad eggs, but there are systems in game that allow you to easily find and keep in touch with nice players. Even still, the variety of game styles and the depth of combat will be off-putting for those not already familiar with older MMOs and this is one of the game's greatest failings.
There is an emphasis is on the game's story, an incredibly lengthy and sprawling tale that unfortunately takes many, many, hours of game time to become truly worthwhile. ARR's story is rather lacking - and the endless amount of post ARR content the player needs to do to access Heavensward is unfortunate. Players can buy their way past this content and continue on with the story in Heavensward but it's still an incredibly rough entry barrier that should be addressed one day. That said, especially once the story reaches Heavensward, it does come into its own as a genuine Final Fantasy title. In my opinion, it stands amongst the greatest in this franchise in terms of story, the emphasis being on consistently great dialogue, well developed characters, and strong narrative arcs that are supported well by longform MMO storytelling. The result is a Final Fantasy game that not only plays significantly differently from the other titles but also in the way that the player experiences its many nuanced developments.
I wouldn't recommend this to someone who isn't willing to embrace it as an MMO or has a prejudice against them, but it looks and feels like iconic Final Fantasy and, as a fan, the payoff for a steep learning curve was immensely worth it for me. I'm looking forward to seeing how Square further develops this property, but even as it is now, this is one of my favorite games of all time.

Full game is better then expected. It's very funny to see some of the reviews so I'll try to debunk some of the myths. Overall though the main part of this (Being a Strategy game), the Strategy is great. You have to move up from cover to cover, Combat spacing is important, Fire superiority is important, and using the right unit for the right job is great.
The Unit AI is stupid; Nope the Units will automatically stop targeting pinned units to fire at units that can Actually hit it. Anti Tank weapons will fire at infantry, but the instant a Tank shows up, their priority changes.
The Enemy AI is stupid; Nope. The AI will actively scout, probe, and build Spearheads before attacking! Not just spawn and send one at a time, they wait to build up at spots they think are weak. In fact, I've seen the AI start a push, I killed their two tanks, the Infantry immediately retreated to their Defensive positions, and the enemy sent a Smoke bombing to cover it!
[Insert Faction/Battlegroup] is OP/Horrible; It's funny because all through Beta people complained that Allies were OP, and now the Chat seems to this Axis are OP. Go figure. I think that fact that the new OP keeps changing, just shows that each battlegroup is unique and decently balanced enough that as players learn, new things become too Good or too Bad. I'm sure we'll find some unbalance down the line, but Eugen is known for constant balance and upgrades to their games.
