This is a hesitant recommendation, because this game has a lot (and I mean A LOT) of rough edges.
On the one hand, the pixelated graphics are actually pretty damn effective and lends themselves to a unique, interesting black and white and red art style. The atmosphere is also genuinely well done, with terrific audio, solid music and creepy details that really stand out. I especially enjoyed a level that takes place in a forest that's sparsely populated by a few different buildings, because that kind of setting just gets me. I love forests because you're surrounded on all sides by trees, making it feel oppressive and bleak.
But then there are the downsides. For one, this game is absolutely loaded with typos, and syntax and grammar errors. Normally I can forgive the occasional typo since, as a writer, I know how hard it is to proof read your own work and catch everything. But there are typos EVERYWHERE in this game, from the text based narration to the scattered notes you find everywhere. It took me out of the game a lot, which is bad for a horror title. The story, what little there is, also feels rather formulaic and that it was written by a teenager (it reminds me a lot of what I used to write in my high school days). In the beginning, there's not much information, then pretty much everything that's going on is explained in a note that is extremely on the nose and feels very out of place (seriously, the note uses the term "by the way" to explain what's going on... by the way is something that should be used in a casual conversation, not in a horror title whose aim is to unsettle the player).
Still, if you love horror like I do this title is worth it, especially if you can find it on sale. The atmosphere is very, very well done and manages to be subtle, which is something sorely lacking in other titles like Outlast. The environments and sound design are particularly well done. Just don't expect much from the story and get ready for all the typos, which, in case you haven't figured it out, are abundant and bothered me to no end.

Normally I dont review games, but this one deserves it. 112 hours after I got this game, and I'm in love.
Pros and Cons dont really do this game justice, So I'll just explain it myself. You start off the game, all alone, with almost nothing. First, you get a drill down. Then that drill is feeding to a furnace that smelts the ores. Then you use the smelted ore to make more drills. Now you have a line of drills all feeding furnaces. Now you have electricity. Now you're starting research. Suddenly you have machines assembling everything you need to get constant automatic research without lifting a finger. Now you have trains wheeling in ores from distant outposts, and then cars and tanks, then the aliens invade and you fight them off with your power armor, then you have robots building and moving stuff, constantly keeping you supplied. Then you have stuff everywhere, you somehow manage to turn this mess into your first rocket, and then you win. But you didn't really win. You could've done better. Been more efficient. So you start again, and again, and again. You keep going and going and dont stop. Because even though there's a point where you win, you never really win. There's always a more efficient way to do it, a more efficient design. The most satisfying part of Factorio is the very end, when everything just works and it's not a game anymore. You just sit back and watch. You don't play, because the game plays itself. This game proves beyond a doubt a really deep message, actually. The human brain, given the right tools, is capable to do anything it wants without having to do anything. And that's where Factorio shines. It's very core concept isn't actually a game, it's a game you don't play. And the idea is so amazing and executed so perfectly it just feels right. This game would be worth it even if it was 100$. No matter who you are, you should at least try the demo, and just try to prove me wrong. Trust me, you won't want to.
Also be ready for the many maths, as calculating ratios once you get passed red science are time consuming to say the least

"A masterpiece leaving me wanting for so much more."
Ah, where do I begin? Supergiant Games, what have you done to me? Thank you for making me cry twice within just 2 days. Along with Bastion, this has easily become one of my favorite games of all time. Please keep doing what you're doing and never settle for less than awesome works. Having that said, let me get to the review already:
Art - Jen Zee's art is right up my alley. Hand painted quality is always a winner in my book. The elements used for the visual theme are all of my interest and blended in very nicely. Cyberpunk, yes, but you also have Vintage, Mafia, Urban Nightlife and a unique style of symbol art used for the glitch and circuitry aesthetic. She captured my heart on Bastion's art but her work on Transistor made it sing.
Animation and VFX - Fluid and stunning. Of course with a game this visually intense one would have liked more cutscenes. Sadly, the lack of it is what to expect from smaller, indie game developers but this does not hinder the audience's experience in any way. I would have wanted more colors for the VFX considering the Transistor being called a brush.
Audio - Once again, Logan Cunningham. I really love his voice, ever since Bastion. Sunkrish Bala did an awesome job for Royce Bracket too. I found it funny that he sort of reminds me of Owen WIlson. I did noticed that picking up cells makes a chirp that reminded me of navigating through Final Fantasy menus. For the music, I listened to the OST before getting my hands on the game and I must say that I didn't like it at first, maybe because at that time, I didn't give it a chance and wasn't in the mood to sit down with it. Now that I have played the game and sat down to chill with it, I would rate the album 10/10. Thumbs up for Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett for lending her soulful voice.
Story and Plot - There is a style in how Transistor narrates its story that is seen in other games such as Shadow of the Colossus. Most of it is open ended and left to our imagination. You either hate it or love it. I respect that Supergiant Games went with this style but again I will say that I am left wanting for more. It's like that one recipe you love so much that you just either want more or want to try more versions of it. Without giving away spoilers, I must say that even without having to go against the Process, Red is a very strong protagonist and I can't imagine how I would feel if I was in her shoes. Clearly, I could feel the weight of emotion and pent up stress that built up toward the end. Cliche as it seems, she does prove that actions are stronger than words.
Gameplay - Because of the battle system, I fondly categorize this game as a "Battle Puzzler" RPG. It slightly reminds me of Vagrant Story and Max Payne in which you take advantage of pausing or slowing the moment to contemplate on how to defeat your enemies. I guess it depends on your playstyle. The battle mechanics are simple enough to understand and intricate to experiment with. As you unlock more abilities, MEM, and slots, you will be able to explore different playstyles. I've seen other players preferring to play more in real-time than rely on Turn(). So far, I find myself very Turn()-heavy which makes the game feel more strategic than a regular hack-and-slash game.
What I Don't Like - I guess the only criticism I would give this game is on some of the UI and Game Design. They abilities are displayed in a way that whatever new Function you get (by either level-up reward or story) is displayed right after the last Function. There is no way to sort or stack them. It may seem okay during the first playthrough. But in the Recursion, you will learn that you can acquire more than of the same Function.The upgrade and passive slots were too small for me and the Spark() and Flood() icons look to similar to each other. The EXP system to me was iffy since the story was very linear. Stage after stage, the little victory screen would pop up. I thought it was unnecessary to display the enemy body count after every battle.
TL;DR and Extra - Beautiful aesthetic, unique storytelling, wonderful story, great music, fun gameplay. Supergiant Games' works are raw, gritty, handcrafted masterpieces that can contend with Triple A games any day in my book. I am excited for their next title "Pyre" that is coming out soon. I hardly doubt it would be done but It would thrill me even more if they could make a PvP mode or even an online PvP oriented pre-quel or sequel that would show more of the Transistor world.

The combat can be real-time, but the option to pause the combat (to allow the player to lineup whatever combat powers the have 'slotted'), and the ability to group power-ups into units of three, makes the combat more tactical.
Negatives would be that I found Transistor a little bit easy to complete.  I only retried three fights, in order to avoid temporarily losing access to an ability, and managed too complete the game in four evenings, about 12-16 hours, and I'm not sure of it's replay value.  I'm setting this negative against the price I paid for Transistors, £2,99, which almost negates it.  That's less that a cup of coffee, and that wont give me the 12 hours of entertainment that Transistor has.
I'm not sure I would be happy paying full price for Transistor, although trying through a replay will be necessary before confirming that, and I should point out that I come from the days of £2.99 Spectrum and Commodore 64 games!!
I'm now off to look at Bastion, by the same company, and expect to be purchasing that.  I'll update as appropriate.

Honestly, as of right now there are too many issues with the game to even consider recommending - and these go beyond the 'It's a beta', especially when judging the game against past Eugen releases. I remember when we were repeatedly promised in Red Dragon's beta that naval combat would be improved - it is still to this day terrible.
Beyond the glitches and the overwhelmingly poor balancing that Eugen has always had (and I'm not referring to balancing between factions, but rather balancing between units) currently the game can be described as a campfest; the maps whilst "historical" lack hills or altitude alterations of any substantial (if any) amount, meaning everything is just a flat field with a few clumps of trees interupting - this means that the already 'bad' terrain of Normandy is even worse; the only barriers to long ranged fire are the aforementioned clumps of trees and the occassional town. This means infantry are essentially target practice, something only accentuated by the limited quantities of infantry you can deploy when compared to tanks (to put it another way, you can get considerably more than 30 tanks onto the field at once with an armoured deck, whereas you'll be struggling to field more than a few hundred infantry, unless you're spamming the militia equivalent).
The terrain issues add another ridiculous element - in open combat, only expensive tanks are useful, in the twisting bocage areas, only cheap tanks are useful, because cheap tanks can knock out frontally virtually all tanks, and setting up ambushes to deal with the only tanks that are immune to point blank fire are worth 300 pts and can just as easily be killed by flanking hits. Eugen appears to have taken the ~100m range penetration values, and then put that as the ~1km range penetration, with extra penetration gained per 100m closer to it than maximum range you are. This means you get ridiculous occurances like M8 scout cars knocking out Panthers frontally. Conversely, as certain tanks have total dominance at long range, it is impossible to advance across open field against them - meaning again, huge numbers of cheap units are better than middle quality units.
Then you have the bizarre balancing decision with planes and AA. AA is poor at killing air units, and the bigger the AA the worse it gets; they are however excellent at suppressing ground units, meaning for some absurd reason, planes are currently the best means to deal with annoying AA pieces; unless they're armoured. Because planes do absurdly limited damage to armoured units; even when those armoured units are vehicles like scout cars. Eugen apparently missed the point in the history books where air forces were destroying tanks - as even direct hits from heavy bombs and artillery will be shrugged off by tanks with a brief period of 'panicking'.
Which brings me onto the panicking mechanic - you will lose control of the unit which will then 'retreat', unless it's a vehicle and is disabled, at which point it will just sit there under heavy fire until it unpanics, which it won't because it's under fire. Units will also 'retreat' into enemy positions, because apparently being shot at by a tank on your right makes you forget there was a tank only 2 seconds previously shooting at you from your left, and makes you run at that tank. Whilst problematic in general this comes to head when tanks are hit by a flanking hit - they will turn and reverse away from whatever hit them, meaning that they will now retreat along the length of a frontline (for a fairly considerable amount of time I should add) getting shot at by a dozen enemy guns that previously wouldn't hurt them, but now can penetrate their sides easily. Involving the same mechanic, infantry and gun positions will sit under fire, refusing to return fire but also refusing to withdraw to a safe position meaning unless you have a means to panic whatever is shooting at them, they will stay there until dead.
In addition to all of the above there are issues with the core of the game - the UI is clunky (unlikely to change), the Battlegroups management somehow succeeds at being worse than Wargame's and is even more cluttered than before, there is far less variety than there could and should be in regards to infantry (many formations are obsolete, most divisions lack access to more than a single form of infantry transport), along with a number of lacking areas in vehicles and other units, planes are arbitrarily equipped (often poorly; much like Wargame's) and the graphics are rather flawed. Controls, whilst not particularly inferior to their predecessor games, are awkward, and often units will go to the wrong positions, particularly noticeable when trying to send infantry into tree lines (where they will randomly walk part of the way out) this is a 'feature' that has existed in Wargame for some time, so I expect no fix.
There are other issues, but the fact that some of the above will never be fixed means the game is already looking to have a short life expectancy, Wargame: Red Dragon is by far more enjoyable as it currently stands and I've seen nothing to indicate that my opinion of the game will change; in the event it does I will revisit this review and alter it.
POST LAUNCH UPDATE:
So in addition to the above there are a number of other issues that have now come to the forefront:
Single player: The campaigns are trivially easy (out of the 8 missions I did, I "struggled" only on one of them, which was because the game told me x, y and z would be important and it turned out I had no need of them, I failed by a narrow margin; second attempt I wiped the floor with the AI.) The AI is the same dumb as a fork AI as was in Wargame, with the specific exception that it no longer appears to map-hack and counter build as much as it did in Wargame. The result is a mess where the AI will human wave assault a defensive position until it runs out of troops and the player wins the match. ALL 8 campaign missions ended up devolving into this form of combat.
Multiplayer: The servers weren't exactly the most stable thing ever in the Beta, however there now appears to be a critical issue with them whereby they fail and kick everyone off the server (with the somewhat ludicrous message of "your computer seems to be too slow": yes, because everyone in the match went from fine to DCing in 10 seconds flat but it's an individual computer rather than the server that is at fault.
They've also added a feature where a medium AI takes over from quitters - but see the "dumb as a fork" remarks I made earlier - the AI just suicides over and over again on human players - prior to my DC I was facing an AI that was doing an infantry charge over open terrain against dug in MGs and tanks.... in destruction mode. The result was a moderate lead to my team turning into an overwhelming lead (I killed over a thousand points in a few minutes of the AI pushing me). This, as could be expected, made more people quit. Leading to other players inflicting similar annihilations. Eugen should never have implemented an AI that just suicidally attacks to replace the quitters.

At the time of this edit, AAC is still in early access (update 8.5), but I'm already extremely happy with my purchase, and I can't recommend this game enough. Additionally, future WitchBeam titles will be unquestioned day-0 purchases for me.
I nominated this game for the "I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won an Award" Steam Award 2016.

I've been having heaps of fun playing the Steam Early Access version of Assault Android Cactus and recently published a review of it. Here's an excerpt:
"Responding to a distress call from the crippled Genki Star, Junior Constable Cactus soon discovers she is overwhelmed by malfunctioning worker robots. Desperate to save the ship, Cactus battles her way through deck after deck of rampaging robots and bosses whilst befriending and recruiting androids along the way to heart of the ship, where presumably they will find the cause the Genki Star's malfunctions.
Assault Android Cactus features four main playable android characters: the titular Cactus, a plucky, but perhaps out of her depth police android; Holly, a nervous inventory manager; Lemon, a trainee medic with a happy outlook; and Coral, a fitness instructor with an outgoing personality. In addition to these four, a range of additional unlockable characters are planned. The current Steam Early Access and Humble Store DRM free versions of the game include Starch (who is my personal favourite), an insane android with a mysterious past. Starch's silly presentation shows that this game doesn't take itself too seriously and values fun above all else.
Where Assault Android Cactus shines (even in its current unfinished state) is in the execution of mechanics, where the same attention to detail and stylistic choices already covered have been brought to bear on creating a robust and satisfying experience that is as enjoyable the fiftieth time as it was the first."

A well-done first person dungeon crawler, reminiscent of classic games such as the original Bard's Tale trilogy.  The graphics are well-done and the combat is fluid and engaging.  Though there are some frustrating parts, the ability to backtrack and find a restore gem as many times as you need to lets you pick away at even the largest enemies.  Keep your eyes open and inspect all the walls you come across--the best weapons and armor are often hidden behind secrets or puzzles, making this more of a thinking man's dungeon crawler rather than simply being a corridor full of enemies.  The ambitious scope of this game gives it an incredible amount of depth, from the food system to the multiple skills that can be advanced for each character type, resulting in a game which can be very accommodating to any playstyle.
I did not get into the custom dungeon creation, so I have no insight into its use nor on the addition of custom dungeons from the Steam Workshop, but having those available does create a massive venue for replayability.
Verdict:  Engaging and fun, but wait for a discount.

One of the best classic-like RPGs out there. Has a pen-and-paper feel to it and very unique combat.
This is a tile-based game wherein you control 4 characters (a mixture of fighter / rogue / mage). You can either use pre-determined characters or create your own which involves distributing stat points and choosing various attributes. You can make everything from a tank, to a melee rogue, archer, spell-caster, etc.
Movement is limited to moving forward / back / left / right along the tiles. This actually works out pretty well, partly because the setting is that of a jail or dungeon so it feels very confined to begin with.
Combat is very unique and pretty addictive. Your characters are arranged in a square - two in the front, two in the back. You really need to plan your fights and reposition your characters as you go. For example, a melee character may not be able to attack from the back row, but he won't take any damage either. Archers and spell-casters do well in the back, but take a lot of damage in the front. Etc. You attack by clicking your characters' weapons, each of which is on a cool-down, which gives you time to re-position your characters in real-time. I also find myself strafing back-and-forth (recall the way movement works, so you can try to force enemies between a few tiles). In larger fights, this can work against you as you can get trapped in a corner. There's a lot of strategy going on.
Spell casting is also very unique. You click a combination of runes to cast a spell. This requires a bit of thought as you can't save rune combinations.
If you liked Eye of the Beholder on SNES, you will like this. A really simple RPG that corners the action RPG style perfectly.

Such a great tribute to Eye of the Beholder, and using modern day tech only makes it better, never spoiliing the classic feel.
I can only hope this is the first of about 30 games, all paying homage to the classic, and evolving the gameplay forward.

Not since Portal have I played a puzzle game that made me feel both stupid and empowered when I figured out the answer was right in front of my face. Legend of Grimrock combines an old-school dungeon crawler mixed with puzzles and RPG elements.
Synopsis: You control a group of 4 prisoners trying to escape Grimrock by solving puzzles and fighting monsters. Puzzles can be as simple as a hidden button on a wall or as complex that things may take time and patience to solve.
Gameplay: The best way I can describe this game is if you mixed D&D and Myst, with tons of aggravation. The Legend of Grimrock isn’t as one dimensional as the art style and movement may lead you to believe. Many of the puzzles will leave you scratching your head and swearing there isn’t a solution. The other aspect of the game which I believe could use some work is the battle system. As intricate as the puzzles can be, the system to fight monsters throughout gets repetitive and leaves a lot to be desired. It’s a mix between real time and turn based, with a focus on the formation of your team. If your characters use all short range abilities, you have to swap one of the two, for the one you want to attack. Many monsters can be defeated without much strategy and sometimes become a hindrance to trying to solve a puzzle. There are four classes you can choose from as you customize your perfect party, but very little direction or tutorial on how to use each class. I found myself having to look up a guide on how to use a mage to even understand what magic could be used. I have logged thirty-eight hours on this title (some of it was afk during a multiplayer game), but at less than $5, 20 hours of engrossing gameplay and a strong community following, this game is more than worth it.
Positive:
+Challenging puzzles are intricate enough to make you feel clever
+Game can be saved at any point.
+Large community following where content can be downloaded.
Negative
-Battle system can get repetitive.
-Not all classes are created equal.
Art Style/Graphics:  Think old school, first person, dungeon crawler. This game is a great blend of classic nostalgia with a jolt of current 3d graphics. Much of the game in spent in the darkness with two to three walls around you, but this doesn’t mean the creators were lazy. Attention is paid to simple cracks in the wall, to how the light bounces off each wall. To speak more about the lighting; this plays a huge role on the tone of the gameplay. The torches on the walls (or the ones you drop on the ground) limit vision to what can be around the next turn, which makes you feel like you are actually there.
Positive:
+Lighting is engaging.
+Can be played on lower-end computers.
+Can be played in Windowed Mode
Negative:
-Characters and enemies could be upgraded.
Soundtrack/Sound effects: This was one of the biggest negatives to the game for me. For the 20 hours I played, much of the time was spent trying to solve puzzles. To solve puzzles you have to explore the dungeon, often falling to lower parts. Hearing my characters yell as they were falling, over and over, got very annoying. This is only increased by the often reused sounds of the characters attacking and grunting in every fight they encounter. On a positive note, the minor sounds of metal doors closing, walls moving, or crackling of the fire, add a realistic aspect and can be heard in surround sound.
Positive:
+Simple sounds of environment
Negative:
-Repetitive
Cost: I personally bought this game in a Humble Bundle (only paying $5), but that being said, I would wait for this game to go on sale. $14 (full price) is a bit too much for the amount of gameplay in the standalone. At 75% off ($3.75) a case can be made. This does not include the amount of community related additions on the workshop; which is extensive
Positive:
+HUGE community created content
Negative:
-Full price not worth standalone

As a long time player of FS15 I am impressed with the new features in FS 17.  It is much better.  Highly recommend.
Pros:
Beautiful map with too many details to mention.
Amazing detailed equipment that you can operate yourself or hire out to workers.  The imagery and audio for the equipment is amazing high quality.
Many activities and equipment available to tend to your fields.
Animals are very well done and tending to them can be very rewarding.
Full economy to support your harvesting and animal husbandry activities.
In addition to playing with all the different equipment you have to manage your finances and build a profitable business.
Many customizable options to suit your preferences. From very easy to very challenging.
New music tracks (simulated radio stations) to listen to while you drive.
New pigs to raise and sell.
New trailers to haul animals.
New contracting jobs to earn money working other farmers fields.  Also a great way to try out different equipment.  Very well implemented in game.
New types of crops to grow.
New ways to fertilize, weed and improve crop yields.
Many information screens providing status information on all your activities.  Animal status page is much improved.  Status of fields is much improved.
Trains that you can load, drive and unload.  A beautiful addition.
Profit for silage greatly reduced. Hurrah.  No longer better than raising crops.
Tip anywhere!  Unload your trailers in storage shelters or anywhere you want and pick it up later with conveyer belts or loaders.
Customize your vehicles with different colors, tires, engines, attachments, etc.
Lease equipment instead of buying it.  Great for short term use or try it before you buy it.
Large modding community providing all kinds of mods for free.  Mods are very easy to install and there is a built in management screen to view and enable or disable mods.
Cons:
Silage bunkers: handling of chaff and silage in bunkers is much worse and frustrating to deal with to get ingredients for cow feed.
Only one new map so far.  Hopefully there are more planned for the future.
Radio stations are repeating play lists of the same songs. very repetittive.
Other:
There are gold nuggets to collect for a reward of $1,000,000.  It is optional.
Forestry income is lower but the equipment costs are very high.  It's not a way to get easy money.
Some bugs have been reported that haven't been fixed yet.
I strongly recommend this game if you enjoy simulations.

You follow the life of a person who has a friend named emily.  in a series of 5 years you experience certain points in emily and the characters life.  a party, a check in to find she hooked up with someone, a break up, a "what we did last year" talk, and a with out her saying "stop talking to me I'm with someone else".
So here is my truely overall complaint about this game.
The story forces you no matter what to be in a bad situation.  No matter what.  Emily always hooks up with either guy that isn't you at the end.  You always end up alone.  It's not to say it is forced to have a happy ending, but it doesn't let you be in a neutral place in life.  Maybe you didn't care about emily.  but that isn't the point really.  you are living the life of someone with regrets.
The first parts of the story seem fine, but all of a sudden you as the character take a huge turn and become obsessed with emily.  You want her now and you know you can't have her.  The event up to the last part are set so no matter what you lose her.
The last chapter is really where I had problems.  It happened a few time in the game prior to the last chapter.  You erase what you want to say in place of a neutral phrase.  It felt unnatural to me.  then again personally I just type things without fully thinking until its sent sometimes.  Also in the last chapter it feels kind of stalker-y the questions laid out.  You become a black spot in Emily's life.  You last questions get erased and are replaced with questions of someone trying to cling to the last moments without being able to speak.  It was a bit frustrating.
I played again, more clingy and another  trying to be distant.  Both led the same way..
Sure this is a free game and sure it is a single story, but I felt cheated out of my own experience to just feel the attempt to break away from someone until they choose to let you go.
Sound wise, it had small computer noises and a clock...honestly set a nice mood.  If anything the lack of sound and only the AIM sounds did keep me immersed.
graphic wise, my brian made fun of the resolution but wasn't bad.
Overall it is a good story...just not my story.  I played it 4 times to see what I could do.  one I played genuinely just answering and another by being a complete jerk (but not really because you are never a complete jerk)  It was entertaining, but I think the overall message of regret and never reaching someone is a little drab.  I think maybe more braching talks and more ending would of made this better.  Even one more chapter....maybe a way to get with emily or emma.  Maybe even talking with other people and hearing a deeper story about emma or you in the world.

The best Call of Duty ever made. After this it's all downhill.
Singleplayer wise it's pretty much the same as any other CoD in terms of gameplay. However, the characters, the story, and the events are highly entertaining and fun, and it's raised even higher in quality thanks to the master of music: Hans Zimmer.
Now, let's delve into what people really love about this game, the multiplayer.
CoD isn't the friendliest of communities out there, but it is amusing to see people get salty after you nuke them.
The game plays like any other CoD with modern weapons, only difference is that the maps are extremely well designed and the guns are mostly well balanced. The only exception is grenade launchers can be insanely OP, but they are really fun to play with and you can counter them if you know how to nade back.
Everyone plays TDM or FFA so let me describe that: TDM You run around and kill everyone you can to get the highest score for your team, whether you coordinate or not, to win with points or till the clock runs out. FFA is basically the same, except you just kill everyone. Nothing special really, but the simplicity is what's appealing. Combined with that as you get higher killstreaks, better rewards are given to you, and there is nothing more satisfying that getting in a chopper and wiping everybody out and then nuking everyone to end the match.
Now, there are occasionally some people in the game who do cheat to win, but it's not as common as you think, nor as inescapable. The simple solution is either to A. Troll them and get them to leave or B. Leave yourself, wait 30 seconds, then re-que for another lobby. Sadly this is match-making based so you can't choose your server (seriously who's bright idea was THAT). You also might find that there are people who accuse you of cheating if you're really good, and that's just because it's really hard to tell sometimes whether someone is trying to hide their hacks or not. However, most of the time it's not a result of hacking.
So yeah, I've wasted so many hours in this game and it's been a blast.
If you do end up getting this game to play multiplayer, you may want to get this -->
It's an FOV changer that the developers approve of since they forgot to include one for PC. Default FOV is 65 which makes people get headaches on PC, so this allows you to go up to 90.

So I don't own this on steam, but I've been playing it since it relaunched as "A Realm Reborn".
I'll start out by saying that this game moves at a much slower pace than pretty much any MMO I've ever played in the past. What I mean by that is that the GCD between abilities is 2.5 seconds each, which is enough time for you to really think about each and every click you make (Granted some classes have so many oGCDs that this statement isn't totally true). Anyone coming from games like WoW, The Secret World, SWTOR, or many other MMOs will probably feel like this makes the game take forever to play. I'd say after playing it on-off for 3 (I think?) years that this game is better for that feeling.
The narrative for the main scenario is perhaps the best story I've ever seen in an MMO, and being that you unlock features -through- doing the story, it makes that progression feel rewarding. The expansions haven't been a let down either, with Heavensward provoking tears from me in multiple places.
The music is also a huge high point to this game. There's so many original music pieces that at its release it held the record for most original music pieces produced for a video game (2013). Nobuo Uematsu is the composer/producer for a majority of the music (He has done music for many other Final Fantasy titles to date) in this game, and I don't think there's a single piece I've heard that I didn't love. I'd recommend anyone that plays this game play it with the music on, as you're really going to miss out without it.
The community for this game is somewhat what you'd expect from an MMO, though some shards have better communities than others. Having played WoW I would say that the worst community here is still %20000 times better than the best community there.
Not wanting to ramble I'll close with this. This is an MMO. If you play MMOs this game is going to feel familiar, but the change of pace will also feel very refreshing. This game offers one of the most polished story based experiences you can find in an MMO (these days it's almost more polished than some single player games!) and anyone playing the game for the story will fall in love instantly with it. I would recommend anyone that loves MMOs give this game a shot. I left a bit out for not wanting to type out a book, but this one really does have something for everyone (Progression Raids, Dungeons, Story Quests, amazing RP potential, constantly improving PvP).
Seriously throw your money at this immediately! or we can no longer be friends >.>

Legend of Grimrock is a dungeon crawling role playing game with an oldschool heart mated with modern execution. A group of prisoners are sentenced to certain death by exile to the secluded Mount Grimrock for vile crimes they may or may not have committed. Unbeknownst to the captives, the mountain is riddled with ancient tunnels, dungeons and tombs built by crumbled civilizations of days long past. If they ever wish to see daylight again and reclaim their freedom, the ragtag group of prisoners must form a team and descend through the mountain, level by level.
The game brings back an oldschool challenge with highly tactical real-time combat and grid-based movement, devious hidden switches and secrets as well as deadly traps and horrible monsters. Legend of Grimrock puts an emphasis on puzzles and exploration, and the wits and perception of the player are more important tools than even the sharpest of swords would be. And if you are a hardened dungeon crawling veteran and you crave an extra challenge, you can arm yourself with a stack of grid paper and turn on the Oldschool Mode, which disables the luxury of the automap! Are you ready for some classic dungeon-crawling first person perspective party-based RPG action? Are you ready to venture forth and unravel the mysteries of Mount Grimrock?

If you have fond memories of crowding around an Amiga with mates playing RPGs with a pen and paper in hand then LoG will definitely scratch that itch.  It's ultimately a shallow experience in that the rogue-like elements never truly change the gameplay and the interface, though simple, isn't particularly fun to use.
On sale it was a no-brainer.  At full price, get it only if it's really your thing, otherwise wait until it's on sale.

Surprisingly Excellent. Would I recommend to somebody who likes fighting games? Hell yes. To somebody who has no idea what a fighting game is? Perhaps, but I'd be more likely to show them to something like Skullgirls, due to this games fairly hefty pricetag and slightly lower production value. When this goes on sale, it is a steal.
Combat is interesting and almost every character feels unique in their own playstyle. Compared to a lot of other fighting games, the skill ceiling is intensely high, fast paced, well balanced and has one of the stronger training and tutorial mechanics for each of the fighters than almost any other fighting game out there. The Art is excellent for a sprite based system and the art assets for the story mode are definitely above average.
However, compared to probably it's most close rival, skullgirls, it has some things that just don't feel up to par with it's rival. It's characters though more plentiful are less interesting, the art is still, though well produced, fairly low rez and there is a huge issue with anyone running this game at any other frame rate other than 60. Dropping it down to 30 causes slow-motion and booting it up to 120-144hz causes ridiculous fast motion gameplay.

It has been a little while since I last played so if they made changes since, I will need to update this when I get to it. Overall it is a fantastic game but very challenging as you progress. There will be times where you build yourself up too much in one spot and leave yourself open in another. Hit and Run tactics are a bad idea. The enemy gets stronger the more you fail to wipe them out. This makes it rewarding to wipe them out in as few strikes as possible. But they will also send swarms at you so you cant just hide away and build up in the shadows. Losing is something you must be okay with as you learn how to build your defenses and prepare to do strikes against the enemy. Plan your resource gathering and be ready to restructure your entire base if needed. Power is precious, gaurd it with your life. Build safe zones within your base in case of a breach. If you love inventory management, crafting, and detail oriented base management with an unforgiving enemy, this is a game you will sink days into and love every second. This is not a casual game.

3. All intense fighting equals "rapidly clicking right mouse button to lock on targets and shooting down the targets with the corresponding weapon".
Will I recommend this game? If you are OK with playing on 4:3 resolutions and not afraid of♥♥♥♥♥♥ripping hardcore missions, this might be waht you seek. Otherwise, it's a thumb down.

Into The Gloom is fantastic, and a steal at $3.  Extremely atmospheric with great variety and sound design.  If you play this game late at night, with headphones atop an open mind, you'll absolutely love it.  Oh, and the best part?  Multiple endings that are actually unique!

Compared to the pixelated horror games that I've played, Into the gloom is pretty weak and mediocre. Despite being 'trendy' with it's graphics, Into the gloom plays a lot like any generic and boring horror game.
You are walking in a poorly lit corridor. You try a door, it's jammed. You try another one, its lock is broken. This door won't budge. This door is jammed. You look at notes on the wall. Game says it's just stuff, nothing of interest. You try a door, it's jammed. Another note on the wall, just some stuff. Computers won't work. You see random messages in the wall written in blood. "You will die." "There is no escape." Another jammed door. Linear corridors. Linear sewers. Message in blood. "He is watching." Jammed doors. A person who hanged himself. You will be seeing a lot of those people.
The actual story of the game is being transmitted to player through random notes. Diary entries. Just stuff, nothing of interest. It is clear that this game is intented to be played through more than once. There are keypads, locked doors, puzzles that you cannot solve during your first walkthrough, but the game won't tell you that. Some of the puzzles feel unfair. A jammed door was actually openable with a key. Who knew.
The game consists of approximately 6-7 areas. Hospital. Sewer. Prison. Subway. Forest/cemetary. Generic? Just stuff. Nothing of interest. All areas are poorly lit. Random messages written in blood. "You will surely die soon." You will find another notes, that someone tore of their diary and left behind in random places. Jammed doors. Doors that won't budge. Doors that have a broken lock. So many excuses why the doors cannot be opened, and why you must continue this linear passage. Message in blood. Just stuff. Nothing of interest. A hung person. So many people hanging from the ceiling. Did the developer think that the amount of bloody messages and hung people is directly proportional to the amount of horror?
Into the gloom might have been an okay game, but the price is too much. Seriously. There are pixelated horror games that are much more inventive, intuitive and scarier than this one. And they are free.
For reference:
ImScared: A Pixelated Nightmare
I See You

Excellent game - an exercise in minimalism. This game has better jump scares and MUUUUCH better chases with its hyper-pixelled goofy-pumpkin-headed villain than most horror AAA titles (most of which, yes, suck). The story is kinda goofy, but in a good way. A lot of the game is maze-ish, so you have to get used to the old-fashioned idea that not every door can be opened, and not every area has a "purpose". The puzzles are nicely balanced, the story unfolds in a pretty fun way, and like I mentioned before, the chase sequences are GREAT. It has a TON of charm (I'm a sucker for games made entirely by a single person, and this one did not diappoint) and I am super excited to see what Mr. Ramos has in store next!
Also, for fun, google '"into the gloom" developer' for an interesting take from Emmanuel on developing a game almost entirely by yourself, and check out the comments section of the Rock Paper Scissors review to see a bunch of old Amiga nerds waxing nostalgic about games that came out before Mr. Ramos was born.
EDIT: Forgot to mention, GREAT sound atmospherics and effects. I'm a developer/video editor by trade myself (not games, yet...), and I have an ancient, wizardly account on FreeSounds. It was heartwarming to see all the FreeSounds credits at the end of the game. As an aside, this is an inspiration to anyone who's ever wanted to make a game. Emmanuel shows that with a budget of $0, as long as you're talented, inspired, clever, and extremely hard-working, you can make something of real quality.

The few jumpscares all have build up and actually work quite well, and the atmosphere set up by the low draw distance and the fantastic sound design truly makes me dread going into the next room. The story CAN be a little predictable, but it's told very well and fits nicely into the story in context.
The puzzles in this game are hard. Hard as ♥♥♥♥. This isn't Amnesia where you have to flip six switches until you get the right order, no. This is genuine classic survival horror levels of puzzelry that i haven't seen in a long time. And while each puzzle is incredibbly difficult, they all make sense in the end, giving the game a truly classic horror feel.
There aren't many action scenes, which is fine with me. The only thing you could consider being action is the occasional chase scene with the Stalker. They're loud and scary and had me running around at the speed of sound crying because holy♥♥♥♥♥♥he sounds like he's right behind me oh ♥♥♥♥ oh ♥♥♥♥. And that's exactly what horror should feel like. Also the small number of these scenes manages to make you not expect them when they eventually do happen.
Overall, Into The Gloom is a pixelized horror game that's both NOT youtuber bait AND genuinely scary. Try a Silent Hill level of atmosphere and puzzling, just minus the combat, while also keeping it's own unique identity.

Pros:
+ Has a ton of funny moments with outrageous voice acting, like the Psycho. The game mostly does not take itself seriously.
+ Spend a lot of time running around the map finding secrets and loot boxes, which is something I really enjoyed. Loot boxes contain equippables (equippables = guns, grenades, shields, relics, and class mods). The secret finding was quite reminiscent of Gears of War and Halo.
+ TONS of equippables with many different levels of rarity and unique mechanics that make looting and grinding fun.
+ Also a lot of character and vehicle skins to find that aren't found in loot boxes, but instead from enemies, quests, and stores.
+ Diverse cast of characters on both sides that make for a fun experience.
+ Multiplayer is fun and requires no setting up, just turn one option on and anyone (within your level range) can join your game, or you can make it private invites only. In multiplayer everyone gets a copy of quest reward items and exp, ammo,
and money drops. However, only one person can pick up equippables dropped from enemies, making for some savage greedy moments potentially if you don't know the people you're playing with.
+ Lots of endgame content with True and ultimate vault hunter modes, which let you replay the story with higher level enemies and better loot.
+ Lots of side quests and quests can be done in any order, very reminiscent of Elder Scrolls games, which I absolutely adore.
+ All the playable characters have some definining characteristic that makes them interesting to try.
+ The community is still alive and well although its kind of a dated game, and its more popular than the pre-sequel.
+ Bank to store items, which can be upgraded along with backpack space and ammo capacity with a currency called Iridium, found while playing.
Cons:
- Previously mentioned, equippables dropped by enemies only go to one player.
- Cleared areas respawn enemies as soon as you leave the game, this can be a good thing as you can infinitely grind certain areas, but also if you leave in the middle of a game you have to clear the entire area again, and a lot of times you have to walk through previous areas to get to new areas.
- I had performance problems whenever a raging goliath appeared, and had to turn my graphic settings down. I can play Skyrim on maxed-out settings, for reference.
- Limited inventory and bank space made it hard for a hoarder like me to do my thing, and goes against all the looting that takes place in the game. Both of which can be upgraded, but require an insane amount of Iridium to upgrade.
- Money is (mostly) not very useful. I have millions in game and nothing to spend it on. Items you buy from shops take up a large portion of what to buy money on, but items that drop from enemies and loot boxes are much better than what you can buy from shops, for the most part. You lose 7% of your cash stack on death, which gets annoying on Ultimate vault hunter mode where you will be dying, a lot. You can also gamble your savings away at the slots, which can have some nice rewards.
Verdict: I highly recommend this game, and as a fan of Halo, Gears of War, and Elder Scrolls series, I very much enjoy this game as it pulls features from all of those. Even though its not the latest in the series, it is by far the most popular of the three, so it is by no means dead. Pick yourself up the game of the year edition, on sale if possible, the dlc add a lot of great features.

Now that the multiplayer update is out, I figured I would go ahead and make a review of the game, now that it's mostly completed. The short answer: If you like strategy games, or are fascinated by the idea of creating your own pathogen to destroy humanity, buy this game, especially during a sale.
The details:
The base game is a genetic strategy game where your goal is to infect the world and destory it before they can do the same to you. It offers plenty of options for doing so, and the game is simple enough in the lower difficulties for newcomers to get a basic idea of what to do, but in harder difficulties, it is challenging enough for even veteran players to have a difficult challenge. The game has many different plague types and modes to try, including user created plagues.
The multiplayer mode is also fun, sporting many strategies that counter other strategies, with quite a bit of depth. Would advise AGAINST newcomers to the game from playing that mode first, as it is much more intense of an experience compared to the main game.  Against friends or randoms, the multiplayer is a great addition to an already great game.
I've played this game ever since 2012, whenever the game first started out on mobile devices and there was only 6 plagues and 3 difficulties. This game has kept my attention and still manages to be a fun distraction and experience to come back to time and time again. So, if you seem at all interested, pick it up, it's a strategy game that's worth the price.

Modern Warfare 2 Campaign Review
Modern Warfare 2 continues about 5 years after where Modern Warfare left off and actually the campaign itself isn't that great. The first Modern Warfare's campaign was exhilarating and visually stimulating. Lastly though it had some poignant things to say about war and it's eventuality of it. As it progressed, things became increasingly dire. However all these things are present in Modern Warfare 2 kicked up to an 11, but without half as much substance. All of this is fine, but unfourtanately not only is the campaign laughably short, but it's story ends up feeling like a side step of what would become a trilogy of games. The campaign also suffers in the way it's structured. It's all about balls to the wall action, which is fun, but feels as if it's inherently at odds with what Modern Warfare 1 did.
After all this you might think I might hate the game, but I did enjoy myself. I don't tend to think too much about what a game brings thematically, since I believe that gameplay is king, but in the case of there being 12 or COD games. I'd say that for the most part if you are buying them for their campaign then Modern Warfare 2 and even 3 should be the last ones to buy as I do feel they are the weakest in the series. Not by much since they all try to dazzle you with setpieces, but the other's fell more consistent and fun than Modern Warfare 2 or even 3
I played this game on a GTX 970, Windows 10, I7 3820 Computer and it ran well for the most part, but just like the old COD's, this game does stutter when it saves or loads, which is odd. Other than that it ran well, and didn't give me much issues. I hesitate to say the game is beautiful, because besides the always impressive locales and setpieces the Modern Warfare series feels like the weakest of the bunch when it comes to artistic design. At least I mean to say that it stays mostly the same after the first Modern Warfare. Unlike Black Ops and Black Ops 2, which fell like they have a more distinct visual style that helps it in terms of selling you that the graphics improve with each title.
I really can not reccomend Modern Warfare 2 for the campaign alone and I'd even say with the multiplayer. I'd feel you would have much better bang for your buck with Black Ops 2. Of course this is just my opinion, but in a sea of COD games I do feel there are better than Modern Warfare 2 or 3 which unfortunately don't hold up all that well with age.

I'm the biggest Deck13 skeptic, but The Surge manages to achieve what Lords of the Fallen (their previous game) failed to.
Let's start with my biggest gripe of LOTF: boss fights. The Surge offers 5 intense, puzzling and creative boss battles with 2 or more phases each. Each boss fight is satisfying, intense and keeps you on the edge of the seat.
Combat system is precise, flexible and repsonsive. Targeting individual body parts is a nice touch. Really loved it.
Graphics are great, nothing spectacular, but it gets the job done well.
Another welcome addition is lack of character stats per say. You define your class by the armor and implants that you wear which is a great and innovative way to treat character progression and lets you adapt to current situation accordingly. Loved it.
There are, of course, shortcommings as well: level design can be a bit confusing, but considering that everything is happening in a factory setting - it's understandable. Sometimes camera acts weird, but nowhere close to the attrocity that Lords Of The Fallen had for a camera.
To sum it up, The Surge is no 5/5 title, but a strong 4, that brings you decent amount of hours of entertainment, challenging boss fights and a unique satisfaction of slicing bad guys to pieces in an exo-suit. Give it a try.

The Surge is a game developed by Deck 13, the same people behind Lords Of The Fallen and published by Focus Home Interactive. Deck 13 have had another go at the souls-like genre, and it's a better game definitely than Lords Of The Fallen. It's a challenging game, punishing even but never unfair and the progress feels just right
Combat feels good and weighted. It's also fairly unique that the gear and weapons you get are mainly sourced from cutting them from enemies. It's a nice system with plenty of scope for different builds and playstyles
The futuristic/apocalyptic setting is very well done and the visuals are excellent, with great animations and sharp texturing. The sound is also top notch. The level design is also very well done, however the game doesn't hold your hand what so ever so it can feel maze like at first
Size wise, it's a big game. Even after 10 or so hours, I'm still not even half way through it's post-apocalyptic world. The Surge is a huge step up from Lords Of The Fallen and if you like the type of games Dark Souls goes with, then The Surge has got your ticket to some bloodshed!

It's been called Soul-like enough times and there is definitely some soul in this one.
However in some aspects it is more, in some less.
You gain in generic level/power and not individual stats. Power is then converted to weapon effectiveness, armor, health recoverables and any number of other things in with implants which can be switched out at any time. Unlike a certain game you don't set yourself up for Mage/Archer/SwordAndBoard permanently but rather can (and sometime must) switch on the fly. Huge advantage for me.
Instead of fighting from save-spot to save-spot there is only one such point in a level and you progressively unlock more shortcuts, alternative routes and roundtrips. It makes the factory feel more like a real place instead of a disjointed set of environments that were haphazardly thrown together. This comes at the price of more difficult orientation and navigation.  I sorely missed a map on occasion, but liked how the world was consistent.
Enemy variety depends on what you are looking for. They are mostly humanoids with a handful of robot types thrown in for good measure. They do tend to wear different gear and use different weapons and employ different move sets, so if you feel generous there is a very large number of different enemies. To me it feels like I have been chopping up the same bloke for the last 60 hours. Satisfying but slightly monotonous.
Bosses are largely amazing (except the very last one - I guess it took me 10 hours to get him right)
The lovely devs put in an option to mute the HORRIBLE country music that plays when you're in the med bay, that makes this game a 10/10 in my book.

The screenshot function when you are doing a slowmo kill is nice too.
You are going to die, lots. But through those deaths you learn how to deal with each and every enemy type.
The robots you once feared, you now jump into and down them with 2-3 hits. You are still going to die, lots. (Sometimes on purpose).
The levels go from feeling huge to a bit smaller once you open the shortcuts, but I found them interesting to navigate and explore.
I've got all the achievements to date for this game, and loved every minute of it.
Definitely a game you should try!

Another in the simulator genre, This one has you take on one of the most covert helicopters ever developed, the Comanche; The controls are a little on the confusing side if you don't have a joystick setup, this game seems to have been designed around you pretending to actually be in the cockpit of a helicopter, this isn't necessarily a bad thing but if you are a laptop gamer on the go then you might need to do some key remapping.

A little note on the controls:
If you're expecting this to play out more like a simulator with realistic helicopter handling (e.g. Battlefield or ARMA series) - unfortunately you won't find that here.
While the game tries to keep a more serious and realistic tone overall - flight model is one thing that was kept simple and arcadey. It controls more like your standard WASD shooter, with the addition of ascend/descend keys to replace jumping/crouching. This simplified flight model is very easy to get into if you find realistic controls overwhelming, however it also lacks a lot of piloting depth that more demanding players may prefer.

First and foremost, I have played this four times already on my PS4, and yes, I bought it on PC because of it's brilliance. As I tend to ramble I will be sectioning this review into certain points, and making a TLDR on each section.
Turn based strategy has been one of my favourite genres since watching my father play them as a little girl. I wouldn't say that Transistor trumped them all in terms of mechanics, and the different 'functions' run a similar pattern to any other RPG turn based. Distance, upclose, AOE, etc. However, I wouldn't say it's repetitive. It makes up for it in pressuring mini-bosses and bosses, and each fight gradually increases in difficulty. The game, if you find vanilla too easy, even offers limiters which cause the enemies to be harder. If you like a challenge, then I'd definitely check those out. Movement with a keyboard is tricky, controller was a lot more fluid for me. Animations for each function are nice and fluid for both the protag and AI.
TLDR ; Movement is a little iffy at times, and the mechanics are standard, however it makes up for it in execution.
As a game that comes with the tag 'Great Soundtrack,' I obviously have to speak about the music. Ashley Lynn Barrett provides the vocals for this game, and without them, the female voice tying witht he story, I don't think I would have bought the game for PC aswell. The story is gripping, but the music is what I play for. It's so immersive and gripping, and is truly worthy for the tag.
TLDR; Inspiring and leaves me struck in awe.
Lore is written extensively however still lets the player interpret it however they may see it. Not only that but the character's are diverse, paticurlary our protag. I can't say much about characters without spoiling the game,  which is a shame, because I have a lot to fangirl about them. I vouch for the lore, and the music helps tie in immersion of the game. Without the female vocals it has, this game would be a lot less fun for me.

A focus that I'll put on my comments here is that there is the ability to perform work on other farmers fields. Having put a nice chunk of time into FS 2013 back in the year 2012, I had spent a lot of time performing chores, then setting the clock to run at 120x speed, while I waited to perform a harvest. Eventually I could diversify the operation which could keep me busy longer, but it took a very long time to accumulate the equipment necessary.
In 2017, money is very easy to acquire by performing work on other farmers fields. So far I've put about 18+ hours into the game and I've already accumulated well over $300,000 in the first day of “game time”.
There's so much money to be made doing this that while there are reasons why I would want to advance time, such as accumulating a couple harvests to have enough food to get into animal tending, I don't feel the need to.
By being able to pull in significant chunks of money fairly quickly, I am now quickly planning how I can get into logging and purchasing bigger fields alongside my plans for tending to animals. In 2013, it was a long slog to get new machines that would make things a bit easier. I'm sure some people exploited things or used cheats to make cash fast, but I wasn't on board with doing that myself.
Overall I feel that the mission design allows the player to put time into the game and get easily apparent rewards that facilitates the player's quest to become more deeply acquainted with the various features of the game.
Besides that, there have been huge upgrades to the graphics since 2013, which is to be expected but casual fans like myself who got on the FS train back in 2012 will be pleased with the new details and animations. Zooming in on various machines while they work is a treat, with soil being deformed and pushed aside, or corn rows being drawn into a corn harvest header. I also really like how machines get dirty and can even be cleaned by cleaning equipment that is operated by the player. Even the interior cabins of machines will have dirty boot prints as you get in and out of them with dirty boots.
Controls wise, I've used KB+Mouse and found them to be great. I am currently using an Xbox 360 controller while sitting on the couch using a TV instead of my monitor and it's even more enjoyable. I have a G27 steering wheel setup but I enjoy sitting back on the couch with this game so I don't feel the need to deepen the simulation with that controller setup. I'm glad that it supports that hardware if I feel so inclined in the future though!
Overall, I find that these games really offer a deep experience of getting to know your farms, your equipment and building a farming empire. The tutorials are very easy to understand (I didn't need most of them but I did some of them anyway) and I liked how they easily allowed me to perform the steps with the game's equipment so I could see what type of hardware I might buy and how I would use it for my in-game farm when I'm ready. New players shouldn't have too much trouble if they have free time and some interest. I find it's really neat to get involved with the farming simulator world, much more immersion than a lot of the shooters and other games which offer transient game experiences.
I haven't tried multiplayer but it's a welcome addition. From viewing YouTube videos it really appears to be a great way to play and something you might really enjoy. I personally like coming home from work and loading up the farm and getting some stuff done whenever I want; without having to coordinate with friends. So MP is less of a thing for me, but once again, a welcome feature.
I tend to marvel at little things in the game, like using a front-end loader to pick up bales or using a shovel to scrape up a pile of something off of the ground. The fact that the game simulates piles of materials is neat. Although I find it slightly bothersome that I can't shift in my seat while using the virtual cockpits; it would be nice to shift around and see different angles while seated. That would help operate multiple different types of machines. Although being able to look around the cockpit is nice enough and popping in and out of third person isn't a problem anyway.
This game really is a deep experience that rewards the player and gives a sense of satisfaction that most games can't. It's also nice to play a game where the world is at peace and one's only worries is how will they spend their day at their beautiful farm.

Great game whether you are a RTS fan or just have an interest in WW II. You build your deck from one of 18 divisions present at Normandy recreated using the historical TO&E. At any one time you probably control what amount to a small battalion of infantry, tanks, artillery, and even air support. Maps are great and were apparently created using aerial photos of the battlefields as they appeared in WW II. I think the game excels at capturing the spirit of the hedgerow fighting where every field and every hedgerow was turned into a small fortress. Learning to properly  reconnoiter, manage line of sight, and employ combined arms is essential. You can micro as much as you want; not as much as in a squad based tactics game, but your units can survive on their own without needing to constantly babysit them. Firefights look and sound gorgeous, zoom in on a fight and turn your volume up, you won't regret it. There should be three campaigns to play offline and I think the AI is a noticeable step up from Wargame's.
Cons:
Needs further optimization could run smoother, but it is a beta and improvements are in the works.
Running the game can be a heavy load on you processor, however mine is only clocked at 2.4ghz, but I can still run the game on high settings.
Final opinion: Some of the best fun I've had in a long time and one of the best RTS I have ever played, even though it's still in beta.

Into the Gloom is a pixelated survival horror game with a heavy emphasis on puzzle solving. The game has a very "minecrafty" feel to it and while it is not truly scary it certainly can get your heart racing at times.
At the start you wake up in a hospital room and then the hunt is on. It is up to you to explore everywhere you can to find keys, valves, passcodes and everything one could expect to hunt for in a horror game. There are even documents scattered throughout the game that provide plot details as well as clue you in on how to solve puzzles.
Speaking of puzzles, the puzzles in this game are far better than most big budget horror games that have released over the past few years. A few of the puzzles in the game alter your environment as you work to solve them which makes finding the solution all the more satisfying. The harder puzzles may take you between 5 to 10 minutes to solve. (unless you are completely lost on one which can happen).
The enemies in this game contrast very well with the slow pace of the puzzles. Let me start by saying there are very few enemies, but you will learn to fear them fast. This is not a horror type of fear, but more of a panic type of fear. You can't combat the enemies; you can only run and after one hit it is game over. Oh yeah, an the enemies are fast. It may seem like a cheap death, but again this kind of panic contrasts very well with the slow pace puzzle solving.
There is a story that unfolds throughout the game, however it felt rather lack luster and is overshadowed by the actual gameplay itself. There are extras you can unlock to fill you in on backstory and also multiple endings to unlock so the game does have replay value. You can expect to finish one full playthrough in 3 hours (if you get the good ending).
To sum it up: The game has a pixelated artstyle. It has heavy focus on puzzle solving and the game has some delightful puzzles to be solved. The horror aspect of the game is more panic than actual horror. The story is overshadowed by the gameplay and is mediocre at best, but it does add replay value with collectibles to unlock for further information. If you are a fan of puzzle solving or survival horror in general, it is hard to pass this game up for the extremely low cost.

First, let me get my complaints out of the way.
1. The puzzles
While the puzzles in this game are generally well balenced and aren't hard to figure out, there are WAY too many. You will have to solve a puzzle in every single area of the game in order to progress. There isn't anything wrong with something that challenges your mind. But when you're forcing the player to constantly solve puzzles to progress. That really kills the mood and pacing.
2. The save feature
This game only saves your progress upon entering a new area. Anything you do in that area until you progress to a new one won't be saved. So if you decide to quit whilst solving a puzzle, your progress won't be saved and you'll have to do the puzzle all over again. This can be very annoying.
Now, onto what I liked about the game.
1.) The atmosphere
The atmosphere in this game is dark, tense, and dreadful. It gives you that feeling of hopelessness, as if there is no way out of this hellhole except in accepting your fate. Or is it?.....
2.) The sound
The sound design in this game does a really nice job of immersing you into the game's grim story. Everything from the moans and groans the ghosts make to the emotionally stirring soundtrack.
3.) The story
For the sake of not posting spoilers, I'm not going to dive into the details of the story. But if I had to describe it, it would be like this: It feels predictable at first glance, but the longer you play and learn more. You'll start to realize that there are far bigger things at work here than what you orginally expected. Perhaps even bigger than you.
Overall, if you want an excellent horror tale of ghosts and ghouls, try Into The Gloom. It's a very memorable experience that knows how to keep you hooked into its grim, tragic story.

It was billed as the Dark Souls of the future, but better. I was no fan of Dark Souls but I thought that this would be worth a shot. I was wrong. This is not Dark Souls of the future, it is Lords of the Fallen (Dark Souls, except you know, horrible) with a thin viniere of tech and voice acting. It still has all of the same problems that those games have but without the feel of being new or the excuse of medieval combat for lack of ranged. In this you are stuck in a repetitive hack and slash with a dearth of skills or abilities, a dearth of any real customization, and a dearth of depth. My biggest complaint of Dark Souls-like games is that enemies respawn and it turns into deadly Farm Simulator. This made the same crucial mistake. Once something is dead, leave it dead so the story can progress. After a while this grind will settle in and you will get bored very quickly. I had hoped that the pace would pick up after the first stage, but it just didn't. The only thing that changed was the color of the bad guys and the difficulty got ramped up. Now I don't want to hear "learn to play", I can do all the combos just fine, but that is the problem. You spend all of your time coming up with some, lets be honest, dull combos but no plot development or memorable characters. I just played this a couple of days ago and I can't even come up with the main character's name. Add all this together and you end up just doing the same thing over and over to win and that is what is wrong with games of this type. One combo with one weapon class is all that you need to rip things to pieces. What I was hoping to see here was a hack and slash with some abilities from the engineer in mass effect. I wanted to freeze, burn, zap and smash my way through a legion of robots and beat some bosses, all while swept along in a cyberpunk dystopian novel. What I got was well, Dark Souls, we already have a Dark Souls, we don't need any more. Please Focus, come up with an original idea for once in your lives, please.

The more things change, the more things stay the same.
Infinity Ward is back with Modern Warfare 2, the sequel to their critically acclaimed and commercially successful, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. The story continues in this installment as we see the return of familiar faces.
Story: Modern Warfare 2 ups the ante with its story from its predecessor. The campaign follows a special forces unit who is lead by Captain Soap MacTavish (who you got to control in the previous game) and the United States Army Rangers, that are  after Vladimir Makarov. He is the leader of the Russian Ultranationalist party which follows in the footsteps of Imran Zakhaev (who was the antagonist in the first game). The pacing of the story is near perfect. As usual, the first mission involves throwing the player into a training pit where he or she gets to learn about the controls of the game. And from that point on, the game resembles something like a Hollywood blockbuster film. There are loud and bombastic action set-pieces, dialogue which develops each character's personality and above all, memorable scenarios and characters. Sometimes you have to take the stealth approach to missions. Other times, you go loud and guns blazing. This delicate balance of missions is done superbly. All the story missions should take you just over 4 hours to complete.
Graphics: Modern Warfare 2 was released in 2009 and it still looks great today. There is much detail to be found in the textures, characters and environments of the game. While the special effects such as fire, smoke and rain do a great job at immersing the player into the digital battlefields rendered by Infinity Ward. The graphics are used to great effect to accentuate the themes presented by the game, such as hopelessness and peace.
Sound: The sound design is once again, done fantastically by the programmers at Infinity Ward. Each gun when used, sounds impactful as bullets pierce through the air. You can hear the thunderous roar of cannons as they are blasted into the enemy. Likewise, the voice actors have done a tremendous job in bringing life to their characters. Ghost is one of my favourite characters as his cynical and cool demeanour is complemented by his country British accent. Every emotion exhibited by the characters, whether it be happiness or sadness is exemplified by the excellent voice acting and is feels authentic to listen to.
Gameplay: The same fast-paced and addictive gameplay of COD 4, returns in Modern Warfare 2 with some slight adjustments. No longer can you lean left and right to sneak a peek at enemies and shoot safely. I believe this is decision was for the best to discourage camping and to push for gameplay that is faster and even more frantic. Additionally, when you are shot, not only is there a red arrow which tells you the direction of the shot but also an additional splattered blood effect which appears on screen. As you keep receiving shots, more and more blood appears on the screen and I think this is a cool feature to let you know to take cover. Again, like COD 4 it feels very satisfying to land a kill in the game as the controls as smooth and snappy.
Overall, Modern Warfare 2 has been the sequel I had hoped for. Everything that was in COD 4 is cranked up to the nth degree with graphics, gameplay and even story improvement. There is also an additional Spec Ops mode which lets you team up with a buddy online to tackle special missions designed around environments found in the campaign. This is the near perfect FPS and is a must-play.
9.5/10.

This game is honestly one of the best I've ever played, and I've played quite a few games in my time. It drags you into the story, while pushing you to be the best family man you can. You work at a border checkpoint in a country called Arstotzka. You must check all documents people bring in to ensure they are all correct, ranging from correct name spellings to facial appearance to even height and weight. As you go, the story develops and the game gets more challenging as it adds on more and more things you need to pay attention, such as diplomats, asylum seekers and a sudden strike of Polio in another country. You have to keep your eye on all of these things, while keeping an eye on the time. I have so far 17.3 hours in this game and would not mind to sink in more. I have already beat the game twice with full playthroughs and have thoroughly enjoyed both of them. Now, for pros and cons.
Pros +
-Neat retro style appearance
-Great soundtrack, very catchy xD
-Fun, quick and intense gameplay
-Endless modes for when you don't want to play story mode
-Money system and spending system which causes you to carefully choose what you spend your money on, which in return affects the fate of your family
-Interesting events that go from terrorist attacks to neat little stories like Serial Killers escaping prison.
-Management system, as you get more and more things to hold on to such as documents, keys, and other miscellaneous things
-Great events that lead you to decide to deny or allow entry using your morals rather than the rules (Basically whether or not you want to be a good person and let someone in need through. This will in turn sometimes reward you with a token, depending on if you find the right person to help. Not everyone is seriously in need.)
-Overall fun gameplay that allows for a good few hours of playing at a time.
Cons -
I dont have any! :D
So if you're looking to buy this game, do it! You won't regret it!
As a final side note, and this is geared towards the developers, you guys really should  do something with this game haha, I want more of this game or something, like a Papers, Please 2! I am definitely a huge fan of this game, and always will be!

Legend of Grimrock is what I'd consider a minimalist RPG. What I mean by this, is the story and premise is set up right at the begining of your play, then after that you're left to your own devices. You basically form your own story while you explore the dungeons. It's very much in the ideals of the original Ultima series, where it's all about exploration, finding secrets, and killing monsters. You get to either spawn four prisoners that you'll take on your journey, or customize them to exactly who you want with you. The races and the types are familiar (warrior, wizard, rogue), but the way you can build them is where the difference comes in.
The game play itself is also aikin back to what RPGs used to be on the computer. Everything works in blocks, you can turn, sidestep, and all of that good stuff during battle, but it all works on a grid. Along with this you can either choose to draw your own map, or play with one that populates as you go depending on how old school you want to be. The graphics bring you into the game and the monsters are well designed and fun to fight. There's a lot of secrets worth looking for meaning you're going to be checking every wall for loose rocks, or for some of the other ways you open the doors. On top of this, the replayability is excellent because of the mod community. Currently there's a mod that keeps most of the original set up but makes things harder and adds more dungeons, or you can just download the added dungeons that other people have created.
Over all this is a great game that, for how it's designed, there isn't much to complain about and I recommend this to anyone that's an RPG fan, especially if you remember the originals like Ultima and Final Fantasy for NES.
