Wargame (well except the first and somewhat the second one maybe) was quite a slow game in essence. And the latest one was very static, in the sense that, when you took your initial positions and set up your units, most of the pushes later in the game would go at a very slow pace.
Now this was not necessarly bad, as the game was still fun, but i found it a bit boring after a while.
This one is even ♥♥♥♥ing slower (mostly due to the tank and vehicle speeds, that were in reality slower than modern ones), but inspite of that i find it more dynamic.
Unlike Red Dragon where breaktroughts could be contained with fire, brimstone and airplanes and were quite hard to manage, here you can easely punch thru a line with a combination of armor, infantry and some well placed smokescreens. Airpower is not hard hitting enough to stop a big ground offensive, and this let's the game flow much better.
I tought the introduction of pak's and static mg's would turn the game into a turtlefest but it didn't really do much except provide a way to cover important ground. I find myself pushing into the enemy line more than i did in Wargame, and i find others doing the same. It feels much better to be honest, and it reminds me of European Escalation and Airland Battle that were much more fluid that Red Dragon.
Maps are not bad either. Unit variety is as good as you can expect from western front in 44, maybe even a bit higher cause i did not expect to find old french tanks in there. Unit animations are clunky as ♥♥♥♥, and the problem with people just quitting 10v10 matches is still prevalent, and still annoying. All in all not bad 8/10. Waiting for the full release. GG

You might be asking yourself what's so fantastic about yet another pixelated horror game? What's the angle here? What's the big deal and why do you need to suffer through yet another one? Well, sometimes, those pixels can be just as scary as something "realistic". Sometimes, they just hit just as hard as something as say, Amnesia. Maybe even harder.
So what does Into The Gloom do?
I can tell you what it did for me. As a gamer who has a handicap? Who suffers from a chronic illness? This hits me a little harder emotionally than it might for other gamers. This is, for me, a truly scary game. While we do have the jump scares (and they do offer you a polite warning before you start the game, yay!), we have a more poignant type of horror being told in this game as well. And it's that squishy type of horror that makes you think and dread the future. It makes you question your life. It makes you question yourself.
You don't expect a game that hardly clocks in an hour of game play per session to do that to you, but hey! There it is!
It's not long, but it'll give you the creeps. As you keep playing, more endings and possibilities open up to you. More ways to frighten yourself. More ways to keep thinking...
And it's cheap. It's certainly worth that price. You can waste about $2.99 on a quick scares and some self reflection, right?
Handicapped gamers: Beware of jump scares that may trigger neurological issues. They will not flash too brightly, but they are there. Your hands may get tired from the controls. Take breaks. (I'm on one now before I try again). Otherwise this is a pretty accessible game for majority of gamers.

Emily Is Away is a short game about talking with your friend Emily. The game takes place over 5 years (2002-2006), with each chapter being a different year. The game has multiple endings, some good, some bad. I've only played through once, and I get the bad ending, and let me tell you, it's absolutely devastating. Not only do you just choose your responses to emily, but you actually have to press keys on the keyboard in order for your character to type them. This is a great mechanic, as you can see "yourself" correct mistakes, and change thoughts
.
The aesthetic of the game is great too. All it is is a small chat program that looks like windows XP. It's a nice little nostalgic feeling, and certainly helps to put the player into game, making them feel as if they're actually using a chat program from 2002 to talk to their friend Emily. While it isn't exactly like XP (and I wouldn't expect it to be), it's a nice little nod to the past.
The game also has a few easter eggs. Depending on what you enter for your user name and first name, you can unlock certain icons. Using the icon gives an achievement and a fun little easter egg, and the game is worth it for the John Cena achievement alone.
All in all, this game is absolutely beautiful, and I'd certainly recommend it to anybody. It's free, and even though it's pretty short, I'd definitely be willing to pay for it.

Nostalgia is a powerful thing. It can make us love something even when it's no longer as crisp and new and relevant as when it came out. One of my favorite games of all time was Final Fantasy 3/6 for the SNES, so believe me when I say this game has nostalgia. But that isn't what makes it great.
MMO-RPGs are a strange sort of game. From the early days of Everquest to the mainstream acceptance of World of Warcraft, there have been countless companies that tried to do it right, back when it was one of the most lucrative (and expensive) game models out there. Many failed - this game did, too, at first. But then they took everything they had built - an interesting world full of lore, colorful characters, and mediocre mechanics - and they burned it to the ground, all to build it up again. The whole world changed, characters that had been loved died, all in an attempt to do right by their community, to make a more interesting game. And I'd say they succeeded.
Final Fantasy is far from a perfect MMO. I can give you pros and cons lists galore, but what it boils down to is a certain, common, fundamental 'heart' that each Final Fantasy struggles to maintain. Some games have it more than others. This game nearly lost it, but then found it again, and every hour I spend in the world fills me with that nostalgic sense of wonder at a dark and mysterious world, one which I'm a part of. As a quite literal escape from the cacophany of the real world (at least in 2017), this game is Fantastic.

What do I have to say about
First of all,
I wasn't sure it was possible for Supergiant to top
but as it turns out, they could. What does Transistor actully have to offer? First of all, one of the most unique and challenging gaming experiences I have ever had. The combat system revolves around what the game calls a Turn() sequence--and yes, the partentheses are part of the word. Turn() allows you to freeze time and plan out your every move, but your enemies, a horde of machine-like entities known collectively as the Process, have ways of confounding you. A great deal of critical thinking goes into making your Turn() as effective as possible, especially considering that you get a fixed number of moves depending on the Functions (think spells, but with a cyberpunk twist) you employ.
Next are the sensory experiences. Darren, Ashley, and Logan outdid themselves yet again.
has a larger--and just as well-performed--voice cast than
the sound design is flawless, and if you loved the
OST, you'll love the music in
as well. The voice actors especially have my approval, particularly Logan Cunningham, the voice of the Transistor, who you may or may not know as Rucks (
), Horatio Nullbuilt (
) and the Archjustice (
the next Supergiant game). What about visuals? I've heard of eye candy, but
is eye
Supergiant continues to appeal to my surreal sensibilities. Every environment is unique and beautiful, make sure to have a look around before moving on from each area.
Finally, there is the story. Don't go in expecting a repeat of
Where
was about repentance, redemption, and rebuilding,
is more about loss, futility, and good intentions gone wrong. You play as Red, a former singer, who loses her voice as well as her lover after an attempt made on her life by the shadowy Camerata society. Lucky for Red, her unnamed lover sacrifced himself to save her life, but as a result his consciousness gets uploaded and trapped inside the Transistor. Wielding her sentient cybernetic greatsword, she sets out to track down the people who tried to kill her, and while she does that, she must find a way to stop the now-mindless Process from reducing the city of Cloudbank to its basest, most desolate form.
I really enjoyed playing
While at times it made me exceptionally frustrated
,  the story, visuals, and sheer challenge it offered kept me hooked for hours at a time. I look forward to the many times I will play back through it. Worth every penny I payed for it.
The only turn-off I see is that the story is very vague and complicated, even more so than

Personally, I love when a story (be it game, book, or movie) doesn't explain everything to you. When you think about it more, you get drawn into the world, and your intimacy with the story grows.

The Surge is a new take on the souls genre and a decent one at that. I actually enjoyed my time with the game until the very ending where suddenly the game ends and I had no idea it was going to end there since I felt like I still had some things to explore but up until that point, the souls-like experience was okay.
Gameplay is The Surge's main aspect and a good one at that. Besides the usual souls formula, it brings a body part targeting mechanism. Basically you can target legs,arms,body or head in order to deal more dmg, get a piece of weapon or armor, or simply gather parts to build said weapons/armors. Its pretty cool and I actually liked it. Difficulty can be a bit more tough since "leveling up" doesnt actually increase your health or stamina but instead gives you energy in which you can place implants that can boost a lot of things for you. What that means is, all enemies will basically destroy you in 2-3 hits assuming you did not invest in any health implants. Variety is decent, never too boring but could have used more enemies. The bosses are kinda super easy and boring to fight. Nothing spectaluar and its the weakest point regarding gameplay.
The Story was interesting up until the end. There was this interesting mystery that kept me going and I was hoping for some cool plot twist but in the end I felt dissapointed and sad that the story just stops without offering much closure, perhaps aiming at a sequel based on your choices and how it ends. There may be a few bugs that will confuse you if you progress or rush through the map but then again the story isnt the main aspect of the game.
Atmosphere wise while initially I hated the "junkyard" theme, it does get interesting the more you progress and some of the places look pretty good and horrific. The locations are very linear but you can get lost in its maze-like linearity as there are a lot of paths, which means you might miss on certain side quests or items of interest.
Sound design and music is decent, nothing worthy of mentioning.
Overall, if you're in dire need of a difficult game or if you want a more easy to understand Souls game, then The Surge is for you. Recommended on a sale. 7.5/10

The Surge feels like a game made by people who played Dark Souls but didn't pay close enough attention.
It has all the basics -- similar controls, corpse runs, punishing gameplay, and so on -- and it even has a few twists on the formula that feel like interesting ideas worth pursuing!
But the core components of the game that even Souls at its worst tends to get right, The Surge gets wrong. Souls combos are simple, but satisfying. Predictable by design. You know the range of your swing, you know where it starts and ends and what it leads into. Nearly every swing in a basic string feels useful -- a wide swing, a stab, an uppercut or a downward strike. The Surge includes things like short jabs, elbow strikes, pommel hits, in the middle of combos that also include wide swings or vertical strikes, and it just feels BAD. Animation priority is a fine enough thing, but when attacks feel unresponsive, and certain parts of combo strings feel completely useless? It stops being fine. It actively hurts the core combat when your own movements are both hard to predict (depending on which body part you're targeting, which direction you're moving, etc) and feel bad to use. When you're trying desperately to learn when to STOP specific combos because you don't want to enter into a long animation of your character delivering an anemic elbow strike with an absurdly short range, you've done a bad job.
This would be bad enough, but the level design compounds the frustration. Early on, facing the Soulslike staple of slow zombie-esque enemies, it's easy enough, but the levels do a terrible job of directing you towards the places you're SUPPOSED to go to advance, so you end up doing loop after loop looking for the tiny doorway you missed in the labyrinthine industrial wasteland and factories the game takes place in.
The enemy placement, too, feels bad; one-on-one duels are difficult enough using the combat system, but the game often likes to throw two or three fast-moving enemies at you. You lack the crowd control of a Souls-style greatsword (the larger weapons are so absurdly slow they feel completely useless, leaving you massively open to attack) or any real ranged attacks, outside of a drone you take a while to unlock and which functions more as a device to pull enemies than do damage.
Oh, and you take tremendous amounts of damage as well. A few hours in, even decked out in the heaviest armor you can manage, enemies will kill you in two or three hits. Similar to a Souls game, perhaps, but given how fast the enemies move, the poor combos and too-heavy animation priority, and how your health doesn't level up outside of optional implants you can equip... there are enemies that can one-shot you, from full-health, if you make one mistake. And it's not necessarily a mistake you can learn from!
The Surge has a lot of cool ideas. It's got a great look to it, and the basic movement and dodging feels good. Even the slow and awkward animations might be acceptable, if the enemies and the levels were designed around them; a slower pace of combat might be better, in fact, to ease in new players to the genre. It's such a shame that all the things around its strengths are profound weaknesses. Like I said at the top, their inspirations are obvious, but it feels like they didn't pay enough attention to them.

The more things change, the more things stay the same.
Infinity Ward is back with Modern Warfare 2, the sequel to their critically acclaimed and commercially successful, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. The story continues in this installment as we see the return of familiar faces.
Story: Modern Warfare 2 ups the ante with its story from its predecessor. The campaign follows a special forces unit who is lead by Captain Soap MacTavish (who you got to control in the previous game) and the United States Army Rangers, that are  after Vladimir Makarov. He is the leader of the Russian Ultranationalist party which follows in the footsteps of Imran Zakhaev (who was the antagonist in the first game). The pacing of the story is near perfect. As usual, the first mission involves throwing the player into a training pit where he or she gets to learn about the controls of the game. And from that point on, the game resembles something like a Hollywood blockbuster film. There are loud and bombastic action set-pieces, dialogue which develops each character's personality and above all, memorable scenarios and characters. Sometimes you have to take the stealth approach to missions. Other times, you go loud and guns blazing. This delicate balance of missions is done superbly. All the story missions should take you just over 4 hours to complete.
Graphics: Modern Warfare 2 was released in 2009 and it still looks great today. There is much detail to be found in the textures, characters and environments of the game. While the special effects such as fire, smoke and rain do a great job at immersing the player into the digital battlefields rendered by Infinity Ward. The graphics are used to great effect to accentuate the themes presented by the game, such as hopelessness and peace.
Sound: The sound design is once again, done fantastically by the programmers at Infinity Ward. Each gun when used, sounds impactful as bullets pierce through the air. You can hear the thunderous roar of cannons as they are blasted into the enemy. Likewise, the voice actors have done a tremendous job in bringing life to their characters. Ghost is one of my favourite characters as his cynical and cool demeanour is complemented by his country British accent. Every emotion exhibited by the characters, whether it be happiness or sadness is exemplified by the excellent voice acting and is feels authentic to listen to.
Gameplay: The same fast-paced and addictive gameplay of COD 4, returns in Modern Warfare 2 with some slight adjustments. No longer can you lean left and right to sneak a peek at enemies and shoot safely. I believe this is decision was for the best to discourage camping and to push for gameplay that is faster and even more frantic. Additionally, when you are shot, not only is there a red arrow which tells you the direction of the shot but also an additional splattered blood effect which appears on screen. As you keep receiving shots, more and more blood appears on the screen and I think this is a cool feature to let you know to take cover. Again, like COD 4 it feels very satisfying to land a kill in the game as the controls as smooth and snappy.
Overall, Modern Warfare 2 has been the sequel I had hoped for. Everything that was in COD 4 is cranked up to the nth degree with graphics, gameplay and even story improvement. There is also an additional Spec Ops mode which lets you team up with a buddy online to tackle special missions designed around environments found in the campaign. This is the near perfect FPS and is a must-play.
9.5/10.

+ Historically accurate details. The maps are based from aerial reconnaissance photos of 1944. The units and tactics used are also heavily realistic from the time period.
+ Visually the game looks amazing. When you zoom the camera out you see that you are playing on a flat 2D map of the area, but when you zoom in the world comes to life in 3D with far more detail than I could have expected. All the units also look great even when you zoom all the way to ground level. It's a joy to watch some of the more dense conflicts.
+ Gameplay involves a lot of strategy, planning, and reacting quickly to the enemy units. It's a bit like rock, paper, scissors as you must be aware of which units counter which, and what terrain will give the best advantage.
+ "Over 400 Units" with realistic sound effects
- Currently no tutorial which makes this game have a very high learning curve. Expect to spend ~30mins watching youtube gameplay to try to figure out how to even start playing.
- I feel the gameplay is a bit slow-paced and a bit mundane at times compared to other RTS games. For the most part you are just waiting to get enough points to spawn in more units while tactically positioning your army across the map. You push up, and once you control more than 50% of the map you start earning points until you eventually win. I sort of wish there were more traditional RTS elements like building forward bases or fortifications.
- Sometimes the units behave oddly. Nothing is more frustrating than seeing your tank being fired at while it slowly rotates in a circle for some unknown reason.

If your looking for a review on Plague Inc: Evolved you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Ok, I knew it wasn't GTA going into it.. but MAN!! I am glad that I picked it up on sale or I would have hard feelings about it.   This game is so.... BLAH... it's not fun, its not entertaining.. it's a meaningless grind with frustrating mechanics and a predictable story.  The most obvious issue right from the beginning is basic mechanics. It's painfully awkward.. From moving the character around to vehicle handling the game feels slow and clunky.  Speaking of vehicle handling, that's a cargo ship of worms and where the mechanics failures really shine!  The vehicles are more like downhill cart racers.. not much speed and not much handling. The vehicles are just as broken as the basic mechanics making It suck to drive,  ride and run.  There no real sense of speed. Everything seems slow until you start skidding at what looks like a slow speed and hitting everything in front of you.  If only he could just teleport.. that might be okay.  That is, until the enemy skill get's to a point where you have to remember a bunch of key combinitations for the advanced fight moves.  Like mortal combat... I never thought that was a good idea.. and it's still not a good idea.. I thought this was a role playign game, not a fight game. Not that it matters because in my opinion, It fails at both.  The missions are basically all the same.. go here and beat these guys up for whatever reason and return. No wash, just rinse and repeat.  The cop missions are no better.. they have you setting up busts thru surveillance or running down street racers... to ram them... aside from the complete mess that driving is, the whole ramming thing is laughable.  The story, at least as far as I got in the game, was predictable and not nearly interesting enough to override the mechanics to keep playing. I simply don't care if Dogface will every get even with you or if Winston will ever figure you out..  Now...., if Dogface and Winston could collaborate and make the game mechanics better.. that would be worth a look.   Another HUGE dislike for me is the crappy point system!  So picture this, the vehicles already handle like pushing a brick uphill  with a long stick..ok..add to that being penalized for hitting anything and everything in the narrow congested streets and alleys.  I hit 4 cars, killed 3 pedestrians, destroyed  3 barricade fences and a light pole before I got to the end of the block!  Then the game compares your driving to any your friends that have the game.  The vehicle radio may be period and/or culturally accurate but I found it to be completely annoying with volume levels well above the other game levels and a little bit stereotypical of asian peoples.  I was VERY happy to see the developers provided a volume slider to turn it off!   And yet...sadly.. another HUGE issue is the camera auto-return!  Its pretty much impossible to get the view that you need when you need it. The view auto-return is VERY aggressive in switching the view back to the game default, which changes based on direction.  Picture this.. you're drivign thru the streets in cold persuit (what else would you call a 20mph chase?) of street racers, you skid off the road into a couple of parked cars.. or cars sitting at the light, or a tree or...anyway, you have to back out of where you are to get back on the job. You want to look forward to see when you have backed far enough to clear the obstacle, but NO, the game changes the view to look behind you.. the result of that is the view going back and forth making the free look pretty useless.  This combination of the aggressive forced view and the auto view switching causes some very, VERY!  frustrating gaming!  Too bad they didnt include a way to turn that off!  The poor mechanics.. and being penalized for them,  the repetition of missions with the multiple button fight moves and the crazy forced camera views, made this game both boring and frustrating. One or the other of those two could possibly be overcome if the game got better.  I have played such games that faltered and then recovered from one or the other issue... but not both.
What are my gaming credentials you may be asking?  I have been gaming for longer than a lot of you reading this have breathed air.  That simply means I've been around more games than you can shake a stick at and this game just sucks.

Having just finished this, all I can really say is:
Transistor is an experience, that everyone needs to try.
The visuals are amazing.
The soundtrack is beautiful.
The gameplay is diverse, theres so many ways to suit it to your playstyle, as you can basically augment and change your attacks/abilities. Flitting around between styles was fun, albeit very challenging at times, as some enemies... are kind of unfair, at times.
The story is left intentionally vauge mostly, but gives enough to leave a strong plot. The detatched storytelling used works well, and the ending is... something.
The main appeal of the game has to be the story and the graphics, but yet theres still some replayability, as new game+ is a thing. On top of this, there are optional limiters to add challenge, if you so wish.
The only potential weak points I can think of are:
- Recharge from Turn() is very annoying, to be frank, as most of your abilities are offline. This can be partially removed by augmenting with an ability called Jaunt(), but its still a pain, especially in a very risky scenario.
- The final boss is... frankly, underwhelming? It seemd rather gimmicked and just a spamfest, with no real difficulty. I dont know if thats because I found a combination able to completely demolish it, but still.
Overall, Transistor is a downright gorgeous game that has to be at least tried at some point.
The game has thousands of hours of content. If you like your MMOs story heavy and a bit traditional this might be the game for you.

I enjoyed this game. Its reasonably short about 13 hours to complete, although I think I didn't complete all the side dungeons so that might lengthen the game a bit.  There are also harder difficulties as well as different game modes. One mode which I just started has a similar storyline but with a different person as the main character. Therefore the game does have some replayability. This game plays like a classical Jrpg game but it also makes fun of a lot of cliche moments and game structure issues that you may know of if you have played a few jrpg. The storyline is basically a comedy having Cthulhu save the world so he can just destroy it later, but with the combination of comedy as well as the characters the game does seem to motivate me to keep playing at least for the first play through. Also you only had a certain amount of random battles per dungeon which was a nice touch.
With this said, the game does have its faults. I played the game in normal mode but before this I played in hard mode. This mode was very difficult even at the start of the game, and not difficult in a good way. The random battles were incredibly tough and I found myself losing a lot. I felt like I could have played it on hard mode even with the difficulty level but the grind just seemed that much more tedious even with the random battle restrictions. Every battle just felt like it took so long and you were continously saving because of the chance that you might lose the next fight. When I started playing in normal mode the game got a lot easier but even still, especially about half if not more into the game the random battles got pretty difficult which I didn't like. I was hoping for difficult bosses which I did get at the start of the game but I actually found as the game went on the bosses got easier. Maybe I was over levelled I am not sure but the last boss seemed like a breeze even though I was have troubles with random battles before getting to the last boss, so that was annoying. You did get 1 up items which basically allowed you to restart a battle which was nice but still didn't help the difficulty that much. Overall I think the difficulty should have been more directed towards the bosses and not so much the random battles.
Overall, the game was good short comedy rpg that I found myself laughing out loud a few times. Besides the difficulty issues I didnt find much else that was wrong with the game. Some advice, if you want to get some extra laughs turn on the commentary option at the start of the game.

Definitely in the "Souls" genre, it does enough of it's own thing that I definitely wouldn't write it off as a "Dark Souls Clone". It has a few systems that are its own and keep things feeling different (dismembering enemies with finishers for parts, the core system, etc). The setting is also fairly interesting with a few story threads and some nice hidden "touches" in the story you can find if you take the time to explore.
It's biggest pitfall is that the setting is very similar throughout. The game is the factory. There are PARTS of the factory, but that is going to be your environment for the whole experience. The DLC did try to directly address that by adding a more varied area and it is an interesting area, but it's DLC. Didn't encounter any major bugs or performance issues, and mechanically it all felt pretty sound. It starts out really tough, as most games in this genre do, but as you get more options via the core system (you can get things like health boosts, cores that charge health by doing combos, etc) it gets less brutal as you go in. Definitely worth playing if you're looking for another Souls-like game.

The Surge is a supremely under-rated Souls-Like that is extremely fun and rewarding once you grasp it's combat.  The biggest difference between the Surge and anything with a FromSoft logo is that going toe-to-toe with an enemy and R1 spamming is pure suicide.  Nah, The Surge is the realm of the sprinting attack and the quickstep attack, unless you want to see a load screen.   For this reason, I found the single-rigged, double-rigged, and heavy weapons to be the most useful as they benefitted the most from the guerilla warfare style combat the game seems to want you to use.  Sure, there are only a handful of boss fights, but as a trade off, the game eschews all those nothing fights against peons you twoshot like you'd find in a souls game for more enemies that can actually kill you.  Pick it up on sale if you're mourning not having a fromsoft release this year.

Do you like Dark Souls? Do you like not-near-but-not-distant-future sci-fi? Do you dislike having to rely on random drops for your gear? The Surge is a very good Souls-like game and having now beat it, I sincerely hope the developers continue making games along these lines.

When I heard this game was tough and supposedly Soulslike I thought "Great something to try out since I finished Dark Souls."
What I didn't realise was that playing the game was the hard part rather than the gameplay.
While the premise of the game is very intriguing and got my interest straight away the game immediately loses my interest within the opening mission.
What I was hoping for was Dark Souls or Nioh styled visceral combat what I instead got was something akin to Runescape's hit a person, wait for them to hit you and then hit back with the occasional dodge. Not only does it feel stiff compared to Dark Souls or Nioh it just feels slow overall like instead of actually fighting I'm getting a play by play recap of something that has already happened.
Maybe that's intentional maybe that's part of its charm to some people that it's not dynamic fast paced roll around a person and back stab but it certainly doesn't appeal to me.
My other gripe that others can feel free to argue is just complaining is the placement of the first boss. The first boss is positioned in such a way that it assumes the player will walk back outside the building they were in to complete an object to then leave the area however that wasn't my first instinct.
What I instead decided to do which most people tend to do in any game with exploration is explore a new area that had opened up. Unfortunately for me what ended up happening was that I got absolutely destroyed by an enemy I didn't see and without any health injections to spare I embraced death. Upon reviving I discovered The Surge's interestingly stupid mechanic timed retrieval of your Tech Scrap.
Which plays into my gripe about the placement of the boss because as it so happens the boss blocked my path to my glorious 3,000+ tech scrap and wasted my two minutes of time.
Not to mention that even at max settings the game runs about as well as your average PS4 game. And yes I know it comes down to my individual specs but DS3 runs gloriously in comparison to it also on max settings.
Overall if I could I would probably give The Surge more time to see if it gets any better but problems like these make it hard to give it another shot.
Buy the game if you somehow enjoyed Lords of the Fallen which had the dullest first boss in history. Don't buy it if you're expecting to jump from DS3 or Nioh into something similar.

They are currently working on optimizations to allow for bigger factories, crazier combinator creations, more players, and more mayhem.
If you are a fan of 2D topdown, automation, base building, turret defense, resource management, and/or trains then I'm sure that you will enjoy Factorio!

Legend of Grimrock is an accessible dungeon crawler with fun and engrossing puzzles; the kind of puzzles that aren't complicated but require a decent understanding of the point-and-click mechanics. Unfortunately most of the underwhelming puzzles require hugging the wall and hunting down hidden wall switches.
The RPG mechanics are pretty barebones. The combat consist of mindless clicking and side-stepping. You'll most likely never reach the end level class skills in your first playthough without excessive grinding. The only redeemable aspect of combat is the spellcasting system. In Grimrock, using magic spells require you enter the correct combinations of runes, as if you are dialing them on a keypad. Learning new rune combinations through the scrolls found in the dungeon is always an enjoyable treat.
I only beat the main campaign but it took me roughly 10 hours not counted on Steam as my internet connection was down for a period of time. The user submitted workshop dungeons could hypothetically add even more unique playtime with this but I haven't had a clue if they are as good as the main game. Grimrock is well worth the full price by itself, though.
One final note is that if you are of faint of heart you might not enjoy this game as it throws you a ton of creepy creatures that run around in the darkness of the dungeon.

Originally, I had a positive review of this game.  It was an interesting start.  It was basically Dwarf Fortress in space with graphics from the list of planned features, and looked to be quite promising.  Even with what was in the game, it was at least worth playing for a couple dozen hours, even if it lacked any real depth to keep you playing for too long.
Then, it was cancelled while still in pre-alpha...
The developer abandoned it because, as far as I can tell, they just plain didn't think it was selling well enough to be worth putting money into finishing the game.  It's kind of crushing that a company that had a positive reputation like DoubleFine would just abandon a half-made game like this.  (And for the record, my first real notification of this was that my previous positive early-access review managed to get a near-constant stream of downvotes for the simple fact that it had been a positive review...)  The "consolation prize" was that they handed out free Hack 'n' Slash games to purchasers of this game (limited time, already over), although it raises the question of why players would trust in the next early access game when the last one was abandoned...
That said, I don't have the same bitterness a lot of people seemed to have. (Likely because I don't live in hype of upcoming games when I'm sitting on a mountain of Steam games I've got in reserve.)
As for the game, itself, it's fairly simple.  Start with nothing but a few resources, build an airlock and air recycler quick to not suffocate when your suits run out of air, build a mining station, and start mining for more resources.  From there, use resources to start making more rooms, and stuffing them full of all the random things in the menu until you have a little of everything.  Then have random visitors stay at your station, and start building MORE of everything.  Then have asteroids slam into your station (just lock everyone out of the threatened rooms), or have some raiders (set everyone to security, and bum rush them all), or have other mystery stations drift nearby (remove their walls from the outside to suck all the likely hostile inhabitants into the vacuum of space instead of letting your guys get killed). By and large, the game just lather, rinses, and repeats from there.
If you really like managers, I can say you might have fun with it for a few hours, but don't get it unless it's absolutely dirt cheap, because you're probably going to experience everything this game really has to offer in about 6 hours or so, and from there, it's just a matter of building a base larger and larger to cram more and more population in.

I'm not a huge fan of the Wargame franchise but Steel Division has the potential to hook me up for a long time.
I liked the fast paced gameplay of World in Conflict but it lacked this "reality" feeling that Wargame had.
Steel Division does a great job at bringing these two world together.
Its a deep strategy game with a lot of things to learn (View range mechanism, decks variety, unit synergy, etc...), but with a very simple basis, the frontline system, that helps beginners like me jump into the fray quickly and enjoy it.
The only real thing needed now is a good matchmaking system. The competitive potential is here, and it might prevent the classic noob stomp that chase people away from custom multiplayer. Its 2017 guys.

These is my first impression of the beta version in short: ( Pls read the second review at bottom)
For those familiar with Eugen Games Wargame series the game mechanics are quite familiar. This a vastly improved game engine, graphics are of course better, details and so on. This game focuses much more on detailed management in that it is very important to use even the slightest cover, you can actually take cover behind buildings and objects, not just "in that area", which was the case in Wargame.
It is a WW2-fans dream, with a LOT of Allied and Axis units, and great freedom to complete MP matches, campaign scenarios or skirmishes in the way you see fit. The use of combined arms are extremely important to succeed, this is not a "tank rush" kinda game.
I´ve read some complain of arty spam; that´s always gonna be a problem. I recommend the to read Anthony Beevor´s books about Normandy ´44 and Ardennes ´44; that was many times real life arty spam aginst all and everything - soldiers, tanks and motorized guns on both sides had to be clever to use the pauses/gaps to avoid being pinned down all the time. Artillery may not be fun in any situation - but it is effective, and therefore it´s used both IRL and in games...
One of the greatest news in the game engine (except for excellent AI) is the use of dynamic fronts. It differs from the Wargame series in that you do not have squares to capture for points, instead the front is controlled by the location of your troops and the strength of your units i comparison to the enemy, and is shown by very flexible red/blue lines across the map which are moving constantly.  This is a great feature. So, to the pros and cons I´ve noticed so far:
* Lots of detailed historically correct units
* Great flow of the game, it is an intense RTS but feels as much as a WW2 squad/battallion strategy game
* Great freedom for different tactics
* Great multiplayer
* If you like complex historically correct RTS games, this is about as good as it gets right now
* Nice graphics and flawless zooming from cloud level to ground level
Cons (not many):
* Not really a game for the casual gamer - using real strategy and combined arms are necessary
* Huge amounts of units and lots of stats to take in
* Risk for arty spam in large MP games
* Sometimes units are not reacting properly to commands (though this is the Beta version)
--------------------------------------------
After a few more hours of playing:
I have to say this game does NOT grow on you - its not really getting better at this point.
Why?
Well, its kinda messy. From start, it I thought it was more detailed, maybe more realistic, but as a WW1 and  WW2  history buff, having read most of the books about WW2 out there and played games based upon it since the 80´s, I quickly got disappointed. So far. Because it´s only a beta, and for a beta, it is not that bad.
But expecting an improvement from the latest Wargame Red Dragon game, I can say it´s just not holding up.
I hope it´s gonna get better, but I still most of all long for a new post-millennium era Wargame.

I purchased the fist full of Bubsy collection because it was $11.99 and because I've always wanted Bubsy to fist me. Totally worth it.
This Bubsy game is actually playable! Each stage comes packed with 9 lives and special t-shirts that grant a shield of protection from one hit. This music and backgrounds are okay and are decent to look at and Bubsy has a very smooth animation cycle. Bubsy comes equipped with his sassy mouth, a trademark that I never found annoying like most people have, and he brings with him a few new abilities. He can climb, pounce, and even double jump (if you glide after jumping, that is). The adventure has you racing from your home to the outer reaches in order to get your prize possession of yarn back. The game is kept very simple to the point of boredom but trust me, at this point that is the least of your problems.
Let's start off with the fact that this game is $30! The game is about 2 hours long(maybe 4 if you 100%) and its $30 are you ♥♥♥♥ing fisting me!? The stages are very one dimensional and if you aren't able to find every secret its most likely because you're not paying attention. The new pounce ability is poorly implemented and absolutely pointless. It has a horrific arc and most of the time you'll be pouncing everywhere but where you want to. Even bouncing on enemies can be a bit daunting as Bubsy can be a bit loose when trying to bounce on top of something. Why couldn't the pounce just destroy everything in its path when activated? You don't need to actually touch a checkpoint to activate it so why is it necessary for pin-point precision for enemies? The only other reason to pounce is to destroy bricks which net yarn balls that do absolutely nothing in the long run. The enemies have been severly neutered, in my opinion, as well. In previous installments(ugh) the enemies had goofy animations to look at that gave the enemies a bit of a cartoony personality. The enemies here are extremely bland and tasteless with one having the ability of walking back and forth....yay. Boss fights are just as bland with each new enemy providing a bit of a challenge and nothing more. IT’S SO BORING! Worry not, though, because Bubsy is coming back...and I'm going to buy the ♥♥♥♥ing game AGAIN! I'm a massochist its what I do.
May I make a suggestion? I don't think this will be the end-all solution but give it a shot; I mean what could possibly go wrong? Since Conker has, officially, had his nuts taken away I suggest that Bubsy should become the new Conker. Make him swear like a sailor, be rude, crude, and if the mood takes you flat out show his♥♥♥♥♥♥at the end of the sequel like in Boogie Nights. I am very immature and I love Conker so ♥♥♥♥ it; give it a shot. Don't act like this is a kids game, you know damn well that your audience are a bunch of horny furries. Fist full of Bubsy...gimme a break, you know you were trying to open the arc of the covenant when you wrote that.
This game is worth $5 AT BEST and paying anymore is a waste of so many things all at once. I'm not mad at this game; how can I be when I predicted this. I hate to say this but I actually like Bubsy as a character. I grew up during the animal mascot era and trust me, he isn't the worst. It just seems like the Bubsy legacy is meant to be one step behind everyone. Congratulations, after twenty years of waiting and research you've made a game that plays.

I cannot believe that there aren't many people that know about this game, as it is simple amazing. It is a more than worthy successer to Supergiant's first game Bastion and its story is suprisingly hard hitting.
Pros:
- The game's soundtrack is phenomenal, and teh game's ability to allow the main character, Red, to hum along when out of combat helps the soundtrack shine.
- The game is beautiful, but runs very well, even for my 3 year old laptop, which isn't at all built for gaming.
- The combat system is simple, yet very fun, somewhat challenging (but not too challenging) and is very creative, making it a breath of fresh air.
- Speaking of difficulty of the game, there are limitations, much like Bastion's panthenion system, which allow you to make the game harder if you feel that it is currently too easy for you.
- The story respects you by allowing you to figure out and put pieces of the puzzle together, instead of constantly guiding you through the story, adding to the mystery of the game, which Bastion also had.
- The world and level design is very good and certain interactions that you can have with the world help to flesh out the world that the game is set in.
- There are extra challenged in the game and the game's story is replayable, if you would like to play the game with a different combination of powers.
Cons:
- The game is a little on the short side, with its main story coming to around 6 hours.
- There aren't any section within the game that allow you to make choice which will affect the story, and - despite Bastion only having a few of these - I feel that they are missed.
In all honesty the cons are really only nickpicks, and don't really affect the game too much, and I feel that Transistor is a step up from Bastion. I also feel like it could have been acknowledged as one of the best games of 2014, if it had been given its rightful attention as its stylistic gameplay and world, combined with the beautiful soundtrack and mysterious story, make it on of my personnal favourites.

To Those expecting this to be just a not-so-good version of Bastion? It's compareable. I wont call it betterm, because Bastion is a gameing masterpiece, but this comes very, very close. This game took several upgraes from where Bastion came from. It has more voice acting, enhanced combat system, and it's more open with it's lore. (Sort of)
And to fans of Ashley Barret, the girl who sang Build that Wall? She has 6 vocal songs in this game. So another awesome plus.(None of them sung by Korb. Boooooo)
This game is alot harder then Bastion, but sacrifices the casual attitude for a confuseing, but well thought out, plot, insane character details, and many many more.
If you played Bastion, get this. You have that feeling that this just 'wont be the same' ? Well it will be I promise you.
If you decide to get it, Enjoy! It's worth the money. Also, Pyre. THat's comeing out. Make sure to play this before it's release, so you could be there to play all of Supergiant's games in order of release.

I really enjoyed this game, and the "mech-souls" gameplay was a refreshing take on one of my favorite genres. I got it on sale for 20 bucks, and it was well worth it. The game presents a satisfying gear progression system and combat system that balances well with the scaling difficulty of the game's bosses.
There are no "levels" in the traditional sense, you upgrade your exosuit's power core by using scrap dropped from enemies in order to fit better implants and pieces of armor for your exosuit. The impants provide both passive buffs like more health and stamina, and can also act as usables to do things like restore health or add an elemental damage buff to your weapon.
In order to aquire new weapons and exosuit parts, you have to take them from enemies by cutting off the approprite body part with a special "execution" style attack once you weaken the enemy. Its quite satisfying.
I only wish there had been more game. I finished a playthrough in just under 22 hours, but I know that I missed plenty of stuff along the way. New Game + will be a good chance to revisit some of those other areas and round out the experience. There also seem to be multiple endings, which makes replaying it inviting. I hope to see more stuff from Deck13 in the future.

I like Papers, Please because I like playing the role of an investigator of sorts, determining what information is contradictory with other information and acting on that. The Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney games always interested me because I could play as, well, an attorney, and slap my hand down on the table when the other person was wrong.
This game allows you to find information that does not correlate with other information on the passports, entry permits, and many other documents, in order to determine whether a person is allowed entry to a fictional country. The game has a story and an Endless Mode, achievements, ACTUAL CHOICES YOU MAKE THAT MATTER (you can choose whether to let someone in or not; you get a citation for doing the wrong option, but there are benefits like achievements for certain characters with more story or dialogue), and some other things.
If you like finding contradictions and doing justice, play this game. If you like strategy, play the game.

I feel like this game was made for me. My friends and I have enjoyed Wargame since the days of EE, but our hours of gameplay were always accompanied by my endless ♥♥♥♥♥ing about modern settings being boring, and how planes stopped being cool when they stopped having propellers. So, I'll ask you; are you like me? Do you long for the days where the good guys wore gaiters and the bad guys wore gray? Then Steel Division: Normandy 44 is the game for you! I always figured that a WWII Wargame was inevitable, and here it is! What a time to be alive! From a gameplay side of things, obviously it's a little more slow-paced than Wargame, so it's a little more easy to comprehend. Gone are capture points, now we have the dynamic front system which, while not perfect, I think adds a depth to the game because you have to cover your flanks, and if your attack gets bogged down by a strongpoint, just go around it! Also, your units are split into three "Phases" which limited what can get called in and when, so it cuts down a lot of the spammy BS. If you do decide to get this game, please spend a couple hours playing against AI to get the hang of things. It will be much more enjoyable for you and your teammates, but once you think you're ready, jump online! It's still the beta, so most people are still learning. Now is the perfect time to practice! Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10 in it's current state. There are possibly some balance issues, but nothing too noticeable. Plus all of the divisions and maps haven't been added yet, so they could help. Usually the people that whine abut balance are just bad. I haven't had any problems with any of the divisions with the exception of the 91 Luftlande, but they're more of a support deck anyway.
In closing, if you like WWII or Wargame or both, I HIGHLY recommend this game. I honestly don't plan on playing anything else until Red Dead 2 comes out. Happy (Panther) hunting!

The latest offering from Eugen systems very much takes off where Wargame Red Dragon left off.  Offering huge improvements on the previous game all wrapped in a highly desireable WW2 setting.
Where this title differs from most is in the scale.  It is neither a skirmish, nor a grand strategy.  It is a truly operational level game where each player fields what probably amounts to a battalion sized battlegroup during the course of any battle.  With such large maps to fight over infantry transport becomes a serious issue and mobility has a real use and aircraft take time to reach target allowing for patrol aircraft time to intercept.
There are a lot of revierws out there for those who want to drill deep - but to mention a few key ones as a development from wargame RD I would say the inclusion of crewed weapon teams, something sadly missing from previous iterations, and the dynamic frontline system.

Originally, I had a positive review of this game.  It was an interesting start.  It was basically Dwarf Fortress in space with graphics from the list of planned features, and looked to be quite promising.  Even with what was in the game, it was at least worth playing for a couple dozen hours, even if it lacked any real depth to keep you playing for too long.
Then, it was cancelled while still in pre-alpha...
The developer abandoned it because, as far as I can tell, they just plain didn't think it was selling well enough to be worth putting money into finishing the game.  It's kind of crushing that a company that had a positive reputation like DoubleFine would just abandon a half-made game like this.  (And for the record, my first real notification of this was that my previous positive early-access review managed to get a near-constant stream of downvotes for the simple fact that it had been a positive review...)  The "consolation prize" was that they handed out free Hack 'n' Slash games to purchasers of this game (limited time, already over), although it raises the question of why players would trust in the next early access game when the last one was abandoned...
That said, I don't have the same bitterness a lot of people seemed to have. (Likely because I don't live in hype of upcoming games when I'm sitting on a mountain of Steam games I've got in reserve.)
As for the game, itself, it's fairly simple.  Start with nothing but a few resources, build an airlock and air recycler quick to not suffocate when your suits run out of air, build a mining station, and start mining for more resources.  From there, use resources to start making more rooms, and stuffing them full of all the random things in the menu until you have a little of everything.  Then have random visitors stay at your station, and start building MORE of everything.  Then have asteroids slam into your station (just lock everyone out of the threatened rooms), or have some raiders (set everyone to security, and bum rush them all), or have other mystery stations drift nearby (remove their walls from the outside to suck all the likely hostile inhabitants into the vacuum of space instead of letting your guys get killed). By and large, the game just lather, rinses, and repeats from there.
If you really like managers, I can say you might have fun with it for a few hours, but don't get it unless it's absolutely dirt cheap, because you're probably going to experience everything this game really has to offer in about 6 hours or so, and from there, it's just a matter of building a base larger and larger to cram more and more population in.

For more than $10, Bubsy: The Woolie Strike Back is nothing short of an utter waste of money. Let me be quick, frank and honest;
Graphics: Fine, though there isn't much 'life' in the character models but it doesn't looks as painful as the PS1 or SNES Bubsy games.
Sound: Really bland score, obvious stock sounds are obvious and I wish there was a way to keep Bubsy's voice acting on but also limit how many one-liners per second he was allowed to spew.
Controls: The game controls well, it doesn't feel like you are delayed or not getting inputs through.
Mechanics: Trash. Your pounce has a 50% chance to just kill you instantly, easier to use as a means to quickly get through levels or simply avoid enemies rather than attack them. Jumping on their heads works fine, but has about a 30% chance of killing you as well because...reasons? Gliding is meh, it was in all the others so it makes sense to keep it around, but like Sonic's spin dash, you sorta question why it exists when the levels aren't really built to take full advantage of the ability.
Collectables: Something close to 300-600 per level of mutli-colored yarn that...has no reason to be there. The yarn does nothing but give you a better score and maybe an achievement. Getting them all isn't hard at all and is mostly there to pad out the game for obvious reasons.
Enemies: Boring and forgettable. You can mostly just avoid them and you'll be fine, they never chase you (except the bee's) but every enemy can also be killed, so just jump on their head and the problem is gone.
Boss fight: There are 3 in total, and all of them are pretty much the same exact ship doing a slight variation of moves in an almost identical space. None of them were hard, but trying to find where to hit them or when to hit them can be tricky and one hit is instant death meaning you have to go through all the motions of their phase again just to get a chance to nail 'em.
Overal: I beat this game in 1.5 hours. If I had stayed to collect all the yarn, it might have taken me 2-2.5 hours to finish. The game is just a blur of noise with nothing standing out as being memorable, it is so short that you question how the math of 2 hours = $30, and this game exists when for $20 you could own Mario Odyessy or $10 more and you could own Sonic Forces or Sonic Mania. Bubsy has no reason to exist, it isn't fun or enjoyable, it isn't well made or thought out, it exists because someone needed money and it clearly shows.
P.S. the game ends claiming that "Bubsy will be Back" which is a thing only you can help stop. Become a hero today, save us all, don't buy this game so there will never be a Bubsy 2.

Earlier this year, when I learned Bubsy was coming back in a new game after more than two decades, I, like many others, was stunned to learn about this.  After that package of disaster known as Bubsy 3D got the franchise stuffed away and locked up in the attic, I never, I repeat, NEVER, in a million years, would think there'd be another official Bubsy game.  We were all taken completely by surprise.  Had my jaw dropped any further down, it would've detached from my face and fallen to the ground.  At the same time, however, after thinking about why they'd bring back the Bubsy franchise, I was rather more optimistic about said franchise's revival than I was pessimistic.  The game looked good in the trailer.  If Accolade were to ever bring Bubsy back, it couldn't be that they were trying to make another bad Bubsy game.  It sure as the Devil wouldn't be too hard to make this better than Bubsy 3D!  Accolade might've asked themselves, "What could possibly go wrong?", but we, the gamers, would be the ones finding out once the game got released.
The plot of the game's story is that a special yarn ball of Bubsy's, the "Golden Fleece" gets stolen by the Woolies (alien characters in the Bubsy franchise that are also his enemies).  Bubsy's mission is to fight the Woolies, yet again like he did in previous games, and get back his Golden Fleece.
The game's short.  I would've loved to see more levels and boss fights.  However, it wouldn't feel too short if you explore the levels more (find all the yarn balls, the t-shirts, the five keys in each stage that open the yarn ball vaults).  As Ferris Bueller once said, "Life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it."  The length of the game doesn't bother me too much, either.  It's more about quality over quantity.  I'd rather a good short game than a long bad one.
The pouncing is a cool idea, in addition to the gliding that this toon bobcat can already do.  It works well most of the time, but if only there weren't times you would miss hitting your enemies or falling to where you don't wanna fall when you use pounce.
Like in the first Bubsy game from '93, there are one-hit deaths in Woolies Strike Back, which I wasn't really hoping for.  That being said, however, these one-hit deaths are easier to avoid.  For one thing, when you collect a black t-shirt in a level, you'll get a shield that protects you from losing a life when you take damage.  In addition to being shielded, all the black t-shirts in the level turn white.  T-shirts, when white, then can be collected as extra lives.  After you lose your shield, however, all the t-shirts go back to being black.  Furthermore, unlike in his first game were Bubsy can run too fast for his own good, having one trillionth of a second to react to something that appears on the screen while running so fast, Bubsy runs at an appropriate speed, one where the player will have the time to see where he or she is guiding Bubsy.
After finally getting to play this game and examine it for myself, I have to say, this isn't a bad game overall.  Sure, it has its flaws (Of course, I didn't expect this to be perfect a game).  But in my book, it's actually decent.  If Accolade is planning on creating more Bubsy games in the future, they should consider what they're customers are saying about this, and learn how they can better the Bubsy franchise.  I do see potential for this franchise, and would love to see Accolade succeed with this.  I just hope they listen.

Full review (including score):
Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back is a 2D platformer that emphasizes its collectibles at the expense of its other content. The game has great presentation, but is completely lacking in content, especially if one is not into collectathons.
Everything visual about this game just works incredibly well together. The graphics, the backgrounds in the levels, the design of the enemies, etc. All of these well-polished elements combined make this a very pleasing game to look at and move around in. Each area was themed well and with some decent level design to match. Additionally, Bubsy’s random comments while playing were a treat to listen to. Some of the lines may have been corny or just stupid, but that fits perfectly into the game’s overall presentation.
This game does not tip the scale towards one difficulty, some levels can be easy, but some can be rather challenging. It was a good mixture of the two. The only outlier being the boss fights, which are much more challenging than the actual levels. Even then, such a challenge is warranted when most of one’s time is spent casually collecting the balls of yarn scattered throughout each level.
I managed to beat the game in just over an hour, and that is with the numerous deaths I suffered at the hands of the second and final boss. There is not a lot to this game, just 14 levels. Most of the emphasis is placed on collecting the balls of yarn found in each level, of which there are several hundred per level. However, the only gain from doing so is points and achievements, so there is not much to look forward to there. In fact, if one completely ignores that aspect of the game, it would probably take less than an hour to complete the game. There simply is not enough content for this game to be worth one’s time if the collectathon element is removed.
The pounce attack is fun when it works, especially when landing those multi-pounces. Unfortunately, it has its downsides. The pounce cannot be canceled once activated. This lead to many deaths in which I felt cheated. Jumping into water that was previously off-screen or landing just in front of an enemy moving towards me being just a couple examples. It was frustrating at times and I ended up avoiding using it for movement and saved it just for enemies I know I will hit.
Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back is an average platformer overall. It does not particularly excel in any area outside of its presentation, but it is not an entirely bad game either, it just simply lacks in content. There are better options out there, especially those with more content, so I would only recommend this game if you are a fan of collectathons.

I cannot believe that there aren't many people that know about this game, as it is simple amazing. It is a more than worthy successer to Supergiant's first game Bastion and its story is suprisingly hard hitting.
Pros:
- The game's soundtrack is phenomenal, and teh game's ability to allow the main character, Red, to hum along when out of combat helps the soundtrack shine.
- The game is beautiful, but runs very well, even for my 3 year old laptop, which isn't at all built for gaming.
- The combat system is simple, yet very fun, somewhat challenging (but not too challenging) and is very creative, making it a breath of fresh air.
- Speaking of difficulty of the game, there are limitations, much like Bastion's panthenion system, which allow you to make the game harder if you feel that it is currently too easy for you.
- The story respects you by allowing you to figure out and put pieces of the puzzle together, instead of constantly guiding you through the story, adding to the mystery of the game, which Bastion also had.
- The world and level design is very good and certain interactions that you can have with the world help to flesh out the world that the game is set in.
- There are extra challenged in the game and the game's story is replayable, if you would like to play the game with a different combination of powers.
Cons:
- The game is a little on the short side, with its main story coming to around 6 hours.
- There aren't any section within the game that allow you to make choice which will affect the story, and - despite Bastion only having a few of these - I feel that they are missed.
In all honesty the cons are really only nickpicks, and don't really affect the game too much, and I feel that Transistor is a step up from Bastion. I also feel like it could have been acknowledged as one of the best games of 2014, if it had been given its rightful attention as its stylistic gameplay and world, combined with the beautiful soundtrack and mysterious story, make it on of my personnal favourites.

Transistor is a work of art. I loved everything: the soundtrack, the visuals, the story, the gameplay. I won't say more about the art and the soundtrack, as you can check those out for yourself without buying the game, but if you need to hear about the story and gameplay to decide to buy this, then here it is.
The story is original and intriguing. It's not thoroughly told, either, which is good! A good story can be ruined if it's shoved down your throat while you impatiently wait to get on with the gameplay. In Transistor, you'll miss half the story if you don't bother inspecting the occasional object/location, or find the slightly out of the way terminal. It's easy and natural to seek out these plot points and clues as to just what this sci-fi setting is like.
The gameplay is also unique; you unlock skills as you level up but, you can only have 4 at a maximum in use. You can use the traits of each skill to upgrade your other skills, adding an attribute, and you can change your loadout of skills and upgrades at any save point. During battles you can freeze time -- or techinically, slow time -- to queue up a powerful combo of skills, in addition to attacking in real time. In addition, as you level up you unlock Limiters, which can be toggled to make the game harder, while giving a small boost to the experience received. This is a nice trick for making the difficulty curve steeper. Of course, I know no other way to play it than getting all the hardest, and thus most rewarding, Limiters first.
While the game runs smoothly, I will admit I've hit a couple bugs. One of which is, the very first ability completely disappeared, part way through my first playthrough. I am able to start a new file and playthrough without it happening, and it hasn't happened to my brother who got me the game, but to be honest it wasn't even that big of a deal. I've been going through with the first playthrough, despite that bug. The second bug was also strange but again, not a huge issue. After my first playsession of a few hours, I got on the next day to play it, but it started like it was the first time I was playing the game. I closed it and tried again, and again, it did not have a saved file. Slightly disappointed, I replayed through part of the game again, made sure there was a save file, then took a break. When I returned later that night, it started from where I had left off the previous night, suddenly finding the old save file. Strange, but it hasn't been an issue since.
Neither of those issues come close to stopping me from recommending this game. I may have gotten it as a gift, but after playing only part way through the story, I went ahead and bought it as a gift for a friend of mine while it was on sale for four bucks. I'm stingy with my money and expect others to do the same, but if you see Transistor at or below ten bucks, buy it.
This game is a work of art, and fully deserves the positive reviews.

Meh. Sci Fi Lords of the Fallen. Had potential but falls so disapointingly short.
Just finished it and just like Lords of the Fallen, it looks good, is graphically beautiful, had a lot of potential but is so clunky it loses any replay value.  Decent game to get on a sale and play once.  Ok story.  Actually good implant and weapon proficiency systems.  However just like Lords of the Fallen, all the weapons in the few archtypes are exactly the same.  No variation in movesets at all.  One does elemental damage.  One does phsycial damage.  One is the best in the archtype that you will end up using anyway despite potential resistances to elemental or physical.  Lame.
The game tries to make it artifically difficult by making literally everything in the game 1 or 2 shot you, no matter what your build is.  The only exception is when you have endgame equipment and go back to the very first area.  Then they kill you in 3-4 hits.  The combat is so clunky. Your combat moveset is locked in a 2-3 second windup animation for 90% of moves that you cant cancel while the enemies all have instant startup moves, unlimited stamina and non-telegraphed counters that will 1 shot you all game.  Most weapons can't stagger enemies and when you do stagger, they can only be staggered once and then have some coded stagger immunity for the rest of the fight making big weapons useless. I finished SL1 runs in all the Dark Souls games and this is a clunky mess in comparison to how those games handle.  The risk / reward system in this game is non existant. It's all (1 shot) risk and no reward to do anything differently. Hitboxes are terrible and it feels like there's no i-frames in your dodge at all which basically means you have 1 way to kill things in the game which make it trivial and boring which is:
"Slide in for the leap attack to get 1 hit in. Slide out so you're out of range because dodging close to an enemy will get you 1shot."  Bait attack, slide in, slide out.  Rinse, repeat Ad nauseum.  Boring.  All archtypes require you to do the exact same move until you have enough dps to kill things within the slide in / slide out window.  Then you can spam R1 instead.
Horizontal and vertical attacks sound cool in concept but actually make 0 difference in the game.  Doesn't affect how you can chop off limbs.  Doesn't affect how you can fight or hit things.  Doesnt' even have different movesets.  Weapons literally have the same attack pattern between horizontal and vertical except 1 or 2 of the slash moves in the combo are, you guessed it, horizontal or vertical.  Doesn't affect anything.  Slide in, slide out, get 1 shot while out of range because the hitboxes hit you from across the room anyway and enemies do not have a limit to how far they can leap in to attack.  The enemy leap attacks all take the same split second to move from where they are at the other side of the room to 1shotting you regardles of distance.  No balance to movespeeds.  Enemies seem to teleport across the room and hit you with those moves like the coding is done so that the time between original location and your location is constant (read instant) and the move speed to get there is calculated to make it happen.
Slide in, slide out, get 1shot. Rinse, repeat.
Interesting game.  Exciting for the first area while you discover new stuff.  Then you realize the whole game is copy paste and had no polish.
Oh well, back to Dark Souls.
Imagine Dark Souls, without fun and diverse enemies, large amount of fun weapons or awesome boss fights. Still, it's kinda fun. 6.5/10

Honestly, I would recommend this game on the music alone. The battle theme is great for setting the tone of the encounter and the town themes are quite varied. The music aside, this game really is quite funny without forcing humor. It plays on the already ridiculous concept well and just has fun with it.
It's nice to see the old style of RPG back but what makes it better is how quick the battles go, in terms of the action boxes. I'm not saying the battles are easy, oh god no. Enemies can hit like semi trucks and knock you flat before you realize what's happening. There are plenty of attacks/spells/combos/what-have-you to pick through so to make a play style that works and is personally appealing.
Things can get super tricky, though. The HP restore at the end of each battle is amazing but the lack of potions purchase can  really throw a wrench into the works. I see how the game could be too easy if you could purchase them considering how potions work but it's the last thing that matters when running out in the middle of a fight. The slow MP restore after every battle helps too but it means you have to be careful when using your favorite MP-using attacks. Thankfully, there's a MP restore/save point before every major boss battle so it's not like you'll go into a tough-as-nails battle completely unprepared for it.
I'm almost six hours in (up to Kingsport) but I'm loving this game to death. Can't wait to see where it goes.

I like Papers, Please because I like playing the role of an investigator of sorts, determining what information is contradictory with other information and acting on that. The Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney games always interested me because I could play as, well, an attorney, and slap my hand down on the table when the other person was wrong.
This game allows you to find information that does not correlate with other information on the passports, entry permits, and many other documents, in order to determine whether a person is allowed entry to a fictional country. The game has a story and an Endless Mode, achievements, ACTUAL CHOICES YOU MAKE THAT MATTER (you can choose whether to let someone in or not; you get a citation for doing the wrong option, but there are benefits like achievements for certain characters with more story or dialogue), and some other things.
If you like finding contradictions and doing justice, play this game. If you like strategy, play the game.

As a veteran player of the Wargame series I got my hopes up thinking this would be a successor - it is not.
If you enjoy the playstyle of Wargame, and are considering buying this game, don't... The playstyle is different, and at a much slower pace. There are no hitpoints or X = Y values, with RNG doing most of the heavy lifting in combat. You can trade shots with a tank, have hits and penetration but if the gods of RNG say no to scoring any damage, you can be killed on the first shot whilst an enemy tank absorbs 30.
The sight / spotting system is supposed to be more realistic, though can be flustering at times, as tanks cannot engage through treelines, or even sit in them. It may get better in time, but as a Wargame player it's a no from me.
