Legend of Grimrock is a dungeon crawling role playing game with an oldschool heart but a modern execution. A group of prisoners are sentenced to certain death by exiling them to the secluded Mount Grimrock for vile crimes they may or may not have committed. Unbeknownst to their captors, the mountain is riddled with ancient tunnels, dungeons and tombs built by crumbled civilizations long perished now. If they ever wish to see daylight again and reclaim their freedom the ragtag group of prisoners must form a team and descend through the mountain, level by level.
The game brings back the oldschool challenge with highly tactical real-time combat and grid-based movement, devious hidden switches and secrets as well as deadly traps and horrible monsters. Legend of Grimrock puts an emphasis on puzzles and exploration and the wits and perception of the player are more important tools than even the sharpest of swords could be. And if you are a hardened dungeon crawling veteran and you crave an extra challenge, you can arm yourself with a stack of grid paper and turn on the Oldschool Mode which disables the luxury of the automap! Are you ready to venture forth and unravel the mysteries of Mount Grimrock?

Although PC users where shunned from the first Battlefield: Bad Company (BF: BC), BF: BC2 more than makes up from this oversight and doesn't require you to have played the original. The singleplayer of BF: BC2 is short, but fun with an unusual set of characters that will leave you somewhat satisfied. However, the multiplayer aspect of the game is where BF: BC2 shines brighter than any other first-person shooter (FPS) to date. Using the Frostbite engine, BF: BC2 offers destructible environments and class-based modern warfare that offers 4 total classes (Assault, Engineer, Medic and Recon). The multiplayer is a blast and well worth the money for FPS enthusiasts.
The special acquisition (SPECACT) kit upgrade for Battlefield: Bad Company 2 (BF: BC2) holds a few advantages for players who are multiplayer fanatics. The SPECACT essentially doubles your classes by allowing you to choose either the default skins or the SPECACT skins that are denoted by their SA tags (e.g. Assault, Assault SA, Engineer, Engineer SA, etc). It also gives you access to a few new weapon choices that are only camouflaged editions of select default weapons such as the M95 SA, the UMP 45 SA, etc. These additions can be used to earn more kill stars for more points. It should be noted that purchasing this DLC kit will give you a CD-Key that you must redeem via BF: BC2's in-game menu while logged into your EA account.
The Vietnam expansion is a multiplayer addition for Battlefield: Bad Company 2. The game's mechanics play the same, but with more maps and weapons built around the Frostbite engine. The multiplayer for Battlefield: Bad Company 2 has always been the core component for the game and the Vietnam expansion provides a worthwhile investment for more action-packed fun for Battlefield fans. It should be noted that the maps are set in a jungle environment that limits destruction 2.0.

Plague Inc is a rather satisfying simulation in which the player's goal is to infect and kill off the entire world. Just exactly how the player chooses to tackle this is up to them.
Gameplay
The player can choose to slowly infect the population, remaining undetected and non-lethal, and then strike once much of the world's population is infected by evolving lethality to kill fast and unexpectedly, making it difficult for the world to react and cure it in time or just try to kill the world as fast as possible which usually results in losing the game as many of the more isolated countries such as Greenland will shut their ports and airports making it very difficult to infect them.
Content
The player is not presented with just one disease type, but many. These disease types range from a neurax worm which allows the player to manipulate infected hosts to their advantage to the necroa virus which allows the player to unleash a devastating zombie apocalypse on the world. It doesn't stop here though as there is a rather extensive community workshop with countless unique diseases thanks to the scenario creator which is available to every player who owns the game.
More coming
The developers of this game are also working on a multiplayer mode which will see two players battle it out to see who's plague is superior. The game is also regularly updated with new content and bug fixes.
Conclusion
While Plague Inc is not perfect, it offers great replayability with different ways to beat different scenarios and higher difficulty modes which can really challenge the player. The price is rather steep so I would suggest waiting until the game is on sale to get the best value for money. 8/10 - Great game.

Where do I begin? This was…. Phenomenal???  Such a satisfying gaming experience??  I just finished the main story and honestly I couldn’t be a happier lass. (Although I’m feeling a little emo, but in a good way?)
As everyone says, the sound is so nice.  The music fits the setting well and the voice acting is beautiful — so immersive!  It’s crazy that there are only 3 voice actors…  I’m in awe.  The art and graphics are beautiful, this game really shines with its aesthetic; the visuals and audio combine to create some sort of cyberpunk fantasy setting with a touch of film noir vibes but all delivered with a brightly colored palette.  They build a rich atmosphere really well.  It’s lovely ~  and defintely the strongest appeal of the game for most players.
The story is well composed but, which might not sit well with everybody, it’s not delivered too directly!  The game asks you to slowly piece together small information available as the plot progresses (tap into that detective side of you!)  It’s part of the experience to be in the dark, and it’s relevant to the story to not know exactly what is going on.  But information is everywhere, from the Function descriptions, looking down a river, to Red's OVC Terminal comments.  When all the pieces connect it’s a really rewarding feeling, and honestly, I can’t stop being impressed by how much is revealed through small details, about the motives of the characters and the unique setting.  Brilliant storywriting and characterization.
I really loved the battle system.  It’s not exactly turn-based, but a sweet fusion of that with real time… In terms of strategy, there are many ways to approach enemies with countless combinations to try out.  I also really appreciate how much customization is available to up the challenge with “limitations” as they are unlocked through the game.  It might be a bit slow for some people, but it works as the gameplay mechanic to deliver this great story.

Modern Warfare 2 is my personal pick for the best game in the Call of Duty franchise, and arguebly one of my picks for the best FPS game of all time. I have so much history with this game. I've put so many hours into the multiplayer back on console, and just beat the campaign for the 4th time. This was also my second Call of Duty game; My first being kind of an obsure one: Call of Duty 3 on the Wii. I still remember playing this game for the first time like it was yesterday, and it just blew me away. It was once I played the game after growing up a bit where I realized how great this game really is.
- The graphics have aged like fine wine. I always like to use this game as a game that has aged really well. The graphics on max settings still look great. It looks nothing like a game released in 2009.
- The campaign is fantastic. I would know because I've played it 4 times. It has some of the most memorable missions in CoD. My personal favorite mission is a close tie between Enemy of my Enemy and Second Sun.
- The campaign can be challenging on a higher difficulty, actually requiring you to use cover. Yes, using cover in a Call of Duty. I know it sounds bizarre. It's also rewarding to play on a high diffculty because you get achievements for every mission you beat. I beat the game on Hardened, and will possibly play through it again sooner or later to get the Veteran achievements.
- Spec Ops gives you some neat little missions to play after beating the campaign. You can even play through them with a buddy!
- Voice acting is pretty good.
- The characters are great, and memorable.
- The game is so well written. It is a very quotable game.
- Multiplayer is a mixed bag. It's pretty broken. Let's be honest. Noobtubing is way too OP. The PC version is also said to be riddled with hackers that can get you VAC banned by giving you level 70. Most of the reviews that claim this are old, so maybe they fixed their anti-cheat or something.
- There's no FOV slider to increase the disgusting 65 FOV. You can increase your FOV in SP and MP using third party programs. There's a guide on how to accomplish this
. I personally use 80, because 90 makes your arms look like they're 5 feet long, which looks odd. If you're worried about being VAC banned online for "cheating," I've used the FOV changer in MP and I haven't gotten banned yet.
- This game is still priced at $20, with the game+DLC being a ridiculous $45. It's 8 years old. That kind of money for an 8 year old game is laughable.
- Singleplayer and Multiplayer are two seperate Steam games, which can look awkward. I don't know why they didn't do what
with their singleplayer and online mode.
Modern Warfare 2 is a great game. I always just loved it. It's a game that I can play any day of the week, and still have fun playing it. The campaign and spec ops is worth a purchase alone.

This is a long formattive essay style review of "The Surge". I don't have much experience on the Steam platform, but have been gaming my entire life, and have loads of experience with many different games. If you find this review helpful please upvote it, so that other gamers can see it. The order I have written about the primary problems in the game are as follows; Lore, Combat issues, Build Diversity, Boring World. If you want the summary of my opinion minus all the explanation, skip to the last paragraph.
If you aren't a Lore nerd, you might as well skip this section, but if you are, you will hate this game. There is no plot. Characters somehow manage to be more flat and 1 dimensional than DS1 NPC's (which is pretty damn bad), and not only is information about the world scarce, but what you do get doesn't really tell you anything. All you know throughout the game is as follows; Blah blah blah "The Surge" happened, so everyone is now a hostile (but surprisingly agile and competent?) zombie. I looked on the wiki after concluding I wouldn't ever finish the game to see if this improved at all beyond where I got (Little more than half way through the game) and it didn't. Its one of the most consistent problems people have with the game, no story, no lore, no interest, BLAH.
The following problem is game breaking; the animation lock time is inconsistent. If I click R1 on my controller once, I get one attack. But if I do it twice, I get 3 attacks. See the problem? Pretty much every weapon in the game has strange and obscure "combos", that are horribly made, and make the game feel unresponsive. If an enemy lunges me, I dodge, and then go in and hit R1 twice, to attack twice. Yet somehow I get locked into a 3rd attack, which I am then punished for. There is no way to cancel it, no way to dodge, and the instances in which this happens are EXTEMELY inconsistent. It's infuriating and unfair.
(Combat continued) Secondly, despite giving the player no effective means to fight multiple enemies (especially in claustrophic spaces where half the game takes place) the game still throws hordes of them at you. This is a cheap kind of difficulty, because the only way around it is to A) run past the enemies and skip them. B) lure them far away enough that you get a 1 vs 1 or 1 vs 2 going because most of them turn back. Or C) Abuse a chokepoint (which are not readily available). This is extremely lazy and poor game design, as there isn't any way to deal with the fights involving multiple enemies in a fun or efficient way. This does not stop the game from constantly throwing groups of enemies at you. Similar games like darksouls do not rely on this cheap trick, and other games are built so that players have options to deal with mob hordes. Say for example in the Batman Arkham Knight game series; the combat system has mechanics built into the game to let you fight mobs of enemies, so that when there are mobs of enemies, you can actually fight them. This game throws hordes at you, but gives you no way to fight the mob hordes, wtf? These two massive flaws in the combat system combine to produce broken and frustrating gameplay that is most certainly difficult, but for all the wrong reasons.
There are essentially two build paths in this game, from the start. Lightweight, with fast attacks, and low armor, or Heavweight with slower attacks, and more armor. The differences in damage between the two seem minor, despite my comparing them between two different boss weapons, one heavy, one light. The problem is that the heavy builds are objectively worse than the light builds. Heavy attacks don't do much more damage, the extra armor provides no substantial benefit, and the slower attacks leave you wide open to enemy attacks. The attacks are so slow, that I find certain enemies nearly impossible to deal with, and the aforementioned issues with unwanted chain attack lock animations, only excacerbate this issue. There are also "implants" which function like perks in the game, but I won't even bother going into detail, because the vast majority of these perks are inferior to the generic ones that give health, stamina, or let you carry more consumable heals at once.
Boredom. This game is boring. There really isn't any other way to say it, the combat is a drag, there is no real plot to follow, no cool tidbits of lore, no compelling characters, and the side quests are stale and lacking in purpose. The Environments seem mostly colorless, just hues of gray and black, with orange or yellow danger lights scattered around. The levels are basically color coded, and do not look appealing at all; they do in fact, look very dead. Since there is literally nothing to compel you to play beyond being a completionist, there is also no incentive to explore. The only justification I could give for exploring would be finding short cuts and secrets. However, you won't care about these things, since the game will fail to grab your interest in the first place.
In conclusion this game has a bland, and lifeless world, absolutely no story, lore, compelling characters, or interesting subplots, AND two aspects of combat so unrefined and lazy, that they completely break the game's combat system. One important criticism that I have neglected going into detail over, but is worth mentioning; The broken camera angles can and will kill you. I do not see any point in playing the game, nor any redeeming factors in it; Do Not Buy.

Like Lords of the Fallen, but better.
Positives:
• Action feels great. Controls and movement are responsive, weapon movesets are varied, and everything from the huge two-handed weapons and the quick dual-wield ones are extremely satisfying to use.
• The Energy system is a great way to encourage you to stick in the fight, similar to Bloodborne vs Souls. Landing hits gives you energy, which can be used on a small estus-free heal, support attacks or abilities from your drone, or if the enemy's health and low, a dismemberment finisher. It works great as a way to encourage you to play aggressively.
• The dismemberment system never got old in my 25 hours with the game, which is surprising. It's an extremely satisfying way to collect new armor sets and weapons without relying on RNG loot drops, and as every successful finisher also boosts your tech scrap multiplier (your currency/experience in this game) you're encouraged to try and perform one on every enemy you find.
• The armored enemy and limb targeting system is great. To get new armor and weapons, you need to target that part when fighting the enemy and successfully perform a finisher to cut it off -- but if you don't need what that enemy has, targeting an unarmored part lets you deal more damage and stagger more quickly. The tradeoff works really well, letting you decide on an ememy-by-enemy basis what to do.
• The areas are *really* well interconnected. What feels like a linear sprawling megacomplex at first constantly grows more familar as you progress and unlock a huge number of shortcuts and alternate paths, more than any other game I've played in this genre.
• As mentioned before, successful finishers increase your scrap multiplier -- but this is reset when you go back to Ops (a bonfire) to refresh your injectables (estus). Alternatively, you can stop by Ops' equipment crafting station to respawn all enemies *without* refilling your injectables or restarting your tech multiplier. The risk/reward for farming is satisfying and player-friendly.
Negatives
• Enemy movesets are a little samey. If two enemies are using the same weapon type, they'll generally be using the same attacks. Not entirely bad, since it lets you capitalize on your mastery more, but a little more variety would have been nice.
• The critical path is linear. I don't care about this at all, but some might.
• The biggest negative for me, the aesthetic is similar throughout the game. While it looks good, it can get pretty confusing identifying where you are at times. I would have appreciated something like a color-coded wall design to highlight different areas, especially in the maintenance tunnels constantly connecting rooms and sectors.
The $40 base price now is a very fair price for the game. If you get it on sale for even less, you should be very satisfied. Greatly looking forward to what this team continues to do.

The Surge is a great game, but one with large flaws that start to become apparent in the latter half. First of all, the game is very fun for the entire first half of it. It feels like a sci-fi Dark Souls with very nice graphics and fun combat. People criticize the controls as "clunky" but you're a guy in a massive suit of robotic construction armor, so I thought they made sense. For a lot of the game I was happily playing along wondering what the heck people were up in arms about.
Unfortunately, the game takes a bit of a turn towards the cheap in the second half of the game. As difficulty begins to ramp up, rather than throw new tactical situations at the player, they simply jack up the damage that enemies do. The worst offender of this was a humanoid boss that for all intents and purposes should do typical damage but somehow was able to one shot you even if you jacked up your HP massively. There are ways to deal with this, like parrying, but it feels cheap and out of place for a Souls game to kill you that easily if you make a slip-up, especially when there's little windup.
Ultimately, the game's design begins to miss the point of a Souls game, that it is fair but hard, and starts to put you in impossible situations that you have no choice but to "cheese" by exploiting enemy movement ranges and such. So ultimately the  game is fun in so many ways, especially in the first half, but takes a bit of a nosedive that it can't quite pull itself out of.
There are some other minor niggles. You can't choose the protagonist gender, which feels like they didn't learn much from Lords of the Fallen. There are also really annoying sounds in certain parts. The default medbay music gets old after about 5 minutes and one of the "operations" bases has an annoying voice over playing constantly (you can shut it off in the options, but the option is so obtuse that I didn't realize it until much later). My armor constantly glitched off my body, something that seems like it would have been easy to discover and fix. It feels like the game was biting off a bit more than the studio could chew.
The graphics of the game are pretty fantastic and the art design is top notch, incorporating extremely inventive futuristic designs. I did experience minor glitches like some unusual flickering with lighting. The characters are somewhat interesting, and there is a decent story, but it never truly grabbed me and sucked me in, and ends up feeling a bit like a mediocre movie that has a point it wants to get across but sort of flubs the execution. I thought the story was, at least, superior to Lords of the Fallen, but still not as engrossing as Dark Souls or Bloodborne by a long shot.

Attack animations go on for a varying length of time depending on whether you held down the button for a long time, or a short time. That's how it's supposed to work. Instead it feels like you flip a coin each time you attack and then either do a 2-3 hit combo or a 1 hit attack. You can dodge like dark souls, but this is equally frustrating as the game locks you out of doing so while you are attacking until you're stunned by an enemy. There were multiple times where I tried to dodge out of the way of my enemy's attack while my character was performing a 3 hit spinning combo that I didn't try and do. I would then die due to the enemy having a small enough weapon (staff or sword of some sort) that didn't result in a stun to knock me out of the attack queue.
Another point in the combat that frustrated the hell out of me was that the game likes to give you deadly ledges fight on and to put enemies near that ledge. Well, the finishers sometimes will move you forward, sometimes to the side, sometimes you'll end the finisher where you started it. After the finisher's done, you might have thrown yourself off the ledge, or you might not.
The level design is for the most part great. Except for when it is just really bad. In one section you are being shot at by an enemy at a turret. The turret is on a raised platform resembling a tower. The stairway up to it hugs the tower structure along one side, and then has an approximately six foot gap between the stairway and the top of the small platform connected at the corner of said platform by a walkway. There's no guard rail that prevents you from falling in to said gap and falling down. To your death. It is also possible to use a finisher on that enemy and walk your happy♥♥♥♥♥into that gap and fall to your death. It is also possible for the enemy to knock you back into that gap and fall to your death.
I want to like this game. It does many things really well, but it feels like it was rushed out before having the amount of time needed to make a well polished and refined dark souls competitior. If they make a Surge 2 I will likely buy it as long as they learn from their mistakes and spend more time refining the game.

Spacebase DF9’s 2,859 “mostly negative” reviews (at the time of writing) are probably more a testament to Steam’s ubiquity as a content delivery tool than to the game’s own (very real) problems. And it does have problems, to be sure, but depending on your outlook and how much you pay for it, they’re not insurmountable.
Its gameplay appears at first to be something along the lines of the legendary Dwarf Fortress, Mucky Foot’s 2001 classic Startopia, or Firefly Studios’  2003 Space Colony, but its flaws – the result of a suddenly-abandoned development process – make it play more like a Roguelike. Your rather nebulous goal is to re-populate the galaxy by building endless space stations, staffing them with an ever-increasing supply of wandering space travellers and keeping them happy and safe from weird diseases, bloodthirsty raiders and each other. Material for building comes from mining asteroids or disassembling passing wrecks and derelicts, and your rooms and corridors are built and then assigned different uses – residential, life support, various social, scientific and utilitarian functions. There’s a strong people-management aspect too, as each new arrival at your base can be assigned to one of eight different duties, each of which will make them feel varying degrees of satisfaction or frustration, and each of which they’ll be good or bad at according to a 1-5 star system. In all respects, the UI is super friendly and makes juggling your people as easy as possible. Which is great, because you can eventually build gigantic structures with literally dozens and dozens and dozens of crewmembers. Crucially though, you have almost zero direct control over your people. You can only order them to report to the infirmary if they’re injured, and even then it may take them a while to limp their way over.
At first, as you learn the ropes, each new game comes hard and fast. Death comes as a result of being ill-prepared to research a disease cure, or not having sufficient defences against a surprise Raider attack, or for any one of dozens of interestingly unfortunate and unforeseeable reasons (usually often as funny as they are frustrating). But the actual process of making your space stations is so much fun that the urge to immediately try again keeps you clicking, again and again, learning more and more each time, developing and abandoning new ideas and strategies as you go. Spacebase DF 9 is very much one of those Civ/Morrowind-type games that suck the hours out of your life without you realising. Be prepared for some really late nights if you decide to have ‘just one quick go’ before bedtime.
Adding to this feeling is the game’s own save system, which by default consists of toggle-able silent autosaves and a Save and Quit menu option. Like a psychopathic lover, Spacebase DF9 doesn’t want you to be anywhere other than inside it, grinding at full speed. Played like this, the feeling is very much of a  Roguelike’s ‘one life, one death’ trip, and all of this helps mitigate the pain of being screwed by one of the game’s terrible bugs or imbalances.
Yes, they are quite terrible, unfortunately. But in the twenty hours that I’ve played it so far, the problems have been all about imbalance and lack of tweaking, rather than outright bugs. One of the worst of these is the fact that the guns on enemy ships, once they’ve boarded you, remain ‘hostile’ even after you’ve killed or captured the invaders (sometimes they can even be reformed and will join your crew to start a new life), or claimed their ship as your own. Only by eventually disassembling enough of the enemy ship will you be able to cut off power to the gun, thus making it safe. But getting to the bloody thing can be a real game-breaker – these defensive turrets have great range and cut through people in spacesuits like a lightsabre through yogurt. It’s at times like these that the lack of direct control over your spacemen becomes a real tooth-grinder, and you can end up with piles and piles of floating corpses made up of the Builders who foolishly crossed in front of the guns to get behind them (in space, the AI paths in direct lines from point-to-point), as well as the Doctors who went to retrieve their corpses.
As far as imbalance in the invisible numbers, the worst offender is the near-constant brawling that goes on. At best this leads to a trip to the brig to cool off for the aggressor and a trip to the infirmary for the victim. At worst, guns will be drawn, and people and facilities start falling. In-fighting is a result of a brilliant system of cabin fever that is determined by various things, including job satisfaction and a host of actual personal feelings and emotions, all of which can be monitored on the crew’s individual profiles. Assigning two people who hate each other to a double cabin is a recipe for disaster, while the sight of bloody corpses littering the place has an obvious impact on depression (especially if the deceased was someone’s friend). But again, due to the abruptly aborted development process, it’s one of several crucial, glaringly imbalanced systems. Which, unless Double Fine release the source code, as they’ve promised to but still not yet done, may never be properly sorted out. This is doubly frustrating because a lua-based modding system is present and correct, but so far nobody’s done anything with it.
Like the similarly blighted and similarly great fun Aliens: Colonial Marines, it’s a game with a bad reputation that in reality is only partially deserved. Early adopters and those who saw the potential for a Dwarf Fortress in space have every right to be annoyed (and to make those thousands of “negative” Steam reviews). But for those of us coming to the game in its ‘finished’ state, and aware of the lingering problems, there is still much fun to be had. Double Fine’s original plan for the game was hugely ambitious, ultimately requiring much more funding than they could successfully raise for it (hence the truncated development). It was only unfortunate that they had already taken it well into the Early Access phase at USD 20 a pop before they realised this. But that’s one of the risks of public alphas, crowdfunding and transparent game development. Like condoms, no one's happy when they go wrong.
If we’re looking at it in financial terms, then in my case I bought it in the 2015 Steam summer sale at -50%, or EUR 4.99, and have played it now for nearly 21 hours. My feeling is that I’ve had at least 20 Euros of fun from it, and that’s quite important. With some AAA titles costing nearly 60 Euro-dollarpounds and offering dozens of hours of gameplay, but failing to deliver even half as much fun, for a flawed gem like Spacebase DF9 to give you that elusive feeling of true, full-belly satisfaction is, I think, quite a feat.

After playing and loving Bastion, I had high hopes for Transistor.  Unfortunately, several glaring issues wth the gameplay just kept me from enjoying the game.  The story seems fine, if rather tough to piece together, so I will not cover that here.
Obviously Transistor will be compared to Bastion, so I will do that as well.  The pros to Bastion's gameplay are
-Wide range of weapons that can be used in combinations for different playstyles
-Upgrade system that adds noticable benefits to both your character and his weapons
-Strong core gameplay (dodging, blocking, attacking, etc.) that rewards skill and timing and prevents overreliance on healing items
-No unnecessarily punishing elements (i.e. undodgeable/unblockable attacks), so deaths are almost always your fault
Transistor on the other hand, seems to go directly against what worked in Bastion for core gameplay.
-No natural block or dodge ability (aside from the teleport dash and invisibility functions), so there is no way to mitigate damage
-Slow-moving character that tends to get caught on obstacles, exacerbated by the lack of a natural dodge
-No healing aside from a late-game function, so some fights become battles of attrition
-Several enemies whose attacks are unavoidable (dogs, creeps, jerks), even with the aforementioned functions, so fights involving these enemies are unnecessarily punishing
-Environments that offer little room for maneuvering
All of this combined results in a gameplay experience that is a chore to endure, particularly later on when high-health enemies with unavoidable attacks appear in numbers.  The teleport dash function can help, but even when dashing away in a straight line enemies can still catch and damage you.  And the environments' cramped design means that you end up dashing in circles trailing enemies that keep picking away at your health in between dashes.  Fights become a race to see if you can kill these enemies before you lose a critical function.
It is a shame that I could not enjoy the game due to these awful design choices.  The function system is an intriguing feature with great depth that could have enabled a wide range of playstyles.  Unfortunately the poorly-designed basic  gameplay means that this system cannot be used to its full potential.

A far superior game to Supergiant Games' first outing Bastion. If you loved Bastion, you'll love Transitor. Stunning graphics, fantastic soundtrack and a mysterious storyline. The story is intentionally vague and forces you to pick it up through items picked up and trawling through menus. Some games take this approach and do it really well. I didn't care for it here. I mean, I really like the 'main character isn't in the story' approach of some stories like murder mysteries of Gone Home, but here the main characters were there talking and just being vague on purpose.
In battles, the range of enemies is extremely small. Which is kinda weird since the options for dispatching them is so high since you can use a weapon socket system to build cool attacks. But once you've minimaxed your loadout the game is just a cake walk.
There is a turn based battle mode which I didn't bother using until the final battle where it's forced upon you. It was kind of lame, imo.
They built something cool but missing some ingredient. And a raspy noir style voiceover didn't bring it home.

Mixed feeling about Transistor are to be expected. The production quality is simply superb. The short but though provoking story, the voice overs, the music and the art style are all excellent but I couldn't help feeling a bit cheated by the pricetag, length and mechanics.
I finished it in less than 5hours and run the + version until I realized even that was too easy (more on that later) and you are basically replaying story mode. Unless you are a completionist there is really no point in replaying and even you do, 10 hours is the max you can get out of the game.
The mechanics is where the game falls short in my opinion. Unlike Bastion that had one of the best ARPG gameplays of recent years the mechanics of Transistor are deep but unbalanced. You'll struggle at first but when you start understanding the Turn() system and skill combos you'll feel empowered...for about 2 hours. Then you'll discover one of the 2-3 (maybe more) combination of skills that completely break the game and make every enemy a joke. Even with every limiter installed you can streamroll through everything and never use Turn(). You can further handicap yourself by not using those powerful combination but most other builds feel incredibly weak or are too focused on evasion/Turn() prolonging the fights unecessarily.
TLDR; An amazing piece of art disguised like a game. If you are looking for a challenge or your next addiction look elsewhere. If you want a short but moving story wait for a discount.

Very fun, albeit simple and very linear turn based RPG. There really aren't any special missions, mini-games, crafting, or other, later RPG game elements, but that doesn't mean this is bad.
What this game does have over others is its uniqueness that I've yet to see, if not just heard about, in other games:
When you arrive at a new area you have a number of potential random battles to be fought. Once you fight them all you don't have to worry about getting harassed any more! But, if you so choose, you can always instantly get into a fight with enemies, regardless of that "battles remaining" number. This is helpful if you needed to level grind a bit, for example.
Winning a fight against your enemies instantly heals your full party to max health. That seems odd at first, but there are definitely a TON of very strong enemies that can kill you from full health very easily. You do NOT, however, restore your mana fully, but only to a very small extent. The mana is a much bigger deal because you primarily use "skills" and "magic" more than you would on basic attacks, which tends to be the common thing in older turn based RPGs.
Branching level ups is a fun system that is somewhat in other RPGs, but more so seen as a type of "skill tree" that you see instead, and thus you can't remove and reallocate any point. It's interesting forcing your mage type characters into a fighter role sometimes, for example. The game definitely offers a variety of physical and magical attacks for each character, too, regardless of their normal intended archetype.
That's really it, for the most part. There are secret dungeons, which is always a nice thing to have, and the other few unique game aspects, some of which I may have forgotten at the moment, but the game is hands down a great purchase, fully surpassing the "bang for your buck" considering the price tag of $3 which also gives you Breath of Death VII to go along with it.

Cthulhu saves the world is a fun little game in the inspiration of JRPG's. I couldn't even begin to describe to you the plot of this wondeful little game. It is one of those, you have to see to believe, kind of game. The combat is fluid, very fast paced. I enjoyed the way this game handles random encounters. There is a counter and whenever you get somewhere, either world map or dungeon, there is a number. For every random encounter you enter and win, the counter goes down by one. Once the counter reads "none", there are no more fights that you will get into randomly. Now, some people might think you can't fight anything at all, but that isn't the case. In the menu there is a fight command. When pressed, you will be thrust into a battle immediately, allowing for leveling if you need to. The characters are silly and enjoyable. Once leveled, there is a little bit of customization with the game, allowing you to choose which level-up bonus you want. You may choose the stats over more HP or the Fire spell over Fire Strike. This allows for, at least the first couple of playthroughs, to be an interesting playthrough, trying different combinations to see which you prefer for the character. The bonus modes I haven't delved into and will update this review when I do so. That said, even without playing them, Cthulhu has stolen my heart with this humurous little game. I hope you pick it up and enjoy it as much as I did.

Seeing as this is on sale, it's an appropriate time to post a review for this game. Very simply, I really, really enjoy this game. Yes, it's a Soulsborn-style game (and I'll be comparing it to other games like it as appropriate), but with the "fresh twist" of modern technology. It sets out to do what it wants to, and it does a solid job of it. Is it perfect? No, but that's okay. Here's a very lengthy explanation why. TLDR is at the bottom.
Sadly, there isn't too much to write about here. You can avoid most of the overall story in the game and just kinda blunder through enemies and bosses. However, if you look into it, and pay attention to the cutscenes, dialog, and character interactions, it's actually pretty interesting to follow. It kind of falls into the average "tragic hero" trope in the beginning, but there's a fair bit more under the hood that the player can explore if they choose. Personally, I thought the story was particularly interesting and complemented what the game had to offer. It isn't something you're spoon-fed though, and it's not as intriguing as other Soulsborn games where you might pause the game for a bit to go look up the lore. But it's there, and it should be given credit where credit is due.
You've got your stamina bar, you've got your dodge, you've got your whack button, you've got your harder whack button, and you've got your lock on. It's pretty simple to pick up and learn this game, and that's not a bad thing. Anyone who has played a game like this will be able to pick it up relatively easily. I would even go so far as to say this game is easier to pick up then other Soulsborn games, as something about the combat feels a bit easier to get used to. Early on, the enemies aren't nearly as punishing, meaning that you can really get a feel for wind-ups, learn telegraphed moves, and find a playstyle that suits you. Sure, if you're looking for the "punch me in the nether regions as soon as I start" style of game, it might not fit that, but it actually feels like a good entry point into this style of combat. As someone who isn't
good at Soulsborn combat, it was actually really pleasant to "learn" this game, really. That said, it doesn't just "hold your hand" throughout the later encounters, as you'll still have to work for your boss kills and such (unless you're like, a no-damage Souls runner, in which case, why are you reading my review anyways).
Now normally this is a point I'd ignore, as I'm usually the type to just put on some background music that doesn't drown out audio queues and play blissfully through the game. But oddly enough, this one struck home. All of the music in the game is
. But there's a particularly atmospheric song in the OST, which plays in every medbay in the game (unless you turn it off, which props to the devs for considering that for those who might not want to hear it too much). There's something oddly haunting about the melody, and it feels at home in this game. The song is Prisoner by Stumfol. There's a beautiful melancholy to hearing this melody every time you revive, and it feels like it has two meanings to you: the medbay is a sanctuary and you are safe here, and that you feel alone in this world and need to trudge along to sort out what happened. Very simply, that's a beautiful atmospheric touch to add to the game, and I even found myself smiling as I revived and heard the song.
The rest of the soundtrack is enjoyable to listen to and adheres to the theme well. Oftentimes you'll be too caught up in the heat of the battle to really give it a listen, but I encourage you to give it a listen sometime.
If there's anything you can fault The Surge for, it's for not having too much content. You don't have too many zones, there's a limited roster of bosses, and it's not nearly as open-world as other Soulsborn games. It's not meant to be your "put in hundreds of hours" kind of game. That said, it introduces new concepts to make the most out of what it can. Hard-mode kills on bosses are something to work for and be proud of (and have the show-off potential through weapons), and smelter kills are progressive towards bragging-rights-worthy content. The "hack off what you want" style of gameplay is super cool, in my opinion, and really allows the player to farm or ignore enemies when necessary to suit their playstyle. See an enemy with a piece of armor you like? Target that limb and hack it off of them. Congratulations, you most likely just got a new schematic to make that piece of armor you wanted! To me, this was a really cool feature to have, and I enjoyed it greatly. This mechanic is a lot of the draw that The Surge has, and though ultimately there aren't TOO many weapons and armor sets, it's a really cool mechanic and I enjoyed it a lot.
Alright. Take your favorite Soulsborn, be it DS 1-3, Bloodborn, S&S, what have you. Now, throw it far into the future. Suddenly it's post-apocalyptic and driven by technology. Does that sound appealing? If it does, then this game is definitely for you. If it doesn't, then that's okay, I'm just being honest here. The apocalyptic machine-ridden style isn't for everyone, and I feel like that could be a deal-breaker here if you're adamant about your fantasy style, so it's necessary to state. Personally, I enjoy this theme greatly, and The Surge does it well. The environments are detailed and beautiful, and the wreckage lying around is a good look for the game which adds to the initial feelings of being left alone in a world you don't fully understand. It's a simple theme, but The Surge does a good job with it.
If a Soulsborn game beset with rampant machines and literal hack-and-slash gameplay sounds fun to you, I highly recommend you pick up this game. It flew under the radar in a lot of aspects because it didn't do anything perfectly, but it did a lot of things well. The new things that it brought to the table were done well, so if you can get past a smaller-length game, you're sure to have fun with it. It's a solid pick-up to satisfy your Soulsborn craving.
TL;DR: It doesn't revolutionize Soulsborn games, but it does a good job at innovating where it can. It's a bit short, but still worth the time.

May I just begin this review by saying, HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥THESE GRAPHICS ARE BEAUTIFUL.It looks amazing for a game like this, beginning with the shadows and going from each detail to the effects of attacks. I never really liked turn based games, but this really suprised me.The game has a large variety of attack skills which are refered to as Functions(Also by attack skills I mean attacks like a slash or a special type)You can combine attacks together, except that attack that you choose to combine with another attack in order, (there's a slot for upgrading other attacks using a attack) has it's properties added on to the main attack.Well, at least some of the properties.You'll be able to do this once you unlock the thing that allows you do this.The attacks you add on to can do a range of different things to other attacks.That's all I'm gonna say about the attacks to not spoil anything else about the attacks.The sound track for this game IS GOD DAMN AMAZING, and you should really consider buying the soundtrack along with the game.The monster designs are creative and as you progress through the story, you figure out the backstory of the main protagonist before where the game began as you played.The boss fights are amazing too and the bosses are also creative.There is a skill you gain early on that allows you to plan your moves, and if used right, along with the properties of the attacks, it is EXTREMELY SASTISFYING and rewarding to get it right.I would buy this game for any of my friends if I had the money, and am going to do so now. I SO GOD DAMN BADLY want a sequal if it ever comes out and wil buy it immedietly.Not only that, but the game has challenges as you progress along to complete, and also the game has quite the replayability, as in one go through the game, I was unable to unlock all the attacks.You get to choose what you want to unlock (but only 1 from each thing)and get experience to level up as you go along and fight the monsters.There is so many combinations for this game and it's attacks.Also there are limiters you can enable as you go along and unlock them to gain more experience and to make the game more challenging.I would recommend this game to ALMOST anyone.

Transistor is a great game. It combines beautiful graphics and story with fun gameplay. Transistor's art style is very nice, using an isometric view. It tells a story through a variety of methods. The gameplay is unique. You have to fight robots in it, however there is a lot of strategy involved. The fights are done in certain areas as you progress through the games. You have to defeat all of the robots to continue. There is an upgrade tree you have to decide which upgrades to use, and there is a very unique planning move you can do, allowing you to plan out your character's movement and attacks in a battle, which is executed rapidly after the planning is done. It has an element of replayability if you enjoy the gameplay after finishing the game. I would highly recommend Transistor.

I didn't expect this game to be great, but the storytelling is high quality. Everything is.
It makes you ask questions constantly - and in my opinion - with no plot holes left when answered. The game has a great combat system, but it is not a walk in the park despite giving you some kind of "ZA WARUDO" ability when using the "Turn()" system.
As Red, you will repeatedly face enemies that will increase in non-artifical difficulty. What seemed difficult to you after your first boss encounter will be nowhere near as hard as the level progression after a while. You will be in situations where you probably will not be using the same moveset as you level up; Experimentation in combat feels great and is highly encouraged without directly forcing you.
As for the story, it does a great job getting the player interested in the bond that develops between Red and Transistor level after level. Of course, Transistor does mostly all of the talking in the game, but he isn't annoying to listen to. He always has something to say and adds statements that builds parts of the world of Transistor - something Red can't narrate for us.
I cannot recommend this game enough. No cons come up to mind, other than the 6 hours it took me to finish the first run of the story.

For me as a bloody newbie is this perfect. Mostly i play 9 Ball and my table has a tournament setting and the pockets are narrow. I have also the option to change the pockets size, table speed, table skid, rail cut, rail speed and rail grab. But i did not change it.
Physics & Graphics:
VP4 has the best physics. In the past i've played also other pool games but it was a feeling of "playing a game". In VP4 it feels like i play on a real pool table. In my opinion VP4 in a RL Pool Simulator.
In VP4 the graphics is good but not perfect. In my opinion the game need bit more shadows (balls & table) and a bit more reflexions. I did not need mindblowing effects & eye candy graphics because I DID NOT SEE THIS IN RL !
Multiplayer Lobby, Player & vponlinesite:
The online lobby is well frequented. Mostly i see 20-50 players. All players are friendly and they know gentlemen pool language. This is nice.
The vponline.celeris website is coupled with the game. There i can get TONS of informations about upcoming tournaments, Matches, Pool and Snooker basic rules, own profile manager and so on.
The game has a own web browser.
This is a free game without advertising ingame.
Totally awesome game, not worth the 25 dollars subscription for just being able to play tournaments and special games that get cancelled cause there are not enough players

Bought the game a few months ago and must say loving it, it's not only pool that you can play but an whole variation of games on a pool table or snooker table.

The rooms where you can play have all different tables with their own atmosphere, even the table speed and pockets are adjustable the way I like it the best.
I was looking for a game that came close to the real thing and must say they “don’t come better than this”!
I would recommend VP4 to everyone that loves to play billiards, in real life or as a game.
For me it’s money well spent!

I agree with what a lot of other folks say about this game, that it's art and tells a compelling story and gives you an interesting dichotomy in helping yourself and helping others.  There's a number of different ways to play it, and it forces you as a player to make interesting decisions.  I bought this game on a steam sale some years back and begrudgingly played through it to my intended (and favorite) ending (20).
I can see why this game has a lot of positive feedback and love and everything, but ultimately it's not something I would recommend to anyone interested in having fun, or enjoying themselves.  It has a solid theme, it plays with its elements very well and keeps things interesting- but it was not for me. I'm glad to have finished playing it but I don't think I'd come back to it or recommend it on the basis of what I enjoy in games.
That said, it may be fun for you- there's certainly a bit of a rush I got in finding discrepancies and tension after approving someone to see if I get a citation.  Glory to Arstotzka.  Glad it's over.

Recommending this for anyone looking for a quick and easy 100% achievement title. The main game is extremely short and can be finished in a very brief single sitting, with the remaining achievements being easter eggs that arepretty self explanitory looking at the achievement list. The easter egg achievements can all be done in about 5-10 minutes after completing the main game.
As for the game itself...
Emily is Away is a text based game revolving around 2 high school friends who try to keep in touch during college. Both have feelings for each other. Stuff happenss, or stuff doesn't happen. No matter how you play the game, the ending pretty much remains the same. It actually has a cool premise, as the game is played out entirely in instant messaging. It's a very brief game, and there is nothing much to do other than to read what Emily types, and progress the game with one of 3 choices at every response. Do the choices really matter? Well, not so much. It changes the flow of everything, except the ending. Not to say there is not just 1 ending. There is more than 1 ending. But the ending is usually always going to be... Well. Just play and see.
Not my usual type of game. And if not for the achievements, I probably would have skipped it.

Factorio the plot is simple: You build a factorio and mostly destroy the environment and kill the inhabitants of the planet you crashed on. The goal or how to "finish" the game is to shoot a satellite into space and of course surviving.
For this task you need to adapt to your surroundings by utilizing resourcess around you as efficient as possible.
Positive:
+ a lot of possibilities to design your factory
+ a lot of fun building, researching, surviving
+ quite decent developing, it's not dead by developer side [actually the updates bring often new interesting features]
+ you have the option that aliens only attack when you initiate combat (beginner friendly)
+ map editor
+ seeds available
+ you can use napalm to destroy aliens
Negative:
- late game motivation is only how many satellites can you shoot
- punishment if ignoring warnings and/or ignoring problems could be massive [destroying entire base --> starting new]
- progress earlier in the game is huge, you don't know what to do first; later on it feels like nothing much is achieved
- not a suitibale game for everyone

This is a short review of my own experience playing the Beta version so far. For WWII wargamers this game will immerse you in the bitter bocage fighting in Normandie where the game rewards you for using real world tactics to win the battle.
The myriad of units in both sets of armies are reproduced in great detail from the Panther tanks that you can call upon, 88 Flak guns, 17 pounders for the Brits and P-38s for the US. Both Axis and Allied armies are depicted via a predetermined choice of the Divisions that you will base your battle group on.
You have the 12th &17th SS and the 91st Luftlande Div for the Germans and 3 Allied divisions made of 2 US and 1 British Div. The 3 phases of the battle means that you would be sending in the recce forces during the first phase and it then escalates to where you get access to heavier units as the battle moves in the 3rd phase. Multi-player is where the game shines though in Beta as the battle map are expanded to accommodate your 'neighbouring' divisions and units can co-mingle and support each other to seal off penetrations or to penetrate the enemy defence lines.
There is a healthy interest to play both sides from what I have seen so far that would prevent the long wait times of COH2 where not many wants to play Allied. Alright now give this game a try, and add me on Steam if you do. You won't regret it!

Review taken from my original post at
The developer at Engage Pixel previously worked at Creative Assembly, which you will be familiar with if you have ever played a Total War video game (they also created the mighty Stunt Car Racer on the Amiga back in 1989) this is Engage Pixel’s first title and they’ve created a great throwback to a very specific style of game that a lot of people may have missed out on the first time around.
The soundless introduction to the game sets the scenario, there has been an alien invasion and your character has been imprisoned for reasons unclear but as all other personnel are unavailable, you have been released from your cell to fight in this intergalactic war.
The game-play is very much in the theme of games such as Thrust and Gravity Force 2 but perhaps has the most in common with Sub Terrania on the Sega Mega Drive (at least this is the game that I was most reminded of) in that it’s quite hectic with a driving, well-suited soundtrack (although more on that later).
Graphics have a hi-res PC circa 96/97 feel, very sharp and distinctive which is reflected in the tightness and accuracy of the controls of the game, a key point in this particular genre as poor controls can often be the deadliest enemy.

"Pro Tip - Before you play, pray to the Gods of inertia"
Game-pad wise, Left trigger controls the boost, right trigger drops bombs, A is the action button whilst the left thumb-stick changes the ship’s direction and the right thumbstick controls the direction of fire.
Captain Kaon has been in development for several years and was entirely developed by one man, the art style here is very British and the character portraits especially reminded me of the Amiga in the early to mid-nineties (the intro also reminded me of Captive and it’s sequel, Liberation).
The first few missions are much-needed tutorials to get you used to the gameplay. I was appreciative of this as I haven’t played a game in this vein for so long. As mentioned above, the controls are accurate and intuitive but the game has several mechanics that do need to be explained so that you are able to successfully complete the missions ahead such as carrying batteries to unpowered doors, how to attack enemy spawn points, etc.
With regards to the music in the game, whilst it is quite suited to the style of Captain Kaon, I must admit I found myself tiring of it quite quickly. As the game’s difficulty is quite steep and missions will either be regularly re-tried or could take a long time as you plan your attack carefully so as not to be overwhelmed by the enemy, I became very aware of the music looping and I did find it a shame that there wasn’t much in the way of variety here (or perhaps each in-game track being longer would have helped). A slight change of audio would make tackling the same mission over and over again maybe less of a chore (although if you are good at the game then I suppose this wouldn’t be an issue…unfortunately, I am not)
The level design is very crisp and requires a lot of skill to navigate, in fact, it’s at this point in the review that I would like to say the game is not for the faint of heart. The game (for me, at least) got difficult very, very quickly, by the third mission I was barely making it back to base in one piece although it does give you a real sense of achievement. The game’s difficulty comes from it’s chosen design and your ability as a player, not from any negative sources such as bad design etc. and so it gets manic and thrilling pretty much instantly.
After completing a mission you can exploit resources which can result in the mother ship getting attacked and having to defend it or in some locations, heal your mother ship (The Argus) should it have been attacked, this is a nice touch as it adds a strategic element to the over-arching plot of the game and also  gives it an edge of simulation beyond the frantic action of the missions
Each level isn’t a straight run through, you will be heading back to your base to re-supply on missiles and also to fix your armour
The screen can seem very busy and the HUD can occasionally get in the way of the action, especially the map.
One strange design choice I noticed was when your ship is low on health, instead of an alarm sounding or maybe a visual cue such as the screen briefly flashing, a character portrait shows on the left-hand side of the screen with a large text bubble which is quite obtrusive on-screen, usually when your ship is low on health you are in the middle of frantic combat, desperately trying to either kill the enemies surrounding you or you are trying to get away from the fire-fight. Either way, having a large portion of the screen being taken up by someone telling you that you are about to die isn’t particularly helpful.
Summary:
This game is great for someone who likes a really tough challenge, the game doesn’t hold your hand and when you succeed a mission it definitely feels worth it.
There is definitely a lot of value here, there are two planets to blast through with Ceres being the first and Mars unlocking after you have completed Ceres.
One of you will have to tell me how this all ends as I fear my limited skill set won’t allow me to see what fate belies Captain Kaon.

==========
It's not often that I write a negative review, but based on my experience with this game I feel it's more than fair. Perhaps the feedback will help the developer in the future. I feel like this is what "Early Access" is for, and I believe in the system even if many don't. It's a useful tool for budding developers. Anyway, let's get into it.
==========
Captain Kaon is a twin-stick gravity shmup. You pilot a ship through various environments and complete various objective to progress. At least, that's what it seems like. I had a couple of serious problems in the tutorial level of the game that prevented me from going any further. In Captain Kaon you are a pilot who was in prison serving her time, until an alien fleet suddenly attacks, leaving a shortage of pilots to defend humanity. Since desperate times call for desperate measures, Kaon gets an early release on the condition that she pilots a ship against the invaders.
The game has a great concept. So far, I really like it. But my main issue here are the controls and how flighty/vulnerable the flight controls are. Using a controller, you steer with the left analog stick and accelerate with the left trigger. You aim and fire your ship's gun with the right analog stick. The control scheme itself is fine, I can work with that, and have in many other games. The problem is how...loose actually flying is. You never know how much acceleration to apply for any given situation, and I often ended up ramming into the environment and other obstacles unintentionally. In a previous patch, this caused massive damage to your ship, but that seems to have dialed back quite a bit.
My other problem, which is what ultimately stopped me from progressing, is the grappling hook. Your ship comes equipped with a free-hanging grappling hook that you can use to pick up and carry items. These items range from batteries to Supply Crates that give you extra resources when you make it to the end of a level with them. One needs only to land on top of the item to have the hook automatically attach to the item so you can fly off with it in tow. In the tutorial level, you are required to pickup a battery with the grappling hook and carry it to a power station to open a door. I tried on numerous occasions to pick up this battery, but the hook would not attach to it. I spent FIVE HOURS in the tutorial trying to do this task, but no matter what I did the hook would not attach. It would help if there was some sort of skip tutorial option, and if there is I did not find it.
==========
Captain Kaon boasts an old school, retro aesthetic, harking back to the NES and even the Amiga days of gaming. This is fine, and everything looks great considering. Your ship is well detailed, as are most items out in the world and environment. Environmental obstacles such as mechanical structures, lasers, doors, and power stations looks great as well. The graphics are probably Captain Kaon's best feature.
==========
Everything here feels like it needs work. It felt really, really basic. And that's probably to match the graphical aesthetic, sure, but it could be a lot better. The intro sequence that explains the game's story doesn't have any sound effects or music, for example! Unbelievable. Some kind of sinister theme playing during that sequence would help enhance it and set the tone of the game.
==========
I honestly didn't see any issues with how the game ran on my rig. Controller worked great, plug n' play, and I didn't have any issues with FPS or similar problems.
==========
Captain Kaon seems like a promising title, but it needs quite a bit more work and some polish. I feel like when it's done it'll be a great title in the shmup genre. I'll be sure to keep it in mind and give it another shot once it's cleaned up and otu of Early Access. But right now, I can't recommend it.
==========

Playing Captain Kaon takes me down memory lane, to the days of my childhood. When you use to hang out at the old corner shop, either before or after school, and starve yourself through the lunch breaks. Just so you could blow your tuckshop money on the old coin op consoles or Pinball machines. The days when 20 cents would give you anywhere up to two hours (YES a whole two hours, of pure unadulterated pixelated fun), before you needed to pop in another coin.
The pinballs were on the decline and the new shiny consoles were making the grade, Space Invaders, Pacman, Galaga and Defender. Your score would be the talk of the day, nay of the month, till it was beaten. Yep, in those days you truly would be the legend in your own lunch time.
It is the last one, Defender, that Captain Kaon mostly reminds me of. A side scrolling space tunnel shooter (well, that what I use to call them). You could plod through the enemy, tactically eradicating  them slowly, or for fits of giggles, go full warp shooting like a wide man screaming ‘DIE MUTHU FRACKER!!’ till you either went splat against a wall or and enemy ship managed to pop you off.
Captain Kaon is no different. You, a rookie fresh out of the academy, is assigned to the Argus, a recommissioned battle cruiser, which is part of a slapped together defence force for earth.  The cool kids, with gnarly ships get to play lazer tag with the enemy alien force, in some far part of the galaxy. While you stay behind and babysit a Miners revolt on Ceres.
You start off with the WASP, the latest technically advanced gunship, from 30 years ago, and blast any invaders who happen to pop up the their badass ugly heads.
Your first two missions are training levels to get use to the ship. You use your WASD keys for the usual directions and Q and E to strafe left and right. The momentum physics are easy to adjust too but hard to master, as you will bump and bounce around the walls like a pinball till you get a handle of it.
Handling is like trying to roller-skate on an ice-rink while eating a very hot pie with cools hands, fun and frustrating at the same time (unlike Star Control, which was like trying to eat a frozen pie, on an oiled ice-rink, on an erratic hover board, remote controlled by a jilted lover). The frustrating part is you will forget which direction your nose is facing and can end up loosing half you life trying to stop ploughing the walls or getting unstuck from corners.
Fire control is done via the mouse and your gun rotates 360 (Missiles and bombs too).  On one hand this is great, you can hover in place while you pick the enemy off in any direction. The down side is while you are flying, you have your attention divided. You are either ploughing into walls while you are concentrating on shooting, or wasting ammo shooting like a Storm Trooper while concentrating on your flying (I am a man, I can only concentrate on one thing at a time! Shoot enemy or avoid wall or pee pants, not all at once!).
The tunnels are in maze form so there is no hitting the throttle and blasting through the levels (sad face), and you need to open doors or hidden areas by either picking up power cells and dropping them off at the required slot, passing through lazer trip wires or grappling levers to pull on or off. The grapple hook is frustrating, there seems to be no ‘let go’ button. So you need to pull away from some levers, which in turn makes them bounce back to their off position (and plough you face first into a wall). When you do get skilled on your controls though, you can start to hoon around the area in a fashion that would make Ken Brock (or any Drift star) proud.
You can refill on ammo and health at any time by returning to the Argus or finding refill stations, if there are any around, but there may be restrictions on hight levels (I suck, so still on level three but having fun dying).
If your are after latest 3D render and shadow effects then walk away now, you are too cool to hang with us Eggheads. The graphic are retro geeky gorgeous. From the intro, menus, popup talkies from your comrades, to the ships. It is all 80’s style pixel art, giving this game a homely feel.
The music is also 80’s fantabulous. At the right ambient level so as not to be annoying to make you turn it off and fits this game like a glove.
Story is lite and typical of 80’s games so no in depth love triangle or buddy revenge. There is a little confusion provide by the summery on Steam and in the actual game. On steam it states that you are Captain Kaon, a woman who was facing Court Martial, when suddenly the war started. In the game you are a Captain Kaon a female rookie from the academy. If this affects you mindset during play, well boohoo princess (your character is a girl after all). Me, I’m a D.I.L.L.I.G.A.F. kind of guy, plus, in the 80’s you don’t need no reason to blow away green alien butt!
There are still more features to be implemented by the developer, that hopefully will add to the game play and not subtract (Screen resolution, key binding, missions on Mars).
I can see this one becoming a classic, so if you are a person wanting to relive your 80’s-90’s childhood or a young person who enjoys retro games, Captain Kaon by Engage Pixel (James Buckle) is a must have in your library.

Players who weren’t around during the days of AIM and MSN Messenger may not ‘get’ Emily is Away the same way that those of an older generation do and this could possibly explain some of the negative reactions – including those that are frustrated that the game doesn’t include a happy ending. It makes it hard to score this release any higher than we have done but at the same time it’s one I’d recommend checking out some time.
I don’t think the title would have worked so well if there was a positive outcome. It’s the 'potential' of a happy ending that makes it the title it is – and the end result just causes the whole thing to hit closer to home. How many of us have had a crush on someone at school, and tried to further that relationship through the use of a messenger client after home-time only to have it fail awkwardly? We were all that teenager once and, even though it won’t appeal to everyone and would benefit from a little more content, Kyle Seeley’s project does a remarkable job at capturing that feeling.

A neat little game about destroying the world with a microorganism.
This little game is a game about sickness, it involves strategy and planning, reaction-time and quick thinking. The spiritual successor of the game "pandemic", it sets you in charge of a bacterica, virus, fungus, worm/parasite with the ultimate goal to kill all of mankind. Strategy elements are symptoms, transmission rates, lethality, detectability, hardening, genetic complexity, etc.
The fascinating thing is that the game - in it's main modes (if I understood it correctly) - does use real data provided from health organizations and pandemic research. Of course the whole thing is not a 1:1 transmission, since there needs to be balance in order for the game to be fun and the games functions have to be advanced by letting you CHOOSE the development of the organisms characteristics which is not possible in real life (a virus/bacteria is not concious, they do not choose how they mutate).
This game is very minimalisitc though. It was originally a mobile game and there is no doubt that it is. The functions are limited to clicking on the screen for "extra DNA" and choosing which symptom/transmission/resistence to choose next for the game, and in which speed the game is supposed to run (Pause + 3 Speed options). There are several menus that display things like public health, infection rates, death rates, airports shut down, harbors blockaded, counties infected, percentage of world population infected/dead, city-cams that show the progression of civilization (which state are they in, order, chaos, total panic/mass-hysteria?).
The game has the following types of sicknesses:
- Bacteria
- Virus
- Fungus
- Neural Worm
- Parasite
- Nano-Virus
- Biological Weapon
- Necroa (Zombie) Virus
- Simarin Flue from Planet of the Apes (as promotional thing in cooperation with the movie company)
It's very interesting and some of the fictional sicknesses include alternate win conditions of enslaving humanity or establishing the apes as a dominant race of the planet or keeping the Zombies alive until all humans are dead or Zombies.
As a PC game it is surely not the best thing you can buy, but it has a fascinating concept, it's educational by showing you the scope and influence of potential pandemics on the world and it is a fun diversion if you have 15 - 20 minutes to spare in between things and don't know what else to do.
I'd recommend it for everyone who can catch this Indie Game on SteamSale (for around 10 bucks), it's worth your while. And if you do not like to buy it on PC, it's also available in the respective AppStores. Beware though the phone version has a little less content and no scenario-creator.

I stumbled across this game a  year or so ago as a mobile app and absolutely loved it.  Really glad to see it in the steam store!
It's an interesting - if grim - plague simulation/strategy, wherein you get to "conquer" the world with a different kind of "empire."  Despite how unbelievably morbid the concept is, it's actually a pretty fun game.  It's good for a casual way to pass time, and its harder difficulties offer a lot more challenge for those who really enjoy strategizing and thinking about the next move... because one wrong step can actually throw your whole game and see your plague destroyed.
Beyond that, there's a bit of learning to be had as well, if only because the information pages on each of the countries are like little encyclopedia entries that offer up real world information.  Of course you don't HAVE to read it, but it's pretty awesome that it's in there.
10/10 for sure, even as early access.  It's a complete game.  It's fun and engaging.  You might even learn something while you're frightening yourself with the strange ease of wiping out humanity.  Unless you turn up the difficulty, in which humanity becomes a little more tenacious.  :)

Yesterday, I finished Bastion, today, I felt like I need more from them so I played Transistor. It took me 5 hours to complete the story without doing anything else but the story, I also didint use and game-hardening effects that you can add while you play. I just wanted to see how it goes. So far, amazing.
PROS:
- Game is an eye-candy. Drawings, characters, enemies, everything is so beautiful I actually felt like using my old oil paints to paint something from this game and hang in my room. I'll just buy probably.
- OST's. As I mentioned in Bastion, they're not just doing a great job but I'm actually going to put all of these songs in my phone, they're worth it.
- Gameplay. I like isometric, but this is something else. I thought I'd be bothered with the turn-based playing but actually, It was on point and fun. Little calculations make it very easy.
- Skill design = FOR THE MOTHER OF INDIES, I loved it. The design is so catchy, and the combination system means, you can play the game however you want! You can create 1-hit K.O. AOE's or if you like playing dodgy, you can create more agile stunner gameplay too. Its all yours.
- Story. I cried. Seriously.
CONS:
- Level gaining. Level gaining itself isn't the bad part, the bad part is, I had to wait and watch how the character gained level after every single encounter, and I don't really like waiting for something so repetitive. It literally pauses the game, pops a little window, shows how many percentage of your character gained level, and then pops of. Still, It didin't ruined the game, It's something minor, and doesn't really bother you at some point because you're just so in the game.
TL;DR: If you like Bastion, buy it. Being isometric, or different gameplay won't bother you in any way, this game's a little masterpiece.

King of Fighters XIII... spoilers up ahead: This game isn't easy. If you're starting with fighting games, start with Street Fighter, otherwise this game will overwhelm you.
KoF XIII is a fast, rushdown-oriented fighting game. You need to learn hops, rolls, drive cancels and hd combos to really win against people, otherwise you will get obliterated. While it is very hard to learn, once you mastered it, an extremely balanced and awesome game awaits you!
Story: Saiki tries to take over the World. OF COURSE. It's nothing special, but still fun too play.
Online: While the community is not that big, you can still get plenty of fights if you're playing arcade with challenging activated. Most battles are very fluid, only sometimes it will crap on you. I recommend it, but be careful: most online players are EXTREMELY powerful and will show you no mercy.
Graphics: Very high quality sprites. While not graphically impressive like the Sprites of Skullgirls, it still looks extremely good.
Sound: Very rock and metal-ish. Gets you pumped for the next match. The Voiceacting is only in japanese, but thats probably better for this game.
All in all, KoF is a joy to play. Not easy to get into, but once you get the hang of it, the endless possibilities of combos, character-teams and more will blow you away!

So if it came down to choosing between Street Fighter and King of Fighters..........I don't know if I could do it. Both fighting series have some amazing characters and mechanics. One of the best things I've ever seen is when they got mashed together back in the early 2000s, creating one of my favorite fighting games of all time: Capcom vs SNK 2.
King of Fighters XIII, in my eyes, saved SNK Playmore from complete extinction. It fixed many of the problems that XII had, and added a lot more. A revamped combat system, more characters, a better netcode.......this is definitely the full package.
If you've been curious about this franchise for a long time, this is definitely a good game to start with. If you're coming from the Street Fighter IV camp, there's still a lot in this game for you to love. Give it a shot!

This game has many shared features with Farming Simulator 15; inlcuding one of the two maps that was ported from 15.
However there are some nice improvements to Farming Simulator 17:
+ More machinery  (both new features & more options from 15)
+ New crops (sunflowers is of note)
+ You can drive trains! (not far but still, plus a train horn...)
+ Equipment lights now can be turned on AT THE SAME TIME! (front and back)
+ AI helpers are slightly less incompetent (fewer crashing into trees, somewhat better at angled fields)
+ Pigs! (Either you like bacon or you're wrong)
+ More customization of buidling placement (upgrades for silo storage)
+ Upgrades to machinery (mostly different tires, more power, some different paint jobs)
+ Tiedowns for log transportation
+ Missions available on fields you don't own, a good way to start making money
Some things that I would say could be improved upon:
- Better NPC AI (cars reacting to you, people not walking out in front of equipment in town, etc.)
- Helpers stopping at angled fields still an issue
- Trees fall through the map if cut low
- More maps (there is only two, one is the same as in FS15)
The last feature that can either be a positive or a negative is that when you reset equipment, it resets to the store. If you like realism, this feature is good for you; also makes trailers hauling equipment more viable. For me I find it slightly annoying when I get stuck on a tree with a combine, then reset, and spend a couple minutes at 16 mph back to the field.
If you liked Farming Simulator 15, 17 is worth the cost.
