**Warning**  Do not buy this game based on this review unless you have, or are willing to buy a Steam controller, Xbox One controller, or PS4 controller for your PC.  This is a highly action-oriented and skill-based game that requires a mastery of timing and synergistic button-pressing.
Ok, now the real review:
Forget about Lords of the Fallen and Dark Souls and Nioh and put all those out of your mind.  You need scrap to level up.  You lose it if you die.  You have to run back for it before dying again.  AND the similarities end there.  Play for five minutes and youl realize this game has it's own heart and soul.  In fact, if you're looking for something to scratch the Souls itch you might be disappointed in a way.  So just let this title stand on it's own two servo-manipulators.
This game does not 'want to be' or 'try to be' any other game.  My hat goes off to the developer for giving us a really unique, challenging, and skill-based game which will strongly appeal to science fiction fans.
Features I love:
1.) You can mix and match armor types
2.) ..But you get a bonus for wearing a complete set
3.) ..And you can upgrade your armor by finding components and using scraps
4.) (So far) there's no ranged weapons that the player can directly wield.  It's all tools you pick up and 'convert' into melee weapons.
5.) Elemental damage consists of things that actually exist like Fire and Plasma, etc.
6.) It's difficult.  If you don't use Google, you WILL die to the bosses the first time. At least the first couple of bosses...
7.) The trash mobs can kill you so fast.  Unlike some games, you can't get sliced with a sword 35 times and live.  You'll die in one or two hits unless you're moving or blocking.
8.) Stagger/stun is a thing.
9.)  The game world/story matters and draws you in.
10.) The graphics are gorgeous.
Dev feedback:
1.) The level up curve (if that's a thing) from the first zone to the next is pretty extreme.  So much so that I went back to the first area to just farm for a while before moving into the second very far.  The difficulty is much higher in the second area.  I went from mostly mastering the first area to being kicked around like a dirty ragdoll in the second.  That's ok, I guess.  It just felt like all my progress in the first part of the game was 'reset.'  But the second area has alot going for it.  So I'm not really calling this a 'con.'  It's just how it is.
2.) There are button combos you can do in order to use 'move sets' for each weapon. But the game doesn't even give you the first clue about this.  For example, double tapping RB1 then quicly tapping RB2 does a cool move set with some weapons.  But you'd never know without experimeinting or finding out on accident.  This isn't a con either. It's just something I'd tell new players  -  that they will have to experiment to figure out move sets.
Anyway, the game is money well spent if you like challenging and rewarding games.  If you prefer casual games where you can just watch a story and press buttons every so often, you'll hate it.

My 2 cent review: I like grinding games but grinding with a purpose.  Not mindless grinding without a payoff, but fruitful grinding with a “ahhhh I did it at the end”  This game provides that 98.3 % throughout the whole game AND it’s a 98.3% entertaining ride and well worth the cost of buying the game and the cost of time playing the game.  But the last few moments to the game don’t give you that bubble wrap popping satisfaction and once you beat the game the first time (wait a few weeks and play it again) you’ll end up farting around in the 98.3% enjoyable part and avoiding the ‘end’ game until you get bored and stop playing for a few weeks and start all over again.
Get this game if you looking for:
-	Building and upgrading
-	Crafting
-	Puzzle games that aren’t puzzle games but have thousands of possible solutions
Wishlist:
The Aliens – I wish they had sort of siege equipment, that they too had to build, craft, learn and grow.
IN short: I have 190+ hours into this game and find it very enjoyable.

If cult classics like Gravitar, Sub-Terrania, Solar Jetman and Thrust tickle your fancy in any way, shape or form, the gameplay and mission structure of Captain Kaon will be right up your alley. I, for one, love these exploratory thrust physics shooters where the objective is as much about piloting safely through twisting caverns with cargo dangling precariously from your ship as it is engaging with hostiles.
Captain Kaon features satisfying twin stick shooting, doing away with a particular oldschool restriction where fixed aiming meant pointing your spacecraft squarely at your target -- not the simplest of tasks in cramped quarters with gravity's perpetual pull! It's a welcome, distinctly action-oriented modernization of the retro formula that Captain Kaon riffs on and, paired with frequent directions provided during any given mission, it makes the game far more accessible than its forebears. A non-linear campaign, an arsenal that grows progressively larger with completed missions, customizable loadouts that let you pick and choose your primary/secondary weapons plus a variety of ships to unlock all work to fill out the package quite nicely.
This was a day one purchase for me and I'm looking forward to playing (and inevitably replaying) the full set of Ceres missions! :)
On the Early Access front, my experience with the game included its fair share of bugs, rough edges and weirdness but nothing unpatchable. Captain Kaon, as of today, has been fully released but there's still a bit of iffiness with regard to controller support. Anyone hoping to use a favourite non-X360 gamepad would be well advised to run a controller emulator like x360ce as generic USB controllers, such as a Logitech Dual Action, aren't supported. Things get a little bit trickier then that, though, as it's possible to switch control priority over from mouse/keyboard to gamepad even while an unsupported generic USB controller is connected (suggesting that the gamepad
detected), causing the mouse pointer to vanish and leaving no means to navigate the menu or revert to mouse/keyboard. This borked setting saves between sessions and it's only after a certain amount of blind clicking around that the game switches back to mouse/keyboard at the title menu. With all that out of the way, I'm happy to report that Captain Kaon plays really rather well with an Xbox 360 controller, although certain menus such as mission selection and loadout adjustment feel a bit clunky in their implementation.
Configuration is quite spartan at present, with display options providing a choice of windowed 1280x720 or scaled fullscreen, audio options nowhere to be found and no freedom to rebind controls. Default bindings are perfectly sensible for QWERTY keyboard users, though.
Nothing technical-wise here is a dealbreaker for me, but I must admit that the controller issues described above made for a bit of a rocky start. This is a super cool game and I
recommend checking it out if you're craving something thrust-y.

[Edit] I realize the original review doesn't really do anything except act as a rhetorical attempt at humour. Firstly, the game took quite some time to "finish." And that's the vanilla version, not including the DLCs and Steam (Valve) workshop scenarios and addons. You can (and many people have) create your own deadly diseases. Pound for pound, money to entertainment value, it's definitely worth it to me for the price.
Secondly, and more importantly, regardless of your stance on the subject of human annihilation, there is a reality that this game reflects and people might benefit from knowing about. I'm not a "Social Justice Warrior" but there is a reality out there that includes things that we do not want to happen but which may happen. This game reflects those things in a way that is surprisingly realistic. Even if you have no science classes in junior or high school you can appreciate the themes of the ever-present dangers of life with this game.
Your "job" in this game is to create a virulent strain that infects the population of the world and then become so deadly that you succeed in killing the human race before a cure can be created. Each step of the game, you have a different "strain" to choose from -- viruses, bacteria, etcetera -- and depending on the strain you have there are different algorythms as to awareness, spreading, and deadliness. The dependency of how you succeed is deterrmined by typical factors like climate, location, population, and overall education.
Consequently, it is more difficult to "infect" areas that are more educated or live in areas (in this game, countries) that are inherently more difficult for strains of your "disease" to infect. Country to country, plane or boat or personal contact and whether or not your "strain" can cross species, determine what is happening and your success. And the key is to spread your "world killer" before someone (i.e., some dorctor who recognizes a common sneezing reaction) realizes it and starts working on a cure.
In terms of morality, this is an awful simulation - your function is essentially to kill everyone. Intellectually; however, this is not only entertaining but also hugely educational. How plagues, bacteria, viruses, and other virulent organisms spread and how societies respond to that spread is amazingly important. Does this simulation live up to reality? I would say not, or least not quite, but it does a great job of simulating knee-jerk reactions. And it's fun - not to kill everyone, but to imagine figuring out how to kill a world that is actively fighting against you from doing just that.
Asuming there's not some super-villain out there doing that, of course. But then, with biology and evolution, there does not have to be a super-villain doing that.

Cthulhu Saves the World is a love letter to the SNES-era turn-based jRPG. It maintains the turn-based formula and SNES graphics, but streamlines all the boring parts (like healing outside of combat), makes combat more interesting and faster, gives each character an advancement choice at every level up, and most importantly, the game has a great sense of humor. This is very much a SNES jRPG, so those who hate the genre should stay away. But those who ever liked the genre should grab this, especially when it's on sale for a dollar along with Breath of Death. This is a pretty bomb♥♥♥♥♥game.  At first glance it doesn't seem like much more than a mildly cute JRPG/Lovecraft parody, but once you get playing it reveals itself to have some pretty awesome mechanics that you don't see in your average RPG.
The battle system is the main thing I want to talk about.  Functionally, it's a straightforward turn-based system a la Dragon Warrior, but some standout tweaks turn the battles from "standard grind" to "every battle is a fight to the death."  Enemies are generally capable of dealing out significant damage, and they grow stronger with every successive turn, pushing you to try and find the quickest way to dispatch them before your characters get wiped out.  The inevitably heavy damage would be almost unbearable in any other game, but CSTW balances it out by restoring your characters' HP to full at the end of every battle so you can get on to your next near-death experience.
Character builds are somewhat unconventional, as well.  Rather than simply picking up stat gains with each new level, each character gains one or more new abilities that either grant them stat boosts or a power to use in battle.  Very often, the game lets you choose between two similar abilities, allowing you to customize the character's skillset toward your playing style while keeping true to their theme.  These aren't your old-school Dragon Quest spells, either - while some will feel familiar, I can't say that any other game has let me pelt my enemies with starfish or drive them insane with the caress of my noodly appendages.
The Insanity mechanism is an interesting gimmick, as well.  At its core Insanity is just another status ailment, but where it differs from its predecessors is that the effects vary from monster to monster.  Some weaken under its influence, while others simply grow more vicious, and you won't know which enemy types have which response until you've already driven them insane.
All in all, the graphics and jokes are a bit hokey, but the gameplay and general silliness make it well worth a playthrough.

I don't play a lot of games, I just play a few games a lot.
I played Borderlands 2 a LOT. Or, as I like to call it in end-game, Gun Farming Simulator. Beats the heck out of Harvest Moon on the farming front, gotta be honest.
To be even more honest, I only pushed through the bland starting areas (all the icy stuff before sanctuary) because I had heard such great things about the game, and none of it matched with the kinda-meh-decent shooter I was playing through. My little pea shooter was hitting midgets for around 30 damage, and it was... not exhilirating.
Then I got a car, and it handled like a piece of rusty tinfoil on wheels. Then I got to the hub city, and then I started playing the game.
711 hours later, I'm two-shotting a raid boss for ONE BILLION DAMAGE with a shotgun that fires ELECTRIC TORNADOS before turning INVISIBLE and throwing EXPLODING KUNAI at his minions. This game has PROGRESSION.
There are 6 (because you should buy the GOTY edition) playable characters, and each of them has three separate skill trees leading to entirely different playstyles. Even within a single skill tree, there are countless diverse loadouts you can test and run.
I've spent the entirety of my time in this game playing as just ONE of these characters. As a sniper, as a melee assassin, as a shotgun run-n-gunner. The shooting mechanics are incredibly tight and satisfying, making it fun just to travel to a map and blast my way through some mobs. None of the rest of the game's features would matter if the mechanics weren't right, but thankfully that's far from the case. The speed and responsiveness allows you to feel truly godlike once you master a play style, and once that gets old you can find a new one to git gud at.
This game also scratched my gambling itch without making me pay a single cent on microtransactions. Farming is the name The procedurally generated guns actually work incredibly well, making nearly every weapon you pick up unique in some way. Best thing is, unless you decide to play in OP levels (bringing enemies well above your own level), you don't need to worry about the variations in guns- most will be viable! Not to mention legendaries assigned to bosses at low drop rates and some hidden bosses on top of that, and there is plenty to hunt for even far into the game.
I also like stupidly challenging games, and my third playthrough onwards scratched that itch too. There's no requirement to go past level 50 or so, and you'll only get to level 30 on your first playthrough, but with each New Game cycle the enemies got double the health, and my guns kept getting stronger.
All of the story DLCs are good in my eyes and worth getting, but Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep is the best. Imagine a skyrim parody with explosive weaponry. It's wonderful.
Ultimately, I have a lot of love for this game. I've solo'ed every raid boss. I've gotten every Unique and Legendary item it has to offer. Done most of the sidequests. I got my money's worth, and if anything I've written sounds appealling to you, you probably will too. Peace.

I really tried to like this game, just as I tried to like Lords of the Fallen. I was excited about The Surge because I read reviews here stating that it was "like Bloodborne", to which I completely disagree. Certainly, as with LotF, there is heavy From Soft-inspiration in the combat presentation... but the feel is just terrible. The attacks feel clunky and overly-animated; the movement suffers from this as well. The entire combat feels proactive as opposed to reactive. There's nothing wrong with having combat that requires prediction - that's a form of tactics - but when 90% of the combat is based on proactivity, in a 3rd person action RPG? That's really boring. And it's really unlike Bloodborne in this aspect, because in BB, you are intended to react quickly with dodges, parries, and attacks.
Moreover, the difficulty when attempting to play this way is unreasonable. In order for something to be positively challenging, it needs to feel fair; it needs to feel like you are learning and getting better. With The Surge, it feels every other enemy kills you in one hit, so you have to resort to cheap tactics like dodging back, strong attacking once, dodging back, strong attacking once, etc. And that brings me to my second point: the AI is terrible. They're really easy to dupe into a lopping pattern. So the difficulty appears to only really come from their stats, which segues into my third point: they have way too much HP. I first tried using heavy weapons - which can kill enemies in a reasonable amount of time - but because the heavy weapons are so slow, it makes it very easy to be hit. And as I mentioned, a hit or two and you're dead. My second try, I played with light weapons. This made dodging and timing attacks easier, but they do so little damage that it increases the chances that you'll mess up and get hit in a fight, since the fights take that much longer. None of this would be an issue if the combat was actually fun, but it's not. It's just a boring monotonous grind that causes me to stop concentrating and mess up, because I'm so bored.
Overall, this feels like a very shallow combat-oriented game. The story has some interesting concepts, but even the plot points feel shoehorned in. If you love games like Dark Souls and Bloodborne for their combat, I don't believe you will like this. You MIGHT, as evidenced by some reviews here, but I honestly can't see why. If you do, great; I'm glad you found a game you can enjoy. Unfortunately, I didn't... despite my best efforts.

You have four science packs, 1, 2, 3, and A. Three of which are manufactured by natural minerals and resources, the last of which is made from alien goop. Manufacturing these by hand is slow and tedious, thus you automate the process with mines and assembly factories.
The pollution from these factories begins to alert the local fauna. They are fast, powerful, and unrelenting even at their weakest. You put up turrets, and load them by hand. Time passes, and the pollution alerts a hive of monsters. You are now under constant attack until you destroy the hive. You automate manufacture of ammunition and feeding into the turrets as you fend off the hordes.
You replace the belts with faster ones, build more science labs, more power sources, but you have run out of copper, putting all science packs on hold. You find a large amount of copper, and create a mining camp with a long conveyer belt. This alerts more monsters to your presence, but you have the means to manufacture colossal amounts of ammo.
You now need iron, but the only way there is through a thick forest that is holding back your pollution from alerting even larger alien dens with highly evolved monsters. Trekking back and forth is tedious, so you build an army of robots to fetch the iron.
You now need oil. You trek out into the wilderness to find one of the rarest resources the game has to offer, and pipe it back to your factory. Technology moves by leaps and bounds as you are able to use more science packs.
Your assembly labs are spewing out more science packs than your massive cluster of labs can consume, you can acquire any technology on a whim, you are fully armed and armored, and your wall of turrets have slain legions of enemies. You manufacture the bullets faster than they are fired, mine copper and iron faster than it is smelted. You invent the locomotive, and shift tremendous amounts of materials to further your research into rocketry. You once thought "I'll never run out of resources", and now you think "How the ♥♥♥♥ did I run out of copper? I had 48,000 plates!", and that 48,000 becomes a rapidly growing number as your lust for freedom grows as your factory does.
After countless hours of work, you finally escape the planet, leaving a masterpiece of machinery that started out as almost literally nothing.

Pro:
-it's a free game
-open-source, too

Con:
-after paying off the initial debt, there is basically no way to loose the game, except from being killed by pirates which happens from time to time and can't be avoided no matter of your skills
-the above forces you to save-scum if you're not willing to grind for ships again
-trading is pretty basic, prices go up and down in a random fashion
-combat is ridiculous, the pirates often attack while you're still taking off from a planet, your small ships are destroyed were quickly
-combat controls are limited, no formations except 'guard flag ship' which often fails because of different jump and movement characteristics
-often you don't even see where your ships are destroyed, because they a fighting offscreen, and you can't react in any way
-fleet management is hampered by different jump speed and range, and ship aggression, often splitting up your fleet. Should you encounter pirates at the jump destination, losses are sometimes unavoidable
-the interface it not desgned very well, at least if you don't act like the devs intended you to act
-some missions simply spawn lots of attackers that are hard to fend off without loosing ships
-ships and items degrade over time, reducing your expensive stuff to trash, this means you'll loose lots of money
-ship outfit screen is limited in functionality
-the grind required for the bigger ships is quite boring, basically you buy lots of cargo space and haul goods from A to B and HOPE you don't loose a ship on the way
-generated missions soon get boring
As a result, I'll thumb this down, but since it's free, just install it and see for yourself.

A really loveable game filled with music, art, and all around good characterization and story writing. From the intro to the credits, the scenes are immersed in art and colors. To draw a parallel--much like Bastion, the many UI aids are still present (Subtitles, non-intrusive graphics, and despite the seemingly 'light filled' gameplay, it's not garish at all!), which in gameplay terms also includes a difficulty scaler (purely the player's choice) that modifies every aspect of combat alongside full control over what you bring into battle, covering around four major battle skills and their own (maximum of two) modifiers each, coupled with passive bonus modifier slots overall--all of whom you gain from the world...and its people, that writing about it in a review may downplay how much is actually possible. Every power and skill is configured to work with any other setting that given the simple battle system, would occur a mixture of primary and secondary effects (The skill would be thematically the same, but modified by the secondary add-on). All four 'major' skills can be modified dynamically given that setting, which makes the combat system able to be tailored to one's custom playstyle.
While not visible in the above screenshots, Transistor has subtitles for everything (sans the song notes and chords for when the protagonist is singing herself) alongside an engaging storyline that somewhat tells itself in media res, with snippets to what was and is happening collected along the way.
It also works on rather 'low-end' PCs which, coupled with wonderful graphics and an also wonderful storyline (and gameplay), creates an immersive setting that performs very well through several hours of playtime with importance given to the lore and writing. Personally, when I played this, the utter smoothness and immersion as if I was playing one of those 1080p quality videos I can hardly load on Youtube made me feel a lot better about how inclusive games are being (both to those with disabilities--given my hearing--and to those who are hard-up in affording 'better' PCs for games).
Edit: While I may not look it--I've played a playthrough and beyond despite the current time showing it. The achievements record per-save basis (and with a stable online connection, of course), so it may not be that obvious. :P

It's important I preface this review with the following: I don't normally enjoy MMOs and I don't particularly like paying subscriptions to games.
The game however completely exceeded any expectations I had for it. I expected to play for a couple months and then be done with it. I'm still playing. I log on near every day, I have multiple classes past lvl 60, which NEVER happens in an MMO for me.
This game is gorgeous and stunning in not only character modeling, but animations, and atmosphere as well. The locations are breathtaking and I find myself just hanging out in places enjoying the scenery from time to time.
This MMO has a plot. It's a great plot. It's not totally flimsy like a lot of MMO plots, and heck, this one even ties into the original FFXIV. Well done. The characters are amazing and I really grew attached to many of them as a result.
Combat is enjoyable. As well it should be. As I found with most MMOs this game did have a slow start through the first 20-30 levels, but the story should be enough to keep you entertained, and its also great for getting those levels fast. The game also does not have to make a whole new character if you want to be a different class. You can level ALL the classes on the same character. It's amazing and I love that it does this, because I often want to play a variety of classes, but don't want to go through all the story questing again, or am far too attached to the one character to have to make a whole new one. Classes are also super varied despite falling into specific roles. My one issue is that queue times for finding Duty Finder groups is painstaking at non-peak hours if you are a DPS class.
The expansions never fail to disappoint. Heavensward and Stormblood are definitely worth picking up, and have been bundled together for your convenience. The new areas and locales are amazing to look at and adventure in.
All in all, this is the only game I will probably ever pay a sub fee for, and honestly, they deserve the money. This game is just that entertaining. I never regret spending my time playing. It never feels like a waste of that time.

Had the game for a while thanks to a previous sale, but I just started playing it, and I must say it is a very in-depth RPG system.  I like the gameplay, though turning the camera is a bit awkward.  Overall, it's worth its price.  It offers an insane amount of replay value.
I don't like the map editor much, but it gets the job done.  The map editor is similar to some old-school editors in games like Darkstone but not quite as complex.  You basically are limited to a 2D floor plan, which makes level design faster but also limits your artistic placement of items and also makes testing how things look a little more difficult.  If nothing else, it makes publishing RPG ideas to the Workshop very easy.
Real quick, the editor has some major quirks.  Quirk #1 is that enemies cannot be finely tuned for the levels.  What this means is enemies are set to basic levels and have stats based on which monster they are.  You cannot be told those stats in the editor, though, so you have to read the monster/combat guides to figure out which enemies are strongest/weakest.  That is not very intuitive, and if I was the dev, I would want to add more granularity to enemy types.
Quirks #2 and #3 kind of roll together.  Quirk #2 is that the editor is 2D, but the levels are 3D, so you can't place items exactly where you want them.  You can, however, pick the wall/direction of the item, and each tile can have up to 4 items of each type... well, most types, anyway.  Quirk #3 is that you don't have any intro/outro scenes for entering and exiting levels.  The real problem is that the first level does not have any story options.  All you can do is throw scrolls and wall text into the level and expect the player to read everything.  You have no way to guarantee that the player will see that text.  It would be nice if the levels could have transition scenes, even just black screens with white text.  I also think some kind of mandatory text message or cutscene device would be useful for getting custom stories or even just area names into the game.
Well, enough ranting about the engine's quirks.  I love the game, and I recommend it to dungeon-crawling fans.

I apologize in advance for my star-eyed enthusiasm.
It's challenging. It's charming. It's old school. Grimrock, to me, is a game of imagination. While obviously nowhere near to the extent of pen & paper, your characters (the most important aspect) are left up to you to flesh out. This is where all the fun begins.
The character system is pretty flexible for its simplicity, and simplicity makes for great gameplay balance. The aformentioned flexibility also adds to replay value with there being many combinations of builds, although your mileage may vary. The classes are well balanced, all except the mage. They are an insult to the name "magic-user" because they aren't nearly versatile enough to make up for their many weaknesses.
(I personally solved my inept mage problem with Cheat Engine by giving him 8 skill points per level) - use "double" as the address type.
The gameplay itself is a delicate mix of puzzle-solving, action, character management and hoarding with a bit of story advancement thrown in. Combat is real-time and fairly simple, but has several strategic and tactical elements, such as party order, flanking, backstabbing, and rudimentry dodging. Items are particularly well done. Everything you might expect in an RPG is there and balanced well, including the modest amount of interesting, unique, and powerful items.
While Grimrock does have a few rough edges, it is nonetheless expertly crafted.

For years I've been wanting to play a modernized old school first person dungeon crawl/RPGs. I tried going back and playing older ones like might and magic games but they just don't cut it over time. All I can say is Legend of Grimrock is EXACTLY what I've been waiting for. It takes all the fun, excitement, and strategy out of those old games and brings it to the current level of gameplay. It removes all the buggyness of older games, it replaces the confusingly blurred graphics where it's easy to miss an important item with beautiful design, poor puzzles with strategic challenges, choppy fighting with challenging battles, etc. I LOVED this game, I had so much fun playing it, and with the added function of a popular mod community and a dungeon editor it is really a top tier experience. If you like RPGs, or dungeon crawls, or have been craving what I have then look no further: this game is TONS of fun.
If it was still early access the lack of features and bugs would be somewhat acceptable, but as a finished product I cannot recommend it

Review after 15 hrs gameplay in beta:
At first I have to say that I am not a fan of the Wargame series which hast different reasons. The main reason why I don't like it is because of the mechanics with command vehicles as the only unit to capure the zones. So basically your zone can be filled with units but unless you dont have a command vehicle you can't capture the zone - this ends in battles where each side is just spamming scouts and trying to snipe the enemys command vehicles.
SD1944 changed those mechanics by swapping the command zones with a moving border which fits the WW2 setting quite well. They also got rid of those kind of command vehicles.
Even though SD1944 plays much like Wargame the overall feeling is much different.
Its also much slower paced compared to the Wargame series - and i love it! You have more time to react and can fully concentrate on micro management. Furthermore your units have no health bar anymore and can be one-shoted.
A new addition to the game is stress management. So basically you have to display your troops stress level to maintain their fighting power. If a unit is stressed out through lets say artillery fire, they are either retreating or pinned down which makes them an easy target.
Pros:
Gameplay is very strategic!
Grafics are looking nice!
It's a lot of fun just to waste time in the deck builder by improving your divisions and trying new combinations.
The 10 vs. 10 battles are amazing!
Realism!
Cons:
The only downside is that people sometimes drop out of the game or even crash their game due to some kind of bug.
Not much content(units/maps/game modes) due to beta stage.
instability(rare game crashes)
I`d rate it 9.5 out of 10 even at the beta stage. I'm very impressed by this game since it is much better as expected.
So if you're a fan of WW2 set RTS - buy it!

Pros:
______________________
< Battlefront line - determins income replacing static control points. This makes the game really fluent and challenging in many ways without making the game too fast paced. Well implemented.
< Battlegroups - the new deck system similar to other wargames, only with different divisions instead of countries. Well Implemented.
< Battle Phases - A, B, C. Unlocks more components of your chosen units as time prolongs. A great idea presenting more fun options ensuring the battle does not become stale after 20 minutes.
< Infantry combat - Squad fights are much better and more entertaining than other wargames. Town battles are much more fluent. Reminds me of company of heroes to a point.
< Command units - improving performance of nearby units. No longer just required to sit on a control point since there are none.
< Unit Suppresion - Units become pinned and vehicles can be forced to retreat from the front if pressured enough. Units surrender if pinned and approached by the enemy making for some interesting tactics when it comes to counter attacking.
< Vehicle movement - Tree lines and forests are no longer passable for vehicles giving infantry a much more important role on the front lines. This really helps to balance out the field and provides more options when it comes to defensive and offensive manouvers.
< Vehicle Armor/Penetration - Units no longer have visible health bars like wargame. If the weapon has a higher penetration value than the armor of the target being shot at then it has a very good chance to destroy it. Keep in mind that the penetration value given for the weapon is at the max range, so for every 100m inside that range it gains an additional penetration value of 1.
Cons:
______________________
> Off map artillery - A bold attempt for this game. Artillery is a factor in this game already, why is this really a thing. A vehicle that creates magical explosions from thin air at really long range compared to other artillery units. You dont see it until its too late 90% of the time. It will make your front collapse and force you to retreat from forward positions. I wouldn't wish it upon my worst enemies. There are artillery units in the game already but they make sense because there is simple counterplay. Not so much with these vehicles. I guess the idea is there but it just doesn't make sense in this kind of game.
*Edit*
______________________
= Planes/AA - Planes kill planes well, AA dont really kill planes unless really heavily stacked. AA causes planes to retreat under pressure though so its hard to say weather this makes the game better or worse. Your planes are more likely so survive ground assaults if your turn off auto evac in options. This is because as your plane is retreating from enemy positions it is easy for the enemy to send a fighter after it. After your plane has completed its assault you should fly it back over your own AA and then order evac. This has a better chance at forcing an enemy fighter to back off before it can do anything to your plane. This doesn't make AA useless like alot of people are complaining about, because they will utterly destroy any infantry even in heavy cover.
= Balance - depends what side of the bed you get up from in the morning. Some units seem really powerful to be allowed in Phase A of the battle. Some units are extremely difficult to deal with depending on what division you are playing as. It really depends if you like certain things being that powerful at that stage of the game. You wont have to dig deep to find the units i am talking about in the discussions. Being beta these things can always change though so only time will tell.

This game is absolutely fantastic. It is a 2D space adventure game inspired by the Escape Velocity series, but in terms of both design and gameplay it exceeds them. And, of course, it is published as free/libre software
if you don't know what that is)
, which is something that all game makers should do. Not to mention that this game also has
, which is also something that all game makers should do. And it's free!
Firstly, the graphics are beautiful. The shimmering multitude of stars (you might want to zoom out to see the shimmering part), the detailed planets, the multicolored remnants of supernovae, the
, the creative design of the ships themselves, and even the variety in asteroids weave together to create something much more beautiful than anything one might expect for a 2D top-down game. Instead of animated surfaces for the planet where you land, photos of various visually impressive places on Earth are used, resulting in the planets having a larger amount of detail. This game is not graphics heavy, however. While you definitely cannot play without the graphics, text takes an integral role as well. Nearly all the events in the game that are related to a story arc are text based, and with a few exceptions, have no supplemental images. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, however. This way, your imagination becomes an integrated part of the game itself, and results in a richer and more detailed experience than any level of animation could create. It is a little like the very old text-based adventure games in that way; you need your imagination, not just a computer.
The gameplay is such that it gives the player a great amount of control. To survive economically, one may choose to take missions to shuttle people or freight, trade goods, accompany caravans to protect them from pirates, or even become a pirate themself (which isn't very easy, but is definitely a viable option). At every story related event, the player has a choice. You are never forced to side with any particular group, or to continue a storyline. Even special missions have choices that go beyond simply accepting or rejecting them. The controls themselves are properly executed as well. Keyboard shortcuts are intuitive, and it is easy to get the hang of spaceship control. Plenty of complexity exists without it being overwhelming, especially in regards to the various systems and modifications you can add to your ship to change its capabilities from the stock model. The choice of ships is small at first, but as the game progresses, many new options will appear for both ship models and modifications. When in space, one can even hail other captains if they so wish. Part of this game is also about exploration. There is a lot to discover, and definitely more than you would expect. All I'm going to say is that taking a look at as many sytems as you can, even uninhabited ones, is worth it.
The story arcs are several, and one has to find them. They're interesting and downright exciting, and when combined with the bits and chunks of lore you gather through general gameplay, a developing portrait of the galaxy is concieved within one's mind. Some special missions add to this as well. As you complete story arcs, you also gain access to certain technologies or advantages, which change the way that might play in subtle but enjoyable ways. There is definitely plenty of well-crafted politics and political relations (ones that you can influence) in the game as well. There is even a dash of conspiracy hidden here and there, if you know where to look, and on a scale much greater than you would expect at first. The story and the world of this game can be likened to a skilfully crafted stained glass window, where different, individually great parts assemble to make the varied and fascinating whole.
This is a masterpiece of a game. I would even go so far as to call it a work of art. Very few videogames achieve the complexity and the beauty of Endless Sky. It is one of the best games that one has ever played, and is absolutely something that you should get, and since it is free, you can do so even if you are unsure. Go on, take off into the endless sky of the cosmos.

Did you ever play Sid Meir's PIRATES!?  To put it simply, this is PIRATES! IN SPACE! When I say PIRATES! I mean the old version, not this GOLD version crap with the DDR style dancing.
* No hand to hand combat
* No Governors daughters
* No Treasure fleet
* No Treasure hunting
* No rescueing your family.
* No Crew Moral (But they will take your ships if you don't pay them)
* Trading
* Capturing ships
* Missions
* Ship to Ship battles
* Your reputation between races
All of this has been greatly expanded on enough to warrant being called its own game. You're no longer limited on the number of ships in your fleet.  Trading has been greatly expanded, and there are more mission types (Escort, Deliveries)  Some of the missions are very PIRATES! like hunting down pirates ships.
There is no choosing a starting faction, you just jump in the smallest starter ship and get started.  In the begining you have no reputation, and jobs are scarce.  You pretty much just take ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jobs, run from the bigger ships, and try and capture as many little ships as you can.
Customization of your ships is pretty extensive, and I haven't found everything yet.  Pirate factions have weapons that might not be approved for use, and will get your ship attacked by a passing johnny law.  Go through a black hole, and wind up in an alien world with technology not yet seen or used by humans.
At some point, your fleet can get huge enough where you'll sell your small ships off to raise enough money for a bigger flagship.  This is important, because the more crew you have on your flagship, the greater your chances are at capturing other big ships (and small ships with ease)
As a result of your conquests and fleet building, your crew and cargo space increases, allowing you to take on larger delivery and escort missions.
Eventually the entire star map will be lit up in missions for you.  Stick to the non time-sensative missions, and every stop will be a payment.
All in all, a very very good game.   Would be neat to see it ported to phones, as I do play the NES PIRATES! when I'm just out and trying to burn some time.

This was the first of the borderlands series that I played and I loved it. I hadn’t played the first so somethings did not make sense at first but eventually they all fell into place and made sense.
The overall game play and mechanics were very well made and reflected the slightly silly fun feel disguised by its gruesome and apocalyptic facade. I also loved how the game can be played many times with a different character each time and with a different skill set. This allows the game to have more replay value and gives you more to achieve then just the one play through. The level system also felt very fair and gives you time to gain experience and weapons without rushing you to the next mission. The farming in this game was also very rewarding and definitely pays off when you experience the feeling of melting enemies with your new legendary. Also to lead on my last point the bosses feel like they are balancing somewhere between hard and difficult by being just hard enough not to be impossible with a weak inventory and being challenging with a very good build.
This game is also very fun to play with friends. It adds a layer of teamwork and fun to the game when played with friends. However the loot system can easily be abused with one friend having a much better inventory then the others. So just remember to keep track of everyone’s loot situation and be fair.
Overall I love this game and the story that follows it. The farming pays off greatly and it rewards players for doing it. Definitely recommended to anyone who likes a challenge and has some spare time.

I'll start off with a few tidbits some people seem to think are relevant:
Out of the entire so-called "Soulborne" series, I've only played Dark Souls III and all its DLC, which I liked a lot.
I'm on NG+ in this game.
I am primarily a PvE player in all games I play.
This game is not like Dark Souls. It does not try to be, and it does not want to be. To even say that it borrows elements from Dark Souls because it's hard is like saying that Dark Souls borrows elements from World of Warcraft because they're both RPGs. However, because many people think of this as "another Souls clone", I will include comparisons to Dark Souls at the end of each pro.
Pros:
The Surge does a good job of storytelling, if you're paying attention. You can get a pretty clear picture of what's going on through audio logs, announcements, NPCs, watching some in-game propaganda videos, or, if you're feeling up to it, reading flavor text. However, the story is not given to you all at the same time, or even in a linear manner. You're going to have bits and pieces out of sequence that you need to put together, like a puzzle. This is different from most other games, but, again, if you're paying attention, you'll come to like it.
This is different from Dark Souls, in that storytelling comes primarily from cutscenes and tons of flavor text.
Level design is mostly realistic. You're stuck in a factory, so there are catwalks, deadly drops, heavy machinery, crates, elevators, and your weapons are just tools being used as weapons. Detailed maps can be found in some areas, but mostly you'll find arrows pointing you in one direction or another. If you're an immersive gamer, like me, you'll love it.
This is no different from Dark Souls, with the exception that non-boss enemies in The Surge can be primarily found in tight spaces, leaving less room for error.
The looting system is deterministic, which is great, and realistic. If you want an armor schematic, you need to cut off pieces of it from enemies who wear it.
If you want components to craft and upgrade your current armor, you need to cut off the same pieces from enemies. If you want leg upgrades, you have to cut off the legs of enemies wearing leg armor. If you want torso upgrades, same thing. Unlike trying to get schematics, you do not need to cut off parts from enemies wearing the same armor as you.
This is different from Dark Souls, in that drops are almost completely random, with few exceptions.
Combat is also realistic, to some degree. Staggering enemies is difficult with lighter weapons with high attack speeds, but at the same time, heavier weapons capable of staggering enemies are harder to hit due to their low attack speed. Furthermore, to get a successful cut, you'll need to weaken enemy body parts. You also can't just back off from an attack past a certain point, due to momentum. Blocking also takes a heavy toll on your stamina, and just holding the block will slowly deplete your stamina. You are, after all, using heavy machinery as weapons. You need to be careful about when to attack and which weapon to use against an enemy.
This is different from Dark Souls, where you can cancel just about any attack by rolling, eliminating the risk of going "all in", and shields simply slow stamina regeneration..
The implant and armor systems are realistic. Your implants need power, but your RIG also needs power to help you move around, so heavy armor will leave you unable to use many implants, while implants will force you to use light armor. That is, unless you farm scrap and level up until you can have both. However, armor still has drawbacks. Heavy armor typically increases stamina and energy consumption and may even decrease damage output.
This is different from Dark Souls, where you need to meet attribute requirements to effectively use weapons and armor, yet suffer no penalties as long as your load capacity is high enough, unless otherwise specified by your weapons and armor.
Cons:
Storytelling has some flaws, primarily in the form of NPCs. Every NPC you talk to says they don't know what's going on, which gets tedious after a while. Although it is realistic, given the situation, it's also frustrating for players due to the inclusion of a "What's going on here?" dialogue option with every single NPC you meet.
Level design can be confusing. Although the developers had the right idea by limiting the amount of maps and such, there's a lack of signs that is unrealistic in a large manufacturing complex where people are expected to move around on foot.
Combat can be frustrating at first in NG+. In NG, you start with what amounts to Mk 0 armor and weapons, and enemies (damage, HP, armor) are scaled to that. Throughout NG, you can upgrade your weapons and armor all the way to Mk V by finding upgrade items called "nano cores". However, there's a limited number of these, so you'll most likely just upgrade your armor and weapons to Mk IV. In NG+, however, the "baseline" from which enemies in the first area are scaled is now Mk VI, meaning that your Mk IV armor and weapons are effectively worse by comparison than your "Mk 0" armor and weapons from NG. This can lead to some quick, frustrating deaths in the early levels, until you upgrade everything to Mk VI.
Upgrading can also be frustrating in NG+. Because you can't farm Mk I - Mk IV components any more, you jump straight to Mk VI. However, this also incurs a massive increase in scrap costs, since you're effectively upgrading multiple times all at once. If you plan on using multiple weapons in NG+, but didn't previously upgrade them, you may spend a lot of time farming.
All in all, this is a good game, well worth the money. Just don't think it's Dark Souls, because it's not.

The Surge definitely shares a lot of similarities with the Soulsborne series, but still manages to be unique and have a personality of its own.
Pros:
-Combat is fluid and the weapons offer a big variety of ways to play. Similarly to Souls, choosing a weapon will depend on your playstyle.
-Each area is huge and offers a lot to explore. Deck13 has clearly put time into making sure every small section of the map is worth exploring.
-The story is interesting, but you might have a hard time catching up. You'll understand everything if you look and listen to everything well enough though.
-Bosses are interesting, and each one has a small extra twist to it compared to the previous one.
Cons:
-Locking on to different body parts can feel a bit awkward at times, especially if you're against a strong or fast enemy.
-There are only 5 bosses. They were great, but I would have loved to see a couple more if not a lot more.
-A lot of the enemies are repeated throughout each area. A bigger enemy variety would've been pleasent.
For those who are worried about optimizations, don't. The game is very optimized for a big variety of hardware, and getting 60fps on any mid-range computer with something like a GTX 950 would be more than fine for this game. Although you'll definitely get the best experience if you at least have a GTX 970, since it shouldn't have any problems to run the game maxed out at 1080p with locked 60fps (For those who wonder, FPS is unlocked, so you can go nuts if you want).
Overall, the game is definitely worth the $50 price tag, but if you're patient, you can wait till the Winter/Autumm sale to save some cash.
Deck13 has definitely improved since the pretty mediocre Lords of The Fallen. I'd love to see them do more with The Surge universe in the future.
Anf of course, if you have yet to realize, the game is difficult, but not unmanagable. Just be prepared for a challenge when you get into it.

As a big fan of both the Wargame series and Paradox it saddens me that I can't recommend this game right now. I hope that the problems that this game has will be fixed as the game moves out of beta but to be honest I am not very hopefull.
The biggest problem this game has is the morale system. The morale system allows you to make any attempt of an assault run away if you simply shoot a few rounds of artillery towards it. It also makes it so that air panicks and flies away if it they come anywhere near an AA-unit.
I don't think anti-air can actually shoot down the planes though, I've actually never seen a plane get shot down by anything but another plane so far.
Tanks have the same problem, they are really hard to kill, but making them run away is way too easy, simply shoot some artillery shells in their direction, or miss a few shot with another tank that can't penetrate it anyway, and the tank will run away.
The frontline system is not terrible from a gameplay perspective, but it makes any kind of stealth or flanking pretty much impossible and makes the game feel even more arcade.
The graphics feels very cartoony (not only because the battlefield is mostly covered in red and blue from the frontline system) and the game has a pretty low degree of realism, with the Jumbo having thicker armor than the King Tiger for example.

"Emily is Away" is an excellent freeze-frame of a particular feeling that was captured during the Messenger days. You shouldn't be looking to play it like a branching narrative with multiple outcomes (you'll be disappointed if you do)—the goal of the game is to talk with Emily, secretly attempting to discover her true feelings whilst remaining a steadfast friend. Of course it's a stupid and deceptive endeavor, but like much of adolescence, "Emily is Away" is less about doing the right thing and more about trying to get someone to like you. The yearly homages are quaint but the main draw is in seeing how close you can get to Emily each year, and grappling with the fact that you're just drifting further and further apart.

Papers, Please is a 2013 award-winning experimental RPG developed by Lucas Pope and published by 3909 for Windows, Mac, Linux, iOS and PlayStation Vita.
Papers, Please is an interesting experience, to say the least. At face value, it looks like another artsy, preachy, SJW game, but upon playing it for a while, I found myself invested in the balls hard gameplay, interesting characters that I cared about and sheer challenge it was to avoid getting citated. In Papers, Please, you take the role of an inspector for the Grestin Border Checkpoint, a border between the fictional dictated countries of Artstotzka and Kolechia. You must find discrepancies in immigrants' passports, as well as doing other tasks like keeping your family alive. For every passport you process correctly, you get some money in which to spend on caring for your family. This creates an interesting system where you start running out of money quickly as more and more papers to process are introduced, which creates a sense of urgency and you'll start accepting more bribes.
There's also an arc where you can choose to complete missions for a group of mercenaries who want to overthrow the government. I'd like to go into that but I don't want to spoil anything. There is an endless mode, but admittedly it's a little throw-away. The random generators that dictate facial appearances and the paperwork are very good, but the faces can sometimes turn out a little... un-human. Also, the final few days of the game can be a little tedious as the amount of papers that need checking gets a little ridiculous.

Short answer, buy this game if you like turn-based RPGs. It has a decent sense of humor and some good replay value with the several unlockable gameplay modes, one of which has a main story very different from the original. Besides that, it has several great features hopefully more RPGs could adopt.
First feature, everybody gets xp once they join your group, even if they're knocked out or not even in the fight. It annoys me to no end when either of these things are the case. When a character faints and I have to reload just to make sure they aren't left behind xp-wise or the ones I haven't had in the party become nearly useless and end up completely ignored because of the effort it would take to grind them, it really takes me out of the game.
Second, every area has a limit on random encounters. Even the overworld has a limit, though it's very high. If you fight the X amount of mobs in the area shown in your menu then there will be no more random encounters. You can also just continue to spam the button "Fight" button to run out the random encounters for the entire area. It Makes exploring a dungeon to try and collect all the loot so much less of a hassle. Each area's amount of random encounters worked out pretty well too. I would usually just finish them off or am left with only a few by the end of it. And if you feel the need to grind a bit afterwards, you can still call more mobs from the menu.
Finally, the mobs scale in strength in each area with every fight, peaking by the time you reach the random encounter limit. While the enemies don't scale with each fight in the overworld, they do become stronger for the entirety of the map as you progress through the story.
Those aren't the only great mechanics, just the ones other RPGs don't have but should adopt. Very few complaints otherwise. Mainly just how much of a maze the dungeons can become later in the game. Really worth the small price tag.

The most fun you can have destroying civilisation without becoming a government MP, Plague Inc. refines the Pandemic formula into a streamlined combination of strategy and twisted bio-horror.

If you want a direct quote to put up for marketing:
This game here is how you do a mobile port
!
It would've been very easy for Pandemic to just release the game with a graphical upgrade, both DLC viruses, and call it a day there.
But they went above and beyond what most Mobile developers are willing to do with a port.
Every selling point I can put on this game has the line "PC Exclusive" hugging it, usually with the word "amazing", "fun", "interesting", or "great" tagging closely.
First of all, the
HD Graphics. They're wonderful. Amazing to look at. They grant a very bare game a lot of personality. From the wall murals in South America, to the deserts of Africa, to the Sky Scrapers and Monuments of North America and Europe, every image of the world you're slowly destroying feels real,
making you wonder if something like this could truly happen.
Secondly, Achievements and things! The
challenges for medals and high scores give something that the original Mobile Plague Inc didn't have. It brings an objective to the game that was more-or-less just "Kill things and see if you can do it gud" before.
And finally, the customization available from the internet!
at it's finest, we have the Steam Workshop! There are already dozens of fan scenarios on the workshop, from the ever-popular "420 Blaze It ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)" meme viruses and "JECKSEPICOEY" YouTube fan-bait, to the absolutely impressive ideas of an infection turning people into Werewolves, killer Plants, and real-life diseases recreated spectacularly.
I've yet to try most of these features, and there's still more to come! (Multiplayer ermagerd!)
For those who wanted Plague Inc on PC, this is a spectacular pick-up!
And that's perhaps where the only real issue with Plague Inc: Evolved lies.
Most people don't want idle Mobile games on PC.
While the graphics, sound design, and even game-play is bumped up dramatically, the core mechanics are still designed with Mobile in mind. The game is still very slow, even on max speed, and ultimately descends into "Set the game on X4 Speed and go look at porn, since you can't play anything else with this beauty running."
This is an issue not with the PC port, but with the game it's self. While some may find it annoying, I find it a feature of the realism.
So would I recommend Plague Inc: Evolved?
For those who enjoyed Plague Inc on Mobile, but prefer PC? Yes.
For those who want to try out Plague Inc in general? Get it on Mobile.
This is the kind of game you have running on a laptop beside you. It isn't too far from having it run on the Phone on your lap, but the upgrades are worth the increased platform size.

I've put 1000+ hours into dark souls 1-3, and the surge did not dissapoint.
Game had a terrible launch due to a couple severe issues that has since been fixed.
Lovely art and combat need not mentioning, I personally enjoyed the plot.
• Game has much better camera & customization than souls.
• The secret areas make sense, as opposed to the souls "hit every wall" (or hit every wiki :P)
• Deeper combo systems, including "perfect" combo bonuses & perfect blocks
• I usually avoid magic in games, but surge's energy system is bloody amazing,
• Very aggressive game, that rewards going balls deep (ala energy system)

Let me preface this review with my lack of interest in these types of games. It can be compared to the likes of the DemonBorne games. I disliked Demon Souls (Yawn, not worth the difficulty). Same went with Dark Souls 1 and 2. (Didn't bother with 3, shame on me for even considering Dark Souls 2). Then came Bloodborne....I hated the mechanics as much as the previous DemonBorne games...but this time the premise rocked. Difficult Lovecraftian setting! What a dream! (But sadly, its a console game...and you have to settle for an age old PS4 look with no PS4 Pro support)
Then I played Lords of the Fallen. It is difficult as hell...but something about it was vastly more interesting and fun than said other games. Still...it was another medieval fantasy game and I stopped playing after a while.
Then came The Surge.
This game rocked and kept me addicted from beginning to end. Solid mechanics and interesting additions make this a solid third person action rogue-like game for the ages.
First off...this game is EFFIN beautiful. A breath of fresh air to the Rogue-Like Action games. Crisp neo-apocalyptic dystopic visuals with complex machine mechanics. Its just so beautiful.
This won't last long as you'll be met with difficult foes...but like the games of this type...it takes strategy and tactics. The cooles tthing here was the ability to target individual body parts with the assistance of showing the weakpoints  (Armored/Unarmored). This in itself added a bit of depth that assisted in making the game a bit more fun.
Now past the gameplay is an actual story. A solid one at that. Building upong a cyberpunkish, apoclyptic, corporate *eff* up plot. Entertaining enough that it assists on driving you forward in the game. It was also nice to see NPCs that aren't trying to kill you, that you can interact with through dialog and complete some (not completely non-linear) side quests.
Anyways, if you love difficult but strategic action games, you'll enjoy this. I'm really hate these types of games, I never liked Bullet Hell games or games that artificially expand game length with impossibly difficult grinding....but this game managed to keep my interest even past the constant dying....it feels awesome. Weird coming from a person that prefers adventure games with insanely difficult puzzles without walkthroughs (Myst/Riven). SO I'm extremely happy to say....PLAY THIS!

While there are still many issues in Spacebase DF-9(such as bugs, outdated graphics, and so on), despite the years of production and work, I understand that this is still an incomplete product. Therefore I am not reviewing this game as a complete product, but rather I am reviewing its creative process. As a building management and construction simulator, Spacebase DF-9 fails the most important criterion in any simulation, uniqueness. Uniqueness is a core aspect in simulation games because it is there in which specialties and creativity come together to make an enjoyable and memorable simulation game. Examples of popular simulation games are Goat Simulator, The Sims, and Train Simulator, which all can be easily identified by each of their unique points. That being said, it is hard to find unique points in Spacebase DF-9. As I am writing this review, in trying to remember things that were unique I find myself fixated more on the bugs than actual gameplay.
Overlooking the bugs, let me break down the gameplay. You build a base, gather resources, and make the base bigger and repeat. You have raiders that attack your base but they don’t present a threat if you properly maintain security. You have asteroid showers that happen every once in a while that start fires and destroy structures such as walls and they need to be patched up. You will get transmissions every once in a while so that people can move in, attack, or attach themselves to the base. The difficulty ramps up as your base becomes larger and more populated; you have to keep track of people’s morale, energy consumption, and security.  That is about it.
As I have stated earlier, it lacks uniqueness. The simulation itself is very basic and there seems to be a large amount of creative work in creating the characters. Unfortunately, the programmers made the characters expandable, having them die very easily and having a lot of them makes the characters feel insignificant and therefore, their uniqueness insignificant. As a simulation, this game will not stand out in sales or reviews unless the creative department decides to do some major reworking. Furthermore if unchanged and published, this game will stand out as one of many examples of morale hazard in pre-release gaming.

As I was about to post this I realized that this game was published a year ago. I could not fathom that a game this unpolished and lacking in content could be deemed complete by anyone who took pride in their work. In the end, it seems that DoubleFine just took everyone’s money and fled.

the sound has always been an issue for this game in dosbox.
contrary to some posts i have read here, the DIGITAL sound does NOT work in this port. (eg: machinegun sounds)
to get the sound working 100% do the following:
1)
go to this address and download the opensource JEMM memory manager: ( JEMM578B.zip )
unpack "JEMM578B.zip" to "steam\steamapps\common\1942 - the pacific air war\JEMM"
your game folder will now look something like this:
- dosbox_windows    (folder, contains dosbox)
- JEMM                       (folder, contains the memory manager)
- MPS                          (folder, contains game)
- manual.pdf
2)
- Open the "dosbox_windows" folder
- Open "dosbox_1942_TPAW.conf" with notepad
now scroll all the way down untill you see the following lines:
xms=true
ems=true
umb=true
change all 3 values to the following:
xms=false
ems=false
umb=false
- Save & exit notepad
3)
- Open the "dosbox_windows" folder
- Open "dosbox_1942_TPAW_launch_windows.conf" with notepad
- Edit and make sure it only contains the following:
[autoexec]
mount C ".."
C:
CD JEMM
jemmex FRAME=E000 LOAD
CD\
CD MPS\PACIFIC
CLS
1942.EXE
EXIT
- Save & exit
4)
Open the configuration utility by right clicking on the game from the steam library and set your digital audio to
sound blaster 16.
5)
Launch game & make sure the digital sounds are ticked in the in-game config screen.

WARNING: keyboard + mouse controls for this game on PC are F#$### up. My best guess is it's another bad porting job, as 90% of the console games ported to PC seem to have some major problems. It's too bad because the game would be fantastic if not for the jacked up controls. The game has a problem detecting the buttons that you hit, and since the game relies HEAVILY on timed pressing of buttons it makes for extremely frustrating gameplay. For example many game missions require you to spam the E button at the right moment in order to avoid failing the mission, but then it fails to detect 75% of the button presses (it does detect SOME of them), and even though you did exactly what you were supposed to, you fail the mission and have to redo it. It took me like 10 tries to get past some missions because of this strange problem. There is NOTHING wrong with my keyboard, outside this game it works perfect. You will CONSTANTLY notice this problem, even a simple thing such as exiting a menu (by hitting backspace) I frequently have to hit backspace 3 or 4 times before it registers. During fights you have to counter enemies by hit E at the right time, and since it frequently doesn't acknowledge you hit the button you will constantly fail to counter easy to counter enemies. I play other games on my PC that require you to counter enemies by hitting a button, for example Shadow of Mordor & Batman Arkham City, and let me tell you I have NO problem countering 99% of all incoming attacks and going on massive kill streaks (like 300+) without getting hit one time, and those games rely on the same mechanic of just timing a button to counter. But on SD, because of the weird failure to recognize keyboard buttons every time, I can barely counter 20% of incoming attacks. Which means I am constantly dying in what should be easy to win fights. I know some stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is going to say it's because I am a noob and don't know how to play, but trust me I've tested this for game for several hours and it is so obvious the game is glitched and ignoring keyboard buttons. Despite the messed up controls I have still enjoyed the game, as occasionally I can actually win a big fight by just spamming buttons as fast as I can, and racing around the streets in cars and crashing into everything never gets old! I will probably even suffer through some more missions to try and get my $4.99 worth. But I can't give this game a thumbs up because the controls are seriously f#$#$# up. Battlefield: Bad Company 2 boasts a fast-paced and thrilling campaign, as well as some of the most immersive and exciting multiplayer action around.
There is no shortage of online destinations for those who enjoy first-person gun-wielding combat, but no matter how many opportunities you get to shoot another player in the face, there is always room for one more. Especially when that one more is as exciting and intense as Battlefield: Bad Company 2. The online multiplayer in this modern military shooter is a standout, featuring huge maps, incredible destructibility, powerful vehicles, and excellent sound design. These elements combine to foster the sense that you are fighting on an actual battlefield, making many other online shooters seem more like combat arenas than believable war zones. Multiplayer battles are invigorating and addictive, but they aren't all that Bad Company 2 has to offer.
The sizable campaign takes you to beautiful and exotic locations where you'll be sorely tempted to take a break from shooting bad guys and blowing things up to admire the scenery. Your hilarious and endearing squadmates are great companions, giving the campaign a rich sense of character not often found in the genre. The result is a very entertaining adventure that, coupled with the excellent multiplayer and top-notch technical presentation, makes Battlefield: Bad Company 2 something special in the world of shooters.
The beginning of Bad Company's second tour finds Sarge, Marlowe, Sweetwater, and Haggard stationed in a wintery valley, supposedly serving out Sarge's last tour of duty. Lofty mountains loom high against the bright blue sky as you sneak your way between snow-laden trees and out across a frozen river. As you infiltrate a small village, the snow muffles the sound of your footfalls, and when a firefight breaks out, your ears ring from the concussion of nearby explosives. One daring escape later, you're dropped into the Bolivian jungle, where mosquitoes whine in your ear as you walk in the dappled light of the jungle floor. Gunfire doesn't echo very far in the forest, but beneath the corrugated tin roof of a logging outpost, each bullet is a cacophony unto itself.
This vivid, engaging world is a testament to Bad Company 2's remarkable technical presentation. The stunning landscapes are matched by the diverse, intriguing terrain in both rural and urban environments. The excellent sound design further enriches your sense of place, and each gunshot, footstep, and exclamation fuels your battlefield awareness and informs your tactical decisions. Though there are some blurry textures, occasional screen tearing, and awkward moments caused by the pervasive environmental destructibility, these are mere blemishes on the ambitious look and immersive sound of Bad Company 2.
Of course, just because the scenery is great doesn't stop you from wanting to blow it up. Trees, barricades, vehicles, buildings, and bridges all splinter and break apart when exposed to gunfire or explosives. Not only is it immensely fun to destroy things, but it's crucial to your survival and success. Say there's a sniper perched in a tower covering your approach. You can try to pick him off without exposing yourself, or you can bust out your underbarrel grenade launcher and blow the platform to smithereens. The explosion showers debris in a realistic and satisfying way, and the sniper is taken care of. Destruction is a double-edged sword, however, as you'll learn the first time that the window you are shooting out of explodes and becomes a gaping hole through which your enemies are more than happy to shoot you.
Most buildings can be completely leveled this time around, provided you have enough firepower, though metal structures like shipping containers are nigh impervious. Occasionally the rampant destructibility will get a bit too ambitious, leaving objects stuck in strange positions. Yet the scale of destruction you can wreak is impressive, and the best part about it is how your destructive power becomes a seamless part of your battlefield strategy. It makes you feel powerful in a logical, invigorating way and makes Bad Company 2 unique among its peers.
Humor is another way that Bad Company 2 distinguishes itself. Your squadmates each have great personalities, and their banter is witty and entertaining. You may have to wait for a quiet moment to hear some of their best conversations, but it is well worth it. Haggard's love for the Dallas Cowboys and command of the Spanish language are two amusing subjects, while a conversation about respecting the dead adds enough emotional depth to elevate these characters above one-dimensional stereotypes. They are competent and helpful on the battlefield, and though the squad-based action seems a natural fit for cooperative play, you won't lament playing solo because the men of Bad Company are such delightful companions.
The campaign is a focused, largely linear adventure that takes you to a variety of gorgeous locations. The aforementioned arctic and jungle landscapes are standouts, but other places live up to the high standard. Driving a tank through a countryside in the full bloom of autumn provides eye candy and cannon fodder aplenty, while speeding around a dry seabed in an ATV brings strange sights, not to mention a particularly fierce firefight in the courtyard of an old fortress. You have to be sharp to defeat the smart, aggressive enemies who use destructibility to their advantage and avoid your line of fire. The action is challenging but not overly so, ensuring you have plenty of time to revel in the havoc you are causing. Despite one oddly forced situation, the campaign moves through exotic locales at a great clip, providing ample opportunity to flex your firearms and enjoy some intense vehicle sequences. This is a very entertaining, very exciting adventure.
But the most exciting thing Battlefield: Bad Company 2 has to offer is online multiplayer competition. Up to 32 players compete in squads in a few different match types. In Rush, the attacking team assaults an enemy position in an effort to destroy two targets of opportunity. If the attackers succeed, two more targets open up, as well as an entire new section of battlefield. These progressive contests are fierce and engaging, and each new area offers new challenges to which both teams must adapt. (There is also shorter, equally intense version of this mode called Squad Rush.)
In Conquest, two teams strive to hold three control points while fending each other off. The natural ebb and flow of combat is unpredictable here, as points can be captured by a lone soldier or by a heavy armored assault. These battlefields are more fluid, and because the action doesn't move on like it does in Rush, they tend to be more thoroughly ravaged by destruction by the end of the match. The last mode, Squad Deathmatch, pits four squads of four against each other in a more traditional, yet still very fun competition. Jumping into a random game doesn't always work properly, and you won't always find a good match, or any match at all for that matter. Fortunately, you can easily call up a list of active servers and consistently hop into whatever game type you like. Each mode offers a different take on the core combat, providing a great variety of ways to do battle.
Bad Company 2's technical excellence is on full display here as well, and the spacious, well-designed maps make superb stages for combat. There are dense snowy forests, debris-laden deserts, coastal industrial complexes, swampy jungle villages, and riverside settlements that play host to the intense action. These maps are impressively varied, offering diverse terrain and more buildings than you would ever need to go in. Each weathers the destructive forces of battle differently each time, making the combat incredibly dynamic and demanding constant adaptability.
