Transistor provides a unique experience that combines an immersive world, genuine artwork and an interesting story. It is a bright example of how creative can indie developers be and how capable they are in creating top-notch standalone games even when they are not living under the shadow of a big publisher's name.
To begin with, Transistor provides the player with a unique story that has good pace and cohesion. The story progresses at a fast manner in order to match the quick pace of the game and, therefore, it does not overwhelm the player with pointless information. This approach has both its merits and drawbacks: It is nice because it keeps a good balance between story and progression, which is something that many similar games fail to do so. On the other hand though, the story leaves a few questionmarks as it is not possible to explain everything that is happening. Maybe this is intentional by the developers in order to make each player fantasize and give her/his own explanations and meanings about the plot and the world in the game. If there is one flaw that must be pointed out, it has to be the story because there are some pieces of the puzzle that are missing in order to give a rationalal explanation to everything that happens in the plot. However, it is important to not forget that the game's main focus is not to establish a "universe" around its story. The story is just there to accompany the rest aspects of the game and give a certain degree of reasoning to what you do.
Furthermore, the characters of the game are well designed. You play as Red, one of the most talented singers in the city where the game takes place. From the very beginning, you are accompanied by the voice of Blue, the person that is stuck inside your sword called 'Transistor'. He is rambling most of the time but he has a nice deep voice, which makes it quite pleasant listening to him. Overall, the voice acting is of high quality and greatly matches the atmosphere of the game.
Music is the strongest aspect of Transistor. In order for a game to become memorable it needs genuine music to accompany it. The music composer, Darren Korb, and the vocalist, Ashley Barrett, have managed to provide us with excellent music experience that give identity and "soul" to the game. At this point, words do not do justice to describe the music eargasm. It is something you should try yourself in order to experience that feeling. And I am sure it will give you as much incentive, as it gave to me, to buy the OST Album of Transistor to honor and support the composer, vocalist and all the musicians that worked hard to create such a masterpiece.
Gameplay is another very strong element of Transistor. It is a fast paced game that gives you a lot of flexibility on how you deal with enemies. You get multiple spells in the game (4 of each you can use at a certain time) but the game gives you the opportunity to enhance each spells with other spells you have acquired in order to create new unique effects for each ability. There are so many combinations you can do and, therefore, so many different patterns you can use to deal with your enemies. This diversity in terms of abilities is one of the biggest reasons why this game justifies replayability so much. In addition, the controls are very responsive and the fights are well designed. There are also certain abilities called "limiters" which make the game significantly harder by limiting, as the name suggests, some of your strengths or enhancing the strengths of your enemies. In return, you receive increased leveling experience and, hence, you can unlock abilities and other new perks faster.
All in all, the game is an artwork, both in terms of visuals and music. It is worth it every single penny you spend on it and on buying the OST album. If you are unfamiliar with indie games or you are still skeptical, please try it! If you are still concerned about the price, the game goes on sale every now and then and the price drops dramatically so do not miss the offer next time!
It is one of the greatest games you can gift yourself and I sincerely believe you will have a blast playing it! Totally recommended!

Supergiant Games were on my radar ever since I picked up Bastion in 2011 and played the ever living crap out of it. Everything from the music to the gameplay really stood out to me in Bastion and I felt like it really fell on the right side of pretentious throughout. So when Transistor was released in 2014 I got really excited since not only was this another Supergiant Games release, but it also had the legend Darren Korb behind the soundtrack again. Unfortunately, back then I was super broke and had no way of getting Transistor so I only got to pick it up recently since now I'm slightly less broke. To quickly summarise my thoughts on this game, I feel like it doesn't live up to the legacy of Bastion and overall is nowhere near as good as Bastion. This said though, Transistor is a completely different game to Bastion and for the rest of this review I'll try to treat it as such, but I will be referencing Bastion in places where I deem it to be appropriate. ON TO THE REVIEW!
Let's just get this out of the way so we can talk about the harder stuff: Darren Korb is a ♥♥♥♥ing genius. He may not be the best music artist ever, but he does his job of making music for games really well. There's tons of memorable songs and all the songs with lyrics to them are catchy and fun. I'd argue this OST is better than Bastion's in some ways since I can listen to it while chilling and not feel offput by it. The narration was fine in this game, but not nearly as good as Bastion's which always felt super dynamic which made the game feel that much more alive. Overall, very good job in the sound department, as to be expected.
In both Bastion and Transistor we had handpainted isometric scenes, both of which looked absolutely stunning. However, Bastion fell short with the characters since they were 3D models rather than sprites. It's easy to see why they did this, however it always felt a bit jarring to see these obviously 3D models on a very flat 2D backdrop. Transistor improves upon this a lot and while you can still tell that the characters are 3D models, it's far less noticeable and fits in quite nicely. However, I prefer the visuals of Bastion much more since they didn't feel as bland as Transistor's. Yes, I get that Transistor is meant to be set in what is essentially a post apocalyptic future, but everywhere I went felt quite samey. Overall, good job on the visuals but the environments could have been a bit better.
This is where the♥♥♥♥♥♥really hits the fan for me personally since the story never really got me. If it's any indication of how the story stuck with me, I had to look up the story for the game on the Transistor Wiki before writing this review to refresh my memory. Now don't get me wrong, the story is actually good once you understand it, but that's the issue here: you have to understand it. Now, if you're like me you'll probably play the game in short bursts over the course of a few weeks, mainly due to the gameplay which I'll get to later. The issue with this is that you will probably lose track of some of the subtleties that are important to get the full impact of the story. It also doesn't help that this game is cryptic as ♥♥♥♥, making sure to never fully reveal what it's trying to convey. This is okay for the most part, but as you reach the later parts of the game it starts to get annoying. The worst part is that this game is really going for a dramatic and gripping story but it seems to fall short because of this cryptic delivery method.
The core mechanic in this game is quite interesting and novel, but that's also it's biggest problem. The fact that it's novel means it gets pretty tiresome pretty quickly. Now, for those who don't know the core mechanic in Transistor is the turn based combat mixed with real time combat. When you go through your first few battles, it's cool. When you get more abilities to mess around with, it's cool. But very soon you'll find a combo that's OP and you'll just spam that over and over until you win. At this point, you get pretty bored and if you too lost interest in the story, you lose a lot of drive to complete the game. The game will occasionaly throw curveballs at you, but they can be dealt with easily using your method with minor tweaks. It's worth noting that there is this system called "limiters" which make the game harder at the benefit of more XP gain from fights, but these feel like a cheap way of increasing difficulty with no real curve to it which makes it hard to really pick them up unless you're MLG pro or something like that.
This is a good game, but I feel like it could have been so much better. The art as always is great, but the gameplay and story made it hard for me to just sit down and play it. I recommend this game to anyone who likes a good soundtrack in their game and likes reading into lore (since there is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of lore to read if you so wish). If you've come from Bastion expecting it to be Bastion, then you'll probably be disappointed like I was. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed this game, but I just feel so much more could have been done to make this game better.

Sadly, this game is not as memorable as Bastion.
Visually, the game is very beautiful. The narrative technique is as good as it gets. The music is great as you might expect from this developer. The story is okay. But the game is let down by its overly-complex combat system and its corresponding configuration UI.
The game makes no (zero!) effort at introducing you to the complex customizations that are possible. It uses a lot of jargon that it doesn't explain and an absurdly complex UI that is completely non-obvious. I actually had to watch a youtube video explaining it after I managed to re-arrange my abilities in a way that made sure I could no longer kill enemies. Oops?
Finishing the game felt like a chore as I button-mashed my way through enemies. Eventually, I kinda-sorta figured out how to use the battle mechanics to string together some combos but by then the game was ending.
(Not as big a deal, but I found the default controls to be unplayable. The auto-cast option was a disaster that contributed a lot to the button-mash-and-pray playstyle I used for the first half of the game. I highly recommend turning it off.)
The combat system is not
once you understand it, but its complexity isn't warranted for a game of its length (which took me 4 hours, skipping the trial rooms). This game would be much more enjoyable on a second playthrough.
I don't recommend the game if you don't have the patience to learn an intricate combat system for a very short game. You'll probably like this if you liked Bastion, though.

Paradox masters of grand strategies and Eugen systems makers R.U.S.E, and the Wargame Series come together to make a phenomenal RTS that is really inovative with the front line system that I so far have not seen in any other RTS's. With Large maps future modding capabilities Eugen systems have taken there learned knowlege and combind it with Knowledge of Paradox to a make a game that is epic, fun, and historical.

EARLY REVIEW: (TL;DR IN THE END)
Following the line of it's modern counterpart "Wargame", this release is definitely more accesible to a new crowd of this specific style of RTS, but not lacking any harshness to challenge the scarred veteran.
You are given a series of divisions to choose from both the Axis and the ally armies.
Different to Wargame, where you built your army based on all the units available for a country, here you are focused on a play style given by the division you choose, although just because you focus on a tank division, it doesn't mean you have no infantry or air support, but you will be more limited in those aspects than the one that revolves around them, so here is where strategical thinking comes to play, make every unit count and synergize as well as possible.
For example, you might go for the Scottish Infantry division, who centers it's forces around veteran infantry, artillery and ground support, or maybe the American Tank division, rampaging the field early with heavy tanks. The German forces wielding an accumulative power of panzers more aimed towards late game with the 12th SS-Panzer-Division led by commander Kurt Meyer, or a more invasive and expanding Fallschirmjäger division, focused on city capture by foot, and air support.
Divisions available are to be always expanding, so new possibilities come as time passes, keeping the game fresh.
The "Battle phases" mechanic makes a clear distinction of, early, middle, and late game.
Some armies benefit the possibility of having some tough units early on, but sometimes waiting to a later phase allows you to bring in more quantity of that same unit, so management and foresight is a must here.
This system was made to simulate the real tides of the battlefield, starting usualy (but not always) with a recon and setting up phase, followed by heavy combat.
Once your army is chosen, it's time to head to the battlefield, where the time will be stopped before the battle begins.
Now, Steel Division runs away of the unison of the typical world war 2 RTS, here you don't build a base, you don't level up buildings, or wait "production time" to get your unit in the battlefield.
You have a single military expenditure resource; as you start with a fixed amount, you are to select and position all your desired units (that you can pay for with the current amount of resource and are available in the current battlephase) from the deck of units you chose or built before entering the battle, into your side of the extensive battlefield, you can also asign movement, deploy, disembark or other orders before starting.
Once ready, hit launch, and the cogs of war start turning.
New to Steel Division is the dynamic front, for instead of capturing defined pieces of land, the entire map is yours to conquer.
The more dominance an army has over the map, the more resources will be granted to it, making all strategic points important, every forest exploitable, every factory center or city, an aid to the war machine.
Now summing up:  (TL;DR)
-Steel Division has a much friendlier learning curve than Wargame did, but it's still hard to master.
-The army builder is focused into roles by choosing divisions instead of countries to play as.
-New content is to be added periodically, keeping a fresh approach to the game.
-It's a unique aspect in comparison to any other non Eugen RTS, aiming more towards realism.
-Battle phases makes you manage not only costs, but time as well, a weak begining might bring a strong late game (and
viceversa).
-A dynamic frontline instead of capture points makes you battle for the entierety of the battlefield, making every
strategic zone important and opens up unlimited possibilities to win.
-Realism is key, tank's front armour is tougher than it's side and back, you can hide amongst trees or bushes or in
buildings to create ambushes or protect yourself.
In short, if you like World War 2, and fulfilling strategy games, pick this up, you won't regret it.

Visually, the Surge is stunning. The environments are colorful, beautifully lit and populated with details that help to immerse you in the narrative. The enemies are highly detailed and the animations are as smooth as butter. The game flawlessly blends dark viscera and interesting glitch effects like chromatic aberration in a gorgeous, futuristic world to create interesting and compelling levels. The level design is great, with lots of interconnectivity and exploration available.
The gamplay was highly rewarding, and has a good level of complexity. I found the combat to be extremely fluid, with a high skill cap that rewards timing and patience. There are many weapon types in the game, all of which have unique movesets and cater to specific play styles. As you use a weapon type, you gain proficiency in it, meaning that switching weapon types later in the game is actually disadvantageous. The proficiency system seems to reward the player for sticking with one weapon type throughout the game, but since all weapons of a specific type have a very similar moveset, this might start to get stale. That being said, the movesets and combos available to each weapon type are so complex and involved that I found myself learning up until the very end of the game, despite only using one handed weapons.
The narrative of the game is very interesting, but personally, I feel that the delivery is lacking. Even after playing it through twice, I still only kinda understand the story. This is probably at least partially intentional, as the game is experienced through the perspective of a lost and confused character. However, I also feel like I did not go through the cutscenes and witness the dialogue in the order I was intended to. The game doesn't rail road you, and allows you to explore and experience it in the way you want to, but I think the narrative cohesion suffers as a result.
All in all, I very much enjoyed The Surge and can whole-heartedly recommend it. It's a souls-like, and as a result is being compared to Dark Souls. I will say that the games are similar in terms of genre, but don't expect a sci-fi Dark Souls clone when going in. There are a plethora of differences between the two games and you should try to leave your expectations at the door and experience the game as it's own entity.

Early in the game you find a room with no enemies.  The lights are on, a robotic voice welcomes you.  A lonesome male voice plays through a crummy speaker.  The message is clear.  Out there, there's bodies and zombies and chaos.  In here though?  In here is *home*.
It doesn't have quite the polish dark souls does combat-wise (install a stam implant ASAP if you plan on blocking), the levels are a bit hard to navigate (trust the signs though, they're pretty good at pointing out shortcuts) and somehow, despite aping Dark Soul's slow delivery of story, they forgot to, you know... actually include the meat of the story.  Somehow, though, I still enjoyed the crap out of the time I spent with this game, and I'm considering coming back on NG+ once the DLC drops, something I never thought I'd say.

If there was a Mixed option to give this, I would, but I'm leaning more towards negative at 15 hours in.
Obviously, it's Souls-esque, but whereas Souls is hard and expects you to learn over time, The Surge is hard and expects you to learn immediately, and nearly demands perfection. Many enemies, especially bosses, can 2-hit kill you. Even areas you return to. Some attacks will sometimes even guarantee you get hit twice (looking at you, heavy-duty users...). So you'll often die quickly to enemies until you even get a sense of how to deal with them, making the learning process even longer due to the backtracking.
And some nitpicky details: having lyrics, especially very simple lyrics and a single verse, to the song you hear in your safe zones (which you will visit frequently) is maddening. I have "~I was booorn...in a pri-soooon~" constantly stuck in my head. Or having the announcer say only a handful of lines when exiting/entering an Ops area. You quickly tire of hearing the same thing over and over again.
The game does have some neat stuff though. The core level system and being able to mix and match implants and gear based on your power source (your level) is kinda cool. The combat can be surprisingly fast sometimes, though as mentioned above, You have to constantly heal or you just die instantly.
I'll revisit this when (or if) I finish.
POST FINISH EDIT:
I did finish the game, though I really didn't see much to change my initial opinion. New Game Plus dials up my comments even further: lots of one shot enemies. I remain of a mixed opinion.

Here's what you get!
* PAW: 1942, plus its Army Air expansion, running in DOSBox, and patched to its latest version.
* You do not get the Gold version, which was just the DOS version packaged with a bollox Win 3.1 multimedia launcher.
* For those who know their old sims and DOSBox, the digital sound works fine.  Getting PAW sound to work in DOSBox could be a real bear.
So, for the game itself:
This is a an old classic for Microprose game collectors, old flight-sim grogs (like myself), and the like.  As with all of these retro releases, there is very little here that modern gamers or folks not fond of this genre will find interesting.  (Truth be told, however, I'd rather fly this old sim than, say, later efforts such as MSCFS 2 or Pacific Fighters!)  But for the graphics -- which are that lovely mid-90's smear of big textured pixels -- PAW's flight model is surprisingly good (if actually a little too punishing), the enemy AI is challenging, and there are many scenarios to choose from.
Highly recommended with the caveats I've mentioned above.
(Note: use CTRL-F12 to increase the DOSBox cycles -- 3000 isn't nearly enough!)

If you like tweaking at the microscopic level and trying to squeeze out that little extra bit of performance, this game is for you. You can figure out optimal designs for producing a given amount of each resource as fast as possible and using as little space/materials as you can.
If you like large scale planning and architecting, this game is also for you. From the map view, that shows each section of your factory and how they all fit together geographically, to the production statistics that let you monitor graphs of your production/consumption of each resource and product, this game gives you the tools necessary to make sure your overall factory design does what you need.
This game has perfected automation. There are so many layers and aspects to it, but it all amounts to building machines that help you build more machines. The rate at which you are able to rework, expand, and optimize increases seemingly exponentially. Once you have perfected your assembly layout for a given resource, blueprint it and then have your construction robots automatically construct additional facilities to increase your production. Factorio demands thoughtful design at both the small and large scales.

Do you play Wargame? Did you play Wargame but got bored/annoyed with it because of it's many flaws?
Steel Division is for you. It's a straight up improvement in usability and gameplay in almost every measure. Conquest is much better with the frontline system, a line-of-sight tool takes out all the mystecism that plagued unit placement in wargame, the phase system shuts down the sort of things that allowed cheese rushes in Wargame such as helo-spam.
While it's still early and some balance tweaks could stand to be made here and there, make no mistake, this is basically Wargame 2.0, with a vastly improved formula, and a new, albeit rather unoriginal setting that regardless is well tailored to the sort of combined arms gameplay of it's predecessor. Health bars are gone, building-clearing is less abstract and more practical, infantry play is more involved and interesting, and the division system is a major step up from the chaotic mess of the nations and coalitions of wargame strewn with hundreds of useless 'noob-trap' units as the game ultimately boiled down to narrow metas.
It's an easy game to praise, even in it's limited beta with only 2 divisions for each side of the conflict out(Several more are  going to be in for release, with some of them trickling in for the beta.), but the gist of it is:
Pros:
-Phase system is an ingenious concept for giving a more 'controlled' and balanced pacing to the game
-Frontline system allows much more dynamic fighting for territory and tends to make battles play out in more interesting ways than static control sectors
-Division system is a massive improvement over nations and coalitions and shaves off needless noob-traps for a more narrow and 'focused' faction design where everything is meant to be viable and competitive.
-While unoriginal, many people tend to prefer WW2. I'm a bit burnt out on the setting, but for many this is still a big pro
Cons:
-Still uses a lobby system for public play, their automatching system will only be in release, and it's unclear if it's purely ranked play like in Wargame.
-Still no punishment system for leavers. And by god there's a metric crap-load of pansies in this game that will jump out the match at the drop of a tank. Probably the most spineless community I've seen in an RTS.
Neutral:
-The public chat is still just as memed out as in Wargame. Be sure to pick up some crazy 'alternative facts' about Hitler's reign, and the geopolitical theories of a slavic 19 year old playing out of a community internet cafe in the basement of an old steel mill.

R.U.S.E. and Wargame just hooked up and had a baby in the form of this game. It takes each good component from RUSE (Like tanks can't camp in the woods and the WW2 setting) while combining a few other good details to the realism and technicality of Wargame (Unit autonomy and insane detail based on history as well as custom armies). So far the two maps that have been released show a lot of promise in the future maps to be released in the full game. They each offer a good area to showcase CQC and hedgerow field areas to showcase how recon and armored units will work.
I was unsure about how I would like the new points scoring system, but I have to say, it is really nice and well done whilst being a simple concept. You push the front line to score points. The one thing that really peaved me in RUSE was scoring based on unit kill count or total domination and the one thing that peaved me in Wargame was cheese flanks and helo rushes that could de-capture your home spawn zone. WW2 is way less mechanized and heavily stands on your capability to micro manage tanks and infantry to repel enemy advances and stabalize front lines rather than flanking with a recon that has a wire-guided missile.
If you are a strategy fan I would strongly encourage you to get this game. Although $40 seems like a lot, Eugen Systems have not let me down on an RTS game and I am confident that this game will be worth the price at the official release date.

The most balanced fighting game of this generation and - once you get the hang of the game mechanics - the most exhilarating one to play as well. Characters share a basic set of offensive and defensive moves that allow you to escape or overcome any situation at any time with the proper read, unlike other popular 2D fighting games where you're sometimes doomed to die in certain situations.
The game also differs from most of its contemporary counterparts in that offense is almost always rewarded more generously than defense, discouraging turtling, full-screen keep-away and holding your ground. The fast pace and multitude of movement options also means that the emphasis on prediction is much higher than on reaction, and a general lack of inputs covering multiple options means that against similarly skilled opponents you can't rely on autopilot like you can in Capcom fighting games, making your every decision matter.
It also helps to sell the experience that the animations and sounds of special and desperation moves are impactful and convey a sense of power like no other 2D fighting game. The soundtrack full of rock tunes also fits the game very well. Last but not least, the devs working on the Steam version of the game did an admirable job with the netcode compared to console versions, making this port the best choice for players without a local offline fighting game scene.
If you look forward to being challenged by a game and you aren't intimidated by a steep learning curve, difficult controls and high risk, high reward gameplay, you can't go wrong with King of Fighters XIII.

You have four science packs, 1, 2, 3, and A. Three of which are manufactured by natural minerals and resources, the last of which is made from alien goop. Manufacturing these by hand is slow and tedious, thus you automate the process with mines and assembly factories.
The pollution from these factories begins to alert the local fauna. They are fast, powerful, and unrelenting even at their weakest. You put up turrets, and load them by hand. Time passes, and the pollution alerts a hive of monsters. You are now under constant attack until you destroy the hive. You automate manufacture of ammunition and feeding into the turrets as you fend off the hordes.
You replace the belts with faster ones, build more science labs, more power sources, but you have run out of copper, putting all science packs on hold. You find a large amount of copper, and create a mining camp with a long conveyer belt. This alerts more monsters to your presence, but you have the means to manufacture colossal amounts of ammo.
You now need iron, but the only way there is through a thick forest that is holding back your pollution from alerting even larger alien dens with highly evolved monsters. Trekking back and forth is tedious, so you build an army of robots to fetch the iron.
You now need oil. You trek out into the wilderness to find one of the rarest resources the game has to offer, and pipe it back to your factory. Technology moves by leaps and bounds as you are able to use more science packs.
Your assembly labs are spewing out more science packs than your massive cluster of labs can consume, you can acquire any technology on a whim, you are fully armed and armored, and your wall of turrets have slain legions of enemies. You manufacture the bullets faster than they are fired, mine copper and iron faster than it is smelted. You invent the locomotive, and shift tremendous amounts of materials to further your research into rocketry. You once thought "I'll never run out of resources", and now you think "How the ♥♥♥♥ did I run out of copper? I had 48,000 plates!", and that 48,000 becomes a rapidly growing number as your lust for freedom grows as your factory does.
After countless hours of work, you finally escape the planet, leaving a masterpiece of machinery that started out as almost literally nothing.

Theres a couple things wrong with this. Enemy units especially infantry will just sit around in allied occupied territory, hiding in forests, with no sign that they are there making the end of a game a man hunt. This game could benefit from more maps with the concept that digging in and preparing defensive positions isnt such a bad idea. 3. THE AXIS SUCK. 9/10 times i have played as an axis battlegroup i have lost the game. Axis need a buff or the allies need a debuff. The axis get steam rolled in almost every single game i have played. Some may say thats historically accurate but i say thats a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t excuse because this is a video game, not a documentary. Axis vehicles need to be buffed or they need more, cheaper infantry to balance things out, preferably with longer ranged panzer fausts and shreks. Other than those 3 things this game is awsome and I highly reccomend it, and i cant wait until launch day.

Good game for the 20 or so hours of game play it offers. I very much liked the salvage mechanic where you need to chop off limbs and body parts to gain spare parts to build and upgrade equipment.

Cyborg Dark Souls, and done well.  If you think you might like this, you probably will.
The combat is fluid and has a lot of depth; you've probably heard about how you can target limbs to extract parts to loot, but this system also slightly changes your moveset, and if you can actually connect your weapon with the part you're targetting, you can get extra benefits like stagger and knockdown.  Apparently if you're good, you can change target limb mid-combo to chain these effects together although I'm not at that level yet.  This gives each weapon a fair bit of depth, although there aren't a huge number of weapons (five basic classes, with a few uniques of each with their own variant movesets).  The levelling system is also as good as it sounds, allowing a huge amount of flexibility; no need to make additional saves for different builds, just swap in the parts you need at the medbay.
The enemies are characterful, well designed and challenging; it takes a while to figure out how to beat them but practice yields dividends.  The only gripe I have is that there could be a few more different types, but given the choice of more varied enemies and diluting the quality of what's already there, I think the game as it is is a good balance.
The story is surprisingly good; nothing new here, but an old tale about hubris executed well.  It's not subtle (some of the main messages of the whole story are literally written in two foot high red letters on a wall in the first area) but the heart of it is well conceived, with good pacing, a light smattering of symbolism and some great voice acting.  It's not Planescape: Torment.  But where say the Mass Effect series promises a lot but delivers very little depth, The Surge promises very little and then delivers on it vastly beyond what you would expect.
Level design is highly interconnected and feels "real", mostly in a good way; each area is built like a spiral around the central medbay ("bonfire"), with progression unlocking shortcuts back that let you start further on in the spiral.  I never had a problem with Dark Souls 2's realistic-as-a-dream geography, but if you did, The Surge is the complete opposite.  Pacing is pretty good, with making it back to medbay usually achievable, but rarely easy.  You often backtrack through explored areas, but usually something has changed about the level, introducing tougher enemies and new rooms.  Exploring is a mild challenge that adds tension; fighting through level-appropriate areas is very satisfying, but when combing an old area for some specific item it's just annoying.  Some kind of 3D map you could unlock after finishing an area would really help here.
The game is pretty buggy.  As well as graphical glitches like juddery movement in elevators, I've had a fair number of CTDs, including a couple of buttons that trigger CTDs every time.  None of them stopped me playing the game, and the autosave makes sure you haven't lost much progress, but they can be pretty annoying.  No fixes yet for my issues, but I'm hopeful; as a developer, Deck 13 seems to be listening to fans pretty closely.
All in all, I'm left wanting more but not at all disappointed by what I got.  I'm looking forward to NG+ in The Surge and very hopeful that a sequel is made.  Deck 13 have shown that (bugs aside) they can execute a Soulslike game very competently (if not capturing *all* of the magic or scope of those games), and innovate in ways that are clearly improvements.  Let's hope they are given the chance to continue.

Transistor is Supergiant Games' second title after the amazing thing that was Bastion. With Transistor, it's certain that they really have a knack for creating unique, inspired, and fun experiences.
Transistor is a unique, inspired, and fun experience. It's easily one of the best games I've ever played, but you've heard that a thousand times before.
In Transistor you play as Red, a famous singer who as a result of some rather bizarre circumstances, has lost her voice. She picks up the Transistor, which is a cool sword that talks. Now she goes on this quest to figure out what the hell is going on and to get her voice back. The combat is something like a hack and slash combined with a strategy game. Red can have up to four skills to use, which she can attack enemies with in real time. If you push Space, you can enter Turn(). Turn() is a planning mode where time freezes. Here you can plan out Red's attacks ahead of time and then play them back, coordinating actions to clear out an entire room of enemies in one maneuver, using up portions of the Plan() bar for each action. On the downside, once you finish doing Turn(), you are extremely vulnerable and unable to defend yourself (under most circumstances) until the Plan bar refills again. It's a surprisingly unique system that manages to be enjoyable and holds a sizeable amount of depth. There are 10+ different "Functions" you can get throughout the game, but they can be used as upgrades, passive effects, or abilities all on their own. The idea of being able to freely mix and match these abilities in nearly infinite combinations makes for a variety of gameplay styles and really brought out the inner mad scientist in me.
The story itself, while seemingly very simple to begin with, evolves to become rather complex. The Transistor talks to Red throughout her quest, sometimes about mundane things, sometimes about their situation. It serves a much different purpose than Rucks did in Bastion. Where Rucks was more of a narrator, to give insight on the world and set the mood for the story, the Transistor is more of a companion. By the end of the game, the Transistor felt like as much of a companion to me as it did to Red. You get insight into the world and Red as a character through what it says, and your interactions with it and the things around you are how the story unfolds. The way everything comes together is great and really left me satisfied with it all playing out the way it did. The story is not as straightforward as Bastion, however - to get a good understanding of all the plot elements you have to piece a lot of information together that's being given to you, and even the most subtle bits of dialogue may prove vital to comprehension. It's ultimately a very interesting tale in which I found myself getting pretty damn emotional about. For those who want to learn more, each Function is associated with a certain person in Transistor's universe, and by examining a Function after using it, you can learn more about some of the characters. This isn't integral to the story but it is a lovely and interesting extra for the people who seek it.
What should be mentioned is that the presentation is absolutely gorgeous. The UI is dripping with a neat modern tech feel, and the world has a beautiful abstract futuristic-noir aesthetic. It was so nice to see and the colors and effects in combat really popped. The soundtrack is a massive part of the experience aswell - I don't really know my genres, but I do know that it's good. It all adds to the atmosphere, and a particularly amazing touch is that using Turn() causes the song currently playing to be replaced by Red humming the melody.
+ Enjoyable and unique combat system

+ Unique world
+ Great story
@ Story requires close attention and may be hard for some to understand
- You liked Bastion

The game'll last you about 6-9 hours average I would say, and after that you can do Recursion, which is your standard New Game Plus mode. With an amazing atmosphere, great soundtrack, fun and experimental gameplay, and immersive story, there's little reason I can't recommend Transistor.

An old-school party-based dungeon crawler (aka "blobber") in the style of Eye of the Beholder, Dungeon Master, and so on. Real-time combat with grid-based movement, immersive graphics, and an interesting story. Also has full mod support for custom campaigns, characters and so on.

Legend of Grimrock is a love letter to the dungeon crawlers of the 1990's. The puzzles are satisfying (especially those that initially seem impossible) and the environments are beautiful. If you've ever played Dungeon Hack or Dungeon Master but wished you could experience them in the crisp definition of 2012's graphical capabilities, get Legend of Grimrock.

Imagine all the childhood fun you had with dungeon crawlers, now modernized but faithful, packaged into a humble, inexpensive indie game. You solve puzzles, explore mysteries, face difficult enemies in reflex-testing combat, craft items, manage inventory, and even create maps with pen and paper (if you want).
Don't forget its steam workshop support, extending its lifetime even further. Truly one of the few games I've put in so little money, yet gotten the most hours of fun from.

It got to the point some hud items actually stopped showing up when I selected units.
Not only that but their "Dynamic front line" makes scouting redundant, if you want to know where the enemy are just watch the red line moving around it's that simple.

In wargame (their other title that is very similar to this) a game that I loved, there was however something slightly off gameplay wise that always bothered me and made my sessions with it shorter than I'd hoped. Now playing steel division I've discovered what bothered me about wargame and what makes me love and stick with this game. Wargames modes were out of place arcade like for a game that presented hyper realistic armies and units and strategies. Take for example how resource points were just large squares on the map that you fought over making the rest of the map OT secondary importance. Finally the most played game mode, destruction, was about scoring points by killing enemy units while trying to keep yours from dying. This was a very arbitrary way to have two modern armies fight and only encouraged camping and arty spamming. In steel division you have a gameplay mode that is realistic and authentic to the divisions you are leading. It's all about a dynamic ever changing front line that you and your enemy wrestle over to try and maintain greater map control than the other and thus gain victory points to win. This adds far more strategy and versatility to the armies you make and fight with. The objective is to control the map and thus the tools you use to that are up to you. Further you can now do actual flanks and surrounds, creating your own pocket where the enemy is cut off from their front line, when this occurs they surrender. This means just as much as fighting is important so is mobility and simply out manoeuvring your opponent is equally if not more so devastating against them. Finally the phase system is nice, it adds rhythm to the game where you can easily see where your opponent is going to be stronger and weaker throughout the round and thus predict what his play style may be, instead of praying to god he doesn't just cheese you with a heli spam and end the match in two minutes.

Okay I might as well throw a review out there.
This game is solid as a time waster, in a very satisfying and yet, incredibly challenging way. You can approach the game in a very simple mindset and have fun with it, or try to approach it tactically and find challenge in the many different ways to play each type of disease. The interface is very simplistic and some of the notifications have some witty humor to them, along side the satire news banner.
Some of the best fun is naming your disease something utterly stupid, so you can laugh to yourself reading the pop-ups.
The game has four difficulties, and a wide varieties of diseases each one can be developed differently for different victories. In addition to the many different countries and locations to start, each one will provide different challenges for your disease. Casual and Normal difficulty are pretty much for the average player, with normal providing some good challenge. Then the game ramps up to Brutal and the dreaded Mega Brutal in which disease seems impossible.
Your goal is simply regardless of how you choose to play. Destroy humanity. Infect everyone and increase your diseases lethal level till no survivors remain. The shorter number of days it takes you to wipe out humanity, and the smaller percentage of the cure determines a scoring system.
The music also sets the tone very well, and in some disease missions the music is slightly altered. The sound effects are simple but excellent for a title like this.
For only $15, this game has plenty of replay value and is a ton of fun.

I just finished Transistor and I don't really know if I should cry or be overjoyed.
But let's start at the beginning... Transistor is a great game, in every possible aspect.
The gameplay consists mostly of walking through the futuristic city of Cloudbank that is the setting of Transistor and fighting strange white creatures known as "process". The combat is great and finds a good balance between tactics and action, enabling the player to use an ability called Turn() to plan their movements and then execute them. However, the number of actions during Turn is limited and the ability has to reload after use, forcing the player to plan carefully.
The graphics are beautiful - Cloudbank is (at least in the beginning) very colorful, and the art style looks fantastic.
I think the screenshots on Steam are pretty accurate here.
The story is very mysterious, but always interesting and sometimes even philosophic. The ending left me absolutely devastated. I won't say more, as everything else would be spoilers.
But THE strongest point of every Supergiant game is of course the soundtrack. The same goes for Transistor, which is the only game I ever bought the soundtrack of. In fact, the soundtrack is  even woven into the story - the protagonist is a singer, and her songs are the most important tracks in the OST. Also, she will, at any time in the game, hum along to the soundtrack if the player presses tab.
If you liked Bastion, yes.
If you didn't play Bastion, yes.
If you don't know what Bastion is, still yes.
If you didn't like Bastion, that was probably because of the combat, which means you should give Transistor a try.

DF-9 does not hold up to its promise. Not by a long shot.
Aside from the fact that fact that Double Fine abandoned (I do actually understand their situation) the game long before their planned goals had been implemented, the unfortunate truth is that what we do have isn't finished either.
Most prominently the power system. Without an actual power meter (like we have for O2) your base will just suddenly lose power if you've built too much. You have no useful way of knowing when to build another reactor. The devs expect you to hover your mouse over each and every room and sum up the power consumption in your head each time you want to take inventory.

Then as you continue to play and expand your base to meet the other goals you'll notice how the game becomes increasingly glitchy.
And speaking of goals: The "build all the things" goal isn't even possible. I tried. I built everything there is and allegedly I'm still missing something.

At first I wrote a silly review because this game just struck me as a silly throw back that's addicting yet worth the money. Now after having logging more hours I feel obligated to leave a more accurate and in-depth review:
This game really ♥♥♥♥ed me up emotionally - and I mean that in a good way. For me it's really rare when media (book, movies, games, whatever) really leaves any lasting impact for more than a few hours however I found myself simply dwelling on Papers Please at idle times days afterwards. The game has a really transforming effect much more powerful than you would ever expect especially given the media it’s presented by and the presentation style itself. In spite of being a pixilated arcade style game, once you get into it – you lose yourself.
I found myself really filling out the role like so few games have had me doing. It’s so easy to succumb to mind numbing bureaucracy and transform into a robot: after a while you’re not even reading the dialogue or looking at people other than to match their faces with their pictures similar to T-800 terminator. Similarly you can lost in people’s stories as they shuffle past you wanting so desperately to help people or do some good (greater good or for personal gain) but being constantly bound by government regulations and your need to support your family and not be sent to the Gulags. Yet still it’s you can find yourself invigorated with power wanting either to obstruct and detain people out of spite or rather allow key players to operate and undermine the very bureaucracy employing you.
Than you stop and go to the bathroom or take a phone call and realize you are playing a videogame with a fairly simple midi-style sound track and SNES era graphics. Nonetheless 2 days later on your lunch break you can’t help but wonder what would have happened if you had let that one revolutionist through, or your bosses lover, or denied that one terrorist, and you have to play again to find out.
All in all the game has 20 endings. It seems like a lot but I wish there were 100. A proper run though can take you anywhere from maybe 3-10 hours. It’s extremely addicting in my opinion not because of (rather in spite of) the amazingly retro arcade play style – rather because of how engrossing and thoroughly intriguing the characters and setting are.

The King of Fighters has always been among the underdog fighting game series compared to its peers like Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat. Whether it be due to its stubbornness to stick on the Neo Geo arcade machine architecture until 2003, the usage of 24-bit graphic sprites until its twelfth numerical entry in the series, or the stronger anime influence on the series than the genre's most famous franchises, The King of Fighters is a series that is highly underrated and deserves much more praise than it gets.
Whereas the series is notable for experimenting with new gameplay engine mechanics, The King of Fighters XIII opts to lift the most popular gameplay elements from the fan favorite entries, The King of Fighters '98 and The King of Fighter 2002, and marries them to the high quality sprite designs introduced with The King of Fighters XII, making for one of the greatest entries in the series. The game's 36 character roster hosts all the franchise staple characters and a good amount of fan favorites, which provide a large amount of variety in character playstyles to choose from so you are bound to find a character that will suit any style of player. The game also sports one the most robust amount of options seen in a 2-D fighting game ranging from an in-depth tutorial, arcade mode, story mode, challenge modes, online multiplayer, and even a custom character color editor for personalizing your favorite characters.
What makes Steam Edition different from the console version of the game is that it includes the three DLC characters into the base package and sports the refined balancing from Japanese arcade only revision of the game "The King of Fighters XIII Climax". Also, while the netcode is vastly improved over its console counterpart, the features present for online multiplayer are the same. The game does not feature any sort of lobby system nor does it allow you to browse replays or spectate other players matches. These aren't really a deal breaker but the lack of them is a real shame.
If you are looking for a game in the series for a good first impression or are just looking for one of the fighting game greats from the seventh console generation of games, you cannot do very much better than The King of Fighters XIII Steam Edition.

I have had a ton of fun with FFXIV and while I haven't put that many hours into the game (in comparison to a handful of other reviewers I have seen) there are a few things I want to address that I haven't really seen talked about all that much.
Pros:
-Mechanics: The game eases you into it's mechanics pretty nicely. It teaches you something and then gives you ample time to learn how to use that particular thing, usually through a handful of quests. By the time it brings up a new mechanic you should have the one before at least somewhat down. The game even goes as far as having a tutorial for raid ediqute based on class, though you do have to go out of your way to do it since mainline quests don't really touch upon it.
-Raids: The with the exception of the first few raids, each raid brings something new to the table, making them feel unique. They are also a good way for you to put the mechanics you've learned to the test.
-Story: If you are even remotely interested in the stories for MMO games, this one won't disapoint. It starts off a bit on the slow side but as the game gives you the opportunity to venture out of your starting area it picks up relatively quickly, and is very engaging.
Cons:
-Income: FFXIV really doesn't have much in the way of income unless you decide to get into the market. Quests are fairly unrewarding even when they give you pouches that you can sell to npc vendors for extra money.
-Story: How is it that story can be on both pros and cons? Put simply, its quests that seemingly serve no purpose in advancing said story, like going to npcs and emoting at them to get them to talk, or doing back and forth fetch quests between the same two npcs. These quests are a good portion of why the story doesn't really take off right away, and while they do still exists in later quests, thankfully they aren't as prevelant as they are in the beginning.
One more topic I want to cover that doesn't really fit in pros or cons is the community, which is a tad bipolar to say the least. Final Fantasy 14 is one of my favourite MMORPGs. However I am aware that it is not suited for everyone, even among those who enjoyed other games of the genre.
Here are my basic pros and cons:
Pro:
+ Really easy for new players to get into (including those who have never played an MMORPG)
+ Plenty of anti-frustration-features
+ Great communtity (the kind that, instead of just quitting, would take the time to patiently explain to me how to be a better tank while doing a dungeon)
+ No pay-to-win mechanics
+ Pleasant (but not too sugary) general atmosphere
+ Amazing soundtrack
+ Overall well-written story and characters
+ Mechanics that reward being nice and helping other players
+ Alts are possible, but not necessary, because you can change between classes at will with a single character
Neutral:
This game has a PvE (Player vs Envrionment) focus. While there is PvP (Player vs Player), which I personally find relatively enjoyable, there aren't nearly as many possibilities in that regard as in some other MMORPGs.
Cons:
- The battle system being easy to learn and enjoyable comes at the cost of some amount of complexity - for example I found myself missing the dodge rolls from GW2 a little while playing this game
- This game's housing market is relatively realistic - by which I mean unless you have a great amout of money or join a guild which has, you are most likely not going to get one
- I don't know how I feel about the english voice acting. Some of it is pretty decent, but some still sounds a bit... off.
- This game is pay-to-play
All in all, this is a really enjoyable game, though, which you can spend (or waste, depending on perspective) lots of time on while still being entertained. I'd recommend it!

This is the worst game of it's kind I've played in a long time. Decided to buy it on a sale, as it most certainly is not worth its price (not even the -51% one, but wanted to try it). Sure, the graphics are not that bad (but you can't really compare them with the contemporary city builders), but it doesn't match the greatness of free games like Simutrans or Open TTD. I can't recommend it at all - not as a city builder, and not as a logistics simulator.
1. There are quite a few types of trains to choose from, and I don't mind that most of them are Japanese. I do mind, however, that those are not timeline locked - you can buy a train from the 1990s in the 1960s and the game will neither warn you, nor stop you.
2. There are quite a lot of buildings to choose from, but the selection is very poor when compared to what Cities: Skylines has to offer, especially with workshop addons.
3. Timetable setting and ability to choose the lengh of traffic lights are both nice additions.
4. Real estate part is pretty nice, though quite lacking.
1. A lot of things seem counter-intuitive including how you need to use the map editor and then save it, and moreover it is extremely clunky to move the camera. I don't know, maybe it is standard in Japan but for me it was very hard to move camera around due to some very questionable design choices.
2. There are no people to be seen anywhere. Even in old Simutrans you have people and AI vehicles, and the lack of those is inexcusable.
3. Creating routes is a chore when compared to Simutrans, where you can do everything very simply, and you will always know why and where you are delivering something or someone.
4. There are very few trucks and cargo trains (3!) to choose from.
5. AI built structures don't align with existing roads. A little thing, but ruining the immersion for me.
6. It seriously lacks the ability to tailor the game like Simutrans, where you cad adjust how economy works, how cities develop, the prices, costs, passengers and their destinations, etc. etc.
7. You are limited to the time between 1960 and the future, which is lacking when compared to Simutrans - with certain packs you can easily start in the 1700s.
8. Economy doesn't seem as inter-connected and realistic as in Simutrans where you have a lot of good types and different factories. Things are too abstracted here and you are not delivering specific items to your town, like cement or hardware, but grey containers that contain something.
9. There is just one type of roads available - no highways or multiple lanes.
10. No air transport and no ships apart from leisure ones.
In conclusion: if you can stand the graphics of Simutrans, try it instead, it's a much, much better game.

Is it even possible to review this game? I'm not sure if it is. As it says on the label, it's much more of a simulator than a game. Think of it as more of a "NASA flight models" kind of simulator, not the "look mom, I'm a train conductor today on my computer screen!" type. In A-Train you deal with a concept common in Asia - you're the head of what is effectively a government branch designed to enforce happiness and capitalism amongst the populace with an iron fist. You come up with development plans, build infrastructure, add little theme parks and shopping malls where you decide is best for the civilians, and then lay down transportation tracks for them to reach it all.
People have complained that this is a very dry game compared to the likes of Cities Skylines or SimCity, because there aren't people with cartoonish names and thought bubbles walking all over the place. However, I think it's not as dry as all that. It has pretty and even emotionally stirring music, friendly advisors (though a bit of that is lost in translation from the original Japanese), and glowing gooey praise written all over the descriptions of the various train models and their histories. It's a bit understated in all of those aspects, yes, but it isn't an emotionless game. Look up the Japanese title of the game on YouTube and you'll see a lot of music videos with peppy feelgood soundtracks showing off everyone's cities.
The way that I got around the lack of life-simulation was to look at the graphics themselves - especially when zoomed out, they look a lot like most cities do in aerial photographs. Even the most beautiful cities look a bit sterile from high enough up. So I think it's just because the developers made a design decision to simulate the feeling of looking at the city from a passing aircraft, which is basically what your omniscient camera in these sorts of games is anyway. On a good-weather day, sometimes a frame or two of the game look indiscernible from a photograph. The graphics look dated most of the time, yes, but on a good day it's photorealistic - if you know what sorts of photos to be thinking about.
Also, there is at least some life going on. For the most part you get the information you need about your success in designing a functioning city by clicking on trains and buildings, seeing how many people are in them, and seeing how much money they're generating. But there's also an element of getting to watch the city developing in front of your eyes without doing anything at all. Unlike SimCIty and its compatriots, you don't have to explicitly zone areas or even build roads. If you've created an appealing area that's in demand and isn't too saturated with people already, you'll start to see little roads creeping across the land without having to do anything to make it happen. Buildings will then appear - at first just farmland and tiny shacks, but over a long enough period more people will arrive and those farms will turn into apartments, offices, and eventually even companies edging into your turf and making profitable enterprises with or without you.
There isn't really an objective in A-Train, not really. In the default mode the game corrals you into playing, you're given a list of maps and scenarios to start out with, which are loosely based on various places in the world (or sometimes not-so-loosely, with tongue-in-cheek descrptions that make it very obvious which real-world city is being referenced). Each one has flavor text about their past history, their present state, and what they're hoping for in their future. The terrain maps are reused in a few cases, with the same land but a different history and set of pre-existing buildings. But for the most part your choices are pretty creative and varied.
Once you've chosen one to play, you might start looking for objectives, loss conditions, and so forth. But, well, the scenario descriptions are more like... guidelines, per se? Once you're in a city, it's yours, and you can throw everything out the window and ignore everyone forever. The city won't mind one bit. As long as you don't go bankrupt, congratulations - a winner is you, for the most part. A-Train is an art program trapped in the furniture of a mid-level urban planner's basement. The true goal of the game is for you to be inspired enough that you'll choose, of your own free will, to be inspired by your advisers' suggestions, to believe the story of the city is real, and to do your best for the people in it. The "goal", simply, is to take what you see and make it better. A-Train is a game about making things better - for no reason other than "because trains are awesome and I like being nice", much of the time.
At the same time, don't be surprised if you play literally every single map twice and *still* keep getting Game Over screens about five minutes in. It takes a while to learn how not to become bankrupt, but once you do, it clicks. There's an entire stock market for the region which is simulated every tick, just like everything else. You can also take out ten or twenty times your savings in loans - tens of billions of dollars - if the timing is right. There are actually many, many ways to survive.
But the most important thing is not to go crazy developing too fast. The game stresses over and over again in little ways, "try not to disturb the populace". That's because this particular game is best played slow-boiled, adding or removing something in baby steps like trimming a bonsai tree. And then with any luck, you watch it grow.
Be warned, though: if you spend too fast, you're dead. Although you're usually tasked with the rebirth of an entire civilization or other laudable goals (exaggerating a bit here, but not by much for some of the maps), it's important to remember that you're just the train guy. Your company started out as the transportation company, it only became logical later on for you to help plan everything else too. (It might help here to remember how important rail stations and their surrounding districts are in Japan. They're cultural hubs, magnets for historical events, places everyone wants to be. Truly the most vital organs of many cities.)
Therefore, ~if you're starting on a poor map where you don't have income other than train fares, don't start plopping apartment buildings down~. Some places start you off with many profitable holdings, but with others, you have to go carefully, saving your pennies from train fares until you can finally add a pedestrian walkway, a cafe, and other little things.
Does it sound fun to oversee the birth of the next rail line as beloved and well-known as - say, the JR Yamanote line? Specifically told from the perspective of somebody sitting in an office building looking at planning data, with the stark numbers-filled interfaces trying desperately to convince you it's your real job? And is it okay if the entire time, you're being gently nudged to take it as slow and easy as possible, like a peaceful babbling brook?
Then yeah, get this and put up with the 30 minutes of reading the manual and the 4 hours of losing a million times. It's your life-experience sandbox, it's who you could've been if things went a little differently in your life. It's a game like no other.
But if that all sounds kinda dumb to you, you might want to skip this one. Heck, it might not even classify as a game at all to you. And that's alright, the price of trying very hard to be a very specific thing is that most people aren't going to be interested. But if you're even a little bit curious after all of the warnings and gotchas, you owe it to yourself to try this, I think. :)

Transistor is a very beautiful game with a combat style unlike anything I've ever seen before. The amount of love put into Transistor is beyond apparent: the full voice acting, the amazing soundtrack, the gorgeous layering and backgrounds... But if you're going to play a game for its story, I cannot recommend this game. The main points of the story are vague and convoluted at best.

If you see it on sale, it's not a bad game to play. Obviously, lots of people adore this game. I just don't think Supergiant Games has a knack for story telling.

What could be said for Transistor that hasn't been said before? Supergiant Games second game is a massive step forward from its previous title Bastion, and while gamers may argue over which is better; both are great. Where Transistor differs, is that Supergiant made a hybrid action RPG.
Red has a "turn" function in the sense of traditional RPG battles; but by equipping Red's weapon with certain functions (they are found throughout the game) some will allow her to battle outside of her turn. Her weapon consists of four attacks that you slot functions into, these can then have up to 2 more functions attached increasing various attributes like damage or even combining skills.
The tale of Transistor is one I don't want to spoil, and lasting only 6 hours even while searching every dark corner of the world, I was left pondering what would I do in the end. Some gamers may not enjoy the combat and originally I felt the same. Despite the game tutorials being pretty straightforward, once you find a basic setup for the functions you can nearly button mash your way to end.
Transistors art design is brilliant, everything within the city and its characters seem inspired by the art deco / streamline era of the 1930's and Supergiant has never disappointed and I go so far as to say outdone and surpassed anyones expectation with the music in Transistor. I urge everyone that reads this to look up the soundtrack and give it listen.
If Supergiant asked if there was anything I could change with Transistor, I would probably say to remove the Performance challenges. I know they are possible, but ultimately I feel that any type of challenges is unnecessary filler and the effort could have gone to adding additional areas and bosses or expanded story elements.
10/10 just for the gameplay + music.

Emily is Away is a short Choose Your Own Adventure style game that is aimed at people in their middle to late 20's and early 30's who used to chat using instant messaging programs during their high-school and collage days. It's a bittersweet reminder of how people used to communicate well before the apparition of broadband internet and mobile phones and how complicated our lives seemed to be although time was on our side. It's a brilliant simulation that captures most of the aspects of the set time-frame: the bland desktop environment, the over-complicated relationships, dyslexia, background noises, lying about musical preferences, constant reiteration of thoughts ... hell, it even has those weird quotes and statuses that people used to put on just to show how cool they were or their general predisposition.
It made me feel really bad. I felt a little bored playing it though. They should have a little solitaire application that you could play during the game. I feel like that could be useful.

At first I wrote a silly review because this game just struck me as a silly throw back that's addicting yet worth the money. Now after having logging more hours I feel obligated to leave a more accurate and in-depth review:
This game really ♥♥♥♥ed me up emotionally - and I mean that in a good way. For me it's really rare when media (book, movies, games, whatever) really leaves any lasting impact for more than a few hours however I found myself simply dwelling on Papers Please at idle times days afterwards. The game has a really transforming effect much more powerful than you would ever expect especially given the media it’s presented by and the presentation style itself. In spite of being a pixilated arcade style game, once you get into it – you lose yourself.
I found myself really filling out the role like so few games have had me doing. It’s so easy to succumb to mind numbing bureaucracy and transform into a robot: after a while you’re not even reading the dialogue or looking at people other than to match their faces with their pictures similar to T-800 terminator. Similarly you can lost in people’s stories as they shuffle past you wanting so desperately to help people or do some good (greater good or for personal gain) but being constantly bound by government regulations and your need to support your family and not be sent to the Gulags. Yet still it’s you can find yourself invigorated with power wanting either to obstruct and detain people out of spite or rather allow key players to operate and undermine the very bureaucracy employing you.
Than you stop and go to the bathroom or take a phone call and realize you are playing a videogame with a fairly simple midi-style sound track and SNES era graphics. Nonetheless 2 days later on your lunch break you can’t help but wonder what would have happened if you had let that one revolutionist through, or your bosses lover, or denied that one terrorist, and you have to play again to find out.
All in all the game has 20 endings. It seems like a lot but I wish there were 100. A proper run though can take you anywhere from maybe 3-10 hours. It’s extremely addicting in my opinion not because of (rather in spite of) the amazingly retro arcade play style – rather because of how engrossing and thoroughly intriguing the characters and setting are.

I've been a fan since FS2013. I own FS 2015 and now 2017 and absolutely LOVE it. It's so well optimized that it plays better on my PC than 2015 does. New map is pretty cool; new vehicles are great. The fact that you can now pick up logs with your hands is so much fun.
There are still some quirks I don't like though:
--Trailers -- What I mean is there are a few trailers that jack-knife your tractor while turning sharp. One trailer (Joskin Modulo 2) is such a pain that it slows your tractor down to 3mph when you make a U-turn to start the next line of fertilization. The trailer jack-knifing is my biggest gripe. Besides that... I love the game.
-- MP settings -- If you join a MP game, you always have to reset your preferences... which can be a little annoying.
Great features:
-- The ability to turn mods on and off. When you load a save game it asks you which mods (ones you currently have installed) you would like to run the game with. It gives your saved games more cuztomization.
-- The ability to dump grain / straw / silage / etc anywhere you want. Yep, you heard me... you don't have a baler? Have a forage wagon full of straw but don't want to sell it? Dump it on the ground where you stand. Then later-on... hop in a front-loader with a bucket and scoop it up.
-- Vehicle customization.... oh yea baby... you can now cuztomize your tractor like putting a bigger engine in it... adding a front-loader... bigger tires / narrow tires / dual-tires... changing the color. It's awesome.
For people who enjoyed FS 2015... I highly recommend buying FS 2017.

Okay first of all, this is quite a good game. However there are some let downs which make it a big pain to play when using Multiplayer.
First are the bugs. There are many stutter bugs & glitches which seem to have become increasingly common since the last patch, showing that there has been little testing before releasing.
Second (and biggest) is the fact you need a separate license to run a dedicated server, which is completely ludicrous. I realise this is a long standing thing and has been around since at least Farming Sim 2013, but the need to have a separate license is ridiculous, especially when you need a license in order to play on it.
Third is the physics. I seem to continuously have an issue (and apparently many others do) whereby trees will fall through the ground. The 'claws' on the front of tractors and on the end of cranes also seem to be extremely weak and often they seem to let go of the object they are holding. It can be a very frustrating endeavour especially when considering the first disadvantage.
As a whole I wouldn't recommend it in its current state. However if some of the bugs and glitches are fixed, then it would make it much easier and less stressful to play!

If only wargame had battles this huge, I would have loved it as much. Unit AI and unit management is also a step up from the previous game.

While the game is compaired with Wargame series a lot, it does play a bit different. There is a phase system, which is quite nice in my opinion because it prevents spam of overpowered units. And also there are different game mechanics in terms of vechicle movement and field of view, where treelines block both vision and fire, therefore it forces a player to make use of the infantry, which plays a significant role in this game. Also this mechanics does make a room for pretty nice sneaky ambushes on units that you couldn't have killed in the open if they are superior to yours.
The suppression is a very important feature in this game, where brute firepower can and will suppress even the toughest armor, forcing it to fall back, leaving it vunerable to executing shots. That is the reason why artillery and air support play a big role in this game.
At the moment, there are 10 divisions to make a choice from, 5 each for allies and axis, and only multiplayer and solo skirmish against AI is available. Total of 18 divisions, tutorials and single player campaign are to be released with the full release.
You might have read the reviews about the balance of this game, but to be honest the more you play, the more balanced it seems. While there could be and will be some more balancing in this game in paches to come, the game is usually misunderstood, and you could make a mistake by playing it like you would play some other RTS game that you got used to (even if it's a Wargame series game).
The thing where most new players make mistake about this game is in assuming that you can win in this game by using brute force. There is NO unbeatable unit, like there wasn't in real life. You must think through your advance, figure out the strenghts and weaknesess of your units, and use the knowlege of the game mechanics in order to make ambushes against stronger units like I said earlier. Also there are a lot of rants about the artillery. While it is true that they can be annoying, you must realize that this is relatively fast paced game in the terms of making your moves before the enemy, where proper recon can help a lot. If you do things right and use the division you've chosen in the right way, you will either be steamrolling your opponent, or be a part of exciting and intense match.
In Steel Division: Normandy 44, the proper use of combined arms is a must. You might only get a temporary advantage by spamming one type of units, but expirienced player would quickly figure you out and use counter measures, which could leave you extremely vunerable since you probably didn't deploy enough support.
And also one more thing that was mentioned in some reviews is micro-management. After some time, when you start to know what you're doing, the micro management becomes moderately paced. There are a lot of ways to issue commands to your units in advance, so you can keep your focus on a more important part of the battlefield. The AI that controls unit's behaviour seems like it could use a bit more tweeking, but in most cases it behaves pretty decently.
You could say that this is a hard game and players get so much better every day. So be prepared for some beating before you get good enough to be a part of epic battles. There is a "quick game" feature that is supposedly doing a matchmaking for you based on your stats, but I havent tested the option to be sure how it works. My advice for a new player would be to try 10v10 public server games, where you will learn a lot much faster than playing smaller games against much more expirienced players.
This is a definite recommendation, but only if you are prepared to invest tens of hours in this game, so you can fully understand it and start enjoying it.

I was on the fence about this game for a while. I liked Pandemic, but I didn't know if I was willing to shell out $15 for a premium spiritual successor. Then I found JackSepticEye playing it on YouTube, and I realized this thing was a lot bigger and better than I gave it credit for. Several infectious apocalypses later, I'd say I got my money's worth.
This is a strategy game where you play as a disease with the singular goal of wiping out humanity. Your first plague is a bacteria, and if you've played Pandemic the mechanics are identical. But as you win with each infection agent on Normal or higher, you unlock more stuff to play with. From viruses which mutate new symptoms rapidly, to neurax worms that can attack specific countries regardless of barriers, and even a plague that lets you start the zombie apocalypse (!), it's safe to say there's plenty of variety. You can tweak the gameplay even further with unlockable perks and special scenarios.
My only serious gripe with the game is that there's plenty of waiting to do while you wait for your disease to infect or kill everyone. The fast-forward function alleviates this, but I wish it went
. Impatient button-mashers stay away - this is a thinking man's game.
I would recommend this game, because it's a fun strategy game if you wanna take over the world. 10/10
